# Marcus Aurelius, Meditations

*A new English translation from the Greek (project-v1)*

Made 2026-11-23. All 418 passages of the Meditations, in the 38 sections of the Stoic Constitution. Every passage was translated from the Greek alone by one model, checked against the Greek by a second, and each point was settled in writing by a third reading. The owner read the first six on 23 November 2026 and said “looks good”; the other 412 have not been read by the owner. None has been checked by a person who reads Greek.

How it was made:
- A first translator was given the Greek of a section’s passages and nothing else: no earlier translation, no article. It was asked for plain English of today that keeps the speaker, the person addressed, every “all” and “not”, and each image, and to translate one reading and note the other wherever the Greek is open.
- A second reader was given only the Greek and that English, without the first translator’s notes, and asked to list every place where the English says more, less or other than the Greek. Across the book it raised 1,458 points; it called 132 passages sound, 275 open to minor fixes, and 5 wrong in a way that changed what Marcus says.
- Each point was then settled in writing: accepted (969), partly accepted (465) or declined (189), with the reason. For the first six passages the editor of this project settled them; for the rest a third reader did, given the Greek, the draft and the points, and it also fixed 137 faults neither earlier reader had caught (marked “Found while settling”). The result is the English shown here. Under each passage you can open both lists: what the Greek leaves open (3,201 notes), and what the second reader questioned.
- All three readers were the same model, Claude Fable 5.2, each in a fresh context that saw only what its brief allowed. Most sections were read in Claude Code; in eleven sections at least one reading was made through the Anthropic API with the same briefs. The briefs are kept in the project (translation-translator.md, translation-checker.md, translation-settler.md).
- So that a Greek word does not become a different English word from one passage to the next, the settled renderings of the first six passages were given to every reader as preferences (for example “the universe” for κόσμος, “the nature of the whole”, “the ruling part”); where a passage’s own argument needed another word, a note says so.
- The 1634 translation numbers and cuts its sections differently from modern editions. Each of its passages was matched to the Greek by reading the openings and endings side by side, after a whole-book alignment had proposed the matches; together the 418 passages cover every chapter of the Greek exactly once. Where a passage joins two or more modern chapters (58 passages), they are shown as one with the chapter breaks kept (6.9–10). Where it cuts inside a chapter (63 passages), the passage carries a letter (11.8a is the first part, 3.11b a later part) and says which Greek it leaves out.
- Before a section was stored, its files were checked by script: every quoted Greek word is an exact part of the passage, every point has its decision, the typography is plain, no archaic forms. Where a reader had typed a Latin letter inside a quoted Greek word, or another Unicode form of the same accented letter, the quotation was corrected to the exact characters of the source; no wording was changed that way.

What it cannot promise:
- All three readers are language models. A model’s Greek can be confidently wrong; the Greek is shown beside the English so that anyone who reads Greek can object.
- The Greek is a digitised copy of Leopold’s edition and has slips of its own (an accent, a breathing, a misprinted letter). Where a slip was read through, a note says so. Where the text itself does not construe (for example 8.35, 9.28a, 7.31b), the English marks the place and does not smooth it over.
- Notes that rely on memory of the manuscripts or of an editor’s conjecture say “from memory, unchecked” (205 notes). None was checked against a critical edition. In 5.8 the source prints ἐκεῖ σε (“you there”) where the text may be the one word ἐκεῖσε (“to that place”); the printed edition was not consulted. Two scraps of the source are outside every passage: the note at the end of Book 1 (Τὰ ἐν Κουάδοις πρὸς τῷ Γρανούᾳ) and a stray chapter numeral inside 12.17.
- The passage numbers are those of modern editions; the 1634 number is given beside each. The sections were grouped on the 1634 English, not on this translation. On the new English, 352 of the 418 passages are still nearest their own section; the table above lists the rest by section. No passage was moved.
- A translated passage is never edited in place. A correction is a new revision with a new id; the old one is kept in the record.

Source text: M. Antoninus Imperator ad se ipsum, edited by Jan Hendrik Leopold, 1908. Digitised text from the Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA); the Greek is not included in this file.

Passages are numbered by book and chapter as in modern editions. A dash joins chapters translated as one passage; a letter marks part of a chapter.

Licence: Dedicated to the public domain (CC0 1.0 Universal, https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/). You may copy, change, publish and sell it without asking and without naming anyone. Words of the Greek or Latin quoted in the notes come from the source texts named below.

On the web: https://ilyadays.vercel.app/apps/stoic-translation.html

## Book 1

### 1.1–4

From my grandfather Verus: good character and freedom from anger.

From the reputation and memory of the man who fathered me: modesty and manliness.

From my mother: reverence for the gods, and readiness to share, and holding back not only from doing wrong but even from coming to such a thought; and also plainness in the way of living, far from the way the rich live.

From my great-grandfather: not going to public lecture rooms, and having good teachers at home, and learning that on such things one must spend unsparingly.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ καλόηθες*: A fine or noble character, good nature. Other reading: a noble character
- *Παρὰ τῆς δόξης καὶ μνήμης τῆς περὶ τοῦ γεννήσαντος*: δόξα is what people said of him, and μνήμη can be their memory of him or Marcus’s own. “The man who fathered me” keeps the Greek, which marks the father by birth off from the father of 1.16. Other reading: From what I heard and what I remember of my father by birth
- *τὸ αἰδῆμον καὶ ἀρρενικόν*: The first is a sense of shame, respect for what is decent; the second is literally “the male”. Other reading: a sense of decency and a manly spirit
- *τὸ θεοσεβὲς*: Reverence towards the gods: “god” is in the word, with no number marked. Other reading: piety
- *μεταδοτικὸν*: Readiness to give a share of what one has. A related word is in 1.14. Other reading: generosity
- *τοῦ ἐπὶ ἐννοίας γίνεσθαι τοιαύτης*: Literally “from coming to be at such a thought”: from so much as thinking of doing wrong. Other reading: but even from entertaining the thought of it
- *τῆς πλουσιακῆς διαγωγῆς*: The way of passing life that belongs to the rich. Other reading: far from a rich person’s habits
- *εἰς δημοσίας διατριβὰς*: The noun means places where teachers hold classes. “Public” means open to all comers, as against teaching at home. The infinitives are in a past tense and name things that happened to him; they are given as plain forms in “ing”, as in the rest of the chapter. Other reading: to the public schools
- *ἐκτενῶς ἀναλίσκειν*: Literally “spend at full stretch”. The same adverb is in 1.14. Other reading: spend freely

</details>

### 1.5

From the man who brought me up: becoming neither a Green nor a Blue, nor a Small-Shield or a Big-Shield man; and bearing hard work, and needing little; and doing things with my own hands, and not meddling; and being slow to accept slander.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τοῦ τροφέως*: The one who rears a child: a foster father or the attendant in charge of a boy. He is not named. Other reading: my tutor
- *μήτε Πρασιανὸς μήτε Βενετιανὸς*: The Greens and the Blues were the rival sides at the chariot races. The Greek gives only the names and so does the English. Other reading: to back neither the Greens nor the Blues at the races
- *Παλμουλάριος ἢ Σκουτάριος*: Latin words in Greek letters for those who backed the gladiators with the small shield and those who backed the ones with the large shield. The Greek as given spells the first with an l where the Latin has an r. Other reading: nor a partisan of the light-armed or the heavy-armed gladiators
- *τὸ αὐτουργικὸν*: Working with one’s own hands, doing one’s own tasks. The Greek names no person and the possessive is added. Other reading: self-reliance in work
- *ἀπολύπραγμον*: Not being a busybody in other people’s affairs. Other reading: minding my own business
- *τὸ δυσπρόσδεκτον διαβολῆς*: Literally “the hard-to-admit of slander”: not readily listening to it. Other reading: a deaf ear to slander

</details>

### 1.6

From Diognetus: not being busy over empty things; and disbelieving what is said by those who deal in marvels and by sorcerers about spells and about the driving out of spirits and things of that kind; and not keeping quails, nor getting excited over such things; and putting up with plain speaking; and becoming at home in philosophy, and hearing the lectures first of Baccheius, then of Tandasis and Marcianus; and writing dialogues as a boy; and wanting a pallet bed and an animal skin, and everything of that kind that belongs to the Greek training.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ ἀκενόσπουδον*: Literally “the not-earnest-about-empty-things”. Other reading: no zeal for trifles
- *τῶν τερατευομένων καὶ γοήτων*: The first are people who talk marvels and make wild claims, the second are sorcerers or plain cheats. Other reading: miracle-workers and charlatans
- *δαιμόνων ἀποπομπῆς*: δαίμονες are spirits, divine or lesser beings. “Demons” would bring in a later sense. Other reading: the casting out of demons
- *ὀρτυγοτροφεῖν*: Quails were kept for fighting and for a game of striking them, a fashionable pastime. The Greek says only “keep quails”. Other reading: not breeding fighting quails
- *ἐπτοῆσθαι*: To be in a flutter over a thing, carried away by it. Other reading: nor being mad about such things
- *παρρησίας*: Frank speech: being spoken to freely by others. Other reading: freedom of speech
- *τὸ οἰκειωθῆναι φιλοσοφίᾳ*: Literally “being made one of the household of philosophy”. Other reading: becoming familiar with philosophy
- *ἀκοῦσαι*: To “hear” a teacher is to attend his lectures, to be his pupil. Other reading: and hearing first Baccheius
- *Τανδάσιδος*: A name not otherwise known and probably doubted (from memory, unchecked). It is given as it stands.
- *ἐν παιδί*: Literally “in a boy”: while still a boy. Other reading: in my boyhood
- *σκίμποδος καὶ δορᾶς*: A low pallet and an animal skin to lie under or on: the hard bedding of a philosopher’s life. The Greek has no articles and does not say how the skin was used. Other reading: a camp bed and a hide
- *τῆς Ἑλληνικῆς ἀγωγῆς*: ἀγωγή is a course of training or a way of life: here the discipline of Greek philosophers. Other reading: the Greek way of life

</details>

### 1.7

From Rusticus: getting the impression that my character needed correcting and treatment; and not being turned aside into emulating the sophists, nor writing about the doctrines, or delivering little speeches of exhortation, or making a show, to strike the imagination, of the man of discipline or the man of action; and keeping away from rhetoric and poetry and clever talk; and not walking about at home in formal dress, nor doing things of that kind; and writing short letters plainly, like the one he himself wrote to my mother from Sinuessa; and, towards those who have been angry and have done wrong, being easy to win back and easy to reconcile, as soon as they themselves are willing to come back; and reading with care, and not being content with a rough grasp of the whole, nor quickly assenting to glib talkers; and getting to read the notes of Epictetus’s teaching, which he shared with me from his own copy.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ λαβεῖν φαντασίαν*: “Impression” for φαντασία, as throughout this translation and in the same phrase in 1.14. The Greek does not say whose character: the possessive is supplied, as the run of the chapter implies. Other reading: getting the impression of needing correction and treatment of character
- *θεραπείας*: The word is medical treatment and also care or tending. The medical sense is taken, beside “correcting”. Other reading: care
- *ζῆλον σοφιστικόν*: ζῆλος is eager emulation or rivalry, and the adjective says only “of the sophist’s kind”: the showy competition of professional speakers. The English takes it as striving to be like them. Other reading: into a sophist’s spirit of rivalry
- *περὶ τῶν θεωρημάτων*: The propositions of philosophy treated as subjects for essays. “Doctrines” as in 1.8. Other reading: about speculative questions
- *προτρεπτικὰ λογάρια*: A diminutive with a sneer in it: little pieces urging people to philosophy. Other reading: little sermons
- *φαντασιοπλήκτως*: A very rare word, built on φαντασία, the “impression” of the opening. It can mean “so as to strike people’s imagination”, as taken here beside the verb of showing off, or “as one struck by his own imaginings”. Other reading: carried away by a fancy, making a show of
- *τὸν ἀσκητικὸν ἢ τὸν ἐνεργητικὸν ἄνδρα*: The first is the man who practises a discipline, the second the active man. From memory, unchecked: some editors read a word meaning “benefactor” for the second. Other reading: the ascetic or the public benefactor
- *ἀστειολογίας*: Urbane, witty or polished talk. Other reading: witty conversation
- *ἐν στολῇ*: στολή is a full outfit, dress for show or for going out. The Greek does not say which garment: the fault is dressing up at home. The same word comes in 1.16. Other reading: in outdoor dress
- *τὰ ἐπιστόλια*: A diminutive, like the “little speeches” above: short letters, notes. It may be no more than a familiar way of saying “letters”. Other reading: letters
- *χαλεπήναντας καὶ πλημμελήσαντας*: The Greek does not say against whom. The writer himself is implied and is left out, as in the Greek. Other reading: those who have been angry with me and wronged me
- *εὐανακλήτως*: Literally “easy to call back”. The passive sense is the natural one: he himself is easily won back. Other reading: ready to call them back
- *περινοοῦντα ὁλοσχερῶς*: Thinking round a thing in the gross, without the detail. Other reading: a general idea of it
- *τοῖς περιλαλοῦσι ταχέως συγκατατίθεσθαι*: The verb is the Stoic term for assent. The people are those who chatter, who talk freely and at length; by the parts of the word it could also be those who talk round a subject. Other reading: nor quickly assenting to those who talk around a thing
- *ἐντυχεῖν*: The verb is to meet with a thing and, of a writing, to read it. Other reading: coming upon
- *τοῖς Ἐπικτητείοις ὑπομνήμασιν*: Literally “the Epictetean notes”: a written record of what Epictetus taught, not notes of his own writing, so “teaching” unpacks the adjective. Presumably what Arrian took down (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: the records of Epictetus’s talks
- *οἴκοθεν*: Literally “from home”: from his own store, so from his own copy. “With me” is added. The verb is “gave a share of”, so the copy was shared, not given away. Other reading: of which he gave me a share from his own house

</details>

### 1.8

From Apollonius: freedom, and unmistakably leaving nothing to the dice, and looking to nothing other than reason, not even for a little while; and being always the same, in sharp pains, at the loss of a child, in long illnesses; and seeing clearly, in a living example, that the same man can be most intense and can be relaxed; and not being irritable when explaining; and seeing a man who plainly counted his experience and skill in passing on the doctrines as the least of his good qualities; and learning how one should take from friends what are counted as favours, neither being lowered because of them nor letting them go by without feeling.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ ἐλεύθερον*: The word covers freedom of mind and the bearing of a free man. The bare word is kept. Other reading: independence of spirit
- *ἀναμφιβόλως ἀκύβευτον*: ἀκύβευτον is literally “not dicing”: not leaving a decision to chance. ἀναμφιβόλως stands directly before it and is taken with it alone, as “unmistakably”, plain to anyone watching. It can also mean “without wavering”, his own steadiness in it. Other reading: and without any wavering leaving nothing to the dice
- *πρὸς τὸν λόγον*: λόγος here is the guide a person looks to, so “reason”, the word this translation keeps for it. Other reading: to the argument
- *σφοδρότατος εἶναι καὶ ἀνειμένος*: The second word is used of a string let slack, so the pair is tight and loose. Only the first is a superlative, and “can be” is said twice so that “most” is not heard over both. The Greek has only “and” between them, and no “yet” is added. Other reading: can be at full stretch and slack
- *ἐν ταῖς ἐξηγήσεσι*: The word is used of expounding a text or a doctrine to pupils. The plainer “explaining” is kept. Other reading: in his expositions
- *σαφῶς*: “Plainly” can go with “counted”, as here, since it stands inside that phrase beside “least”, or with “seeing”, like “seeing clearly” in the clause before. Other reading: and seeing plainly a man who counted
- *τὴν ἐμπειρίαν καὶ τὴν ἐντρέχειαν τὴν περὶ τὸ παραδιδόναι τὰ θεωρήματα*: “In passing on the doctrines” is attached in the Greek to the skill and probably covers the experience too; the English leaves that as open as the Greek. τὰ θεωρήματα are the propositions of philosophy, the things taught: “doctrines” here and in 1.7, since “principles” is kept for δόγματα. Other reading: his experience, and his skill in passing on the theory
- *τὰς δοκούσας χάριτας*: Literally “the seeming favours”: favours as people count them, without saying that they are not real ones. The same turn is used of honours in 1.16. Other reading: the so-called favours
- *ἐξηττώμενον*: Literally “being worsted, made the lesser”: losing one’s standing or independence to the giver. “Lowered” is used because “overcome” would be heard as overcome by feeling. Other reading: neither being made beholden by them
- *ἀναισθήτως παραπέμποντα*: Either letting the favour pass unnoticed or brushing it aside tactlessly. Other reading: nor dismissing them tactlessly

</details>

### 1.9

From Sextus: kindliness; and the example of a household governed by its father; and the idea of living according to nature; and dignity without pretence; and skill in reading his friends, with care for them; and patience with lay people and with those who hold unexamined opinions; and adapting himself readily to everyone, so that his company was more pleasant than any flattery, and yet at that very moment those same people held him in the greatest respect; and finding out and setting in order, with a sure grasp and by method, the principles necessary for life; and never giving so much as a sign of anger or of any other passion, but being at once most free of passion and most affectionate; and praise given quietly, and wide learning without display.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τοῦ οἴκου τοῦ πατρονομουμένου*: A household under a father’s rule. It can also mean one run in a fatherly way. Other reading: a household run in a fatherly way
- *τὴν ἔννοιαν*: The accusative breaks the run of the list, as if a verb such as “got” were understood. ἔννοια is a notion or conception, and “idea” is kept for it. Other reading: the conception
- *τὸ στοχαστικὸν τῶν φίλων κηδεμονικῶς*: Literally “aiming at his friends, caringly”: good at guessing them, at seeing what they feel or need before they say it. The Greek does not say what he guessed. The related noun in 1.14 is “guess”. Other reading: thoughtful attention to his friends
- *τῶν ἰδιωτῶν*: Laymen: people without philosophical training. Other reading: ordinary people
- *τὸ ἀθεώρητον οἰομένων*: The Greek as given is rough: literally “and the unexamined of those who suppose”, with no article of its own for “those who suppose”. It is read with the article of “lay people” serving both groups and “the unexamined” as what they suppose. From memory, unchecked: the text is doubted here and editors correct it. Other reading: and with the unreasoned notions of people who merely suppose
- *εὐάρμοστον*: Literally “well fitted”: fitting himself to every kind of person. Other reading: getting on well with everyone
- *αἰδεσιμώτατον*: A superlative: most revered. The grammar has him as the one revered “to those very people”, and sets this against the pleasantness of his company, which “yet” gives. Other reading: and yet he was at that very time most venerable to them
- *καταληπτικῶς καὶ ὁδῷ*: The first is a Stoic term for grasping a thing securely; the second is “by a road”, by method. Other reading: with understanding and systematically
- *ἀπαθέστατον*: Free of the passions in the Stoic sense, with “passion” for πάθος just before. It does not mean unfeeling, as the next word shows. Other reading: wholly unmoved by passion
- *τὸ εὔφημον ἀψοφητὶ*: εὔφημον is speaking well, praise, the word given as “speaking well of” in 1.13. It could also be fair or seemly speech in general. The adverb is literally “without noise”. Other reading: fair speech without noise

</details>

### 1.10

From Alexander the grammarian: not to find fault, and not to pounce reproachfully on people who have come out with a wrong form of a word, a mistake in grammar or a jarring sound, but deftly to come out with just the very thing that should have been said, by way of an answer, or of backing them up, or of a joint discussion about the matter itself, not about the expression, or through some other such well-tuned reminder in passing.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τοῦ γραμματικοῦ*: A γραμματικός taught language and the reading of the poets; “grammarian” is the usual word, wider than the modern sense of grammar. Other reading: From Alexander the teacher of literature
- *τὸ ἀνεπίπληκτον*: The word can be active, “not rebuking”, or passive, “not open to rebuke”. What follows is about how to correct others, so the active sense is taken. Other reading: to be beyond reproach
- *ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι*: “To lay hold of”, “to seize on”: catching a speaker out. Given as “pounce on”. Other reading: not to take people up in a reproachful way
- *βάρβαρον ἢ σόλοικόν τι ἢ ἀπηχὲς*: Three school terms: a “barbarism” (a wrongly formed word; the Greek word is literally “foreign”, “not Greek”), a “solecism” (a wrong construction), and something “off in sound” (a wrong pronunciation or an ugly-sounding phrase). Each is given in plain words. Other reading: a barbarism, a solecism or something that sounds wrong
- *ἐπιδεξίως*: “Dexterously”, with a light, tactful hand. Other reading: tactfully
- *αὐτὸ μόνον ἐκεῖνο ὃ ἔδει εἰρῆσθαι προφέρεσθαι*: “To bring forward that very thing alone that ought to have been said”: to use the right form oneself and nothing more. The verb is the one used of the speakers’ slip (προενεγκαμένων), so both read “come out with”; “just” is for μόνον. Other reading: to bring out only the expression that should have been used
- *συνεπιμαρτυρήσεως*: A rare word, “bearing witness along with”: confirming what the other person said, and using the right form while doing so. Other reading: or of adding one’s own testimony
- *συνδιαλήψεως*: Another rare word, “taking up together” in talk or in thought: joining the other person in going over the point. It stands with two words for things said, so it is given as “a joint discussion”. Other reading: or of thinking the matter over together
- *περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ πράγματος, οὐχὶ περὶ τοῦ ῥήματος*: These words follow the third way and may belong to it alone or to all three; the English keeps the Greek order so that either can be heard. ῥῆμα is the particular word or phrase that was used. Other reading: all of them about the matter itself and not about the wording
- *ἐμμελοῦς παρυπομνήσεως*: ἐμμελής is “in tune”, and so “graceful”, “tactful”; it answers ἀπηχές, “out of tune”, earlier in the sentence, and the image is kept with “jarring” and “well-tuned”. παρυπόμνησις is a reminder slipped in on the side. Other reading: some other such tactful hint

</details>

### 1.11

From Fronto: to have taken note of what a tyrant’s envy, shiftiness and play-acting are like, and that on the whole these people we call patricians are somehow rather lacking in affection.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Παρὰ Φρόντωνος*: Fronto was Marcus’s teacher of Latin rhetoric. “From Fronto”, with no verb, as in the other entries of this book. Other reading: What came from Fronto
- *τὸ ἐπιστῆσαι*: “To have stopped and given attention to”, “to have observed”. The same verb is “take note of” in 7.66. Other reading: to have come to see
- *ἡ τυραννικὴ βασκανία καὶ ποικιλία καὶ ὑπόκρισις*: The adjective “of a tyrant” can go with the first noun only or with all three; it is taken with all three. βασκανία is malicious envy and ὑπόκρισις is acting a part. ποικιλία is “many-colouredness”, so either changeableness or intricate cunning, and “shiftiness” has something of both. Other reading: what the envy that goes with tyranny is like, and its caprice and hypocrisy
- *οἱ καλούμενοι οὗτοι παρ’ ἡμῖν εὐπατρίδαι*: εὐπατρίδαι, “those of good fathers”, is the Greek word for the Roman patricians, the old noble families. “Among us”, which the English gives through the one who calls them so, means at Rome. The literal sense sits oddly beside the lack of affection that follows. Other reading: these people who are called the well-born among us
- *ἀστοργότεροί πως*: στοργή is the love that is natural within a family, as between parents and children. The form is a comparative, “rather lacking” or “more lacking than others”, and πως, “somehow”, softens it. Other reading: are somehow more lacking in family affection than other people

</details>

### 1.12

From Alexander the Platonist: not often or without need to say to anyone, or write in a letter, “I am busy”; and not to keep excusing oneself in this way from the duties that relations with those one lives among call for, by pleading the business that surrounds one.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Παρὰ Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Πλατωνικοῦ*: “From Alexander the Platonist”, with no verb: what Marcus owes to him. From memory, unchecked: a Platonist philosopher who served Marcus as secretary for Greek letters. Other reading: What came from Alexander the Platonist
- *ὅτι ἄσχολός εἰμι*: ὅτι here introduces the words as spoken; it could also be reported speech. ἄσχολος is literally “without leisure”. Other reading: not to say or write that one has no time
- *παραιτεῖσθαι*: “To beg off”, “to ask to be excused from”. The infinitives name no person; “oneself” and “one” keep that. Other reading: and not to keep begging off in this way
- *τὰ κατὰ τὰς πρὸς τοὺς συμβιοῦντας σχέσεις καθήκοντα*: καθήκοντα is the Stoic term for the acts that are fitting for a person, here given as “duties”. They are those that go with one’s relations (σχέσεις) to “those who live with one”: household, friends, colleagues. Other reading: what is fitting in one’s ties to the people who share one’s life
- *προβαλλόμενον τὰ περιεστῶτα πράγματα*: Literally “holding out in front the affairs standing round”: using the business one is in the middle of as a shield or pretext. Other reading: with the circumstances one is in as the pretext

</details>

### 1.13

From Catulus: not making light of a friend who finds some fault, even if they happen to be finding fault without reason, but trying actually to bring them back to their usual self; and speaking well of one’s teachers wholeheartedly, as in what is recorded about Domitius and Athenodotus; and true love for one’s children.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *φίλου αἰτιωμένου τι*: A friend who blames or complains about something. The Greek masculine is general and “they” is used. Other reading: a friend’s complaint
- *ἀλόγως*: Without reason: unreasonably, or with no ground. Other reading: groundlessly
- *ἀποκαθιστάναι ἐπὶ τὸ σύνηθες*: Literally “to restore to the usual”. The verb has no object in the Greek. The nearest is the friend, brought back to their usual disposition; it could also be the friendship that is brought back. Other reading: to bring things back to their usual state
- *ἐκθύμως εὔφημον*: εὔφημον is speaking well of someone, the word given as “praise” in 1.9. The adverb is “from the heart”, eagerly. Other reading: warm praise of one’s teachers
- *οἷα τὰ περὶ Δομιτίου καὶ Ἀθηνοδότου ἀπομνημονευόμενα*: Literally “such as the things recounted about Domitius and Athenodotus”. It is open whether these are stories Catulus told or a known record, and who praised whom. The story is not traced here. Other reading: like the stories told of Domitius and Athenodotus
- *περὶ τὰ τέκνα*: The Greek has “the children”, with no possessive: his own, or one’s own. Other reading: for his children

</details>

### 1.14

From my brother Severus: love of family, love of truth and love of justice; and through him coming to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, Brutus, and getting an impression of a state with equal laws, governed on the basis of equality and an equal right to speak, and of a kingship that honours above all things the freedom of those it rules; and also from the same man: evenness and steadiness in the honour paid to […]; and doing good and sharing readily, unsparingly; and hopefulness, and trust that he was loved by his friends; and being open with those who met with his censure; and that his friends had no need to guess about what he wanted or did not want, but that it was plain.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ μου*: The Greek says “brother”, and that is what is translated. From memory, unchecked: Severus was not his brother by birth and editors have doubted the word. Other reading: my kinsman
- *τὸ φιλοίκειον*: Love of one’s own: family, household, those close to one. English has to choose. Other reading: love of his own people
- *Θρασέαν, Ἑλβίδιον, Κάτωνα, Δίωνα, Βροῦτον*: Men remembered for standing against rulers. Which Dio is meant is not certain (from memory, unchecked). The names are left bare as in the Greek. Other reading: Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dion, Brutus
- *φαντασίαν λαβεῖν*: The same phrase as in 1.7, with “impression” for φαντασία as throughout this translation. Here it is the mental picture of such a state, a conception of it, not a passing glimpse. One article governs this and “coming to know”, so “through him” covers both. Other reading: forming the idea of a state with equal laws
- *πολιτείας ἰσονόμου*: A constitution in which the law is equal for all. πολιτεία can be “state”, “constitution” or “republic”. Other reading: a constitution of equal law
- *ἰσηγορίαν*: The equal right of every citizen to speak in public. Other reading: equal freedom of speech
- *βασιλείας*: Kingship, rule by one man. The bare word is kept, not “monarchy” or “empire”. Other reading: a monarchy
- *ἐν τῇ τιμῇ τῆς ·*: The Greek as given breaks off: the article τῆς has no noun before the stop. The gap is marked in the English and nothing is supplied. From memory, unchecked: printed texts have φιλοσοφίας, “philosophy”, here. Other reading: in the honour paid to philosophy
- *τὸ ὁμαλὲς καὶ ὁμότονον*: Literally “the level and the evenly strung”: no ups and downs, the same pitch throughout. Other reading: being level and of one pitch
- *ἐκτενῶς*: “Unsparingly” stands last in the Greek, after “sharing readily”, and may go with the sharing alone or with the doing good as well. The English leaves it at the end in the same way. The same word is used of spending in 1.4. Other reading: doing good, and sharing readily and unsparingly
- *τὸ ἀνεπίκρυπτον*: Literally “the unconcealing”: he did not hide his censure from the people he censured. The Greek noun is an adverse judgment, stronger than disapproval. Other reading: hiding nothing from those he condemned
- *ἀλλὰ δῆλον εἶναι*: δῆλον can be neuter, “it was plain”, as here, or masculine, with him as the subject. Other reading: but that he was plain to read

</details>

### 1.15

From Maximus: self-mastery and being carried off course in nothing; and good spirits in illness as in other hard circumstances; and a character well blended, mild and dignified; and getting through what lay before him without complaining; and that everyone believed of him that whatever he said was what he thought, and that whatever he did he was not acting badly. And not being amazed, and not being startled, and never hurrying or hanging back or at a loss or downcast or putting on a grin, or again angry or suspicious; and doing good, and forgiving, and not lying; and giving the impression of one not bent rather than of one being straightened; and that no one would ever have thought they were looked down on by him, nor have gone so far as to suppose themselves better than him; and being pleasantly witty.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *περίφορον*: Literally “carried round”: swung about, unsteady in purpose. Other reading: and not wavering in anything
- *ἔν τε ταῖς ἄλλαις περιστάσεσι καὶ ἐν ταῖς νόσοις*: Literally “both in the other circumstances and in illnesses”. The order is turned for English. The noun often means hard circumstances, which is why illness is counted among them, and “hard” is written; it can also be plain “circumstances”. Other reading: in illness as in other circumstances
- *τὸ εὔκρατον τοῦ ἤθους*: The image is of a good mixture, as of wine or climate: a temper with nothing in excess. Other reading: an even temper
- *οὐ σχετλίως*: Without the manner of one who is hard done by: no grumbling. Other reading: without making hard work of it
- *ὅτι οὐ κακῶς πράττει*: Literally “that he is not acting badly”. It probably means with no bad intent. The wider wording is kept, as wide as the Greek adverb. Other reading: that whatever he did he did with no bad motive
- *τὸ ἀθαύμαστον καὶ ἀνέκπληκτον*: Not given to wonder and not knocked off balance by a shock. Other reading: never surprised and never alarmed
- *προσσεσηρός*: Literally “baring the teeth at”: a fawning or forced grin. Other reading: or fawning with a smile
- *ἀδιαστρόφου μᾶλλον ἢ διορθουμένου*: The image is a thing not twisted against a thing being made straight. The second word is the “correcting” of 1.7. “Impression” for φαντασία, as throughout. Other reading: of a man who could not be led astray rather than of one who had been corrected
- *ὑπέμεινεν*: Literally “would have endured”: would have brought themselves to. The Greek singular “anyone” is turned with “they”. Other reading: nor have ventured to think
- *τὸ εὐχαριεντίζεσθαι*: A rare verb: to be graceful in jesting, or simply to be agreeable. From memory, unchecked: the word has been doubted. Other reading: and a gracious manner

</details>

### 1.16

From my father: gentleness, and holding firm, unshaken, to what had been decided after examination; and no empty pride in what are counted as honours; and love of work, and perseverance; and listening to those who had something to bring to the common good; and giving each person what they deserved, without being turned aside; and knowing from experience where there is need to tighten and where to slacken; and putting a stop to love affairs with youths; and his sense of being one among others, and that his friends were not bound to dine with him every time, nor obliged to travel with him, and that those who had been kept away by some need always found him the same; and careful inquiry in council, and persistence, and not “he gave up the search too soon, content with the impressions that lay to hand”; and keeping his friends, never tiring of them quickly nor being infatuated with them; and self-sufficiency in everything, and cheerfulness; and foresight from far off, and arranging the smallest things in advance without making a drama of it; and that acclamations and all flattery were held in check under him; and always watching over what the empire needed, and managing its spending thriftily, and putting up with the blame that came for some things of this kind; and being neither superstitious about the gods, nor, with people, a courter of the public or eager to please or fond of the crowd, but sober in everything and firm, and never lacking in taste, and no lover of novelty; and using the things that add to the ease of life, of which fortune gave him plenty, without conceit and at the same time without apology, so that when they were there he took them without affectation, and when they were not he did not need them; and that no one could have said he was a sophist, or a home-bred buffoon, or a pedant, but a ripe man, complete, beyond flattery, able to take charge of his own affairs and other people’s. Besides these: honouring those who truly practise philosophy, and not reproaching the others, nor yet being easily led by them; and again, being good company and gracious, but not to excess; and taking care of his own body in due measure, not as someone in love with life would, nor for the sake of looks, nor yet carelessly, but so that through his own attention he needed very little from medicine, or from drugs and external dressings; and above all, giving way without envy to those who had some ability, such as ability in speaking, or the ability that comes from the study of laws or customs or some other matters, and joining eagerly in their efforts, so that each should be well thought of according to their own strengths; and doing everything by the ancestral ways, without setting out to be seen doing even this, keeping the ancestral ways. And again: not being easily shifted and restless, but staying long in the same places and at the same business; and after his attacks of headache, coming straight back fresh and at full strength to his usual work; and that he did not have many secrets, but very few and very rarely, and those only about public matters; and good sense and measure in putting on shows, in building works, in handouts and things of that kind, which is the way of a person who looks to the thing itself that has to be done, not to the good name that comes of having done it. Not one to bathe at odd hours, not fond of building, not one to be inventive about food, nor about the weave and colours of clothes, nor about the beauty of bodies. The formal dress from Lorium, coming up from the villa below; a tunic at Lanuvium for the most part; how he dealt with the cloak at Tusculum that was asking to be excused; and all that way of behaving. Nothing harsh, nor yet relentless, nor violent, nor such that one could ever have said “to the point of sweat”; but everything reasoned out, each part taken separately, as if at leisure, without disturbance, in order, with strength, in agreement with itself. What is recorded of Socrates would fit him: that he was able both to go without and to enjoy those things which most people are weak at going without and give way in enjoying. To be strong, and to hold out and stay sober in each of the two, is the mark of a man who has a soul that is sound and unbeaten, as in the illness of Maximus.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς*: The father by adoption, the emperor Antoninus Pius. The father by birth is named differently in 1.2. Other reading: From my adoptive father
- *ἐπὶ τῶν ἐξητασμένως κριθέντων*: Literally “on the things judged in an examined way”: decisions, or judgments, reached after scrutiny. Other reading: to judgments reached after scrutiny
- *τὰς δοκούσας τιμάς*: Literally “the seeming honours”: honours as people count them, the same turn as with favours in 1.8. Other reading: the so-called honours
- *ποῦ μὲν χρεία ἐντάσεως, ποῦ δὲ ἀνέσεως*: The image is a string tightened and let go, the same pair as in 1.8. The image is kept, and what is tightened is left unsaid, as in the Greek. Other reading: where to press and where to ease off
- *τὸ παῦσαι τὰ περὶ τοὺς ἔρωτας τῶν· μειρακίων*: The stop after τῶν in the Greek as given is a slip and is read through. The last word means adolescents and young men, older than boys. It is open whether he ended such affairs of his own or put a stop to the practice around him, and the English leaves it open too. Other reading: and having brought his own passion for youths to an end
- *ἡ κοινονοημοσύνη*: A very rare word, perhaps Marcus’s own, and in the nominative, which breaks the run of the list. Built from “common” and “minded”, it seems to mean not setting himself above others, which the examples that follow bear out. The sense is not certain: it could also be consideration for others, or public spirit. Other reading: his consideration for others
- *τὸ ἐφεῖσθαι τοῖς φίλοις*: Literally “that it was left to his friends” not to dine and not to travel with him: they were let off the obligation, not kept from doing so. Other reading: leaving his friends free not to dine with him and not to travel with him
- *πάντως*: “In every case”, taken here as “every time”. It can also be “necessarily”, which would make it a twin of “obliged” in the next phrase. Other reading: were not bound to dine with him as a matter of course
- *συναποδημεῖν*: To be away from home together with him: on his journeys, not necessarily in foreign countries. Other reading: to go away with him
- *οὐ τὸ προαπέστη τῆς ἐρεύνης*: The text is doubtful here: the article stands before a finite verb, “he left off the search too soon”, which does not construe as ordinary Greek. The English takes the article as quoting the phrase, a thing that could not be said of him; the other course is to suppose the words damaged. From memory, unchecked: editors doubt the text here. Other reading: and he never left off the search too soon
- *ταῖς προχείροις φαντασίαις*: “Impressions” for φαντασίαι, as throughout: the first appearances of a matter, the ones nearest to hand. Other reading: with first appearances
- *μηδαμοῦ ἁψίκορον*: The first word is literally “nowhere”, that is, in no case: “never” here and at “never lacking in taste” further on. Other reading: in no case tiring of them quickly
- *ἐπιμανές*: Mad about a person: excessive or infatuated attachment, set against quickly tiring of them. Other reading: nor doting on them
- *τὸ φαιδρόν*: Literally “the bright”: a beaming, cheerful look or temper. The Greek names no face. Other reading: a bright face
- *ἀτραγῴδως*: Literally “untragically”: without stage manner, without fuss. Other reading: without fuss
- *συσταλῆναν*: A slip in the Greek as given for the infinitive συσταλῆναι, which is read. The phrase before it, “in his time” or “in his own case”, is taken as “under him”. Other reading: were cut short where he was concerned
- *τῆς χορηγίας*: The supply of means: here the public outlay or the treasury’s resources. Other reading: a careful steward of the public funds
- *τῆς ἐπὶ τῶν τοιούτων τινῶν καταιτιάσεως*: Either blame over some matters of this kind, as taken here, or blame from certain people in such matters. Other reading: the blame some people laid on him in such matters
- *ὀχλοχαρές*: By its parts, “delighting in the crowd”, which the English keeps. After the two words before it, it may rather mean playing to the crowd. Other reading: or playing to the crowd
- *καινοτόμον*: One who cuts new ground: an innovator, or a chaser of novelty. Other reading: no innovator
- *ἀπροφασίστως*: Literally “without pretexts”: without making excuses for using them. It can also mean without hesitation. Other reading: and without hesitation
- *οὐερνάκλος*: The Latin word vernaculus in Greek letters: a slave born in the house, a type known for pert, low joking. “Home-bred buffoon” gives the word and the type together. The sense is not certain. Other reading: a home-born slave
- *σχολαστικός*: A man of the schools, bookish and unpractical. Other reading: a bookish man
- *φιλοσοφούντων*: Literally “those who philosophise”: who live as philosophers, not only study. Other reading: true philosophers
- *εὐπαράγωγον*: Easily led aside, taken in. Other reading: nor yet being taken in by them
- *φαρμάκων καὶ ἐπιθεμάτων ἐκτός*: The last word is taken with the dressings alone: things laid on the outside of the body. It could instead mean “apart from”, governing both nouns, which would turn the phrase. Other reading: or went without drugs and dressings
- *τὴν ἐξ ἱστορίας νόμων ἢ ἐθῶν*: ἱστορία is inquiry and the knowledge it gives. The feminine article picks up “ability”, which the English repeats. Other reading: the knowledge that comes from research into laws or customs
- *συσπουδαστικὸν αὐτοῖς*: Literally “being eager together with them”: he threw his own effort in behind theirs. Other reading: and actively backing them
- *πάντα δὲ κατὰ τὰ πάτρια πράσσων*: The construction changes here to a participle in the nominative, “he, doing everything”. It is kept in the run of the list. τὰ πάτρια are the customs handed down from the fathers, “the ancestral ways” both times. Other reading: He did everything by the customs of his fathers
- *οὐδὲ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐπιτηδεύων φαίνεσθαι*: Literally “not practising to be seen even at this very thing”. He kept the ancestral ways and made no show of keeping them. Other reading: without even seeming to make a point of it
- *θεωριῶν ἐπιτελέσει*: θεωρίαι here are public spectacles, the games and shows an emperor gives. Other reading: in the giving of public spectacles
- *διανομαῖς*: Distributions: handouts of money or food to the people. Other reading: in largesses
- *οὐκ ἀωρὶ λούστης*: The Greek has no verb in this sentence or the next ones. “At odd hours” is “out of season”, at the wrong time of day. Other reading: no bather at unseasonable hours
- *ἐπινοητής*: A deviser or inventor: one who thinks up refinements. The word governs the food, the clothes and the bodies alike, so “inventive about” is used for all three. Other reading: not one to think up dishes
- *οὐ περὶ σωμάτων ὥρας*: “Bodies” very likely means slaves, whose looks a rich man would choose for. The bare word is kept. Other reading: nor about the good looks of his slaves
- *ἡ ἀπὸ Λωρίου στολὴ ἀνάγουσα ἀπὸ τῆς κάτω ἐπαύλεως*: A jotting without a verb, and doubtful: the participle is active, “bringing up”, and has no object, so the Greek as given does not construe securely. “Coming up” is the nearest sense, and the point of the remark is not known. The noun is the “formal dress” of 1.7; Lorium was a country house of his (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: the robe he wore coming up from his villa at Lorium, down below
- *τῷ φελώνῃ ἐν Τούσκλοις παραιτουμένῳ ὡς ἐχρήσατο*: The word as given is “cloak”, which fits the list of clothes, but the participle “asking to be excused” is in the dative and agrees with it, and a cloak cannot ask. The English gives what stands, and the word is suspect. From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts read a word meaning “tax collector”, which construes. Other reading: how he treated the tax collector at Tusculum who asked his pardon
- *ἀδυσώπητον*: Not to be moved by entreaty, implacable. It can also mean not to be put out of countenance, shameless. Other reading: nor yet shameless
- *ἕως ἱδρῶτος*: Given as a thing people say: driving a matter until one sweats. It is kept word for word. Other reading: at fever heat
- *πάντα διειλημμένα λελογίσθαι*: The infinitive has nothing to hang on, like much in this chapter. Literally “everything, divided up, to have been reasoned out”. Other reading: but he had thought everything through, point by point
- *τὸ περὶ τοῦ Σωκράτους μνημονευόμενον*: Marcus does not say where the saying comes from, and it is not traced here. Other reading: the saying about Socrates
- *ἑκατέρῳ*: “In each of the two”: in going without and in enjoying. Holding out answers to the first and staying sober to the second, but the Greek joins the verbs to both. Other reading: to hold out in the one case and stay sober in the other
- *ἄρτιον*: Sound, well fitted, whole of its kind. “Complete” is kept for another word, τέλειος, earlier in the passage. Other reading: a soul that is complete and unbeaten
- *οἷον ἐν τῇ νόσῳ τῇ Μαξίμου*: A clipped ending. It is open whether this is how Antoninus bore himself while Maximus was ill, or how Maximus was in his own illness, which 1.15 speaks of. The English is left as bare as the Greek. Other reading: as he showed during the illness of Maximus

</details>

### 1.17a

From the gods: that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good people close to me, relatives, friends, nearly all of them; and that I was not carried away into any offence against any of them, although I had a disposition from which, if it had so happened, I might well have done something of the kind; but it is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up. And that I was not brought up for longer with my grandfather’s concubine; and that I preserved the bloom of my youth; and that I was not made a man before the season, but even took some time more. That I was placed under a ruler and father who was to take all the conceit out of me and bring me to the thought that it is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches and statues of this sort and similar show; but that one may draw oneself in until one is very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good. That I happened to have such a brother, able by his character to rouse me to take care of myself, and at the same time gladdening me with his respect and affection. That my children were not born lacking in natural gifts, nor deformed in their little bodies. That I did not make more progress in rhetoric, in poetry and in the other pursuits, in which I might perhaps have been held fast, if I had felt myself getting on easily. That I was quick to set those who brought me up in the rank they seemed to me to desire, and did not put it off with the hope that, since they were still young, I would do it later. That I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, Maximus. That I had an impression, clearly and often, of the life according to nature, of what kind of life it is, so that, as far as it rests with the gods and with the gifts, help and inspirations that come from there, nothing prevents me from living according to nature already, and that I still fall short of this is by my own fault and by not keeping to the reminders from the gods, which are all but teachings. That my body has held out so long in a life like this. That I touched neither Benedicta nor Theodotus, but that later too, when I fell into the passions of love, I recovered. That, though I was often angry with Rusticus, I did nothing more that I would have regretted. That my mother, who was to die young, still lived with me in her last years. That whenever I wanted to help someone who was poor or in need of something else, I was never told that I had no money to do it with; and that no similar need befell me myself, so as to take from another. That my wife is as she is, so compliant, so warmly affectionate, so unaffected. That I had no lack of suitable people to bring up my children. That remedies were given me through dreams, among others against spitting blood and against dizziness; and of this, at Caieta, as you will use. That, when I set my heart on philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, nor sit down to writing, or to resolving syllogisms, or to busying myself with the things in the sky. For all these things “need the gods’ help and fortune.”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *σχεδὸν ἅπαντας*: “Nearly all” may limit the whole list or only the last items (relatives, friends). It is left at the end, where it can be heard either way. Other reading: that nearly all my grandfathers, parents, sister, teachers, people close to me, relatives and friends were good
- *προέπεσον*: The verb is to fall or rush forward: to be carried headlong into something. Other reading: that I did not fall into any offence against any of them
- *καίτοι διάθεσιν ἔχων τοιαύτην*: The participle takes its time from the past verb, so “had”. The Greek does not say whether the disposition was still there at the time of writing. Other reading: although I have a disposition
- *ἥτις ἔμελλέ με ἐλέγξειν*: Literally “which was going to convict (or expose) me”. The English reads “would have shown me up”; “put me to the test” is also possible. Other reading: that would have put me to the test
- *τὸ τὴν ὥραν διασῶσαι καὶ τὸ μὴ πρὸ ὥρας ἀνδρωθῆναι, ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ ἐπιλαβεῖν τοῦ χρόνου*: One Greek word is used twice in two senses: the bloom of youth, and the due season. “Bloom” and “season” are chosen so that the second can be heard picking up the first. “Made a man” is meant sexually, and “took some time more” means he put it off even past the due time. Other reading: that I kept my youth unspoiled, and did not prove my manhood before the time, but even went beyond it
- *ἄρχοντι καὶ πατρὶ*: The ruler and father is Antoninus Pius, who adopted Marcus; the Greek does not name him. Other reading: under a ruler who was also my father
- *τὸν τῦφον*: Literally “smoke”: the puffed-up self-importance that clouds the head. The English reads “conceit”. Other reading: all the vanity
- *λαμπάδων καὶ ἀνδριάντων τοιῶνδέ τινων*: Literally “torches and statues, some such as these”, pointing at things familiar at court. Which torches and statues are meant is not said. Other reading: nor torches, statues and things of that sort
- *ἐγγυτάτω ἰδιώτου συστέλλειν ἑαυτὸν*: Literally “to contract oneself nearest to a private person”: to cut one’s state down almost to that of someone who holds no office. The picture of drawing in is kept. Other reading: bring oneself down very nearly to a private citizen’s way of living
- *ταπεινότερον*: The word is “low”: of a person’s bearing, lowly, abject, without dignity. Other reading: and not on that account be any meaner or slacker
- *ἡγεμονικῶς*: “In the manner of a leader.” The word is kin to the Stoic term “the ruling part”, but here it has the ordinary sense of one who commands. Other reading: what has to be done with authority for the common good
- *διὰ ἤθους*: “By his character.” The brother is Lucius Verus, Marcus’s brother by adoption (from memory, unchecked). The Greek does not say whether the character roused him as an example or as a warning, and that is left open. Other reading: by his way of life
- *τὸ φθάσαι*: The verb is “to get in first, to do in good time”. The English reads “was quick to”. Other reading: that I lost no time in setting
- *τοὺς τροφέας*: Those who reared him, as in 5.31; the same word is used below of the people who rear his children. It is narrower than “teachers”. Other reading: my tutors
- *μὴ ἀναβαλέσθαι ἐλπίδι τοῦ με*: The Greek verb has no object: “did not put off, with the hope of my doing it later”. The hope may be one held out to them or his own expectation, and the English leaves that open. Other reading: and did not put them off with the hope that I would do it later
- *τὸ φαντασθῆναι*: The verb belongs with the Stoic noun for an impression (φαντασία): something presented itself to his mind. “Impression” keeps the glossary word. Other reading: that I pictured to myself, clearly and often
- *διαδόσεσι καὶ συλλήψεσι καὶ ἐπιπνοίαις*: Three parallel nouns, all “from there”: things handed on, acts of helping, and breathings-upon. Other reading: what is passed on from there, their help and their promptings
- *μήτε Βενεδίκτης ἅψασθαι μήτε Θεοδότου*: A woman’s name and a man’s name. Nothing more is known of them; they are usually thought to have been slaves of the household (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: that I laid no hand on Benedicta or on Theodotus
- *ὑγιᾶναι*: Literally “to become healthy”: love’s passions are treated as an illness he got over. Other reading: I was cured
- *τὸ τὴν γυναῖκα τοιαύτην εἶναι*: The infinitive does not show tense, so the Greek does not settle whether his wife was alive at the time of writing. The English reads “is”. Other reading: that my wife was as she was
- *πειθήνιον*: Literally “obedient to the rein”: ready to be persuaded, compliant. Other reading: so obedient
- *βοηθήματα*: The word is “aids”, and in medicine “remedies”; with spitting blood and dizziness the medical sense is taken. It is kin to the word for the gods’ “help” in the closing quotation. Other reading: That help was given me through dreams
- *καὶ τούτου ἐν Καιήτῃ ὥσπερ χρήσῃ*: These words do not construe as they stand and are generally thought to be corrupt (from memory, unchecked). They are given word for word, “and of this, at Caieta, as you will use”, and not mended; the last word could also hide a word for an oracle. Caieta is a town on the coast south of Rome. Other reading: and for this, at Caieta, as if by an oracle
- *ὅπως ἐπεθύμησα φιλοσοφίας*: The first word is normally “how” or “in order that”; here it must be “when” or “as soon as”, a rare use. Other reading: that, however much I longed for philosophy
- *ἀποκαθίσαι ἐπὶ τὸ συγγράφειν*: Literally “sit down apart to writing”, that is, to composing treatises. Some editors read “the writers” here instead of “writing” (from memory, unchecked); the text is translated as given. Other reading: nor sit down over the writers
- *τὰ μετεωρολογικὰ*: The study of things aloft: the heavens and the weather, as a branch of natural philosophy. Other reading: questions about the heavens
- *θεῶν βοηθῶν καὶ τύχης δεῖται*: Marked in the edition as a quotation; the source is not identified. Literally “need helping gods and fortune”. The word for “helping” is kin to the word for the “remedies” given through dreams just above. Other reading: need gods to help, and luck

</details>

## Book 2

### 2.1

At dawn, say to yourself beforehand: I shall meet a meddler, an ungrateful person, an insolent one, a deceitful one, an envious one, an unsocial one. All these things have come upon them through ignorance of what is good and bad. But I, who have seen the nature of the good, that it is honourable, and of the bad, that it is shameful, and the nature of the very person who does wrong, that they are akin to me, sharing not the same blood or seed but mind and a portion of the divine, can neither be harmed by any of them, for no one will wrap me in what is shameful, nor be angry with one who is akin to me, nor hate them. For we have come into being to work together, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. So to work against one another is against nature; and to be indignant and to turn away is working against.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *προλέγειν ἑαυτῷ*: An infinitive used as a command, with the reflexive “oneself”, which in Greek of this date serves for any person. The English reads “say to yourself”; how far the speech runs is not marked, so no quotation marks are used. Other reading: One should say to oneself at dawn, in advance
- *περιέργῳ*: περίεργος is someone who is busy with what is not their concern. Other reading: a busybody
- *βασκάνῳ*: βάσκανος is grudging and malicious, the word used of the evil eye. Other reading: a spiteful one
- *ὅτι καλόν*: καλόν and αἰσχρόν are both “beautiful, ugly” and “honourable, shameful”. The English takes the moral pair and keeps “shameful” for αἰσχρῷ below, so that the reason given for not being harmed can be followed. Other reading: that it is beautiful … that it is ugly
- *ὅτι μοι συγγενής*: “Akin”, picked up by τῷ συγγενεῖ below. The words “blood or seed” and “mind and a portion of the divine” all depend on μέτοχος, “sharing in”: kinship by shared mind, not by family. Other reading: a kinsman, not of the same blood or seed, but a sharer in mind
- *θείας ἀπομοίρας*: ἀπόμοιρα is a share portioned off from something larger: a portion of what is divine. Other reading: a fragment of the divine
- *περιβαλεῖ*: The image is of throwing something around a person, as a garment or a net. It is kept as “wrap”. Other reading: involve in what is shameful
- *ἀπέχθεσθαι αὐτῷ*: The verb usually means to be hated by someone; with this dative it is to be at enmity with them. The English reads “hate”. Other reading: nor be at enmity with them
- *ἀντιπρακτικὸν*: The same root as ἀντιπράσσειν just before, and set against συνεργίαν (working together). “Work” is kept in all three. Other reading: and indignation and turning away are forms of opposition

</details>

### 2.2

Whatever this is that I am, it is bits of flesh, a little breath, and the ruling part. Let the books go. Be pulled no longer. It is not allowed. Instead, as one already dying, despise the bits of flesh: gore, little bones, a web, a small plaiting of sinews, little veins and arteries. Look too at what kind of thing the breath is: wind, and not even always the same, but at every moment vomited out and gulped in again. Third, then, is the ruling part. Think of it this way: you are old. No longer let this be a slave, no longer let it be pulled about on strings by unsocial impulse, no longer let it be discontented with what is fated now or look with suspicion on what is fated to come.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πνευμάτιον*: A diminutive of πνεῦμα, breath: for the Stoics the warm breath that keeps a body alive. The flesh is a diminutive too. Other reading: a puff of breath
- *μηκέτι σπῶ*: The verb is “pull”, “drag”; in this form “be pulled”, that is, distracted, or “pull yourself”. After the books it could also be “do not grasp at them”. Other reading: stop grasping at them
- *οὐ δέδοται*: “It has not been granted.” What is not granted is not said: the time for books, most likely. Other reading: That has not been given to you
- *κροκύφαντος*: A woven net, such as a hairnet. The next phrase explains it as a small plaited thing made of sinews, veins and arteries. Other reading: a mesh
- *νεύρων*: νεῦρα are sinews or tendons, and also nerves; the two were not sharply told apart. Other reading: of nerves, veins and arteries
- *πάσης ὥρας*: Literally “every hour”, in the loose sense of at all times. Other reading: every hour
- *καθ’ ὁρμὴν ἀκοινώνητον*: “Unsocial” is the negative of this translation’s “social”: impulse that takes no account of the community. The verb after it is the one for working a puppet by its strings, as in 12.19 and 7.3. Other reading: by selfish impulse
- *τὸ εἱμαρμένον ἢ παρὸν δυσχερᾶναι ἢ μέλλον ὑπιδέσθαι*: “What is fated” is said once and goes with both halves, the present and the coming. The last verb is to look at something from under the brows, with mistrust or dread, the same verb as in 2.17. Other reading: no longer let it complain of its present lot or dread the one to come

</details>

### 2.3

What comes from the gods is full of providence. What comes from chance is not without nature, or without the spinning together and interweaving of the things that providence governs. Everything flows from there. And there is besides what is necessary, and what benefits the whole universe, of which you are a part. And what the nature of the whole brings is good for every part of nature, and so is what preserves that nature. And the universe is preserved by changes: those of the elements and, in the same way, those of compound things. Let this be enough for you, and let these be your principles. As for your thirst for books, throw it away, so that you do not die grumbling, but truly gracious, and thankful to the gods from your heart.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὰ τῶν θεῶν*: Literally “the things of the gods”, which can be their works or what comes from them. The next sentence has the same form, “the things of chance”, and the two are matched. “Everything flows from there”, two sentences on, takes up the sense “comes from”. Other reading: The works of the gods are full of providence. The works of chance
- *οὐκ ἄνευ φύσεως ἢ συγκλώσεως καὶ ἐπιπλοκῆς*: Literally “not without nature or spinning-together and interweaving”. The “or” may offer a second way of saying the same thing and not an alternative. Both nouns are images from thread and cloth. Other reading: not apart from nature, that is, from the spinning and weaving together
- *ἐκεῖθεν*: “From there” has no stated place. It most naturally points back to providence, or to the gods. Other reading: Everything flows from that source
- *πρόσεστι δὲ τὸ ἀναγκαῖον*: Literally “there is added the necessary”. It is open whether necessity is a second thing beside providence or a feature of what flows from it. Other reading: and with it goes necessity
- *συμφέρον*: Literally “what brings together”, and the next sentence uses the simple verb “brings” (φέρει); the echo is lost in the English. This translation usually gives the word as “is good for”. “Benefits” is used here so that it is not confused with ἀγαθόν, “good”, in the next sentence. Other reading: what is good for the whole universe
- *σωστικόν*: The adjective and the verb in the next sentence (σῴζουσι) are the same word, “keep safe, preserve”. “Preserve” is used for both, and the second sentence is turned into the passive. Other reading: what keeps that nature safe. And what keeps the universe safe is the changes
- *καὶ δόγματα ἔστω*: δόγματα are settled beliefs one lives by, “principles” in this translation. The text is translated as given; some editions may print a word meaning “always” here in place of “and” (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: let them always be your principles
- *γογγύζων*: A word for low muttering or complaining under the breath. Other reading: so that you do not die muttering
- *ἵλεως*: Used of gods it means “kindly, well-disposed”; of people “gracious, good-humoured, at peace”. Here it is set against grumbling. “Gracious” is used here and for the same word in 3.16. Other reading: truly at peace / truly cheerful

</details>

### 2.4

Remember how long you have been putting these things off, and how many times you have been given a set time by the gods and make no use of it. Now at last you must perceive what universe you are a part of, and from what governor of the universe you came into being as an outflow, and that a limit of time has been marked out for you. If you do not use it to clear away the clouds, it will be gone, you will be gone, and it will not be possible again.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *προθεσμίας*: A legal word: the day fixed in advance by which something must be done, or the period allowed. The Greek is plural, one term after another being granted; the English reads “a set time” in the singular after “how many times”. Other reading: how many times you have been given deadlines by the gods and make no use of them
- *τίνος κόσμου*: τίνος asks “which” or “what”, and in such a phrase can lean toward “what kind of”. Other reading: what kind of universe you are a part of
- *ἀπόρροια ὑπέστης*: ἀπόρροια is a flowing off, a stream that runs out from a source. ὑπέστης is “you came to exist”. Literally “of what governor of the universe you came to exist as an outflow”. Other reading: and from what governor of the universe you exist as an emanation
- *ἀπαιθριάσαι*: The verb is made from the word for a cloudless sky: to bring fair weather, to drive off the clouds. No object is given, and the weather stands for clearing one’s own mind; the English keeps the image and does not add “your mind”. The verb can also be taken as “to become clear”. Other reading: if you do not use it to become clear, as the sky does
- *οἰχήσεται οἰχήσῃ*: The two verbs stand side by side with no connecting word in the Greek as given: “it will be gone” (the time) and “you will be gone”. From memory, unchecked: editions print a καὶ between them, and its absence may be a slip of the digitised copy. The English keeps the two without “and”. Other reading: it will be gone and you will be gone
- *αὖθις οὐκ ἐξέσται*: Literally “it will not be allowed (or possible) again”, with nothing said about what: the chance to use the time. Other reading: and there will be no second chance

</details>

### 2.5

At every hour take firm care, as a Roman and a man, to do what is in hand with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice, and to win yourself respite from all other impressions. You will win it if you carry out each action as the last of your life, rid of all aimlessness, of turning away in passion from what reason decides, of pretence, of self-love and of discontent with what has been allotted to you. You see how few the things are which, once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing: for the gods will demand nothing more of whoever keeps to these.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *στιβαρῶς*: The adverb means “sturdily, stoutly”. The English takes it with “take care”; by position it could also colour “to do what is in hand”. Other reading: take care, as a Roman and a man, to do what is in hand sturdily
- *ἄρρην*: The word is “male”, not the ordinary word for a man. The English reads “a man” because “a male” reads oddly here; the same word comes back in 3.5a, where it is “male”. Other reading: as a Roman and a male
- *ἀκριβοῦς καὶ ἀπλάστου σεμνότητος*: One article and one pair of adjectives stand before four nouns. The English keeps a single “with” for the whole list, so that “exact and unfeigned” can be heard with dignity alone or with all four, as in the Greek. “Affection” is the noun of the word given as “warmly affectionate” in 6.30a and 1.17a. Other reading: with exact and unfeigned dignity, with warm affection, with freedom and with justice
- *σχολὴν*: The word is “leisure, free time”. Since it is leisure from other impressions (φαντασίαι), the English reads “respite”. The verb, “procure, win”, comes twice in the Greek and is “win” both times. Other reading: to procure yourself leisure from all the other impressions
- *ἐμπαθοῦς ἀποστροφῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ αἱροῦντος λόγου*: The phrase rests on the idiom “reason proves (or requires) it”, literally “the reason that takes”. The English reads “what reason decides”, and “in passion” for an adjective that means “in the grip of a passion”. “All” stands once in the Greek, before “aimlessness”, and stays there. Other reading: of emotion-driven turning away from the reasoning that carries the point
- *τὰ συμμεμοιραμένα*: Literally “the things that have been allotted along with (you)”, the share dealt out together with a person’s life. “To you” is supplied. Other reading: discontent with the things allotted together with you
- *εὔρουν*: Literally “flowing well”. It is a Stoic word for the happy life, “a good flow of life” (from memory, unchecked). The image is kept. Other reading: a prosperous life
- *θεουδῆ*: In Homer the word means “god-fearing”; later writers also used it as if it meant “godlike”. The English reads “god-fearing” because the next clause speaks of what the gods will demand, though that clause fits “godlike” as well. Other reading: a life that flows smoothly and is like the gods’
- *καὶ γὰρ οἱ θεοὶ*: The two opening particles together can mean simply “for in fact”, or the first can mean “too” (“for the gods too”). The English takes the first, since the passage names no one else who makes demands. Other reading: for the gods too will demand nothing more

</details>

### 2.6

Do violence, do violence to yourself, soul; but you will have no chance left to honour yourself. For each person has one life, and yours is almost finished, while you do not respect yourself but place your good fortune in the souls of others.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὕβριζε, ὕβριζε σεαυτήν*: An imperative, said in bitter irony and answered by “but”; the Greek has no “go on” and no possessive with “soul”. Some are thought to read an indicative here, “you are doing violence to yourself” (from memory, unchecked). “Do violence” matches 2.16, and the verb is set against τιμῆσαι, “to honour”. Other reading: You are doing violence, violence to yourself, soul
- *οὐκέτι καιρὸν ἕξεις*: καιρός is the right moment or opportunity, not time in general. Other reading: you will no longer have the time
- *εἷς γὰρ ὁ βίος ἑκάστῳ*: As printed: “for each has one life”. The wording of this clause is thought to be doubted in the transmission and to rest on an editor’s repair (from memory, unchecked). The English translates what is given. Other reading: for life is a single thing for each person
- *σχεδὸν διήνυσται*: A perfect: has been all but completed, like a journey travelled to its end. Other reading: is nearly at its end
- *μὴ αἰδουμένῃ σεαυτήν*: Dative participles agreeing with σοι: literally “for you, not respecting yourself but placing”. They are made a clause with “while”; a plain relative, “you who do not respect yourself”, is also possible. αἰδεῖσθαι is to feel respect or shame before someone, the verb of αἰδώς in 11.1. Other reading: yours, who do not respect yourself but place
- *τὴν σὴν εὐμοιρίαν*: Literally “your good portion”, the lot that falls to a person: good fortune, and so well-being or happiness. Other reading: your happiness

</details>

### 2.7

Do the things that fall on you from outside distract you at all? Then give yourself leisure to learn some further good thing, and stop wandering. But now there is the other kind of drifting to guard against as well. For people play the fool through their actions too, those who are worn out by life and have no target at which to direct every impulse and, in general, every impression.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Περισπᾷ τί σε*: The accent on τί may only be thrown back from the following σε, giving the indefinite “somewhat”, “at all”, or it may be the question word “why”. The English takes “at all”, since the word stands second in its clause, and gives the Greek “and” that follows as “Then”. From memory, unchecked: editors differ on whether this is a question or a statement. Other reading: Why do the things that fall on you from outside distract you?
- *τοῦ προσμανθάνειν ἀγαθόν τι*: προσ- adds “in addition”: to learn something good on top of what you know. Other reading: to learn something good
- *τὴν ἑτέραν περιφορὰν*: περιφορά is a being carried round. The first kind is being pulled about by outside things; “the other” is busy action without an aim. The English has “drifting”. Other reading: the other way of going round in circles
- *ληροῦσι*: ληρέω is to talk nonsense, to be silly. With “through their actions too” the point is that one can babble in deeds as well as words. Other reading: For they are talking nonsense in their actions as well
- *οἱ κεκμηκότες τῷ βίῳ*: The participle says that they have grown weary; “life” can be what has wearied them or the field in which they have toiled. “Worn out by life” is meant in the sense of exhausted, not of wishing to die. Other reading: those who have worn themselves out in living
- *ἀπευθύνουσιν*: As accented this is a present, “at which they direct”; a future (“will direct”) is one accent away. English needs “at which to direct”. Other reading: no target at which they will direct every impulse
- *καθάπαξ φαντασίαν*: καθάπαξ is “once for all”, “altogether”, “in general”: it widens the claim from every impulse to every impression. φαντασία is “impression” as elsewhere, though here it comes close to “thought”. Other reading: every impulse and every thought whatever

</details>

### 2.8

Hardly anyone has been seen to be unhappy through not attending to what goes on in another person’s soul. But those who do not keep track of the movements of their own soul are bound to be unhappy.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Παρὰ μὲν τὸ μὴ ἐφιστάνειν*: παρά with the accusative gives the cause (“through not attending”). ἐφιστάνειν is to set the mind on something, to stop and consider it. In the Greek the cause comes first in the sentence; the English puts it after the main clause, where it cannot be taken with “hardly”. Other reading: Through not stopping to consider what goes on in another person’s soul
- *οὐ ῥᾳδίως τις ὤφθη κακοδαιμονῶν*: Literally “not easily has anyone been seen being unhappy”: an understatement, with a past tense that states what experience has shown. “Hardly anyone has been seen” keeps the passive and the fact of experience. Other reading: it is not easy to find anyone who is unhappy
- *κακοδαιμονεῖν*: The word is built on δαίμων (the spirit that goes with a person): literally “to have a bad spirit”, the opposite of εὐδαιμονία, “happiness”. “Unhappy” is used so that it answers “happiness” elsewhere; the word is stronger than a passing mood. Other reading: to be wretched
- *κινήμασι*: “Movements” is literal: whatever stirs in the soul, whether thoughts, feelings or impulses. The Greek does not narrow it and the English does not. Other reading: stirrings
- *μὴ παρακολουθοῦντας*: παρακολουθεῖν is to follow closely with the mind, and so to keep track of or to be aware of. “Keep track of” is read because “follow” alone could be heard as “obey”. Other reading: those who do not follow, or: those who are not aware of
- *ἀνάγκη κακοδαιμονεῖν*: Literally “it is a necessity that they are unhappy”. “Are bound to be” is read because “must be” can be heard in English as a guess. Other reading: must be unhappy

</details>

### 2.9

These things must always be remembered: what the nature of the whole is, and what mine is, and how this one stands to that one, and what kind of part it is of what kind of whole; and that there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις*: Glossary rendering. The Greek is plural, “of all things together”. Other reading: the nature of all things
- *ὁποῖόν τι μέρος ὁποίου τοῦ ὅλου οὖσα*: Literally “being what sort of part of what sort of whole”. Other reading: what sort of part it is, and of what sort of whole
- *ἧς μέρος εἶ*: The Greek moves from “mine” to “you are”, and the English keeps the shift. “You” after “prevents” is supplied from this clause. Other reading: of which I am a part
- *τὰ ἀκόλουθα τῇ φύσει*: Literally “the things that follow nature”, as a companion follows: what is consistent with it, not what is deduced from it. Other reading: what follows from the nature

</details>

### 2.10

Theophrastus speaks as a philosopher when, in his comparison of wrongdoings (as one might compare such things in a more everyday way), he says that offences committed from desire are more serious than those committed from anger. For the one who is angry is seen to turn away from reason with a certain pain and a shrinking inside that goes unnoticed; but the one who does wrong from desire, overcome by pleasure, is seen to be somehow more unrestrained and more womanish in their wrongdoing. Rightly, then, and in a way worthy of philosophy, he said that the wrong done with pleasure is open to a greater charge than the wrong done with pain. And in general the one is more like a person who has first been treated unjustly and has been forced by pain into anger; the other is moved to do injustice by an impulse of their own, carried towards doing something from desire.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>
