- *Φιλοσόφως*: An adverb, “philosophically”, going with “says”. The English turns it into “speaks as a philosopher when … he says”, which adds the verb “speaks”. Other reading: It is philosophically that Theophrastus says
- *ὡς ἄν τις κοινότερον τὰ τοιαῦτα συγκρίνειε*: A qualification: “as one might compare such things in a more common way”. It is taken to concede that comparing wrongdoings at all is a looser, everyday way of talking, since strict Stoic teaching held all wrongdoings equal (from memory, unchecked). κοινότερον could also mean “by more widely shared notions”. Other reading: so far as one may compare such things by the standards people commonly share
- *βαρύτερα*: Literally “heavier”, the ordinary Greek word for a grave offence. The English has “more serious”. Other reading: heavier
- *πλημμελούμενα*: A different verb from ἁμαρτάνω: literally “to strike a false note”, then “to offend”. The English has “offences” here and keeps “wrongdoing” and “do wrong” for ἁμαρτάνω and its nouns in the rest of the passage. Other reading: the false steps made from desire
- *τῶν κατὰ θυμόν*: θυμός is “anger” but also the spirited temper more broadly, and the Greek word for desire, ἐπιθυμία, is built on it, so the pair sounds alike in Greek. The English has “from anger” and “from desire”; the κατά is literally “in accordance with”. Other reading: than those committed in a fit of temper
- *λεληθυίας συστολῆς*: συστολή is the Stoic term for the drawing in of the soul in distress, usually put as “contraction”. The English keeps the image as “a shrinking” and adds “inside” so that a reader can tell what shrinks. λεληθυίας is “that escapes notice”, without saying whose notice: most likely the angry person’s own. Other reading: an unnoticed contraction
- *φαίνεται τὸν λόγον ἀποστρεφόμενος*: φαίνεται with a participle normally means “is plainly, is seen to be” and not merely “seems”. The same verb stands in the next clause with adjectives only, where it could be the weaker “appears”. The English has “is seen to” in both places so that the one verb is heard of both people. Other reading: seems to turn away from reason … appears somehow more unrestrained
- *ἀκολαστότερός*: The word is the opposite of self-control: “more undisciplined, more licentious”. The English has “more unrestrained”. Other reading: more self-indulgent
- *θηλύτερος*: Literally “more female”, a reproach meaning soft. The image is kept as it stands. The subject is a generic masculine, rendered “the one who … their”. Other reading: softer
- *μείζονος ἐγκλήματος ἔχεσθαι*: Literally “is held by a greater accusation”, a legal turn of phrase. The English has “is open to a greater charge”. Other reading: deserves heavier blame
- *ὅλως τε*: From here the Greek moves from reported speech to plain statements. This may be Marcus adding his own point, or still a summary of Theophrastus. The English leaves it as plain statement, as the Greek does. Other reading: And in general, he said, the one is more like
- *αὐτόθεν πρὸς τὸ ἀδικεῖν ὥρμηται*: ὥρμηται is the verb of ὁρμή, “impulse” in the glossary, so “impulse” is brought into the English. αὐτόθεν is taken as “from themselves, of their own accord”, but it can also mean “straight off, at once”, that is, without being provoked first. Other reading: the other has set out straight away to do injustice

</details>

### 2.11

To do and say and think each thing in the knowledge that it is possible to leave life at this very moment. As for going away from among human beings: if gods exist, it is nothing to fear, for they would not throw you into anything bad. And if either they do not exist or they do not care about human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe empty of gods or empty of providence? But they do exist, and they do care about human affairs; and they have put it wholly in a person’s own power not to fall into the things that are truly bad. And if any of the rest were bad, they would have provided for that too, so that it would be in everyone’s power not to fall into it. But what does not make a human being worse, how could that make a human being’s life worse? The nature of the whole would not have overlooked these things, either through ignorance or because, though it knew, it could not guard against them beforehand or set them right; nor would it have made so great a mistake, through lack of power or lack of skill, that good things and bad things happen alike and in a jumble to good people and to bad. Now death and life, good repute and ill repute, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty, all these happen alike to the good and to the bad among human beings, and they are neither fine nor shameful. So they are neither good nor bad.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὡς ἤδη δυνατοῦ ὄντος ἐξιέναι τοῦ βίου*: Literally “on the footing that it is possible to leave life right now”. The Greek is impersonal, with infinitives for the instruction; the English keeps “To do” and names no person. Other reading: To do and say and think each thing as someone who can leave life at this very moment
- *κακῷ γάρ σε οὐκ ἂν περιβάλοιεν*: The argument of the whole chapter turns on one word, κακόν, used of things and of people. “Bad” stands for it every time, and “good” for its opposite. The verb is literally “throw around”, to involve someone in something. Other reading: for they would not involve you in any evil
- *τί μοι ζῆν*: Literally “what to this speaker is living”: what good is living. The Greek changes here from the second person to the first. Other reading: why should I go on living
- *προείδοντο*: “Saw beforehand”, and so “made provision”. It answers in sense to “providence” earlier in the chapter, though it is not the same Greek root. Other reading: they would have foreseen that too
- *ἐπὶ παντὶ*: Taken as “in every person’s power”, matching “in a person’s own power” just before. It could also mean “in every case”. Other reading: so that in every case it would be possible not to fall into it
- *πεφυρμένως*: From a verb for kneading or mixing up: without sorting, all in a mess. Other reading: indiscriminately
- *θάνατος δέ γε καὶ ζωή*: The small words bring in the next step of the argument, as “Now” does in English. They do not object to what was just said. Other reading: But death and life
- *πόνος καὶ ἡδονή*: πόνος is both hard toil and pain. Set against pleasure, it is taken as “pain”. Other reading: toil and pleasure
- *οὔτε καλὰ ὄντα οὔτε αἰσχρά*: καλόν and αἰσχρόν are the morally fine and the morally ugly, a different pair from good and bad; the last sentence draws the conclusion from them. The participle may give a reason (“since they are”); the English has a plain “and”. Other reading: since they are neither honorable nor shameful

</details>

### 2.12a

How quickly all things vanish, the bodies themselves into the universe, the memories of them into eternity. What all the things perceived by the senses are like, and above all those that lure with pleasure or frighten with pain or are loudly celebrated through vanity: how cheap and contemptible and filthy and quick to perish and dead.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πῶς πάντα ταχέως ἐναφανίζεται*: The “how” and “what” clauses are indirect questions that depend on a verb later in the chapter, which is not part of this passage. The English leaves them all standing on their own, as headings for thought, and supplies no governing verb. Other reading: [To consider] how quickly all things vanish
- *τῷ μὲν κόσμῳ*: The datives go with the verb, “vanish in” or “into”: bodies are lost in the universe, memories in eternity. They could also be heard as “for the universe”, “for eternity”. Other reading: the bodies themselves in the universe, the memories of them in time
- *τῷ πόνῳ*: πόνος is both “pain” and “toil, hardship”. Set against pleasure, “pain” is the nearer sense. Other reading: or frighten with hardship
- *τῷ τύφῳ διαβεβοημένα*: τῦφος is literally smoke: vanity, delusion, puffed-up pride. διαβεβοημένα is “shouted abroad”, made famous. The things meant are those celebrated only through people’s vanity. Other reading: or are noised abroad by empty pride
- *εὔφθαρτα καὶ νεκρά,*: The Greek as given stops at a comma, in mid-sentence. The English closes with a full stop so that the passage can stand on its own; nothing has been supplied. Other reading: and quick to perish and dead,

</details>

### 2.12b

To attend [to these things] belongs to the power of mind. What these people are, whose judgments and voices give a good name. What dying is, and that, if a person looks at it by itself alone and, by dividing up the notion, dissolves the things imagined into it, they will no longer judge it to be anything other than a work of nature; and if anyone is afraid of a work of nature, they are a child. This, though, is not only a work of nature but also something good for nature.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *νοερᾶς δυνάμεως ἐφιστάναι*: The passage begins in mid-sentence. The infinitive has no object in the Greek given, because what is to be attended to stands in the part of the chapter before the cut; “to these things” is added in square brackets. The questions that follow (“what these people are”, “what dying is”) may also depend on this verb. Other reading: … is for the power of mind to attend to.
- *αἱ ὑπολήψεις καὶ αἱ φωναὶ τὴν εὐδοξίαν παρέχουσι*: ὑπόληψις is the Stoic term rendered “judgment” here; the verb ὑπολήψεται below is the same word, so it is “judge” there. φωναί is “voices” or “words”; εὐδοξία is good repute. Other reading: whose opinions and words confer fame
- *τῷ μερισμῷ τῆς ἐννοίας*: Either “by dividing the notion” (taking the idea of death apart) or “by the division that thought performs”. The English takes the first. Other reading: by taking it apart in thought
- *τὰ ἐμφανταζόμενα αὐτῷ*: The verb belongs to the family of φαντασία (“impression”): the things that show themselves in it, or are imagined into it. αὐτῷ is taken as “in it”, meaning death. Other reading: the impressions that attach themselves to it
- *ἀλλὰ καὶ συμφέρον αὐτῇ*: αὐτῇ is nature; the noun is repeated, because “good for it” would be unclear in English. συμφέρον is rendered “good for”, as in the glossary; in 12.23, where it stands beside ἀγαθόν, it is “benefits”. Other reading: but also to nature’s advantage

</details>

### 2.12c–13

How a human being touches god, and with what part of themselves, and in what state this part of the human being is when that happens.

Nothing is more wretched than a person who goes round everything in a circle and, as it is said, “searches into the things beneath the earth”, and looks by guesswork for what is in the souls of their neighbours, but does not notice that it is enough to keep only to the guardian spirit within them and to serve it truly. To serve it is to keep it clean of passion and aimlessness and discontent with what comes from the gods and from people. For what comes from the gods deserves reverence because of their excellence; and what comes from people is dear because of kinship, and sometimes also, in a way, pitiable because of their ignorance of what is good and bad. This disability is no less than the one that takes away the power to tell white from black.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πῶς ἅπτεται θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος*: The Greek given begins in the middle of a list: these are indirect questions that hang on a verb in the part of the chapter not given. Nothing is added; they are left as a list of questions, with a capital letter at the start. Other reading: [to consider] how a human being lays hold of god
- *ὅταν πῶς ἔχῃ διακέηται*: The Greek has two verbs side by side that both mean “is in a certain state”, with nothing joining them, so the clause does not construe as given; one looks like a gloss on the other (from memory, unchecked: editors bracket ἔχῃ). διακέηται is itself an odd form. The English translates the sense once. Other reading: and when this part of the human being is in what state, how disposed
- *φησὶν*: “He says” marks the words in quotation marks as a quotation from an author who is not named; the Doric form γᾶς shows it is verse. The English has “as it is said” so that “he” is not taken for the wretched person. From memory, unchecked: the line is Pindar’s, quoted by Plato in the Theaetetus. Other reading: and, as the poet says, “searches into what lies under the earth”
- *διὰ τεκμάρσεως*: τέκμαρσις is inference from signs, conjecture. The English has “by guesswork”. Other reading: and tries to work out from signs what is in the souls of their neighbours
- *πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ ἔνδον ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονι εἶναι*: πρός with εἶναι is to be occupied with something, and μόνῳ says with this and nothing else: “keep only to”. δαίμων is the divine being within each person, not “demon” in the later sense; the English has “guardian spirit”, as in 12.3, with “guardian” supplied. Other reading: to be with the god within them, and with that alone
- *γνησίως θεραπεύειν*: θεραπεύω is to serve or attend on a god, and also to tend or care for. The English keeps “serve” for the verb and for the noun θεραπεία after it. Other reading: and to tend it sincerely. Tending it means
- *εἰκαιότητος*: The noun from εἰκῇ, “at random”: acting or thinking without purpose. The English has “aimlessness”. Other reading: clean of passion and thoughtlessness
- *ἀρετήν*: ἀρετή is excellence or virtue; the Greek does not say whose. The English takes it as that of the gods and has “their excellence”. Other reading: deserves reverence because of its goodness
- *πήρωσις*: πήρωσις is a maiming or disabling, often used of blindness. The English keeps the general word, since the comparison with not telling white from black supplies the blindness. Other reading: This blindness is no less than the one that robs a person of telling white from black

</details>

### 2.14

Even if you are going to live three thousand years, or even three times ten thousand, still remember that no one loses any life other than this one they are living, and no one lives any life other than the one they are losing. So the longest comes to the same thing as the shortest. For the present is equal for everyone, so what perishes is equal too, and in this way what is lost shows itself to be an instant. For no one could lose either the past or the future, for how could anyone take from a person what that person does not have? So these two things must be remembered. One is that all things from eternity are of the same kind and come round in a circle, and that it makes no difference whether a person will see the same things for a hundred years, or for two hundred, or for time without limit. The other is that the one who lives longest and the one who will die soonest lose an equal amount. For the present is the only thing a person is going to be deprived of, if indeed this is the only thing they have, and a person does not lose what they do not have.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τοσαυτάκις μύρια*: Literally “so many times ten thousand”, where “so many times” picks up the “three times” of three thousand. The English says “three times ten thousand” outright. Other reading: or even that many times ten thousand
- *ἀποβάλλει βίον*: ἀποβάλλειν, literally to throw off or let drop, is the word the argument turns on and comes six times. The English reads “lose” every time. Other reading: no one throws away any life other than
- *τὸ ἀπολλύμενον οὖν ἴσον*: This is a different verb from ἀποβάλλειν: ἀπόλλυσθαι, to perish or be lost. The English reads “perishes” to keep it apart from “lose”, though it could be heard as one more word for the same loss. ἴσον is “equal” throughout the passage. Other reading: so what is being lost is equal too
- *ἀκαριαῖον*: The word means of the shortest possible length, of a hair’s breadth of time. The English gives the noun “an instant” for the adjective. Other reading: shows itself to be momentary
- *ἀνακυκλούμενα*: Literally “being wheeled round again”. The English keeps the circle. Other reading: and recur in cycles
- *ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ*: Literally “in the unlimited”, with “time” understood after the hundred and two hundred years. ἐν with a number of years means over that span, so the English reads “for”; “in a hundred years” would be heard as “a hundred years from now”. Other reading: or for ever
- *εἴπερ γε ἔχει καὶ τοῦτο μόνον*: εἴπερ γε can state a condition (“if indeed”) or a ground taken as agreed (“since”). The English keeps “if indeed”. The subject is unstated and is taken to be the same impersonal “a person” as in the next clause. Other reading: since this is in fact the only thing they have

</details>

### 2.15

That everything is judgment. For what is said in answer to Monimus the Cynic is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὅτι πᾶν ὑπόληψις*: A bare “That …” again, as in 12.22, with no verb of remembering; none is added. From memory, unchecked: Monimus is credited with saying that everything supposed is smoke or vanity, in words built on this same root, and Marcus’s phrase echoes him. Other reading: Remember that all is opinion.
- *τὰ πρὸς τὸν Κυνικὸν Μόνιμον λεγόμενα*: The preposition can mean “to” or “in answer to, against”. It is taken as the replies made to Monimus, which gives the contrast with the next clause: the objections are plain, but so is the use. It can also be the words addressed to him, or more sharply the things said against him. Other reading: what was said to Monimus the Cynic is plain
- *Μόνιμον*: From memory, unchecked: Monimus of Syracuse, a Cynic philosopher of the fourth century BC, a follower of Diogenes. The Cynics were a school known for blunt speech and contempt for convention.
- *τοῦ λεγομένου*: “What is said”, singular: it is taken as Monimus’s saying itself, that everything is judgment, set against the plural “things said” in answer to it. Both are the same Greek participle, which “said” and “saying” let the reader hear. Other reading: the usefulness of what is said
- *τὸ νόστιμον*: A food word. From memory, unchecked, it is used both of what feeds well and of what tastes good, and so of the good part of a thing, the pith. “What is nourishing” keeps a food image and suits the talk of usefulness. Other reading: if one takes the savour of it
- *μέχρι τοῦ ἀληθοῦς*: Literally “up to the true”: the saying is to be taken so far as it is true and no further. Other reading: within the limits of what is true

</details>

### 2.16

The human soul does violence to itself most of all when it becomes, so far as it lies with it, an abscess, a thing standing apart, and a kind of growth on the universe. For to be vexed at anything that happens is a standing apart from nature, in some part of which the nature of each of the other things is contained. Next, when it turns away from some person, or even moves against them with the aim of doing harm, as the souls of angry people do. Third, it does violence to itself when it is beaten by pleasure or by pain. Fourth, when it plays a part and does or says something in a feigned and untrue way. Fifth, when it lets some action or impulse of its own fly at no target, but does anything whatever at random and without attention, when even the smallest things ought to be done with reference to the end. And the end of rational living beings is to follow the reason and law of the oldest city and constitution.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὑβρίζει ἑαυτὴν*: ὑβρίζειν is to treat with insolence or outrage, to maltreat wantonly. The English reads “does violence to”, here and in 2.6, where the same verb is set against τιμῆσαι, “to honour”. Other reading: The human soul dishonours itself
- *ἀπόστημα καὶ οἷον φῦμα τοῦ κόσμου*: ἀπόστημα, the medical word for an abscess, is literally “a thing that has stood apart”, and the next clause explains it with ἀπόστασις, a standing apart or defection. The English gives the one Greek word twice, as “an abscess” and as “a thing standing apart”, so that the reason can be followed. These are not two items in the Greek. Other reading: an abscess and a kind of growth on the universe
- *ἧς ἐν μέρει αἱ ἑκάστου τῶν λοιπῶν φύσεις περιέχονται*: ἐν μέρει with the genitive is taken literally, “in a part of which”: each thing’s nature lies within its own portion of nature as a whole. It can also be read as “as a part”. Other reading: in which the nature of each of the other things is contained as a part
- *ἡδονῆς ἢ πόνου*: πόνος is toil or pain. Set against pleasure, it is taken as pain. Other reading: by pleasure or by hardship
- *ὑποκρίνηται*: The verb of the stage actor: to play a part, and so to pretend. “Plays a part” is kept, as in 9.39b. Other reading: when it pretends
- *οὐδένα σκοπὸν ἀφιῇ*: σκοπός is a target and ἀφιέναι is to let fly, as with an arrow or a spear. The image is kept. Other reading: directs some action or impulse of its own to no aim
- *ἀπαρακολουθήτως*: Literally “without following along”: without keeping track of what one is doing, or without connection to anything. The English takes the first and reads “without attention”. Other reading: inconsequently
- *τῆς πόλεως καὶ πολιτείας τῆς πρεσβυτάτης*: The universe thought of as a city. πρεσβυτάτης is “oldest” and also “most revered”; πολιτεία is the constitution or the community of citizens. The English takes the plain sense of age, and “constitution”, which goes with the “law” that follows. Other reading: the most venerable city and commonwealth
- *λόγῳ καὶ θεσμῷ*: λόγος is “reason” as in the glossary; θεσμός is an old, solemn word for a law laid down. Other reading: the principle and ordinance

</details>

### 2.17

In human life, the time is a point, the substance is in flux, perception is dim, the compound of the whole body is ready to rot, the soul is a whirl, fortune is hard to make out, fame is undiscerning. To put it briefly: everything of the body is a river, everything of the soul is a dream and smoke, life is a war and a stranger’s stay abroad, and fame after death is forgetting. What, then, can escort a person through? One thing and only one: philosophy. And this lies in keeping the spirit within free from abuse and unharmed, stronger than pleasures and pains, doing nothing at random, nothing falsely or with pretense, not needing another person to do something or not do it; and further, accepting what happens and what is allotted as coming from that same place, wherever it is, from which it came itself; and, on top of all this, waiting for death with a cheerful mind, as nothing other than a dissolving of the elements of which every living thing is put together. And if for the elements themselves there is nothing terrible in each one continually changing into another, why should anyone look with suspicion on the change and dissolution of all? For it is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad. At Carnuntum.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἡ δὲ οὐσία ῥέουσα*: οὐσία is the stuff a human being is made of. “In flux” prepares the river in the next sentence. Other reading: its matter is flowing
- *ῥόμβος*: A thing that is whirled round (a top, or a bull-roarer spun on a cord) or the whirling motion itself. “A whirl” covers both. Other reading: the soul is a spinning top
- *ἡ δὲ φήμη ἄκριτον*: ἄκριτος can be active, “not judging”, “undiscerning”, or passive, “not decided”, “not to be judged”. The English takes the first: what people say is said without discernment. Other reading: fame is an uncertain thing
- *ὄνειρος καὶ τῦφος*: τῦφος is literally smoke or vapor, and by extension delusion and empty pride. The image is kept beside “dream”; the same word is “puffed-up pride” in 12.24. Other reading: a dream and a delusion
- *ξένου ἐπιδημία*: A foreigner’s stay in a town that is not his own. Other reading: a visit to a strange land
- *τὸ παραπέμψαι δυνάμενον*: The verb is used of escorting or convoying a traveler. The Greek names no object; “a person” and “through” are supplied. Other reading: What, then, can guide one on the way?
- *τὸν ἔνδον δαίμονα*: δαίμων is a divine being of lower rank than a god; here the divine part allotted to each person. “Spirit” stands for it, as in 5.10b. Other reading: the divinity within
- *ἀνύβριστον*: Not subjected to ὕβρις, which is insult and wanton violence together. “Abuse” covers both. Other reading: unviolated
- *ὅθεν αὐτὸς ἦλθεν*: “It itself” is masculine and is taken of the spirit, which all the words around it describe. It could be the person. Other reading: from which he himself came
- *ἐπὶ πᾶσι*: “On top of all”: the last item of the list. It can also be heard as “above all”, which would rank this item highest. Other reading: and above all
- *ἵλεῳ τῇ γνώμῃ*: The same word as “cheerfully” in 5.33: well disposed, kindly, also cheerful. Other reading: with a serene mind
- *τὴν πάντων μεταβολὴν καὶ διάλυσιν*: “Of all” can be of all the elements, set against “each one” just before, or of all things. The English leaves “all” bare. Other reading: the change and dissolution of all things
- *Τὰ ἐν Καρνούντῳ*: Literally “The things at Carnuntum”, a label and not part of the argument. Carnuntum was a Roman army base on the Danube. From memory, unchecked, editors differ on whether it closes this book or heads the next. Other reading: Written at Carnuntum.

</details>

## Book 3

### 3.1

It is not only this that has to be reckoned with, that life is being used up day by day and a smaller part of it is left. This too has to be reckoned with: if a person were to live longer, this at least is unclear, whether their mind will later on be equal, unchanged, to the understanding of things and of the study that is directed toward close acquaintance with divine and human things. For if a person begins to lose their wits, there will be no lack of breathing, of taking nourishment, of having impressions and impulses, and of everything else of that kind. But making use of oneself, getting every point of duty exact, setting out clearly what appears before one, stopping to consider this very question, whether it is now time to lead oneself out of life, and everything of that kind that needs thoroughly trained reasoning: this is extinguished first. So one must hurry, not only because one comes nearer to death at every moment, but also because the grasp of things and the power to follow them give out first.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *λογίζεσθαι*: λογίζεσθαι, then λογιστέον, and further on the noun λογισμοῦ are one family of words (to reckon, to reason). The English reads “reckoned with” for the two verbs and “reasoning” for the noun, so the link is only half kept. Other reading: It is not only this that one must reason about
- *ὁμοία αὖθις*: αὖθις is “later on” or “again”, and ὁμοία is “the same, alike”, said of the mind. The English reads “later on” and “unchanged”. Other reading: whether their mind will again be equal to it in the same way
- *ἡ διάνοια*: The glossary gives “thought” for διάνοια and allows “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty that may fail with age, so the English reads “mind”. Other reading: whether their thought will later on be equal
- *πρὸς τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ τῆς θεωρίας*: τῆς θεωρίας is in the genitive, so as the Greek stands it depends on σύνεσιν together with τῶν πραγμάτων: understanding of things and of the study. An accusative would make the study a second thing the mind must be equal to, and editors have doubted the case (from memory, unchecked). The English keeps the genitive as given. Other reading: equal to understanding things and to the study that is directed toward close acquaintance with divine and human things
- *ἐμπειρίαν*: ἐμπειρία is familiarity won by experience and practice, not knowledge in the abstract. The English reads “close acquaintance”. Other reading: toward experience of divine and human things
- *παραληρεῖν ἄρξηται*: παραληρεῖν is to talk beside the point, as in delirium or senility; the English gives the sense, “lose their wits”. The subject is not stated: it can be the person, as the English has it, or the mind, the nearest noun. Other reading: For if it begins to wander
- *διαπνεῖσθαι*: Literally “to be breathed through”. It can mean plain breathing or the wider passing of air and vapour through the body and its skin. The English keeps the plain word. Other reading: transpiring
- *τοὺς τοῦ καθήκοντος ἀριθμοὺς ἀκριβοῦν*: Literally “to make exact the numbers of duty”. In Stoic speech a duty (τὸ καθῆκον, what is fitting to do) has “numbers”, the separate points that must all be met for the act to be complete. The English reads “every point” for “the numbers”. Other reading: getting the numbers of duty exact
- *τὰ προφαινόμενα διαρθροῦν*: διαρθροῦν is to divide by joints, to set out part by part. τὰ προφαινόμενα is “the things that show themselves”, which can be what comes into view in general or first appearances in particular. Other reading: analysing first appearances part by part
- *ἐξακτέον αὑτὸν*: Literally “one must lead oneself out”, the Stoic expression for leaving life by one’s own act. “Of life” is added so that the English says what is meant, and “must now” is turned into “it is now time to”. Other reading: whether one must now lead oneself out
- *λογισμοῦ συγγεγυμνασμένου πάνυ χρῄζει*: πάνυ, “very”, stands between the participle and the verb and can go with either. The English takes it with the participle: “thoroughly trained”. Other reading: that very much needs trained reasoning
- *προαποσβέννυται*: The image is of a flame going out beforehand. “First” stands for the prefix προ-, before the other functions or before death; the Greek does not say which. προαπολήγειν in the last sentence has the same prefix and reads “first” there too. Other reading: is extinguished beforehand

</details>

### 3.2

One should also take note of things like this: that even what comes about on top of the things that come about by nature has something graceful and attractive about it. For example, when bread is baking, some parts of it break open at the side; and so these parts too, which stand open like this and are in a way contrary to what the baker’s craft sets out to do, somehow look right and stir up an eagerness for the food in a way of their own. Again, figs gape open when they are at their ripest; and in olives ripened on the tree, the very nearness to rotting adds a certain beauty of its own to the fruit. And ears of grain bending down, and the frown on the lion’s brow, and the foam running from the mouths of wild boars, and many other things are far from good-looking if one looks at them by themselves; and yet, because they come as consequences of the things that come about by nature, they help to adorn them and they charm the mind. So if someone has a deeper feeling for, and understanding of, the things that come about in the whole, there is almost nothing, even among the things that happen as consequences, that will not seem to that person to be put together in a way that somehow gives pleasure. And that person will look even at the real gaping jaws of wild animals with no less pleasure than at all those that painters and sculptors show in imitation; and will be able to see a kind of prime and ripeness in an old woman and an old man, and to see with their own chaste eyes the seductive charm of the young. And many such things, which will not convince everyone, will strike only the one who has become truly at home with nature and its works.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὰ ἐπιγινόμενα*: Literally “the things that come about on top of” the works of nature, what arises in addition to them: side effects, by-products. The English keeps “come about” for both halves of the phrase, as the Greek repeats one verb. “By-products” is avoided because it brings in a workshop the Greek does not have here. Other reading: even the by-products of the things that come about by nature
- *παρὰ τὸ ἐπάγγελμα τῆς ἀρτοποιίας*: ἐπάγγελμα is what a craft professes or promises to deliver. παρά here can be “contrary to” or, more mildly, “beside, outside”. The English reads “contrary to what the baker’s craft sets out to do”. Other reading: in a way outside what the art of baking professes
- *ἐπιπρέπει πως*: The verb ranges from “are conspicuous” to “are becoming, suit”. The English takes the second, since the point is that they please. Other reading: somehow catch the eye
- *κέχηνε*: “Gape” is kept here because the same root returns below in χάσματα, the “gaping jaws” of the wild animals. Other reading: figs split open when they are at their ripest
- *δρυπεπέσιν*: A rare word for fruit ripened on the tree, fully ripe; a related form means “ready to drop from the tree”. The English keeps the literal “ripened on the tree”. Other reading: in olives ripe enough to drop
- *ἐπισκύνιον*: The word names the skin above the eyes that is drawn down in a frown, and so the frown itself. The English gives the part and the look together, without a separate adjective. Other reading: the skin of the lion’s brow
- *συῶν*: The word covers pigs and wild boars alike. Foam at the mouth points to the wild animal, so the English reads “wild boars”. Other reading: the foam running from the mouths of pigs
- *ἐπακολουθεῖν συνεπικοσμεῖ καὶ ψυχαγωγεῖ*: ἐπακολουθεῖν is literally “follow upon”, and the school phrase κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν in the next sentence is “by way of following upon”; “consequences” is used in both places so that the link can be heard. Neither of the next two verbs has an expressed object: the first is “join in adorning”, where the English supplies “them”, and the second is literally “lead the soul”, said of anything that attracts or entertains, where the English supplies “the mind”. Other reading: because they follow upon the things that come about by nature, they add to the adornment and draw the soul
- *πάθος καὶ ἔννοιαν βαθυτέραν*: πάθος is usually a bad “passion” in Stoic writing; here it is neutral, a sensitivity or feeling. “Deeper” agrees in form with the nearer noun only, but an adjective placed after two nouns can cover both, and the English takes it so. Other reading: a feeling for the things that come about in the whole, and a deeper understanding of them
- *ἡδέως πως διασυνίστασθαι*: The verb is very rare and its exact sense is uncertain: “to be constituted, to hold together”, possibly “to present itself”. ἡδέως (“with pleasure”) could describe how the thing is composed or how it strikes the viewer. “Pleasure” is kept because the same adverb returns in the next sentence. Other reading: that will not seem to that person to present itself in a somehow pleasant way
- *ἀκμήν τινα καὶ ὥραν*: ὥρα is “season”, and so the bloom of a person at their best; it echoes ὡραιότατα (“ripest”) used of the figs above. “Ripeness” keeps that echo. Other reading: a kind of prime and bloom
- *τὸ ἐν παισὶν ἐπαφρόδιτον τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ σώφροσιν ὀφθαλμοῖς*: ἐπαφρόδιτον has Aphrodite in it: charm of the kind that draws desire, which is why the eyes are called σώφρονες, “self-controlled, chaste”. παισίν can be “boys”, “children” or the young in general, and the English keeps the wide word. The Greek has one verb for all three things seen, with the eyes placed next to this last one; the English repeats “see” so that the eyes stay beside it. Other reading: and will be able to see, with eyes that keep their self-control, a kind of prime and ripeness in an old woman and an old man, and the alluring charm of boys
- *οὐ παντὶ πιθανά*: Literally “not persuasive to everyone”: things that not everyone would find believable or appealing. The verb that follows (προσπεσεῖται) is “will fall upon, will occur to”; the English reads “will strike”. Other reading: many such things, not credible to everyone, will occur only to the one who
- *γνησίως ᾠκειωμένῳ*: The verb is from the Stoic term for coming to treat something as one’s own or as kin (οἰκείωσις). “At home with” keeps the household image in the word. Other reading: who has genuinely made nature and its works their own

</details>

### 3.3

Hippocrates, after curing many illnesses, fell ill himself and died. The Chaldaeans foretold the deaths of many, and then what was fated caught up with them too. Alexander and Pompey and Gaius Caesar, after so many times wiping out whole cities completely and cutting down in battle many tens of thousands of horsemen and foot soldiers, one day went out of life themselves as well. Heraclitus, after saying so much as a student of nature about the burning up of the universe, was filled inside with water and died smeared with cow dung. Lice killed Democritus, and other lice killed Socrates. What of this? You went on board, you sailed, you came to harbour: get off. If to another life, nothing is empty of gods there either. And if in a state without sensation, you will stop putting up with pains and pleasures and being a slave to a vessel that is so much worse than the thing that serves it: for the one that serves is mind and divine spirit, the other earth and gore.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *οἱ Χαλδαῖοι*: The Chaldaeans of Babylon, the name by which astrologers in general were known. Other reading: The astrologers
- *Γάιος Καῖσαρ*: Julius Caesar, here called by his first name and the name Caesar. Other reading: Julius Caesar
- *περὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ἐκπυρώσεως τοσαῦτα φυσιολογήσας*: φυσιολογεῖν is to give a natural philosopher’s account of things, and the English reads “saying so much as a student of nature”. ἐκπύρωσις is the turning of the universe into fire. Other reading: after so much speculation on the conflagration of the universe
- *ὕδατος τὰ ἐντὸς πληρωθείς*: Literally “filled with water as to his insides”, that is, dropsy. The water is kept because of the contrast with the fire he wrote about. Other reading: swollen with dropsy
- *ἄλλοι φθεῖρες*: “Other lice”: the men who brought Socrates to his death are called vermin. The image is kept and nothing is added to explain it. Other reading: and vermin of another sort killed Socrates
- *τί ταῦτα*: Two words, “what [are] these things?”: what do they come to, why list them. Other reading: Why these things?
- *κατήχθης*: “You were brought in to land”, the regular word for a ship putting in. Other reading: you have come to shore
- *ἐν ἀναισθησίᾳ*: Neither branch has a verb: “if to another life”, “if in absence of sensation”. The first has “to” (ἐφ’) and this one “in”. The English keeps both prepositions and supplies no verb. Other reading: If you go on to another life … and if into unconsciousness
- *λατρεύων*: λατρεύειν is to be in service or in bondage to something. The English reads “being a slave to” so that it is not taken for the different verb behind “the thing that serves it” (τὸ ὑπηρετοῦν) just after. Other reading: and serving a vessel
- *ἤπερ ἐστὶ τὸ ὑπηρετοῦν*: As given, “than is that which serves”: the vessel (the body) is so much worse than what serves it (the mind). The clause is tight, and editors have altered it (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: a vessel as much worse as the thing that serves it is better
- *τὸ μὲν γὰρ νοῦς καὶ δαίμων*: The Greek has only “the one … the other”, and the first is the thing that serves, just named. “That serves” is added to “the one” so that the sentence cannot be read with the vessel as mind. Other reading: for the one is mind and divine spirit, the other earth and gore
- *δαίμων*: The daimon: the divine spirit assigned to each person, here set beside mind as the same thing. “Divine” is added to keep it from sounding like a ghost. Other reading: mind and the god within
- *λύθρος*: Blood mixed with dirt, the filth of a battlefield. “Gore” is used here and in 8.37. Other reading: earth and filthy blood

</details>

### 3.4

Do not wear away the part of your life that is left in impressions about other people, when you are not referring them to something of common benefit (for in truth you are deprived of other work). That is, forming impressions of what so-and-so is doing, and for what purpose, and what they are saying, and what they have in mind, and what they are contriving, and all such things as make you wander away from watching over your own ruling part. So you must avoid, in the chain of your impressions, even what is random and to no purpose, but far the most what is meddling and malicious. And you must accustom yourself to form only those impressions about which, if someone suddenly asked, “What are you thinking now?”, you would answer at once and frankly, “This, and this”; so that from them it would be plain straight away that everything is simple and kindly and belongs to a social animal, one that cares nothing for imaginings of pleasure or of enjoyment in general, or for any rivalry, or envy and suspicion, or anything else that you would blush to explain you had in your mind. For a man of this kind, who no longer puts off being, so to speak, among the best already, is a kind of priest and servant of the gods. He also makes use of what is enshrined within him, which makes the person unstained by pleasures, unwounded by any pain, untouched by any insult, insensible to any wickedness, an athlete in the greatest contest, the contest not to be thrown by any passion, dyed deep in justice, welcoming with his whole soul everything that happens and is dealt out, and not often, nor without a great need that serves the common benefit, forming an impression of what another person is saying or doing or thinking. For it is only what is his own that he has for his activity, and what is spun for him out of the whole he thinks of without a break; and the first he makes fine, and the second he is convinced are good. For the lot dealt to each person is carried along with them and carries them along with it. He remembers too that everything rational is kin, and that to care for all human beings is in keeping with the nature of a human being, but that the good opinion to hold on to is not that of everyone, but only of those who live in agreement with nature. As for those who do not live so, he keeps in mind all the time what sort of people they are at home and outside the house, by night and by day, and what they are like and with what kind of people they are mixed up. So he sets no store either by praise that comes from such people, who are not even pleased with themselves.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐν ταῖς περὶ ἑτέρων φαντασίαις*: The passage runs on one root: φαντασία, with its verb φαντάζομαι. The English keeps “impression” and “form an impression” throughout, though in plain speech the sense is close to picturing or imagining what others are up to. Other reading: in imaginings about other people
- *ἤτοι γὰρ ἄλλου ἔργου στέρῃ*: ἤτοι normally opens an “either … or”, and no “or” follows, so the parenthesis does not construe as given and the text is doubted (from memory, unchecked: some editors mark a gap or change the particle). The English takes the particle as an emphatic “in truth”. στέρῃ is “you are deprived of”, “you go without”. Other reading: for either you are being deprived of some other work, [or …]
- *καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα ποιεῖ ἀπορρέμβεσθαι*: The English takes ὅσα as the relative that joins the list to the verb, “all such things as make you wander away”; “you” is supplied. The list can also be ended at “and all such things”, with “makes” said of the whole habit. Other reading: and everything of that kind: this makes you stray from watching over your own ruling part
- *ἐθιστέον ἑαυτὸν*: The Greek is impersonal here and at χρὴ just before (“one must”), and turns to the second person in the same sentence (“you would answer”). Marcus often uses ἑαυτόν for “yourself”, and the English has “you” throughout so that the sentence holds together. Other reading: And one must accustom oneself
- *ὅτι τὸ καὶ τό*: Literally “this and that”, standing for a definite content that could be named. In English of today “this and that” is a vague answer, so the English has “This, and this”. Other reading: “Such and such”
- *φαντασμάτων*: φάντασμα is the thing imagined, a figment, not the φαντασία (“impression”) of the rest of the passage, so the English gives it a different word, “imaginings”. Other reading: impressions of pleasure or of enjoyment in general
- *φιλονεικίας*: The word is love of strife or, by the spelling that became confused with it, love of winning. “Rivalry” covers both. Other reading: any love of quarrelling
- *τὸ ὡς ἐν ἀρίστοις ἤδη εἶναι*: Literally “the being already as among the best”. The ὡς softens the claim (“so to speak”); it could also be heard as “being as one of the best is”. Other reading: who no longer puts off taking his place now among the best
- *τῷ ἔνδον ἱδρυμένῳ αὐτῷ*: ἱδρύω is the verb for setting up a statue, altar or shrine, which carries on the image of the priest: what is “set up” within him is the god in him, which Marcus elsewhere calls the δαίμων. “Enshrined” keeps the image; the Greek does not name what it is. Other reading: that which is seated within him
- *πάσης ὕβρεως ἀνέπαφον*: ὕβρις is outrage or insolence. It can be insult done to him, which cannot reach him, or insolence of his own, which he is free of. The English takes it as what is done to him, in line with “unwounded” before it. Other reading: untouched by any arrogance
- *πρὸς ἐνέργειαν † ἔχει*: The edition marks the text as corrupt at this point with a dagger, so the wording is uncertain. The English gives the words as they stand: only his own things he “has” “for activity”. Other reading: For he keeps only his own affairs in view for action
- *συνεμφέρεταί τε καὶ συνεμφέρει*: The same rare verb in the passive and the active: the lot “is carried along with” and “carries along with”. Neither verb has its companion expressed; the English supplies the person, the only one the sentence names (“each”). There may also be a play on συμφέρει, “is good for”. Other reading: is borne along with the whole and bears the person along with it
- *δόξης*: δόξα is opinion, here the opinion others hold of one, reputation. The English has “good opinion” so that the contrast (that of everyone, or only that of those who live by nature) stays clear. Other reading: but that the reputation to cling to is not the one that comes from everyone
- *φύρονται*: φύρω is to mix, knead or muddle; of people, to mix with others in a disorderly way, with a tone of dirt. The English keeps “mixed up”. Other reading: what they are like and what sort of company they wallow in

</details>

### 3.5a

Do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. Do not let elegance dress up your thought. Do not be a person of many words or a busybody. Further, let the god in you be the guardian of a living being that is male, old, engaged in public affairs, a Roman and a ruler, who has set himself in order, as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released, needing neither an oath nor any human being as witness.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀκοινώνητος*: The negative of the word the glossary gives as “social”: acting without regard for the community one belongs to. “Unsocially” keeps the tie with “social actions” in 6.30a. Other reading: or without regard for the common good
- *ἀνεξέταστος*: Literally “unexamined”. Said of the one acting, it can mean without having examined the matter, or without having examined oneself. The object is left open. Other reading: or without having examined yourself
- *ἀνθελκόμενος*: Literally “dragged in the opposite direction”: acting while something in you pulls against the act. Other reading: or with reluctance pulling against you
- *κομψεία*: Elegance, cleverness, prettiness in general. Fine wording is probably meant, since it is said to dress up thought and the next clause is about many words, but the Greek does not say so and the English keeps the general word. Other reading: Do not let fine phrasing dress up your thought.
- *μήτε πολυρρήμων μήτε πολυπράγμων*: Two matching words, “many-worded” and “many-doinged”. The second is the usual Greek word for a meddler, and “busybody” gives that sense; the match between the two words is lost in English. Other reading: Do not be a person of many words or of many doings.
- *ὁ ἐν σοὶ θεὸς*: “The god in you” is literal. It means the divine part in a person, which Marcus elsewhere calls the guardian spirit or the ruling part; the Greek here says only “god”. Other reading: the god within you
- *προστάτης*: One who stands in front of or over another: a protector, patron or one in charge. The English reads “guardian”. Other reading: let the god in you be in charge of a living being
- *πρεσβύτου*: The word is “old man”, a man well on in years. How old it claims the writer is cannot be fixed. Other reading: an elder
- *πολιτικοῦ*: The word is not the noun for a citizen but an adjective, “of the city, taking part in its affairs”: a statesman, or a being made for life in a community. The English reads “engaged in public affairs”. Other reading: made for civic life
- *ἀνατεταχότος ἑαυτόν*: Literally “having ordered (or drawn up) himself”. It may be a military picture, in keeping with the signal that follows. The verb is unusual in this use, and the text has been doubted here (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: who has taken up his post
- *τὸ ἀνακλητικὸν*: The army’s trumpet signal that recalls troops from the field. “To withdraw from life” translates the Greek “out of life”. Other reading: waiting for the recall to be sounded from life
- *εὔλυτος*: Literally “easily loosed”, like something lightly tied: with nothing to hold him back. Other reading: unencumbered

</details>

### 3.5b

And let there be cheerfulness within, and no need of service from outside, and no need of the quiet that others provide. So one must be upright, not set upright.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐνέστω δὲ*: The passage starts in the middle of a chapter. The verb is “let there be in”, and what it is to be in is not in the Greek given. The English has “within” and supplies no “you”. Other reading: And let there be in you
- *τὸ φαιδρὸν*: Literally “the bright”, of a face or a mood: cheerful, beaming. Other reading: brightness
- *τῆς ἔξωθεν ὑπηρεσίας*: The noun is service or help done by another. The adjective before it is “not needing in addition”, given as “no need of” both times it occurs. Other reading: needing no help from outside
- *ἡσυχίας*: Quiet, rest or peace. The English takes “quiet”, a calm that depends on other people leaving one alone. Other reading: the peace that others give
- *ὀρθὸν οὖν εἶναι χρή, οὐχὶ ὀρθούμενον*: A play on one word: “upright” and “being made upright” by something else. The verb is to set upright or straighten, and its form here also allows being kept upright, propped. The Greek is impersonal, so “one”. Other reading: So one must be upright, not held upright

</details>

### 3.6

If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage, and, in a word, than your thought being content with itself in the things where it has you acting according to right reason, and in fate, in the things that are allotted without your choosing; if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best. But if nothing appears better than the spirit itself that is seated in you, which has put its own impulses under itself, which examines the impressions, which has pulled itself away, as Socrates used to say, from the feelings of the senses, and has put itself under the gods, and cares for human beings; if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else. Once you have tipped and turned aside toward anything else, you will no longer be able, without being pulled about, to honor above all else that good which is proper to you and is yours. For it is not permitted that anything whatever of a different kind, such as praise from the many, or offices, or wealth, or the enjoyment of pleasures, should take up a position against the rational and civic good. All these, even if for a little while they seem to fit, suddenly take control and carry you off course. But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it. “But the better is what benefits.” If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so, and guard your verdict without conceit. Only see that you make the examination without slipping.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὴν διάνοιάν σου*: διάνοια is the thinking faculty here. The glossary’s “thought” is kept so that the word matches 3.7, where it stands beside νοῦς (“mind”). Other reading: your mind being content with itself
- *καὶ ἐν τῇ εἱμαρμένῃ ἐν τοῖς ἀπροαιρέτως ἀπονεμομένοις*: The Greek as given has ἐν, “in”, before “fate”, and the English follows it: the thought is content with itself in two fields, where it acts by right reason and, in fate, where things are allotted without choice. Without that ἐν the words mean “content with fate”, with fate as the partner of “itself”. From memory, unchecked: editors print the text without it. Other reading: and content with fate in the things that are allotted without your choosing
- *τοῦ ἀρίστου εὑρισκομένου ἀπόλαυε*: εὑρισκομένου is a present participle, “being found”, and answers “if you find” at the start, so the English keeps the finding open. It can also be heard as a finished event. Other reading: enjoy the best thing, now that it is found
- *αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἐνιδρυμένου ἐν σοὶ δαίμονος*: δαίμων is a divine being; here it is the divine part housed in each person, which Marcus elsewhere equates with mind and reason. “Spirit” is used for it throughout this section. ἐνιδρυμένου is the word for a god’s statue or shrine set up in a place, so “seated” is weaker than the Greek. Other reading: the god itself that has its shrine in you
- *τῶν αἰσθητικῶν πείσεων*: πεῖσις here is from πάσχω, “what is undergone”, not from πείθω, “persuasion”: what the senses are made to feel. From memory, unchecked: the saying of Socrates is a loose recollection of Plato’s Phaedo, where the soul is told to withdraw from the senses, and not an exact quotation. Other reading: from the affections of the senses; or, on the other derivation, from the persuasions of the senses
- *πρὸς ὃ ῥέψας ἅπαξ καὶ ἀποκλίνας*: ῥέπω is the tipping of a scale pan and ἀποκλίνω a leaning off to one side; the image is a balance, and both verbs go with “toward which”. The Greek is a relative clause on “nothing else”; the English begins a new sentence and writes “anything else” for the relative. Other reading: toward which, once you have inclined and turned aside, you will no longer be able
- *ἀπερισπάστως*: Literally “without being dragged around”, that is, without distraction. It can go with “be able” or with “honor above all”; the sense is the same. Other reading: to honor undistracted
- *τὸ ἴδιον καὶ τὸ σόν*: Two words for one thought: ἴδιον is what belongs to a being as its own and no other’s, σόν is simply “yours”. The English reads “proper to you” for the first so that the pair does not say the same thing twice. Other reading: that good which is your own and yours
- *ἀντικαθῆσθαι γὰρ τῷ λογικῷ καὶ πολιτικῷ ἀγαθῷ οὐ θέμις*: ἀντικαθῆσθαι is to sit over against, used of an army encamped opposite another. θέμις is what divine law allows, so “not permitted” is still weaker than the Greek. Other reading: For it is not lawful that anything of another kind should sit encamped against the good of a rational being and a citizen
- *πολιτικῷ*: πολιτικός means “of a citizen, made for life in a city”. “Civic” is used for it throughout this section to keep it apart from κοινωνικός, “social”. Other reading: the good of a rational being and a citizen
- *ἑτερογενές, οἷον*: In the Greek the examples follow “of a different kind” at the end of the clause. The English moves the whole phrase before the verb so that the examples are not read as examples of the good. Other reading: For it is not permitted that there should take up a position against the rational and civic good anything whatever of a different kind, such as praise from the many
- *κατεκράτησεν ἄφνω καὶ παρήνεγκεν*: Two aorists of what regularly happens, with no object in the Greek. The English puts them in the present and supplies “you” with the second verb. Other reading: have suddenly prevailed and carried away
- *κρεῖττον δὲ τὸ συμφέρον*: An objection from an imagined speaker, as the edition’s quotation marks show. The Greek names no one who is benefited and the English leaves that open too; “you” in the reply is supplied from the commands that follow. “Benefits” is used and not the glossary’s “is good for”, because this passage also speaks of “the good” (ἀγαθόν) and the two would run together. Other reading: “But the better is what is good for a person.”
- *εἰ μὲν τὸ ὡς λογικῷ, τοῦτο τήρει· εἰ δὲ τὸ ὡς ζῴῳ, ἀπόφηναι*: Very compressed: “if the [benefit] as to a rational [being], keep this; if the one as to an animal, declare”. What is to be declared is not said; the English takes it as an admission that this is the kind of benefit meant. ζῷον is “animal” here because the contrast is with the rational being; in other passages of this section, where no such contrast is drawn, the word is “living being”. Other reading: If it is your benefit as a rational being, watch over it; but if as a living being, declare it
- *ἀτύφως φύλασσε τὴν κρίσιν*: τῦφος is smoke, and so puffed-up delusion or conceit. κρίσις is the deciding or its result; “verdict” keeps it apart from ὑπόληψις, “judgment”, as in 11.16. The clause can also be heard as “keep your judgment free of delusion”. Other reading: and keep your decision without self-deception
- *ἀσφαλῶς τὴν ἐξέτασιν ποιήσῃ*: ἀσφαλῶς is literally “without tripping”: securely, on firm footing. ἐξέτασις, “examination”, is the noun of the verb used above of the spirit that “examines the impressions”. Other reading: Only see that you make the examination securely.

</details>

### 3.7

Never value as a benefit to yourself anything that will one day force you to break faith, to abandon your self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, to desire something that needs walls and curtains. For whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue, does not make a tragedy of things, does not groan, will need neither solitude nor a crowd. Greatest of all, they will live neither pursuing nor fleeing. Whether they will have the use of the soul, enclosed in the body, for a longer stretch of time or a shorter one matters to them not at all. For even if they have to depart this moment, they will go as free of ties as if they were about to do any other of the things that can be done with self-respect and in good order, on their guard through their whole life against this one thing only: that their thought should take any turn foreign to a living being that has mind and is civic.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὡς συμφέρον σεαυτοῦ*: τὸ συμφέρον with a genitive, “an advantage of your own”. The English reads “a benefit to yourself” and not the glossary’s “good for”, so that the word answers the objection that closes 3.6, the chapter before this one in the book: “the better is what benefits”. Other reading: as good for yourself
- *τὴν πίστιν παραβῆναι*: πίστις is trust, good faith, a pledge given. “Break faith” covers both breaking a promise and betraying a trust. Other reading: to break your word
- *τὴν αἰδῶ ἐγκαταλιπεῖν*: αἰδώς is the sense of shame that holds a person back from what is unworthy of them. The English reads “self-respect” and keeps the same word for the adverb αἰδημόνως later in the passage. Other reading: to abandon your sense of shame
- *ὑποκρίνασθαι*: The word for acting on a stage, and so for pretending. Other reading: to be a hypocrite
- *προελόμενος*: προαιρέομαι is to choose one thing in preference to others. The Greek does not say “before everything”. Other reading: has chosen first
- *τὰ ὄργια τῆς τούτου ἀρετῆς*: ὄργια are the secret rites of a mystery cult; the person is pictured as the worshipper of the spirit within. τούτου, “of this one”, is taken as the spirit. ἀρετή is “virtue” or “excellence”. Other reading: the worship of its excellence
- *τραγῳδίαν οὐ ποιεῖ*: Literally “does not compose a tragedy”: does not turn their life into a stage lament. The English keeps the word “tragedy” and supplies “of things”. Other reading: does not play the tragic actor
- *δεήσεται*: The Greek moves from the present (“does not make a tragedy, does not groan”) to the future here and in what follows; the English keeps the shift. Other reading: needs neither solitude nor a crowd
- *οὕτως εὐλύτως ἄπεισιν*: εὐλύτως is “in a way easily loosed”, like something untied without trouble; “free of ties” keeps that picture. Other reading: they will go as easily
- *τροπῇ*: τροπή is a turning or change of direction; literally the thought “comes to be in a turn” that is foreign to such a being. The verb εὐλαβούμενος already means “guarding against”, so the Greek has no “not”. Other reading: that their thought should fall into any condition foreign to
- *νοεροῦ καὶ πολιτικοῦ ζῴου*: νοερός is “of mind” by the glossary, matching νοῦς, “mind”, earlier in the passage, so the English reads “that has mind”. πολιτικός is “civic”, as in 3.6: made for life among fellow citizens. Other reading: a thinking creature and a citizen

</details>

### 3.8

In the mind of someone who has been disciplined and thoroughly cleansed you would find nothing full of pus, nor indeed anything stained, nor anything festering under the skin. Nor does fate overtake their life while it is unfinished, as one might say of a tragic actor who leaves before finishing and playing the play through. And further, nothing slavish, nothing affected, nothing tied to anything, nothing split off, nothing liable to be called to account, nothing lurking in a hole.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐν τῇ διανοίᾳ*: “Mind” for διάνοια, as the glossary allows where the faculty is meant. Other reading: in the thought
- *τοῦ κεκολασμένου καὶ ἐκκεκαθαρμένου*: κολάζω is “check, correct, chastise”, and is also used of cutting plants back. ἐκκαθαίρω is “clean out”, also a medical word for purging, which fits the pus and the wound that follow. The Greek names no one, so “someone … their”. Other reading: of the one who has been chastened and purged
- *ὕπουλον*: Said of a wound that has closed over on top but is unsound beneath. Other reading: sore beneath a scar
- *ἀσυντελῆ τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ ἡ πεπρωμένη καταλαμβάνει*: ἀσυντελής is “incomplete”, taken up by τελέσαι (“finishing”) just after; the word can also mean “contributing nothing”, which is not the sense taken here. ἡ πεπρωμένη is “the fated [share or day]”. Other reading: nor does the appointed hour catch their life incomplete
- *τὸν τραγῳδὸν πρὸ τοῦ τελέσαι καὶ διαδραματίσαι ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι*: τραγῳδός is a performer in tragedy. διαδραματίσαι is a rare word, “to play the drama through”. The Greek construction (“that the actor leaves”) is turned into “who leaves”. Other reading: that the actor in a tragedy goes off before he has completed and acted out the piece
- *ἔτι δὲ οὐδὲν δοῦλον οὐδὲ κομψὸν*: The list has no verb of its own and hangs on “you would find” at the start; the English leaves it without one. κομψόν is “smart, clever, elegant”, here in a bad sense. Other reading: And further you would find nothing servile and nothing showy
- *οὐδὲ προσδεδεμένον οὐδὲ ἀπεσχισμένον*: “Bound to” and “split off from”, and the Greek does not say to or from what: presumably other people or outside things. “To anything” is added only because English cannot leave “tied to” bare. Other reading: nothing dependent, nothing cut off
- *οὐδὲ ὑπεύθυνον οὐδὲ ἐμφωλεῦον*: ὑπεύθυνος is the word for an official who is liable to have his accounts examined, so “liable to be called to account”. ἐμφωλεύω is said of an animal lying hidden in its den. Other reading: nothing that must answer for itself, nothing hiding away

</details>

### 3.9–10

Revere the power of forming judgments. Everything lies in this, that there should no longer arise in your ruling part a judgment that does not follow nature and the constitution of the rational animal. And this promises freedom from haste, affinity with human beings, and following the gods.

So throw everything away and hold on to only these few things; and remember as well that each person lives only this present, an instant. The rest has either been lived or is uncertain. Small, then, is what each person lives, and small the little corner of the earth where they live; small too is even the longest fame after death, and even that is handed down a line of little human beings who will die very soon and who do not know even themselves, let alone someone who died long ago.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὴν ὑποληπτικὴν δύναμιν*: The power that forms a ὑπόληψις, “judgment” in this translation: the faculty of taking a view of things. Other reading: Revere the faculty of opinion
- *ἐν ταύτῃ τὸ πᾶν, ἵνα*: “In this is everything”, then a clause with the word that usually means “so that”. The English takes the clause as spelling out what the “everything” is. It may instead give a purpose. Other reading: Everything lies in this, so that there may no longer arise in your ruling part a judgment
- *ἀνακόλουθος*: “Not following”, “out of line with”. The same root returns at the end of the sentence in “following the gods”, so “follow” stands in both places. Other reading: a judgment inconsistent with nature
- *αὕτη δὲ ἐπαγγέλλεται*: “This” can point back to the constitution of the rational animal, the nearest noun, to nature, or to the power of forming judgments at the start. The English leaves “this” bare, as the Greek does. Other reading: And this power promises
- *ἀπροπτωσίαν*: A Stoic term, literally “not falling forward”: not giving assent to an impression too quickly. Other reading: freedom from rash assent
- *οἰκείωσιν*: A Stoic term for treating something as one’s own, as belonging to one’s household. “Affinity” stands for it, and “kinship” is left for another Greek word in this section. Other reading: a sense of belonging with human beings
- *Πάντα οὖν ῥίψας ταῦτα μόνα τὰ ὀλίγα σύνεχε*: The Greek says “everything”, not “everything else”. As given there is no comma, so “these” could just be taken with “everything” (throw all these away); the sense requires it with “only the few”. Other reading: So let everything else go and keep hold of these few things alone
- *τὸ ἀκαριαῖον*: “The momentary”: the present that lasts an instant. Other reading: this present, which is only a moment
- *ἐν ἀδήλῳ*: Literally “in the unclear”: not visible, not known. Other reading: or lies hidden
- *κατὰ διαδοχὴν ἀνθρωπαρίων*: “By a succession”, as in a relay; “is handed down” stands for a verb the Greek leaves out. The word for human beings is a belittling diminutive. Other reading: and it depends on a relay of poor little people

</details>

### 3.11a

To the precepts already named let one more be added: always to make a definition or outline of the thing that comes up in an impression, so as to see it as it is in its substance, bare, whole and entire, and taken apart, and to say to oneself its own name and the names of the things it was put together from and into which it will be broken up. For nothing so produces greatness of mind as being able to test methodically and truly each of the things that come up in life, and always to look into them in such a way as to take in at the same time what kind of use this thing supplies to what kind of universe, what worth it has in relation to the whole, and what in relation to the human being, who is a citizen of the highest city, of which the other cities are like houses.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *παραστήμασιν*: A rare word: “things that stand by one”, rules or aids kept at one’s side. It refers back to what came before in the book, outside this passage. Other reading: To the aids already named
- *ὅρον ἢ ὑπογραφὴν*: Terms of logic: ὅρος is a strict definition, ὑπογραφή a looser outline or sketch of a thing. Other reading: a definition or description
- *τοῦ ὑποπίπτοντος φανταστοῦ*: φανταστόν is the thing that gives rise to an impression (φαντασία). ὑποπίπτω, “fall under, present itself”, comes again below (ὑποπιπτόντων); “come up” is used for both. Other reading: of the object that presents itself to the mind
- *ὅλον δι’ ὅλων διῃρημένως*: Literally “whole, through wholes, dividedly”. The grouping is open: “whole and entire, and taken apart”, or “taken apart through and through”. Other reading: bare, entire, analysed through and through
- *λέγειν παρ’ ἑαυτῷ*: The whole instruction is impersonal, infinitives after “let there be added”. The English keeps “oneself” and does not have “you”. Other reading: to say to yourself
- *μεγαλοφροσύνης*: “Greatness of mind”, a different word from μεγαλοψυχία, “greatness of soul”, in 5.9. The same sentence comes again at 10.11. Other reading: high-mindedness
- *ὁδῷ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ*: ὁδῷ is “by a road”, that is, in an orderly way, by method; ἀληθείᾳ is “by truth”. Other reading: by method and in truth
- *ὁποίῳ τινὶ τῷ κόσμῳ ὁποίαν τινὰ τοῦτο χρείαν παρεχόμενον*: One packed clause: “this thing, supplying what kind of use to what kind of universe, has what worth”. The English keeps the two “what kind of” questions together and lets the questions of worth follow. Other reading: what worth it has for the whole, given the kind of universe this is and the kind of service the thing does it
- *ὥσπερ οἰκίαι εἰσίν*: οἰκία is a house or household. The section cut falls at the colon after these words and the Greek sentence goes on; the English ends with a full stop. Other reading: are like households

</details>

### 3.11b

What is it, and what is it compounded of, and how long is it in its nature to last, this thing that is now making the impression on me? And what virtue is needed for it: gentleness, for example, courage, good faith, simplicity, self-sufficiency, and the rest? So in each case one must say: this comes from god; this comes by the shared lot, and the spinning and winding together, and this kind of coincidence and chance; and this comes from one of my own tribe, a kinsman and partner, who does not know, however, what is in accordance with nature for them. But I do know. That is why I treat them according to the natural law of partnership, with good will and justly; and yet at the same time, in things that are neither good nor bad, I aim at what accords with worth.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τί ἐστὶ καὶ ἐκ τίνων συγκέκριται*: The part given begins in the middle of a sentence: these are indirect questions that depend on a verb in the part not given. No words are added. The indirect questions are turned into direct ones and made two sentences, and “this thing that is now making the impression on me” is moved to the end of the first. Other reading: [...] what it is, and what it is compounded of, and how long it is in its nature to last, this thing that now makes the impression on me, and what virtue is needed for it
- *πέφυκε παραμένειν*: Literally “is by nature such as to stay”. Other reading: how long is it made to last
- *φαντασίαν*: φαντασία, the Stoic term for the way a thing presents itself to the mind, “impression” in this translation. Other reading: this thing that is now producing an appearance in me
- *πίστεως*: The word covers both trust and trustworthiness. In a list of virtues it is taken as keeping faith. Other reading: trustworthiness / trust
- *ἀφελείας*: Plainness, the absence of show or complication. Other reading: plainness
- *τοῦτο μὲν παρὰ θεοῦ ἥκει*: The three “this” clauses are alternatives: of each thing one says whichever of the three applies. The same Greek can also mean “partly ... partly ... partly”. Other reading: one thing comes from god, another by the shared lot, another from one of my own tribe
- *σύλληξιν*: A rare word, “a drawing of lots together”, given as “the shared lot”. Other reading: by the joint allotment
- *συμμηρυομένην σύγκλωσιν*: Two thread images together: σύγκλωσις is a spinning together, and the participle means “being wound up together”, as thread is wound. The Greek does not say with what. The English joins the two as “the spinning and winding together” and supplies no noun. Other reading: the spinning together that is wound up with the lot
- *σύντευξίν τε καὶ τύχην*: σύντευξις is a falling in with something, a coming together of events; it is from the same root as τύχη, “chance”. “This kind of” may go with both nouns or with the first only. Other reading: this sort of meeting, and chance
- *κοινωνοῦ*: “Partner, one who shares”. It is the same root as κοινωνία below, so the English reads “partner” and “partnership”; “fellow member” and “community” would also be possible. The Greek words for this person are masculine in form but single out no man, so the English refers back with “them”. Other reading: a fellow member ... the natural law of community
- *ἐν τοῖς μέσοις*: τὰ μέσα, literally “the things in the middle”, is the Stoic name for things neither good nor bad in themselves, such as health or money. The English gives the meaning of the term. Other reading: in the things in the middle
- *συστοχάζομαι*: The verb is “I aim at”, with a prefix meaning “together” or “at the same time”. What is aimed at is “what accords with worth”, which may be the value of each thing or what the person deserves. The English leaves that open. Other reading: I aim, together with them, at what each thing is worth

</details>

### 3.12

If you do the work that is present, following right reason, earnestly, vigorously, with good will, and with nothing as a side business, but keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment; if you join this together, waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing, but content with the present work that is according to nature and with heroic truth in what you say and utter, you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ παρὸν ἐνεργῇς*: ἐνεργῇς here and ἐνεργείᾳ below are the same word, verb and noun, and “present” is repeated with them. The English reads “do the work that is present” and “the present work” so that the close is heard picking up the opening. The word is strictly “be active” and “activity”. Other reading: If you are active in what is present
- *καὶ μηδὲν παρεμπόρευμα*: There is no verb in the Greek: literally “and nothing a side-trade”. παρεμπόρευμα is goods dealt in on the side of one’s main trade. The English supplies “with” and “as” and takes the phrase with the doing of the present work; it can also be heard as a first object of “keep”. Other reading: and admit nothing as a sideline
- *τὸν ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονα καθαρὸν ἑστῶτα τηρῇς*: ἑαυτοῦ stands for “your own”, a common late use. δαίμων is “spirit” as in 3.6. ἑστῶτα is “standing”, with no “and” between it and “pure”; it may also be a quality of its own, standing firm or steady. Other reading: keep your own spirit pure and standing firm
- *ἀποδοῦναι*: “To give back” what was lent or entrusted. The Greek does not say to whom. Other reading: as if you had to return it at once
- *ἐὰν τοῦτο συνάπτῃς*: συνάπτω is to fasten or join together, the verb of “joining one good to another” in 12.29. The Greek does not say what is joined to what: it may be the present work and the pure spirit joined to each other, or the practice kept unbroken from one moment to the next. Other reading: if you keep this joined up without a break
- *ἡρωικῇ ἀληθείᾳ*: “Heroic truth” is a strange phrase and is translated as it stands: truthfulness of the kind the heroes of old had. From memory, unchecked: editors have doubted the adjective. Other reading: the truthfulness of a hero
- *εὐζωήσεις*: One word, “you will live well”, in the sense of a good and happy life. Other reading: you will have a happy life

</details>

### 3.13

As doctors always have their instruments and blades at hand for emergency treatments, so have your principles ready for knowing things divine and human, and for doing everything, even the smallest thing, as one who remembers the bond that ties the two to each other. For you will not do any human thing well without referring it at the same time to the divine, nor the other way round.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὰ ὄργανα καὶ σιδήρια*: σιδήρια is “irons”: the surgeon’s iron tools, knives and lancets. Other reading: their instruments and irons
- *πρὸς τὰ αἰφνίδια τῶν θεραπευμάτων*: Literally “for the sudden ones among treatments”. Other reading: for treatments needed suddenly
- *πρὸς τὸ τὰ θεῖα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα εἰδέναι*: “For knowing” governs “things divine and human”; the same “for” is taken to run on to “doing everything”. “Knowledge of things divine and human” was a standing definition of wisdom (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: for understanding divine and human things
- *συναναφορᾶς*: “A referring together”: carrying the human act back to the divine along with it. The root is that of ἀναφοράς in 12.8, where the English has “aims”. Other reading: without relating it to the divine as well
- *οὔτ’ ἔμπαλιν*: “Nor the reverse”: nor anything divine without reference to the human. Other reading: nor the opposite

</details>

### 3.14

Stop wandering. For you are not going to read either your little notebooks or the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks and the extracts from the writings, which you were putting away for yourself for old age. So hurry to the end, and letting go of empty hopes, come to your own rescue, if you care at all about yourself, while it is possible.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μηκέτι πλανῶ*: πλανᾶσθαι is to wander, to stray, and so to be led off the point or be mistaken. Literally “wander no more”. Other reading: Stop going astray
- *ὑπομνημάτιά*: A diminutive of the word for notes or memoranda. It may mean notebooks like this one or other notes he kept; the Greek does not say. Other reading: your own little notes
- *πράξεις*: “Deeds”, as something to be read, so written accounts of them. It may be a collection he had made himself; the English keeps the plain word. Other reading: the histories of the ancient Romans and Greeks
- *τὰς ἐκ τῶν συγγραμμάτων ἐκλογάς*: συγγράμματα are written works, treatises. The Greek says only “the writings” and does not say whose; the authors he read are the likely sense. Other reading: the selections from their books
- *ἃς εἰς τὸ γῆρας σαυτῷ ἀπετίθεσο*: The relative ἃς is feminine plural: what was being put away is the extracts, or the deeds and the extracts together, not the writings, which are neuter. The English “which” after the comma is to be heard the same way. Other reading: all of which you were putting away for your old age
- *σπεῦδε οὖν εἰς τέλος*: τέλος is both “end” and “goal, the aim of life”, and εἰς τέλος can also mean “to completion”. The English reads “the end”, which can be heard as the finish or as the aim. Other reading: So hurry on to your goal
- *σαυτῷ βοήθει*: Literally “help yourself”, the verb for running to someone’s aid. “Help yourself” is avoided because in English it is heard as “take what you like”. Other reading: rescue yourself

</details>

### 3.15–16a

They do not know how many things are meant by “stealing”, by “sowing”, by “buying”, by “being at rest”, by “seeing what must be done”, which is not done with the eyes but with a different kind of sight.

Body, soul, mind. To the body belong sensations, to the soul impulses, to the mind principles.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>
