- *Οὐκ ἴσασι*: “They” are not identified; presumably people in general. Other reading: People do not know
- *πόσα σημαίνει*: Literally “how many things it signifies”: the ordinary words have further senses that are missed. The verb is singular, with each infinitive in turn as its subject. Other reading: how much is meant by
- *τὸ κλέπτειν, τὸ σπείρειν, τὸ ὠνεῖσθαι*: Infinitives with the article, quoted as words. The English puts them in quotation marks as verbal nouns. Other reading: to steal, to sow, to buy
- *τὸ ἡσυχάζειν*: To be quiet, to be at rest, to keep still. Other reading: “keeping quiet”
- *ὃ οὐκ ὀφθαλμοῖς γίνεται*: The neuter relative most naturally picks up the last item, seeing what must be done. It could reach back to the understanding of all these words. Other reading: and this is not a matter for the eyes but for another kind of sight
- *σώματος αἰσθήσεις, ψυχῆς ὁρμαί, νοῦ δόγματα*: Three genitives with no verb; “belong” is supplied. The glossary words are kept: impulse (ὁρμή), mind (νοῦς), principle (δόγμα). Only the opening of 3.16 is given, so the thought is left where the Greek stops. Other reading: Of the body, sensations; of the soul, impulses; of the mind, principles.

</details>

### 3.16b

To be stamped with impressions belongs to cattle as well. To be pulled by the strings of impulse belongs also to wild beasts, and to effeminate men, and to Phalaris and Nero. And to have the mind as leader towards what appear to be the fitting things to do belongs also to those who do not believe in gods, and those who desert their country, and those who do what they do once they have shut the doors. If, then, the rest is shared with those just mentioned, what is left as the good person’s own is to love and welcome the things that happen to them and are spun together for them; and not to muddy the spirit seated within the chest, nor disturb it with a crowd of impressions, but to keep it gracious, following god in good order, neither saying anything contrary to what is true nor doing anything contrary to what is just. And if all people disbelieve that the good person lives simply and modestly and cheerfully, the good person is not angry with any of them, and is not turned aside from the road that leads to the end of life, at which one must arrive pure, quiet, ready to be released, fitted to one’s own portion without being forced.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τυποῦσθαι φανταστικῶς*: Literally “to be stamped in the way of impressions”. The image is a seal pressed into wax; the adverb is from φαντασία, “impression”. Other reading: to receive the imprint of appearances
- *νευροσπαστεῖσθαι ὁρμητικῶς*: The verb is used of puppets worked by strings. The adverb is from ὁρμή, “impulse”. Other reading: to be jerked about like a puppet by impulses
- *ἀνδρογύνων*: Literally “man-women”. In ordinary use it is an insult for men thought unmanly. The English gives the sense and not the literal compound. Other reading: men who are half women
- *Φαλάριδος καὶ Νέρωνος*: Phalaris was a tyrant of Acragas in Sicily, a byword for cruelty; Nero is the Roman emperor. Other reading: a Phalaris or a Nero
- *ἐπὶ τὰ φαινόμενα καθήκοντα*: καθήκοντα is the Stoic term for acts that are fitting or appropriate, often translated “duties”. “Appear” can go with it two ways: things that seem to be fitting, or fitting things as they show themselves. Other reading: towards the duties that present themselves
- *τῶν ποιούντων*: “Those who do”, with no object: the Greek does not say what they do behind shut doors, and a word may have dropped out. “What they do” is supplied by the English and stands for no Greek word; it is chosen because it gives the verb an object without saying what the object is. Editors are believed to supply a word meaning “anything at all” (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: those who do anything at all once they have shut the doors
- *τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ*: Masculine in form, but meaning anyone who is good, so the English reads “the good person” and “them”. In the last sentence the noun is repeated where the Greek has “him” and “he”, so that “them” can stand for the people who disbelieve. Other reading: the good man’s own ... he is not angry with any of them
- *συγκλωθόμενα αὐτῷ*: Literally “being spun together for him” or “with him”, the image of the thread of fate. Other reading: spun into the good person’s thread
- *δαίμονα*: A δαίμων is a divine being below the gods; here it is the divine thing lodged inside a person, which Marcus elsewhere identifies with the mind. The English reads “spirit”. Other reading: the god seated within the chest / the guardian spirit
- *φύρειν*: To mix something so as to foul it, as water is muddied or dough kneaded. Other reading: not to defile / not to confuse
- *ἵλεων*: The word used of a god who is kindly and well-disposed. “Gracious” is used here and for the same word in 2.3; of the spirit within it could also be “serene”. Other reading: to keep it serene
- *κοσμίως ἑπόμενον θεῷ*: This participle and the two after it (“saying”, “doing”) are masculine singular, and can describe either the spirit or the good person who keeps it. The English participles can be taken either way, as in the Greek. Other reading: while the good person follows god in good order, saying nothing contrary to what is true
- *ἀπιστοῦσιν αὐτῷ*: Literally “disbelieve him, that he lives ...”. It could also be “distrust him because he lives ...”. The English takes the first. Other reading: if all people distrust the good person for living simply
- *τὸ τέλος τοῦ βίου*: τέλος is both “end” and “goal”. Here it is where the road arrives and where one must be “ready to be released”, so the end; the other sense may also be heard. Other reading: the goal of life
- *εὔλυτον*: Literally “easily loosed”, like a knot that comes undone without trouble: ready to be let go from life. Other reading: easily set free

</details>

## Book 4

### 4.1

The thing that is master within, when it is in accordance with nature, stands towards what happens in such a way that it always shifts easily to what is possible and given. For it is not fond of any assigned material, but directs its impulse towards the things that come first, with a proviso, and what is brought in instead it makes into material for itself, like fire when it masters the things that fall on it, things by which a small lamp would have been put out. But a bright fire very quickly makes what is heaped on it its own, consumes it, and from those very things rises higher.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὸ ἔνδον κυριεῦον*: Literally “that which is lord within”, another way of naming the ruling part. It is kept distinct from the usual term. Other reading: The ruling power within us
- *ὅταν κατὰ φύσιν ἔχῃ*: Literally “when it is in the state that accords with nature”. Other reading: when it is in its natural state
- *ὕλην γὰρ ἀποτεταγμένην οὐδεμίαν φιλεῖ*: The participle means “marked off, assigned”. The verb is “loves”, and can also mean “is used to”. Other reading: For it does not love any appointed material
- *πρὸς τὰ προηγούμενα*: Literally “towards the things that go in front”: the things it aims at first, as against what is brought in instead. It can also be heard as the Stoic “preferred things”, though the usual word for those is a different participle. “What comes first” is used for this word here and in 7.55 and 5.20. Other reading: towards the things that are to be preferred
- *ὑπεξαιρέσεως*: Literally “an exception made beforehand”: aiming at a thing with the proviso “if nothing prevents”. “Proviso” is used here and in 5.20. Other reading: with reservation
- *τὸ δὲ ἀντεισαγόμενον*: Literally “what is brought in instead”, that is, in place of the thing first aimed at. The prefix can also be heard as “against”: what is brought in to oppose it. Other reading: and whatever is brought in against it it makes into material for itself
- *ἐξῳκείωσεν ἑαυτῷ*: The verb is from the root “one’s own”. The three verbs here are past tenses used for what always happens, so the English puts them in the present. Other reading: has quickly taken over what was heaped on it

</details>

### 4.2

Let no act be done at random, or otherwise than according to a rule that goes to make up the art.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐνέργημα*: Noun and verb are from one root (ἐνέργημα … ἐνεργείσθω), literally “let no activity be acted”. English cannot keep the echo without stiffness. Other reading: Let no action be carried out
- *εἰκῇ*: “At random”, without plan or purpose. Other reading: without a purpose
- *θεώρημα*: A θεώρημα is a rule or proposition belonging to an art. The English reads “rule” and leaves “principle” for δόγμα, as in the glossary. Other reading: according to a principle
- *συμπληρωτικὸν τῆς τέχνης*: Literally “that helps to fill up the art”: a rule that is one of the parts making the art complete. The art is not named; the art of living is presumably meant. Other reading: a rule that completes the art

</details>

### 4.3

People look for retreats for themselves: country places, seashores, mountains. You too are in the habit of longing very much for such things. But all of this is the mark of someone with no training at all, when you are free, at whatever hour you wish, to retreat into yourself. For nowhere that a person retreats to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul, above all for someone who has such things within that, on bending to look into them, they are at once in complete ease; and by ease I mean nothing other than good order. So give yourself this retreat continually, and renew yourself. And let the things be short and elementary which, as soon as they meet you, will be enough to wash away all distress and to send you back without resentment at the things you are returning to. For what will you resent? The badness of people? Think over the conclusion: that rational animals have come to be for the sake of one another, and that forbearance is a part of justice, and that they go wrong against their will, and how many before now, after feuding, suspecting, hating, fighting with spears, have been laid out and turned to ash; and then stop at last. Or will you also resent what is dealt out from the whole? Renew for yourself the either-or, “either providence or atoms”, and all the grounds on which it was proved that the universe is, as it were, a city. Or will the things of the body still touch you? Consider that the mind does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly, once the mind has taken itself back and come to know its own power; and, for the rest, all that you have heard and agreed to about pain and pleasure. Or will petty fame distract you? Look at how fast everything is forgotten, and at the gulf of endless time on either side, and the emptiness of the echo, and how changeable and undiscerning those are who seem to give praise, and the narrowness of the place in which that petty fame is confined. For the whole earth is a point, and how small a corner of it is this dwelling place? And here, how many are there, and what sort of people, who will give the praise? For the rest, then, remember the withdrawal into this little country place of your own; and before everything do not be torn about and do not strain, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal animal. And among the things readiest to hand, which you will bend to look into, let there be these two. One, that things do not touch the soul but stand outside it, unmoving, and disturbances come only from the judgment within. The other, that all these things you see will change in almost no time and will no longer be; and keep thinking of how many things you have yourself already seen change. The universe is alteration; life is judgment.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἰδιωτικώτατόν*: The word is the superlative of the adjective from ἰδιώτης, a private person with no training, here one untrained in philosophy. The English reads “someone with no training at all”, with “at all” for the superlative. Other reading: But all of this is as unphilosophical as can be
- *οὔτε ἡσυχιώτερον οὔτε ἀπραγμονέστερον*: The two comparatives can be adverbs with the verb (“retreats more quietly or with less business”) or describe the place retreated to. The English takes them of the place. Other reading: For nowhere does a person retreat more quietly or with less trouble than into their own soul
- *ἐγκύψας*: The verb is to stoop and peer into something. It comes again near the end of the passage (ἐγκύψεις), and the English has “bend to look into” both times. Other reading: as soon as they look into them
- *τὴν δὲ εὐμάρειαν οὐδὲν ἄλλο λέγω ἢ εὐκοσμίαν*: εὐμάρεια is ease or comfort; εὐκοσμία is orderliness, good behaviour, a well-kept state. Marcus defines the first by the second, so the English keeps two plain nouns. Other reading: and by comfort I mean nothing other than being well ordered
- *πᾶσαν λύπην ἀποκλύσαι*: The English follows the text as given, “wash away all distress”. From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts are not agreed here and some editors print a pronoun (“wash it wholly clean”, of the soul) in place of λύπην, or a verb meaning “shut out”. Other reading: to wash the soul wholly clean
- *τὸ κρῖμα*: κρῖμα is a decision reached, a ruling. The glossary keeps “judgment” for ὑπόληψις, which comes twice later in this passage, so the English has “conclusion” here to keep the two words apart. Other reading: Think over the judgment you have reached
- *ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνουσι*: ἄκοντες is “unwilling”, “not of their own will”; it can also be heard as “without meaning to”. The English keeps the stronger, literal sense, which is the Socratic claim that nobody goes wrong willingly. Other reading: that they go wrong without meaning to
- *ἀνανεωσάμενος τὸ διεζευγμένον*: The Greek has a participle (“having renewed”) with no main verb, as also at ἐννοήσας and ἀπιδὼν below; a verb such as “stop” or “you will not resent it” is understood from the answer before. The English turns all three into commands. τὸ διεζευγμένον is the logicians’ term for an either-or statement, and the verb repeats “renew yourself” above, so “renew” is kept. Other reading: Having called back to mind the disjunction, “either providence or atoms”
- *κινουμένῳ πνεύματι ἡ διάνοια*: πνεῦμα here is the breath that runs through the body and carries sensation; its smooth or rough movement is pleasure or pain. The English keeps “breath”. διάνοια is “thought” in the glossary, but here the faculty is meant (it takes itself back and knows its power), so the English has “mind”. Other reading: that thought does not mingle with the vital spirit, whether its motion is smooth or rough
- *τὸ δοξάριόν*: A diminutive of δόξα, reputation, with a belittling tone. The English has “petty fame”. Other reading: that little bit of reputation
- *τῆς πάντων λήθης*: The genitive πάντων can be the things forgotten (“everything”), the people forgotten (“everyone”) or the people who forget (“how fast everyone forgets”). The English takes it of things. Other reading: how fast everyone is forgotten
- *ἡ κατοίκησις αὕτη*: Literally “this dwelling” or “this habitation”. It can mean the inhabited part of the earth or the particular place where one lives; “this dwelling place” can be heard either way. Other reading: this inhabited part of the earth, or: this place where you live
- *μὴ σπῶ μηδὲ κατεντείνου*: σπῶ is a middle or passive command from σπάω, to pull, wrench or tear: “do not be torn about”, or “do not be convulsed”. κατεντείνου is “do not strain”. The English keeps the image of being pulled apart. Other reading: do not be distracted and do not overstrain yourself
- *τὸ ἀγρίδιον ἑαυτοῦ*: ἀγρίδιον is a little field or small farm; it picks up the “country places” (ἀγροικίας) of the first line, so the English has “little country place”. ἑαυτοῦ is used here for the second person: the place may be one that belongs to you or one that is yourself. Other reading: this little plot that is yourself
- *ἀλλοίωσις*: A different word from the μεταβολή (“change”) just before; it means becoming other. The English has “alteration” so that the two Greek words stay two English words. Other reading: The universe is change; life is opinion.
- *ὁ βίος ὑπόληψις*: Two bare nouns set side by side, like “the universe is alteration” before them. ὑπόληψις is what one takes things to be, the same word as “the judgment within” a few lines above; it does not mean being judged. Other reading: life is what you judge it to be

</details>

### 4.4

If mind is common to us, then reason too, by which we are rational, is common. If that is so, then the reason that commands what is to be done or not done is also common. If that is so, law too is common. If that is so, we are citizens. If that is so, we share in some civic body. If that is so, the universe is, as it were, a city. For in what other common civic body will anyone say that the whole race of human beings shares? And it is from there, from this common city, that our very mind and reason and sense of law come; or from where else? For just as what is earthy in me has been portioned off from some earth, and what is wet from another element, and what is breath from some source, and what is warm and fiery from some source of its own (for nothing comes from nothing, just as nothing goes away into what is not), so too mind has come from somewhere.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ νοερὸν*: Literally “the thing of mind”, the part of us that thinks. “Mind” is used for it throughout this passage. Other reading: If the power to think is common to us
- *λογικοί*: The adjective made from λόγος, “reason”: “having reason”. “Rational” is used, as throughout this translation; the Greek link with “reason” is closer than the English shows. Other reading: by which we are reasoning beings
- *ὁ προστακτικὸς τῶν ποιητέων ἢ μὴ λόγος*: “The reason that gives orders about things to be done or not”: this reads as a school definition of law, which is why “law” follows at once. The Greek leaves “to be done” to be supplied after “or not”. Other reading: the reason that prescribes what we must do and what we must not
- *πολιτεύματός τινος*: πολίτευμα is made from the word for citizen and can mean a constitution, a government, a state, or the body of citizens. “Civic body” is used and kept in the next sentence. Other reading: we share in some kind of state
- *ὁ κόσμος ὡσανεὶ πόλις ἐστί*: κόσμος is the ordered whole of things, “the universe” throughout this translation. ὡσανεί softens the claim: “as if, so to speak”. Other reading: the world is like a city
- *νομικὸν*: Three adjectives under one article, answering to mind, reason and law in the chain above: “the thing in us that is of mind, of reason and of law”. νομικόν is literally “having to do with law”; “sense of law” marks that it is the capacity in us, not law itself, which was an earlier step. Other reading: the very thing in us that thinks, reasons and keeps law
- *τὸ πνευματικὸν ἀπὸ πηγῆς τινος*: πνευματικόν is “what is of breath or wind”. “From some source” is oddly vague beside “from some source of its own” in the following phrase, and the words have been doubted (from memory, unchecked). The English translates what stands. Other reading: the airy part from some spring
- *ἥκει ποθέν*: ἥκω is a present with perfect sense: “has come, is here”. Other reading: comes from somewhere

</details>

### 4.5

Death is the same kind of thing as birth, a mystery of nature: a combining out of the same elements, a dissolving into the same. And in short, it is not a thing anyone would be ashamed of: for it is not contrary to what follows in sequence for a living being with mind, nor contrary to the reason on which it is built.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *οἷον γένεσις*: γένεσις is both “birth” and “coming to be” in general. Set beside death, it is taken as “birth”. Other reading: such a thing as coming into being
- *φύσεως μυστήριον*: μυστήριον is a secret rite, as in the mystery cults, not just a puzzle. “Mystery” is kept and the religious sense is left to this note. Other reading: one of nature’s secret rites
- *σύγκρισις ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν στοιχείων, εἰς ταὐτὰ λύσις*: It is open whether both nouns describe both events, or the combining is birth and the dissolving is death. The two phrases are left side by side as the Greek has them. From memory, unchecked: the wording of this clause is disputed and part of it may be an editor’s repair; the English translates what is printed. Other reading: the one a combining out of certain elements, the other a dissolving into those same elements
- *ὅλως δὲ*: A phrase that sums up: “in general”, “on the whole”, “in short”. With the “not” that follows it could also be heard as “not at all”. Other reading: and on the whole; and it is not at all a thing anyone would be ashamed of
- *αἰσχυνθείη*: “Would be ashamed.” It is not obvious why death should be a matter of shame, and one might expect “distressed”. The English translates the word that stands. Other reading: not a thing to be embarrassed by
- *παρὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῷ νοερῷ ζῴῳ*: τὸ ἑξῆς is “what follows in sequence”: death is the next step in the series for such a being. The dative could also depend on ἑξῆς itself, giving “what follows from being such a creature”. νοερός is “of mind” in the glossary; “with mind” makes an English phrase. Other reading: not at odds with what follows from being a creature of mind
- *τὸν λόγον τῆς κατασκευῆς*: λόγος is kept as “reason”, as in the glossary, though here it is close to “plan” or “rationale”; “principle” is avoided because this translation keeps that word for δόγμα. κατασκευή is the way a thing is constructed, and “it” is supplied. Other reading: the plan of its makeup; the principle of its construction

</details>

### 4.6

It is the nature of these things to be done in this way by people of this kind, of necessity; and whoever does not want this wants the fig tree to have no sap. But in general remember this: that within a very short time both you and this man will be dead, and a little later not even your names will be left.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ταῦτα οὕτως ὑπὸ τῶν τοιούτων*: The passage does not say what things or which people: some conduct of a certain kind of person is in view. τοιούτων can be masculine (such people) or neuter (such things). People is taken, because of “this man” below, and the preposition then marks them as the doers. Other reading: These things naturally come about in this way from such causes
- *ὀπὸν*: The milky, acrid juice of the fig tree. Other reading: wants the fig tree to have no juice
- *οὗτος*: “This one”, masculine: the particular person whose behaviour started the thought. Other reading: both you and he
- *οὐδὲ ὄνομα ὑμῶν*: Singular in the Greek, “not even a name of you two”. English wants the plural. Other reading: not even a name of yours will remain

</details>

### 4.7–9

Take away the judgment, and “I have been harmed” is taken away. Take away “I have been harmed”, and the harm is taken away.

What does not make a human being worse than they were does not make their life worse either, and does not harm them either from outside or from within.

The nature of what is beneficial is bound by necessity to do this.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἦρται τὸ βέβλαμμαι*: The article turns the first-person verb into a quoted thing, so it stands in quotation marks. ἦρται is a perfect: the thing “has been taken away” at once. Other reading: and the thought “I am hurt” is gone
- *χείρω αὐτὸν ἑαυτοῦ*: Literally “worse than himself”: worse than he was. “They” is used for ἄνθρωπος. Other reading: does not make a man worse than himself
- *οὔτε ἔξωθεν οὔτε ἔνδοθεν*: “Neither from outside nor from inside”: the Greek gives no object for “harm”; “them” is supplied. Other reading: nor does it do harm, outwardly or inwardly
- *ἡ τοῦ συμφέροντος φύσις*: Literally “the nature of the beneficial”. The glossary has “is good for” for συμφέρει; with no object here the English has “what is beneficial”. It may be a roundabout way of saying “what is beneficial, by its nature”. Other reading: What is good for the whole is, by its nature
- *Ἠνάγκασται*: A perfect passive: “has been compelled”. Other reading: has been forced
- *τοῦτο ποιεῖν*: “To do this”: the Greek does not say what “this” is. It may look back to the chapter before or to whatever has just happened. Other reading: to bring this about

</details>

### 4.10

That “everything that happens, happens justly”. If you watch closely, you will find it so. I do not mean only according to the order in which one thing follows another, but that it is according to what is just, and as if by someone handing out what accords with worth. So keep watching, as you have begun, and whatever you do, do it with this: with being good, in the sense in which the good person is properly understood. Keep this in every action.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὅτι*: The chapter opens with “that”, as a note of a point to hold on to, with no main verb. The quotation marks are the editor’s. Other reading: Remember that everything that happens, happens justly
- *δικαίως*: “Justly”, and also more loosely “rightly”. The explanation that follows (“according to what is just”) shows the strict sense is meant. Other reading: happens rightly
- *παραφυλάσσῃς*: “To keep watch beside”, to observe closely. It comes again as a command below and “watch” is used for both. Other reading: if you observe carefully
- *κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς*: Literally “according to the next-in-order”, that is, as one thing follows from another. The same “according to” then governs “what is just”. Other reading: not only in the order of cause and effect
- *ὑπό τινος ἀπονέμοντος*: Literally “as it would be by someone distributing what accords with worth”. “Worth” can be what each deserves; the Greek has no “to each”. Other reading: as if by someone who gives each what they deserve
- *καθὸ νενόηται ἰδίως ὁ ἀγαθός*: Literally “in the way the good one has been conceived in the particular sense”. ἰδίως is taken as “in the strict, proper sense of the word”. ὁ ἀγαθός is masculine in form but means anyone who is good. Other reading: in the special sense in which a person is thought of as good
- *σῷζε*: “Keep safe, preserve”. Other reading: Hold on to this in everything you do

</details>

### 4.11

Do not judge things to be such as the person who abuses you decides they are, or wants you to decide they are, but see them as they are in truth.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὑπολάμβανε*: The verb of the glossary’s “judgment” word, so “judge”. The Greek has no noun for what is judged (“such things as …”); “things” is supplied. Other reading: Do not take things the way the one who abuses you takes them
- *ὁ ὑβρίζων*: The verb covers insult, outrage and high-handed ill-treatment, in word or act; “abuses” covers both word and act. “You” as its object is supplied from the σε that follows. Other reading: the person who insults you, the person who treats you with contempt
- *κρίνει ἢ οἷά σε κρίνειν βούλεται*: κρίνειν is a different verb from ὑπολαμβάνειν, though close in sense. “Decide” is used for it so that the two can be told apart; its noun, κρίσις, is “verdict” in 6.52 and 7.16. Other reading: as the person who abuses you judges them, or wants you to judge them
- *ἴδε αὐτά*: “See them”: the pronoun standing alone after its verb is the ordinary “them”. With more weight on it, it would be “look at the things themselves”. Other reading: but look at the things themselves, as they truly are

</details>

### 4.12

One must always have these two kinds of readiness. The first is to do only what the reason of the kingly and lawgiving art suggests, for the benefit of human beings. The second is to change one’s mind, if it turns out that someone is at hand who sets one right and leads one away from some mistaken notion. But the leading away must always come from something persuasive, as being just or of common benefit, and what is preferred must be of that kind only, not because it appeared pleasant or well thought of.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὁ τῆς βασιλικῆς καὶ νομοθετικῆς λόγος*: The two adjectives are feminine with no noun. “Art” is the usual word to supply; “knowledge” is also possible. The phrase may mean the principle of ruling and lawgiving, or reason itself in its role as king and lawgiver. Other reading: the reason that is king and lawgiver
- *ὑποβάλλῃ*: The verb ranges from “suggest” and “prompt” to “dictate”. The English takes the mild end. Other reading: dictates
- *μεταθέσθαι*: Literally to shift one’s position. The English has “change one’s mind” here and in 8.16; in 6.21, where the verb answers both judging and acting, it is the bare “change”. Other reading: to shift one’s ground
- *ἐὰν ἄρα*: The small word after “if” marks the case as one that may or may not arise, given as “if it turns out that”. Other reading: if perhaps someone is at hand
- *ἀπό τινος οἰήσεως*: The noun is what one supposes to be so, and it usually has a bad sense: a notion held on one’s own say, often with conceit. “Mistaken” carries that bad sense and is not a separate Greek word. Other reading: from some conceit
- *ἀπό τινος πιθανότητος, ὡς δικαίου ἢ κοινωφελοῦς*: Literally “from some persuasiveness, as of a thing just or of common benefit”. The English makes the abstract noun “something persuasive”. Other reading: from some plausible ground, such as that it is just or serves the common good
- *τὰ προηγμένα*: A passive participle, “things led forward” or “put first”, and as a Stoic term “the preferred things”; the English keeps that plain passive sense. It can also be taken as the things that led one on to the change, the inducements. From memory, unchecked: other editors print a word meaning “the like” here. Other reading: and what moves one to it must be of that kind only
- *οὐχ ὅτι ἡδὺ ἢ ἔνδοξον ἐφάνη*: The second adjective is either “held in repute” or “bringing repute”; set beside “pleasant” the English takes the first, “well thought of”. Both adjectives are singular with no stated subject, given as “it”: the view one changes to. Other reading: not because it appeared pleasant or glorious
- *δεῖ*: The Greek is impersonal throughout, with no “you”. The English keeps “one”, which is stiff but is what the Greek has. Other reading: You must always have these two kinds of readiness

</details>

### 4.13

“Do you have reason?” “I do.” “Then why do you not use it? For when it is doing its own work, what else do you want?”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Λόγον ἔχεις*: The word is taken as the faculty, “reason”, the settled rendering. The quotation marks and the division between two speakers are in the edition’s Greek. Other reading: “Are you in possession of reason?”
- *τί οὖν οὐ χρᾷ*: The verb has no object expressed; “it” is supplied. Other reading: “Why then do you not make use of it?”
- *τούτου γὰρ τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ποιοῦντος*: A participle phrase (a genitive absolute), which the Greek leaves open between “when”, “if” and “since”. The English reads “when”. “Its own work” is literally “what is its own”. Other reading: For if it does what is its own to do
- *τί ἄλλο θέλεις*: Literally “what other thing do you want?”, which can be heard as “what else” or “what more”. Other reading: what more do you wish for?

</details>

### 4.14–15

You came to exist as a part within something. You will vanish into what gave birth to you; or rather, you will be taken back up into its seminal reason, through change.

Many little lumps of incense on the same altar: one fell earlier, another later, but it makes no difference.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐνυπέστης ὡς μέρος*: The verb is “you came to exist in (something)”, and the Greek does not name the something. “Within something” renders the prefix ἐν and no more; the next sentence says what the something is. Other reading: You have subsisted as a part.
- *τῷ γεννήσαντι*: The participle can be masculine or neuter: “the one who gave birth to you” or “that which gave birth to you”. The English takes the neuter with “what”. The verb is the ordinary one for a father or a mother having a child. Other reading: into the one who gave birth to you; into the one who fathered you
- *μᾶλλον δὲ ἀναληφθήσῃ*: μᾶλλον δὲ corrects what was just said: not vanishing but being taken back. “Taken back up” is the same rendering as for this verb in 7.10. Other reading: or rather you will be received back into its generative reason by a change
- *τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ τὸν σπερματικὸν*: The Stoic term λόγος σπερματικός: reason as the seed from which things grow. “Seminal” is meant in its literal sense, “of seed”, so that λόγος stays “reason” and the seed stays in a single adjective. αὐτοῦ is “its” or “his”, following the choice made for τῷ γεννήσαντι. Other reading: into its generative reason; into his seminal reason
- *βωλάρια*: A diminutive of βῶλος, a lump or clod: small lumps or grains of frankincense. Other reading: grains of incense
- *προκατέπεσεν*: “Fell down before”: either dropped onto the altar earlier, or collapsed (burnt down) sooner. The bare “fell earlier” leaves both open. Other reading: one has burnt down sooner, another later

</details>

### 4.16

Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you turn back to the principles and to reverence for reason.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐντὸς δέκα ἡμερῶν*: Literally “within ten days”. It may be a round figure for “very soon”; the number is kept. Other reading: In a few days
- *οἷς νῦν θηρίον καὶ πίθηκος*: There is no verb in this clause; “you seem” is carried over from the main verb. The first noun is a wild animal. Other reading: to whom you are now a wild animal and a monkey
- *ἀνακάμψῃς*: The verb is to bend back or turn back on one’s course, so it implies a return to something left behind. Other reading: if you return
- *τὰ δόγματα*: The Greek has only the article, “the principles”, and the English keeps it. Since the verb speaks of turning back, the article may stand for “your”: the principles once held and since left. Other reading: to your principles
- *τὸν σεβασμὸν τοῦ λόγου*: The genitive is taken as the thing revered: reverence for reason. The Greek does not say whether this is a person’s own reason or the reason that runs through everything, and “reason” without an article keeps both. The noun is from the same root as “revere” (σέβεις) in 12.28. Other reading: the worship of reason

</details>

### 4.17

Not as though you were going to live ten thousand years. What must come hangs over you. While you live, while it is possible, become good.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μὴ ὡς μύρια μέλλων ἔτη ζῆν*: The sentence has no main verb: “Not as one who is going to live ten thousand years”. A verb such as “live” or “act” is left to be understood, and the English leaves it out as the Greek does. Other reading: Do not live as though you were going to live ten thousand years
- *τὸ χρεὼν ἐπήρτηται*: τὸ χρεών is “what must be”, fate, with a sense of a debt that falls due: here death. ἐπήρτηται is “has been hung over”. The Greek does not say over whom; “you” is added. Other reading: Fate hangs overhead
- *ἀγαθὸς γενοῦ*: γενοῦ is “become”, which can also stand for a plain “be” in a command. Other reading: be good

</details>

### 4.18

How much leisure a person gains who does not look at what their neighbour said or did or thought, but only at what they themselves are doing, so that this very thing may be just and holy, or in keeping with the good man: not to look round at a dark character, but to run straight along the line, not thrown this way and that.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *εὐσχολίαν*: “Good leisure”: free time, freedom from being busy. Other reading: How much time and ease a person gains
- *ἢ † κατὰ τὸν ἀγαθὸν*: The edition marks the text as corrupt here with a dagger, and “or in keeping with the good man” does not join to what goes before or after. The words are translated as they stand. From memory, unchecked: some editors read a proper name here and take what follows as a quotation. Other reading: or, as the good man would have it:
- *μὴ μέλαν ἦθος περιβλέπεσθαι*: The construction changes to infinitives with no stated subject. μέλαν is “black”, “dark”; the phrase has no article and can be the dark character of some other person that one looks round at, bad character in general, or, less likely, a manner of looking. The first is taken. Other reading: do not glance about at the dark characters around you
- *ἐπὶ τῆς γραμμῆς τρέχειν ὀρθόν*: The image is of a runner keeping to the line marked on the track. ὀρθόν can go with the runner (“upright”, “straight”) or be an adverb with “run”. Other reading: but to run on the line, upright
- *μὴ διερριμμένον*: “Not flung about”: not thrown from side to side, or not scattered in many directions. Other reading: not darting from side to side

</details>

### 4.19–20

Whoever is worked up about fame after death does not picture that each of those who remember them will very soon die too; then in turn the one who takes over from that one, until the whole memory also goes out, as it passes on through those that are lit and go out. But suppose even that those who will remember are immortal, and the memory immortal: what then is that to you? And I do not speak of its being nothing to the dead; but to the living, what is praise, except perhaps for the sake of managing some matter? For leave aside now, out of season, the gift of nature, which from here on belongs to some other discussion.

Everything that is beautiful in any way at all is beautiful of itself and ends in itself, and does not have praise as a part of itself. At any rate, what is praised becomes neither worse nor better. I say this also of the things called beautiful in the more ordinary way, such as material things and things made by craft (for what does the truly beautiful need? No more than law does, no more than truth, no more than goodwill or a sense of shame). Which of these is beautiful because it is praised, or is ruined when it is blamed? For does a little emerald become worse than itself if it is not praised? And what of gold, ivory, purple, a lyre, a small knife, a little flower, a little tree?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐπτοημένος*: A participle meaning fluttered, startled or excited, used of people carried away by a passion. “Worked up” gives the agitation in plain English. Other reading: Whoever is in a flutter about fame after death
- *οὐ φαντάζεται*: The verb belongs with φαντασία, the Stoic “impression”: the fact does not appear to this person. Other reading: does not form the impression that
- *ὁ ἐκεῖνον διαδεξάμενος*: The verb is to receive something in succession from another, as an heir or the next runner does. “Takes over from” keeps that; the plainer sense is only that this one comes next. Other reading: then in turn the one who comes after that one
- *διὰ ἁπτομένων καὶ σβεννυμένων προιοῦσα*: The image is of a flame handed on. The two participles can be neuter, things such as lamps or torches, or masculine, the people who remember; “those that” leaves the image whole, and “go out” repeats the verb of “goes out” just before, as the Greek does. From memory, unchecked: the first participle is an editor’s correction of the manuscripts here. Other reading: as it passes on through people who are lit and put out
- *καὶ οὐ λέγω, ὅτι οὐδὲν πρὸς τὸν τεθνηκότα, ἀλλὰ*: Literally “and I do not say that it is nothing to the dead, but”. This is the idiom of passing over a smaller point to make a larger one, not a denial that praise is nothing to the dead. “It” has no word of its own in the Greek and picks up “that” in the question before. Other reading: And I do not say merely that it is nothing to the dead, but what is praise even to the living
- *πλὴν ἄρα δι’ οἰκονομίαν τινά*: The noun is the managing of a household or of affairs, and so expediency: praise may be useful as a means of getting something done. It can also mean a larger ordering of things. Other reading: unless, it may be, on account of some arrangement of things
- *πάρες γὰρ νῦν ἀκαίρως τὴν φυσικὴν δόσιν ἄλλου τινὸς ἐχομένην λόγου λοιπόν*: The Greek as given does not construe cleanly: the adverb “out of season” belongs to the command “leave aside”, which makes no sensible order, and the last word, “for the rest” or “from here on”, hangs loose. The English sets the words down in order without mending them, and what “the gift of nature” refers to is not clear. From memory, unchecked: the text is doubted, and editors have read an indicative, “you are neglecting”, and a participle agreeing with “you”. Other reading: For now you are neglecting, at the wrong moment, the gift of nature, and holding on to some other account.
- *ἄλλου τινὸς ἐχομένην λόγου*: The words are read as “belonging to some other discussion”. They can also mean “hanging on someone else’s word”, with “someone else” a person: the gift of nature made to depend on what another says, which would tie the sentence to praise. Other reading: the gift of nature, which then hangs on someone else’s word
- *Πᾶν τὸ καὶ ὁπωσοῦν καλὸν*: The adjective means beautiful, fine and morally noble at once. The examples run from emeralds to law and truth, so no one English word fits all; “beautiful” is kept throughout the chapter so the argument can be followed. Other reading: Everything that is fine in any way at all
- *ἐφ’ ἑαυτὸ καταλήγει*: Literally “comes to a stop at itself”: its beauty is complete in itself and points to nothing further. Other reading: and comes to rest in itself
- *τῶν κοινότερον καλῶν λεγομένων*: A comparative adverb: “in a more common way”, that is, in the looser everyday sense of the word, as against the truly beautiful named next. Other reading: the things more commonly called beautiful
- *ἐπὶ τῶν ὑλικῶν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν τεχνικῶν κατασκευασμάτων*: The last noun, “things constructed”, may go with both adjectives or only with the second. The English takes it with the second only, since the list that follows has raw materials and living things as well as made objects. Other reading: such as products of matter and products of craft
- *τὸ γὰρ δὴ ὄντως καλὸν τίνος χρείαν ἔχει; οὐ μᾶλλον ἣ νόμος*: The question is left without a stated answer: the truly beautiful needs nothing, any more than law does. The ἣ here, the one after it and the one in “neither worse nor better” above are slips in the copy for ἢ, “than” or “or”. Other reading: for what is truly beautiful needs nothing more, any more than law does
- *αἰδώς*: The word covers a sense of shame, modesty and respect for others. Other reading: modesty
- *σμαράγδιον*: A diminutive, as are the knife, the flower and the tree at the end of the list. “Little” or “small” is kept for each. Other reading: an emerald
- *πορφύρα*: The purple dye from shellfish, or cloth dyed with it. Other reading: purple cloth

</details>

### 4.21

If souls go on existing, how has the air had space for them from eternity? And how does the earth have space for the bodies of those who have been buried over so long an age? For just as here the change and dissolution of these bodies, after they have gone on existing for a certain time, makes space for other dead, so the souls that pass over into the air, after holding together for a while, change and are poured out and are set alight, being taken back into the generative reason of the whole, and in this way they give space to those that come to settle there after them. That is what a person might answer on the supposition that souls go on existing. But one should consider not only the multitude of bodies buried in this way, but also that of the animals eaten every day by us and by the other animals. For how great a number is consumed and, in a way, buried like this in the bodies of those that feed on them! And yet the space takes them in, through their being turned into blood, through their alteration into what is airy or fiery. What is the way to inquire into the truth in this matter? Division into what is matter and what is cause.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Εἰ διαμένουσιν αἱ ψυχαί*: διαμένειν is to last on, here to go on existing after death. Marcus does not affirm it: the answer is given “on the supposition” that they do. The noun ἐπιδιαμονή, used below of the buried bodies, is from the same verb, so “go on existing” is used there too. Other reading: If souls survive
- *χωρεῖ*: χωρεῖν is “to have room for”, and χώρα, “room, space”, comes three times below. “Space” is used throughout so that the thread shows. The present tense with “from eternity” is rendered “has had”. Other reading: how does the air contain them
- *ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐνθάδε*: γάρ here introduces the answer to the two questions, not a reason for them; “for” is the nearest plain word. ἐνθάδε, “here”, means in the earth. Other reading: The answer is that, just as here in the earth
- *χέονται καὶ ἐξάπτονται*: Literally “are poured” (melt, spread out) and “are kindled”. Both images are kept. Other reading: are diffused and catch fire
- *τὸν τῶν ὅλων σπερματικὸν λόγον*: The Stoic σπερματικὸς λόγος: the reason of the whole thought of as seed, from which all things grow. “Generative” is used for plain English; the usual technical rendering is “seminal”. Other reading: the seminal reason of the whole
- *ταῖς προσσυνοικιζομέναις*: A triple compound: those who are settled in besides, as additional fellow inhabitants. Other reading: to the souls that come to share the dwelling
- *δέχεται ἡ χώρα αὐτὰ*: Literally “the space receives them”. χώρα may be the room there is or the place, the region of the earth. Other reading: And yet the place has room for them
- *ἐξαιματώσεις*: “Turnings into blood”: the eaten animal becomes the eater’s blood. This and the following abstract noun are turned into verbal phrases. Other reading: through the conversions into blood, through the alterations into the airy or the fiery
- *ἡ ἱστορία τῆς ἀληθείας*: ἱστορία is inquiry or investigation. The phrase is compressed and is taken as “the way of inquiring into the truth”. Other reading: What is the investigation of the truth on this point?
- *εἰς τὸ ὑλικὸν καὶ εἰς τὸ αἰτιῶδες*: Two adjectives used as nouns: what a thing is made of, and what acts in it as cause. The sentence has no verb and is left so. Other reading: into the material and the causal

</details>

### 4.22

Not to roam away, but at every impulse to give what is just, and at every impression to keep the sure grasp.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀπορρέμβεσθαι*: ῥέμβομαι is to roam or spin about; with ἀπο-, to roam off. The sentence is infinitives used as instructions, kept impersonal. Other reading: Not to be whirled off course
- *ἐπὶ πάσης ὁρμῆς τὸ δίκαιον ἀποδιδόναι*: ἀποδίδωμι is to give what is owed. ἐπί with the genitive is “in the case of” every impulse. Other reading: in every impulse to render what is just
- *σῴζειν τὸ καταληπτικόν*: A Stoic term: the impression that is καταληπτική is the one that grasps its object so clearly that it cannot be false. Literally “to keep safe the grasping [quality]”: the sure grasp is a quality of the impression, not the thing grasped. Other reading: to preserve the power of sure apprehension

</details>

### 4.23

Universe, everything that fits well with you fits well with me. Nothing that is timely for you is too early or too late for me. Nature, everything your seasons bear is fruit to me. All things from you, all things in you, all things into you. One man says, “Dear city of Cecrops.” But you, will you not say, “Dear city of Zeus”?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πᾶν μοι συναρμόζει ὃ σοὶ εὐάρμοστόν ἐστιν*: Both words come from the root for fitting together, which covers a carpenter's joint and a musical tuning. I chose 'fits'. Other reading: Everything that is in tune with you is in tune with me
- *κόσμε*: Universe, or world, or the ordered whole; the same choice as in 10.21. Other reading: world
- *οὐδέν μοι πρόωρον οὐδὲ ὄψιμον ὃ σοὶ εὔκαιρον*: The words for “too early” and “too late” are also used of crops that come before or after their season, which leads into the fruit of the next sentence. Other reading: Nothing that is timely for you is unripe or overdue for me
- *αἱ σαὶ ὧραι*: The word means seasons and also hours or times in general. 'Seasons' goes with the fruit. Other reading: your hours
- *ἐκ σοῦ πάντα, ἐν σοὶ πάντα, εἰς σὲ πάντα*: The Greek has no verbs, only “out of you”, “in you”, “into you”. None is supplied. Other reading: All things come from you, exist in you and go back into you
- *ἐκεῖνος μέν φησιν*: The speaker is not named, only pointed to as 'that one'; the words quoted look like a line of verse. Cecrops was the legendary first king of Athens, so his city is Athens. Other reading: The poet says
- *ὦ πόλι φίλη Κέκροπος*: 'Dear' can go with 'city' (dear city, belonging to Cecrops) or with the name (city dear to Cecrops). The same holds for the phrase about Zeus that copies it. Other reading: O city dear to Cecrops ... O city dear to Zeus
- *σὺ δὲ οὐκ ἐρεῖς*: Up to here 'you' was the universe and then nature. This 'you' is set against 'that man' and is most naturally Marcus speaking to himself; the Greek does not say so, and does not say what the city of Zeus is. The question expects the answer yes.

</details>

### 4.24

“Do few things,” he says, “if you mean to be cheerful.” Might it not be better to do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a living being that is civic by nature requires, and in the way it requires? For this brings not only the cheerfulness that comes from doing things well, but also the cheerfulness that comes from doing few things. For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a person strips it away they will have more leisure and be less troubled. So on each occasion one must also remind oneself: “Is this perhaps one of the things that are not necessary?” And one must strip away not only the actions that are not necessary but impressions too, for then superfluous actions will not follow after them either.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πρῆσσε, φησίν*: The quotation is in Ionic dialect (πρῆσσε for πρᾶσσε), and “he says” names no one. From memory, unchecked: it is a saying of Democritus. Other reading: “Do little,” it is said
- *εὐθυμήσειν*: εὐθυμία is good spirits, a settled and contented mind and not a passing mood. “Cheerful” and “cheerfulness” are kept for the verb and the noun. Other reading: if you mean to be of good heart
- *μήποτε*: In later Greek this opens a cautious suggestion, “perhaps”. The edition prints the sentence as a question. Other reading: Perhaps it is better
- *αἱρεῖ καὶ ὡς αἱρεῖ*: ὁ λόγος αἱρεῖ is a set phrase, “reason proves, reason dictates”; literally reason “takes” or “chooses”. Other reading: chooses, and as it chooses
- *καλῶς πράσσειν*: πράσσειν is “do” throughout the passage, so “doing things well” is kept; the sense is acting rightly, not prospering. Other reading: from acting rightly
- *εὐσχολώτερος καὶ ἀταρακτότερος*: Two comparatives: “more at leisure and more undisturbed”. Other reading: will have more free time and more calm
- *ἀλλὰ καὶ φαντασίας*: The Greek does not repeat “not necessary” with the impressions and has no article. The words are most naturally carried over from the actions, and the English leaves them to be carried over in the same way. Other reading: but unnecessary impressions too
- *παρέλκουσαι*: Literally “dragging alongside”: trailing after to no purpose, superfluous. Other reading: idle actions

</details>

### 4.25–26

Try how the life of the good person, too, goes for you: the person who is pleased with what is allotted from the whole and content with their own action being just and their disposition kind.

You have seen those things; look at these too. Do not disturb yourself: make yourself simple. Someone does wrong? They do wrong to themselves. Something has happened to you? That is well: everything that happens was, from the beginning, fated along with you out of the whole and spun into your thread. In sum, life is short. The present must be turned to profit, with good reasoning and justice. Be sober, without strain.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πῶς σοι χωρεῖ*: χωρεῖ is “goes”, “turns out”, “succeeds”: see how this life works out when you try it. Other reading: Try how the life of the good person suits you
- *καὶ ὁ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἀνθρώπου βίος*: The small word καί, “also”, goes with the life and implies that other lives have been tried already. It is kept as “too”, set next to “the life of the good person”. Other reading: Try how even the life of the good person goes for you
- *Ἑώρακας ἐκεῖνα, ἴδε καὶ ταῦτα*: The Greek does not say what “those” and “these” are. They are left bare. Other reading: You have seen that side; now look at this one too
- *ἅπλωσον σεαυτόν*: “Make yourself single”: simple, of one piece. The verb can also mean to unfold or spread out. Other reading: be simple
- *ἑαυτῷ ἁμαρτάνει*: The dative marks who is affected: the wrong lands on the one who does it. Other reading: It is their own loss
- *καλῶς*: “Well”, as an answer to the question. “Good” is avoided because this passage uses it for another Greek word, in “the good person”. Other reading: Good
- *συγκαθείμαρτο καὶ συνεκλώθετο*: Two verbs with the prefix “together with”: fated along with you and spun along with you. The second is the image of the Fates’ thread; “thread” is supplied. Other reading: was fated together with you and spun together with you
- *κερδαντέον τὸ παρὸν*: A word from trade: the present is to be made a gain of. Other reading: One must profit from the present
- *νῆφε ἀνειμένως*: “Be sober” (not drunk, and so clear-headed) with an adverb meaning “loosely”, “without strain”. The two pull against each other on purpose. Other reading: Keep a clear head, but be at ease

</details>

### 4.27

Either an arranged order, or a stirred brew jumbled together. But in fact an order. Or can a kind of order exist in you, and disorder in the all? And this when all things are, as they are, separated out and spread out, and feel with one another.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κόσμος διατεταγμένος*: The word κόσμος is both “order” and the ordinary word for the universe, which is its English in the other passages. Here the argument turns on the same word being said of the all and of “you”, and on its opposite, ἀκοσμία, “disorder”, so the English is “order” every time. Other reading: Either a universe set in order
- *κυκεὼν συμπεφυρμένος*: A kykeon was a drink of barley meal stirred into liquid; “a stirred brew” is also its English in 6.10. The participle means kneaded or mixed up together. The manuscripts are said to be troubled at this point and the printed words to be partly an editor’s repair (from memory, unchecked); the English follows what is printed. Other reading: a hotchpotch all mixed up together
- *ἀλλὰ μὴν κόσμος*: A clipped statement with no verb. The two particles give the next step of an argument as a fact, “but in fact”, and nothing is supplied. Other reading: But there is an order
- *τις κόσμος*: Literally “a certain order”. The indefinite word may limit the claim (“some sort of order”) or simply mean “an order”. Other reading: can there be an order in you
- *τῷ παντὶ*: Literally “the all”. It is a different word from the ones given as “the whole” and “the universe” in the other passages, so the English keeps it literal. Other reading: and disorder in the universe
- *καὶ ταῦτα οὕτως*: The first two words mean “and that too”, adding a circumstance that makes the thing more striking. The third can mean “so much” or “in the way they are”, and the English takes the second. Other reading: And this when all things are so separated out
- *διακεκριμένων καὶ διακεχυμένων καὶ συμπαθῶν*: Three descriptions of all things: sorted apart, poured out in different directions, and sharing in one another’s states (the Stoic term, literally “affected together”; “sympathy” is avoided because it now means pity). It is open whether all three are evidence of order, or whether the first two concede how separate things are and the third answers them. They are joined with plain “and”, as in the Greek. Other reading: when all things, though so distinct and so dispersed, still feel with one another

</details>

### 4.28–29a

A dark character, a womanish character, a stubborn character, like a wild beast, like cattle, childish, dull, counterfeit, clownish, like a petty trader, tyrannical.

If the one who does not know the things that are in the universe is a stranger to the universe, no less a stranger too is the one who does not know the things that happen.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μέλαν ἦθος*: Literally “black character”: dark, malignant. The English says “dark”, which the word also means, so that it is not heard as a matter of skin. The chapter is a bare list with no verb and does not say whether it describes one person or sets out kinds of character. Other reading: A black, malicious character
- *θῆλυ ἦθος*: Literally “a female character”, an ancient term of reproach for softness. The English keeps what the Greek says and does not swap in “soft”. Other reading: a soft, unmanly character
- *περισκελὲς ἦθος*: The adjective means very hard, rigid, and of character obstinate or harsh. Other reading: a hard, unbending character
- *βοσκηματῶδες*: “Like a grazing animal”, that is like livestock, as against the wild beast just before it. Other reading: like a herd animal
- *βλακικόν*: The range runs from slack and lazy to slow-witted and stupid. “Dull” can be heard both ways. Other reading: sluggish, slack; stupid
- *βωμολόχον, καπηλικόν*: The first is the low jester who will say anything for a laugh. The second is the petty retailer, with a suggestion of cheating that the English leaves to this note. Other reading: a buffoon’s, a cheating shopkeeper’s
- *ξένος κόσμου*: The noun means a foreigner or stranger, someone not at home in a place. The genitive is “of the universe”, and English needs “to the universe”. The same word comes back in 12.13 and is “stranger” there too. Other reading: a foreigner in the universe
- *γνωρίζων*: The verb is to know in the sense of being acquainted with, or to recognise. The English uses “know” both times it occurs. Other reading: does not recognise
- *τὰ γινόμενα*: “The things that come about” is set against “the things that are”. The Greek does not repeat “in it”, and the English does not supply it. The passage is only the opening of chapter 29, but this sentence is complete as given. Other reading: what comes to pass in it

</details>

### 4.29b

An exile is whoever exiles themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens. Blind is whoever shuts the eye of the mind. A beggar is whoever is in need of another and does not have from themselves everything that is useful for life. An abscess standing apart from the universe is whoever stands apart and separates themselves from the reason of the common nature by being displeased with what happens: for that nature brings this forth, the same one that brought you forth too. A piece split off from the city is whoever splits their own soul off from the soul of rational beings, which is one.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *φυγὰς ὁ φεύγων*: A play on one root: φυγάς is a banished person, an exile (it can also mean a fugitive), and φεύγειν is both “to flee” and the ordinary verb for being in exile. The English reads “exile” and “exiles themselves” so that the echo is heard and the list stays about a person’s standing in the city; the sense of running away is given up. The passage begins partway through chapter 4.29; nothing was added apart from the “is” that each of these verbless Greek sentences needs in English. Other reading: A fugitive is whoever flees from the reason that belongs to citizens.
- *τὸν πολιτικὸν λόγον*: πολιτικός means “of citizens, of their life together in a city”; the city meant is the one that all rational beings share, named at the end of the passage. λόγος is “reason” as in the glossary, here and in “the reason of the common nature” below. “The reason that belongs to citizens” is read in place of the closer “the reason of the city”, which is hard to take in. Other reading: the reason of the city, or: the principle of life as a citizen
- *καταμύων τῷ νοερῷ ὄμματι*: καταμύω is “to shut the eyes”, and the dative says with which eye: literally “who shuts their eyes with the eye of the mind”. The English makes the eye the object. νοερός is “of the mind” as in the glossary. Other reading: whoever keeps their eyes shut where the eye of the mind is concerned
- *ἑτέρου*: The form can be masculine (another person) or neuter (something else). “Another” is kept because the Greek sets this one word against “from themselves” in the next clause; an English reader will hear a person first. Other reading: whoever is in need of something else
- *παρ’ ἑαυτοῦ*: Literally “from beside oneself”, that is, supplied by oneself. The English keeps the literal “from themselves”. Other reading: from their own resources
- *ἀπόστημα κόσμου ὁ ἀφιστάμενος*: A play on one root: ἀπόστημα is the medical word for an abscess, literally “a standing away” (matter that has drawn apart in the body), and ἀφιστάμενος is “standing away, withdrawing”, a word also used of revolt. The English keeps the abscess and spells out the literal sense of the noun as “standing apart from the universe”, so that “stands apart” can echo it as “split off” does in the next sentence. The Greek has only “an abscess of the universe”. Other reading: An abscess on the universe is whoever withdraws, or revolts
- *ἐκείνη γὰρ φέρει τοῦτο, ἣ καὶ σὲ ἤνεγκεν*: The Greek has only “that one”, feminine, which picks up the common nature just named, and the English supplies “nature”; the same verb (φέρω: bring, bear, produce) comes twice, so “bring forth” is used twice. “This” is as bare and singular in the Greek: the particular thing that happens and displeases. The Greek turns to “you” here with no warning, and the English keeps that. Other reading: for the nature that produces this is the same one that produced you
- *ἀπόσχισμα πόλεως ὁ τὴν ἰδίαν ψυχὴν τῆς τῶν λογικῶν ἀποσχίζων, μιᾶς οὔσης*: The Greek repeats one root (ἀπόσχισμα, ἀποσχίζων), which “split off” keeps. “Soul” has to be supplied with “of rational beings”: literally “from that of the rational ones, it being one”. The last two words can be a plain statement (“which is one”) or a concession (“though it is one”); the English takes the first. Other reading: A fragment torn from the city is whoever tears their own soul away from the soul of rational beings, although that soul is one.

</details>

### 4.30

One person practises philosophy without a tunic, another without a book. Here is another, half naked: “I have no bread,” he says, “and yet I hold to reason.” And I, for my part, do not have the nourishment that comes from learning, and yet I hold to reason.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *χιτῶνος*: The chiton is the basic garment worn next to the skin. To go without it is to go in a cloak alone. Other reading: without a shirt
- *φιλοσοφεῖ*: One verb in Greek: to do philosophy, or to live as a philosopher. Other reading: lives as a philosopher
- *ἄλλος οὗτος ἡμίγυμνος*: There is no verb: “this other one, half naked”. The English makes it a short sentence introducing the speaker of the next words, and the quotation marks around his words are added, since the edition has none here. It is open whether this is a third figure or a closer look at one of the first two. Other reading: This other one, half naked, says: “I have no bread, and yet I hold to reason.”
- *καὶ ἐμμένω τῷ λόγῳ*: The Greek has a bare “and”, which here sets the holding against the lack. The English writes “and yet”, in this sentence and in the last. Other reading: and I hold to reason
- *τῷ λόγῳ*: With the article, in a philosopher’s mouth, the word could be reason itself or the teaching (the argument) the speaker has taken up. The English keeps “reason”, the settled rendering. Other reading: and yet I stand by my teaching
- *τροφὰς τὰς ἐκ τῶν μαθημάτων*: Open between the food that learning itself gives the mind and a living earned from one’s learning or lessons. The English phrase leans to the first but does not shut out the second. “Bread” above is plural in the Greek (“loaves”), answered here by a plural word for food. Other reading: I get no living from my studies
- *ἐγὼ δὲ*: The edition puts a dash before these words to mark a turn, perhaps a change of speaker: it may be Marcus himself or one more philosopher answering the half-naked one. The English leaves the sentence outside the quotation marks, as Marcus’s own, and begins a new sentence in place of the dash. The particle is given as “and”, because this speaker says of himself what the last one said; “but” is the other way to hear it. Other reading: “But I,” says another, “have no nourishment from learning, and yet I hold to reason.”
- *οὐκ ἔχω καὶ ἐμμένω*: As given: “I do not have … and I hold”, with no object for the second verb; “to reason” is supplied from the sentence before. From memory, unchecked, the place of the negative has been doubted, and with it moved the sentence becomes a self-reproach. Other reading: I have the nourishment of learning and I do not hold to it

</details>

### 4.31

Love the little trade you have learned, and rest in it; and go through what is left of your life having entrusted everything that is yours to the gods with your whole soul, and making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τεχνίον*: A diminutive of the word for a craft or skill: “little craft”, said modestly. The Greek does not say which craft; it may be philosophy as the craft of living, or a person’s own trade. “Trade” is used because “small craft” in English is a boat. Other reading: the modest skill you have learned
- *προσαναπαύου*: Literally “rest yourself upon”: lean on it, find your rest in it. Other reading: be content with it
- *ὡς θεοῖς μὲν ἐπιτετροφὼς*: Literally “as one who has entrusted”: the Greek “as” presents the entrusting as the footing on which the rest of life is to be lived. The English leaves “as” out so that “you” can run through the whole sentence. Other reading: as someone who has entrusted everything of their own to the gods
- *ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς*: “With your whole soul” goes by position with “entrusted”. It could be heard with “go through”. Other reading: go through what is left of your life with your whole soul
- *ἀνθρώπων δὲ μηδενὸς μήτε τύραννον μήτε δοῦλον*: The Greek sets “the gods” against “no human being”. The order of the two halves is kept, but English loses the pointed contrast of the two particles. Other reading: to the gods, entrusting everything; of human beings, tyrant to none and slave to none

</details>

### 4.32

Think, for the sake of an example, of the times of Vespasian, and you will see all the same things: people marrying, raising children, falling ill, dying, making war, keeping festivals, trading, farming, flattering, insisting on their own way, suspecting, plotting, praying for certain people to die, grumbling at how things are, falling in love, hoarding treasure, wanting consulships, wanting kingships. Well then, that life of theirs is no longer anywhere. Pass on again to the times of Trajan: again all the same things. That life too is dead. In the same way look over the other inscriptions of times and of whole nations, and see how many people strained with all their strength and a little later fell and were broken up into the elements. But above all one should go back over those whom you yourself knew being dragged after empty things, people who neglected to do what fits their own constitution, to hold on tight to that and to be content with that. And here it is necessary to remember that the attention given to each action also has its own worth and proportion. For in this way you will not give up in frustration, if you do not occupy yourself with the lesser things more than is fitting.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *αὐθαδιζομένους*: “Behaving in a self-willed, overbearing way.” The English makes it an action like the rest of the list; the same word-family is “self-willed” in another passage of this section. Other reading: throwing their weight about
- *βασιλείας*: “Kingships”, which in a Roman setting is also the word for the emperor’s rule. Other reading: wanting to be consul, wanting to be emperor
- *ἐπιγραφὰς χρόνων*: ἐπιγραφή is an inscription, a title or a heading. The English keeps “inscriptions”, as of what is written over the dead; it may instead be the headings under which periods are entered, like “the times of Vespasian”. Other reading: the other headings of periods and of whole nations
- *κατενταθέντες*: “Having strained hard”, a word of the stretched string or sinew. The same family comes back in other passages of this section, and “strain” is kept for it. Other reading: after straining every nerve
- *κενὰ σπωμένους*: σπάω is “to pull, to drag, to wrench”. The form can be passive (dragged) or middle (pulling at, grasping for). κενά, “empty things”, is in the object case, which does not make them the ones doing the dragging. Other reading: grasping at empty things
- *ἀναπολητέον*: An impersonal form, “one must turn over again”, followed at once by the second person “you yourself knew”. The English keeps both as they stand. Other reading: you must think back over
- *κατασκευὴν*: “Constitution, make-up”: how a thing is built and so what it is built for. Other reading: what fits the way they themselves are made
- *ἡ ἐπιστροφὴ*: “The turning towards”, that is, attention or care given to a thing. “Given to” renders καθ’ ἑκάστην πρᾶξιν, “for each action”. Other reading: the care spent on each action
- *οὐκ ἀποδυσπετήσεις*: The verb is to give up out of impatience or discouragement. The Greek does not say at what; the next clause gives the condition. Other reading: you will not lose heart

</details>

### 4.33–34

Expressions that were once in ordinary use are now obsolete words. So too the names of those who were once much sung are now, in a way, obsolete words: Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Dentatus, and little by little Scipio and Cato too, then Augustus too, then Hadrian and Antoninus too. For all things quickly fade and turn into tales, and quickly too complete forgetting buries them. And I say this of those who shone in some wonderful way; for the rest, the moment they have breathed their last, are “unseen, unheard of”. And what is everlasting remembrance at all? All of it empty. What then is there that one should put serious effort into? This one thing: thought that is just, actions that are social, speech such as never to lie, and a disposition that welcomes everything that happens as necessary, as familiar, as flowing from an origin and spring of that kind.

Willingly join in giving yourself over to Clotho, and let her spin you together with whatever events she wishes.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *γλωσσήματα*: A grammarian’s term: obsolete or rare words that need a gloss. “Obsolete words” is used both times; the need for a gloss is not carried over. Other reading: old words that need explaining
- *κατ’ ὀλίγον*: “Little by little” or “after a little”: the later names are sliding the same way as the early ones. Other reading: and soon Scipio and Cato too
- *κατέχωσεν*: An aorist, which can state a general truth (“buries”) or a completed fact. The English takes the general truth, in line with the present tense before it. Other reading: complete forgetting has buried them
- *ἄιστοι, ἄπυστοι*: Two Homeric words, marked as a quotation in the edition; they appear to come from the Odyssey, said of the lost Odysseus (from memory, unchecked). The second is “not heard of, of whom there is no news”. Other reading: “out of sight, out of hearing”
- *ὅλον κενόν*: Either “the whole of it is empty” or “wholly empty”. The English says “All of it” so that the answer picks up “at all” in the question, as the Greek ὅλον picks up ὅλως. Other reading: Wholly empty.
- *πράξεις κοινωνικαὶ*: “Social” is the settled word for κοινωνικός in this translation. It means directed to the community and its good, not sociable. Other reading: actions for the common good
- *λόγος, οἷος μήποτε διαψεύσασθαι*: λόγος here is speech, not the faculty of reason, as the verb shows. The verb is middle, “to lie, to deceive”; it could be stretched to “to be mistaken”. Other reading: and reason such as never to be deceived
- *ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς τοιαύτης καὶ πηγῆς*: Literally “from such a beginning and spring”. “Such” may mean of the same kind as the event itself (necessary, familiar), or may point to an origin already known to the writer. Other reading: as flowing from an origin and spring of the same kind as itself
- *συνεπιδίδου*: The prefix adds “together with”: to join in the giving, that is, to work with Clotho and not merely submit. It can also be heard as only strengthening the verb. Other reading: Willingly give yourself over to Clotho
- *συννῆσαι*: Clotho is one of the three Fates; her name means the Spinner. The verb is “to spin together with”: a person’s thread is spun in with the events. Other reading: offering yourself to be woven into whatever events she wishes

</details>

### 4.35–36

Everything lasts a day, both what remembers and what is remembered.

Observe continually that all things come about by change, and accustom yourself to the thought that the nature of the whole loves nothing so much as to change the things that exist and make new things like them. For everything that exists is, in a way, the seed of what will come from it. But you picture as seeds only those that are cast into earth or womb, and that is very much a layman’s view.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐφήμερον*: Literally “of a day”, lasting one day. The day is kept in the English. Other reading: Everything is short-lived
- *κατὰ μεταβολὴν γινόμενα*: γινόμενα can be “coming to be” or “happening”; κατὰ μεταβολήν is “by way of change”. The English takes it as all things coming about through change. Other reading: Observe continually all things as they come to be through change
- *νέα ὅμοια*: Literally “new like [things]”: new things of the same sort as the old. Other reading: and make new ones of the same kind
- *πᾶν τὸ ὃν*: ὃν is read as ὂν, “being” (a slip of the digitised text): “everything that is”. The English says “exists”, here and for τὰ ὄντα just before, to avoid “is is”. Other reading: everything that is
- *φαντάζῃ*: The verb is from the same root as φαντασία, “impression”: to form a picture of something. “Picture” is used here and in the other passages of this section. Other reading: But you imagine that the only seeds are those
- *γῆν ἣ μήτραν*: ἣ is read as ἢ, “or” (a slip of the digitised text). Other reading: into the ground or the womb
- *λίαν ἰδιωτικόν*: ἰδιωτικός is what belongs to the private person without training, here the person without philosophy. It can be heard as “unphilosophical” or more sharply as “crude”; “view” is supplied for the bare adjective. Other reading: and that is very unphilosophical

</details>

### 4.37

Any moment now you will be dead, and you are not yet simple, nor untroubled, nor free of the suspicion that you could be harmed from outside, nor gracious towards everyone, nor someone who places wisdom only in acting justly.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἤδη τεθνήξῃ*: A future perfect, “you will be dead”, with ἤδη (“already, presently”): the state is almost here. Other reading: Soon you will have died
- *καὶ οὔπω οὔτε ἁπλοῦς*: The Greek has no verb after “and not yet”; “you are” is supplied. ἁπλοῦς is “simple, single”, without doubleness. Other reading: and not yet straightforward
- *ἀνύποπτος τοῦ βλαβῆναι ἃν ἔξωθεν*: ἃν is a slip in the digitised text for ἂν, the particle that goes with βλαβῆναι. Literally “unsuspecting of possibly being harmed from outside”: free of the idea that outside things could do harm. Other reading: without the expectation that you might be harmed from outside
- *ἵλεως*: A word used of gods who are favourable, and of people who are kindly and mild. Other reading: kindly
- *τὸ φρονεῖν ἐν μόνῳ τῷ δικαιοπραγεῖν τιθέμενος*: τὸ φρονεῖν is “being wise, having good sense”. μόνῳ (“only”) goes with acting justly: wisdom lies in that and nowhere else. Other reading: counting acting justly as the only good sense

</details>

### 4.38

Look closely into their ruling parts, and at the wise as well: what sort of things they run from, and what sort of things they chase.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *αὐτῶν*: “Their”: the people are not named, and the line has no context. It is presumably people in general. Other reading: Look closely into people’s ruling parts
- *διάβλεπε*: To look straight at or see through. τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, its object, is “the ruling part”. Other reading: See right through
- *καὶ τοὺς φρονίμους*: “The wise” stands in the same case as “ruling parts”, a second thing to look at, and its point is open. It can mean “even the wise”, with contempt, or “and look at the wise” as the contrast and model; “as well” leaves both possible. From memory, unchecked: the words have been doubted. Other reading: and even at the wise
- *οἷα μὲν φεύγουσιν, οἷα δὲ διώκουσιν*: The subject can be the wise alone or everyone whose ruling part is being looked at. The verbs are “flee” and “pursue”, the same pair as in 8.52. Other reading: what sort of things they avoid and what sort they pursue

</details>

### 4.39

What is bad for you does not have its existence in another’s ruling part, nor yet in any turn and alteration of what surrounds you. Where, then? In the place where you have that which judges about bad things. So let that not judge, and all is well. Even if what is nearest to it, the little body, is cut, is burned, festers, rots, still let the part that judges about these things keep quiet. That is, let it decide that nothing is either bad or good which can happen equally to a bad man and a good one. For what happens equally to the one who lives against nature and to the one who lives in accordance with nature is neither in accordance with nature nor against nature.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κακὸν σὸν*: Literally “a bad thing of yours”, “your evil”. “Bad” is used for κακόν throughout the section so that it matches “a bad man” below. Other reading: No evil of yours has its being in another’s ruling part
- *ὑφίσταται*: A term for having real existence or subsistence. Other reading: does not lie in
- *τοῦ περιέχοντος*: “What surrounds” is usually the surrounding air or environment. Since the next sentence calls the body “what is nearest”, it could also mean the body as the envelope around the ruling part. “What surrounds you” leaves both open; “you” is supplied. Other reading: of the body that encloses you
- *τοῦτο οὖν μὴ ὑπολαμβανέτω*: Literally “let this not judge”: no object is given. The sense is “let it not form the judgment that something is bad”. Other reading: So let it make no such judgment
- *τὸ σωμάτιον*: Diminutive of “body”, used slightingly; “little body” throughout this section. Other reading: this poor body
- *διαπυίσκηται*: A medical word: to suppurate, to fill with pus. Other reading: suppurates
- *κρινέτω*: κρίνω stands beside ὑπολαμβάνω: “judge” is kept for the second (the verb of ὑπόληψις) and “decide” for the first. Other reading: let it judge that nothing is either bad or good
