- *κακῷ ἀνδρὶ καὶ ἀγαθῷ*: The Greek has ἀνήρ, a man, so “man” is kept. Other reading: to a bad person and a good one

</details>

### 4.40

To think constantly of the universe as one living thing, having one substance and one soul; and of how all things are handed up to its one perception; and how it does all things by one impulse; and how all things are joint causes of all the things that come about; and what the spinning together and winding together is like.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐπινοεῖν*: The verb is an infinitive with no person, the form of a note to oneself or a rule. It is kept impersonal as “To think”. Other reading: Think constantly of the universe as one living thing
- *ζῷον*: The word means any living creature, an animal. The English is “living thing”. Other reading: as one animal
- *ἐπέχον*: The participle means holding, occupying or possessing. The English is the plain “having”. Other reading: holding one substance and one soul / made up of one substance and one soul
- *ἀναδίδοται*: The verb means to be given up or handed on, as a report is handed up to someone. The noun it leads to, αἴσθησιν, is sense-perception or awareness. Other reading: how all things are reported back to its single awareness
- *πάντα πράσσει*: In Greek a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb, so this is either “it (the universe) does all things” or “all things act”. The English takes the universe as subject: a living thing that has one perception and acts by one impulse. Other reading: and how all things act by one impulse
- *συναίτια*: Literally “causes together with”, each thing sharing in the causing of each event. The English is “joint causes”. Other reading: how all things help to cause all that comes about
- *σύννησις καὶ συμμήρυσις*: Two rare nouns from thread-work: the first is spinning threads together, the second winding or reeling them together. Both are kept as images. Whether the second is winding into a ball or weaving into a web is not settled. Other reading: what the spinning together and weaving together is like

</details>

### 4.41

You are a little soul carrying a corpse, as Epictetus used to say.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ψυχάριον*: A diminutive of ψυχή, belittling or pitying. Other reading: a poor soul
- *βαστάζον νεκρόν*: βαστάζειν is to carry a load; νεκρός is a dead body, here the living body seen as already a corpse. Other reading: lugging a dead body about
- *ὡς Ἐπίκτητος ἔλεγεν*: The imperfect can mean “used to say” or simply “said”. The saying is thought not to be in the surviving books of Epictetus (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: as Epictetus said

</details>

### 4.42–43

There is nothing bad for things that are in the course of change, just as there is nothing good for things that come to exist out of change.

Eternity is a kind of river of things that come to be, and a violent current. For as soon as each thing has been seen it has been carried past, and another is being carried past, and yet another will be carried along.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τοῖς ἐν μεταβολῇ γινομένοις*: Literally “for the things coming to be in change”. It may mean things that are undergoing change, or things that come about in the process of change. The English takes the first; the thought is that being changed is no harm to them. Other reading: Nothing is bad for things that come about in the course of change
- *τοῖς ἐκ μεταβολῆς ὑφισταμένοις*: ὑφίστασθαι is to come into existence or to subsist. The things meant are those that exist as the result of a change. The clause denies them a good as the first denies the others a harm. Other reading: just as it is no good either for things that subsist as a result of change
- *ὁ αἰών*: αἰών is the whole endless extent of time. “Eternity” is kept so that the word is the same as in the other passages of this section, where it stands beside χρόνος, “time”; here it means endless time in its flow, not timelessness. Other reading: Time is a kind of river of things that come to be
- *ὤφθη*: An aorist: “was seen”, that is, no sooner has each thing appeared than it is gone. Other reading: no sooner is each thing seen than it has been swept past
- *τὸ δὲ ἐνεχθήσεται*: Literally “and the other will be carried”. τὸ δέ after ἄλλο marks a further thing, so that three things stand in three tenses: carried past, being carried past, to be carried. It could also be taken of the thing just mentioned. Other reading: and that one too will be carried off

</details>

### 4.44–45

Everything that happens is as ordinary and familiar as the rose in spring and fruit in summer. For illness is like that too, and death, and slander, and plotting, and all the things that gladden or grieve fools.

What comes next always follows what went before as kin to it. For it is not like a counting-off of separate items that has only compulsion in it, but a connection that has reason in it. And just as the things that exist have been arranged to fit together, so the things that come to be show not bare succession but a wonderful kinship.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὀπώρα ἐν τῷ θέρει*: ὀπώρα is the ripe fruit of late summer, and also the name of that season. θέρος is summer, and also the harvest. Other reading: the fruit at harvest time
- *ἣ λυπεῖ*: As printed in the digitised text the first word is the relative “which” (feminine), which does not fit the sentence. It is read as ἢ, “or”. Other reading: all the things that gladden fools or pain them
- *οἰκείως*: Literally “in the manner of one who belongs to the household”. The noun from the same root (οἰκειότητα) ends the passage, so the English reads “kin” and “kinship”. Other reading: follows in a way that belongs to what went before ... a wonderful belonging-together
- *καταρίθμησίς τίς ἐστιν ἀπηρτημένως*: Literally “a kind of counting-off, detachedly”, that is, a list of items with nothing joining them. The adverb is rare. Other reading: a mere enumeration of things hanging apart from each other
- *τὸ κατηναγκασμένον*: Literally “what has been forced”. The point is a sequence in which each thing has to come next and nothing more can be said. Other reading: that has nothing but necessity in it
- *συνάφεια εὔλογος*: εὔλογος is “reasonable, having good reason”. The English keeps the word “reason” visible. Other reading: a reasonable connection
- *συντέτακται συνηρμοσμένως*: Two “together” words: “have been arranged together” and “in a fitted-together way”. Other reading: have been ordered together harmoniously

</details>

### 4.46

Always remember the saying of Heraclitus, that the death of earth is to become water, and the death of water is to become air, and of air, fire, and back again. And remember too the one who forgets where the road leads; and that people are at odds with the very thing they are most constantly in company with, the reason that governs the whole; and that the things they run into every day seem foreign to them; and that we must not act and speak like people asleep, for then too we think we are acting and speaking; and that we must not act and speak like children of their parents, that is, simply as we have had it handed down.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τοῦ Ἡρακλειτείου*: Literally “the Heraclitean [thing]”, the saying of Heraclitus. The rest of the passage strings together further sayings of his (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: what Heraclitus said
- *μεμνῆσθαι*: An infinitive used as an instruction, with no person. The English uses the bare command. Other reading: Always to remember
- *τοῦ ἐπιλανθανομένου*: “The one who forgets”: a figure from a saying, not a particular person. Other reading: the man who forgets where the road leads
- *ὁμιλοῦσι*: The verbs here are third person plural with no subject, and “people” is supplied. The verb is “to keep company with, to have dealings with”. The one rendered “are at odds with” (διαφέρονται) is literally “are carried apart from”. Other reading: that they differ from that with which they have most continual dealings
- *λόγῳ τῷ τὰ ὅλα διοικοῦντι*: λόγος here is the governing principle, “reason” by the glossary. In Heraclitus’s own usage it also carries “account”. τὰ ὅλα is a plural, “all things taken together”, given as “the whole” as elsewhere in this translation. Other reading: the account that orders all things
- *δοκοῦμεν*: The verb can be “seem” or “think”. With an infinitive it is said of what people believe they are doing, which suits sleepers, and the English reads “think”. Other reading: for then too we seem to act and speak
- *ὡς παῖδας τοκεώνων*: Literally “like children of parents”, with an old poetic form of “parents” and no verb. “Act and speak” is carried over from the clause before, and “their” is supplied. The phrase is hard and its text has been doubted (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: must not be like children of their parents
- *κατὰ ψιλόν, καθότι παρειλήφαμεν*: This is the writer’s own gloss on the phrase before. κατὰ ψιλόν is “barely, with nothing added”. The last words say “according as” the thing has been received, with the verb in the first person plural. Other reading: that is, on bare trust, just as it has been received

</details>

### 4.47

Just as, if one of the gods told you that you will die tomorrow or at any rate the day after, you would no longer count it a great thing that it should be the day after rather than tomorrow, unless you are utterly abject (for how much is the gap between?), so too think it nothing great that it should be many years from now rather than tomorrow.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *εἰς τρίτην*: Literally “on the third (day)”. Greek counts today as the first, so this is the day after tomorrow. Other reading: or at any rate on the third day
- *παρὰ μέγα ἐποιοῦ*: An idiom: to reckon something as making a great difference. Other reading: you would no longer make much of the day after as against tomorrow
- *ἐσχάτως ἀγεννὴς*: ἀγεννής is “low-born” and so “ignoble, without spirit, cowardly”. English must pick one; “abject” keeps both the lowness and the want of spirit. Other reading: unless you are a coward to the last degree
- *πόσον γάρ ἐστι τὸ μεταξύ*: “How much” is asked expecting the answer “very little”. The question is kept as it stands and set in brackets, so that the sentence can run on to “so too” as the Greek does. Other reading: for how small is the difference!
- *εἰς πολλοστὸν ἔτος*: Literally “in the many-eth year”, an ordinal made from “many”: in a year a long way down the count. Other reading: that it should be in some far-off year rather than tomorrow

</details>

### 4.48

Keep in mind continually how many doctors have died, after many times knitting their brows over the sick; how many astrologers, after foretelling other people’s deaths as if that were something great; how many philosophers, after insisting on countless things about death or immortality; how many champions, after killing many; how many tyrants, after using their power over lives with terrible arrogance, as if they were immortal; and how many whole cities have, so to speak, died: Helice and Pompeii and Herculaneum and countless others. Go over as well all those you know, one after another. One buried this person and was then laid out, another buried that one, and all of it in a short time. For the sum of it is this: always see human things as lasting a day and cheap, yesterday a little slime, tomorrow a mummy or ash. So pass through this instant of time in accord with nature and come to rest with good grace, as an olive might fall when it has grown ripe, speaking well of the earth that bore it and grateful to the tree that grew it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐννοεῖν συνεχῶς*: The verb is an infinitive used as an instruction, with no person. The English uses the bare command, which names no “you” either; the same holds for the later infinitives in the passage. Other reading: To keep in mind continually
- *μαθηματικοί*: At this date the word commonly means astrologers, and foretelling deaths fits that. It can also mean mathematicians or men of learning. Other reading: mathematicians
- *μυρία διατεινάμενοι*: The verb is to maintain a thing with all one’s force, from a root meaning “stretch”. The Greek says only “countless things”, with no word for arguments, and the English takes the verb as vehement assertion. Other reading: after straining over countless arguments about death or immortality
- *ἀριστεῖς*: The word names those who win the prize for valour, the best fighters. The killing that follows shows that the field is war. Other reading: the bravest fighters
- *ἐξουσίᾳ ψυχῶν*: ψυχῶν can be “lives” or “souls”. The English takes the power of life and death. Other reading: their authority over souls
- *μετὰ δεινοῦ φρυάγματος*: φρύαγμα is first the snorting of a spirited horse, then insolent pride. The English gives the sense and loses the horse. Other reading: with a terrible snorting
- *ἐξετάθη*: Literally “was stretched out”, that is, laid out as a corpse. Other reading: was then stretched out
- *ὁ δὲ ἐκεῖνον*: The Greek sets “this one” against “that one” and leaves the verb to be carried over. “That one” may be a different dead person, as the English has it, or the first burier, which makes a chain of burials. Other reading: and another buried him
- *τὸ γὰρ ὅλον*: Here the phrase is adverbial, “on the whole, in sum”, not “the whole” of the glossary. Other reading: For, in a word,
- *μυξάριον*: A diminutive of the word for mucus or slime. It points to the seed a human being starts from; the English keeps the plain image. Other reading: a drop of mucus
- *τάριχος*: The word means fish or meat preserved in salt, and is also used of an embalmed body. Beside “ash” the English takes the body, as “a mummy”, and loses the kitchen sense with its contempt. Other reading: a piece of salt fish
- *ἵλεων καταλῦσαι*: καταλῦσαι is to unyoke at the end of a day’s journey, to put up for the night, and so to end life. ἵλεων ranges from “gracious, kindly” to “cheerful”; “with good grace” is meant to hold the willing, ungrudging mood. Other reading: and come to your lodging cheerful
- *τὴν ἐνεγκοῦσαν*: Literally “her who bore it”, with no noun. The phrase is a common way of naming the land that bore one, so “the earth” is supplied; “nature” is also possible. Other reading: speaking well of her who bore it

</details>

### 4.49a

To be like the headland against which the waves break without pause; but it stands, and around it the water that had swelled up is put to sleep.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὅμοιον εἶναι*: An infinitive used as a note of what is to be done, with no person, kept as “To be like”. Other reading: Be like
- *τῇ ἄκρᾳ*: A point of land running out into the sea: a headland or cape. Other reading: the promontory
- *κοιμίζεται*: Literally “is put to sleep”, of the sea being stilled. The English keeps the image. Other reading: is calmed
- *τὰ φλεγμήναντα τοῦ ὕδατος*: Literally “the parts of the water that became inflamed”, a medical word for swelling and heat, in a past form: what had risen before it reached the headland. The English keeps the swelling and loses the heat. Other reading: the seething of the water

</details>

### 4.49b

“I am unfortunate, because this has happened to me.” No, rather: “I am fortunate, because although this has happened to me I go on undistressed, neither broken by what is present nor afraid of what is coming.” For a thing of this kind could have happened to anyone, but not everyone would have gone on undistressed at it. Why then is that a misfortune rather than this a piece of good fortune? And do you call anything at all a human being’s misfortune that is not a failure of the human being’s nature? And does anything seem to you to be a failure of the human being’s nature that is not against what that nature wills? Well then: you have learned what it wills. Surely this that has happened does not prevent you from being just, great-hearted, self-controlled, sensible, not rash, not deceived, modest, free, and the rest, the things with which, when they are present together, the human being’s nature has in full what is its own? From now on, remember, at everything that leads you towards distress, to use this principle: not “this is a misfortune”, but “to bear it nobly is good fortune.”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἀτυχὴς ἐγώ*: The passage begins part-way through the chapter. The Greek has no quotation marks; they are added for the two things said. The argument plays on ἀτυχής, εὐτυχής, ἀτύχημα, εὐτύχημα, so “unfortunate, fortunate, misfortune, good fortune” are kept. Other reading: Unlucky me, that this has happened to me.
- *ἄλυπος*: “Without λύπη”. λύπη is “distress” throughout the section, and “pain” is kept for πόνος. Other reading: I go on free of pain
- *ἀπότευγμα*: A “miss”, a failure to hit the mark. It shares its root with ἀτύχημα (“misfortune”), which English cannot show: a misfortune of a human being must be a missing of human nature’s mark. Other reading: a miscarriage of human nature
- *τὸ βούλημα τῆς φύσεως αὐτοῦ*: Literally “the will of his nature”, that is, of the human being’s nature. “What that nature wills” avoids “his” for ἄνθρωπος. Other reading: against the purpose of his nature
- *μεγαλόψυχον*: Literally “great-souled”: a person too large in spirit to be shaken by what happens. Other reading: great-souled
- *ἀπρόπτωτον*: A Stoic term: not “falling forward”, that is, not rushing into assent before a thing is clear. Other reading: unhurried in assent
- *ἀδιάψευστον*: The word can be passive (“not deceived, not in error”) or active (“not deceiving, truthful”). After “not rash” it is taken as passive. Other reading: truthful
- *αἰδήμονα*: Having αἰδώς: a sense of shame and of respect for others. “Modest” narrows it. Other reading: self-respecting
- *ἀπέχει τὰ ἴδια*: ἀπέχω is the word used on receipts, “to have received in full”. Human nature, when these qualities are present, has been paid what is its own. Other reading: has received all that belongs to it
- *λοιπὸν*: λοιπόν can be “from now on” or a plain “so then”. The English takes the first. Other reading: So then, remember
- *γενναίως*: “Nobly”, as befits good birth; it also covers “bravely”. Other reading: to bear it bravely

</details>

### 4.50

A layman’s help toward contempt of death, but an effective one all the same, is to call back to mind those who clung on and lingered in life. What more do they have, then, than those who died before their time? In any case they lie somewhere or other, Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus or anyone else of that kind, who carried many out to burial and then were carried out themselves. Altogether, the interval is small, and even this, through how many things, in what company and in what a little body it is drained out! So do not treat it as something that matters. For look behind at the yawning expanse of eternity, and ahead at another that has no limit. In this, then, what difference is there between a child three days old and a Nestor of three generations?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἰδιωτικὸν*: ἰδιωτικός is what belongs to a private person or a non-expert, here as against a philosopher’s argument. It can carry a slight of “crude” or “vulgar”. Other reading: An unphilosophical help
- *γλίσχρως ἐνδιατριψάντων τῷ ζῆν*: γλίσχρως is “stickily”, used of clinging and of stinginess. Literally “those who spent their time stickily in living”; the English gives the adverb as “clung on”. ἀναπόλησις before it is a going over again in the mind, here “call back to mind”. Other reading: those who hung on greedily to being alive
- *πάντως πού ποτε κεῖνται*: πού ποτε can be “somewhere or other” or “somewhere, at some time”, and πάντως can be “in any case” or “surely”. κεῖνται, “they lie”, is the ordinary word for the dead lying in their graves. Other reading: Surely they lie somewhere at last
- *Καδικιανός*: The name is transliterated as it is given. From memory, unchecked: other editions print Καιδικιανός, Caedicianus. The four men are not explained in the text; the context makes them people known for living long. Other reading: Caedicianus
- *ἐξήνεγκαν, εἶτα ἐξηνέχθησαν*: ἐκφέρειν, “to carry out”, is the set word for carrying a body out to its funeral. “To burial” is added once so that the sense is clear. Other reading: who carried out many, then were carried out
- *ὅλον, μικρόν ἐστι τὸ διάστημα*: With the comma as given, ὅλον is an adverb, “on the whole, in sum”. Without it the words would say “the whole interval is small”. Other reading: The whole interval is small
- *καὶ τοῦτο δι’ ὅσων καὶ μεθ’ οἵων ἐξαντλούμενον καὶ ἐν οἵῳ σωματίῳ;*: The Greek as given ends this sentence with a question mark, but its words (“through how many”, “with what sort”, “in what a”) are those of an exclamation, not of a question. There is also no finite verb after “and even this”, only a participle. The English makes it an exclamation and supplies “it is”. Other reading: Altogether, is the interval not small, and even this drained out through how many things, in what company and in what a little body?
- *ἐξαντλούμενον*: The image is of baling or draining water out to the last, used for toiling through something. “Through how many” and “with what sort” do not say whether things or people are meant: the English reads the first as things, most likely troubles, and the second as people, “in what company”. σωματίῳ is a diminutive that belittles the body. Other reading: and even this is toiled through amid how many troubles, with what sort of things and in what a poor little body
- *μὴ οὖν ὡς πρᾶγμα*: There is no verb: literally “not, then, as a matter”, with πρᾶγμα in the sense of something that counts. The English supplies “treat it” and gives πρᾶγμα as “something that matters”. Other reading: So, not as though it were something
- *τὸ ἀχανὲς τοῦ αἰῶνος*: τὸ ἀχανές is “the yawning”, an adjective used as a noun, so English must supply a noun: “expanse”. αἰών is the whole of time, given as “eternity”. Other reading: the gaping gulf of time
- *τὸ πρόσω ἄλλο ἄπειρον*: ἄπειρον can be taken with an understood “expanse” (another, without limit, ahead) or as a noun (what lies ahead is another infinity). The English takes the first. Other reading: and what lies ahead, another infinity
- *τριγερηνίου*: A made-up word that plays on “Gerenian”, Homer’s standing name for Nestor, the old king who outlived three generations, and on γέρων, “old man”: one who is three times a Nestor. The English names Nestor and gives the three as generations. τριήμερος before it is “of three days”, taken as a child three days old. Other reading: between the one who lives three days and the one who lives three generations

</details>

### 4.51

Always run to the short road. And the short road is the one according to nature, so that you say and do everything in the soundest way. For a purpose of this kind frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐπὶ τὴν σύντομον*: The noun is left out, as Greek does with “road”: “the short [road]”. ἐπί with the accusative is “to” or “for”: make for the short road and take it. Other reading: Always run by the short road.
- *ὥστε κατὰ τὸ ὑγιέστατον πᾶν λέγειν καὶ πράσσειν*: ὥστε with the infinitive gives the result. ὑγιέστατον is “healthiest”, and so soundest. No subject is expressed; “you” comes from the command before. Other reading: so as to say and do everything in the healthiest way
- *ἀπαλλάσσει γὰρ ἡ τοιαύτη πρόθεσις*: πρόθεσις is a purpose set before oneself. The verb has no object; “you” is supplied from the command that opens the passage. Other reading: For such a resolve sets a person free
- *στραγγείας*: A rare word, “loitering, hanging back, delay”, translated as given. From memory, unchecked: the word is an editor’s correction, and the manuscripts have στρατείας, “campaigning, warfare”. Other reading: from toils and campaigning
- *οἰκονομίας καὶ κομψείας*: οἰκονομία is managing a household and so, in speech and conduct, arranging things for effect; κομψεία is smartness, refinement put on for show. Both are meant in a bad sense. Other reading: from all management and cleverness

</details>

## Book 5

### 5.1

At dawn, when you are reluctant to get up, have this ready to hand: “I am getting up to do a human being’s work. Why then am I discontented, if I am on my way to do the things I was born for, the things for whose sake I was brought into the universe? Or was I made for this, to lie under the blankets and keep myself warm?” “But this is more pleasant.” So were you born to feel pleasure? And in general, were you born to be acted on or to act? Do you not see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees doing what is their own to do and, for their part, putting the universe together? And then you are not willing to do what belongs to a human being? You do not run to what is according to your nature? “But one must rest too.” I say so too. Nature, though, has given measures for this as well; it has given them for eating and drinking as well; and yet you go beyond the measures, beyond what is enough. But in your actions it is not so: there you stop short of what you can do. For you do not love yourself, since otherwise you would love your nature too, and what it wills. But those who love their own crafts wear themselves away at the works of those crafts, unwashed and unfed. Do you honour your own nature less than the engraver honours engraving, or the dancer dancing, or the money-lover money, or the lover of empty fame their scrap of fame? These people too, when the passion takes them, would sooner advance the things they care about than eat or sleep. But to you do social actions seem cheaper and worth less effort?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *δυσόκνως*: A very rare adverb, apparently “with a sluggish reluctance”. The English reads “reluctant”. From memory, unchecked: editors have doubted the form. Other reading: when you wake up sluggish and unwilling
- *δυσκολαίνω*: The verb is to be hard to please, out of humour. “Discontented” keeps it a mood; it can also be heard as complaining aloud. Other reading: Why then am I grumbling
- *στρωματίοις*: A diminutive, “little bedclothes”, with a touch of scorn that “blankets” does not show. Other reading: to lie in little bedclothes and keep myself warm
- *ἀλλὰ τοῦτο ἥδιον*: The Greek has no speaker marks. The opening is taken as words to say to oneself, this sentence and the later one about rest as objections from the part that wants to stay in bed, and the rest as the reply in the second person. Other reading: But staying here is more pleasant.
- *ὅλως δὲ σὺ πρὸς πεῖσιν ἢ πρὸς ἐνέργειαν*: The noun πεῖσις is being acted on, passive experience, as against activity. The one Greek sentence is split into two questions. From memory, unchecked: the text here is disputed and other editions print something different. Other reading: So you were born for pleasure, and in general for feeling things, or for doing them?
- *τὰ φυτάρια, τὰ στρουθάρια*: Both are diminutives, kept as “little”. The second word is strictly “little sparrows” and loosely any small birds. Other reading: the little plants, the little sparrows
- *συγκροτούσας κόσμον*: The same word as “the universe” a few lines above, here without the article: literally “putting together an order”, each as far as lies with it; the English keeps “the universe” so the echo is heard. The participle is feminine, agreeing with the bees, but is taken to cover the whole list. From memory, unchecked: other editions print a different participle here, meaning “helping to set in order”. Other reading: and, for their part, putting together an order; or: each putting in order the world that is its own
- *ἡ φύσις ἔδωκε μέντοι*: The text as given has no stop between the two clauses, which looks like a slip of the copy. The English reads a break after “nature” and keeps the repeated verb. Other reading: Nature has given measures for this too, just as it has for eating and drinking
- *ἐντὸς τοῦ δυνατοῦ*: Literally “but in actions no longer, but inside the possible”: in rest the measure is passed, in action the limit of what can be done is not even reached. The English supplies “it is not so” and “there you stop”, and turns “inside the possible” as “short of what you can do”. Other reading: but in your actions you do not, and stay within what is possible
- *συγκατατήκονται*: The verb is “melt away together with”: they waste away along with their work. The English reads “wear themselves away at”. Other reading: waste away together with the works of their crafts
- *τορευτὴς*: A craftsman who works metal in relief, a chaser or embosser. “Engraver” is the nearest plain word. Other reading: the metal-chaser honours metal-chasing
- *δοξάριον*: A belittling diminutive of the word for fame, and it picks up the word just before it, “lover of empty fame”, as “money” picks up “money-lover”. The English reads “scrap of fame”. Other reading: their little bit of glory
- *πρὸς ἃ διαφέρονται*: The verb is taken in its sense “to be concerned about, to care for”. It more often means “to differ, to be at odds”, which does not fit here. Other reading: the things they are carried away by

</details>

### 5.2

How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troublesome or out of place, and at once to be in a complete calm.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀπαλεῖψαι*: To wipe out or rub out, as writing from a tablet or a mark from a surface. The image is kept. Other reading: to erase
- *φαντασίαν*: φαντασία, “impression”: what presents itself to the mind, the Stoic term. Other reading: every thought; every appearance
- *τὴν ὀχληρὰν ἢ ἀνοίκειον*: ὀχληρός is troublesome, pressing in on one. ἀνοίκειος is not one’s own, foreign, and also unfitting. “Out of place” is taken as the English that says “does not belong here”. Other reading: every impression that is disturbing or alien
- *ἐν πάσῃ γαλήνῃ*: γαλήνη is the stillness of the sea, and “a calm” is meant to keep that. πάσῃ is “all”, here “complete”; it answers πᾶσαν, “every”, earlier in the sentence, an echo the English does not keep. Other reading: in all calm; in perfect stillness

</details>

### 5.3

Judge yourself worthy of every word and deed that accords with nature, and do not let the blame or the talk that comes afterward from some people pull you away; but if it is a fine thing to have been done or said, do not judge yourself unworthy of it. For those people have a ruling part of their own and act on an impulse of their own. You, for your part, do not look round at those things, but go the straight road right through, following your own nature and the common nature; and the road of these two is one.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *μὴ σεαυτὸν ἀπαξίου*: The verb is built on the same word as “worthy” in the opening words, so the English has “judge yourself worthy” and “do not judge yourself unworthy”. The words “of it” are supplied. Other reading: do not think it beneath you
- *τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν*: The article is singular and stands next to “deed”. The English takes it with both “word” and “deed”. Other reading: of every word, and of every deed that accords with nature
- *ἡ ἐπακολουθοῦσά τινων μέμψις ἢ λόγος*: Here the word that elsewhere means “reason” is plainly what people say, so “talk”. The participle is “following upon”, that is, coming after the word or deed; it could also be heard as blame that dogs a person. Other reading: the blame or the talk of certain people that dogs you
- *περισπάτω*: Literally to draw off to one side, so to distract. The English keeps the pull, since the passage goes on to a straight road. Other reading: distract you
- *εἰ καλὸν πεπρᾶχθαι ἢ εἰρῆσθαι*: The word for “fine” covers right, honorable and beautiful. The two verbs are passive and look back on a finished act, “to have been done or said”, and the English keeps them so. Other reading: if it is right that it should have been done or said
- *ἰδίᾳ ὁρμῇ χρῶνται*: Literally “use an impulse of their own”. “Their own” here means private to them, set against “your own nature” below, where the same adjective returns. Other reading: use an impulse of their own
- *ἃ σὺ μὴ περιβλέπου*: The relative is neuter plural, so it points to their ruling part and their impulse, not to the people: “those things”. The Greek stresses “you” against “those people”, which the English gives as “You, for your part”. “Look round at” is the literal sense of the verb. Other reading: But you, do not gaze about at them
- *εὐθεῖαν πέραινε*: “Straight” is feminine with “road” understood, the road named in the last words, so the English says “road” in both places. The verb is the glossary’s “carry through”, which English does not say of a road; “go right through” keeps its sense of going on to the finish. Other reading: carry your course straight through

</details>

### 5.4

I make my way through the things that accord with nature until I fall and rest, breathing my last into that from which I draw breath every day, and falling on that from which my father gathered the bit of seed, my mother the bit of blood and my nurse the bit of milk; from which every day, for so many years, I have been fed and watered; which bears me as I tread on it and make free use of it for so many purposes.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *διὰ τῶν κατὰ φύσιν*: “Through the things according to nature”: these may be the events, the acts or the stages of a natural life. The vague “things” is kept. Other reading: travelling by the road that accords with nature
- *ἐναποπνεύσας μὲν τούτῳ*: “Having breathed out into this”, with the sense of breathing one’s last. It plays against ἀναπνέω, “breathe in”, rendered “draw breath”. The “this” is the air, which the Greek does not name; the English leaves it unnamed. Other reading: giving back the last breath to the air
- *ἐξ οὖ*: A slip in the digitised text for ἐξ οὗ, “from which”, as twice below. It is read so.
- *πεσὼν δὲ ἐπὶ τούτῳ*: The second “this” is the earth, again unnamed, and left so. πεσὼν repeats the earlier πεσὼν, so “fall” is used both times. Other reading: and falling upon the earth
- *τὸ σπερμάτιον*: A diminutive, like αἱμάτιον and γαλάκτιον after it: a little seed, a little blood, a little milk. “The bit of” serves for all three; the article could also be possessive (“his”, “her”). Other reading: his drop of seed, her drop of blood, her drop of milk
- *συνέλεξε*: One verb, “gathered”, serves father, mother and nurse. The thought is that each drew the seed, blood and milk from the earth. Other reading: collected
- *βόσκομαι καὶ ἀρδεύομαι*: Words used of livestock and of fields: “pastured and irrigated”. “Fed and watered” keeps a trace of that. The Greek present with “for so many years” covers the whole span up to now, which English says with “have been”. Other reading: have grazed and been watered
- *πατοῦντα*: The verb is “tread, walk on” and also “trample”. “Tread on” is kept. With the harsher sense of the next verb as well, the clause would say that the earth bears the speaker although he tramples on it and misuses it. Other reading: which bears one who tramples on it and misuses it for so many purposes
- *ἀποχρώμενον*: The verb ranges from “use to the full” to “misuse, abuse”. “Make free use of” leans to the first, which suits “for so many purposes”, but leaves a hint of the second. Other reading: and misuse it in so many ways

</details>

### 5.5

They cannot admire your sharpness of mind. So be it. But there are many other things of which you cannot say, “Because I am not made for it by nature.” Offer those, then, which are wholly in your power: being genuine, dignity, bearing hard work, not loving pleasure, not complaining of your lot, needing little, kindness, freedom, plainness, no idle talk, greatness. Do you not see how many things you are already able to offer, for which there is no excuse of want of natural gift or of unfitness, and yet you still stay down below of your own will? Or are you actually forced to grumble, to be stingy, to flatter, to blame your poor body, to try to please, to show off and to be tossed about so much in your soul, because you were built without natural gift? No, by the gods. Rather, you could have been rid of these long ago, and be faulted only, if at all, for being rather slow and finding things rather hard to follow. And this too you must work on, not disregarding it and not taking pleasure in your dullness.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Δριμύτητά σου οὐκ ἔχουσι θαυμάσαι*: “They” has no noun: people in general. The noun is sharpness or pungency, here of wit, and “of mind” is added so that it is not heard as harshness. The verb phrase is “they are not able to admire”, which can also be heard as “they have nothing to admire in”. Other reading: They have no sharpness of yours to admire
- *οὐ γὰρ πέφυκα*: Literally “for I am not by nature so”: the excuse as it would be spoken, beginning with its “for”, which the English gives as “Because”. The same root returns twice below as “natural gift”. Other reading: “I cannot, for I was not born for it”
- *τὸ ἀκίβδηλον*: A word from coinage and metal: not debased, not counterfeit. “Genuine” is said of coin and of people alike. Other reading: being unalloyed
- *τὸ ἀπέρισσον*: Literally “having nothing over”, nothing more than is needed. It may be plainness of living or of manner. Other reading: having nothing in excess
- *τὸ μεγαλεῖον*: Greatness or grandeur, with no noun to say of what, and the English leaves it bare. Greatness of mind is probably meant. Other reading: high-mindedness
- *κάτω μένεις*: Literally “you stay below”, with nothing to say below what: below what you could be, or simply low down. The English keeps the bare image. Other reading: you still fall short
- *γλισχρεύεσθαι*: From an adjective meaning sticky, hence close with money, mean, and also clinging or importunate. The English takes the money sense. Other reading: to be grasping
- *τὸ σωμάτιον*: A diminutive of “body”, which in Marcus is slighting. “Poor body” carries it. Other reading: your little body
- *καταγινώσκεσθαι*: The verb is to judge against someone, from finding fault to condemning. Its form here speaks of what would go on being said, not of a verdict already given, so “be faulted”. Other reading: and have been found guilty only
- *δυσπαρακολουθητότερος*: The adjective normally means “hard to follow”; here it must be said of the person who follows with difficulty, that is, is slow to understand. Both adjectives are comparatives, given as “rather”, and “things” is supplied. Other reading: rather slow to understand
- *καὶ τοῦτο δὲ ἀσκητέον μὴ παρενθυμουμένῳ μηδὲ ἐμφιληδονοῦντι τῇ νωθείᾳ*: “This” is the slowness: it too is to be worked on. The first participle can mean “disregarding” or “letting the mind wander off”, and the English takes the first. The Greek is impersonal; the English has “you”, since the whole passage addresses “you”. Other reading: And this too is to be trained, by one who does not let the mind wander and does not enjoy being sluggish

</details>

### 5.6

One kind of person, when they have done someone a good turn, is ready also to charge the favour to that person’s account. Another is not ready to do that, but all the same thinks of the other, privately, as a debtor, and knows what they have done. A third, in a way, does not even know what they have done, but is like a vine that has borne its grapes and looks for nothing more after it has once borne its own fruit. A horse that has run, a dog that has tracked, a bee that has made honey, and a human being who has done good, do not shout about it, but pass on to another thing, as a vine passes on to bearing its grapes again in season. So one must be among these, the ones who in a way do it without being aware of it. “Yes, but this is the very thing one must be aware of. For it is characteristic of the social being,” someone says, “to perceive that it is acting socially and, by Zeus, to want its fellow to perceive it too.” What you say is true, but you take what is being said now in the wrong way. Because of this you will be one of those I mentioned before, for they too are led astray by a certain plausible reasoning. But if you want to understand what it is that is being said, do not be afraid that because of it you will leave undone any social act.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τι δεξιὸν*: Literally “something right-handed”: something well done, obliging, kind. The English reads “a good turn”. Other reading: when they have done something helpful for someone
- *λογίσασθαι αὐτῷ τὴν χάριν*: A bookkeeping expression: to reckon the favour to the other person, as an entry they owe. The second type keeps the same idea (“as a debtor”), so the English keeps the image of an account. Other reading: to count the favour against them
- *ἵππος δραμών, κύων ἰχνεύσας, μέλισσα μέλι ποιήσασα*: These three stand in the nominative with no verb of their own, and “a human being” follows with a particle that can mean “and” or “but”. The English lets all four share the verb “do not shout about it”, which construes the Greek as given without adding a word. They can also be taken as loose further examples after the vine, with a new sentence beginning at “a human being”. Other reading: A horse that has run, a dog that has tracked, a bee that has made honey. But a human being who has done good does not shout about it
- *ἐπιβοᾶται*: The verb is “cry out” and, in this voice, also “call on others”, as witnesses or for help. The English reads “shout about it”. Other reading: does not call people to witness it
- *ἀπαρακολουθήτως*: “Without following it with the mind”. The objector answers with the positive verb of the same root, so “aware” is used in both places. “In a way” softens it: Marcus does not say flatly “unconsciously”. Other reading: who do it, in a way, without noticing
- *ἐν τούτοις οὗν δεῖ εἶναι*: As punctuated in this text the sentence is a statement by Marcus, and the objector begins at “Yes, but”. It could be punctuated as the objector’s question, answered “Yes”, with a new objection after that. The Greek marks the changes of speaker with dashes; the English uses quotation marks. Other reading: “So one must be among those who in a way do it without being aware of it?” Yes. “But this is the very thing one must be aware of”
- *φησί*: “He says” or “it is said”, with no subject. It may only mark the imagined objector, or the objector may be citing an authority. The English reads “someone says”. Other reading: For it is characteristic, it is said, of the social being
- *ἴδιον γάρ*: The word means what is a thing’s own and sets it apart from others. The English reads “characteristic of”. Other reading: For it is the mark of the social being
- *τὸν κοινωνὸν*: The one who shares in the association, here the person who receives the good. The word is from the same root as “social” and “socially” in the same sentence; English “fellow” does not show that link. Other reading: to want its partner to perceive it too
- *ἐκείνων ὦν πρότερον ἐπεμνήσθην*: The people “mentioned before” must be the first two kinds of giver, who keep an account. The second word is a slip of the copy for the relative pronoun and is read so. Other reading: one of those earlier ones I spoke of
- *λογικῇ τινι πιθανότητι*: Literally “by a certain rational plausibility”: an argument that looks reasonable. The glossary’s “rational” is awkward here, so the English reads “plausible reasoning”. Other reading: by something that has the look of logic
- *συνεῖναι*: This form could come from the verb “to be with”, but here it is the infinitive of “to understand”. In the last clause, “because of it” may point to this understanding or to acting without awareness; the English leaves “it” open. Other reading: if you are willing to grasp what is really meant
- *ἔργον κοινωνικόν*: The noun is “work” or “deed”, and it is of one root with the verb “is acting” above. “Act” is used here because “social work” would be heard as the modern profession. Other reading: any social task

</details>

### 5.7

A prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, down on the ploughland of the Athenians and the plains.” Either one should not pray, or one should pray like this: simply and like a free person.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Εὐχὴ Ἀθηναίων*: The Greek has no quotation marks; I take the prayer to run from 'Rain, rain' to 'the plains', with Marcus's comment after it. There is no article, so it could also be 'An Athenian prayer'. Other reading: An Athenian prayer
- *ὗσον, ὗσον*: A command to Zeus himself, “rain!”, said twice. Other reading: Send rain, send rain
- *κατὰ τῆς ἀρούρας τῆς Ἀθηναίων καὶ τῶν πεδίων*: ἄρουρα is ploughed or sown land. One preposition governs both nouns, so the plains may be the Athenians’ own or simply “the plains”; the English leaves that open. Other reading: on the ploughland and plains of the Athenians
- *ἤτοι οὐ δεῖ εὔχεσθαι ἢ οὕτως*: The second half has no verb; “one should pray” is supplied from the first. δεῖ can be “should” or “must”. Other reading: Either one must not pray, or only like this
- *ἁπλῶς καὶ ἐλευθέρως*: The first word is “simply, plainly, sincerely”; the second is “in the manner of a free person”: frankly, without servility, perhaps open-handedly. Marcus does not say what this is set against. οὕτως may also measure the two words: “as simply and freely as this”. Other reading: plainly and frankly

</details>

### 5.8

When people say, “Asclepius ordered horse-riding for this person, or cold baths, or going barefoot”, it is the same kind of thing as saying, “The nature of the whole ordered an illness for this person, or a maiming, or a loss, or something else of that kind.” For in the first case “ordered” means something like this: he set this in order for this person as suited to health. And in the second, what falls to each person has in some way been set in order for them as suited to fate. For we say that these things “fall” to us in just the way that builders say the squared stones in walls or in pyramids “fall” into place, fitting with one another in a particular arrangement. For in general there is one fitting-together; and just as the universe is made complete, as the body it is, out of all bodies, so fate is made complete, as the cause it is, out of all causes. Even people with no training at all understand what I mean, for they say, “It brought him this.” So then, this was brought to this person, and this was ordered for this person. Let us accept these things, then, as we accept the things Asclepius orders. After all, many of those too are rough, but we welcome them in the hope of health. Let the carrying out and completion of what seems good to the common nature seem to you the same kind of thing as your own health, and so welcome everything that comes about, even if it seems rather harsh, because it leads you there: to the health of the universe, and to the good progress and success of Zeus. For it would not bring this to anyone if it did not bring good to the whole. For not even any ordinary nature brings anything that is not suited to what it governs. So you should hold dear what falls to you, for two reasons. One is that it came about for you, and was ordered for you, and stood in some relation to you, spun together from far back out of the oldest causes. The other is that what comes to each person individually is also a cause, for the one that governs the whole, of good progress and of completion and, by Zeus, of continuance itself. For the complete whole is maimed if you cut through the connection and continuity at any point at all, of its causes just as of its parts. And you do cut through it, as far as it lies with you, whenever you are discontented, and in a way you destroy it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *συνέταξεν*: The verb means “arranged together” and is also the ordinary word for a doctor’s order. Marcus then explains it by the same verb without its prefix (ἔταξε, τέτακται), “set in its place, set in order”. The English uses “ordered” for the first and “set in order” for the second, so that the link can be heard. Other reading: Asclepius prescribed riding for this person ... “prescribed” means: he assigned this to this person
- *Ἀσκληπιὸς*: Asclepius is the god of healing. Sick people slept at his shrines and were given treatments to follow, often in dreams. Other reading: the god of healing ordered
- *τούτῳ*: Literally “for this one”, the way Greek says “for so-and-so”. The form is masculine but is used of any person, so the English reads “this person”. Other reading: for this man
- *ἀποβολὴν*: Literally “a throwing away”, so a loss of any kind: of property, of a limb, of a person. The Greek does not say which, and the English leaves it open. Other reading: a bereavement / the loss of something
- *πρὸς τὴν εἱμαρμένην*: εἱμαρμένη is the Stoic word for fate, literally “what has been allotted”. It is “fate” here and where it comes again below. Other reading: as suited to destiny
- *συμβαίνειν αὐτὰ ἡμῖν λέγομεν*: A play on words that carries the argument. The verb means “to happen” and, literally, “to come together”, which is how builders use it of stones. “Fall” (“fall to us”, “fall into place”) is used for every use of the verb in this passage to keep the link visible; elsewhere in this translation the verb is “happen”. Other reading: we say these things “happen” to us in the same sense in which builders say the squared stones “come together”
- *ἁρμονία ἐστὶ μία*: ἁρμονία is a joining or fitting of parts, and from that “harmony”. It picks up the verb “fitting” used of the stones just before, so “fitting” is kept. Other reading: there is one harmony
- *τοιοῦτον σῶμα συμπληροῦται*: Literally “is filled up into such a body”. “Such” can mean “the kind of body it is” or “so great a body”. The English takes the first, and does the same for “such a cause” in the matching clause. Other reading: is made up into so great a body ... so great a cause
- *οἱ τέλεον ἰδιῶται*: ἰδιῶται are people without special training, here in philosophy. The word does not mean “stupid”. Other reading: even complete laymen
- *τοῦτο ἔφερεν αὐτῷ*: An everyday saying with no stated subject: literally “this it was bringing to him”. τοῦτο could be the subject or the object; it is taken as the object, with an unnamed “it” doing the bringing, because the verb comes back later with a nature as its subject. “Him” is the saying’s own word for whoever is being spoken of. Other reading: This brought it on him
- *τῶν τῇ κοινῇ φύσει δοκούντων*: The same verb comes three times in this sentence: “let it seem to you”, “the things that seem good to the common nature”, which is the usual way of saying what someone has resolved, and “even if it seems rather harsh”. The English keeps “seem” for all three. Other reading: what the common nature has decided
- *ἐκεῖ σε ἄγειν*: As printed in the digitised text these are two words, “there” and “you”: “it leads you there”. The same letters as one word (ἐκεῖσε, “to that place”) would give “it leads there” with no “you”, and the reason given would be about the universe alone. Both are possible Greek; the English follows the two words as printed, and the printed edition was not checked. Other reading: because it leads there: to the health of the universe
- *τοῦ Διὸς εὐοδίαν καὶ εὐπραγίαν*: Zeus here stands for the reason that runs the universe. εὐοδία is literally “a good road”, so a going well; εὐπραγία is “doing well”, success in what one does. Other reading: the prosperity and welfare of Zeus
- *συνέφερεν*: A play on words: φέρειν is “to bring” and συμφέρειν is “to bring together” and so “to be good for”. The English reads “bring” and “bring good to” to keep the echo. The subject is not stated, as in the saying above; the next sentence shows that a nature is meant. The tense can refer to the present or the past. Other reading: it would not have brought this to anyone if it were not good for the whole
- *ἡ τυχοῦσα φύσις*: Literally “the nature one happens to meet”, that is, any nature you like, such as that of a plant or an animal. The contrast is with the nature of the whole. Other reading: not even a chance nature
- *στέργειν*: The word covers both “to feel affection for” and “to be content with, to put up with”. The English takes the warmer sense, because it answers “welcome” above. Other reading: you should be content with what falls to you
- *ἄνωθεν*: ἄνωθεν is “from above” and also “from the beginning, from far back”. Beside “the oldest causes” the English takes the sense of time. Other reading: spun together from above, out of the oldest causes
- *συγκλωθόμενον*: Literally “being spun together”, the image of the thread the Fates spin. The Greek does not say with what it is spun together, and the English leaves that unsaid too. Other reading: woven in with your thread from the beginning
- *τῷ τὸ ὅλον διοικοῦντι*: The form can be masculine (“him who governs the whole”) or neuter (“that which governs the whole”). Zeus has just been named, and “good progress” was his two sentences before, which favours the masculine. The English reads “the one that governs” and so leaves it open; the Greek has no “his” or “its” with the three nouns that follow. Other reading: for him who governs the whole, a cause of his good progress
- *πηροῦται*: The same word as the “maiming” in the first sentence (πήρωσιν), so “maimed” is kept. Other reading: the complete whole is mutilated
- *διακόψῃς*: The verb is “cut through, sever”, and it comes again in the next sentence. Literally “if you cut through anything whatever of the connection and continuity”. Other reading: if you break the connection and continuity at any point
- *ἀναιρεῖς*: Literally “you take away, do away with”. It can also mean “kill”. The object is not stated; “it” is supplied, meaning the connection. Other reading: and in a way you do away with it

</details>

### 5.9–10a

Do not be disgusted, do not give up, do not lose patience, if doing each thing from right principles does not come to you time after time; but when you have been knocked aside, come back again, and be glad if most of what you do is more in keeping with a human being, and love what you are coming back to. And do not come back to philosophy as to a schoolboy’s minder, but as people with sore eyes go to the little sponge and the egg, as another goes to a poultice, as to a medicinal wash. For in this way you will make no show of obeying reason, but will find rest in it. Remember that philosophy wants only what your nature wants; but you were wanting something else, not in accord with nature. For what is more agreeable than these things? For is it not through this that pleasure trips us up? But look whether greatness of soul, freedom, simplicity, fairness of mind, reverence are more agreeable. For what is more agreeable than wisdom itself, when you think of how the power of understanding and knowledge never stumbles and flows smoothly in everything?

Things are, in a way, so veiled that to not a few philosophers, and not ordinary ones, they have seemed altogether impossible to grasp; except that to the Stoics themselves, at least, they seem hard to grasp. And every assent of ours can shift: for where is the person who does not shift? Pass on, then, to the objects themselves: how short-lived they are, how cheap, how they can be in the possession of a catamite, a prostitute or a robber. After that go on to the characters of the people you live with: one can hardly put up with even the most charming of them, not to say that a person can hardly bear even themselves. In such gloom and filth, then, and in so great a flow of substance and of time, of movement and of the things moved, what there is that can be highly valued, or pursued in earnest at all, I cannot even imagine. For on the contrary …

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *καταπυκνοῦταί*: Literally “is packed thick”; the verb is rare. The English takes it of right action coming close together, “time after time”. It can also be read as “is fully achieved”. Other reading: if you do not fully succeed in doing each thing from right principles
- *εἰ τὰ πλείω ἀνθρωπικώτερα*: The Greek has no verb and no noun here: “if the greater part more human”. “Of what you do” is supplied. The comparative has nothing to be compared with, and can mean “more as a human being should be” or, modestly, “human enough”. Other reading: if most of it is human enough
- *παιδαγωγὸν*: The paidagogos was the slave who walked a boy to school and kept him in order, not a teacher. The English reads “a schoolboy’s minder”. Other reading: as to a schoolmaster
- *τὸ σπογγάριον καὶ τὸ ᾠόν*: Remedies for sore eyes: a small sponge for bathing them, and egg, probably the white, laid on them. The second detail is from memory, unchecked. Other reading: the eye-sponge and the egg-white
- *καταιόνησιν*: A medical word for pouring liquid over a sore part. The English reads “a medicinal wash”; the Greek does not say whether the liquid is warm. Other reading: a fomentation
- *οὐδὲν ἐπιδείξῃ τὸ πειθαρχεῖν τῷ λόγῳ, ἀλλὰ προσαναπαύσῃ αὐτῷ*: Both verbs are read as second-person futures: “you will make no show, you will rest”. “It” can be reason or the obeying; in the English it follows “reason”. Other reading: you will not be showing off your obedience to reason; you will be resting on that obedience
- *τί γὰρ τούτων προσηνέστερον*: “These” is open: the things that nature and philosophy want, or the thing wanted against nature, which makes the question an objection that the remark about pleasure answers. The English keeps “these things” and marks no change of voice. The word for “agreeable” also means gentle or soothing, which suits the remedies just named. Other reading: “But what is more pleasant than those things?”, said by the self that wanted them
- *σφάλλει*: The verb (trip, make fall, mislead) has no object in the Greek; “us” is supplied. The image comes back below in “never stumbles”, which is a different Greek word. Other reading: Is it not through this that pleasure deceives?
- *εὐγνωμοσύνη*: The word covers good sense, fairness, kindness and readiness to make allowances. The English reads “fairness of mind”. Other reading: kindness
- *φρονήσεως*: Phronesis, one of the four chief virtues: practical wisdom, good sense in action. The English reads “wisdom”, the word also used for it in 5.12. Other reading: good sense
- *τῆς παρακολουθητικῆς καὶ ἐπιστημονικῆς δυνάμεως*: Literally “the power that follows along and knows”: the faculty of following things with understanding and of sure knowledge. Whether one power or two is meant is not marked. Other reading: the faculty of attention and of knowledge
- *πλὴν αὐτοῖς γε τοῖς Στωικοῖς*: The first word can be “except that” (the Stoics, unlike those others, say “hard to grasp” and not “impossible”) or “and yet even”. The English takes the first. Marcus names the Stoics in the third person. Other reading: and even to the Stoics themselves they seem hard to grasp
- *συγκατάθεσις μεταπτώτη*: Assent (συγκατάθεσις) is the Stoic term for the mind’s agreeing to an impression. μεταπτώτη and ἀμετάπτωτος are one word and its negative, “liable to shift” and “not shifting”; “shift” is kept for both. Other reading: all human assent is fallible; for where is the infallible man?
- *τὰ ὑποκείμενα*: Literally “the underlying things”: the objects one deals with, the things themselves as against a grasp of them. The word after it can be “how” or “as being”; the English reads “how”. Other reading: Turn then to the things themselves, as short-lived and cheap
- *κιναίδου*: A term of contempt for a man who lets himself be used sexually by other men; it is also thrown loosely at any lewd man. “Catamite” is the nearest single English word. Other reading: a lewd man
- *ὧν μόλις ἐστὶ καὶ τοῦ χαριεστάτου ἀνασχέσθαι*: “Of them” can be the people or their characters: the Greek relative fits either, and “the most charming” can be masculine or neuter. The English leaves it open. Other reading: even the most agreeable of these characters can hardly be put up with
- *τοὐναντίον γὰρ*: The section cut falls in the middle of a sentence, so the Greek breaks off here. The two words are translated and the break is marked with three dots, which are not in the Greek. Other reading: For the opposite

</details>

### 5.10b

One must comfort oneself and wait for the natural dissolution, and not chafe at the delay, but rest in these things alone. One: that nothing will happen to me that is not according to the nature of the whole. The other: that it is in my power to do nothing against my god and spirit, for there is no one who will force me to go against him.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *δεῖ παραμυθούμενον ἑαυτὸν*: The Greek begins in mid-sentence and in the impersonal (“one must”), and moves to the first person further on. The words just before the cut, “for, on the contrary”, belong to this sentence and are not translated; the English starts a new sentence with a capital and adds nothing else. Other reading: one has to wait, encouraging oneself, for
- *τὴν φυσικὴν λύσιν*: λύσις is a loosening or undoing: death as the coming apart of what a person is made of. Other reading: the release that nature brings
- *τῇ διατριβῇ*: διατριβή is the spending of time, and so a delay; it can also be simply one’s stay or way of passing the time. Other reading: and not be vexed at the time spent here
- *τὸν ἐμὸν θεὸν καὶ δαίμονα*: δαίμων is the divine being allotted to each person, here set beside “god” as one and the same. “Spirit” stands for it, as in 2.17. Other reading: against the god and divinity that is within
- *τοῦτον παραβῆναι*: “To transgress against this one.” The Greek does not say who is forced; the first person is supplied from the sentence before. Other reading: there is no one who can compel anyone to disobey him

</details>

### 5.11

“Just what, then, am I using my own soul for now?” Ask yourself this at every turn, and examine: “What do I have now in this part, the one they call the ruling part? And whose soul, then, do I have now? Not a small child’s, surely? Not a youth’s? Not a silly woman’s? Not a tyrant’s? Not a farm animal’s? Not a wild beast’s?”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πρὸς τί ποτε ἄρα νῦν*: ποτε sharpens the question and ἄρα draws it as an inference. The English gives them as “Just what” and “then”. Other reading: What ever, then
- *ἐπανερωτᾶν ἑαυτὸν*: An infinitive used as an instruction, with the reflexive ἑαυτόν, which in later Greek serves for any person. The English reads “ask yourself”, since Marcus is addressing himself; the Greek does not mark the person. Other reading: To ask oneself this at every turn, and to examine
- *ὃ δὴ ἡγεμονικὸν καλοῦσι*: τὸ ἡγεμονικόν is the Stoic term for the governing part of the soul. “They” are those who use the term, presumably the philosophers, and δή marks the name as the familiar one. Other reading: which is called the ruling part
- *μήτι παιδίου*: μήτι introduces a question said with misgiving, hoping for the answer no, and it is repeated before each of the six nouns. The English repeats “Not” six times and adds “surely” to the first only. Other reading: Can it be a small child’s? Can it be a youth’s?
- *μειρακίου*: A μειράκιον is a lad in his teens or a little older. Other reading: Not a boy’s?
- *γυναικαρίου*: A diminutive of “woman” used with contempt. The Greek is dismissive and the English does not soften it. Other reading: Not a little woman’s?
- *κτήνους*: κτῆνος is a domestic animal, cattle or a beast of burden, set against θηρίον, a wild animal. Other reading: Not a beast of burden’s?

</details>

### 5.12

What kind of things they are that seem good to most people, you can gather from this as well. For if a person had in mind certain things that truly are good, such as wisdom, self-control, justice, courage, then with these in mind first they could not listen to the words “because of the good things”, for it will not fit. But a person who has first in mind the things that appear good to most people will listen, and will readily accept what the comic poet said as a fitting thing to add. So even most people have an impression of the difference. For otherwise this line would not jar and be refused in the one case, while when it is said of wealth and of the pieces of good luck that make for luxury or reputation we accept it as aptly and wittily said. Go on, then, and ask whether one should honour and judge to be good the kind of things which, when they have first been brought to mind, can fittingly be followed by the line that their owner, because of the plenty, “has nowhere to shit”.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κἂν ἐντεῦθεν λάβοις*: “You could grasp even from this”: from the test that follows. Other reading: you may learn from the following too
- *ὑπάρχοντά τινα ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθά*: ὡς ἀληθῶς is “truly”. The phrase can be “certain things that truly are good” or “certain existing things as truly good”. Other reading: if someone thought of certain real things as truly good
- *προεπινοήσας*: “Having thought of beforehand”. The verb comes three times with this prefix and once without (ἐπινοήσειεν); “in mind” and “first” are kept for it, and “brought to mind” for the passive at the end. Other reading: having first conceived of these
- *ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγαθῶν*: The opening words of a comic line whose end is given at the close of the passage: a man has so many good things that he “has nowhere to shit”. The Greek here is only “because of the good things”. Other reading: “for all his goods”
- *ἐπακοῦσαι*: To give ear to. It can also be taken as “to hear in addition”, that is, to hear the line tacked on. Other reading: could not bear to hear added
- *τοῦ κωμικοῦ*: “The comic poet”, not named. The line may be Menander’s (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: the writer of comedy
- *οὕτως καὶ οἱ πολλοὶ φαντάζονται τὴν διαφοράν*: καί is “even”: even ordinary people have an impression of the difference between the two kinds of good. φαντάζονται is the verb of “impression”. Other reading: So the many too perceive the difference
- *οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο μὲν οὐ προσέκοπτε*: The second οὐ is hard: taken strictly, the two negatives cancel and give the wrong sense. It is read as the first negative repeated, “for otherwise this would not jar”; editors may remove or bracket it (from memory, unchecked). “Otherwise”, “line” and “in the one case” are supplied. Other reading: for otherwise this would not fail to jar
- *παρεδεχόμεθα*: The verb is in the first person plural, where the rest of the passage speaks of “a person” and “most people”. Its tense is past, inside the “otherwise”, which is how Greek states what would be so now; the English has the present. Other reading: while we would be accepting it
- *εὐκληρημάτων*: Pieces of good luck, lucky gains. Other reading: the advantages that bring luxury or fame
- *ὑποληπτέον*: From the verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment”. Other reading: to be supposed good
- *οὐκ ἔχειν ὅποι χέσῃ*: The coarse word is in the Greek. τὸν κεκτημένον is masculine, “the man who owns them”, with no man singled out; the English has “their owner”. Other reading: that he who has them is so well off that he “has no place left to relieve himself”

</details>

### 5.13

I am made up of what is causal and what is material, and neither of these will perish into what is not, just as neither came to be out of what is not. So every part of me will be assigned, through change, to some part of the universe, and that in turn will change into another part of the universe, and so on to infinity. It was through a change of this kind that I too came to be, and my parents, and, for one who goes back, into another infinity. For nothing prevents one from saying so, even if the universe is governed in finite cycles.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐξ αἰτιώδους καὶ ὑλικοῦ*: Two neuter adjectives: “the causal” and “the material”, the Stoic pair of what acts or forms and what is acted on. They are kept as plain adjectives and not glossed as form and matter. Other reading: of a cause and of matter; of a formal and a material element
- *εἰς τὸ μὴ ὂν φθαρήσεται*: τὸ μὴ ὂν is “what is not”. The plain phrase is kept and used again for ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος so that the symmetry shows. Other reading: will be destroyed into nothing
- *ὑπέστη*: “Came to exist, subsisted.” The same verb returns as ὑπέστην below; “came to be” is used both times. Other reading: arose; had its existence
- *καταταχθήσεται*: A word of ordering and posting: to be assigned to a place in a rank. “Assigned” keeps that. Other reading: will be distributed into; will be reduced to
- *καὶ ἤδη εἰς ἄπειρον*: ἄπειρον is “the unlimited”, and the last sentence answers it with πεπερασμένας, “limited”, from the same root. “Infinity” here and “finite” there let the English show the link. Other reading: and so on without limit
- *οἱ ἐμὲ γεννήσαντες*: Literally “those who produced me”, from the verb used of a father or a mother having a child. In the plural it is an ordinary Greek way of saying “parents”, and the English uses that noun. Other reading: and those who brought me into being
- *ἐπανιόντι εἰς ἄλλο ἄπειρον*: The dative participle means “for someone going back up”, that is, tracing the line of ancestors backwards. The Greek then says only “into another unlimited”, with no noun and no word for “on”; “another infinity” adds neither. Other reading: and so, tracing the line upwards, into another series without limit
- *κατὰ περιόδους πεπερασμένας*: περίοδος is a circuit or recurring period, and the preposition is “in” or “by”: the governing goes cycle by cycle. This is taken as the Stoic teaching of world cycles, each with an end (from memory, unchecked). διοικῆται is the same verb of governing as in 6.5. Other reading: even if the universe is administered by periods that have a limit

</details>

### 5.14–15

Reason and the art of reasoning are powers that are content with themselves and with the works that are their own. So they set out from their own starting point and travel towards the end set before them, which is why actions of this kind are called katorthōseis, “acts that go straight”, as signifying the straightness of the road.

None of the things that do not fall to a human being, as a human being, should be called a human being’s. They are not requirements of a human being, human nature does not promise them, and they are not perfections of human nature. So the end for a human being does not lie in them either, nor does that which makes the end complete, the good. For if any of these things did fall to a human being, it would not fall to a human being to look down on them and rise up against them, nor would a person who proves to be in no need of them be praiseworthy, nor would a person who stints themselves in any of them be good, if these things really were goods. But as it is, the more of these things, or of others like them, a person bears to take away from themselves, or even bears having one of them taken away, the better that person is.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἑαυταῖς ἀρκούμεναι*: The verb with a dative usually means “to be content with”, but it can also be heard as “to be enough for”. The English takes “content with”, as in the opening of 8.7. Other reading: powers that are sufficient for themselves and for the works that are their own
- *ἡ λογικὴ τέχνη*: This can mean logic as a discipline, or more loosely the skill of using reason. “The art of reasoning” allows both. Other reading: the art of logic
- *κατορθώσεις*: A Stoic term for fully right actions. The word contains the Greek for “straight”, and the sentence explains the term by that, so the Greek word is kept in the English. The gloss “acts that go straight” is added for the reader and is not in the Greek. Other reading: which is why such actions are called “right acts”, as signifying the rightness of the road
- *Οὐδὲν τούτων ῥητέον ἀνθρώπου*: Chapter 15 begins here. The Greek says “none of those things … which do not fall to a human being” and never names the things; from what follows they seem to be outward things one can have or lose. No noun is supplied. Other reading: None of these things, which do not fall to a human being as a human being, should be called a human being’s
- *οὐκ ἐπιβάλλει*: The verb means “falls to one’s share, is one’s proper business”, and it comes three times in the argument. “Fall to” is used each time. Other reading: that are not a human being’s proper concern as a human being
- *ἀπαιτήματα ἀνθρώπου*: The Greek can mean things demanded of a human being, or things a human being requires or has a claim to. “Requirements of a human being” leaves it as open as the Greek. Other reading: They are not demanded of a human being
- *τελειότητές*: The word is built on the Greek for “end”, which follows in the next sentence: a perfection is a thing’s having reached its end. English cannot show the link. “Complete” is kept for a different Greek word in the next sentence. Other reading: and they are not ways in which human nature reaches its end
- *ὁ ἐλαττωτικὸς ἑαυτοῦ*: Literally “the one inclined to make himself less”, that is, to go short. The word is rare, and it can also be heard as taking less than one’s due. Other reading: a person who takes less than their share of any of them
- *ἢ καὶ ἀφαιρούμενός τι τούτων ἀνέχηται*: “Bears” is the only finite verb here and is taken with both participles: bearing to take things from oneself, and bearing to have one taken. It could be attached to the second only. Other reading: the more of these things, or of others like them, a person takes away from themselves, or even bears having one of them taken away, the better that person is

</details>

### 5.16

Whatever kind of impressions you often form, your thought will be of that kind; for the soul is dyed by its impressions. So dye it with an unbroken run of impressions such as these. For example: where it is possible to live, there it is also possible to live well; but it is possible to live at court; therefore it is also possible to live well at court. And again: each thing is carried toward that for the sake of which it was built; and what it is carried toward, in that lies its goal; and where its goal is, there also is the benefit and the good of each thing; therefore the good of a rational animal is community. For that we were born for community has long since been shown. Or was it not plain that the worse things are for the sake of the better, and the better for the sake of one another? And things with a soul are better than things without one, and rational things better than things with a soul.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οἷα ἂν πολλάκις φαντασθῇς*: The verb is the one from which φαντασία (“impression”) is made: “whatever sort of things you often have appear to you”. The English reads “impressions you often form” so that verb and noun stay one word. Other reading: Whatever kind of things you often picture to yourself
- *ἡ διάνοια*: διάνοια is “thought, understanding”, and also the mind as the thing that thinks. “Thought” is used, as elsewhere in this translation. Other reading: your mind will be of that kind
- *βάπτεται*: Literally “is dipped”, the dyer’s word; the same verb is the command in the next sentence, and “dye” is kept for both. Other reading: is steeped
- *τῇ συνεχείᾳ*: Literally “by the continuity of such impressions”, made concrete as “an unbroken run”. Other reading: by having such impressions continually
- *ἐν αὐλῇ*: αὐλή is a courtyard and then a ruler’s court: his household and the life lived around him. Marcus means his own. The building is not the point. Other reading: in a palace
- *πρὸς τοῦτο φέρεται*: The form can be passive (“is carried”) or middle (“moves, tends”). “Is carried” is kept both times; it need not imply an outside force. Other reading: each thing tends toward that for the sake of which it was built
- *τὸ συμφέρον*: “What is good for a thing”, built on the same verb as “is carried” just before; the echo cannot be kept in English. “Benefit” is used here because “the good” follows at once as a separate word. Other reading: what is good for each thing
- *κοινωνία*: The word covers “sharing, partnership, fellowship, community”. “Community” is used here and in the next sentence. It is the noun behind the adjective given as “social” elsewhere in this translation. Other reading: fellowship
- *πάλαι δέδεικται*: “Has been shown long ago”: the Greek does not say whether earlier in his own notes or in the teaching of his school is meant. The English leaves it open. Other reading: was proved long ago
- *τὰ χείρω τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν*: Plain comparatives, “worse” and “better”; they can also be heard as “lower” and “higher” in a scale of beings. Other reading: the lower exist for the sake of the higher
- *τῶν δὲ ἐμψύχων τὰ λογικά*: Taken as a comparison, in parallel with the clause before: rational things are better than things that have a soul and no more. The words can also be read as picking the rational ones out from among things with a soul. Other reading: and among things with a soul the rational ones are better

</details>

### 5.17–19

To chase after impossible things is madness. And it is impossible that bad people should not do things of this kind.

Nothing happens to anyone that they are not fitted by nature to bear. The same things happen to someone else, and either because they do not know that it has happened, or because they are showing off greatness of mind, they stand firm and remain unhurt. It is a terrible thing, then, that ignorance and the wish to please should be stronger than wisdom.

Things themselves do not touch the soul in any way at all, nor do they have a way in to the soul, nor can they turn or move the soul. But it alone turns and moves itself, and whatever verdicts it thinks itself worthy to pass, it makes the things that stand before it to be of that kind for itself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *φαύλους*: φαῦλος is “of poor quality, mean”: in Stoic use, everyone who is not wise. It is not the same word as κακός, which is “bad” elsewhere in this section; κακός does not occur in this passage. Other reading: that inferior people should not do such things
- *τοιαῦτά τινα*: “Some such things”: the Greek does not say which. Marcus has some particular offence in mind. Other reading: should not act in some such way
- *ὃ οὐχὶ πέφυκε φέρειν*: πέφυκε is “is so made by nature”. The subject is the person, not the thing. “Fitted by nature to bear” is used here and in 10.3. Other reading: that it is not in their nature to bear
- *ἀρέσκειαν*: ἀρέσκεια is the wish to please or to make an impression on others. It picks up “showing off greatness of mind”. Other reading: ignorance and vanity
- *δεινὸν*: “Terrible”, also “strange, shocking”. Other reading: It is a strange thing, then
- *φρονήσεως*: φρόνησις is practical wisdom, good sense in living. Other reading: stronger than good sense
- *αὐτὴ ἑαυτὴν μόνη*: “Itself, itself, alone”: the soul is both what turns and what is turned, and nothing else does it. Other reading: but it turns and moves itself, by itself
- *κριμάτων*: κρῖμα, a finding or verdict; “verdict” throughout the section, with “judgment” kept for ὑπόληψις. Other reading: whatever judgments it thinks itself worthy of
- *οἵων ἂν κριμάτων καταξιώσῃ ἑαυτήν*: Literally “of whatever verdicts it thinks itself worthy”. “To pass” is supplied; the phrase can also be heard as the verdicts the soul thinks fit for itself. Other reading: and whatever verdicts it thinks it deserves
