- *τὰ προσυφεστῶτα*: A rare word: the things that “stand there besides”, that is, that present themselves to the soul from outside. Its exact force is not certain. Other reading: the things that present themselves to it

</details>

### 5.20

In one respect nothing is more our own than a human being, in so far as we must do good to them and bear with them. But in so far as some of them stand in the way of the works that are our own, a human being becomes for me one of the indifferent things, no less than sun or wind or wild animal. By these an activity may be hindered, but there are no hindrances to impulse and disposition, because of the proviso and the turning round. For the mind turns round every obstacle to its activity and shifts it into what comes first, and what holds back this work becomes a help to the work, and what stands in this road becomes a way forward on the road.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *οἰκειότατον*: The superlative of “one’s own, akin”: literally “a human being is the thing most our own”. The same adjective comes back in “the works that are our own”, so “own” is kept in both places. Other reading: a human being is the thing closest to us
- *εἰς τὰ οἰκεῖα ἔργα*: The Greek says only “the own works” without saying whose. They are taken as ours, following “us” before, though “me” follows. Other reading: stand in the way of my proper works
- *τῶν ἀδιαφόρων*: The Stoic term for things that are neither good nor bad in themselves. Other reading: one of the things that make no difference
- *διὰ τὴν ὑπεξαίρεσιν καὶ τὴν περιτροπήν*: Two technical words. The first is literally “an exception made beforehand”: aiming at a thing with the proviso “if nothing prevents”, so that being prevented does not defeat the impulse. “Turning round” is explained by the next sentence, which uses the verb from the same root. Other reading: because it acts with reservation and can reverse things
- *εἰς τὸ προηγούμενον*: Literally “into what goes in front”: the obstacle itself becomes the mind’s first business. It can also be heard as “what leads forward”, something that furthers the activity, or as “something to be preferred”. “What comes first” is used for this word here and in 7.55 and 4.1. Other reading: and shifts it into something that furthers the activity
- *πρὸ ἔργου γίνεται τὸ τοῦ ἔργου τούτου ἐφεκτικὸν καὶ πρὸ ὁδοῦ τὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ ταύτης ἐνστατικόν*: Two idioms are played on: “for the work” means “useful” and “forward on the road” means “helpful”. The Greek sets each against “this work” and “this road”, and the English keeps “work” and “road” in both halves so the play shows. Other reading: what checks this work becomes useful, and what blocks this road helps one along

</details>

### 5.21

Of the things in the universe, honour what is supreme: this is what uses all things and directs all things. In the same way, of the things in you too, honour what is supreme: this is what is akin to that other. For in your case too, this is what uses the others, and your life is governed by it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ κράτιστον*: The word is the superlative both of “strong” and, in common use, of “good”: the mightiest and the best. “What is supreme” covers both, and is the same English both times. Other reading: honour the most powerful / honour what is best
- *τίμα*: The verb means to honour or to value highly, and is used of honouring gods. Other reading: revere / hold in highest value
- *πᾶσι χρώμενον*: Literally “making use of all”, as a workman uses tools. The same verb returns in the last sentence and “uses” is kept for both. Other reading: that which employs all things
- *διέπον*: The verb means to manage or conduct affairs. The English is “directs”, kept distinct from “governed” at the end, which is a different Greek verb. Other reading: and manages all things
- *ἐκείνῳ ὁμογενές*: Literally “of the same family (or kind) as that one”, pointing back to what is supreme in the universe. Other reading: what is of the same kind as that
- *ἐπὶ σοῦ*: The phrase means “in your case”, a different phrase from “in you” just before. Other reading: For in you too

</details>

### 5.22–25

What is not harmful to the city does not harm the citizen either. At every impression of having been harmed, apply this rule: if the city is not harmed by this, I have not been harmed either. And if the city is harmed, one should not be angry, but should show the one who harms the city what it is that is being overlooked.

Think often of the speed with which the things that are and the things that come to be are carried past and drawn away. For the substance of things is like a river in unbroken flow, the activities are in continual changes, the causes in countless turns, and almost nothing stands still, even what is close at hand. And the boundlessness of the past and of the future is a yawning gulf in which all things vanish. How then is a person not a fool who, among these things, is puffed up, or torn about, or complains bitterly, as though at something that troubled them for a time, and a long one?

Remember the whole substance of things, of which you have the smallest share; and the whole of time, of which a brief, momentary interval has been marked off for you; and fate, of which you are how small a part?

Someone else does me some wrong? That is for them to see to: they have their own disposition, their own activity. I now have what the common nature wants me to have now, and I do what my own nature wants me to do now.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀλλὰ δεικτέον*: From memory, unchecked: these words are thought to be an editor’s supplement, the manuscripts running straight from “one should not be angry” to “with the one who harms the city”. The English translates the text as given. Other reading: one should not be angry with the one who harms the city: what is it that is being overlooked?
- *τί τὸ παρορώμενον*: Literally “what the thing being overlooked is”. The Greek does not say who overlooks it; in context it is the person doing the harm. Other reading: what it is that they are failing to see
- *οὐσία*: The stuff of which things are made, “substance” or “being”. “Of things” is supplied here and in “the whole substance of things” in the next chapter, so that the word is not read as a bare term of the schools. Other reading: For all that exists is like a river
- *καὶ τὸ πάρεγγυς*: The phrase is uncertain. As punctuated in the text given, it closes the clause: “almost nothing stands still, even what is close at hand”. With other punctuation and a small correction (from memory, unchecked) it opens the next clause, about the gulf of past and future that lies close beside one. Other reading: and almost nothing stands still. And close beside you is the boundless gulf of the past and of the future
- *ἀχανές*: “Yawning, gaping”: used as a noun for an abyss. “Is” is supplied. Other reading: is an abyss
- *σπώμενος*: Literally “pulled” or “convulsed”: dragged this way and that. Paired with “puffed up” it seems to mean being torn about by events. Other reading: or racked
- *ὡς ἔν τινι χρόνῳ καὶ ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἐνοχλήσαντι*: The phrase is hard as given and the text is doubted (from memory, unchecked; a future participle has been proposed). The English takes τινι as the “something” that troubled the person and χρόνῳ as “for a time”; τινι can also go with χρόνῳ, “in some span of time”. Other reading: as though the thing that troubled them belonged to some span of time, and a long one
- *αἰῶνος*: αἰών is time without limit. The English has “the whole of time” and not “eternity”. Other reading: the whole of eternity
- *ἀκαριαῖόν*: From a word for something too short to be cut: a hair’s breadth, an instant. Other reading: a short, hair’s-breadth interval
- *πόστον εἶ μέρος*: πόστος asks “which in the series?”, “what fraction?”. The question mark stands in the text given, so the sentence turns into a question at its end. Other reading: of which you are what fraction of a part?
- *ἁμαρτάνει τι εἰς ἐμέ*: ἁμαρτάνω is to miss, to go wrong; with the words for “against” and the speaker it is to wrong someone. Other reading: Someone else makes some mistake against me?
- *ὄψεται*: Literally “he will see”: an idiom for “that is his affair, let him look to it”. The Greek subject is singular (“another”); “they” is used as the glossary allows. Other reading: He will see to that
- *ἡ κοινὴ φύσις*: The nature common to all things, the nature of the whole, set here against the speaker’s own nature. The same phrase is “the common nature” in 8.46. Other reading: universal nature

</details>

### 5.26

Let the ruling and governing part of your soul not be turned by the smooth or rough motion in the flesh, and let it not be blended in, but let it draw a line around itself and confine those feelings within the parts of the body. But when they pass up into the mind by the other shared feeling, as in a body that is one, then one should not try to go against the sensation, which is natural; but let the ruling part not add, from itself, the judgment that it is something good or bad.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν καὶ κυριεῦον τῆς ψυχῆς σου μέρος*: Here ἡγεμονικόν is an adjective with “part” and is paired with a second word, “being master”. At the end of the passage it stands alone as “the ruling part”. Other reading: The part of your soul that leads and is master
- *ἄτρεπτον*: “Not turned”: unmoved, unaltered. “Turn” is kept because the same verb is used of the soul in 5.19. Other reading: let it be unmoved
- *λείας ἢ τραχείας κινήσεως*: “Smooth or rough motion” is the language of the pleasure schools (Cyrenaic and Epicurean) for pleasure and pain. Marcus uses their terms. Other reading: by pleasure or pain in the flesh
- *συγκρινέσθω*: To be combined or compounded with something. The Greek does not say with what, the motion or the flesh, and the English leaves it unsaid too. Other reading: and let it not be blended with that motion
- *πείσεις*: What is undergone: the states the flesh is put into. “Feelings” narrows it a little. Other reading: those affections
- *ἐν τοῖς μορίοις*: “In the parts”: the parts of the body where the feelings arise. “Of the body” is supplied. Other reading: within the limbs
- *ὄταν*: The text given has a slip in the breathing; it is read as ὅταν, “when”. Other reading: whenever
- *κατὰ τὴν ἑτέραν συμπάθειαν*: Obscure, and the text is doubted (from memory, unchecked). συμπάθεια is the technical term for a feeling shared between joined parts, not pity, so “shared feeling”. What “the other” is set against is not said; it may be the shared feeling of mind with body, as distinct from that of one bodily part with another. Other reading: by that other sympathy which joins mind and body
- *εἰς τὴν διάνοιαν*: διάνοια as the faculty, “mind”. Other reading: into thought
- *τὴν ὡς περὶ ἀγαθοῦ ἢ κακοῦ*: Literally “the judgment as about a good or a bad thing”. Other reading: the judgment that treats it as good or evil

</details>

### 5.27

“To live with the gods.” And the one who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them their own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that the spirit wants, the spirit that Zeus has given to each person as protector and leader, a fragment of himself. And this spirit is each person’s mind and reason.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Συζῆν θεοῖς.*: A bare infinitive, which the edition sets in quotation marks as a saying. It can be a heading or a command; the English keeps the infinitive, and the next sentence then says who does live so. Other reading: “Live with the gods.”
- *συζῇ δὲ θεοῖς ὁ συνεχῶς δεικνὺς*: Literally “and he lives with the gods who constantly shows them”. The English turns this into “the one who … is the one who …” so that the long description does not trail far from its subject. Other reading: And a person lives with the gods who constantly shows them
- *τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν*: The Greek is “his own soul”: the soul of the person, not of the gods. “Their own” is written to avoid “he” for a subject not singled out as a man, so “them” is the gods and “their” is the person’s. Other reading: shows them his own soul
- *ἀρεσκομένην μὲν*: Two participles say what the soul is shown to be: content, and doing. The Greek can equally be put as a clause with “that”. Other reading: constantly shows them that their own soul is content with what is allotted and does all that the spirit wants
- *τοῖς ἀπονεμομένοις*: Literally “the things being dealt out”. The Greek does not say by whom or to whom, and the English adds neither. Other reading: pleased with what is assigned to it
- *ὁ δαίμων*: The daimon: a divine being that attends each person. The English reads “the spirit”, since the passage itself goes on to call it a protector and to say what it is. The word is repeated twice (“the spirit that Zeus”, “this spirit”) where the Greek has a relative pronoun and a “this”. Other reading: the guardian spirit; the divinity
- *προστάτην καὶ ἡγεμόνα*: The first word is one who stands in front: a protector, guardian, patron or chief. The second is a leader, one who gives the lead and is followed; it is the root of the Stoic term “the ruling part” (τὸ ἡγεμονικόν), so “ruler” is also possible, and “guide” is its milder sense. Other reading: as guardian and guide; as chief and ruler
- *ἀπόσπασμα ἑαυτοῦ*: The noun is from a verb meaning to tear or pull away, and names a detached portion of something. “Fragment” is the plain word for it; the more literal rendering spells out the root. Other reading: a piece torn off from himself
- *νοῦς καὶ λόγος*: Two nouns for one thing; both are kept, with this translation’s usual words for them. They may be meant as a single idea. Other reading: each person’s reasoning mind

</details>

### 5.28a

Surely you are not angry with the person who stinks like a goat? Surely you are not angry with the one whose breath smells? What do you want them to do? The person has that kind of mouth, has that kind of armpits; from such things such a smell must come. “But a human being has reason,” someone says, “and can work out, by stopping to think, where they are at fault.” Good for you! Well then, you have reason too: stir a rational disposition with a rational disposition; show them, remind them. For if they listen, you will cure them, and there is no need of anger.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τῷ γράσωνι*: γράσων is someone who smells like a goat, said of rank armpits, as “armpits” below shows. The goat is kept, and the same words are used for γράσωνα in 11.15. Other reading: the person whose armpits smell
- *μήτι ὀργίζῃ*: μήτι opens a question that expects the answer no. The Greek repeats the verb in both questions and so does the English. Other reading: Are you angry with
- *τί σοι ποιήσει*: Literally “what will he do for you?”. The person is taken as the subject and “for you” loosely, because the next sentence explains that they cannot help the smell. The words can also have the anger as subject, or mean what they mean in 11.18, where they are “what will that person do to you?”. Other reading: What good will it do you? (or: What will they do to you?)
- *τοιοῦτον στόμα ἔχει*: The Greek has no pronoun, only “has”. To avoid “he” where no man is singled out the English has “the person” and then “they”, although the Greek is singular throughout. Other reading: He has that kind of mouth, he has that kind of armpits
- *ὁ ἄνθρωπος λόγον ἔχει*: The words can mean a human being in general or this particular person. The general sense is taken: a human being, unlike a mouth or an armpit, has reason. Other reading: But this person has reason
- *φησί*: “He says”: an unnamed objector. The edition sets the objection between dashes; the English uses quotation marks. Other reading: it is said
- *τί πλημμελεῖ*: Literally to strike a false note in music; so to offend, to be at fault. Other reading: where they are out of tune
- *εὖ σοι γένοιτο*: A wish, “may it go well with you”, used as approval of the objection, perhaps with some irony. Other reading: Bless you
- *εἰ γὰρ ἐπαίει*: ἐπαΐω is to give ear and to understand. The English reads “listen”. Other reading: for if they understand

</details>

### 5.28b–29

Neither a tragic actor nor a prostitute.

The way you have in mind to live once you have gone out, you can live that way here. But if they do not allow it, then go out of life as well, yet as one who is suffering nothing bad. There is smoke, and I leave. Why do you think it anything much? But as long as nothing of that kind leads me out, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want. And I want what accords with the nature of the rational and social living creature.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οὔτε τραγῳδὸς οὔτε πόρνη.*: The last words of chapter 28, with no verb. The part of the chapter not given ends by saying that a person can be shown their fault without anger, so the words seem to set aside two manners, the stage performer’s and the prostitute’s. They are translated word for word, since the Greek does not say whether “be” or “there is need of” is to be understood. Other reading: Be neither a ranter nor a flatterer
- *Ὡς ἐξελθὼν ζῆν διανοῇ*: διανοῇ is “you have in mind, you intend”. ἐξελθών is “having gone out”, and the Greek does not say out of what. It is taken as leaving this place, because “go out of life as well” follows. Other reading: As you intend to live when you have departed
- *ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἐπιτρέπωσι*: “They” are not named: the people around him. Other reading: but if people will not let you
- *τότε καὶ τοῦ ζῆν ἔξιθι*: The same “go out” as ἐξελθών above, and ἐξάγει below is “leads out”; “out” is kept in all three. ἐξαγωγή, “leading out”, is the Stoic word for a reasoned leaving of life. Other reading: then depart from life too
- *καπνὸς καὶ ἀπέρχομαι*: Literally “smoke, and I go away”: the Greek leaves “there is” to be understood. From memory, unchecked, this is the image of the smoky room found in Epictetus: if the room smokes too much, one leaves it. Other reading: The room is full of smoke and I leave it
- *τί αὐτὸ πρᾶγμα δοκεῖς;*: πρᾶγμα here is “a matter of weight, a trouble”, which “anything much” gives. The words could also be read as a question about what the thing is. Other reading: What do you think the thing itself is?
- *μένω ἐλεύθερος*: μένω answers “leads me out”, so “I stay”, with “free” added to it. It could also be read as one phrase, “I remain free”. Other reading: I remain free
- *θέλω δὲ κατὰ φύσιν τοῦ λογικοῦ καὶ κοινωνικοῦ ζῴου*: The Greek repeats “I want” and gives it no object: “and I want in accordance with the nature of the rational and social living creature”. “What accords with” supplies the object. Other reading: and my wanting follows the nature of a rational and social animal

</details>

### 5.30

The mind of the whole is social. At any rate it has made the worse things for the sake of the better, and has fitted the better to one another. You see how it has ranked things one below another, one beside another, and has given to each according to its worth, and has brought the best things to be of one mind with one another.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κοινωνικός*: The word means made for partnership or community, acting for a shared life. “Social” is the nearest plain word and is the English settled for it across this translation, though it is weaker than the Greek. Other reading: The mind of the whole is a mind for community
- *γοῦν*: The particle offers what follows as evidence for the claim, without the full force of “because”. The English is “at any rate”. Other reading: For instance / Certainly
- *τὰ χείρω τῶν κρειττόνων*: The words are “worse” and “better”, words of value that also cover weaker and stronger, inferior and superior. The plain pair is kept so that “the best things” at the end can be heard as the top of the same scale. Other reading: the inferior things for the sake of the superior
- *ὑπέταξε, συνέταξε*: Two verbs from one root of ranking, “ranked under” and “ranked together”, set side by side with no connective. Neither has an object in the Greek; “things” is supplied once. Other reading: how it has subordinated, how it has coordinated
- *ὁρᾷς*: The form is the same for a statement and a question. The English takes it as a statement. Other reading: Do you see how it has ranked things
- *ἀξίαν*: The phrase is “what is according to worth”, a matter of rank or value. Other reading: has given to each what it deserves
- *τὰ κρατιστεύοντα*: Literally “the things that are best” or “that hold first place”, a word built on the superlative of “better” above. Whether it means the same group as “the better” is not stated. Other reading: the things of the first rank
- *ὁμόνοιαν*: Literally “sameness of mind”, the usual word for concord among citizens. “Of one mind” keeps the echo of “mind” in the opening sentence. Other reading: into agreement with one another

</details>

### 5.31

How have you behaved up to now toward the gods, your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, those who brought you up, your friends, those close to you, your household slaves? Does this hold of you up to now, toward all of them: “to have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong”? Call to mind, too, what things you have passed through and what things you have been strong enough to endure; and that the story of your life is now full and your service complete; and how many fine things you have seen; and how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many honours you have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people you have been considerate.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πῶς προσενήνεξαι*: The Greek gives no question mark. The opening is read as a question put to oneself; it could depend on an unspoken “consider”. Other reading: Consider how you have behaved up to now toward the gods
- *ἀδελφοῖς*: The plural is “brothers”, and can cover brothers and sisters together. “Brothers” is kept. Other reading: your brothers and sisters
- *τροφεῦσι*: Those who rear a child: nurses, foster-carers, the tutor who has charge of a boy. The English reads “those who brought you up”. Other reading: your tutors
- *οἰκείοις*: People who belong to one’s house or circle: kin, household, intimates. The English reads “those close to you”, and the same in 1.17a, where the word stands beside a separate word for relatives. Other reading: your relatives
- *εἰ πρὸς πάντας σοι μέχρι νῦν ἐστι τό*: Literally “whether toward all of them there is for you up to now the (saying)”. The “whether” has no verb to depend on, so the English makes a direct question; it could hang on the first sentence or on an unspoken “consider”. Other reading: and whether up to now it holds of you toward all of them
- *μήτε τινὰ ῥέξαι ἐξαίσιον μήτε τι εἰπεῖν*: A line of Homer, from the Odyssey, said of Odysseus as king and adapted to fit the sentence (from memory, unchecked). The adjective means “beyond what is right or due” and stands once in the Greek; the English repeats “wrong” to make the second half clear. Other reading: neither to have done anything out of bounds to anyone, nor to have said it
- *ἡ ἱστορία τοῦ βίου*: The noun can be a story or record, or an inquiry and what is learned by it. The English reads “the story of your life”. Other reading: that your acquaintance with life is now complete
- *λειτουργία*: A public service or duty performed for the community. The English reads “service”. Other reading: your public duty is finished
- *πόσα ὦπται καλὰ*: The verb is passive with no person named: “how many fine things have been seen”. The “you” is carried over from the clause before, where the Greek has “for you”. Other reading: how many fine things have been seen
- *ἡδονῶν καὶ πόνων*: The second noun is toil or hardship as much as pain. “Pains” is used because it stands here as the partner of “pleasures”. Other reading: how many pleasures and hardships
- *ὑπερεῖδες, πόσα δὲ ἔνδοξα παρεῖδες*: Two compounds of “see”: to look over the top of, so to look down on, and to look past, so to disregard. “Look” is kept in both. Other reading: how many pleasures and pains you have despised, how many honours you have disregarded
- *ἀγνώμονας εὐγνώμων*: A matched pair on one root: without right feeling (unkind, unfair, ungrateful) and with right feeling (kind, fair, generous). “Inconsiderate” and “considerate” keep the pair. Other reading: to how many ungrateful people you have been kind

</details>

### 5.32

Why do unskilled and ignorant souls throw into confusion one that has skill and understanding? Which soul, then, has skill and understanding? The one that knows beginning and end, and the reason that runs through the whole of substance and, through all of time, manages the sum of things in appointed periods.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *συγχέουσιν*: Literally “pour together”: to confound, upset, throw into confusion. Other reading: trouble
- *ἄτεχνοι καὶ ἀμαθεῖς*: Without τέχνη (art, skill) and without learning, answered by ἔντεχνος and ἐπιστήμων, having skill and having expert knowledge. The feminine adjectives that follow agree with an understood “soul”, supplied in English as “one”. “Understanding” is used for ἐπιστήμων so that “knows” is left for the different verb in the answer. Other reading: souls without art and without learning … one that has art and knowledge
- *ἀρχὴν καὶ τέλος*: ἀρχή is beginning or first principle; τέλος is end or goal. The plainer pair is kept. Other reading: origin and purpose
- *ὅλης τῆς οὐσίας*: οὐσία is the Stoic name for the stuff of which everything is made, which reason runs through and shapes. “Substance” is kept as the one word for it. Other reading: through the whole of what exists
- *κατὰ περιόδους τεταγμένας*: Fixed, ordered cycles; the same thought as the periodic rebirth in 11.1, so “periods” is kept. Other reading: in ordained cycles
- *οἰκονομοῦντα τὸ πᾶν*: οἰκονομεῖν is to manage a household. τὸ πᾶν, “the all”, is another name for the universe; “the sum of things” keeps it apart from “the whole” (τὸ ὅλον) and “the universe” (κόσμος). Other reading: administers the universe

</details>

### 5.33

Any moment now, ash or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; and the name is a noise and an echo. The things highly prized in life are empty and rotten and small, little dogs biting one another, quarrelsome children laughing and then at once crying. But good faith, a sense of shame, justice and truth: “to Olympus from the earth of the wide ways.” What is there, then, that still holds one here, seeing that the things the senses perceive change easily and do not stand still, the organs of sense are dim and easily take false imprints, the little soul itself is a vapor rising from blood, and a good name among such people is empty? What then? You wait cheerfully for what is either an extinguishing or a move elsewhere. And until the right time for that is at hand, what is enough? What else but to revere the gods and speak well of them, to do good to human beings, to bear with them and to hold back; and, as for everything inside the limits of the bit of flesh and the little breath, to remember that it is neither yours nor up to you.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὅσον οὐδέπω*: An idiom, “all but now”, “in next to no time”. The sentence has no verb and no subject; “you” is understood but not said, and it is not added. Other reading: Very soon you will be ash or a skeleton
- *σκελετὸς*: Literally “a dried-up thing”: a skeleton or a dried corpse. Other reading: ash or a dried-up corpse
- *πρὸς Ὄλυμπον ἀπὸ χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης*: Part of a line of epic verse, with no verb in Marcus’s sentence. From memory, unchecked, it is from Hesiod’s Works and Days, where Shame and Nemesis leave the earth for the gods. Olympus is the mountain home of the gods; the last word is an epic compound, “with wide ways”. Other reading: have gone “to Olympus from the wide-wayed earth”
- *τὸ ἐνταῦθα κατέχον*: “What holds here”: the Greek names no person. The English has “one” and not “you”. Other reading: What is there, then, that still keeps you here
- *εἴ γε*: “If, that is”, or “seeing that”: the conditions that follow are taken as fact. Other reading: if the things the senses perceive change easily
- *περιμένεις ἵλεως*: A plain present as given, “you wait”. With a different accent it would be a future, and it could also be punctuated as a question. ἵλεως is “well disposed”, “kindly”, also “cheerful”; “cheerfully” stands for it here and “cheerful” in 2.17. Other reading: Will you not wait serenely
- *τὴν εἴτε σβέσιν εἴτε μετάστασιν*: σβέσις is the putting out of a flame; μετάστασις is a removal to another place. Marcus leaves open which of the two death is. Other reading: for the end, whether it is extinction or a change of place
- *ἀνέχεσθαι αὐτῶν καὶ ἀπέχεσθαι*: Two verbs that differ by one letter, a rhyming pair (from memory, unchecked, a watchword of Epictetus). The second, “hold oneself off”, may stand alone, “to refrain”, or take “them” as its object, “to keep away from them”. The English leaves it without an object. Other reading: to bear with them and to keep away from them
- *ἐντὸς ὅρων*: “Inside the limits” as given: the body and breath themselves and what belongs to them are not yours. From memory, unchecked, some editors read “outside” here. Other reading: everything outside the limits of the bit of flesh and the little breath

</details>

### 5.34

You can always have your life flow well, if indeed you can also travel a good road, if indeed you can also judge and act step by step, as along a road. These two things are common to the soul of god, and of a human being, and of every rational living being: not to be hindered by anything else; and to have its good in a just disposition and just action, and to have its desire stop there.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Δύνασαι ἀεὶ εὐροεῖν*: The Greek says simply “you can always flow well”. “Have your life” is supplied because 10.6 uses the same verb of a life and English does not say that a person flows. Other reading: You can always flow well
- *εὐοδεῖν, εἴ γε καὶ ὁδῷ*: A chain of sound and sense: εὐροεῖν (flow well), εὐοδεῖν (have a good road), ὁδῷ (by a road). ὁδῷ is an idiom for “methodically, in due order”; the English gives the sense as “step by step”, as in 6.26, and adds “as along a road” so that the play can be followed. Other reading: if you can also go on your way well, if you can also judge and act methodically
- *ὑπολαμβάνειν*: The verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment” in the glossary: to form a judgment about things. Other reading: to think
- *τοῦ θεοῦ*: “The god” with the article, which in Marcus is god in general or the god of the universe. Lower case by the glossary. Other reading: the soul of the god
- *ἄλλου*: ἄλλου can be masculine, “by another person”, or neuter, “by anything else”. The English takes the wider sense, which includes the other. Other reading: not to be hindered by another
- *ἐν τῇ δικαικῇ διαθέσει καὶ πράξει*: δικαικῇ is a rare adjective, “of justice”, read here as the edition’s δικαϊκῇ. It governs both nouns, so “just” is repeated. Other reading: in the disposition and action that belong to justice
- *ἐνταῦθα τὴν ὄρεξιν ἀπολήγειν*: ὄρεξιν is taken as the subject of the infinitive, “desire coming to a stop there”. It can also be the object, “to bring desire to a stop there”. Other reading: and to end its desire there

</details>

### 5.35–36a

If this is neither badness of mine nor an activity that comes from badness of mine, and the community is not harmed, why am I upset over it? And what harm is there to the community?

Do not be swept off wholesale by the impression, but help as far as you are able and as far as is deserved, even if it is in the middle things that they are coming off worse; do not, however, form the impression that it is a harm, for that is a bad habit. But as the old man, on leaving, asked for his foster-child’s top, remembering that it was a top, so too in this case. Otherwise you become someone calling out on the Rostra. Man, have you forgotten what these things were? “Yes, but they are much sought after by these people.” And is that a reason for you to become a fool as well? I once was,

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κακία*: “Badness”, the usual word for vice. “Badness” is kept to match “bad” for κακόν elsewhere in the section. Other reading: If this is neither a vice of mine
- *τὸ κοινὸν*: “The common thing”: the community, or the common good. Other reading: and the common good is not harmed
- *διαφέρομαι*: The verb covers being at odds, being anxious and being put out about something. Other reading: why am I anxious about it?
- *τίς δὲ βλάβη τοῦ κοινοῦ*: The question can ask what harm there is to the community in this case, or what harm to the community is at all. The English takes the first. Other reading: And what is harm to the community?
- *συναρπάζεσθαι*: The commands in this chapter are infinitives (“not to be swept off … to help … not to form the impression”); the English writes them as imperatives. φαντασίᾳ and φαντάζεσθαι below are noun and verb of one word, so “impression” and “form the impression”. Other reading: Not to be carried away wholesale by the impression
- *βοηθεῖν*: “To help” has no object, and the English gives none. The plural “they are coming off worse” in the next clause shows that other people are meant. Other reading: but help them
- *κατ’ ἀξίαν*: “According to worth”: either what the people deserve or what the matter is worth. “As far as is deserved” leaves both open. Other reading: and as far as the matter is worth
- *εἰς τὰ μέσα ἐλαττῶνται*: Literally “they are made less in respect of the middle things”: the Stoic “middle” or indifferent things, neither good nor bad, such as money or health. The school term is kept as the Greek has it. Other reading: even if their loss is in things that are neither good nor bad
- *ὁ γέρων ἀπελθὼν τὸν τοῦ θρεπτοῦ ῥόμβον ἀπῄτει*: An allusion that is lost, probably to a scene in a play. θρεπτός is a child brought up in the house, a foster-child or a home-bred slave; ῥόμβος is a spinning top, or a bull-roarer. ἀπῄτει is “asked for as due” or “asked to have back”; the English has the plain “asked for”. Other reading: as the old man, when he went away, asked for his nursling’s top back
- *μεμνημένος ὅτι ῥόμβος*: “Remembering that it was a top”: the point seems to be that he humoured the child without forgetting how little the thing was. The participle may be concessive, “though he remembered”. Other reading: though he did not forget that it was only a top
- *ἐπεί τοι γίνῃ καλῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐμβόλων*: The Greek as given does not construe securely and the text is doubted (from memory, unchecked), so the English here is a guess. It takes ἐπεί τοι as “otherwise”, καλῶν as “calling out” and τὰ ἔμβολα as the Rostra, the speakers’ platform at Rome named after ships’ beaks: a man declaiming in public over such losses. Other reading: Since there you are, crying out on the Rostra.
- *ναί*: “Yes” is an odd answer to “have you forgotten?”; it may mean “yes, it is known what they are”. “Yes” is kept. The dashes in the text mark a second speaker, shown here with quotation marks. Other reading: “No, but these people set great store by them.”
- *τούτοις περισπούδαστα*: “To these people, things much striven for”: the word describes how eagerly the people pursue the things, not what the things are worth. Other reading: but these people are very keen on them
- *Ἐγενόμην ποτέ,*: The passage ends here with a comma, at the start of a new sentence, with nothing in the passage to say what the speaker once was or became. The fragment is kept and nothing is supplied. In the full chapter the sentence goes on to its own complement; as cut, it can be heard as an answer to the question about becoming a fool. Other reading: I once became,

</details>

### 5.36b

… wherever caught, a person whose lot is good. And “whose lot is good” means having assigned yourself a good lot; and good lots are good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὁπουδήποτε καταληφθείς*: The passage begins in the middle of a sentence and has no finite verb: the 1634 division puts the opening words of the sentence, “Once I was”, at the end of the section before. Nothing is supplied here, and the three dots mark the cut. καταληφθείς is “caught”, “overtaken” or “found”, and the Greek does not say by what. Other reading: wherever overtaken; in whatever place found
- *εὔμοιρος ἄνθρωπος*: εὔμοιρος ordinarily means “fortunate”, but it is built on μοῖρα, a share or lot, and the next two clauses argue from that. The English reads “whose lot is good” so that “lot” can be repeated. Other reading: a fortunate person
- *τὸ δὲ εὔμοιρος*: The article quotes the word just used and there is no verb; “means” is supplied. Other reading: And “fortunate” is: having assigned a good fortune to yourself
- *σεαυτῷ ἀπονείμας*: Second person: “to yourself”, with the participle in the nominative. ἀπονέμω is “assign” or “deal out” and is not formed from μοῖρα, so the English does not echo “lot” in it. Other reading: having dealt yourself a good portion
- *ἀγαθαὶ τροπαὶ ψυχῆς*: τροπαί are turns or changes of direction, and ψυχῆς has no article. “Turnings” is written because “good turns” in English means favours. Other reading: good dispositions of the soul; good changes of the soul
- *ἀγαθαὶ ὁρμαί*: ὁρμή, “impulse”: the movement of the soul toward an action, the Stoic term. Other reading: good strivings

</details>

## Book 6

### 6.1

The substance of the whole is obedient and ready, and the reason that governs it has in itself no cause for doing anything bad. For it has no badness, and it treats nothing badly, and nothing is harmed by it. And all things come about and are carried through in accordance with it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *οὐσία*: Here the stuff of which everything is made, the passive side of the universe as against the reason that works on it. The English is “substance”; “matter” would also serve. Other reading: The matter of the whole
- *εὐτρεπής*: The dictionary sense is “ready, prepared”. A reader might expect “easily turned” or “pliable”, which belongs to a similar-looking word, εὔτρεπτος, used in 6.36. The English keeps to the word printed. Other reading: obedient and pliable
- *λόγος*: The word covers reason, account and speech. Here it is the rational principle that runs the universe, and the English is “reason”. Other reading: the rational principle that governs it
- *αἰτίαν*: The word means cause, ground or motive. “Cause” is the English for it in the other passages too. Other reading: has in itself no reason to do anything bad
- *κακοποιεῖν*: Three words from one root follow one another: “to do bad”, “badness” and “badly”. “Bad” is kept in all three so the chain shows. The first could also be “to do harm”, and the middle one is the usual word for vice. Other reading: no cause for doing harm; for it has no vice
- *οὐδέ τι κακῶς ποιεῖ*: This can mean “treats nothing badly”, a common Greek idiom for doing harm to someone, or “does nothing in a bad way”. The English takes the first; the next clause then says the same from the side of the thing harmed. Other reading: and it does nothing in a bad way
- *ἐκεῖνον*: The pronoun is masculine because “reason” is a masculine noun in Greek. The English is “it”, not “him”. Other reading: in accordance with him
- *περαίνεται*: The verb means to be carried through to the finish, accomplished. The English is the same as in 6.9; it does not mean that things perish. Other reading: come about and are accomplished

</details>

### 6.2

Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting shivering or warm, and whether drowsy or having slept enough, and whether spoken ill of or praised, and whether dying or doing some other kind of act. For this too is one of the acts of life, the one in which we die. So in this too it is enough to manage well what is at hand.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μὴ διαφέρου*: The middle form: “do not let it make a difference to you”. Other reading: Do not care
- *τὸ πρέπον ποιεῖς*: τὸ πρέπον is “what is fitting, what is proper”. “You do” is the one verb for all four pairs, so the English puts it first and lets the later pairs lean on it. Other reading: whether you are shivering or warm when you do your duty
- *κακῶς ἀκούων ἢ εὐφημούμενος*: The idiom is literally “hearing badly”, that is, being ill spoken of. εὐφημούμενος is “being spoken well of”. Other reading: whether you are blamed or well spoken of
- *πράττων τι ἀλλοῖον*: Literally “doing something of another kind”. “Act” is put in because the next clause takes the verb up with πράξεων, “acts”, and the reason given depends on that link. Other reading: doing something else
- *μία γὰρ τῶν βιωτικῶν πράξεων καὶ αὕτη ἐστί, καθ’ ἣν ἀποθνῄσκομεν*: βιωτικαὶ πράξεις are the acts that belong to living. Dying is counted as one of them, and the verb turns from the second person to the first person plural. Other reading: for the act by which we die is itself one of the tasks of life
- *τὸ παρὸν εὖ θέσθαι*: Literally “to place well what is present”, an idiom for handling a thing well. τὸ παρόν can be the present moment or the thing in front of you. Other reading: to make good use of the present

</details>

### 6.3

Look inside. With any thing, do not let either its own quality or its worth run past you.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἔσω βλέπε*: Open: “look inside” can mean inside things or inside yourself, and the Greek does not say which. Because the next clause is about the quality and worth of things, the English is left as bare as the Greek, “look inside”, which leans towards inside things. Other reading: Look within yourself.
- *ἡ ἰδία ποιότης*: In Stoic use a thing’s quality is what makes it the kind of thing it is, and “its own” marks what is peculiar to this thing. The adjective is the one given as “its own” in 8.11 (“its own make-up”). Other reading: its particular quality, what it is in particular
- *ἡ ἀξία*: “Worth” or “value”, a Stoic term for how much a thing counts for. The English reads “worth”. Other reading: its value
- *παρατρεχέτω σε*: An image: “let it not run past you”, as something that goes by before you notice; the image is kept. The Greek is negative throughout, “of no thing let neither … nor …”, which the English gives as “with any thing, do not let either … or …”. Other reading: Let neither the quality nor the worth of anything escape you.

</details>

### 6.4–5

All existing things will very quickly change, and either they will go up in vapour, if substance is indeed a unity, or they will be scattered.

The reason that governs knows in what condition it acts, what it does, and on what material.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὰ ὑποκείμενα*: Literally “the things lying under”: the things that are there, the objects that impressions are about, or the underlying material things. “Existing things” takes the widest sense and brings in no observer. Other reading: all underlying things; all material objects
- *ἐκθυμιαθήσεται*: The verb is from burning incense: to be turned into fumes. The image is kept as “go up in vapour”. Other reading: will be burnt off as smoke
- *εἴπερ ἥνωται ἡ οὐσία, ἢ σκεδασθήσεται*: Two pictures of the world are set side by side: substance as one continuous thing, or a scattering (of atoms, though Marcus does not say so). εἴπερ can be a real “if” or nearly “since”; the English keeps it conditional. Other reading: since substance is unified; otherwise they will be dispersed
- *Ὁ διοικῶν λόγος*: λόγος is “reason” as in the glossary. διοικῶν is “managing, administering”; the Greek does not say what is governed, and the English does not supply it. Other reading: the reason that administers the universe
- *πῶς διακείμενος*: Literally “being how disposed”: a participle with no verb of its own. It is taken with ποιεῖ, the one verb that serves all three questions, and “acts” is supplied from that verb. It could instead stand alone as a first thing known, the state reason itself is in. Other reading: knows what state it is in, what it is doing, and on what material
- *τί ποιεῖ*: ποιεῖ is both “does” and “makes”. “Does” is kept because the phrase that follows says “on what material”, not “out of”; “makes” is possible. Other reading: what it is making

</details>

### 6.6

The best way to fight back is to not become like them.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τοῦ ἀμύνεσθαι*: The middle of ἀμύνω covers both “defend oneself, ward off” and “pay back, take revenge on”. “Fight back” is chosen because it can be heard either way. The Greek is impersonal and names no “you”. Other reading: The best way to defend oneself. Or: The best way to retaliate.
- *τὸ μὴ ἐξομοιοῦσθαι*: The verb means “to be made like” or “to make oneself like” and has no object here: the Greek does not say like whom. “Them” is supplied as the smallest word English allows, and stands for whoever is being fought, one person or many. The negative belongs to the infinitive, “the not becoming like”, which “is to not become” makes plain. Other reading: is to not become like the one who did the wrong. Or, as a passive: is to not be made like them.
- *Ἄριστος τρόπος*: τρόπος is “way, manner”, and also “character”. The plain sense “way” is what the genitive that follows needs. Other reading: The best manner of fighting back

</details>

### 6.7

Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: going from one social act to another social act, with god in mind.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἑνὶ*: “In one thing”. The Greek does not add “only”, and neither does the English. Other reading: Let one thing be your pleasure and your rest
- *προσαναπαύου*: To rest upon something, to find one’s rest in it. The same verb is used of philosophy in 6.12 and has the same English there. Other reading: and lean on it for rest
- *ἀπὸ πράξεως κοινωνικῆς μεταβαίνειν ἐπὶ πρᾶξιν κοινωνικὴν*: Literally “passing from a social act to a social act”. “Social” (κοινωνικός) is the glossary word: an act that serves the common life of people with one another. Other reading: passing from an act for the common good to an act for the common good
- *σὺν μνήμῃ θεοῦ*: Literally “with memory of god”. The noun has no article, so “a god” is also possible. Other reading: with remembrance of god

</details>

### 6.8

The ruling part is what wakes itself and turns itself; it makes itself whatever it wants to be, and it makes everything that happens appear to itself the way it itself wants.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἡγεμονικόν*: The Stoic term for the commanding faculty of the soul, literally “the leading thing”. “The ruling part” is its English in every passage of this set. Other reading: The governing faculty
- *ἐγεῖρον*: The verb means to wake from sleep or to rouse into action. The image of waking is kept. Other reading: what rouses itself
- *τρέπον*: The verb means to turn, and so either to direct oneself somewhere or to change oneself. “Turns itself” leaves both open. Other reading: and changes itself / and directs itself
- *οἷον ἂν καὶ θέλῃ*: Literally “of whatever sort it may in fact wish”, an indefinite form. The second clause has a plain statement with an emphatic “itself”: “such as it itself wants”. The English is “whatever it wants to be” for the first and “the way it itself wants” for the second. Other reading: makes itself such as it may wish
- *ἑαυτῷ φαίνεσθαι*: “To appear to itself”: the verb is the one behind the Stoic word for an impression. The claim is that the ruling part settles how each event looks to it. Other reading: makes everything that happens seem to it

</details>

### 6.9–10

Each thing is carried through in accordance with the nature of the whole. For it is certainly not in accordance with any other nature, whether one that surrounds from outside, or one contained within, or one that stands apart outside.

Either a stirred brew and a mutual entanglement and a scattering, or unity and order and providence. Now if it is the first, why do I even want to spend my time in a random compound and a jumble of that kind? And why do I even care about anything other than how, one way or another, to “become earth”? And why am I even troubled? For the scattering will come upon me, whatever I do. But if it is the second, I feel reverence, I stand firm, and I take heart, relying on the one that governs.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τῶν ὅλων*: Literally plural, “of the wholes”, a set phrase for the universe. The English is “the whole”, the same as for the singular τοῦ ὅλου in the other passages. Other reading: the nature of all things
- *περαίνεται*: The verb means to be carried through to its limit, accomplished, finished. “Carried through” is used here and for the same verb in 6.1. “Brought to its end” would be heard as “dies”, which the Greek does not say. Other reading: Each thing is accomplished
- *ἔξω ἀπηρτημένην*: The participle is from a verb meaning to hang off from something; it can mean “detached, separate” or “hanging from, attached to”. The English takes it as a nature standing apart outside. The Greek gives no object for “surrounds”, “contained” or “stands apart”, and none is supplied. Other reading: or one attached to it from outside
- *κυκεὼν*: A kykeon was a drink of barley meal and other things stirred into liquid, which has to be kept stirred to hold together. “A stirred brew” keeps both the stirring and the drink, and is also the English for the word in 4.27. Other reading: a porridge / a hotchpotch
- *ἀντεμπλοκὴ καὶ σκεδασμὸς*: The first word means things tangling or interlocking with one another, the second their being scattered apart. Both seem to belong to the atomists’ account of the universe (from memory, unchecked). “Scattering” is used for σκεδασμός both times it occurs in the passage. Other reading: an interlocking and a dispersal
- *ὅπως ποτὲ*: The small word after “how” can make it indefinite (“how ever, in whatever way”) or can be temporal (“at some time”). The English takes it as indefinite, since the two words together commonly mean “in whatever way”. Other reading: except how, some day, to “become earth”
- *αἶα γίνεσθαι*: The edition marks these words as a quotation, and the word for “earth” is a poetic form. It seems to echo a line of Homer about turning to water and earth (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: to “turn to earth”
- *σέβω καὶ εὐσταθῶ*: The first verb, “I revere” or “I worship”, has no object in the Greek. English “I revere” cannot stand alone, so the English is “I feel reverence”, which keeps the word used for the same verb in 6.36. The second verb means to be stable or steady, of footing or of mind. Other reading: I worship, I am steady
- *θαρρῶ*: The verb means to be of good courage and, with the dative that follows it, to be confident in someone. The English gives both sides: “I take heart, relying on”. It answers “why am I even troubled?” above. Other reading: I put my trust in the one that governs
- *τῷ διοικοῦντι*: The form can be masculine (“him who governs”) or neuter (“that which governs”). “The one that governs” keeps it open. The same verb is used of managing a household or a city. Other reading: relying on him who administers it

</details>

### 6.11

When circumstances force you to be, as it were, thrown into confusion, go back quickly into yourself, and do not step out of the rhythm more than you are forced to. For you will have a firmer hold on the harmony by continually going back to it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὑπὲρ τὰ ἀναγκαῖα*: Literally “beyond what is necessary”. The word echoes ἀναγκασθῇς (“you are forced”) at the start, so “force” is used in both places. Whether “beyond” means longer or further is not said. Other reading: do not stay out of the rhythm longer than is necessary
- *τῶν περιεστηκότων*: Literally “the things standing around”, the usual word for circumstances. The Greek has no “your”. Other reading: by what surrounds you
- *οἱονεὶ διαταραχθῆναι*: οἱονεί (“as it were”, “in a way”) softens the strong verb, which means to be thoroughly disturbed or thrown into disorder. The English keeps both. Other reading: to be, so to speak, badly shaken
- *ἐξίστασο τοῦ ῥυθμοῦ*: Literally “stand out of the rhythm”, an image from music or dance. The verb is one of movement, so the English reads “step out of”. The present imperative with μή can also mean “do not keep standing out of”. Other reading: do not stay out of step
- *ἐγκρατέστερος τῆς ἁρμονίας*: Literally “more in command of the harmony”. ἁρμονία is the fitting-together or tuning of notes, not harmony in the modern sense of chords. The familiar word is kept so that the musical image, begun with “rhythm”, stays visible. Other reading: you will be more the master of the tuning
- *ἐπανέρχεσθαι*: The same verb as ἐπάνιθι (“go back”) earlier in the sentence, so “go back” is repeated. “It” (αὐτήν) is the harmony. Other reading: by constantly returning to it

</details>

### 6.12

If you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time, you would wait on the stepmother, and still you would be continually going back to your mother. That is what the court and philosophy are to you now. Go back here often and rest in philosophy, because of which the things there seem bearable to you, and you seem bearable among them.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐθεράπευες*: The verb means to attend on, serve, look after, and also to pay court to someone, the sense that prepares “the court” in the next sentence. “Wait on” is meant to carry both. The Greek says “that one” for the stepmother; the English names her. Other reading: you would pay court to the stepmother
- *ἡ ἐπάνοδός σοι πρὸς τὴν μητέρα συνεχὴς ἐγίνετο*: Literally “your going back to your mother would be continual”. The noun is from the same root as ἐπάνιθι (“go back”) below, so the English keeps “going back” and “go back”. Other reading: your return to your mother would be constant
- *ἡ αὐλὴ καὶ ἡ φιλοσοφία*: αὐλή is the court, the emperor’s palace and the life around it. By the order of the words the court answers to the stepmother and philosophy to the mother; the Greek does not spell that out and neither does the English. Other reading: the palace and philosophy
- *ὧδε*: Either “to this place” or “in this way” (as you would go back to your mother). The English takes “here”, meaning to philosophy, because the next clause sets it against “the things there”. Other reading: Go back in this way often
- *ταύτῃ*: “In this one”, feminine. The court and philosophy are both feminine nouns in Greek, and “this one” is the nearer of the two, philosophy. The English writes the noun so that it is clear which is meant. Other reading: and rest in her
- *δι’ ἣν*: The preposition with this case gives a cause (“on account of which”), not a means (“by means of which”). Other reading: thanks to which
- *τὰ ἐκεῖ*: “The things there”, that is at court, as against “here”. Other reading: what you meet at court
- *καὶ σὺ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀνεκτός*: The verb is carried over from the clause before, so “seem” is repeated. “Among them” is most naturally the things there (neuter), but the form could also be heard as the people there. Other reading: and you are bearable among the people there

</details>

### 6.13a

Just as, over cooked dishes and other such things to eat, one takes the impression that this is the dead body of a fish, and this the dead body of a bird or a pig; and again, that Falernian wine is a little juice from a little bunch of grapes, and the purple-bordered robe is little hairs of a little sheep soaked in a little blood from a shellfish; and, over what belongs to sex, that it is the rubbing of a bit of gut and, with a kind of spasm, the discharge of a little slime: just as these impressions reach the things themselves and go right through them, so that one sees what they really are, so one must do through the whole of life, and where things give the impression of being very trustworthy, strip them bare, see their cheapness plainly, and strip off the story on which they pride themselves. For conceit is a formidable cheat, and it is when you think you are most occupied with serious things that you are most bewitched.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οἷον δὴ τὸ φαντασίαν λαμβάνειν*: The sentence runs “As it is to take the impression …, as these impressions are …, so one must do”. The infinitive has no stated subject; the English has “one”. οἷον δή could also be an exclamation. Other reading: How good it is to take the impression
- *ὄψων*: ὄψον is cooked food eaten with bread, above all fish and meat. Other reading: over meats
- *ὁ Φάλερνος χυλάριόν ἐστι σταφυλίου*: Falernian was a famous Italian wine; “wine” is supplied from the masculine article, which implies it. The nouns here and below (juice, grape-bunch, hairs, sheep, blood, gut, slime) are diminutives, used to belittle; they are marked with “a little”, “little” and “a bit of”. Other reading: Falernian is the juice of a bunch of grapes
- *ἡ περιπόρφυρος*: “The purple-bordered”: the robe with a purple border worn by Roman magistrates; “robe” is supplied. Purple dye came from a sea-snail. Other reading: the purple-edged toga
- *ἐντερίου παράτριψις καὶ μετά τινος σπασμοῦ μυξαρίου ἔκκρισις*: ἐντέριον is a diminutive of “gut, intestine”, here used of the inner flesh; μυξάριον is a diminutive of “mucus, slime”. There is no verb: the words stand as the content of the impression, and “that it is” is supplied. Other reading: friction of a membrane and, with a kind of convulsion, the ejection of a little mucus
- *λίαν ἀξιόπιστα τὰ πράγματα φαντάζεται*: φαντάζεται is the verb of “impression” (φαντασία): things “present themselves”. λίαν is “very much”, shading into “too much”. Other reading: where things seem all too plausible
- *τὴν ἱστορίαν ἐφ’ ᾗ σεμνύνεται*: ἱστορία is an account or story; the word may have been doubted here (from memory, unchecked). σεμνύνεται can be middle, “pride themselves”, or passive, “are made grand”. Other reading: the talk by which they are made to look solemn
- *ὁ τῦφος παραλογιστὴς*: τῦφος is literally smoke: conceit, a puffed-up illusion of importance. It is part of σεμνοτυφία in 9.29. παραλογιστής is one who cheats by false reasoning, and δεινός is both “fearsome” and “clever”. Other reading: For pride is a clever sophist
- *καταγοητεύῃ*: “You are bewitched”, as by a sorcerer: passive, second person, where the instruction before was impersonal. Other reading: you are most taken in

</details>

### 6.13b

See, at any rate, what Crates says about Xenocrates himself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *γοῦν*: “At any rate”, “for instance”: it brings in a case that supports what came just before. This passage is one sentence from the end of a chapter, and what it supports is not in the Greek given; nothing was supplied. Other reading: See, for instance
- *ὁ Κράτης τί περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ξενοκράτους λέγει*: Marcus does not give the saying. From memory, unchecked: Crates is most likely the Cynic philosopher, Xenocrates was a head of Plato’s school known for his gravity, and the remark itself is lost. αὐτοῦ is “himself”, with the force of “even Xenocrates”. Other reading: what Crates says even about Xenocrates

</details>

### 6.14

Most of the things the crowd admires come down to the most general kind, the things held together by cohesion or by natural growth: stones, timber, fig trees, vines, olive trees. The things admired by people of a slightly better sort come down to the things held together by soul, such as flocks and herds. The things admired by people more refined still come down to the things held together by rational soul; not, however, rational soul as such, but in so far as it is skilled in a craft or adept in some other way, or merely in terms of owning a great number of slaves. But whoever honours rational soul as such, and as civic, no longer pays attention to any of the other things, but before everything else preserves their own soul rational and social in its condition and its movement, and works together with whoever is of the same kind toward this.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *εἰς γενικώτατα ἀνάγεται*: Literally “are led back to the most generic”: are classed under the broadest, least specific kind of thing. The English reads “come down to” and keeps that phrase for the two later steps, where the Greek leaves the verb to be understood. Other reading: are referred to the most generic class
- *ὑπὸ ἕξεως ἣ φύσεως*: Bare Stoic terms for the two lowest ways a thing is held together: ἕξις, the “holding” that makes a stone or a log one thing, and φύσις, “nature” in the narrow sense of the growing principle of plants. The English reads “cohesion” and “natural growth”, because plain “nature” would be taken as nature at large. The text as given prints ἣ where ἢ (“or”) must be meant, and likewise ὦν for ὧν and οἶον for οἷον; they are read so. Other reading: held together by a state or by nature
- *τῶν ὀλίγῳ μετριωτέρων*: μέτριος is “moderate, within measure”, and of people “decent, respectable”. The passage ranks people by what they admire (the crowd, those a little better, the more refined still), so the English gives the sense in use. Other reading: by people who are a little more moderate
- *ὑπὸ ψυχῆς*: ψυχή here is the next step up: the life of an animal, not yet reason. “Soul” is kept because the passage climbs by repeating this one word (soul, rational soul, one’s own soul). Other reading: the things held together by animal life
- *χαριεστέρων*: The word means “more graceful, more accomplished”, and was a usual way of saying “the more cultivated people”. Other reading: by people of still more taste
- *οὐ μέντοι καθολικῆς*: καθολικός is “general, universal”. It is set against καθό, “in so far as”: rational soul valued in general, simply as rational soul, as against rational soul valued in one respect. “As such” is used both times the word occurs. It can also be taken as “universal”, the reason that all rational beings share. Other reading: though not rational soul as universal; and below, rational soul that is universal and civic
- *ἢ κατὰ ψιλὸν τὸ πλῆθος ἀνδραπόδων κεκτῆσθαι*: A compressed clause, taken as a third way of valuing rational souls: not for any skill but for the bare fact of owning many of them, as slaves. ψιλόν (“bare, mere”) is read with the owning; it could go with the number instead. πλῆθος is a great number, a mass. Other reading: or in terms of owning a bare quantity of slaves
- *πολιτικὴν*: “Belonging to a city, fit for life as a citizen”. The English reads “civic” here and “social” for the different word κοινωνικῶς in the next clause. Other reading: rational soul as such, and as political
- *οὐδὲν ἔτι τῶν ἄλλων ἐπιστρέφεται*: The verb is literally “turns toward”; with this case it means “pays heed to, cares about”. Other reading: no longer turns to look at any of the other things
- *τῷ ὁμογενεῖ εἰς τοῦτο συνεργεῖ*: τῷ ὁμογενεῖ is singular and can be masculine (“the one who is of the same kind”) or neuter (“what is of the same kind”). With a verb of working together the English takes it as a person. “Toward this” most likely means toward keeping the soul rational and social, so the sense is helping one’s fellow to do the same. Other reading: and works together with what is of the same kind toward this

</details>

### 6.15

Some things are hurrying to come to be, others are hurrying to have come to be, and of what is coming to be some part has already been quenched. Flows and alterations renew the universe continually, just as the unbroken movement of time keeps boundless eternity always new. In this river, then, which of these things running past would anyone prize, a thing it is not possible to stand on? It is as if someone began to love one of the little sparrows flying past, and it has already gone out of sight. Each person’s life itself, too, is something of the kind: like the vapour that rises from blood and the breath drawn in from the air. For drawing in the air once and giving it back, which we do every moment, is the same kind of thing as giving back the whole power of breathing, which you acquired yesterday and the day before when you were born, to the place from which you first drew it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὰ δὲ σπεύδει γεγονέναι*: The perfect infinitive of the same verb as “to come to be”: these things hurry to have done their coming to be, that is, to be over. “To have come to be” keeps the one verb heard three times in the sentence. Other reading: others are hurrying to be over and done
- *ἀπέσβη*: The verb is used of a flame going out. “Quenched” keeps the image. Other reading: some part has already gone out
- *τὸν ἄπειρον αἰῶνα*: αἰών is time in its whole endless extent, here set beside χρόνος, time as it passes. “Eternity” is used for αἰών and “time” for χρόνος throughout this section. Other reading: keeps the boundless age always new
- *στῆναι οὐκ ἔξεστιν*: The relative ἐφ’ οὗ (“on which”) may refer to the thing one might prize, on which no footing can be had, or back to the river, in which one cannot stand still. The English takes the nearer reference, the thing. Other reading: In this river, then, in which there is no standing still, which of these things running past would anyone prize?
- *στρουθαρίων*: A diminutive of στρουθός, a sparrow or any small bird. Other reading: one of the little birds flying past
- *τοιοῦτον δή τι καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ ζωὴ ἑκάστου*: τοιοῦτον may look back to the things running past or forward to the comparison that follows (“such a thing as vapour”). “Something of the kind” followed by a colon leaves both open. Other reading: Each person’s life itself is just such a thing as the vapour that rises from blood
- *ἀναθυμίασις*: A rising vapour or exhalation. The Stoics held that the soul is fed by an exhalation from the blood, and the sentence alludes to that; the plain image is kept. Other reading: the exhalation from blood
- *παρέκαστον*: “At each moment” or “each time”; one word here for παρ’ ἕκαστον. Other reading: time after time
- *χθὲς καὶ πρῴην*: Literally “yesterday and the day before”, an idiom for “very recently”. It is kept literal, to match the similar phrase in 10.7. Other reading: only the other day

</details>

### 6.16

It is not breathing through the surface as plants do that is of value, nor breathing as cattle and wild beasts do, nor being stamped by an impression, nor being pulled on strings by impulse, nor herding together, nor taking in food; for this last is like passing out the waste from the food. What then is of value? Being clapped? No. Then not being clapped by tongues either; for the praises of the many are a clapping of tongues. So you have let petty fame go as well. What is left that is of value? I think it is this: to move and to hold back in keeping with the way one is oneself made, which is also where tending and the crafts lead. For every craft aims at this, that the thing made should be fit for the work it was made for. The planter and the one who tends the vine, the breaker of colts and the one who tends the dog are after this. And the upbringing of children, and teaching: what are they pressing towards? Here, then, is what is of value. And if this is in a good state, you will not be acquiring any of the other things for yourself. Will you not stop valuing many other things as well? Then you will be neither free nor sufficient to yourself nor without passion. For you are bound to envy, to be jealous, to look with suspicion on those who can take those things away, to plot against those who have what you value. In short, anyone who is in need of any of those things is bound to be in confusion, and what is more to find much fault even with the gods. But respect for your own mind, and the value you set on it, will make you pleasing to yourself, well fitted to your fellows and in tune with the gods, that is, praising all that they deal out and have arranged.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τίμιον*: The argument turns on one root: τίμιον (“worth valuing”, “precious”), τιμῶν, τὸ τιμώμενον, τιμή. “Value” is kept for all of them, including the last, where “honour” would be the usual word. Other reading: is nothing to prize
- *διαπνεῖσθαι*: Literally “to breathe through”: to give off vapour through the surface, as plants do, set against ἀναπνεῖν, the breathing of animals. “Breathing” is used for both so that the pair can be heard; the technical word for the plant is “transpire”. Other reading: It is not transpiring as plants do
- *νευροσπαστεῖσθαι*: The verb is from the puppet moved by strings. The image is kept. Other reading: nor being jerked about like a puppet by impulse
- *τὸ ὑπὸ γλωσσῶν κροτεῖσθαι*: κροτέω is to strike together, to clap, so to applaud. Marcus moves from clapping with hands to praise as “clapping of tongues”; “clap” is kept so the step can be seen. Other reading: Then not being applauded by tongues either
- *κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν κατασκευὴν κινεῖσθαι καὶ ἴσχεσθαι*: κατασκευή is the way a thing is built or made up, and the same root returns twice in the next sentence (“the thing made”, “was made for”), so “made” is kept; ἰδίαν, “one’s own”, is given by “oneself”. ἴσχεσθαι is to be held or to hold oneself in check; the Greek is impersonal here. Other reading: to act and to refrain according to one’s own constitution
- *αἱ ἐπιμέλειαι*: ἐπιμέλεια is care given to something; the Greek is plural, the different forms of such care. The same root comes twice below for the one who “tends” the vine and the dog, and “tending” keeps the link. Other reading: which is also where training and the crafts lead
- *ὅ τε φυτουργὸς καὶ ὁ ἐπιμελούμενος τῆς ἀμπέλου*: This can be two people (the planter, and the one who tends the vine) or one person named twice. Two are kept, as the Greek has two articles. Other reading: The gardener who tends the vine
- *περιποιήσεις*: A plain future: “you will acquire”, “you will secure”. The thought is probably that a person whose own working is in good order will not go after the other things; the English keeps the plain future. Other reading: you will not care to get any of the other things for yourself
- *οὐ παύσῃ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ τιμῶν*: As punctuated this is a question, “Will you not stop …?”, which in Greek is a way of urging. The next sentence then gives the result if you do not stop; the Greek does not spell out that “if”. Other reading: You will not stop valuing many other things too? Then you will not be free
- *πεφύρθαι*: φύρω is to mix or muddle; in the perfect passive, to be in a muddle or turmoil. Other reading: is bound to be in turmoil
- *αἰδὼς καὶ τιμὴ*: αἰδώς is respect or reverence; τιμή is honour, and here it closes the chain on “value”. διάνοια is “thought” in the glossary; the faculty is meant here, so the English has “mind”. Other reading: But reverence and honour for your own understanding
- *τοῖς κοινωνοῖς*: κοινωνοί are those who share something with you, partners, here those who share the common life. The English has “your fellows”. Other reading: well fitted to those who share society with you

</details>

### 6.17

Up, down, round in a circle: such are the motions of the elements. The movement of virtue, though, is in none of these, but is something more divine, and going forward by a road hard to make out it travels well.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *φοραὶ τῶν στοιχείων*: φορά is a being carried, a course: the natural motions of the elements. There is no verb and “such are” is supplied. Other reading: Upward, downward, in a circle run the courses of the elements
- *ἡ δὲ τῆς ἀρετῆς κίνησις*: κίνησις is a different word from φοραί; the English has “motions” for the first and “movement” for this one. Other reading: the motion of virtue
- *θειότερόν τι*: Neuter, “something more divine”. It can be a predicate (virtue’s movement is a more divine thing) or adverbial (in some more divine way). It is taken as a predicate. Other reading: but in some more divine way
- *ὁδῷ δυσεπινοήτῳ*: A road that is hard to form a notion of, hard to conceive. “Hard to make out” fits both a road and a thought. Other reading: by a path hard to understand
- *εὐοδεῖ*: Literally “has a good road”, echoing ὁδῷ just before; in ordinary use it means “prospers”. The road is kept. Other reading: it prospers on its way

</details>

### 6.18

What a thing it is that they do. The people who live at the same time as them and alongside them they are unwilling to speak well of, yet they set great store by being spoken well of themselves by those who come after, whom they have never seen and never will see. This is close to what it would be to be pained that those who came before did not also speak well of you.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οἷόν ἐστιν ὃ ποιοῦσι*: Literally “what sort of thing it is that they do”, an exclamation of surprise. “They” are not named. Other reading: How strange is what they do.
- *εὐφημεῖν*: The same word comes three times, as a verb active and passive and then in the phrase “well-speaking words”. “Speak well of” is kept each time. Other reading: to praise
- *μεθ’ ἑαυτῶν*: Literally “with themselves”: in their own company. Other reading: and in their own company
- *τῷ λυπηθῆναι ἄν*: The particle makes the infinitive hypothetical: it is close to how it would be if one were pained. Other reading: This is close to being pained
- *οὐχὶ καὶ οἱ προγενέστεροι περὶ σοῦ*: The passage turns to “you” here, after “they” throughout. The Greek “also” goes with those who came before: they as well as those who come after. Other reading: that the earlier generations as well did not speak well of you

</details>

### 6.19

Do not, if something is hard for you yourself to carry out, judge it impossible for a human being; but if something is possible for a human being and proper to them, consider it within your own reach too.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *δυσκαταπόνητον*: “Hard to work through to the end”, hard to master by effort. Other reading: hard for you to master
- *ὑπολαμβάνειν*: An infinitive used as a command, the verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment”. The second half has a plain imperative, νόμιζε, “consider”. Other reading: do not suppose
- *δυνατὸν καὶ οἰκεῖον*: οἰκεῖον is what belongs to a being by its nature. The English reads “proper to them” for the human being. Other reading: possible and natural to man

</details>

### 6.20

In the gymnasium someone has scratched us with their nails, and butted us with their head and landed a blow; but we do not mark them down, nor take offence, nor suspect them afterwards of plotting against us. We are on our guard, certainly, yet not as against an enemy, nor with suspicion, but with a kindly stepping aside. Let something like this happen in the other parts of life too: let us overlook many things in those who are, as it were, our training partners. For it is possible, as I said, to step aside, and neither to suspect nor to hate.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐν τοῖς γυμνασίοις*: Plural: in the gymnasia, or in bouts of exercise. The first two verbs have no object in the Greek; the English supplies one twice so that they can stand. Other reading: In training bouts someone scratches with the nails
- *τῇ κεφαλῇ ἐρραγεὶς πληγὴν ἐποίησεν*: ἐρραγείς is from the verb “to break, to burst”: bursting or crashing in with the head. πληγή is a blow, or the wound it leaves. The past tenses describe what typically happens. Other reading: and, crashing in with the head, has left a bruise
- *ἐπισημαινόμεθα*: To set a mark on something. It is taken as marking the person down as an offender; it could be making a sign of protest. Other reading: there is no making a point of it
- *ἐκκλίσεως εὐμενοῦς*: ἔκκλισις is the Stoic term for avoidance, and here also the literal dodge of a wrestler. The English has “stepping aside”, and “step aside” for the verb ἐκκλίνειν below. Other reading: but with good-natured avoidance
- *πολλὰ παρενθυμώμεθα τῶν οἷον προσγυμναζομένων*: The verb is “to let pass in one’s thoughts”, and the form is taken as an exhortation. προσγυμναζόμενοι are those who train against a person; οἷον, “as it were”, marks the figure. Other reading: much should be disregarded in those who are, so to speak, wrestling partners
- *ἀπέχθεσθαι*: As in 2.1: to be at enmity. The English reads “hate”. Other reading: nor to bear ill will

</details>

### 6.21

If anyone can refute me and make it plain to me that I am not judging or acting rightly, I will gladly change. For I am looking for the truth, by which no one was ever harmed; the one who is harmed is the one who persists in their own delusion and ignorance.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐλέγξαι*: To test by questioning and so to prove wrong. “Refute” is the nearest single word. Other reading: can prove me wrong
- *παραστῆσαί μοι*: Literally “to set beside me”, to bring a thing home to someone so that they see it. Other reading: and show me
- *ὑπολαμβάνω*: The verb of the noun the glossary gives as “judgment”: to take a thing to be so. Hence “judging”; the verb for judging in 5.3 and 8.38 is a different one. Other reading: that what I suppose or do is not right
- *χαίρων μεταθήσομαι*: Literally “I will shift, rejoicing”. The verb is the one given as “change one’s mind” in 4.12 and 8.16; here it answers both judging and acting, so the English has the bare “change”. Other reading: I will gladly change my mind
- *ἐπὶ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἀπάτης καὶ ἀγνοίας*: The first noun is deception, here the state of being deceived, whoever did the deceiving. “Delusion” says that; “their own deception” could be heard as their deceiving of others. Other reading: in their own self-deception and ignorance

</details>

### 6.22–23

I do my own duty; the other things do not distract me. For they are either without life, or without reason, or have gone astray and do not know the road.

Animals without reason, and in general things and objects, treat with a large mind and freely, as one who has reason treats what has none. Human beings, since they have reason, treat socially. And in everything call on the gods. And do not trouble yourself about how long you will be doing this: for even three hours of this kind are enough.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *καθῆκον*: A Stoic term: the act that is fitting for one, what falls to one to do. Other reading: I do what is fitting for me
- *ἄλογα*: “Without λόγος”, without reason. The next chapter turns on having and not having reason, so “without reason” and “has reason” stand throughout. Other reading: or irrational
- *πράγμασι καὶ ὑποκειμένοις*: Two near synonyms: things, and what lies to hand as material. Other reading: things and materials
- *χρῶ μεγαλοφρόνως καὶ ἐλευθέρως*: The verb is “use” or “deal with”; the same verb is used of people in the next clause, so “treat” stands for both. The first adverb is literally “with a great mind”, the second “as a free person does”. Other reading: use them generously and like a free person
- *χρῶ κοινωνικῶς*: “Socially” follows this translation’s fixed word for κοινωνικός. It does not mean sociably: it means dealing with them as fellow members of a community. Other reading: treat as fellows in a community
- *ἐφ’ ἅπασι*: “In all things” or “on every occasion”; it could also be “over all of them”. Other reading: And on every occasion call on the gods
- *μὴ διαφέρου*: Literally “do not make a difference to yourself about”: do not be anxious, do not let it matter. Other reading: And let it make no difference to you how long
