- *τρεῖς ὧραι τοιαῦται*: “Three hours of this kind”: hours spent so. The number is as the Greek has it. Other reading: even three such hours

</details>

### 6.24

Alexander of Macedon and his mule driver, once dead, came to the same state: for either they were taken back into the same seed-reasons of the universe, or they were scattered alike into atoms.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὀρεωκόμος*: A man who looks after and drives mules: the lowest of his servants, set beside the king. Other reading: his muleteer
- *εἰς ταὐτὸ κατέστησαν*: Literally “were brought to the same”: the same condition, or the same place. Other reading: ended up in the same place
- *ἀνελήφθησαν*: “Were taken up” or “taken back”. The English reads “taken back”, since on the Stoic view they return to what they came from. Other reading: they were taken up into
- *σπερματικοὺς λόγους*: A Stoic term: the reasons at work in the universe that act as seeds, from which each thing grows and into which it returns. λόγος is “reason” throughout this translation and “principle” is kept for δόγμα, so the English reads “seed-reasons” and not the more usual “seminal principles”. Other reading: the same generative principles of the universe
- *διεσκεδάσθησαν ὁμοίως εἰς τὰς ἀτόμους*: The second alternative is the Epicurean one: a universe of atoms with no reason running it. ὁμοίως is “in the same way”, both alike. Other reading: or they were both alike dispersed among the atoms

</details>

### 6.25

Consider how many things come about at once in each of us in the same instant of time, things of the body and things of the soul together. And then you will not be surprised if many more things, or rather all the things that come about, exist at once within the one and entire thing, the very thing we call the universe.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀκαριαῖον*: Literally “too short to be cut”, of a moment with no length. The English is “instant”. Other reading: in the same indivisible moment of time
- *σωματικὰ ὁμοῦ καὶ ψυχικά*: Two adjectives, “bodily” and “of the soul”, joined by “together”. The second covers everything the mind or life-principle does, not only what would now be called spiritual. Other reading: bodily and mental things alike
- *μᾶλλον δὲ*: The phrase corrects what has just been said: “or rather”. It is kept as a correction and not smoothed away. Other reading: many more, indeed all
- *τὰ γινόμενα*: The participle means things that come to be or happen. “Come about” is used for this verb in both sentences, and in the neighbouring passages, because the argument runs from what comes about in us to what comes about in the universe. Other reading: all the things that happen
- *ἑνί τε καὶ σύμπαντι*: Two adjectives used as a name: “the one” and “the all-together”. The English is “the one and entire thing”. Other reading: in the One and All
- *ἐνυφίσταται*: A compound verb: to subsist or have being within something. The English is “exist … within”. The word before it, ἅμα, is “at once”, the same word as in the first sentence. Other reading: have their being at the same time within

</details>

### 6.26

If someone sets you the question how the name Antoninus is written, surely you will not strain as you bring out each of its letters? What then if they get angry: surely you will not get angry back? Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters? So here too, remember that every duty is made complete out of certain counted parts. These you must keep to, and, without being thrown into confusion and without answering those who are annoyed with annoyance of your own, carry through step by step what lies before you.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ Ἀντωνίνου ὄνομα*: Antoninus is Marcus’s own name as emperor, so the example is spelling his own name. Other reading: the name of Antoninus
- *μήτι κατεντεινόμενος προοίσῃ*: μήτι expects the answer no, so the English reads “surely you will not”. κατεντεινόμενος is “straining hard”, whether of the voice or of effort in general; προφέρω is to utter aloud. Other reading: surely you will not shout out each letter at full stretch?
- *στοιχείων*: στοιχεῖα here and γραμμάτων below both mean the letters of the name; the first is strictly the elements or sounds, the second the written characters. The English has “letters” for both. Other reading: each of its elements
- *ἐὰν ὀργίζωνται*: The Greek moves from “someone” to an unnamed plural “they”. Other reading: if people get angry
- *πρᾴως προιὼν*: πρᾴως, “gently”, stands between “count off” and “going on” and can go with either. The English puts it before both. Other reading: Will you not go on gently and count off each of the letters?
- *πᾶν καθῆκον*: καθῆκον is the Stoic term for an act that it falls to one to do, a fitting or appropriate act. “Duty” is the plain word nearest to it. Other reading: every fitting act
- *ἐξ ἀριθμῶν τινῶν συμπληροῦται*: ἀριθμοί, “numbers”, are the counted items that make a thing complete, picking up ἐξαριθμήσῃ, “count off”, just before. The English reads “counted parts” so the link shows; “parts” is supplied. From memory, unchecked: Stoics spoke of a right act as having all its “numbers”. Other reading: is made complete out of certain numbers
- *περαίνειν ὁδῷ*: περαίνειν is “carry through” by the glossary. ὁδῷ, literally “by a road”, is the idiom for “methodically, in order”; it is “step by step” here and in 5.34, where the road itself is also kept. Other reading: carry through, keeping to the road, what lies before you

</details>

### 6.27

How cruel it is not to let people go after the things that appear to them to suit them and to be good for them. And yet in a way you do not allow them to do this, whenever you are indignant that they do wrong. For they are certainly being carried toward things as suiting them and good for them. “But it is not so.” Then teach them and show them, without being indignant.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὁρμᾶν*: The verb belonging to ὁρμή, “impulse” in the settled list: to set out after a thing. “To have impulses toward” would be stiff, so the English reads “go after”. Other reading: not to allow people their impulse toward
- *οἰκεῖα καὶ συμφέροντα*: οἰκεῖα are things that belong to one, are proper to one’s nature. The English reads “suit them”; συμφέροντα is “good for them” as settled. Other reading: what appears to them to be their own and to their advantage
- *πάντως*: “In every case” or “certainly”. The second is taken. Other reading: For in every case they are carried
- *οὐκ ἔχει οὕτως*: The edition sets these words between dashes as an objection by another voice: the things are not really good for them. The English uses quotation marks. Other reading: “But they are mistaken.”

</details>

### 6.28

Death is a rest from the impacts on the senses, from the tugging of impulse on the puppet strings, from the step-by-step course of thought, and from service to the flesh.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀνάπαυλα*: The word is “rest, respite from” something, and can also be simply “cessation”. “Rest” keeps the sense of relief. Other reading: Death is the ceasing of
- *αἰσθητικῆς ἀντιτυπίας*: ἀντιτυπία is the resistance or striking back of something hard. Here it is either the blows that things deal the senses or the senses’ own answering reaction. “Impacts” is used, and “impression” is avoided, since this project keeps it for φαντασία. Other reading: the imprinting of the senses
- *ὁρμητικῆς νευροσπαστίας*: νευροσπαστία is the working of a puppet by its strings. The adjective says the pulling is done by impulse (ὁρμή). Other reading: being jerked about like a puppet by impulse
- *διανοητικῆς διεξόδου*: διέξοδος is a way through, a course followed step by step, used of thought working its way through a matter. “Step-by-step” spells out the prefix; the Greek does not say that the course is laborious. Other reading: the discursive working of thought
- *τῆς πρὸς τὴν σάρκα λειτουργίας*: λειτουργία is a public service that a citizen is obliged to perform. The English says only “service”; the sense of a duty imposed is not carried by a separate English word. Other reading: the duty of waiting upon the flesh

</details>

### 6.29–30a

It is shameful that, in a life in which your body does not give out, your soul should give out first.

Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed: for it happens. So keep yourself simple, good, unspoiled, dignified, unpretentious, a friend of what is just, reverent toward the gods, kindly, warmly affectionate, strong for the work that is fitting. Struggle to remain the kind of person philosophy wanted to make you. Stand in awe of the gods, keep people safe. Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *προαπαυδᾶν*: The verb is the one used of the body just before, with “first” added in front: to give up, to fail from exhaustion. One English verb serves for both. Other reading: that your soul should be the first to say no
- *ἀποκαισαρωθῇς*: A word made from “Caesar”, apparently coined here: to be made into a Caesar through and through. The English spells it out. Other reading: that you are not Caesarified
- *μὴ βαφῇς*: Literally “that you are not dipped, dyed”. The dye in mind is probably the imperial purple, but the Greek does not name it and the English does not add it. Other reading: that you are not stained with the purple
- *ἀκέραιον*: The word means unmixed, undamaged, pure. The English reads “unspoiled”. Other reading: pure
- *ἄκομψον*: Literally “without elegance, without polish”: no fine airs. It is the opposite of the “elegance” warned against in 3.5a. The English reads “unpretentious”. Other reading: plain
- *αἰδοῦ θεούς*: The verb is to feel awe or shame before someone. “Stand in awe of” is used so that it is not taken for the same word as “reverent toward the gods” earlier in the list, which is a different Greek word. Other reading: Revere the gods
- *σῷζε ἀνθρώπους*: The verb is “save, keep safe, preserve”. The English reads “keep people safe”. Other reading: save people
- *εἶς καρπὸς τῆς ἐπιγείου ζωῆς*: The first word as given is a slip of the digitised text for the word “one”, and is read so; the verb “is” is supplied. The Greek uses two words for life in these two sentences, a life as it is lived and the state of being alive, and the English reads “life” and “living”. Other reading: one fruit of earthly life
- *πράξεις κοινωνικαί*: “Social” follows the glossary. The sense is actions done as a member of the community and for it, not sociable ones. Other reading: acts that serve the common good

</details>

### 6.30b

Everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity, and his ambition to grasp matters; and how he would not let anything at all go by without first looking into it very well and understanding it clearly; and how he bore with those who blamed him unjustly, without blaming them in return; and how he hurried toward nothing; and how he did not accept slanders; and how exact an examiner he was of characters and actions, and not one to reproach, not one to jump at a noise, not suspicious, not a sophist; and how he was content with little, for example in housing, bedding, clothing, food and service; and how hard-working he was and how patient; and that he was the kind of man who could stay at the same thing until evening, not even needing, because of his plain diet, to pass his waste except at the usual hour; and his being firm and always the same in his friendships; and his putting up with those who openly opposed his opinions, and being glad if anyone showed him something better; and how he was reverent toward the gods without superstition; so that your last hour may come upon you with a conscience as good as his.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πάντα ὡς Ἀντωνίνου μαθητής*: The passage begins partway through a chapter and these words have no verb: “do” is understood, and the English leaves it without one. Antoninus is Antoninus Pius, the emperor who adopted Marcus. The list that follows also has no verb (“remember” is understood) and is kept as a list. Other reading: Do everything as a pupil of Antoninus
- *εὔτονον*: Literally “well-strung”, of a string at the right tension: energy that does not slacken. Other reading: his steady effort for what is done according to reason
- *τῶν κατὰ λόγον πρασσομένων*: The participle is present and general, “things that are done according to reason”. It could also be heard of what was being done in his time. Other reading: what was done according to reason
- *τὸ εὔδιον τοῦ προσώπου*: The adjective is a weather word, “fair, clear, calm”. The English reads “calm”. Other reading: the fair weather of his face
- *τὸ ἀκενόδοξον*: Literally “the not being empty-gloried”: no appetite for empty reputation. Other reading: his freedom from empty glory
- *τὸ περὶ τὴν κατάληψιν τῶν πραγμάτων φιλότιμον*: “Love of honour” turned onto getting a firm grasp of things. The noun for “grasp” is also the Stoic term for sure knowledge of a fact; the plain word is kept. Other reading: his eagerness to get a sure understanding of the facts
- *παρῆκε*: The verb is “let pass, let go by, dismiss”. It is taken of letting a matter go without examining it. Other reading: he would never dismiss anything at all
- *οὐκ ἐδέχετο*: Literally “did not receive”: he did not take slanders in, did not give them a hearing. Other reading: he would not listen to slanders
- *ψοφοδεής*: Literally “afraid of a noise”: easily alarmed. Other reading: not timid
- *σοφιστής*: A professional teacher of clever speaking, and so anyone who shows off cleverness. “Sophist” is kept, as in 1.17a. Other reading: not a clever talker
- *ὑπηρεσίᾳ*: The word is “service”, here the servants who wait on a person. Other reading: attendants
- *ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ*: Literally “in the same”. It can be the same task or the same place, and the remark about not needing to leave except at the usual hour suits either. The English takes the task. Other reading: who could stay in the same place until evening
- *τὸ βέβαιον καὶ ὅμοιον*: Literally “the firm and the alike” in his friendships: he was steady toward his friends and did not change toward them. Other reading: his constancy and evenness in his friendships
- *εὐσυνειδήτῳ*: “With a good conscience”, said of “you”, with “as him” at the end: the last hour is to find you as it found him. Other reading: so that the last hour may find you with as clear a conscience as it found him

</details>

### 6.31

Sober up and call yourself back. And when you have woken up again and understood that it was dreams that were troubling you, then, awake again, look at these things as you looked at those.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἀνάνηφε*: Literally “become sober again”, as after drink. The passage then moves to the image of waking from sleep; both images are kept. Other reading: Come to your senses
- *πάλιν*: The word comes twice. The first may go with “woken up” or with “understood”; the second stands before “awake” but could go with the command, “look again”. The English takes them as “woken up again” and “awake again”, and splits the single Greek sentence in two. Other reading: and when you have woken and understood once more that it was dreams, now that you are awake, look again at these things
- *ἠνώχλουν*: An imperfect: the dreams “were troubling” you over a stretch of time. The English adds “it was” to bring out that they were only dreams. Other reading: that dreams were troubling you
- *βλέπε ταῦτα, ὡς ἐκεῖνα ἔβλεπες*: “These things” are what lies before you awake; “those” are most naturally the dreams. So the sense would be: regard waking troubles as you regarded the dream ones. The Greek does not say this outright and the pronouns are left bare. Other reading: look at the things of waking life as you used to look at the things in your dreams

</details>

### 6.32

I am made of a little body and a soul. Now to the little body all things are indifferent, for it cannot tell a difference. To the mind, whatever is not its own activity is indifferent; and whatever is its own activity, all of that is in its power. Even of these, though, it is concerned only with the present, for its future and past activities are themselves already indifferent as well.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐκ σωματίου εἰμὶ καὶ ψυχῆς*: σωμάτιον is a diminutive, “little body”, and belittling; the soul gets no diminutive. “Little” is kept. Other reading: a body and a soul
- *οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναται διαφέρεσθαι*: A play on ἀδιάφορα, the Stoic term for things “indifferent” (neither good nor bad), and διαφέρεσθαι, which can mean to make distinctions or to be affected differently. “Indifferent” and “tell a difference” keep the echo. Other reading: for nothing can make a difference to it
- *τῇ δὲ διανοίᾳ*: After “soul” in the first sentence Marcus switches to διάνοια. The glossary prefers “thought” but allows “mind” where the faculty is meant, as it is here; the passage has no νοῦς to confuse it with. Other reading: To thought
- *ἐνεργήματα*: The products of ἐνέργεια: its acts, what it itself does. The English has the singular “activity” in the general clauses and the plural at the end. Other reading: its own acts
- *αὐτῇ ἐστιν*: The full phrase is the Stoic expression for what is “up to” someone, in their power. Other reading: all of these are up to it
- *περὶ μόνον τὸ παρὸν πραγματεύεται*: Literally “it busies itself only about the present”. τὸ παρόν may be the present activity or the present time, and the English leaves that as open as the Greek does. Other reading: it is concerned only with the present one
- *καὶ αὐτὰ ἤδη ἀδιάφορα*: ἤδη is taken as logical, “already, at once”: not being present, they fall straight into the class of indifferent things. καὶ αὐτά, “they too”, puts past and future activities with external things. Other reading: are themselves indifferent as well by now

</details>

### 6.33–34

Pain is not against nature for the hand or for the foot, so long as the foot is doing the foot’s work and the hand the hand’s. So too for a human being, as a human being, pain is not against nature, so long as they are doing a human being’s work. And if it is not against nature for them, it is not bad for them either.

What great pleasures robbers, catamites, father-beaters, tyrants have enjoyed!

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὁ πόνος*: The word covers hard labour and pain. The hand and foot at their work suggest “toil”; but the conclusion, that it is not bad, and the pleasures of the next chapter answer the question whether pain is an evil, and the same word is set against pleasure in 9.1. “Pain” is used in both passages. Other reading: Toil is not against nature for the hand or for the foot
- *τὰ τοῦ ποδὸς*: Literally “the things of the foot”. “Work” is supplied; the Greek has no noun. Other reading: so long as the foot does what belongs to a foot
- *οὐδὲ κακόν ἐστιν αὐτῷ*: The adjective is the ordinary word for “bad”, used by the Stoics for what is truly an evil. Other reading: it is not an evil for them either
- *Ἡλίκας ἡδονὰς ἥσθησαν*: Chapter 34 begins here: a single exclamation with no stated conclusion, and none is added. Other reading: How great are the pleasures that have been felt by
- *κίναιδοι*: An abusive word for a man who takes the passive part in sex with men, and more loosely for any man held to be sexually shameless. “Catamites” is the nearest single English word. Other reading: debauched men
- *πατραλοῖαι*: Literally “father-strikers”. The word is used both of those who beat a father and of those who kill one; the English stays with the literal sense. Other reading: parricides

</details>

### 6.35

Do you not see how craftsmen in the manual trades adapt themselves to laymen up to a point, but all the same hold on to the reason of their craft and will not agree to abandon it? Is it not shocking if the master builder and the doctor are to have more respect for the reason of their own craft than a human being has for their own reason, which a human being shares with the gods?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *οἱ βάναυσοι τεχνῖται*: βάναυσος is the word for people in the manual, workshop trades and usually carries some contempt. The English names the trades and leaves the slight unsaid. “Craftsmen” is kept for τεχνῖται because it is from the same root as τέχνη, “craft”, which comes twice more in the passage. Other reading: the common craftsmen; mere tradesmen
- *ἁρμόζονται μὲν μέχρι τινὸς πρὸς τοὺς ἰδιώτας*: ἁρμόζονται πρός is literally “fit themselves to”. The ἰδιῶται are those outside the craft, here most naturally the customers who have no training in it. Other reading: fit in with the untrained up to a point; go along with their customers so far
- *ἀντέχονται τοῦ λόγου τῆς τέχνης*: The λόγος of a craft is its rationale, the rule or account by which the work is done. The English has “reason” because the second sentence sets this λόγος beside the human being’s own λόγος, and the argument needs one English word for both. Other reading: hold on to the principle (or rule) of their craft
- *τούτου ἀποστῆναι οὐχ ὑπομένουσιν*: Literally “do not submit to standing away from it”. The English states a refusal, since the Greek has no word for being unable. Other reading: and cannot bear to leave it; and will not bring themselves to depart from it
- *οὐ δεινὸν*: δεινόν runs from “terrible” to “strange” or “outrageous”. With εἰ it is a usual way of protesting at something absurd, so the English has “shocking”. Other reading: Is it not a terrible thing if; Is it not strange if
- *ὁ ἀρχιτέκτων*: The ἀρχιτέκτων is the chief builder who directs the work, not only a designer. With the doctor this may be a step up from the trades of the first sentence, or two more examples of a craft. Other reading: the architect
- *αἰδέσονται*: A future, “will respect”, turned as “are to have more respect”. The verb αἰδεῖσθαι means to respect or revere, with a sense of feeling shame before something. Other reading: will revere the reason of their own craft more
- *τὸν ἑαυτοῦ, ὃς αὐτῷ κοινός ἐστι πρὸς τοὺς θεούς*: Literally “his own, which is common to him with the gods”: “reason” is supplied from earlier in the sentence. ὁ ἄνθρωπος is the human being in general, so the English does not write “he”. It has “their own reason” and then repeats “a human being”, so that the last clause cannot be taken to mean the builder and the doctor. Other reading: than man has for his own, which he has in common with the gods

</details>

### 6.36

Asia, Europe: corners of the universe. Every sea: a drop of the universe. Athos: a small clod of the universe. All of present time: a point of eternity. All things are small, easily changed, vanishing.

All things come from there: they have set out from that common ruling part, or they come as a consequence. So the gaping jaws of the lion too, and poison, and every kind of harm, like a thorn, like mud, are by-products of those revered and beautiful things. So do not picture them as foreign to what you revere, but consider the source of all things.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *γωνίαι*: Literally “angles”, then corners or nooks. The Greek has no verb in this run of phrases, and colons keep it as terse as it is. Other reading: Asia and Europe are nooks of the universe
- *πᾶν πέλαγος*: Without the article this is “every sea”, each open sea taken singly. It could also be read as “the whole sea”. Other reading: The whole sea: a drop of the universe
- *Ἄθως βωλάριον*: Athos is a high mountain on a headland in northern Greece. The second word is a diminutive of “clod of earth”. Other reading: Athos: a little lump of soil
- *στιγμὴ τοῦ αἰῶνος*: The first word is a prick or dot, the mark a point makes. The second is the whole of time, here “eternity”. “Of” is kept, as in the three phrases before it. Other reading: a pinprick in the whole of time
- *ἐναφανιζόμενα*: The compound means disappearing into something. The Greek does not say into what, and the list before it covers both the universe and time, so the English is “vanishing” and names nothing. Other reading: disappearing into it
- *ὁρμήσαντα ἣ*: The participle means “having set out, started”, and is the verb of ὁρμή, “impulse”, as in 7.75, where the ruling part of the universe directs an impulse at things. The small word after it is printed with a breathing that would make it “which”, and that gives no sense; it is read as “or”. Other reading: set going by an impulse of that common ruling part, or as a consequence
- *ἐπακολούθησιν*: Literally “following after”: things that are not aimed at directly but come as a sequel. The Greek does not say to what, and the English does not either. The same phrase has the same English in 7.75. Other reading: or as a side-effect that follows
- *πᾶσα κακουργία*: The noun means doing harm, and most often wrongdoing or malice in a person. Beside jaws, poison, thorn and mud, the English takes it widely as “every kind of harm”. On the other reading it is human wickedness. Other reading: and all wickedness, like a thorn, like mud
- *ὡς ἄκανθα, ὡς βόρβορος*: The small word means “like” or “as”. It can give thorn and mud as examples of harm, or it can compare: jaws, poison and harm are by-products in the way that a thorn and mud are. English “like” allows both. Other reading: such as a thorn, such as mud
- *ἐπιγεννήματα*: Literally “things born on top of” or “born after” something. It seems to be a Stoic term for what comes along with a thing without being its purpose (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: are after-growths of those revered and beautiful things
- *τῶν σεμνῶν καὶ καλῶν*: The first adjective is said of what commands reverence and is from the same root as “revere” in the next sentence, so the English is “revered”. The second means beautiful or fine. The plural “those things” is not explained; it seems to point back to the ruling part and what it does. Other reading: of those holy and noble things
- *τούτου οὗ σέβεις*: The forms can be masculine or neuter: “him whom you revere” or “what you revere”. The English keeps the neuter. Other reading: as foreign to him whom you worship

</details>

### 6.37–38

Whoever has seen what is now has seen everything: all that has come to be from the everlasting past and all that will be without end. For all things are of the same stock and of the same kind.

Reflect often on the linking together of all things in the universe and their relation to one another. For in a way all things are interwoven with one another, and all are on that account dear to one another. For this thing is next in order to another, through the movement of tension, the breathing together and the unity of substance.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐξ ἀιδίου*: “From the everlasting”, that is, from all time past; “past” is added to make that plain. It is paired with εἰς τὸ ἄπειρον, “into the boundless”, given as “without end”. Other reading: all that has been from eternity and all that will be to infinity
- *ὁμογενῆ καὶ ὁμοειδῆ*: Two near-synonyms: “of the same birth or family” and “of the same form or kind”. “Of the same kind” is kept for ὁμοειδής, as in 7.49 and 9.35. Other reading: akin and alike in form
- *ἐπισύνδεσιν*: A binding of one thing onto another, a chain of connection. The word is rare. Other reading: the bond that joins all things in the universe
- *φίλα*: “Dear” or “friendly”: things are on good terms with one another because they are woven together. The word can also mean simply “akin”. Other reading: and all are on that account friendly to one another
- *ἄλλῳ ἑξῆς ἐστι τοῦτο*: Literally “this is next in order to another”. As given, “this” has nothing to point to, and the phrase is thought to be damaged or emended by editors (from memory, unchecked). The English keeps it as it stands; the sense must be that each thing comes in sequence after another. Other reading: for one thing follows in order on another
- *τὴν τονικὴν κίνησιν*: A Stoic technical term: the movement of tension (τόνος) in the breath that pervades and holds together all substance. No plain English word exists for it, so the two Greek words are given literally. Other reading: through the tensile movement
- *σύμπνοιαν*: Literally “breathing together”: the shared breath, and so the agreement, of all parts of the universe. The literal image is kept because the Stoic breath is in view. Other reading: the common accord

</details>

### 6.39–40

Fit yourself to the things your lot has joined you to, and love the people your lot has put you among, but truly.

Every instrument, tool or utensil is as it should be if it does what it was made for; and yet in that case the one who made it is away. But in things held together by nature, the power that made them is inside and stays there. For that reason you should respect it all the more, and consider that if you keep to its will and live by it, everything is as your mind would have it. And in the same way, for the All too, what is its own is as its mind would have it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *συγκεκλήρωσαι*: Literally “you have been allotted together with”. The next clause uses a different verb with the same image of drawing lots (συνείληχας). “Lot” is used for both. Other reading: the things with which you have been joined by lot
- *συνάρμοζε σεαυτὸν*: The same “fit together” verb that is used of building stones in 5.8. Other reading: adapt yourself
- *Ὄργανον, ἐργαλεῖον, σκεῦος*: Three near-synonyms for a made thing that is used for something. The differences between them are slight and the three English words are approximate. Other reading: Every implement, tool, vessel
- *εὖ ἔχει*: Literally “is in a good state”, the phrase given as “all is well” in 9.28. Other reading: is in good order
- *ἐκποδών*: Literally “out from the feet”, that is, out of the way, gone off. It does not say the maker is dead, only that the maker is not there, as the next sentence shows. Other reading: the maker is out of the way
- *κατασκευάσοσα*: As printed in the digitised text this form is irregular. It is read as κατασκευάσασα, “that made”, the same verb as “was made for” and “the one who made it” just before. Other reading: the power that constructed them
- *αἰδεῖσθαι*: The word joins respect, reverence and a sense of shame before someone. Other reading: you should revere it all the more
- *ἔχῃς καὶ διεξάγῃς*: Two verbs with no object: literally “if you are in a state and carry on through” in line with its will. They are given as “keep to” and “live by”. Other reading: if you are and continue in accord with its will
- *κατὰ νοῦν*: An idiom, “to one’s liking”, whose literal sense is “according to mind”. Marcus uses it twice, the second time of the All, where the literal sense is felt. The English reads “as your mind would have it” to keep the word “mind”. Other reading: everything goes as you would wish. And so too for the All its own affairs go as it would wish
- *τῷ παντὶ*: Literally “for the all”, a name for the sum of things. It is a different word from “the whole” and from “the universe”, so the English keeps “the All”. Other reading: for the universe

</details>

### 6.41

Whatever you set up for yourself as good or bad among the things that are not yours to choose, it must follow that when you meet with such a bad thing or miss such a good one, you blame the gods, and hate people too: those who are the cause, or are suspected of being about to be the cause, of your missing the one or meeting with the other. And indeed we do many wrongs because of the difference these things make to us. But if we judge only the things that are up to us to be good and bad, no cause is left either for accusing a god or for taking an enemy’s stand against a person.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τῶν ἀπροαιρέτων*: The word means the things that do not fall under choice (προαίρεσις), what a person cannot decide. It is the opposite of “the things that are up to us” (τὰ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν) later in the passage; the English keeps two different phrases because the Greek has two. Other reading: the things that lie outside your will
- *ὑποστήσῃ σαυτῷ*: The verb is to lay something down as a basis, to posit. “For yourself” can go with the verb, as the English takes it, or with “good or bad”. Other reading: Whatever you suppose to be good or bad for you
- *κατὰ τὴν περίπτωσιν τοῦ τοιούτου κακοῦ ἢ τὴν ἀπότευξιν τοῦ τοιούτου ἀγαθοῦ*: Two nouns of the Stoic school: περίπτωσις is falling into what one wanted to avoid, ἀπότευξις is failing to get what one wanted. The Greek has nouns; the English turns them into verbs with “you” as subject. Other reading: upon the falling into such a bad thing or the failure to obtain such a good thing
- *ὑποπτευομένους ἔσεσθαι*: A passive with a future infinitive: “suspected that they will be (the cause)”. The Greek does not say who suspects, and the English keeps the passive. Other reading: or whom you suspect will be the cause
- *διὰ τὴν πρὸς ταῦτα διαφοράν*: Literally “because of the difference toward these things”. The English takes it as the opposite of Stoic indifference: these things are allowed to make a difference. The noun can also mean a quarrel or disagreement; the verb of the same idiom is at 9.40. Other reading: because of our quarrels over these things
- *οὐδεμία αἰτία καταλείπεται*: αἰτία is a cause and also a ground for a charge. It answers “those who are the cause” (τοὺς αἰτίους) above, so the English says “cause” in both places. Other reading: no ground is left
- *στῆναι στάσιν πολεμίου*: Verb and noun are from one root: “to stand the stand of an enemy”. The noun στάσις is also the ordinary word for faction and civil strife, which may be heard here. Other reading: to take up an enemy’s position against a person

</details>

### 6.42

We are all working together towards one finished result, some of us knowingly and with awareness, others without attending to it, just as Heraclitus, I think, says that even those who are asleep are workers and fellow workers in the things that happen in the universe. One works together in one way, another in another, and, into the bargain, so does even the one who finds fault and the one who tries to stand against the things that happen and do away with them, for the universe had need of such a person too. What remains, then, is for you to understand among which of them you are placing yourself. For the one who governs the whole will in any case use you well, and will take you in as some part of the fellow workers and of those who help the work along. But you, do not become the kind of part that the cheap and ridiculous line is in the play, the one Chrysippus mentions.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀποτέλεσμα*: The completed product of a work, the thing brought to a finish. The English reads “finished result”. Other reading: towards one outcome
- *συνεργοῦμεν*: The passage repeats this root five times. The English keeps “work together” for the verb and “fellow workers” for the noun in each place so that the chain shows. Other reading: We all cooperate towards one result
- *παρακολουθητικῶς*: “Following with the mind”: aware of what one is doing. Its opposite in the next clause (ἀνεπιστάτως) is “without attention”, given as “without attending to it”. Other reading: some knowingly and with understanding, others unwittingly
- *ὁ Ἡράκλειτος*: Heraclitus of Ephesus, the early philosopher. Marcus quotes from memory, as his own aside shows. From memory, unchecked: this passage is itself the source for the saying, which is counted among the fragments of Heraclitus. Other reading: as Heraclitus, I believe, calls even sleepers workers and collaborators in what goes on in the universe
- *ἐκ περιουσίας*: Idiom, literally “out of surplus”: over and above, with room to spare. The English reads “into the bargain”. The sense is that even the objector contributes, as an extra. Other reading: and there is room to spare even for the one who finds fault
- *ὁ τὰ ὅλα διοικῶν*: A masculine participle, “he who administers the whole”, meaning god or the governing reason. The English reads “the one who governs the whole”. The Greek for “the whole” is plural here (“all things”); the glossary’s word is kept. Other reading: he who governs all things
- *τῶν συνεργῶν καὶ συνεργητικῶν*: Two near-synonyms from the same root: fellow workers, and those apt to help the work. The genitive could be persons or things; the English takes them as persons. Other reading: as a part of the things that work together and help the work along
- *οὗ Χρύσιππος μέμνηται*: Chrysippus was the third head of the Stoic school. From memory, unchecked: Plutarch reports him saying that a comedy contains ridiculous lines which are poor in themselves but add charm to the whole play, and that vice has the same place in the universe. Other reading: the line Chrysippus speaks of

</details>

### 6.43

Surely the sun does not think it should do the rain’s part? Or Asclepius the part of the fruit-bearing goddess? And what of each of the stars? Are they not different, yet working together toward the same thing?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μήτι*: This particle marks a question expecting the answer no, here and in the next question; “Surely … not” carries that. Other reading: Does the sun think it should do the rain’s part?
- *ἀξιοῖ*: The verb ranges from “thinks it right” and “sees fit” to “claims” and “demands”. Other reading: Surely the sun does not claim the rain’s part?
- *τὰ τοῦ ὑετοῦ*: Literally “the things of the rain”: what belongs to the rain to do. Other reading: the rain’s work
- *τῆς Καρποφόρου*: “The Fruit-Bearer” (feminine) is a title of a goddess of crops, usually Demeter, sometimes Earth. Asclepius is the god of healing. Other reading: the part of Demeter, bringer of crops
- *τί δὲ τῶν ἄστρων ἕκαστον;*: The question has no verb: literally 'and what each of the stars?' Other reading: And what does each of the stars do?
- *οὐχὶ διάφορα μέν, συνεργὰ δὲ πρὸς ταὐτόν;*: The adjectives are neuter plural and may describe the stars alone or everything just named (sun, rain, the two gods, the stars). The Greek also does not say what 'the same thing' is. Other reading: Are all these not different, yet working together toward the same end?

</details>

### 6.44

If, then, the gods deliberated about me and about the things that had to happen to me, they deliberated well. For a god without deliberation is not easy even to imagine; and for what cause would they have had an impulse to do me harm? For what would they, or the community, which is what they take most thought for, have gained from it? But if they did not deliberate about me individually, they certainly did deliberate about the affairs of the community, at least, and these things too, which happen as a consequence of those, I ought to welcome and hold dear. But if in fact they deliberate about nothing (to believe that is not pious; or else let us not sacrifice, or pray, or swear oaths, or do the other things that we do at every turn towards the gods as present and living with us), if in fact they deliberate about nothing that concerns us, then I am free to deliberate about myself, and my inquiry is into what is of benefit. What benefits each is what accords with its own make-up and nature, and my nature is rational and civic. My city and fatherland, as Antoninus, is Rome; as a human being, the universe. So the things that are useful to these cities are the only things that are good for me.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐβουλεύσαντο*: The verb is “to take counsel” and so both “to deliberate” and “to decide”. It comes seven times and “deliberate” is kept throughout. Other reading: If the gods made a decision about me
- *ἄβουλον*: From the same root: “without counsel”, which can mean one who does not deliberate or one who deliberates badly. Other reading: an ill-advised god
- *ἔμελλον ὁρμᾶν*: Literally “were they going to set themselves moving”. “Impulse” is used for the verb, as for the Stoic term ὁρμή. Other reading: why would they have set out to do me harm?
- *περιεγένετο*: Literally “what was left over as a gain”. The Greek is a plain past tense, “what did they gain”; the English reads “would have gained”, since the harm is only supposed. Other reading: what did they, or the community, gain from that?
- *τῷ κοινῷ*: “The common thing”, singular: the body to which all belong, an ordinary word for a community or commonwealth. In the next sentence the plural τῶν κοινῶν, “the common things”, is given as “the affairs of the community”, so that the one word is heard in both places. Other reading: the common good ... what is common to all
- *προνοοῦνται*: The verb behind πρόνοια, “providence”: to think ahead on behalf of something. Other reading: for which above all they exercise providence
- *ἐπακολούθησιν καὶ ταῦτα συμβαίνοντα*: Literally “these things too, happening by way of following on from those”. “These things” are what happens to me. Other reading: and what happens to me as a by-product of those decisions
- *πιστεύειν μὲν οὐχ ὅσιον ἢ*: The ἢ after “not pious” is “or else”: if one did believe it, the acts of worship that follow would make no sense. The brackets are the editor’s. Other reading: it is impious to believe so; otherwise let us give up sacrificing
- *σκέψις περὶ τοῦ συμφέροντος*: Literally “for me there is inquiry about what benefits”. The Greek does not say “benefits me”; the next sentence says whom. This translation usually gives συμφέρει as “is good for”. “Benefit” is used here because the last sentence of the passage needs “good” for another word, ἀγαθά. Other reading: and my inquiry is into what is good for me
- *πολιτική*: “Belonging to a city (πόλις)”, that is, made for life with others as a citizen. The word for “city” follows at once, so the English reads “civic” to keep the link. Other reading: rational and social
- *Ἀντωνίνῳ*: Antoninus is Marcus’s own name as emperor (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus). Other reading: as the emperor Antoninus

</details>

### 6.45

Whatever happens to each is good for the whole. That would be enough. But if you watch you will also see this, as a general rule: whatever happens to one person is good for other people too. Here, though, let “good for” be taken in the more ordinary sense, as applied to things that are neither good nor bad.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *συμφέρει*: “Is good for”, literally “brings together”. The sounds of “happens” (συμβαίνει) and “is good for” (συμφέρει) answer each other in the Greek. Other reading: is to the advantage of the whole
- *ἤρκει τοῦτο*: A past tense, “this was enough”, used in Greek for what would be enough by itself. Other reading: That was enough
- *ὡς ἐπίπαν*: “On the whole, in general, for the most part”. It limits the claim: this holds as a rule, not without exception. Other reading: in most cases
- *ὅσα ἀνθρώπῳ, καὶ ἑτέροις ἀνθρώποις*: The Greek has no verbs here: literally “whatever to a person, also to other persons”. The English supplies “happens” and “is good for” from the first sentence, in the same order, because the clause has the same shape as that sentence, with “a person” in place of “each” and “other people” in place of “the whole”. “Is good for” could be supplied twice, which is a different claim. Other reading: whatever is good for one person is good for other people too
- *κοινότερον*: “More commonly”, that is, in the looser everyday sense of the word and not the strict Stoic sense in which only virtue is good for anyone. Other reading: in a broader sense
- *τῶν μέσων*: Literally “the things in the middle”, the Stoic name for things neither good nor bad in themselves, such as health or money. The English gives the meaning of the term, as in 3.11. Other reading: as applied to the things in the middle

</details>

### 6.46

Just as what goes on in the amphitheatre and places of that kind repels you, since the same things are always being seen, and the sameness makes the spectacle cloying, feel the same about the whole of life too. For all things, up and down, are the same and from the same. How long, then?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *προσίσταταί σοι*: Literally “stands against you”. It is used of food that turns the stomach and so of anything that offends or wearies. The English uses a verb of physical distaste. Other reading: wearies you; turns your stomach
- *ὡς ἀεὶ τὰ αὐτὰ ὁρώμενα*: Literally “as being always the same things seen”. The Greek is passive and names no viewer, and the English keeps it so. Other reading: because you always see the same things
- *προσκορῆ*: The word means causing surfeit, too much of one thing. “Cloying” keeps the image of being overfed. Other reading: makes one sick of the sight
- *πάσχειν*: The Greek as given has a bare infinitive with no verb to govern it. The English reads it as the notebook’s infinitive of instruction, “feel”. It can also be taken as a statement of what happens, and some editors are said to alter it to an indicative in the second person (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: this is what happens to you with the whole of life too
- *ἄνω κάτω*: Literally “up down”, an idiom for “everywhere, from top to bottom” or “over and over, back and forth”. The English keeps the literal pair, which can be heard both ways. Other reading: For everything, over and over, is the same
- *ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν*: “Out of the same”: the same materials or the same causes. The Greek has no verb here and does not say which, and the English adds neither. Other reading: and come from the same causes
- *μέχρι τίνος οὖν*: Literally “up to what point, then?”. It may ask how long this will go on, or how long one is to go on watching. Other reading: Until when, then?

</details>

### 6.47

Keep in mind continually that people of every kind, of every kind of occupation and from every sort of nation, are dead, so that this thought comes down as far as Philistion and Phoebus and Origanion. Now pass on to the other classes. That is the place we must move to, where there are so many formidable orators, so many grave philosophers, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates, so many heroes earlier, so many generals and tyrants later; and besides these Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes, other natures that were sharp, great-minded, hard-working, unscrupulous, self-willed, mockers of human life itself, perishable and lasting a day, such as Menippus and all of his kind. About all of these, keep in mind that they have long been lying dead. What, then, is terrible in this for them? And what for those who are not even named at all? One thing here is worth a great deal: to live life through with truth and justice, kindly towards the liars and the unjust.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὥστε κατιέναι τοῦτο*: The construction is loose. “This” is taken as the subject, and “thought” is supplied to say what comes down: the review of the dead reaches these three names. It can also be “so as to go down in this as far as”. Other reading: so as to come down in this as far as Philistion
- *Φιλιστίωνος καὶ Φοίβου καὶ Ὀριγανίωνος*: Three people who cannot be identified here, presumably recently dead and of no standing, so that the review reaches down to the present and to the obscure (from memory, unchecked).
- *τὰ ἄλλα φῦλα*: φῦλα is “tribes, races”. Here it is used of kinds of people (orators, philosophers, heroes, generals) and not of nations, so the English says “classes”. Other reading: the other tribes
- *μεταβαλεῖν ἡμᾶς δεῖ*: The verb is the one for “change” used in other passages; here it is a change of place. It can mean that everyone must in the end go where these dead are, or only that the review must now move on to them; “move to” leaves both open. Other reading: must change over to that place
- *δεινοὶ ῥήτορες*: δεινός of a speaker is “clever, formidable”. The same word comes back below as “terrible” (τί οὖν τοῦτο δεινὸν), and the echo may be meant; English cannot hold both with one word. Other reading: so many clever speakers
- *ἄλλαι φύσεις ὀξεῖαι*: Only “sharp” is marked as feminine and so tied to “natures”. The adjectives after it have one form for masculine and feminine and may instead name further kinds of people. Other reading: other sharp natures, and the great-minded, the hard-working, the unscrupulous, the self-willed
- *πανοῦργοι*: Literally “ready to do anything”. It is usually a word of blame (unscrupulous, knavish), which the English follows, and sometimes a word for clever resource. Other reading: ready for anything
- *χλευασταί, οἷον Μένιππος*: Menippus was a Cynic writer known for mockery (from memory, unchecked). The genitive before it makes human life itself the thing mocked. Other reading: scoffers at this very life of human beings, perishable and short as it is, such as Menippus
- *κεῖνται*: The verb is simply “lie”, the regular word for the dead lying in the ground. “Dead” is added in the English to make that plain. Other reading: they have long been lying there

</details>

### 6.48

When you want to cheer yourself, think of the strong points of the people you live with: the energy of one, for example, the modesty of another, the generosity of a third, and something else in someone else. For nothing cheers so much as the likenesses of the virtues showing in the characters of the people you live with, and coming together, as many at once as possible. And so they must be kept ready to hand.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *εὐφρᾶναι*: The same verb comes back in the second sentence (εὐφραίνει), so one English word, “cheer”, is used for both. Its range runs from “gladden” to “delight”. Other reading: When you want to gladden yourself
- *τὰ προτερήματα*: Literally the points in which someone is ahead: advantages, superior qualities. The English takes the plain “strong points”. Other reading: the merits (or: the advantages) of the people you live with
- *τὸ δραστήριον*: The quality of being effective in action, of getting things done. “Energy” narrows it a little. Other reading: the effectiveness of one
- *τὸ αἰδῆμον*: The quality of having αἰδώς: a sense of shame, respect for others and for oneself. “Modesty” is one side of it. Other reading: the sense of shame (or: the self-respect) of another
- *τὸ εὐμετάδοτον*: Literally readiness to give a share of what one has. Other reading: the readiness to share of a third
- *τὰ ὁμοιώματα τῶν ἀρετῶν*: The Greek says likenesses (images, copies) of the virtues, not the virtues themselves, and the English keeps that. It need not be dismissive. Other reading: the images of the virtues
- *τῶν συζώντων*: A different verb from τῶν συμβιούντων in the first sentence, with the same sense, “those who live with”. The Greek names no person in either place; the English supplies “you” in both, since the passage is addressed to “you”. Other reading: in the characters of those who share one’s life
- *ἀθρόα ὡς οἷόν τε συμπίπτοντα*: Literally “falling together in as dense a crowd as possible”. It is open whether the likenesses crowd together in the same people or come before the mind all at once. The English leaves that open. Other reading: and meeting the eye all together, as far as that can be
- *διὸ καὶ πρόχειρα αὐτὰ ἑκτέον*: An impersonal form (“they are to be kept”) with no “you”. The καί is taken with διό (“and so”); it could instead mark “them too”. “They” is most naturally the strong points, but could be the likenesses. Other reading: So these too must be kept at hand

</details>

### 6.49

You are not upset, are you, that you weigh so many pounds and not three hundred? So too, then, with having to live to so many years and no more. For just as you are content with the amount of matter that has been marked off for you, so too with time.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μήτι δυσχεραίνεις*: μήτι opens a question that expects the answer no. δυσχεραίνειν is to take something hard, to be annoyed or put out. Other reading: Surely you do not resent
- *τοσῶνδέ τινων λιτρῶν εἶ*: Literally “you are of so many pounds”; the English reads “weigh”. The λίτρα is the Roman pound. From memory, unchecked: about 327 grams, so three hundred of them is a little under a hundred kilograms. Other reading: that you are of such and such a number of pounds
- *οὕτω δὴ καὶ ὅτι*: The second sentence has no verb of its own: “so too, then, that you must live to so many years”. The verb “be upset” is carried over from the question, and the English leaves it unstated too. Other reading: Then do not be upset either that you must live to so many years and no more
- *τῆς οὐσίας*: οὐσία is “substance”, the stuff a thing is made of, here the matter of the body, which fits the pounds just mentioned. The same word is also the ordinary Greek for a person’s property. Other reading: the amount of property that has been marked off for you
- *στέργεις*: στέργειν is to be content with, to put up with gladly, and also to feel affection for. The English takes the cooler sense. Other reading: you accept with affection

</details>

### 6.50

Try to persuade them, but act even against their will whenever the reasoning of justice leads that way. If, however, someone uses force and stands in the way, change over to being content and free of distress, and use the hindrance for another virtue; and remember that your impulse was with a reservation, and that you were not desiring what is impossible. What were you desiring, then? An impulse of some such kind. And this you attain: the things we were led forward for, these come about.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *αὐτούς*: “Them” is not explained; the Greek does not say who they are. Other reading: Try to persuade people
- *τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὁ λόγος*: Literally “the reason of justice”: what justice, reasoned out, requires. “Reasoning” keeps λόγος close to “reason”, as in the glossary, and leaves “principle” for δόγμα. Other reading: whenever the principle of justice leads that way
- *τὸ εὐάρεστον καὶ ἄλυπον*: Two neuter adjectives used as states: being well pleased with what comes, and being without pain of mind. Other reading: pass over to contentment and calm
- *συγχρῶ εἰς ἄλλην ἀρετὴν τῇ κωλύσει*: Literally “make use of the hindrance towards another virtue”: the block on the just act becomes material for a different virtue. The Greek does not name it. Other reading: turn the hindrance to the exercise of another virtue
- *μεθ’ ὑπεξαιρέσεως*: ὑπεξαίρεσις is the Stoic “reservation”: an impulse (ὁρμή) made with the unspoken clause “if nothing prevents”. The one word is kept. Other reading: that you set out conditionally
- *τίνος οὖν;*: Literally “Of what, then?”, the case depending on “you were desiring” just before. The verb is repeated so that the question stands in English; “were you desiring” is added. Other reading: What, then?
- *τῆς τοιᾶσδέ τινος ὁρμῆς*: “An impulse of some such kind”, that is, an impulse with a reservation: what was wanted was the impulse itself, not the outcome. Other reading: Just such an effort as this.
- *ἐφ’ οἷς προήχθημεν, ταῦτα γίνεται*: The hardest clause. προάγω is to lead forward, and the preposition with this case gives the purpose or the terms, not a place reached; the Greek does not say who did the leading, and it changes without warning from “you” to the first person plural. It can be read of what the impulse set out for, of what human beings were brought into being for, or of the terms on which the impulse was made. Other reading: what human beings were brought into being for, that is being done

</details>

### 6.51

The lover of fame takes their own good to be another person’s activity; the lover of pleasure, their own feeling; the person who has sense, their own action.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *φιλόδοξος*: Literally a lover of δόξα, which is reputation and also other people’s opinion. Other reading: The lover of reputation
- *ἀλλοτρίαν ἐνέργειαν ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν*: The line turns on “another’s” against “one’s own”, the second word coming three times. Another’s activity is the praising that other people do. The Greek names the activity first; the English puts “their own good” first so that “their” is clearly the lover of fame. Other reading: takes another person’s activity to be their own good
- *ὑπολαμβάνει*: The verb of ὑπόληψις, “judgment” in the glossary. Other reading: judges
- *ἰδίαν πεῖσιν*: Literally “their own being acted on”: what is passively felt, set against activity and action. Other reading: what they themselves undergo
- *νοῦν ἔχων*: The everyday idiom for being sensible, literally “having mind”. The glossary gives “mind” for the noun; the English reads “sense” because the idiom is the point. Other reading: the person who has mind
- *ἰδίαν πρᾶξιν*: A different noun from the “activity” of the first clause: a deed, something one does. Other reading: what they themselves do

</details>

### 6.52

One is free to form no judgment about this and not to be troubled in one’s soul; for things themselves do not have a nature that produces our verdicts.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἔξεστι*: Impersonal: “it is allowed, it is open”, a matter of freedom more than of bare possibility. “One is free” keeps it impersonal, since the Greek names no “you”. Other reading: It is possible to form no judgment about this
- *περὶ τούτου*: “About this” with nothing named: the matter in front of him. The form could also be masculine, “about this person”. Other reading: to form no judgment about this man
- *ὀχλεῖσθαι τῇ ψυχῇ*: The verb is from the word for a crowd: to be bothered, pestered. “Trouble” is used for this word and its compound (ἐνοχλεῖν) throughout the section, and “disturb” for ταράσσειν, to keep the two apart. The Greek has “the soul”, where the article stands for the owner; “one’s” follows the impersonal opening. Other reading: and not to be bothered in the soul
- *κρίσεων*: κρίσις is close in sense to ὑπόληψις, which the glossary renders “judgment”. Since both stand in this one sentence, κρίσις is given as “verdicts”, so that the two Greek words can be told apart. Other reading: a nature that produces our judgments
- *φύσιν ποιητικὴν*: Literally “a nature productive of”: things are not of a kind to make our verdicts for us. Other reading: things themselves are not of a nature to create our verdicts

</details>

### 6.53

Accustom yourself to be with what another person is saying, without inattention, and, as far as possible, be in the soul of the one who speaks.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πρὸς τῷ ὑφ’ ἑτέρου λεγομένῳ γίνεσθαι*: Literally “to come to be at what is said by another”, an idiom for giving one’s attention to a thing. The same verb returns in “be in the soul”, so the English has “be” both times. Other reading: to give your whole attention to what is said by another
- *ἀπαρενθυμήτως*: A rare adverb: “without thinking of something beside it”, or “without disregarding it”, as the related verb means in 5.5. “Without inattention” leaves both open. Other reading: without neglecting any of it
- *ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ λέγοντος γίνου*: Literally “come to be in the soul of the speaker”, now as a command. The English keeps “soul” and does not turn it into “mind”. Other reading: get inside the speaker’s mind

</details>

### 6.54

What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee either.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τῷ σμήνει*: σμῆνος means both the beehive and the swarm of bees that lives in it. The contrast is between the community of bees and the single bee. The English reads “hive”, which also names the colony and not only its box, while “swarm” in English suggests bees on the move. Other reading: What is not good for the swarm
- *μὴ συμφέρον οὐδὲ τῇ μελίσσῃ συμφέρει*: The same verb, συμφέρω, “be to the advantage of, benefit”, stands on both sides, first as a participle and then as a finite verb, and “is good for” renders it both times, as elsewhere in this translation. It is not ἀγαθόν, the word for “good” in 9.17. Other reading: What does not benefit the hive does not benefit the bee either.
- *οὐδὲ*: οὐδέ can be “not … either” or the stronger “not even”. The weaker sense is taken, since the sentence moves from the group to its member. Other reading: is not good even for the bee

</details>

### 6.55

If the sailors were speaking ill of me while I was steering, or the sick while I was their doctor, would I be attending to anything other than how I myself might bring about what keeps those on board safe, or what makes those under treatment healthy?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κυβερνῶντα οἱ ναῦται ἢ ἰατρεύοντα οἱ κάμνοντες*: The participles are bare accusatives, “one steering”, “one doctoring”, with no article and no pronoun. The first person in the if-clause is supplied, because the verb ἐνεργοίην later in the sentence is first person. “Their” in “their doctor” is also supplied. Other reading: If the sailors were speaking ill of the one steering, or the sick of the one doctoring
- *ἰατρεύοντα*: One word, “doctoring”, turned as “while I was their doctor”. “Treating” is not used here because the sentence ends with a different Greek word, θεραπευομένοις, “those under treatment”. Other reading: while I was treating them
- *κακῶς ἔλεγον*: The imperfect with εἰ, answered by ἂν and an imperfect, makes an unreal condition, which may refer to the present or to the past. The English takes it as present. Other reading: If the sailors had been speaking ill … would I have attended
- *ἂν προσεῖχον*: The form is either first person singular, “would I attend”, or third person plural, “would they attend”. The English takes it as first person to agree with ἐνεργοίην. Other reading: would they be attending to anything other than
- *ἄλλῳ τινὶ*: The dative can be neuter, “anything else”, or masculine, “anyone else”. With ἢ πῶς following, “anything other than how” is the reading that construes. Other reading: would I pay attention to anyone else, or to how
- *αὐτὸς ἐνεργοίην*: As given, the verb is first person singular, “I myself might bring about”, and the English follows it. From memory, unchecked, the text is doubted here and a third person form, “he himself”, is also read, which would make the sailors and the sick the subject of the main verb. Other reading: would they be attending to anything other than how he himself might bring about
- *τὸ τοῖς ἐμπλέουσι σωτήριον*: τὸ σωτήριον is “what saves” or “what brings safety”. οἱ ἐμπλέοντες are all who sail in the ship, a wider word than the sailors of the first clause, so the English keeps the two apart, as also “the sick” and “those under treatment”. Other reading: what saves those sailing in the ship; the safety of those on board
- *τὸ τοῖς θεραπευομένοις ὑγιεινόν*: ὑγιεινόν is what makes for health, as σωτήριον is what makes for safety. The English gives the two phrases the same shape. Other reading: what is healthy for those under treatment; what restores those under treatment to health

</details>

### 6.56

How many of those with whom I came into the world have already gone away.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πόσοι*: “How many” can be a question or an exclamation. The edition prints a full stop, so the English takes it as an exclamation and keeps the full stop. Other reading: How many of those with whom I came into the world have already gone away?
- *εἰσῆλθον*: The form can be first person singular or third person plural. Only the first makes sense with “with whom”, so the speaker is the one who came in. Other reading: with whom they came into the world
- *εἰς τὸν κόσμον*: The glossary prefers “the universe” for this word. “The world” is used because the sense is being born among people, and “came into the world” is the plain English for that. Other reading: with whom I entered the universe
- *ἀπεληλύθασιν*: A perfect, “have gone away”, built on the same verb as “came in”. It means they have died, but the Greek keeps the image of leaving, and so does the English. Other reading: have already departed; have already left it

</details>

### 6.57

To people with jaundice honey appears bitter, and to those bitten by a mad dog water appears frightening, and to small children their little ball appears beautiful. Why, then, am I angry? Or do you think that a false belief has less power than the bile has over the person with jaundice and the poison over the one bitten by a mad dog?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ σφαιρίον καλόν*: σφαιρίον is a diminutive, a little ball. καλόν here is “beautiful, fine” to the child’s eye, not the moral sense. Other reading: a ball seems a fine thing
- *ἢ δοκεῖ σοι*: The Greek moves from the first person to the second in one breath; both are kept. Other reading: Or does it seem to the speaker himself
- *τὸ διεψευσμένον*: A neuter participle, “that which has been deceived” or “the state of being deceived”. The English reads “a false belief”. Other reading: that being deceived has less power
- *τὸ χόλιον*: A diminutive of χολή, bile, which was held to cause jaundice. ἰός is the poison passed on by the mad dog’s bite. Other reading: the gall

</details>

### 6.58

No one will prevent you from living according to the reason of your own nature. Nothing will happen to you contrary to the reason of the common nature.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Κατὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς σῆς φύσεως*: λόγος is “reason” by the glossary; it could also be heard as the principle or law of your nature. The Greek puts the two prepositional phrases first, in sharp parallel: “according to … contrary to …”. Other reading: according to the principle of your own nature
- *τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως*: “The common nature” is the nature shared by all things, the nature of the whole. Other reading: of universal nature

</details>

### 6.59

What sort of people those are whom they want to please, and for what sort of gains, and through what sort of activities. How quickly eternity will cover everything, and how much it has covered already.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οἷοί εἰσιν οἷς θέλουσιν ἀρέσκειν*: An exclamation or a thing to consider, with no main verb beyond “are”. The “they” who want to please are not named: people in general. Other reading: What are they like, the people they want to please?
- *δι’ οἷα περιγινόμενα*: The participle means things that result or are left over as profit. The preposition with this case gives the reason or aim: for the sake of what results. Other reading: and for what sort of results
- *δι’ οἵων ἐνεργειῶν*: The same preposition with a different case, now the means. The noun is “activity”, as in 6.51. Other reading: and by what sort of actions
- *ὁ αἰὼν*: The word covers an age, a lifetime and the whole of unending time. It is a larger word than the ordinary one for time, so the English reads “eternity”. Other reading: How quickly time will cover everything
- *καὶ ὅσα ἐκάλυψεν ἤδη*: Literally “and how many things it has covered already”. It can be a second exclamation, as the English takes it, or a second object of “will cover”. Other reading: and all that it has covered already

</details>

## Book 7

### 7.1

What is wickedness? This is what you have often seen. And with everything that happens, keep this at hand: this is what you have often seen. In general, high and low, you will find the same things. The histories are full of them, the ancient ones, those in between and the recent ones; cities and households are full of them now. Nothing is new. Everything is both familiar and short-lived.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τί ἐστι κακία*: κακία is badness of character. The glossary has no entry; “wickedness” is used here as in 8.55 and 8.56. Other reading: What is vice?
- *ὃ πολλάκις εἶδες*: The same formula comes twice, and the English is the same both times: “This is what you have often seen”. The verb is a simple past, “you often saw”, which English puts more naturally as “you have often seen”. Other reading: what you saw many times
- *πρόχειρον ἔχε*: Literally “have ready to hand”, Marcus’s usual phrase for a thought to be kept ready for use. Other reading: have this thought ready
- *ἄνω κάτω*: An idiom, literally “up, down”. It can mean “high and low, wherever you look”, or “round and round, over and over”. The English takes the first, which suits the histories, cities and households that follow. Other reading: over and over you will find the same things
- *αἱ ἱστορίαι αἱ παλαιαί, αἱ μέσαι, αἱ ὑπόγυιοι*: ἱστορίαι are written histories or records. αἱ μέσαι is literally “the middle ones”, the histories of the period between ancient and recent, rendered “those in between”. ὑπόγυιοι is literally “under the hand”, that is, close to the present. Other reading: the histories of ancient times, of the times between and of our own day
- *ὧν νῦν μεσταὶ*: The Greek hangs two relative clauses (“of which … are full”) on “the same things”. The English makes them a separate sentence with “them”; nothing is dropped. Other reading: the same things, of which the histories are full … and of which cities and households are now full
- *αἱ πόλεις καὶ αἱ οἰκίαι*: οἰκίαι is “houses” or “households”. It is taken as households, the private scale set beside the public one. Other reading: the cities and the houses
- *ὀλιγοχρόνια*: Literally “of little time”, rendered “short-lived”. Other reading: lasting only a little while

</details>

### 7.2a

How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out, the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame? I am able to form the judgment I ought about this. If I am able, why am I disturbed? The things outside my mind are nothing at all to my mind. Learn this and you are upright.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὰ δόγματα*: The glossary word “principles”. The Greek has only the article, so the English reads “the principles” without “your”, though the principles he himself holds are meant. Other reading: How can your principles be killed
- *πῶς ἄλλως δύναται νεκρωθῆναι*: The input prints a full stop at the end of this sentence, but πῶς makes it a question and it is punctuated so. The verb means to be made a corpse, to be deadened; “killed” keeps the death. The Greek says “how else … unless”, and the English lets “unless” carry the “else”. Other reading: The principles cannot be made dead in any other way than by the putting out of the impressions that answer to them.
- *ἀναζωπυρεῖν*: Literally to kindle back into life: the word joins the fire image (σβεσθῶσιν, “are put out”) to the life image (νεκρωθῆναι, “be killed”). English has no one word for both, so the “life” half is lost in “fan back into flame”. “The impressions” is repeated where the Greek has only “which”. Other reading: which it is up to you to keep rekindling to life
- *διηνεκῶς*: “Without a break”. It stands next to the verb of rekindling and is taken with it, as “keep”; it can also go with “it is up to you”. Other reading: the impressions it is at every moment up to you to fan back into flame
- *δύναμαι περὶ τούτου ὃ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν*: Here he turns from “you” to the first person, and the change is kept. “This” is whatever is in front of him and is not named. The verb is the glossary’s “judgment” word. Other reading: I can think what I should about this.
- *τῆς ἐμῆς διανοίας*: The glossary gives “thought” for διάνοια, and “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty, which has an inside and an outside, so “mind” is used both times. Other reading: The things outside my thought are nothing at all to my thought.
- *οὐδὲν ὅλως πρὸς τὴν ἐμὴν διάνοιαν*: An idiom, “nothing at all in relation to”: they have no bearing on it, are no concern of it. The short English idiom “are nothing to” is kept. Other reading: have no bearing whatever on my mind
- *ὀρθὸς εἶ*: A present, “you are upright”, where English might expect a future. The adjective means standing straight, on one’s feet, and also right or correct; “upright” leaves both open and adds no verb of standing. Other reading: Learn this and you are in the right.

</details>

### 7.2b–3

You can come back to life. See things again as you used to see them: for in this lies the coming back to life.

The empty seriousness of a procession, plays on a stage, flocks, herds, spear fights, a little bone thrown to little dogs, a scrap of bread into the fish tanks, the toils and load-carrying of ants, the scurrying of frightened little mice, puppets pulled on strings. Among these things, then, one must stand kindly and without snorting at them, and yet keep in view that each person is worth just as much as the things they have taken seriously are worth.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὡς ἑώρας*: A past tense of repeated action: as you used to see them, at some earlier and better time. Other reading: as you once saw them
- *κενοσπουδία*: “Empty earnestness”. The same root comes back in the last words of the chapter, so “seriousness” stands here and “taken seriously” there. Other reading: The hollow pomp of a procession
- *διαδορατισμοί*: A rare word, “fighting it out with spears”. It may be battle or a show of combat. Other reading: bouts with the spear
- *ψωμίον εἰς τὰς τῶν ἰχθύων δεξαμενάς*: No verb of its own: “thrown” is understood from the bone before it and is not repeated. The last word is a tank or pond. Other reading: a crumb tossed into the fish ponds
- *μυιδίων*: A diminutive. It is taken from the word for mouse; the form is close to the word for a fly. Other reading: the darting about of startled little flies
- *σιγιλλάρια νευροσπαστούμενα*: The first word is Latin (sigillaria, small figures or dolls) in Greek letters; the second is the verb for working puppets by strings. Other reading: little dolls jerked about on strings
- *καταφρυαττόμενον*: From the snorting of a proud horse: to behave with insolent contempt toward something. The snort is kept. Other reading: without looking down one’s nose at them

</details>

### 7.4

One must follow what is said word by word, and what is done impulse by impulse; and in the latter case see at once what aim it is directed at, and in the former watch closely for what is meant.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κατὰ λέξιν*: “Word by word” or “phrase by phrase”: λέξις is a single expression. It is matched by “at each impulse” for actions; ὁρμή, “impulse”, is the Stoic term for the movement of the mind toward doing something. Other reading: follow what is said expression by expression
- *τοῖς γινομένοις*: Literally “the things that happen” or “come about”. Paired with “impulse” and set against “what is said”, it is taken as “what is done”. Other reading: and what happens, at each impulse
- *ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ ἑτέρου*: The Greek says only “in the one case, in the other”, without saying which is which. The sense shows that the order is crossed: the aim belongs to what is done, and what is meant belongs to what is said. The English says “latter” and “former” so that a reader does not pair them the wrong way. Other reading: and in the one case see at once what aim it is directed at, and in the other watch closely for what is meant
- *ἡ ἀναφορά*: “The reference”: what the action is referred to as its goal. There is no verb; the English supplies “is directed”. Other reading: to what target the reference is

</details>

### 7.5–7

Is my mind enough for this or not? If it is enough, I use it for the work as a tool given by the nature of the whole. If it is not enough, either I step back from the work in favour of someone who can carry it out better, unless for some other reason it is my duty, or I do it as best I can, taking on to help me someone who, by making use of my ruling part as well, can do what is timely and useful for the community now. For whatever I do, by myself or with another, must be directed to this alone: what is useful to the community and fits well with it.

How many who were much sung of have already been handed over to forgetting, and how many who sang of them are long since out of the way.

Do not be ashamed of being helped. For what is set before you is to do what falls to you, like a soldier at the storming of a wall. What then, if you are lame and cannot climb up onto the battlement alone, but with another it is possible?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἡ διάνοιά μου*: The glossary gives “thought” for this word, and “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty, used as a tool, so the English reads “mind”. The “ruling part” later in the chapter is a different Greek term (τὸ ἡγεμονικόν). Other reading: Is my understanding enough for this
- *ἐὰν ἄλλως τοῦτο μὴ καθήκῃ*: Literally “if this is not otherwise fitting”; the verb is the Stoic term for what is fitting or is one’s duty. It is not clear whether “this” is the work or the stepping back. The English takes it of the work: the speaker gives way unless the task is a duty on other grounds. Other reading: provided that giving way is not for some other reason the wrong thing to do
- *κατὰ πρόσχρησιν τοῦ ἐμοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ*: Literally “by additional use of” the speaker’s ruling part: the helper does the thing, drawing on that ruling part as well as their own ability. The ruling part is the Stoic term for the governing faculty of the soul. Other reading: someone who, with my ruling part to help, can do
- *εἰς τὸ κοινῇ χρήσιμον καὶ εὐάρμοστον*: Literally “to what is in common useful and well fitted”. “In common” echoes “the community” (κοινωνίαν) just before, so the English has “community” in both places and takes “in common” with both adjectives. Other reading: to what is useful to all in common and in tune with it
- *πολυύμνητοι*: Literally “much hymned”. The next clause uses the same root (“those who hymned them”), so the English has “sung of” and “sang of”. The second half of the sentence has no verb in the Greek; “are” is supplied. Other reading: How many who were once much praised
- *ἐκποδών*: Idiom, literally “out from the feet”: out of the way, gone. The English keeps “out of the way”; it means they are dead. Other reading: are long since gone
- *τὸ ἐπιβάλλον*: Literally “what falls upon” you: your share, your assigned part. The English reads “what falls to you”. Other reading: to do your part
- *χωλαίνων*: A participle, “limping” or “being lame”, made into a clause, “you are lame”. In the last words “with another” repeats the phrase of the first chapter, so it is not expanded to “with another’s help”. Other reading: if, because you limp, you cannot climb the battlement alone

</details>

### 7.8–9

Do not let what is to come trouble you. For you will come to it, if you have to, carrying the same reason that you now use on what is present.

All things are interwoven with one another, and the bond is sacred, and hardly anything is foreign to anything else. For they have been arranged together, and together they give order to the same universe. For there is one universe, made of all things, and one god, through all things, and one substance, and one law, the reason common to all living beings that have mind, and one truth, if indeed there is also one perfection for living beings that are of the same kind and share in the same reason.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *μὴ ταρασσέτω*: The Greek is a third-person command with no object: “let the things to come not trouble”. “You” is supplied, because the next verb is in the second person. Other reading: Let what is to come cause no trouble
- *τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον*: λόγος is “reason”, but can also be “account” or “argument”. “Reason” is used here and for the same word in the second chapter. Other reading: bringing the same reasoning
