- *σύνὸεσις*: As printed in the digitised text this is not a Greek word. It is read as σύνδεσις, “a binding together”, taking the fourth letter to be a slip for δ. Other reading: the binding-together is sacred
- *συγκατατέτακται*: “Have been arranged together”, as troops are drawn up in one formation. “Order” is kept for the next verb, which is made from κόσμος. Other reading: they have been ranked together
- *συγκοσμεῖ τὸν αὐτὸν κόσμον*: A play on words. κόσμος means both “order” and “the universe”, and the verb, made from the same word, means “to join in putting in order” and also “to adorn”. The English gives the verb as “give order to” and the noun as “universe”, here and in the next sentence. Other reading: together they adorn the same universe / together they order the same order
- *νόμος εἷς, λόγος κοινὸς*: After a run of items joined by “and”, this one has no “and”. “The reason common to all” can be a second name for the one law, or one more item in the list. The English sets it beside “one law” with a comma, as the Greek does. Other reading: and one law, and one reason common to all living beings that have mind, and one truth
- *νοερῶν*: νοερός is “having mind”, from νοῦς, “mind”. Other reading: all intelligent living beings
- *εἴγε καὶ τελειότης μία*: εἴγε can be a real condition (“if indeed”) or close to “seeing that”. The English keeps the condition. Other reading: seeing that there is also one perfection

</details>

### 7.10

Everything material very quickly vanishes into the substance of the whole, and every cause is very quickly taken back up into the reason of the whole, and the memory of everything is very quickly buried in eternity.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ ἔνυλον*: Literally “what is in matter”. It is taken as simply “material”. Other reading: everything embodied in matter
- *ἐναφανίζεται*: “Disappears into”: the prefix ἐν gives the “into”. The same verb is used of the person in 4.14, and “vanish into” serves in both. τάχιστα comes three times and is “very quickly” each time. Other reading: is lost in
- *πᾶν αἴτιον*: “Every cause”, set against the material: the active, forming element in each thing. The bare word “cause” is kept. Other reading: everything causal; every formative principle
- *ἀναλαμβάνεται*: “Is taken up” or “taken back”. “Taken back up” matches the rendering of ἀναληφθήσῃ in 4.14. τῶν ὅλων is plural (“of all things”) and is “the whole” as in the glossary. Other reading: is resumed into the reason of all things
- *παντὸς μνήμη*: παντὸς can be neuter (“of everything”) or masculine (“of everyone”). After two neuters “everything” is kept. Other reading: the memory of everyone
- *ἐγκαταχώννυται τῷ αἰῶνι*: The verb is to bury under heaped earth, and “buried” keeps it. αἰών is the whole of time, “eternity” or “the ages”. Other reading: is covered over by the ages; is entombed in time

</details>

### 7.11

For the rational animal, the same action is in accordance with nature and in accordance with reason.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κατὰ λόγον*: “Reason” here and “rational” at the start are one root in Greek. Other reading: the same act is both natural and reasonable

</details>

### 7.12

Upright, not held upright.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὀρθός*: The Greek has no verb: a bare masculine nominative, “upright” (also “straight”, “right”), and the English is left without a verb too. It is probably meant as a rule, with “be” or “one must be” understood. The negative μή would show that in older Greek, but in the Greek of Marcus’s time it is also the usual negative with a participle, so it does not settle the question alone. Other reading: Be upright, not held upright.
- *ὀρθούμενος*: A present participle of ὀρθόω, “set upright, straighten, put right”, from the same root as ὀρθός, taken as passive: kept upright by someone or something else. The present tense marks a state that goes on, so the English reads “held upright”, and “upright” is repeated so that the play on the one root shows. Other reading: Upright, not set upright. Or: Straight, not straightened.
- *μὴ ὀρθούμενος*: From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts are said to read ἢ (“or”) here, and μή (“not”) is an editor’s correction supported by the similar sentence in 3.5. The English follows the text as given, so the “not” is uncertain. Other reading: Upright, or held upright.

</details>

### 7.13

The relation that the limbs of the body have in things that are united is the relation that rational beings have in things that stand apart, being built to do some one work together. The thought of this will strike you more if you often say to yourself: “I am a limb [melos] of the whole made up of rational beings.” But if, by using the letter rho, you say that you are a part [meros], you do not yet love people from the heart; doing good does not yet delight you fully; you still do it as no more than the proper thing, not yet as doing good to yourself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐν ἡνωμένοις*: A school distinction (from memory, unchecked): bodies that are one continuous whole, such as an animal, against wholes made of members that stand apart, such as an army or a chorus. The second term is ἐν διεστῶσι in the next clause. “United” is used because the Greek word is made from “one”, like “union” in the neighbouring passages. Other reading: in bodies that are all of one piece
- *τοῦτον ἔχει τὸν λόγον*: λόγος here is “relation, proportion”, not “reason”, though it is the word from which λογικά (“rational beings”) is made, and the echo may be intended. Other reading: the same account holds for
- *τὰ μέλη τοῦ σώματος*: μέλος is a limb or bodily member. “Limb” is used because the passage goes on to set it against “part”. Other reading: the members of the body
- *πρὸς μίαν τινὰ συνεργίαν*: Literally “for some one working-together”: the activity of working together, not a thing produced. Other reading: for a certain single cooperation
- *προσπεσεῖται*: Literally “will fall upon you”: the thought will hit you, come home to you. Other reading: will come home to you more
- *συστήματος*: σύστημα is a whole put together out of members: a body of people, an organised group. It is a different word from the one given as “the whole” elsewhere (τὸ ὅλον). Its English descendant, “system”, sounds mechanical today. Other reading: the system made up of rational beings
- *διὰ τοῦ ῥῶ στοιχείου*: The point is a play on two Greek words one letter apart: μέλος (limb) and μέρος (part), with rho (r) in place of lambda (l). Since the passage is talking about the words themselves, both are added in square brackets; the brackets and what is in them are not in the Greek. Other reading: by changing the l to an r
- *καταληκτικῶς*: A rare adverb and a doubted reading (from memory, unchecked). As it stands it comes from the verb “to come to an end, to stop”, and is taken as “to the end, fully”; it could also mean “as the point at which one stops”. Editors have proposed καταληπτικῶς, a Stoic term for a firm grasp (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: doing good does not yet delight you as an end in itself; or, with the proposed reading, with full conviction
- *ὡς πρέπον αὐτὸ ψιλὸν*: Literally “as a bare fitting thing”: what is proper and nothing more. “Duty” is avoided, since that is a different Stoic word. Other reading: simply as a bare duty

</details>

### 7.14

Let whatever likes fall from outside on the things that are able to be affected by this falling. For those things, once affected, will complain if they like. But I, unless I judge that what has happened is bad, have not yet been harmed. And it is possible for me not to judge so.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὃ θέλει*: Literally “what wishes”: let whatever likes to, fall. The same verb returns in “if they like”. Other reading: Let anything that wants to fall from outside
- *τοῖς παθεῖν ἐκ τῆς προσπτώσεως ταύτης δυναμένοις*: A neuter plural, “the things that can be affected”: the parts of the body. προσπιπτέτω and προσπτώσεως are the same word, verb and noun, so “fall” and “falling” are kept. Other reading: on the parts that can suffer from this impact
- *ἐὰν θελήσῃ*: A singular verb with the neuter plural subject “those things”: “if they like”. Other reading: if it wishes
- *μέμψεται*: To blame or find fault. Other reading: will find fault
- *οὔπω βέβλαμμαι*: οὔπω is “not yet”, which is kept; it can be weaker, “not so far”, “not at all as things stand”. Other reading: I am not harmed
- *μὴ ὑπολαβεῖν*: ὑπολαμβάνω is the verb of ὑπόληψις (“judgment”). The Greek has no “so”; it is added. Other reading: And I am free not to suppose it

</details>

### 7.15

Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good; just as if gold or emerald or purple were always saying this: “Whatever anyone does or says, I must be emerald and have my own color.”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἡ πορφύρα*: The word covers the purple dye and cloth dyed with it. The English keeps the bare color word, since the point is a thing that has its own color. Other reading: the purple dye
- *ἐμὲ δεῖ σμάραγδον εἶναι*: Three things are named, but in the speech only the emerald speaks, and the English does not even this out. The Greek word is a green stone and may not be exactly the emerald of today. Other reading: I must be an emerald
- *ὡς ἂν εἰ*: An unreal comparison. The verb is in the past tense of an unreal case, so “were always saying”. Other reading: as though gold or emerald or purple kept saying
- *τὸ ἐμαυτοῦ χρῶμα ἔχειν*: The verb is the plain “have”. “Keep”, which the setting suggests, would add the idea of holding on under pressure. Other reading: and keep my own color

</details>

### 7.16

The ruling part does not make trouble for itself; I mean, for example, it does not frighten itself into desire. But if anyone else can frighten or distress it, let them do so; for it will not, by its own judging, turn itself in such directions. Let the little body itself take care that it suffers nothing, if it can, and let it say so if it suffers anything. But the little soul, the thing that fears, that is distressed, that in general forms judgments about these things, will suffer nothing at all; for you will not lead it to such a verdict. The ruling part, so far as depends on itself, is in need of nothing, unless it makes a need for itself; and in the same way it is undisturbed and unhindered, unless it disturbs and hinders itself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν*: The glossary’s “the ruling part”: the part of the soul that judges and directs. Other reading: the governing part, the directing mind
- *αὐτὸ ἑαυτῷ οὐκ ἐνοχλεῖ*: The Greek doubles the pronoun, “itself … to itself”: the trouble would be its own doing. English carries this in “for itself”. “Trouble” is the word used for this verb throughout the section. Other reading: The ruling part does not itself trouble itself
- *οὐ φοβεῖ ἑαυτὸ εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν*: “Frighten itself into desire” is what the words say, and it is hard sense: fear does not lead into desire, and the next sentence speaks of frightening and distressing, not of desire. From memory, unchecked, editors have doubted the text here and suspect that words have dropped out or been altered. The English follows the Greek as given and does not smooth it. Other reading: it does not frighten itself or lead itself into desire
- *τις ἄλλος*: Masculine, “anyone else”, a person; “them” is used for it as the glossary allows. It could loosely cover anything outside the ruling part. Other reading: But if something else can frighten or distress it
- *ὑποληπτικῶς οὐ τρέψει εἰς τοιαύτας τροπάς*: The adverb is made from the glossary’s “judgment” word: “in the way of judging”. Verb and noun are the same word in Greek, “turn itself into such turns”, meaning the changes of fear and distress; the English keeps one “turn” and gives the noun as “directions”. “Its own” gives the force of the doubled αὐτὸ … ἑαυτὸ. Other reading: for it will not of itself, through its judgment, change into such states
- *τὸ σωμάτιον*: A diminutive, as is ψυχάριον below. It is belittling rather than fond; both are kept as “little”. Other reading: the poor body … the poor soul
- *μὴ πάθῃ τι, αὐτὸ μεριμνάτω, εἰ δύναται, καὶ λεγέτω, εἴ τι πάσχει*: The verb πάσχειν (to suffer, to have something done to one) comes three times in two sentences and “suffer” is kept for all three. “Say so” fills in an object the Greek leaves out. Other reading: Let the body itself see to it, if it can, that nothing happens to it, and let it speak if anything does.
- *ὅλως*: Either “in general, in a word”, summing up the list, or “at all”, or “wholly”. It is taken as summing up, which is the usual sense where the word has no “not” beside it. Other reading: that forms any judgment at all about these things
- *οὐδὲν μὴ πάθῃ*: The two negatives with this verb form are read as the strong denial, “will certainly suffer nothing”, given as “nothing at all”. Other reading: need suffer nothing
- *οὐ γὰρ ἄξεις αὐτὸ εἰς κρίσιν τοιαύτην*: The verb is second person, “you will not lead it”, a sudden turn to “you” in a chapter otherwise about “it”; the turn is kept as the Greek gives it. From memory, unchecked, the form has been questioned. κρίσιν is “verdict” as in 6.52, to keep it apart from “judgment”. Other reading: for it will not be brought to judge so
- *ἀπροσδεές*: This word and ἔνδειαν in the next clause share the root for need, so “need” is used for both. Other reading: is self-sufficient, unless it creates a want for itself
- *ἀτάραχον καὶ ἀνεμπόδιστον*: Each adjective is answered by its own verb in the next clause (ταράσσῃ, ἐμποδίζῃ); the pairs are kept as “undisturbed … disturbs” and “unhindered … hinders”. Other reading: untroubled and unobstructed

</details>

### 7.17

Happiness is a good spirit, or a good ruling part. So what are you doing here, impression? Go away, by the gods, as you came: for I do not need you. But you have come out of old habit. I am not angry with you. Only go away.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Εὐδαιμονία ἐστὶ δαίμων ἀγαθὸς*: The sentence takes the word for happiness apart: εὐδαιμονία is made of εὖ (“well”) and δαίμων, the spirit or divinity that goes with a person, which Marcus elsewhere places inside the person. English cannot show this, so the sense is translated and the play is left to this note. “Spirit” stands for δαίμων with nothing added; a being is meant, not a mood. Other reading: Happiness (eudaimonia) is a good daimon, or: a good guardian spirit
- *ἢ ἡγεμονικὸν ἀγαθόν*: ἤ is “or”. It can offer a second possibility or restate the first in other words (“that is to say”). The English leaves the bare “or”, which is open in the same way; τὸ ἡγεμονικόν is “the ruling part” as in the glossary. Other reading: that is, a good ruling part
- *ὧδε*: In later Greek this word is “here”; in older Greek it is “in this way”. “Here” is read, as fits a visitor who is being sent away. Other reading: So why are you acting in this way, impression?
- *ὦ φαντασία*: φαντασία is “impression” as in the glossary: what presents itself to the mind. Here it is spoken to like an unwanted visitor. The word can also mean the power of imagining. Other reading: imagination
- *τοὺς θεούς σοι*: A clipped phrase with no verb, literally “the gods to you”: a colloquial appeal or oath with its verb left out. The English reads the bare “by the gods” and supplies no verb. The phrase is known from the spoken style of other Stoic teaching (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: Go away, I beg you by the gods
- *ὡς ἦλθες*: Literally “as you came”. It can mean by the same way you came in, or in the same state in which you came, that is, unasked and having gained nothing. “As you came” leaves both open. Other reading: by the way you came, or: no better off than you came
- *οὐ γὰρ χρῄζω σου*: χρῄζω covers both needing and wanting. The English takes “need”. Other reading: for I do not want you
- *κατὰ τὸ ἀρχαῖον ἔθος*: Literally “according to the old habit”. The Greek does not say whose habit: the impression’s own old way of turning up, or the speaker’s old habit of letting it in. “Out of old habit” names no owner, though it is heard first of the one who comes. Other reading: You have come according to the old habit.

</details>

### 7.18

Is someone afraid of change? Why, what can come about without change? And what is dearer to the nature of the whole, or more its own? Can you yourself take a bath unless the firewood changes? Can you be fed unless the food changes? Can anything else that is useful be accomplished without change? Do you not see, then, that your own changing too is the same kind of thing, and in the same way necessary to the nature of the whole?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τί γὰρ*: The particle gives the ground for surprise at the fear: “[how so,] for what can …?”. The English uses “Why,” for it. Other reading: But what can come about without change?
- *γενέσθαι*: “Come to be, come about, happen”: the word covers being born as well as happening. Other reading: what can come into being without change?
- *οἰκειότερον*: “More one’s own, more akin, more at home with.” Change belongs to the nature of the whole more than anything else does, and the English reads “more its own”. Other reading: dearer or closer to the nature of the whole
- *τὰ ξύλα*: Literally “the wood”: the logs burned to heat the bath. Other reading: unless the wood changes
- *αὐτὸ τὸ σὲ μεταβαλεῖν*: Literally “the very fact of you changing”. The verb is the one used of the firewood and the food. The change meant is death, but the Greek does not say so and neither does the English. Other reading: that for you too to be changed
- *ὅμοιόν ἐστι καὶ ὁμοίως ἀναγκαῖον*: “Is alike, and alike necessary.” The dative “to the nature of the whole” goes most naturally with “necessary”. Other reading: is just the same, and equally needed by the nature of the whole

</details>

### 7.19–22

All bodies pass through and out of the substance of the whole, as through a winter torrent, grown together with the whole and working with it, as our limbs do with one another. How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has eternity already swallowed down. Let the same thought strike you about any human being whatever and any thing.

Only one thing troubles me: that I myself might do something that the constitution of a human being does not want, or in a way it does not want, or that it does not want now.

Your forgetting of all is near, and near is the forgetting of you by all.

It is proper to a human being to love even those who stumble. This happens if it strikes you at the same moment that they are your kin, that they go wrong through ignorance and against their will, that in a little while both of you will be dead, and above all that the person has not harmed you, for that person has not made your ruling part worse than it was before.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *οὐσίας*: οὐσία here is the stuff of which everything is made. “Substance” keeps it apart from “nature”, which this translation uses for φύσις. Other reading: through the matter of the whole
- *διεκπορεύεται*: A verb with two prefixes, “through” and “out”: bodies pass through the stream and out of it again. Other reading: all bodies make their way
- *ὁ αἰὼν*: αἰών is a long age, or the whole of time; “eternity” keeps it apart from the ordinary word for time. Chrysippus was a head of the Stoic school; Epictetus a Stoic teacher of the generation before Marcus. Other reading: has time already swallowed down
- *περισπᾷ*: Literally “pulls away”, “distracts”, the sense it has in 6.22. With the clause of fear that follows, it comes to “troubles”. Other reading: Only one thing distracts me
- *ἡ κατασκευὴ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου*: κατασκευή is how a thing is built or equipped. “Constitution” in the sense of makeup. Other reading: the way a human being is made
- *ἡ πάντων περὶ σοῦ λήθη*: “All” in both halves can be all things or all people. In the first half it is what you forget; in the second it is most naturally everyone who forgets you. “All” is kept bare in both. Other reading: Your forgetting of all things is near, and near is everyone’s forgetting of you
- *συμπροσπίπτῃ*: The same verb as “strike you” in 7.19 with a prefix added, “together with”: the thought must come at the very moment of the offense. Other reading: if it also occurs to you
- *ἄκοντες*: “Unwilling”: they do not mean to go wrong. The Stoic view is that nobody errs on purpose. Other reading: and without meaning to
- *οὐκ ἔβλαψέ σε*: The Greek moves from the plural (“they go wrong”) to a singular with no subject named: the one person in front of you. The English has “the person” and “that person”, since the Greek does not say “he”. Other reading: that he has not harmed you, for he has not made your ruling part worse

</details>

### 7.23

The nature of the whole, out of the whole of substance as if out of wax, at one moment shaped a little horse; then it melted that down and used its material for a little tree, then for a little human, then for something else. Each of these existed for the briefest time. But there is nothing terrible for a little box in being taken apart, just as there is nothing good in its being put together.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐκ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας ὡς κηροῦ*: οὐσία is the stuff of which everything is made; “substance” is used for it here and in the neighbouring passages. ὅλης may mean “the whole of” or “universal”. Other reading: out of the universal substance, as out of wax
- *ἱππάριον*: A diminutive, like δενδρύφιον, ἀνθρωπάριον and κιβωτίῳ after it. It may suggest a wax figurine or simply belittle the thing; “little” is kept all four times. Other reading: a toy horse (then a toy tree, a toy man, a toy box)
- *ἔπλασε*: The tense is a simple past. It is read as narrative with νῦν μὲν (“at one moment”), but it could be the past tense that Greek uses for what always happens. Other reading: now shapes a little horse, then melts it down and uses its material
- *συγχέασα*: Literally “having poured together”, that is, having blurred or destroyed the shape. With wax the English narrows this to “melted that down”; the Greek does not say whether the wax is melted or squashed. Other reading: having broken it up
- *πρὸς ὀλίγιστον ὑπέστη*: ὑπέστη is “came to exist” or “subsisted”; the superlative ὀλίγιστον is “for the very least time”. Other reading: each of these came into existence for a moment only
- *τὸ διαλυθῆναι τῷ κιβωτίῳ*: The image shifts without warning from wax to a small box or chest, and the two verbs are joinery words (taken apart, fitted together). The dative is taken with “terrible”: nothing terrible for the box. Other reading: it is nothing terrible that the little chest should be broken up
- *ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὸ συμπαγῆναι ἀγαθόν*: Neither half of this sentence has a verb in the Greek, so the tense is supplied. “Is” is used in both halves, since both are general statements. Other reading: just as there was nothing good in its being put together

</details>

### 7.24–25

A scowl on the face is very much against nature. When it is often there, the look of the face dies in it, or in the end has been put out, so that it cannot be kindled at all. Try to grasp at least this very point, that it is against reason. For if even the awareness of doing wrong is going to go, what cause is there still for living?

Everything you see, the nature that governs the whole will change in almost no time, and will make other things out of their substance, and again others out of the substance of those, so that the universe may always be young.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὸ ἐπίκοτον τοῦ προσώπου*: ἐπίκοτος is “bearing a grudge, wrathful”: the angry cast of a face. Other reading: A look of rancour on the face
- *ὅταν πολλάκις ἐναποθνῄσκειν ᾖ πρόσχημα ἢ τὸ τελευταῖον ἀπεσβέσθη*: The Greek as given does not construe: word for word, “whenever often to-die-in-it be outward show, or in the end it was quenched”. The English is a reconstruction: πρόσχημα (the outward appearance) is taken as what dies and is put out, “often” is taken with the scowl, “of the face” is supplied, and a new sentence is begun where the Greek clause hangs on “against nature”. Editors are believed to treat the text as damaged here (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: when it is often put on, its comeliness begins to die, and at last is extinguished
- *ὥστε ὅλως ἐξαφθῆναι μὴ δύνασθαι*: The image is of a lamp or fire: put out, and unable to be lit. It is kept. Other reading: so that it can never be rekindled
- *αὐτῷ γε τούτῳ παρακολουθεῖν πειρῶ*: παρακολουθέω with a dative is to follow with the mind, to stay aware of. The dative is taken as its object, explained by the “that” clause, and the next sentence, on losing awareness, continues the thought. It could be a dative of means. Other reading: Try to conclude from this very fact that it is against reason
- *ἡ συναίσθησις τοῦ ἁμαρτάνειν*: συναίσθησις is the awareness a person has of their own state. The link of thought with the scowl is not spelled out in the Greek, and none is supplied. Other reading: if even the consciousness of doing wrong is lost
- *τίς ἔτι τοῦ ζῆν αἰτία*: αἰτία is a cause or ground. “Cause” is used so that “reason” stays with λόγος in the sentence before. Other reading: what reason is left for living?
- *ὅσον οὔπω*: An idiom, literally “as much as not yet”: all but now, at any moment. Other reading: in a moment
- *ἡ τὰ ὅλα διοικοῦσα φύσις*: The same phrase as in 11.18. τὰ ὅλα is rendered “the whole” as settled, and ὁ κόσμος at the end “the universe”. Other reading: the nature that governs all things

</details>

### 7.26

Whenever someone does you some wrong, consider at once what they judged to be good or bad when they did the wrong. For once you have seen this you will pity them, and will be neither surprised nor angry. For either you yourself still judge the same thing to be good as they do, or another thing of the same kind; so you must forgive. But if you no longer judge such things to be good and bad, you will more easily be kind to one who fails to see.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὑπολαβὼν*: The verb belonging to ὑπόληψις, “judgment” in the settled list. It comes three times in the passage and the English has “judge” each time. Other reading: with what notion of good or bad they did the wrong
- *θαυμάσεις*: θαυμάζω is to wonder at; here to be surprised, as in 9.42. Other reading: you will neither wonder nor be angry
- *συγγινώσκειν*: The ordinary word for “forgive”, literally “to know or think along with”. The literal sense fits the argument, since you share the other’s judgment. Other reading: so you must make allowance, as one who thinks the same
- *τῷ παρορῶντι*: παροράω is to see beside the thing, to overlook or see wrongly. It is taken as failing to see what is truly good and bad; the same verb gives “what they are failing to see” in 11.13 and 10.4. Other reading: to the one who sees amiss

</details>

### 7.27–28

Not to think of absent things as already there, but to reckon up the best of the things that are present, and on their account to remind yourself how they would be sought after if they were not present. At the same time, though, be on your guard that through being so glad of them you do not accustom yourself to prize them so much that, if ever they are not present, you will be troubled.

Draw in upon yourself. It is the nature of the rational ruling part to be content with itself when it acts justly and by that very fact has calm.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μὴ τὰ ἀπόντα ἐννοεῖν*: The first sentence is in infinitives used as instructions, with no person; the second turns to “you”. The English keeps the impersonal form for the first (“Not to think …”), adding “yourself” only where English needs an object for “remind”. Other reading: Do not think of absent things as already there
- *ὡς ἤδη ὄντα*: Literally “as already being”: as if they already existed or were already yours. Other reading: as if they were already yours
- *τῶν παρόντων τὰ δεξιώτατα*: δεξιός is “on the right hand”, so lucky, favourable, and also fine or choice. The English has “the best”. Other reading: the most fortunate of the things that are present
- *τούτων χάριν*: χάριν with the genitive is “for the sake of” or “on account of”. The English takes it as giving the occasion for the reminder. ἐπεζητεῖτο is “would be sought after”, so “missed”. Other reading: and, for their sake, to remind yourself how much you would miss them if they were not there
- *ἐθίσῃς ἐκτιμᾶν*: The verb “accustom” has no object in the Greek; “yourself” is understood. ἐκτιμάω is to value highly, to overvalue. Other reading: that you do not get into the habit of overvaluing them
- *συνειλοῦ*: Literally “roll yourself up” or “coil yourself up” into yourself, as a thing is wound tight. The English has “draw in”, which keeps the movement. Other reading: Coil yourself up into yourself.
- *γαλήνην*: γαλήνη is the calm of a still sea. The English keeps “calm”. Other reading: and by that very fact is at peace

</details>

### 7.29–31a

Wipe out the impression. Stop the pulling of the puppet strings. Draw a line around the present time. Recognise what is happening, whether to you or to another. Take the thing before you apart and divide it into what causes and what is matter. Think of the last hour. The wrong that person did, leave it there, where the wrong came to be.

To stretch thinking out alongside what is being said. To have the mind get inside the things that come about and the things that act.

Brighten yourself with simplicity and modesty and with indifference towards what lies between virtue and vice. Love the human race. Follow god.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *νευροσπαστίαν*: The word means the working of a puppet by its cords. The image is kept; what pulls the strings (impulses, passions) is not said here. Other reading: Stop being jerked about like a puppet.
- *περίγραψον τὸ ἐνεστὼς τοῦ χρόνου*: περιγράφω is to draw a line around, and so to mark off or to limit. The drawing of the line is kept; “the present of time” is given as “the present time”. Other reading: Limit yourself to the present moment.
- *γνώρισον*: The verb covers both coming to know a thing and recognising it for what it is. The command is for a single act, so the English reads “recognise”. Other reading: Get to know what is happening
- *τὸ ὑποκείμενον εἰς τὸ αἰτιῶδες καὶ ὑλικόν*: τὸ ὑποκείμενον is literally “what lies under”, the object in front of one. The causal and the material are the two Stoic principles, the active cause and the matter it works on; one article covers both. Other reading: divide the underlying object into the causal and the material
- *τὸ ἐκείνῳ ἁμαρτηθὲν*: The dative is taken as the doer (“the wrong done by that one”), and the English reads “that person” since the form need not single out a man. The dative could just possibly be the one wronged. Other reading: The wrong done to that person
- *ὑπέστη*: Literally “took its stand” or “came into existence”. The point is that the wrong exists in the one who did it. Other reading: where the wrong has its footing
- *Συμπαρεκτείνειν τὴν νόησιν τοῖς λεγομένοις*: The two sentences of this chapter are infinitives used as instructions, with no “you”; they are kept impersonal. νόησις is given as “thinking” to keep it apart from νοῦς, “mind”, in the next sentence. Other reading: Keep your thinking in step with what is being said.
- *εἰσδύεσθαι*: The verb is to get into a thing, to slip or sink inside it. The English keeps the “in” and adds no “down”. Other reading: To have the mind sink into
- *τὰ γινόμενα καὶ ποιοῦντα*: Literally “the things coming about and making”, under one article, and the second has no object. ποιεῖν is the Stoic verb for what acts as a cause; the English reads “the things that act” and supplies no object, so the Greek is not tied to the causes of just those events. Other reading: into the things that come about and the things that make them
- *Φαίδρυνον*: The verb is to make bright, and so also to wash clean or to cheer. The brightness is kept. Other reading: Cleanse yourself with simplicity
- *αἰδοῖ*: αἰδώς is the sense of shame that holds a person back from what is unworthy. “Modesty” narrows it. Other reading: a sense of shame; self-respect
- *θεῷ*: No article: “god” or “a god”. Lower case as in the glossary. Other reading: Follow a god.

</details>

### 7.31b–34

He says, “All things are by convention, and in reality only the elements.” But it is enough to remember that all things are by convention. Already very few.

On death: either a scattering, if there are atoms; or, if there is a unity, either a snuffing out or a move elsewhere.

On pain: what cannot be borne carries one off, and what lasts can be borne. And the mind keeps its own calm by separation, and the ruling part has not become worse. As for the parts that are harmed by the pain, let them give their verdict on it, if they can.

On fame: look at their minds, what they are like, and what kind of things they run from and what kind of things they chase. And see that, as heaps of sand piled one on another hide the earlier ones, so in life the earlier things are very quickly covered by those piled on after.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐκεῖνος μέν φησιν*: Literally “that man says”. The part given does not name him. The saying resembles one attributed to Democritus (from memory, unchecked), but no name is put into the English. Other reading: That well-known man says
- *νομιστί*: A rare adverb, “by custom, by convention, as people hold”. Because it is related to the word for law (νόμος), Marcus’s own restatement could be turning it to mean “by law”. “By convention” is kept in both places. The text of this sentence may be doubted (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: it is enough to remember that all things are governed by law
- *τὰ στοιχεῖα*: “The elements”, the basic things everything is made of. Other reading: only the first components are real
- *ἤδη λίαν ὀλίγα*: Three words with no verb, “already very few”, and nothing to say very few of what. The English gives the three words and supplies nothing. The likeliest sense is that the things to remember are by then very few; it could also be that very few things are left as real. The text may be doubted here (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: By then there is very little left to remember
- *ἕνωσις*: Literally “a making one”. It is the opposite case to atoms: a universe that is a single joined whole. Other reading: if all is one
- *σβέσις ἢ μετάστασις*: σβέσις is the putting out of a flame. μετάστασις is a change of place, and can also be a change of state. Other reading: either being put out or being changed into something else
- *ἐξάγει*: Literally “leads out”, with no object. “One” is supplied. The verb is a common way of speaking of leaving life. Other reading: what cannot be borne takes one out of life
- *ἡ διάνοια*: διάνοια is “thought” elsewhere in this translation. Here and under “On fame” it is the faculty, so the English reads “mind”. Other reading: thought keeps its own calm
- *κατὰ ἀπόληψιν*: ἀπόληψις is a cutting off or shutting off, and the Greek does not say of what: the mind may cut itself off from the body’s pain, or shut the pain off. “Separation” leaves that open. The word is unusual in this sense. Other reading: by cutting itself off / by shutting the pain off
- *ἡγεμονικὸν*: τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, the Stoic term for the part of the soul that judges and decides, “the ruling part” in this translation. Other reading: the governing self has not become worse
- *ἀποφηνάσθω*: The verb means to declare an opinion or give a ruling. The point is that the judgment about the pain belongs to the damaged parts, if to anything. Other reading: let them say what they have to say about it
- *Περὶ δόξης*: δόξα is both “opinion” and “reputation”. The heading is about what others think of you, so “fame”. Other reading: On reputation
- *τὰς διανοίας αὐτῶν*: “Their” has nothing before it to refer to. It means the people whose opinion makes up fame. The English keeps the bare “their”. Other reading: look at the minds of those people
- *καὶ ὅτι*: “That” depends on “look” at the start of the chapter. The English begins a new sentence and repeats the verb as “see”, which is the only word added. Other reading: look at their minds ... and at the fact that
- *θῖνες*: Heaps or banks of sand, on a shore or in a desert. The two “piled on” words in the sentence are closely related Greek verbs. The last verb is a past tense used for a general truth. Other reading: as dunes drifting one over another

</details>

### 7.35

“‘So, a mind that has greatness and a view of all time and of all being: do you think human life seems anything great to the one who has it?’ ‘Impossible,’ he said. ‘Then such a person will count death, too, as nothing terrible?’ ‘Not in the least.’”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἧι οὖν ὑπάρχει διανοίᾳ*: The whole passage is a quotation, marked as one in the Greek as given: a piece of dialogue from Plato (Republic 486a: from memory, unchecked). The Greek starts “The mind, then, to which there belongs …” and goes on “to this one” (τούτῳ), a person; the sentence is broken at a colon to keep that turn. διάνοια is the faculty here, so “mind” and not “thought”. Other reading: So, to someone whose thought has greatness and a view of all time and all being
- *μεγαλοπρέπεια*: Literally “what befits the great”: grandeur, largeness of mind. “Greatness” keeps the link with “anything great” (μέγα τι) in the question. Other reading: magnificence
- *θεωρία*: Looking at, viewing, contemplating. The English reads “a view of”. Other reading: the contemplation of all time and of all being
- *πάσης δὲ οὐσίας*: οὐσία is “being” in Plato; a Stoic reader such as Marcus would also hear “substance”, the stuff of the world. Plato’s sense is kept since the words are his. Other reading: and of all substance
- *τούτῳ*: “To this one”: masculine or neuter, so either the person who has such a mind or the mind. The answer speaks of ὁ τοιοῦτος, “such a person”, so it is taken as the person. Other reading: seems anything great to such a mind
- *ἦ δ’ ὅς*: The set phrase “said he” of Plato’s narrated dialogues, which shows the passage is lifted from one. Other reading: said he

</details>

### 7.36–37

“It is kingly to act well and yet be spoken ill of.”

It is shameful that the face should be obedient, and be shaped and put in order as the mind commands, while the mind itself is not shaped and put in order by itself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Βασιλικὸν εὖ μὲν πράττειν, κακῶς δὲ ἀκούειν*: The edition marks this as a quotation. From memory, unchecked: the saying is credited to Antisthenes. “Kingly” is the same adjective as in 4.12. Other reading: “It is a king’s part to do good and to be ill spoken of.”
- *εὖ μὲν πράττειν*: The phrase usually means “to fare well”; set against being ill spoken of it must mean acting well, perhaps doing good to others. The Greek sets “well” against “ill”, which “and yet” brings out. Other reading: to do good
- *κακῶς δὲ ἀκούειν*: An idiom, literally “to hear badly”: to have bad things said of one. Other reading: and to get a bad name
- *σχηματίζεσθαι καὶ κατακοσμεῖσθαι*: The same two verbs are used of the face and then of the mind, so the English keeps the same two verbs. They can be passive or reflexive: “be shaped” or “shape itself”. Other reading: compose itself and arrange itself
- *ἡ διάνοια*: The faculty that gives orders to the face, so “mind” and not the glossary’s first choice “thought”, as in 7.60. Other reading: thought

</details>

### 7.38–43

“For one must not be angry with things, for they do not care at all.”

“May you give joys to the immortal gods and to us.”

“To reap life like a ripe ear of grain, and for one to be and another not.”

“But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.”

“For what is right is with me, and what is just.”

No joining in the wailing, no racing pulse.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τοῖς πράγμασιν γὰρ οὐχὶ θυμοῦσθαι χρεών*: A line of verse quoted with no name: from memory, unchecked, it is from a lost play of Euripides. The quotation marks here and in the next four chapters are added; the Greek has none. πράγματα can be things, affairs or circumstances. Other reading: For one must not be angry with circumstances
- *χάρματα δοίης*: A wish, “may you give”, in a line of epic metre whose source is not identified here. χάρματα are joys or causes of joy. Other reading: May you bring delight to the immortal gods and to us.
- *Βίον θερίζειν ὥστε κάρπιμον στάχυν*: The Greek is a bare infinitive with no governing verb, so it does not construe alone: the quotation is cut out of a sentence (from memory, unchecked, a line of Euripides in which a word for “it is necessary” governs it). The English leaves it a fragment and does not supply the verb. Other reading: Life must be reaped like a ripe ear of grain
- *κάρπιμον*: Literally “fruit-bearing”: an ear carrying its grain, and so ready for the reaper. “Ripe” gives that sense in the word English uses of grain. Other reading: like a fruitful ear of grain
- *τὸν μὲν εἶναι, τὸν δὲ μή*: “One to be, and another not”: “be” in the sense of exist, live. The masculine “one … another” can be an ear of grain or a person; the English leaves it open as the Greek does. Other reading: and that one man lives while another does not
- *παῖδ’ ἐμώ*: The form is a dual: exactly two children. The word can mean sons or children; from memory, unchecked, this too is a verse from a lost tragedy. Other reading: my two sons
- *ἔχει λόγον καὶ τοῦτο*: Literally “this too has reason”, λόγος: there is a reason for it, it can be accounted for. Other reading: there is an account to be given of this too
- *Τὸ γὰρ εὖ μετ’ ἐμοῦ καὶ τὸ δίκαιον*: τὸ εὖ is the adverb “well” made into a noun: what is well, what is right. It is not the word for “the good” (τὸ ἀγαθόν), so the English does not say “the good”. The Greek has no verb; “is” is supplied. Other reading: For right is on my side, and justice.
- *Μὴ συνεπιθρηνεῖν, μὴ σφύζειν*: Two infinitives used as instructions, and not, as far as can be told, a quotation. The first is to join others in lamenting over something; the second is used of the pulse beating hard, hence of feverish agitation. The English keeps the pulse. Other reading: Do not lament along with them; do not throb with agitation.

</details>

### 7.44–48

“But I would have a just answer to give this man: ‘What you say is not right, fellow, if you think that a man who is of even a little use must take into account the risk of living or dying, rather than look at this alone whenever he acts: whether he is doing what is just or unjust, and the deeds of a good man or of a bad one.’”

“For this is how it truly is, men of Athens. Wherever a person has taken up a post, judging it to be best, or has been posted by a commander, there, as it seems to me, they must stay and run the risk, taking nothing into account, neither death nor anything else, ahead of disgrace.”

“But, my dear man, see whether what is noble and what is good may not be something other than saving and being saved. For perhaps this, living for whatever length of time, is what one who is truly a man must let go, and he must not cling to life, but, leaving these matters to god and trusting the women who say that not even one person could escape what is fated, must consider what comes next: in what way he might live the time he is going to live as well as possible.”

Look round at the courses of the stars as if running round with them, and think continually of the changes of the elements into one another. For the impressions of these things wash away the dirt of life on the ground.

A fine saying of Plato’s. And indeed whoever is talking about human beings must also look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above: herds, armies, farms, marriages, divorces, births, deaths, the din of law courts, empty lands, the varied peoples of the barbarians, festivals, laments, markets, the mixture of every kind and the order put together out of opposites.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐγὼ δὲ τούτῳ δίκαιον ἂν λόγον ἀντείποιμι*: The first three paragraphs are quotations copied without the author’s name: Socrates speaking in Plato (Apology 28b and 28d, Gorgias 512d to e: from memory, unchecked). Each is set in its own quotation marks. Other reading: But I would speak a just word against this man
- *ὦ ἄνθρωπε*: Literally “O human being”, a curt way of addressing someone, with no warmth in it. “Fellow” keeps it curt and keeps it apart from the “man” of the next clause, which is a different Greek word (ἄνδρα). Other reading: What you say is not right, man
- *ὅτου τι καὶ σμικρὸν ὄφελος*: Literally “of whom there is some use, even a small one”. Kept close. Other reading: a man who is worth anything at all
- *κίνδυνον ὑπολογίζεσθαι τοῦ ζῆν ἢ τεθνάναι*: Two words tie the first quotation to the second. ὑπολογίζεσθαι comes back as ὑπολογιζόμενον, so both read “take into account”, and κίνδυνον comes back in κινδυνεύειν, so both read “risk”. “The risk of living or dying” is the chance of coming out alive or dead. Other reading: must weigh up his chances of life or death
- *Ὁὕτω γὰρ ἔχει*: The Greek as given has a doubled breathing on the first word and no opening quotation mark for this second quotation, though it has a closing one; the stray breathing is probably what is left of the opening mark. The word is read as Οὕτω and the paragraph is marked as a quotation of its own. Other reading: For so it is, men of Athens, in truth
- *ἄρχοντος*: The word covers anyone who rules or commands, an officer or a magistrate. The picture is of a soldier’s post, so “commander”. Other reading: or has been posted by someone in authority
- *πρὸ τοῦ αἰσχροῦ*: Literally “before the shameful”: nothing is to be counted as weighing more than disgrace. The English keeps the short “ahead of”. Other reading: taking nothing into account, neither death nor anything else, in comparison with what is shameful
- *ὦ μακάριε*: Literally “blessed one”, a polite and slightly teasing form of address in conversation. Other reading: But, my blessed friend
- *μὴ γὰρ τοῦτο μέν, τὸ ζῆν ὁποσονδὴ χρόνον, τόν γε ὡς ἀληθῶς ἄνδρα ἐατέον ἐστὶ*: μή with the indicative makes a guarded statement, “perhaps”, “it may be that”; it can also be heard as a question. The English takes the guarded statement. The forms in -τέον say what has to be done and are given as “must”, the word used for δεῖ in the other quotations. Other reading: For must not one who is truly a man let this go, living for however long a time?
- *τῷ θεῷ*: The Greek has the article, “the god”. The English follows the rendering settled for this translation, “god”, lower case. Other reading: leaving these matters to the god
- *πιστεύσαντα ταῖς γυναιξίν*: Literally “having trusted the women, that …”: a saying that women were known to repeat. The English keeps the women and adds only “who say”. Other reading: believing the old wives’ saying
- *τὸ ἐπὶ τούτῳ*: Literally “the thing upon this”: the question that comes next once that one is set aside. Other reading: consider what follows from this
- *ὥσπερ συμπεριθέοντα*: This paragraph is in infinitives used as instructions, with no person named; the participle is masculine singular, “as if one were running round with them”. The English uses commands without “you”. Other reading: as though you were running round with them
- *αἱ τούτων φαντασίαι*: φαντασία is “impression” throughout this translation: here the pictures of these things as they form in the mind. Other reading: For picturing these things washes away
- *τοῦ χαμαὶ βίου*: Literally “of the life on the ground”, set against the stars above. Kept as an image. Other reading: the dirt of earthbound life
- *Καλὸν τὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος.*: Literally “Fine, that of Plato’s”: “saying” is supplied for the bare article. The words may look back to the three quotations above or forward, making what follows a saying of Plato; the Greek as given puts a full stop after them, and the English is left equally open. From memory, unchecked: editors have doubted how these words join what follows. Other reading: Plato has a fine saying: whoever is talking about human beings must also look down at the things on earth as if from somewhere above
- *ὥσπερ ποθὲν ἄνωθεν κάτω*: κάτω, “downward”, stands with no verb of its own; the English joins it to the one verb there is, as “look down at”. From memory, unchecked: some editors change κάτω to κατὰ, which would give “herd by herd”. Other reading: as if from somewhere above: by herds, armies, farms
- *ἀγέλας*: Herds of animals; the word is also used of crowds of people. Kept as “herds”. Other reading: crowds
- *διαλύσεις*: A “breaking up” or “loosing”. It stands next to “marriages” as “deaths” stands next to “births”, so it is read as divorces; the word is also used of settling quarrels and making peace. Other reading: peace treaties
- *τὸ παμμιγὲς καὶ τὸ ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων συγκοσμούμενον*: παμμιγές is “mixed of every kind”. The last word has κόσμος, “order”, inside it: “that which is being ordered together out of opposites”. “Order” is used here, as this translation allows where the sense of order is the point. Other reading: the medley of all things and the harmony arranged out of opposites

</details>

### 7.49–51

Look back over what has gone before: so many changes of ruling powers. It is possible to foresee what will be as well. For it will certainly be of the same kind, and it cannot step out of the rhythm of what is happening now. So to observe human life for forty years is equal to observing it for ten thousand. For what more will you see?

And: “What grew from earth goes back to earth, and what sprouted from a seed of the upper air, back to the vault of heaven.” Or else this is a dissolution of the interlockings among the atoms, and some such scattering of elements that cannot be affected.

And: “Turning the channel aside with food and drink and spells, so as not to die.” … “But the sailing wind that blows from the gods must be borne, in toils without lament.”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὰ προγεγονότα ἀναθεωρεῖν*: An infinitive used as an instruction, with no person expressed. The English uses an imperative; the second person does appear later in the chapter (ὄψει, “you will see”). Other reading: To look back over what has gone before
- *τῶν ἡγεμονιῶν*: ἡγεμονία is leadership or rule, and in the plural can mean reigns, dynasties or empires. The wider “ruling powers” is kept. Other reading: so many changes of dynasties
- *πάντως*: πάντως can strengthen the statement (“certainly, in any case”) or give its extent (“altogether”). The English takes the first. Other reading: For it will be altogether of the same kind
- *τοῦ ῥυθμοῦ*: ῥυθμός is measured movement, and also shape or pattern. “Rhythm” is kept as the image, with “step out of” for ἐκβῆναι. Other reading: it cannot depart from the pattern of what is happening now
- *ἱστορῆσαι*: The verb means to inquire into or observe as a witness. The Greek says that the one observing “is equal to” the other, and the English keeps that. Other reading: to have studied human life for forty years is the same as studying it for ten thousand
- *Καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐκ γαίας*: The opening Καὶ is taken as the notebook’s own “And” introducing an excerpt, here and before the next verses, so it stands outside the quotation marks. It could also be the first word of the quoted lines. Other reading: “And what grew from earth goes back to earth”
- *εἰς οὐράνιον πάλιν ἦλθε πόλον*: Verse, believed to be from a lost play of Euripides (from memory, unchecked). The lines as quoted have one verb, πάλιν ἦλθε, “went back”, which stands in the second half and serves both; the English puts “goes back” in the first half and lets it serve the second. ἦλθε is an aorist stating a general truth, so the English has the present. Other reading: and what sprouted from a seed of the upper air has gone back to the vault of heaven
- *Ἢ τοῦτο διάλυσις*: There is no verb. τοῦτο is taken as subject (“or else this”, that is, what the verses describe, death) with “is” understood, giving the atomist alternative to the poet’s account. It could also be read as “or this:” introducing the alternative. Other reading: Or this: a dissolution of the interlockings among the atoms
- *τῶν ἀπαθῶν στοιχείων*: ἀπαθής can mean “not acted upon, unchangeable” (as atoms are) or “without feeling”. The English takes the first. Other reading: of the unfeeling elements
- *παρεκτρέποντες ὀχετὸν*: Verse, believed to be from Euripides’ Suppliant Women (from memory, unchecked); the quotation has only a participle and no finite verb, and the English leaves it so. ὀχετός is a channel or conduit for water, here the course that carries a life to its end, and the image is kept. Other reading: they divert the stream with food and drink and spells, so as not to die
- *ὥστε μὴ θανεῖν*: After these words the text as given has a row of dots, which marks a break between two separate verse quotations (or a gap). The English shows it with an ellipsis between two sets of quotation marks and supplies nothing. Other reading: the two quotations printed as one continuous passage
- *οὖρον*: οὖρος is a sailing wind, usually a fair one that blows from behind. “Sailing wind” keeps that; plain “wind” would be easier English but loses it. Other reading: But the wind that blows from the gods must be borne
- *καμάτοις ἀνοδύρτοις*: Literally “with toils unlamented”: the toils are endured and not wailed over. The English keeps one phrase and the plural. Other reading: with toil and without lament

</details>

### 7.52

Better at throwing an opponent, but not more social, nor more modest, nor better disciplined in the face of what happens, nor kinder toward the oversights of those nearby.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Καββαλικώτερος*: A wrestling word in a Doric (Spartan) form: “more able to throw down”; “an opponent” is supplied, because “throw” alone is heard in English of throwing a thing. From memory, unchecked, it echoes a Spartan saying reported by Plutarch, where the man who beat a wrestler is called not better but better at throwing. The sentence has no verb and no subject, so who is compared with whom is left open. Other reading: A better wrestler
- *κοινωνικώτερος*: The settled rendering “social” is kept. The sense is not “fond of company” but “given to acting for the community, for the common good”. Other reading: more public-spirited
- *αἰδημονέστερος*: The word covers modesty, a sense of shame, decency and respect for others. The English reads “modest”, which narrows it. Other reading: with more sense of shame
- *εὐτακτότερος ἐπὶ τοῖς συμβαίνουσιν*: The adjective is the soldier’s “in good order”, “disciplined”; the preposition is “at” or “over” what happens. The phrase “in the face of what happens” is read with this adjective only, not with the ones before it. Other reading: nor more orderly when things happen
- *εὐμενέστερος*: Well disposed, gracious, kind. With faults as the object it comes near “more forgiving”. Other reading: nor more forgiving of
- *τὰ τῶν πλησίον παροράματα*: The noun means things overlooked: mistakes made by not seeing. “Those nearby” is literally “those near”, the people one lives among, often put as “neighbours”; no “his” is written, because the Greek does not say whose they are. Other reading: the slips of his neighbours

</details>

### 7.53–54

Where a piece of work can be completed in accordance with the reason that gods and human beings have in common, there is nothing to fear there. For where it is possible to gain benefit through an activity that travels a good road and goes forward in accordance with the way we are made, no harm is to be suspected there.

Everywhere and without a break it is in your power to be well content, in reverence for the gods, with the present turn of events, to behave justly towards the people present, and to work with a craftsman’s care on the present impression, so that nothing slips in that has not been grasped.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *οὐδὲν δεινόν*: δεινόν is “terrible, to be feared”. No verb is expressed. Other reading: there nothing is terrible
- *εὐοδούσης*: Literally “having a good road”, travelling well: a stock Stoic image for activity that flows as it should. The road is kept. Other reading: an activity that prospers
- *κατὰ τὴν κατασκευὴν*: Literally “in accordance with the constitution”, with no word for whose. The first person plural is supplied, and the wording matches the same word in 10.33. Other reading: in accordance with one’s constitution
- *ὑφορατέον*: To look at something from under the brows: to suspect or eye with apprehension. Other reading: no harm need be feared there
- *τῇ παρούσῃ συμβάσει*: The same word, “present”, comes three times (παρούσῃ, παροῦσιν, παρούσῃ) and is kept three times. σύμβασις is what has come about, the event or turn of things. Other reading: with what is happening to you now
- *θεοσεβῶς*: An adverb, “in a god-revering way”. The plural “gods” is the usual sense of the compound; the word does not itself say singular or plural. Other reading: piously
- *ἐμφιλοτεχνεῖν*: A rare compound: to practise one’s craft lovingly on something. The impression is treated as stuff to be worked on with care. Other reading: to apply your skill to the present impression
- *ἀκατάληπτον*: A Stoic term: an impression that has not been “grasped”, that is, not tested and securely taken hold of before assent. Other reading: so that nothing unexamined slips in

</details>

### 7.55

Do not look around at other people’s ruling parts, but look straight ahead to where nature is leading you, both the nature of the whole, through the things that happen to you, and your own nature, through the things you have to do. What each being has to do is what follows from its make-up. Now everything else has been made for the sake of the rational beings, just as in every other case the inferior things are for the sake of the superior, and the rational beings have been made for the sake of one another. So what comes first in the human make-up is being social. Second is not giving way to what the body undergoes; for it is proper to movement that is rational and of mind to draw a boundary around itself and never to be beaten by the movement of the senses or the movement of impulse. For both of those are of the animal kind, while the movement of mind wants to hold first place and not to be overpowered by them. And rightly so, for it is by nature fitted to make use of all of those. Third in the rational make-up is not being hasty and not being deceived. So let the ruling part hold to these and carry its straight road through, and it has what is its own.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀλλότρια ἡγεμονικά*: The Stoic term for the commanding part of the soul, rendered “the ruling part”. The plural is unusual in English. Other reading: Do not look around at what rules in other people
- *ὁδηγεῖ*: Literally “guides along a road”, which prepares the “straight road” at the end of the passage. Other reading: to where nature is guiding you on your road
- *τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ κατασκευῇ*: The noun means how a thing is constructed, and the verb from the same root follows at once. “Make-up” and “made” are used so the link shows. Other reading: what is in line with its constitution
- *τὸ μὲν οὖν προηγούμενον*: Literally “what goes in front”: first in rank among the features of the human make-up, with “second” and “third” following. “What comes first” is used for this word here and in 5.20 and 4.1. Other reading: So the principal thing in the constitution of a human being
- *τὸ κοινωνικόν*: A neuter adjective used as a noun: “the social”, the fact of being made for fellowship. The English turns it as “being social”. Other reading: is fellowship with others
- *τὰς σωματικὰς πείσεις*: The noun means being acted on, as opposed to acting: here whatever the body is made to feel. “Undergo” is used for this word here and in 9.16. Other reading: not yielding to the feelings of the body
- *λογικῆς γὰρ καὶ νοερᾶς κινήσεως*: The second adjective is built on the Greek noun for mind. “Of mind” is the wording kept for it throughout the translation. Other reading: for it is proper to rational and intelligent movement
- *περιορίζειν ἑαυτὴν*: Literally “to mark a boundary round itself”. It can be heard as keeping itself apart or as keeping within its own limits. Other reading: to keep itself within its own limits
- *τὸ ἀπρόπτωτον καὶ ἀνεξαπάτητον*: The first is a Stoic term, literally “not falling forward”, meaning not assenting before one should. “Hasty” is used for this root here and in 11.10. Other reading: freedom from rash assent and from being deceived
- *εὐθεῖαν περαινέτω καὶ ἔχει τὰ ἑαυτοῦ*: “Straight” is a feminine adjective with “road” understood, and the verb means to carry a thing through to completion. The last verb is a plain present, “it has”, not a future or a command. Other reading: let it finish a straight course, and it is in possession of what belongs to it

</details>

### 7.56–59

As someone who has died and whose life has been lived up to now, one must live what is left, as a surplus, according to nature.

To love only what happens to oneself and is spun into one’s own thread. For what fits better?

At each thing that happens, to keep before one’s eyes the people to whom the same things happened, and who then were vexed, found it strange, complained. So where are they now? Nowhere. Well then, do you too want to be like them? Do you not rather want to leave the turns that belong to others to those who turn and are turned, and yourself be wholly taken up with how to use the things that happen? For you will use them well, and they will be material for you. Only pay attention, and want to be honorable in your own eyes in everything you do; and remember both things, for what the action is done on also makes a difference.

Dig within. Within is the spring of the good, and it can always well up, if you always dig.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *μέχρι νῦν βεβιωκότα*: The Greek tense marks the living as finished: the life is counted as over at this moment. “Whose life has been lived up to now” is meant in that sense. Other reading: and has lived up to now
- *ἐκ τοῦ περιόντος*: Literally “out of what is left over”: the rest of life treated as an extra, beyond a life already counted as finished. Other reading: live the rest as a bonus
- *Μόνως*: An adverb, “solely”. The English takes it with the object: love that and nothing else. It could also limit the verb: do nothing but love it. Other reading: To do nothing but love what happens to oneself
- *συγκλωθόμενον*: “Spun together with” one: the image of the Fates spinning a person’s thread. “Thread” is supplied to make the image readable. Other reading: what happens to oneself and is spun together with one
- *ἐξενίζοντο*: From the word for a stranger: they treated what happened as something foreign. Other reading: were astonished
- *τὰς μὲν ἀλλοτρίας τροπὰς καταλιπεῖν τοῖς τρέπουσι καὶ τρεπομένοις*: Three forms of one word, “turn”, all kept. What turns are meant is not said: other people’s changes of mood or direction, or changes that are not one’s own affair. Other reading: leave other people’s changes to those who cause them and those who undergo them
- *περὶ τὸ πῶς χρῆσθαι αὐτοῖς*: The Greek says only “them”. It cannot be the turns (the Greek gender is wrong for that). It is most likely the things that happen, named at the start of the chapter and called “material” in the next sentence, and the English says so. It could be the people who turn and are turned. Other reading: with how to deal with those people
- *σεαυτῷ καλὸς εἶναι*: καλός (fine, honorable) echoes καλῶς (“well”) just before. English could keep the echo only with “good”, which this passage needs for another Greek word in “the spring of the good”. “To yourself” is taken as “in your own eyes”. Other reading: want to be fine toward yourself
- *καὶ μέμνησο ἀμφοτέρων, ὅτι καὶ διάφορον ἐφ’ οὗ ἡ πρᾶξις*: Obscure as it stands, and the English is left as obscure. “Both” has no clear pair: it may be the two commands just given, or the use and the material. The last clause may give a reason (“for”) or the content (“that”), and its main word can mean “makes a difference” or “different”; from memory, unchecked, some editors change it to the Stoic term “indifferent”. Other reading: and remember both things, and that what the action is done on is indifferent
- *Ἔνδον σκάπτε*: The Greek as given says “dig”. From memory, unchecked, the manuscripts have “look” here and “dig” is an editor’s correction. Other reading: Look within

</details>

### 7.60

The body too must be firmly set, and not thrown about, either in movement or in posture. For what the mind provides in the face, keeping it composed and graceful, something of that kind must be required in the whole body as well. But all this must be kept up without affectation.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πεπηγέναι*: Literally “to be fixed” or “made solid”, as of something set firm. The sense is a compact, steady bearing. Other reading: must be held firm
- *διερρῖφθαι*: Literally “to be flung in different directions”: loose, sprawling limbs. The English keeps the throwing. Other reading: not sprawling
- *ἐν σχέσει*: The noun is a state or a way of holding oneself; set against “movement” it is the body at rest, its posture. Other reading: or at rest
- *ἡ διάνοια*: The glossary’s first choice is “thought”, with “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty that governs the face, so “mind”. Other reading: thought
- *συνεστὼς*: A participle meaning “held together”, “composed”, here of the face. From memory, unchecked: the word may be an editor’s correction of a transmitted word meaning “intelligent”. Other reading: keeping it intelligent and graceful
- *εὔσχημον*: Literally “of good form”: becoming, decorous or graceful in bearing. Other reading: seemly
- *ἐπὶ ὅλου τοῦ σώματος*: The same preposition is used of the face and of the whole body, so the English has “in” both times: the body is where the thing is to be seen, not the one asked for it. Other reading: must be required of the whole body as well
- *σὺν τῷ ἀνεπιτηδεύτῳ*: Literally “together with the unstudied”: all of it is to look as if no effort went into it. Other reading: with nothing studied about it

</details>

### 7.61

The art of living is more like the art of wrestling than the art of dancing, in that it stands ready for the things that fall on it and are not foreseen, and does not fall.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἡ βιωτικὴ*: An adjective with “art” understood, formed like the two words that follow for wrestling and dancing. “The art of” is written three times to keep the parallel. Other reading: Living is more like wrestling than dancing
- *κατὰ τὸ*: Literally “in respect of the standing …”: the phrase gives the point of likeness. The English makes it “in that it stands”. Other reading: in respect of standing ready
- *τὰ ἐμπίπτοντα*: Literally “the things that fall upon”, used of blows and of events; the Greek does not name what they fall on, and “it” is supplied. The word shares its root with ἀπτὼς (“not falling”) later in the sentence, so “fall” is kept in both places. Other reading: whatever comes at it
- *οὐ προεγνωσμενα*: Literally “not known beforehand”. The word has lost its accent in the copy; it is read as the ordinary participle. Other reading: and are not known in advance
- *ἕτοιμος καὶ ἀπτὼς ἑστάναι*: The two adjectives are nominative, which in this construction refers them to the subject of the sentence, “the art of living” (the first can serve as a feminine); they may still point loosely to the person who lives, as to a wrestler. The second means “not falling”, “not thrown”, and is given as “does not fall”; from memory, unchecked, it is a word used of wrestlers. In the Greek both adjectives go with “stand” and both face “the things that fall on it”; the English divides them to stay readable. Other reading: in that one stands ready and firm on one’s feet against what falls on one unforeseen

</details>

### 7.62–63

Keep turning your attention to who these people are whose testimony in your favour you want, and what ruling parts they have. For you will neither blame those who stumble against their will nor need their testimony, if you look into the springs of their judgment and impulse.

“Every soul,” he says, “is deprived of truth against its will.” So too, then, of justice and self-control and kindness and everything of that kind. It is most necessary to remember this continually, for you will be gentler toward everyone.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐφιστάναι*: An infinitive used as a command, with no person; the next clause has “you want”, so the English uses an imperative. The verb is to fix attention on something, often by halting to do so; with “constantly” the English gives the attention and not the halt. Other reading: Constantly to stop and consider
- *μαρτυρεῖσθαι*: Literally “to be witnessed to”, that is, to be spoken well of. The witness word is kept because ἐπιμαρτυρήσεως (testimony) picks it up in the next clause. Other reading: whose approval you want … nor will you need their approval
- *τίνα ἡγεμονικὰ ἔχουσιν*: τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, the ruling part of the soul, the mind that directs a person, stands here in the plural: what kind of ruling part each of them has. Other reading: what sort of governing minds they have
- *ἀκουσίως πταίουσιν*: ἀκουσίως (not willingly) is the same word as ἄκουσα in the saying that follows; the English has “against their will” and “against its will” so that the link shows. Other reading: those who stumble involuntarily
- *φησίν*: “He says”, with no name. The saying is Plato’s, and Marcus seems to have it in the form in which Epictetus quotes it (from memory, unchecked). The speaker is left unnamed as in the Greek. Other reading: “Every soul,” Plato says
- *σωφροσύνης*: σωφροσύνη covers self-control, moderation and soundness of mind. The English reads “self-control”. Other reading: moderation

</details>

### 7.64

At every pain, have this ready to hand: that it is not shameful and does not make the mind at the helm any worse, for it does not ruin it either in so far as it is rational or in so far as it is social. With most pains, though, let Epicurus’s saying help you as well: that it is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if you remember the limits and do not add to it by opinion. And remember this too: that many things that are the same as pain go unnoticed as such, though we resent them, such as being drowsy, being overheated and having no appetite. So when you are displeased at any of these, say to yourself: “You are giving in to pain.”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὴν διάνοιαν τὴν κυβερνῶσαν*: Literally “the thought that steers”, the image of a helmsman. διάνοια here is the faculty, so “mind”. Other reading: the understanding that steers you
- *διαφθείρει*: To destroy or corrupt. The subject is still the pain. Other reading: it does not corrupt it
- *τὸ τοῦ Ἐπικούρου*: “The thing of Epicurus”: a saying of his. Epicurus (341 to 270 BC) founded the rival school; Marcus borrows from him here. Other reading: the remark of Epicurus
- *οὔτε ἀφόρητον οὔτε αἰώνιον*: The adjectives are neuter though “pain” is masculine: “it is a thing neither unbearable nor everlasting”. Other reading: that pain is neither past bearing nor without end
- *τῶν ὅρων*: “The limits”: Epicurus taught that pain has limits in strength and in length. The Greek does not say whose limits; “its limits” is the likely sense. Other reading: if you remember its limits
- *προσδοξάζῃς*: An Epicurean word: to add an opinion on top of what is actually felt. Other reading: and do not add your own imaginings
- *λανθάνει, δυσχεραινόμενα*: Literally “many things, being the same as pain, escape notice, being resented”: they are resented without its being noticed that they are pain. “As such” is supplied, and the bare participle is turned into a clause with a first-person plural subject. Other reading: many things that are found disagreeable are, unnoticed, the same as pain
- *καυματίζεσθαι*: To suffer from heat: either hot weather or the heat of a fever. Other reading: being feverish
- *λέγε ἑαυτῷ, ὅτι πόνῳ ἐνδίδως*: The Greek is reported speech with a second-person verb, and has the third-person reflexive ἑαυτῷ for “yourself”. The English turns it into direct speech. Other reading: tell yourself that you are giving in to pain

</details>

### 7.65

See that you never come to feel toward the inhuman anything like what the inhuman feel toward human beings.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πάθῃς*: πάσχω is to undergo or be affected: here, to come to be in a certain state of feeling toward someone. Other reading: See that you are never affected toward the inhuman as
- *οἷον οἱ ἀπάνθρωποι πρὸς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους*: The text is translated as given. Some editors are believed to change the second “the inhuman” to “human beings”, giving “as human beings feel toward human beings” (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: what human beings feel toward human beings

</details>

### 7.66–67a

How do we know that Telauges was not better than Socrates in his disposition? For it is not enough that Socrates died a more glorious death, and argued more nimbly with the sophists, and showed more endurance in spending the night out in the frost, and, when ordered to bring in the man from Salamis, was thought to have stood against it more nobly, and “swaggered in the streets”, a point one might well take note of most of all, if indeed it was true. But what has to be looked at is this: what kind of soul Socrates had, and whether he could find it enough to be just in his dealings with human beings and devout in his dealings with the gods, neither getting idly angry at vice nor yet being a slave to anyone’s ignorance, neither receiving anything allotted from the whole as something foreign or enduring it as something unbearable, nor handing his mind over to feel with the feelings of the poor flesh.

Nature did not blend the mind with the compound in such a way that it is not allowed to draw a boundary round itself and to bring what is its own under its own control.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τηλαύγης*: From memory, unchecked: Telauges was said to be a son of Pythagoras, and a lost dialogue by Aeschines, a follower of Socrates, was named after him. He stands here for a man of whom little is known.
- *Πόθεν ἴσμεν, εἰ μὴ*: Literally “From where do we know whether … not”. English says this more easily with “that … not”. Other reading: How do we know whether Telauges was not better than Socrates
- *τὴν διάθεσιν*: The settled inner state of a person, as against what they did or how they looked. “Disposition” is the nearest plain word. Other reading: in character
- *ἐνδοξότερον ἀπέθανε*: ἔνδοξος is “held in honour”, “of high repute”: the word has both glory and fame in it. The English takes “glorious”. Other reading: died a more famous death
- *ἐν τῷ πάγῳ διενυκτέρευε*: An allusion to Socrates standing through a frosty night on campaign (Plato, Symposium 220: from memory, unchecked). The tense can also mean a habit. Other reading: used to spend his nights out in the frost with more endurance
- *τὸν Σαλαμίνιον κελευσθεὶς ἄγειν γεννικώτερον ἔδοξεν ἀντιβῆναι*: “The man from Salamis” is Leon, whom Socrates was ordered to arrest and did not (Plato, Apology 32c: from memory, unchecked). With Socrates as its subject ἔδοξεν is “seemed”, “was thought to”, or, less often, “resolved to”; γεννικώτερον is taken as the adverb “more nobly”, like the three adverbs before it. The English takes “was thought”, which keeps the list to what others could see of him. Other reading: and, when ordered to bring in the man from Salamis, more nobly resolved to refuse
- *ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἐβρενθύετο*: A quotation, marked as such in the Greek as given: the comic poet Aristophanes mocking Socrates in the Clouds (from memory, unchecked). The verb means to carry oneself proudly, to strut. Other reading: held his head high in the streets
- *περὶ οὗ καὶ μάλιστ’ ἄν τις ἐπιστήσειεν, εἴπερ ἀληθὲς ἦν*: ἐπιστήσειεν is “stop and give attention”, the verb given as “taken note” in 1.11; it can shade into “raise a doubt”. εἴπερ is “if indeed”, so the last clause is taken as a condition and not as the thing doubted. Other reading: about which one might well raise a doubt most of all, whether it was true
- *ἀρκεῖσθαι*: The same verb as οὐ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ (“it is not enough”) above, now in the form “be content with”. “Enough” is kept in both so the echo can be heard. Other reading: whether he was able to be content with being just
- *εἰκῇ*: “At random”, “without thought”, and also “to no purpose”. “Idly” leaves room for both: anger at vice that has no aim and achieves nothing. Other reading: neither getting angry at vice without thought
- *δουλεύων τινὸς ἀγνοίᾳ*: Literally “being a slave to someone’s ignorance”: giving way to what another person, not knowing better, wants or thinks. Kept as the image. Other reading: nor yet bowing to any person’s ignorance
- *τῶν ἀπονεμομένων ἐκ τοῦ ὅλου*: “The things dealt out from the whole”: each person’s share of what happens. τὸ ὅλον is “the whole” throughout this translation. Other reading: any of the things assigned to him by the universe
- *τοῖς τοῦ σαρκιδίου πάθεσιν ἐμπαρέχων συμπαθῆ τὸν νοῦν*: A play on πάθεσιν (what the flesh feels or undergoes) and συμπαθῆ (feeling along with it), kept with “feel with the feelings”. σαρκίδιον is a belittling form, “little flesh”, given as “the poor flesh”. Other reading: nor letting his mind share in what the bit of flesh undergoes
- *Ἡ φύσις οὐχ οὕτως συνεκέρασε τῷ συγκρίματι*: The verb “blended” has no object in the Greek as given: it is not said what nature blended with the compound. “The mind” is supplied from the last words of the chapter before (τὸν νοῦν), with which the “itself” that follows agrees in the Greek; the other candidate is “you”. “The compound” (σύγκριμα, “the thing put together”) is the body, or body and breath, as a thing made of parts. Other reading: Nature did not blend you with the compound in such a way
- *ὡς μὴ ἐφεῖσθαι περιορίζειν ἑαυτὸν καὶ τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ὑφ’ ἑαυτῷ ποιεῖσθαι*: The reflexive is the third-person form, which later Greek also uses for “yourself”; the English follows the supplied “mind” with “itself”. The passage is cut here in mid-chapter and the Greek ends at a colon; nothing was supplied at the end. Other reading: that you are not allowed to mark yourself off and to bring what is yours under your own control

</details>

### 7.67b

For it is very possible to become a godlike man and to be recognised by no one. Remember this always, and this as well: that living happily lies in very few things. And do not, because you have given up hope of being a logician and a student of nature, for that reason give up on being free, modest, social and obedient to god.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *λίαν γὰρ ἐνδέχεται*: The passage begins mid-chapter with “for”. λίαν is “very much”: it is entirely possible. Other reading: For it is quite possible
- *θεῖον ἄνδρα*: θεῖος is “divine, godlike”; ἄνδρα is the word for a man, not for a person in general. Other reading: a divine man
