- *ἐν ὀλιγίστοις κεῖται*: “Lies in very few things”: the superlative of “few”. Other reading: depends on the fewest things
- *διαλεκτικὸς καὶ φυσικὸς*: The dialectician is the expert in logic and argument, the φυσικός the expert in the study of nature: the two parts of Stoic philosophy besides ethics. Other reading: a dialectician and a natural philosopher
- *ἀπογνῷς*: ἀπήλπισας and ἀπογνῷς both mean to give up hope; the English has “given up hope” and “give up on”. The adjectives that follow are nominative, with “being” left out. Other reading: do not for that reason despair of being free
- *αἰδήμων*: Having αἰδώς, a sense of shame and respect before others and oneself. The English reads “modest”, as for αἰδῆμον in 9.29. Other reading: self-respecting
- *κοινωνικὸς*: “Social” in the sense of living and acting as a member of the community, for the common good; not “sociable”. It is the word kept for κοινωνικός throughout this translation. Other reading: a good member of the community
- *εὐπειθὴς θεῷ*: “Readily obedient to god”; there is no article, so “god” and not “the god”. Other reading: ready to obey god

</details>

### 7.68

To live life through unforced and in the greatest gladness, even if everyone is shouting whatever they like against you, even if the wild beasts are tearing apart the little limbs of this lump of dough that has thickened around you. For what, in all of this, prevents the mind from keeping itself in calm, in a true verdict on what stands around it, and in a ready use of what is put before it, so that the verdict says to what befalls, “This is what you are in reality, even if in opinion you look like something else,” and the use says to what comes to hand, “You are what I was looking for. For to me what is present is always material for rational and civic virtue, and in general for the craft of a human being or a god”? For everything that happens is made akin to a god or a human being, and is neither new nor hard to handle, but familiar and easy to work.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἀβιάστως διαζῆσαι*: The sentence is a bare infinitive with no main verb: it can be a command to oneself, a wish, or a statement of what is possible. The English leaves it as an infinitive. ἀβιάστως is “without being forced”, free of any constraint. Other reading: Live your life through without constraint
- *καταβοῶσιν*: The Greek has no object for “shout against”, and none for “around” in the next clause; “you” is supplied twice, since Marcus is addressing himself. Other reading: even if everyone cries out whatever they like
- *τοῦ περιτεθραμμένου τούτου φυράματος*: φύραμα is a kneaded lump, dough or paste: the body. The participle comes from a verb used of something that sets or curdles around a thing, and can also be heard as “fed to growth around”. μελύδρια before it is a diminutive, “little limbs”. Other reading: of this paste that has been fed up around you
- *τὴν διάνοιαν*: διάνοια is “thought” in the glossary; here the faculty is meant, so “the mind”. Other reading: prevents thought from keeping itself
- *κρίσει*: κρίσις is the act of judging and its result. “Verdict” is used because the glossary keeps “judgment” for ὑπόληψις; here the verdict is then made to speak. Other reading: in a true judgment about its circumstances
- *ὥστε τὴν μὲν κρίσιν λέγειν τῷ προσπίπτοντι*: The result clause is still part of the question, so the English carries the question through both speeches and puts the question mark after the second. Other reading: … what is put before it? Then the verdict says to what befalls: …
- *κατὰ δόξαν ἀλλοῖον φαίνῃ*: κατ’ οὐσίαν and κατὰ δόξαν set what the thing is against what it is thought or reputed to be. “In reality” stands for the literal “in substance”; δόξα covers both “opinion” and “reputation”. Other reading: This is what you are in substance, even if by common report you look like something else
- *σὲ ἐζήτουν*: The Greek has no quotation marks. The English ends the speech of “use” after “a human being or a god”; it could end after “looking for”, or run on to the end of the chapter. Other reading: “You are what I was looking for.” For to me what is present is always …
- *τῷ ὑποπίπτοντι*: Two verbs are set side by side: προσπίπτω, what falls on the mind (“befalls”), and ὑποπίπτω, what falls under its hand as stuff to work with (“comes to hand”). Other reading: to what falls under it
- *πολιτικῆς*: “Of a citizen”, the virtue of one who lives in a community. “Political” would mislead in today’s English. Other reading: rational and social virtue
- *θεῷ ἢ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐξοικειοῦται*: The datives can go with “happens” (“everything that happens to a god or a human being”) or with the verb, as the English takes them. The verb means to make a thing one’s own, akin to one or at home with one. Other reading: For everything that happens to a god or a human being is made their own
- *εὐεργές*: Said of material that is easy to work, which keeps up the image of “material” and “craft”. Other reading: easy to deal with

</details>

### 7.69

Perfection of character has this: to live through every day as the last, and neither to be feverish nor to go numb nor to play a part.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τοῦτο ἔχει ἡ τελειότης τοῦ ἤθους*: Literally “perfection of character has this”, that is, this belongs to it. τελειότης (“perfection, completeness”) and τελευταίαν (“last”) share one root; the English does not show it. Other reading: Perfection of character consists in this
- *σφύζειν*: Literally “to throb”, as a pulse does in a fever: feverish agitation, set against numbness. Other reading: to throb
- *ναρκᾶν*: “To grow numb or torpid.” Other reading: to be sluggish
- *ὑποκρίνεσθαι*: The verb for acting a part on the stage, and so for pretending. It is the verb of ὑπόκρισις, “pretence”, in 9.2. Other reading: to pretend

</details>

### 7.70–71

The gods, who are immortal, are not vexed that through so long a time they will certainly always have to put up with bad people, such as they are and so many. More than that, they care for them in every kind of way. But you, who are about to come to an end any moment now, do you give up, and that when you are one of the bad ones?

It is ridiculous not to flee one’s own vice, which is in fact possible, but to flee that of others, which is impossible.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐν τοσούτῳ αἰῶνι*: αἰών is an age, a very long or endless stretch of time; it can also mean a lifetime, which for the immortal gods comes to the same. Other reading: in so long a life
- *πάντως ἀεὶ τοιούτων ὄντων καὶ τοσούτων φαύλων*: φαῦλοι is the Stoic word for everyone who is not wise: bad, worthless people. πάντως, “certainly”, “without fail”, goes with “will have to”. Other reading: they will without fail have to put up always with worthless people, who are what they are and so many
- *κήδονται αὐτῶν παντοίως*: The verb is to care for, to look after, as for one’s own family. “Them” is the bad people. Other reading: they look after them in all sorts of ways
- *ὅσον οὐδέπω λήγειν μέλλων*: Literally “about to cease all but now”. The Greek says only “cease”, meaning to stop living; “come to an end” keeps it as plain as that. Other reading: you, who are on the very point of dying
- *ἀπαυδᾷς*: The verb is to say no more, to give up from exhaustion. The sentence is punctuated as a question in the Greek and the English keeps it. Other reading: do you refuse to go on
- *φεύγειν*: The verb is both to run from a thing and to get clear of it. The English uses “flee” in both halves, which like the Greek verb covers the attempt and the success. κακία is rendered “vice” to keep it apart from φαῦλοι, “bad people”, in the chapter before. Other reading: not to escape one’s own wickedness, which is possible, but to try to escape other people’s

</details>

### 7.72

Whatever the rational and civic power finds to be neither of mind nor social, it judges, with good reason, to be inferior to itself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἡ λογικὴ καὶ πολιτικὴ δύναμις*: The second adjective means “belonging to a city, fitted for life as a citizen”. “Civic” is used, and kept apart from “social”, a different Greek word later in the sentence. Other reading: the faculty of reason and of citizenship
- *μήτε νοερὸν*: The adjective is built on the Greek noun for mind: “having mind”. “Of mind” is the wording kept for it throughout the translation. Other reading: neither intelligent nor social
- *εὐλόγως*: Literally “with good reason”, on the same root as “rational”. It can go with “judges”, as taken here, or be heard as a comment by the writer. Other reading: it reasonably judges to be beneath itself

</details>

### 7.73–74

When you have done good and another has had good done to them, why do you look for a third thing beside these, as fools do: to be seen to have done good as well, or to get a return?

No one tires of being benefited, and benefit is action according to nature. So do not tire of being benefited, in that you give benefit.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *εὖ πεπονθώς*: The Greek pairs “having done well” with “having been done well by”, the active and passive of one phrase. The English keeps “done good” and “had good done to them”. Other reading: and another has been well treated
- *τὸ καὶ δόξαι εὖ πεποιηκέναι*: The verb is “to seem” or “to be thought”: to have the reputation of it as well as the fact. The English reads “to be seen to have done good”. Other reading: to be thought to have done good as well
- *ἀμοιβῆς*: A return or repayment, of any kind: thanks, a favour back, a reward. The English leaves it as “a return”. Other reading: or to be repaid
- *ὠφελούμενος*: The whole chapter turns on one root (benefited, benefit, you benefit), so “benefit” is used throughout. The glossary keeps “benefits” for another verb (συμφέρει), which does not occur here. The form is passive, “being benefited”. Other reading: No one tires of receiving help, and help is action according to nature
- *ἐν ᾧ ὠφελεῖς*: Literally “in that in which you benefit”, with no object; it can also be read “while” or “in so far as”. The English reads “in that you give benefit”, with “give benefit” so that the verb is not heard as “you gain”. Other reading: while you are benefiting others

</details>

### 7.75

The nature of the whole set out by impulse to make the universe. But now either everything that comes about comes about as a consequence, or even the most important things, the ones at which the ruling part of the universe directs a particular impulse, are irrational. Remembering this will make you calmer about many things.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὥρμησε*: This is the verb of the noun ὁρμή, “impulse”, which comes back later in the passage. On its own it means “set out for, started on”. The English gives both, “set out by impulse”, so that the act is clear and the repetition can be heard. Other reading: The nature of the whole had an impulse toward making the universe
- *κοσμοποιίαν*: Literally “universe-making”. The word for the universe, κόσμος, also means order, so the making of an ordered arrangement is in the word. Other reading: toward the making of an ordered universe
- *νῦν δὲ*: This can be temporal (“but now”, after that first impulse) or logical (“but as things are”). The plain “but now” allows both. Other reading: But as things are
- *ἐπακολούθησιν*: Literally “following after”. Things come about as a sequel to something earlier, here presumably the first impulse, though the Greek does not say to what, and the English does not supply it. The same phrase has the same English in 6.36. Other reading: comes about by following on from that
- *ἢ ἀλόγιστα καὶ τὰ κυριώτατά ἐστιν*: This is the hardest place in the passage. As printed, the second alternative says that even the chief things are “unreasoned”, a conclusion nobody could accept, which pushes toward the first alternative; the word could also be taken with the verb before it, leaving the rest as a separate statement. Editors have doubted or altered the text here (from memory, unchecked), and the English follows the printed words. Other reading: or it comes about without reasoning; and the most important things are those at which the ruling part of the universe directs a particular impulse
- *ἀλόγιστα*: The word means not reasoned out, not thought through. “Irrational” is used, since “without reason” in English would mean “for no cause”. Other reading: are unreasoned
- *ἰδίαν ὁρμὴν*: The adjective means “its own” or “particular, separate”. The English takes the second sense: after one general impulse at the start, a particular impulse aimed at particular things, as against things that merely follow. Other reading: directs an impulse of its own
- *τὸ τοῦ κόσμου ἡγεμονικόν*: The Stoic term for the commanding part of a soul, here said of the universe. “The ruling part” is its English in every passage of this set. Other reading: the commanding faculty of the universe
- *γαληνότερον*: The word is from the calm of a still sea. The English is “calmer” and does not spell out the image. Other reading: more tranquil, like a sea without wind

</details>

## Book 8

### 8.1

This too helps you not to care for empty reputation: that you can no longer have lived your whole life, or at least your life since youth, as a philosopher, but to many others, and to you yourself, it has become plain that you are far from philosophy. So you are muddied, so that winning the reputation of a philosopher is no longer easy for you; and your situation fights against it too. If, then, you have truly seen where the matter lies, let go of what reputation you will have, and be content if you live at least the rest of your life, however much it may be, as your nature wants. So understand what it wants, and let nothing else pull you away. For you have learned by trial how many things you wandered among and nowhere found the good life: not in syllogisms, not in wealth, not in reputation, not in enjoyment, nowhere. Where is it, then? In doing what human nature asks for. How, then, will you do these things? If you have principles from which your impulses and actions come. What principles? Those about good things and bad: that nothing is a good thing for a human being which does not make them just, self-controlled, brave, free, and nothing is a bad thing which does not make them the opposite of these.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πρὸς τὸ ἀκενόδοξον φέρει*: The word is built on δόξα, which runs through the passage as “reputation” (δόξαν, ἐν δόξῃ, and the verb in τί δόξεις). Literally “leads towards being without empty reputation”. The English reads “helps you not to care for empty reputation”; “you” is supplied. Other reading: This too tends to free you from vanity
- *φιλόσοφον βεβιωκέναι*: φιλόσοφον goes with “life” (a philosophic life), not with “you”. The English reads “as a philosopher”. Other reading: to have lived your whole life as a philosophic one
- *πέφυρσαι*: Perfect passive of a verb meaning to mix, knead, soil or jumble. It can mean “you are stained” or “you are in confusion”; “muddied” is meant to keep both. Other reading: So you are in a muddle
- *ἀνταγωνίζεται δὲ καὶ ἡ ὑπόθεσις*: ὑπόθεσις is what a life is founded on: one’s position, role or plan of life. Presumably that of emperor is meant, which the Greek does not say. The English reads “your situation”, the word used in 11.7; the verb is that of an opponent in a contest. Other reading: and the basis of your life works against it too
- *τὸ μὲν τί δόξεις ἄφες*: Literally “let go the ‘what will you seem’”. The verb is from the same root as “reputation”, so the English reads “what reputation you will have”. Other reading: give up the question of how you will seem
- *εἰ κἂν τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ βίου ὅσον δήποτε*: κἄν here is “at least, if only”. ὅσον δήποτε is “however much it turns out to be”. Other reading: if you live even what is left of your life, be it long or short
- *συλλογισμοῖς*: Formal logical arguments. “Syllogisms” is kept because it names the thing. Other reading: in logical arguments
- *ὃ οὐχὶ ποιεῖ δίκαιον, σώφρονα, ἀνδρεῖον, ἐλεύθερον*: The adjectives are singular, “makes [a person] just”; the English has “them” for the person. “A good thing” stands for the Greek noun, “a good” (ἀγαθοῦ ὄντος ἀνθρώπῳ); it is not the glossary’s “is good for” (συμφέρει). Other reading: that there is no good for man except what makes him just, temperate, brave and free

</details>

### 8.2

At each action ask yourself: “How does this stand with me? Will I come to regret it? A little while and I am dead, and everything is cleared away. What more do I look for, if the work in hand is the work of a living being that has mind, is social, and is under the same law as god?”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πῶς μοι αὕτη ἔχει*: Literally a question of how this action “holds” for the one who asks, that is, how it stands in relation to the doer. The phrase is brief and could be narrowed in more than one way. Other reading: What is this action to me?
- *μὴ μετανοήσω*: The form can be future or aorist subjunctive, and the particle makes it an anxious question or one that hopes for the answer no. The English is a plain question about the future. Other reading: I will not regret it, will I?
- *ἐκ μέσου*: Idiom, literally “out of the middle”: removed, out of the way. The English reads “cleared away”. Everything after the colon is kept inside the quotation marks as the question put to oneself, since the Greek stays in the first person. Other reading: and everything is gone
- *νοεροῦ*: The glossary’s word for this adjective is “of mind”. The English turns it as “that has mind” so that the three adjectives read as one phrase. Other reading: a living being of mind
- *ἰσονόμου θεῷ*: Literally “having equal law with god”. It can mean living under one and the same law as god, or having equal rights with god as a fellow citizen has. The English takes the first; the second is the stronger claim. Other reading: and has equal rights with god

</details>

### 8.3

And Alexander, Gaius and Pompey: what are they beside Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates? For the latter saw things and their causes and their matter, and their ruling parts were the same. But with the others, how many things to take thought for, and slavery to how many!

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Γάιος*: Gaius is Gaius Julius Caesar, named by his first name beside Alexander the Great and Pompey. The name is left as the Greek has it. Other reading: Alexander, Caesar and Pompey
- *τί πρὸς*: Literally “what in relation to”: what do they amount to when set against the three philosophers. The chapter opens with δέ (“and”, “but”), as if continuing a thought. Other reading: what are they compared with Diogenes, Heraclitus and Socrates?
- *οἱ μὲν*: “The ones”, set against ἐκεῖ δὲ, “but there”: the three philosophers, named last, as against the three rulers. The English makes this plain with “the latter” and “with the others”. Other reading: For these men saw things
- *τὰ πράγματα καὶ τὰς αἰτίας καὶ τὰς ὕλας*: “The things, and the causes, and the matters”: cause and matter are the two sides the Stoics found in each thing, so the last two are taken as the causes and the matter of the things. Other reading: saw things and causes and materials
- *τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ ἦν αὐτῶν ταὐτά*: As given, “their ruling parts were the same”, and the Greek does not say the same as what: the same in all three men, or always the same and so not pulled about like those of the rulers. With one change of accent (ταῦτα) it would be “these were their ruling parts”. The text is probably doubted here (from memory, unchecked: readings meaning “were their own” have been proposed); the English translates what stands. Other reading: and their ruling parts were their own
- *ἐκεῖ δὲ ὅσων πρόνοια καὶ δουλεία πόσων*: Literally “but there, forethought for how many things and slavery to how many”, with no verb. “There” points back to the three rulers. The “how many” can be things or people. Other reading: But there, how much to plan for, and to how many masters they were slaves!

</details>

### 8.4–5

That they will do the same things none the less, even if you burst.

First, do not be disturbed: for all things are according to the nature of the whole, and in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, just as Hadrian is not, nor Augustus. Next, fix your eyes on the matter and see it; and, remembering as well that you must be a good human being and what the nature of a human being demands, do that without turning aside, and speak as seems to you most just: only kindly, modestly and without pretense.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὅτι οὐδὲν ἧττον*: The chapter opens with a bare “That”, as a thought to keep in mind. It is kept. Other reading: Remember that they will do the same things none the less
- *διαρραγῇς*: Literally “burst apart”, said of bursting with anger or effort. Other reading: even if you burst with rage
- *εἰς τὸ πρᾶγμα*: πρᾶγμα is the thing in hand: the matter, the business, the task. Other reading: fix your eyes on the task
- *ἀμεταστρεπτὶ*: “Without turning round”: without looking back or swerving. Other reading: without looking back
- *εἰπέ, ὡς δικαιότατον φαίνεταί σοι*: “Speak, as seems most just to you”: the Greek is about the way of speaking. The clause may go with “speak” alone, as the English has it, or with both “do” and “speak”. Other reading: do that without turning aside, and say what seems to you most just
- *αἰδημόνως*: From αἰδώς, a sense of shame and of respect for others. Other reading: with respect

</details>

### 8.6

The nature of the whole has this as its work: to move what is here over to there, to change it, to lift it from here and carry it there. All things are transformations, not so that one need fear something new. All things are familiar, and what is more, the allotments are equal.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *μετατιθέναι, μεταβάλλειν*: Two verbs with the same prefix, “to place elsewhere” and “to change”. English cannot keep the echo; the plain sense of each is given. Other reading: to transpose what is here to there, to transform it
- *πάντα τροπαί*: τροπή is a turning, and so a change from one state into another. “Transformations” is used here because “turnings” with nothing after it is not clear English; in 10.7, where the word has “into” after it, it is “a turning”. Other reading: All things are turnings
- *μή τι καινόν*: Literally “not so as to fear lest something new”: the verb is left out. It is taken as fear that something new and strange may come about. Other reading: so there is no need to fear anything unheard of
- *ἴσαι αἱ ἀπονεμήσεις*: “The distributions are equal.” It may mean that what is given out is the same for everyone, or that what is taken from one place is matched by what is given to another, or that the shares are fair. The bare statement is kept. Other reading: the portions are dealt out fairly

</details>

### 8.7

Every nature is content with itself when its road goes well. And a rational nature’s road goes well when, among its impressions, it assents to nothing false and nothing unclear; when it directs its impulses only to social acts; when it has confined its desires and aversions to the things that are up to us alone; and when it welcomes everything allotted by the common nature. For it is a part of that nature, as the nature of the leaf is a part of the nature of the plant; except that there the nature of the leaf is part of a nature that is without sensation, without reason, and able to be hindered, while the nature of the human being is part of a nature that is unhindered, has mind and is just, seeing that it makes the apportionments of time, substance, cause, activity and circumstance equal for each thing and according to what each deserves. But look, not at whether you will find one thing equal to one thing in every case, but at whether all that belongs to this one, taken together, is equal to the whole of what belongs to the other.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἑαυτῇ εὐοδούσῃ*: The verb literally means “to have a good road” and commonly just “to prosper”. The road is kept, since road language runs through the neighbouring passages. Other reading: Every nature is content with itself when it prospers
- *μήτε ψευδεῖ μήτε ἀδήλῳ συγκατατιθεμένη*: “Assent” is the Stoic term for accepting an impression as true. The second adjective means “not evident”, what has not been made clear. Other reading: assenting neither to what is false nor to what is not evident
- *τὰ κοινωνικὰ ἔργα*: The adjective means “belonging to fellowship or community”. “Social” is the word used for it throughout this translation; it does not mean sociable. The noun is literally “works”. Other reading: works that serve the community
- *τὰς ὀρέξεις δὲ καὶ τὰς ἐκκλίσεις*: Two Stoic terms, literally “reachings-for and turnings-away”. The Greek says the rational nature “has made them of the things up to us only”; “confined … to” is the English for that. Other reading: when it has made its desires and avoidances to be only of the things in our power
- *τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως*: The nature common to all things, that is, the nature of the whole. “The common nature” is kept wherever this phrase occurs. Other reading: by universal nature
- *νοερᾶς*: An adjective from the Greek noun for mind: “having mind”. “Mind” is kept for this root throughout the translation. Other reading: a nature that is unhindered, intelligent and just
- *εἴγε*: Either “seeing that” (giving the ground for calling it just) or “if, that is” (a condition, which the closing “But look” would then help to test). The English takes it as the ground. Other reading: if, that is, it makes the apportionments equal for each thing
- *χρόνων, οὐσίας, αἰτίου, ἐνεργείας, συμβάσεως*: A bare list. The first word is a plural, “times”, that is, spans of time. “Substance” is the stuff a thing is made of and “cause” the forming principle in it, a pair Marcus uses often; the last word means what befalls a thing. Other reading: of spans of time, matter, form, activity and what happens
- *συλλήβδην τὰ πάντα τοῦδε πρὸς ἀθρόα τὰ τοῦ ἑτέρου*: The Greek is compressed and has no adjective here; “is equal” is carried over from the clause before. Other reading: but whether, taken all together, the whole of this one against the total of the other

</details>

### 8.8

It is not possible to read. But it is possible to hold back insolence. But it is possible to get the better of pleasures and pains. But it is possible to be above petty reputation. But it is possible not to be angry with the insensitive and the ungrateful, and more than that, to care for them.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἀναγινώσκειν οὐκ ἔξεστιν*: ἔξεστιν is “it is allowed” or “it is possible”, with no person named. It is kept impersonal, with one phrase for all five occurrences. Other reading: You are not free to read.
- *ὕβριν ἀνείργειν*: ὕβρις is insolence or overbearing behaviour; the Greek does not say whose. The verb is to keep back or shut out. Other reading: to keep arrogance out
- *πόνων*: πόνος is toil and also pain. Paired with “pleasures”, it is taken as pains. Other reading: pleasures and hardships
- *δοξαρίου*: A diminutive of δόξα (“reputation”) used with contempt. Other reading: to be above your little bit of fame
- *ἀναισθήτοις*: Literally “without perception”: people who are dull, or who do not feel what is done for them. “Insensitive” can be heard both ways. Other reading: the stupid and the ungrateful

</details>

### 8.9

Let no one hear you finding fault with life at court any more, and do not hear yourself doing it either.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *καταμεμφομένου*: To blame, find fault with, complain of. Other reading: complaining about life at court
- *τὸν ἐν αὐλῇ βίον*: “The life at court”: αὐλή is the emperor’s court, as in 6.12. Other reading: life in the palace
- *μηδὲ σὺ σεαυτοῦ*: Literally “nor you yourself”, with “hear” understood: you are not to hear yourself doing it, that is, not to complain even inwardly. μηδέ can be “nor” or “not even”; the English takes “nor” and supplies “hear” and “doing it”. Other reading: not even you yourself

</details>

### 8.10

Regret is a kind of reproach against oneself for having let something useful go by. But what is useful must be something good, and the honourable and good man must attend to it. And no honourable and good man would regret having let a pleasure go by. So pleasure is neither useful nor good.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *μετάνοιά*: The word is a change of mind after the fact. “Regret” is used for the noun and its verb throughout, since the argument depends on the repetition. Other reading: Repentance
- *ἐπίληψίς τις ἑαυτοῦ*: ἐπίληψις is literally a laying hold of, and so a censure. The genitive is the object: oneself is what is laid hold of. Other reading: a kind of catching oneself out
- *παρεικότος*: From a verb meaning “to let pass, to neglect”. It returns below as παρεικέναι, and one English phrase, “let go by”, is kept for both, because the argument turns on it. Other reading: for having neglected something useful
- *τὸ δὲ χρήσιμον ἀγαθόν τι δεῖ εἶναι*: The English follows the order of the Greek as given: the useful must be something good. From this premise “not useful” follows, but the closing “nor good” does not strictly follow; it would if the premise ran the other way. The reverse order may be what the printed edition has (from memory, unchecked), though the accents in this copy fit the order as given. Other reading: But what is good must be something useful
- *ἀγαθόν τι δεῖ εἶναι*: “Must be something good” or “must be a good”, in the sense of a real good. The same word “good” then recurs in the phrase for the good man and in the conclusion, so “good” is kept each time. Other reading: must be a good of some kind
- *τῷ καλῷ καὶ ἀγαθῷ ἀνδρί*: A set Greek phrase for the thoroughly decent man, literally “the fine and good man”. The Greek has ἀνήρ, a man, so “man” is kept. The verbal adjective before it, ἐπιμελητέον, says that the useful thing is his to look after, rendered “must attend to it”. Other reading: the true gentleman must make it his care
- *οὔτε ἄρα ·χρήσιμον οὔτε ἀγαθὸν ἡδονή*: The raised dot before χρήσιμον is a stray mark in the copy and is ignored. There is no verb; “is” is understood. Other reading: Pleasure, then, is neither a useful thing nor a good

</details>

### 8.11

This thing, what is it in itself, in its own make-up? What in it is substance and material, and what is cause? What does it do in the universe? And how long does it last?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *αὐτὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ*: A set philosophical phrase, “itself by itself”: the thing taken alone, apart from everything around it. The English reads “in itself”. Other reading: what is it, itself by itself
- *τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ*: The noun means how a thing is built or put together: construction, constitution. The dative is loose (“in”, “by”, “in respect of”), and the English reads “in its own make-up”. Other reading: by its own constitution
- *τὸ οὐσιῶδες αὐτοῦ καὶ ὑλικόν*: One article covers both adjectives, so this is one element with two names, not two elements; literally “the substance-like and material of it”. In Stoic use “substance” (οὐσία) is the underlying stuff, close to “material”. The English says “what in it is”, without a word such as “part”, which the Greek does not have. Other reading: What is its substance, that is, its material
- *τὸ αἰτιῶδες*: Literally “the cause-like”: the Stoic active element that shapes the material and makes the thing what it is. The plain word “cause” is kept. Other reading: the causal element, the shaping principle
- *ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ*: “The universe” is the rendering settled for this word across the translation. “The world” is also possible; the Greek does not decide between the ordered whole and the world people live in. Other reading: What does it do in the world?
- *ὑφίσταται*: The verb means “subsists”, “has existence”; with “how long a time” the English reads “last”. The tense is present, so the question is how long such a thing stands in being, not how long it has left. Other reading: and for how long a time does it exist?

</details>

### 8.12

When you find it hard to wake from sleep, remind yourself that to render social actions is according to the way you are made and according to human nature, whereas sleeping is shared with the animals without reason as well. And what is according to each one’s nature is more its own, more closely grown to it, and indeed more agreeable too.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *δυσχερῶς*: The adverb covers both difficulty and unwillingness: waking with trouble, or waking with annoyance. The English reads “find it hard”. Other reading: When you are annoyed at being woken from sleep
- *κατασκευήν*: The word means the way a thing is built or equipped. The English reads “the way you are made”. Other reading: your constitution
- *ἀποδιδόναι*: The verb is “to give back, to give what is due”, so the social actions are thought of as something owed. “Render” keeps that shade. Other reading: to perform social actions
- *κοινὸν*: There is a play here: “social” (κοινωνικὰς) and “shared, common” (κοινὸν) come from the same root. Social action is a human being’s own; sleep is merely common to all animals. English cannot keep the echo. Other reading: sleeping is common to the animals without reason too
- *προσφυέστερον*: Literally “more grown onto” it, from the same root as the word for nature just before. The English keeps the image of growth. Other reading: more natural to it

</details>

### 8.13

Continually, and with every impression if possible, reason about nature, reason about the passions, practise dialectic.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *φυσιολογεῖν, παθολογεῖν, διαλεκτικεύεσθαι*: Three bare verbs with no “and”, infinitives used as an instruction to oneself, written as three commands. The first two are built on the word for reasoning or giving an account, hence “reason about”. The three seem to answer to the three parts of Stoic philosophy (physics, ethics, logic), each brought to bear on the impression; that is an inference, not something the Greek says. Other reading: apply the study of nature, the study of the passions, and dialectic
- *παθολογεῖν*: A rare verb: “to give an account of the πάθη”. The noun’s range runs from “what one undergoes” and “feelings” to the Stoic sense of the passions, the feelings that disturb; the English takes the Stoic sense. Other reading: reason about feelings, about what one undergoes
- *διαλεκτικεύεσθαι*: “To practise dialectic”, the Stoic name for the art of reasoning correctly: testing a statement by question and argument, and seeing what follows from what. “Logic” would be a wider and more modern label. Other reading: test it by argument
- *ἐπὶ πάσης, εἰ οἶόν τε, φαντασίας*: Literally “in the case of every impression, if it can be done”. “Impression” is the Stoic term φαντασία. “Every” is kept, with its own limit “if possible”. Other reading: in the case of every impression, if that can be done

</details>

### 8.14–15

Whoever you meet, say to yourself at once, beforehand: “What principles does this person hold about what is good and what is bad? For if they hold principles of such-and-such a kind about pleasure and pain and the things that produce each, and about fame, disrepute, death, life, it will seem to me nothing surprising or strange if they do such-and-such things, and I will remember that they are compelled to do so.”

Remember that, just as it is shameful to find it strange if the fig tree bears figs, so it is if the universe bears such-and-such things that it is a bearer of. And for a doctor and a helmsman too it is shameful to find it strange if so-and-so has come down with a fever or if a contrary wind has got up.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πρόλεγε*: The verb is “say beforehand”: before dealing with the person. The words to be said are kept in quotation marks to the end of the chapter, since the Greek stays in the first person. Other reading: put this question to yourself first
- *δόγματα*: The glossary’s “principles”: the settled beliefs a person acts from. It need not mean considered doctrines; it covers whatever the person in fact holds to be good and bad. Other reading: What beliefs does this person hold
- *πόνου*: The word means both pain and toil. Paired with pleasure it is taken as pain. Other reading: pleasure and hardship
- *δόξης, ἀδοξίας*: The pair is good repute and its absence, which can be disgrace or mere obscurity. The English reads “fame, disrepute”, the nearer pair of opposites. Other reading: fame, obscurity
- *ἢ ξένον μοι δόξει*: The copy has a raised stop just before these words, which cuts the sentence in two and does not construe. The English reads straight through, with “surprising or strange” as one phrase. “Strange” is from the same root as the verb “find it strange” in the next chapter, so one English word is used. Other reading: it is nothing surprising; or it will seem strange to me if they do such things
- *τάδε τινὰ φέρει*: The Greek has “of such a kind” for the principles and then the same two words, “such-and-such things”, for what the person does and for what the universe bears. The English keeps one phrase in both places so the parallel between the person and the universe can be heard. Other reading: bears this or that
- *ὧν ἐστι φορός*: Literally “of which it is a bearer”, echoing the verb “bears” used of the fig tree and the universe; “bears” and “bearer” keep the echo. The clause can describe the things borne, as here, or pick them out from a larger stock. Other reading: bears this or that among the things it is a bearer of
- *πεπύρεχεν οὗτος*: Literally “this man has caught a fever”: the doctor’s patient, whoever he may be. The English reads “so-and-so” and does not add “patient”. Other reading: if this person has a fever

</details>

### 8.16

Remember that to change your mind, too, and to follow the one who sets you right is no less free. For the activity is yours, carried through according to your own impulse and judgment, and indeed according to your own mind.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὁμοίως ἐλεύθερόν ἐστι*: “Equally” has nothing stated to compare with; what is meant is as free as holding to the first view, and the English does not add that. “Free” is a bare adjective in the Greek: the thing is free, or is what a free person does. Other reading: is no less the act of a free person
- *καὶ τὸ μετατίθεσθαι καὶ ἕπεσθαι τῷ διορθοῦντι*: One article covers both verbs, so the first “and” of the Greek is “too”: changing and following are one course, set beside another that is not named. The verbs are those of 4.12, kept as “change your mind” and “set right”. The Greek has no “your”; the second person comes from “Remember” and “yours”. Other reading: that both to change your mind and to follow the one who sets you right are equally free
- *κρίσιν*: The act of judging or deciding. The glossary keeps “judgment” for another Greek word, which does not occur in this passage, so “judgment” is used here. Other reading: decision
- *περαινομένη*: The glossary’s “carried through”: the activity is brought to completion on your own terms. Other reading: accomplished
- *καὶ δὴ καὶ κατὰ νοῦν τὸν σὸν*: A climax: “and what is more, according to your own mind”. The phrase “according to mind” is also an idiom for “to one’s liking”; with the article and “your” the English takes it as the faculty. Other reading: and, what is more, just as you would have it

</details>

### 8.17

If it is up to you, why do you do it? If it is up to another, whom or what do you blame? The atoms or the gods? Both are madness. No one is to be blamed. For if you can, set the other right. If you cannot do that, set right at least the thing itself. And if not even that, what end does blaming still serve for you? For nothing is to be done without an aim.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Εἰ μὲν ἐπὶ ·σοί, τί αὐτὸ ποιεῖς*: The raised dot before σοί is a slip of the digitised text; the words are ἐπὶ σοί, “up to you”. The Greek never says what “it” is: whatever is going wrong. Other reading: If it is in your power, why do you do this?
- *τίνι μέμφῃ*: The form τίνι is “whom” and “what” alike, and the first answer offered, the atoms, is a thing, so the English gives both. In the same way “no one” (Οὐδενί) in “No one is to be blamed” is equally “nothing”. Other reading: whom do you blame?
- *ταῖς ἀτόμοις ἢ τοῖς θεοῖς*: The two rival accounts of how things happen: the atoms of Epicurus, moving by chance, or the gods. The pair is often set side by side in this book. Other reading: Chance or providence?
- *ἀμφότερα μανιώδη*: Neuter plural: both things, that is, both kinds of blaming, are like madness. Other reading: Either would be insane.
- *διόρθωσον*: The command “set right” has no object in the Greek. The contrast with “the thing itself” in the next clause shows that the first object is whoever is responsible; “the other” is supplied, taken from “another” two sentences before. Other reading: For if you can, set the person right
- *πρὸς τί ἔτι σοι φέρει*: Literally “toward what does it still carry for you”: what does it lead to, what does it serve. Other reading: what good does blaming still do you?
- *εἰκῇ*: The adverb means at random, with no purpose in view. Other reading: For nothing should be done at random.

</details>

### 8.18

What has died does not fall outside the universe. If it stays here, it also changes here, and is dissolved into what is its own, which are the elements of the universe and of you. And these too change, and do not grumble.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ ἀποθανὸν*: Neuter: “the thing that has died”, not “the person who has died”. Other reading: That which dies
- *εἰ ὧδε μένει καὶ μεταβάλλει ὧδε*: The division between the “if” clause and its conclusion is not marked. καί is taken as “also”, beginning the conclusion: if it stays here, then here is where it changes. The whole could also be one long “if” clause with nothing after it. Other reading: If it stays here and changes here and is dissolved into what is its own
- *εἰς τὰ ἴδια*: “Into its own things”: its own proper constituents. No noun such as “parts” or “elements” is added, since “elements” comes in the next clause. Other reading: into its own constituents
- *καὶ σά*: “And yours”: the elements belong to the universe and to you alike. Other reading: which are elements of the universe and yours too
- *οὐ γογγύζει*: A homely word for muttering in complaint. The elements are said not to do it. Other reading: and do not complain

</details>

### 8.19

Each thing has come to be for something: a horse, a vine. Why are you surprised? Even the Sun will say, “I have come to be for some work,” and so will the other gods. So what are you for? For pleasure? See whether the idea holds up.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τί θαυμάζεις;*: Can be “why are you surprised?” or “what are you marvelling at?”. The English takes the first, as a reply to an imagined doubt about the opening claim. Other reading: What are you wondering at?
- *ὁ Ἥλιος*: The Greek word is both the ordinary word for the sun and the name of the sun as a god, Helios. “The Sun” with a capital keeps both, and “the other gods” shows that a god is meant. Other reading: Even Helios will say
- *πρός τι ἔργου γέγονα*: The Greek as given is unusual: literally “for something of work”, an indefinite with a genitive, read here as “for some piece of work, some task”. Other editions may print ἔργον, plain “for some work” (from memory, unchecked); the sense is the same either way. Other reading: for a certain task
- *τὸ ἥδεσθαι;*: Literally “the being pleased”, the verb used as a noun. The preposition “for” is carried over from the question before. Other reading: To enjoy yourself?
- *ἴδε εἰ ἀνέχεται ἡ ἔννοια*: The verb is “bears up, holds out, puts up with”; ἔννοια is “thought, notion, understanding”. The English takes it as the idea just proposed, that you came to be for pleasure, and asks whether it stands. It can also be read with the understanding as the one that bears: whether your own notion of what you are will put up with that answer. Other reading: See whether your understanding will put up with that.

</details>

### 8.20a

Nature has aimed at the ending of each thing not a bit less than at its beginning and its course.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐστόχασται*: Perfect of a verb from archery, “to aim at a target”, with its objects in the genitive. The image is kept. Other reading: has had regard to; has had in view
- *ἑκάστου*: Masculine or neuter: “of each thing” or “of each person”. The wider “each thing” is taken. Other reading: the ending of each person
- *τῆς ἀπολήξεως*: “Ceasing, leaving off”: the point where a thing stops. Other reading: its cessation
- *διεξαγωγῆς*: “A carrying through”: the passage between beginning and end. It can also mean the conduct of a life. Other reading: its continuance; the way its life is passed
- *τῆς ἀρχῆς τε καὶ διεξαγωγῆς,*: The Greek as given stops at a comma, in the middle of a sentence, because the section is cut here; the chapter goes on with a comparison. The English closes with a full stop and supplies nothing of what follows. Other reading: than at its beginning and its course,

</details>

### 8.20b–21

like someone throwing a ball up. So what good is it to the little ball to be carried upward, or what harm to be carried downward, or even to have fallen? And what good is it to the bubble to hold together, or what harm to have burst? And the same holds for a lamp.

Turn it inside out and look at what it is like, and what it becomes when it has grown old, when it has been ill, when it has prostituted itself. Short-lived is the one who praises and the one who is praised, the one who remembers and the one who is remembered. And besides, in a corner of this region, and not even here do all agree, nor does any one person even agree with themselves; and the whole earth is a point.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὡς ὁ ἀναβάλλων τὴν σφαῖραν*: The passage as given begins in mid-sentence, with the second half of a comparison whose first half is not here. The English leaves it as a fragment and does not supply what is compared. Other reading: as the one who throws the ball up does
- *τῷ σφαιρίῳ*: A diminutive of the word for “ball” just used. Other reading: to the ball
- *διαλυθείσῃ*: “Dissolved, come apart”, the opposite of the “holding together” before it. Other reading: or what harm when it has come apart
- *Ἔκστρεψον*: “Turn inside out”, as one turns a garment. The Greek names no object; the neuter participles that follow suggest the body, not the lamp of the sentence before, which belongs to the previous chapter. The English leaves it as “it”. Other reading: Turn the body inside out
- *πορνεῦσαν*: As given, “when it has prostituted itself”. The word is abrupt after old age and illness, and editors are recalled as having doubted it (from memory, unchecked); the English follows what stands. Other reading: when it has given itself to debauchery
- *ἐν γωνίᾳ τούτου τοῦ κλίματος*: The clause has no subject or verb in the Greek and is left without them in the English. κλίμα is a zone or region of the earth. Other reading: And besides, all this happens in a corner of this part of the world
- *οὐδὲ αὐτός τις ἑαυτῷ*: Literally “nor even a person himself with himself”; the verb “agree” is carried over. Other reading: and no one agrees even with himself
- *στιγμή*: A point in the geometer’s sense, a mere dot. Other reading: and the whole earth is a dot

</details>

### 8.22a

Pay attention to the thing before you, or to the principle, or to the activity, or to what is meant.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ*: Literally “what lies under” or “what lies before one”: the thing itself that one is dealing with and that an impression is of. It can also be the matter in hand, the business being done, or in Stoic physics the underlying material. The English takes the first, and “you” is supplied, since the Greek says only “what lies before”. Other reading: to the matter in hand (or: to the underlying material)
- *τῷ δόγματι*: “Principle” is the rendering settled for this word across the translation: a settled view one holds and acts from. It could also be heard as the particular belief or judgment involved in the case. Other reading: or to the belief
- *τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ*: “Activity”: a thing’s being at work, or the act one is engaged in. “Action” is the narrower choice. Other reading: or to the action
- *τῷ σημαινομένῳ*: “What is signified”: a Stoic term from logic for the meaning that a word or statement carries, as against the sound of the words. The English reads “what is meant”. Other reading: or to the thing signified, the meaning
- *ἢ τῷ δόγματι ἢ τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ ἢ τῷ σημαινομένῳ*: The Greek joins the four with “or”, not “and”, and “or” is kept. This is part of a chapter and the Greek ends here; nothing was supplied. Other reading: to the thing before you and the principle and the activity and what is meant

</details>

### 8.22b

You deserve these things that are happening to you; you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ταῦτα*: This is part of a chapter, and nothing in the Greek given says what “these things” are. The English keeps the bare words and supplies nothing. Other reading: what is happening to you
- *Δικαίως ταῦτα πάσχεις*: Literally “justly you undergo these things”. The verb can be the neutral “have happen to one” or the stronger “suffer”; the English takes the neutral sense and puts “justly” into the verb “deserve”. Other reading: You suffer these things justly.
- *μᾶλλον δὲ θέλεις*: The comparative goes with the “than” that follows: “you want rather … than”. The same two words can also mean “or rather”, a correction of what was just said, but then “than” has nothing to answer. The connecting particle is light: the English joins the two clauses with a semicolon and writes neither “but” nor a “because” the Greek does not have. Other reading: or rather, you choose to become good tomorrow instead of being good today
- *ἢ σήμερον εἶναι*: The Greek has only “than to be today”, with “good” understood; the English repeats “good”. The contrast of “become” and “be” is in the Greek. Other reading: than be so today

</details>

### 8.23

Am I doing something? I do it, referring it to the doing of good to human beings. Is something happening to me? I accept it, referring it to the gods and to the spring of all things, from which everything that comes about is wound together.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀνθρώπων εὐποιίαν*: εὐποιία is the doing of good, a kindness done, with ἀνθρώπων as those to whom the good is done. The English keeps the stress on the doing. Other reading: the benefit of human beings
- *ἀναφέρων*: Used twice: first of carrying an action to its aim, then of carrying an event back to its origin. “Referring it to” is kept in both places so that the pairing shows. Other reading: with the doing of good to human beings as the aim … tracing it back to the gods
- *συμβαίνει τί μοι*: τί has an accent only because the enclitic μοι follows; it is the indefinite “something”, parallel to Πράσσω τι. Read as the interrogative it would be a different question. Other reading: What happens to me?
- *τὴν πάντων πηγήν*: πηγή is a spring of water, and the English keeps the picture. πάντων can be “of all things” or “of all”; and the καί before it may add a second thing to the gods or explain them. Other reading: the gods, that is, the source of everything
- *συμμηρύεται*: A rare verb from μηρύομαι, to wind thread or yarn; with συν-, “wound together”. The picture is of all events as thread drawn from one place and wound into one. The bare verb is kept, with no “like thread” added, and “spun” is not used because spinning is another word in Greek. Other reading: from which everything that comes about is spun out together

</details>

### 8.24

As bathing appears to you (oil, sweat, dirt, slimy water, all of it disgusting), such is every part of life and every object.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὁποῖόν σοι φαίνεται τὸ λούεσθαι*: “Of what kind bathing appears to you” is answered later by “of that kind is every part of life”. The English keeps the pair as “As” and “such” in one sentence and puts the list between them in brackets. Other reading: What bathing looks like to you, that is what every part of life is like
- *ὕδωρ γλοιῶδες*: The adjective comes from the word for the mix of oil and dirt scraped off the skin at the baths, so the water is thick and sticky with that scum. Other reading: scummy, sticky water
- *πάντα σικχαντά*: “All things nauseating”: this sums up the list. The adjective is rare, and its sense is that of causing loathing. Other reading: everything sickening
- *πᾶν ὑποκείμενον*: Literally “everything that underlies” or “that lies before one”. In Stoic use it is the material substrate, and more loosely any object one has to do with. The English takes the looser sense; the same word is “the matter that underlies” in 9.36. Other reading: and every underlying material

</details>

### 8.25

Lucilla buried Verus, then Lucilla. Secunda buried Maximus, then Secunda. Epitynchanus buried Diotimus, then Epitynchanus. Antoninus buried Faustina, then Antoninus. It is all like this. Celer buried Hadrian, then Celer. And those shrewd ones, or the ones who foretold things, or the ones puffed up with vanity, where are they? The shrewd ones, for example: Charax and Demetrius the Platonist and Eudaemon and anyone else of that kind. All of it lasting a day, long dead: some not remembered even for a short while, some changed into tales, and some by now faded even out of the tales. So remember these things: that either your little compound will have to be scattered, or your little breath be put out, or else move away and be posted somewhere else.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Λούκιλλα Οὐῆρον, εἶτα Λούκιλλα*: The Greek has no verb at all: a name in the nominative, a name in the accusative, “then” and the first name again. “Buried” is supplied in each pair and the second half is left bare. Which Lucilla and Verus are meant is not certain: probably the writer’s mother and father (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: Lucilla, Verus; then Lucilla.
- *Φαυστῖναν Ἀντωνῖνος*: Here alone the accusative comes first; the English puts the pair in the same order as the others. Antoninus is presumably the emperor Antoninus Pius and Faustina his wife (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: Faustina was buried by Antoninus, then Antoninus.
- *δριμεῖς*: “Sharp, keen, piercing”, of wits or of temper. Other reading: those sharp-witted ones
- *προγνωστικοὶ*: “Able to know beforehand”: said of forecasters of any kind, astrologers or doctors giving a prognosis. Other reading: the ones with foresight
- *τετυφωμένοι*: Literally “filled with smoke”, the ordinary word for being puffed up with vanity. It is from the same root as the word given as “vanity” in another passage of this section. Other reading: the conceited ones
- *πάντα ἐφήμερα*: Neuter: “all things of a day”, though the next clauses go back to the masculine people. “Lasting a day” is kept for this word across the section. Other reading: All creatures of a day
- *τούτων οὖν μεμνῆσθαι ὅτι*: Literally “so remember these things, that”. The plural may point back to the people and things just listed or forward to the clause; “these things” followed by a colon leaves both open. The verb is an infinitive used as an instruction. Other reading: So remember these people, and that
- *τὸ συγκριμάτιόν σου*: A diminutive of “compound”: the thing put together that makes up a person. So also “little breath” (πνευμάτιον), the breath of life. Other reading: the little compound that you are
- *μεταστῆναι καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ καταταχθῆναι*: The subject is not restated; it is taken to be the little breath. The second verb is a military one, “to be assigned a post”. Other reading: or change its place and be stationed elsewhere

</details>

### 8.26–27

A human being’s joy is to do what is proper to a human being. And what is proper to a human being is goodwill towards their own kind, looking down on the movements of the senses, telling the persuasive impressions apart, and contemplating the nature of the whole and the things that come about in accordance with it.

Three relations: one to the surrounding vessel, one to the divine cause, from which all things happen to all, one to those with whom life is shared.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὰ ἴδια ἀνθρώπου*: The adjective means “peculiar to, belonging specially to”. It is repeated in the singular in the next clause, and “proper to” is kept for both. Other reading: to do the things that are a human being’s own
- *ὑπερόρασις τῶν αἰσθητικῶν κινήσεων*: The noun is literally “looking over the top of”, and so disdain. “Movements of the senses” are the stirrings that sensation sets up. Other reading: disregard for the stirrings of the senses
- *διάκρισις τῶν πιθανῶν φαντασιῶν*: Literally “a telling apart of the persuasive impressions”. It is open whether this means judging among them or telling them from true ones. Other reading: sorting the merely plausible impressions from the true
- *Τρεῖς σχέσεις*: Chapter 27 begins here; it is a bare list with no verb. The noun means a standing relation to something. Other reading: Three ties
- *τὸ ἀγγεῖον τὸ περικείμενον*: “The vessel set around” is the body. From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts have a different word here, “cause”, and “vessel” is a correction that editors print. Other reading: one to the body that encloses us
- *πρὸς τοὺς συμβιοῦντας*: Literally “towards those living together with”. The Greek names no person, so the English is kept impersonal. Other reading: one to the people you live among

</details>

### 8.28

Pain is either a bad thing for the body, and then let the body declare it so, or for the soul. But it is possible for the soul to keep its own clear sky and calm, and not to judge that it is a bad thing. For every verdict and impulse and desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to here.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *οὐκοῦν ἀποφαινέσθω*: Literally “well then, let it declare”: the subject is the body, and what it is to declare is left unsaid. “The body” and “it so” are supplied. Other reading: then let the body give its own opinion
- *αἰθρίαν καὶ γαλήνην*: Two weather words: a clear sky and a calm sea. Other reading: its own serenity and stillness
- *μὴ ὑπολαμβάνειν*: The verb of ὑπόληψις, so “judge”; κρίσις in the next sentence is “verdict”. Other reading: and not to suppose that it is bad
- *κρίσις*: The act of judging; “verdict” as elsewhere in this section, since “judgment” is kept for ὑπόληψις. Other reading: For every judgment
- *ὄρεξις καὶ ἔκκλισις*: The Stoic pair: reaching towards a thing and leaning away from it. Other reading: wanting and avoiding
- *οὐδὲν ὧδε ἀναβαίνει*: Literally “nothing comes up here”, that is, into the place inside where these acts happen. From memory, unchecked: some texts read “nothing bad”. Other reading: and nothing bad climbs up to here

</details>

### 8.29

Keep wiping out impressions, saying to yourself continually: “Now it is up to me that in this soul there be no wickedness, no craving and no disturbance at all, but that, seeing what kind of thing everything is, I use each according to its worth.” Remember this power in accordance with nature.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *συνεχῶς*: “Continually” can go with “wipe out” or with “saying”. It is put with “saying”, which it stands next to; “keep wiping out” gives the form of the command, which is the one for an action that goes on. Other reading: Keep wiping out impressions continually, saying to yourself
- *ἐπ’ ἐμοί ἐστιν ἵνα*: ἐπ’ ἐμοί is the Stoic phrase for what is in a person’s own power; the ἵνα clause gives what is in that power, a later Greek use. Other reading: Now it lies in my power that
- *ἐπιθυμία*: ἐπιθυμία is appetite or craving, one of the passions. “Desire” is kept for ὄρεξις, which is used in other passages of this section. Other reading: no desire
- *ὁποῖά ἐστι*: ὁποῖα is “of what kind”: seeing the sort of thing each is comes before using each according to its worth. Other reading: seeing all things as they are
- *χρῶμαι*: The form is the same in the indicative and the subjunctive. It is taken as subjunctive, still hanging on the words before “that”, because the “but” answers the three things the soul is to be without; as indicative it would be a new statement of what is already done. Other reading: instead, seeing what kind of thing everything is, I use each according to its worth
- *κατ’ ἀξίαν*: ἀξία is the worth or value a thing has. The phrase is “according to its worth”, not “as it deserves” in a moral sense. Other reading: I deal with each as it deserves
- *ταύτης τῆς ἐξουσίας κατὰ φύσιν*: “In accordance with nature” stands at the end with no article. It can describe the power (one you have by nature) or the remembering or using of it; the English leaves it as loose as the Greek. Other reading: Remember this power, as nature would have you.

</details>

### 8.30

To speak, both in the senate and to anyone at all, with decorum, not over-distinctly; to use sound speech.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Λαλεῖν*: An infinitive used as a note of what is to be done, with no person, kept as “To speak”. The verb is the everyday word for talking. Other reading: Speak
- *κοσμίως*: The adverb covers orderly, decent and modest. Said of how a person behaves it is propriety of manner, so “with decorum”. Other reading: in an orderly way
- *μὴ περιτράνως*: A very rare word: the simple adjective means clear, distinct, piercing, and the prefix adds “exceedingly” or “too much”. The English takes it of delivery that is too carefully distinct; it may instead be a voice that is too piercing. The sense is not certain. Other reading: not in a piercing voice
- *ὑγιεῖ λόγῳ χρῆσθαι*: Literally “healthy”, the word used of eye and stomach in 10.35; of speech or reasoning English says “sound”. The noun can be speech or reason, and after “to speak” the English takes speech. Other reading: to use healthy reason

</details>

### 8.31

The court of Augustus: wife, daughter, grandchildren, stepsons, sister, Agrippa, relatives, intimates, friends, Areius, Maecenas, doctors, sacrificers. The death of a whole court. Then go on to the others . . . not the death of a single person: as, for example, that of the Pompeys. And that line that is written on tombs, “the last of his own family”: reckon up how much those before them were racked so as to leave some successor, and then someone has to be the last. Here again the death of a whole family.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἔγγονοι, πρόγονοι*: ἔγγονοι is “grandchildren” or “descendants”. πρόγονοι is usually “ancestors”, but also “children of an earlier marriage”, that is, stepchildren. The list is of people at court who died, so the English reads “stepsons”. Other reading: descendants, ancestors
- *οἰκεῖοι*: “Those of the house”: close kin, intimates, or the people of the household. Coming between “relatives” and “friends” it is taken as those close to him. Other reading: household
- *Ἄρειος*: Areius, a philosopher attached to Augustus (from memory, unchecked). Agrippa was his general and son-in-law, Maecenas his friend and adviser. Other reading: Arius
- *θύται*: “Sacrificers”: the priests who perform the sacrifice and read the signs from it. Other reading: diviners
- *εἶτα ἔπιθι τὰς ἄλλας*: The edition marks a gap after these words, and the sentence does not construe across it. “The others” is feminine plural, which would suit “courts”. The two sides of the gap are translated as they stand and nothing is supplied. Other reading: Then go on to the other courts . . .
- *μὴ καθ’ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου θάνατον*: These words stand just after the gap with no verb to govern them, and the preposition καθ’ cannot be placed with certainty. The English gives only “not the death of a single person”. Other reading: not one person’s death at a time
- *οἷον Πομπηίων*: A genitive plural: “as [that] of the Pompeii”. It is taken as the family of Pompey, a whole line that died out, set against the death of a single person. The same form is the name of the city of Pompeii, which is named in 4.48 (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: as, for example, that of Pompeii
- *ἔσχατος τοῦ ἰδίου γένους*: Given as the wording of an epitaph. γένος is “family, line, stock”, and “family” is kept for it to the end of the passage. Other reading: “the last of his line”
- *πόσα ἐσπάσθησαν*: The verb is “were pulled, wrenched, convulsed”, and “racked” keeps the bodily image. The verb of reckoning before it is an infinitive used as an instruction. “Those before them” is plural although the epitaph is singular. Other reading: how much anguish those before them went through
- *ὅλου γένους θάνατον*: An accusative with no verb of its own. It hangs on the earlier “reckon up” or “go on to”, and the English leaves it as a bare phrase. Other reading: here again, consider the death of a whole family

</details>

### 8.32

You must put your life together one action at a time, and if each action does its own part as far as it can, be content. And no one at all can prevent you from having it do its own part. “But something from outside will stand in the way.” Nothing will, at least not in the way of acting justly, with self-control and with good sense. Some other kind of activity will perhaps be prevented; but through being well pleased with the very thing that prevents it, and through moving over with good grace to what is given, another action at once takes its place, one that will fit into the putting together of which we are speaking.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Συντιθέναι*: The verb and the noun σύνθεσιν at the end are one word; the English reads “put together” and “the putting together” so the link shows. Other reading: You must compose your life
- *κατὰ μίαν πρᾶξιν*: “By one action”, that is, action by single action. Other reading: action by action
- *τὸ ἑαυτῆς παρέχει*: Literally “supplies what is its own”, with the noun left unsaid. The English reads “does its own part”; the words can also mean that the action reaches its own end. Other reading: achieves its own end
- *ἐνστήσεταί τι ἔξωθεν*: The edition marks a change of speaker with dashes. The English uses quotation marks for the objection and none for the reply. Other reading: “But some outside thing will block it.”
- *οὐδὲν εἴς γε τὸ δικαίως καὶ σωφρόνως καὶ εὐλογίστως*: There is no verb: “nothing, at least for the justly and self-controlledly and reasonably”. The English supplies “acting”. εὐλογίστως is “with sound reckoning”. Other reading: Nothing, at least, that stops you being just, self-controlled and reasonable
- *ἄλλο δέ τι ἴσως ἐνεργητικὸν*: “Something else of an active kind”: some outward doing, as against the manner of acting just named. Other reading: but perhaps some other exercise of your activity
- *κώλυμα*: κώλυμα is the noun of the verb “prevent” used twice before it in the passage: the thing that prevents. The English writes it out as “the very thing that prevents it” so that the three can be heard together. Other reading: the obstacle itself
- *εὐαρεστήσει*: A noun in the dative, “by a being well pleased”, not a verb. “Well pleased” is used for this word family here and in 10.6, to keep it apart from ἀρκεῖσθαι, “be content”. Other reading: by accepting the obstacle itself gladly
- *εὐγνώμονι μεταβάσει*: εὐγνώμων is fair-minded, sensible, good-tempered; μετάβασις is a stepping across. Other reading: by a sensible change over to what is given

</details>

### 8.33

To take without conceit, and to let go readily.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἀτύφως*: Without τῦφος: literally smoke, and so conceit, a head puffed up. The English reads “without conceit”. Other reading: without vanity; without arrogance
- *λαβεῖν*: The two infinitives stand alone. They can be a maxim (“to take”) or commands to oneself. No object is expressed: what is taken and let go is left open, and λαβεῖν covers both “take” and “receive”, as “take” does in English. Other reading: Receive without conceit; let go readily.
- *εὐλύτως*: From a word for what is easily untied or loosened: with no knot to work at, and so without clinging. The English reads “readily”. Other reading: with ease; with a loose hand

</details>

### 8.34

If you have ever seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a severed head, lying somewhere or other apart from the rest of the body: that is what a person makes of themselves, as far as it is in their power, when they do not want what happens and split themselves off, or when they do something unsocial. You lie somewhere or other, thrown away from the union that accords with nature; for you were by nature a part, but now you have cut yourself off. But here is the neat thing: you are allowed to unite yourself again. To no other part has god granted this, to come together again once it has been separated and cut through. But consider the kindness with which he has honoured the human being: for he put it in the human being’s power not to be broken off from the whole in the first place, and, for one who has been broken off, he made it possible to come back again and grow together and take up again the place of a part.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Εἴ ποτε εἶδες*: The “if” clause never gets a main clause; the sentence breaks off and starts again with “that is what”. The break is kept with a colon. Other reading: Have you ever seen a hand cut off? That is what
- *κεφαλὴν ἀποτετμημένην*: The head has a different verb from the hand: “cut away”. “Severed” keeps the two apart. Other reading: a head cut away
- *χωρίς πού ποτε*: πού ποτε (“somewhere, at some time”) is repeated in the next sentence of you yourself, so the thrown-away self lies where the hand lay. “Somewhere or other” is used both times; the “at some time” is only faintly there. Other reading: lying at some time, in some place, apart
- *ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ*: “As far as rests with oneself.” The same phrase comes back at the end, of what god has made to rest with the human being; “power” is used in both places. Other reading: as far as it lies with them
- *τὸ συμβαῖνον*: “What happens”, with the sense “what happens to them”. The Greek has no “to them”. Other reading: what befalls them
- *ἀκοινώνητόν τι*: The adjective negates the word for community: “something that has no share in community”. “Unsocial” is used as the negative of “social”, the word for κοινωνικός throughout this translation; it does not here mean keeping to oneself. Other reading: something that goes against community
- *ἀπέρριψαί*: The form is either passive (“you have been thrown away, you lie thrown away”) or reflexive (“you have thrown yourself away”). The passive is taken, because the next clause adds an express “yourself” and this one does not, and because it matches the severed limb “lying” somewhere. Other reading: You have thrown yourself somewhere or other away from the union
- *ἐπεφύκεις γὰρ μέρος*: A past form of the verb “grow”, the verb behind φύσις (“nature”) just before and “grow together” at the end: “you had grown as, you were by nature, a part”. Other reading: for you grew as a part
- *κομψὸν*: κομψός is “neat, elegant, clever”, said of a nice touch or a pretty arrangement. Other reading: But here is the fine thing
- *θεὸς*: No article: “god”, “a god”, or the one god of the next sentence, who honoured the human being. Lower-case “god” is used, as throughout this translation. Other reading: no god has granted this to any other part
- *ἵνα τὴν ἀρχὴν μὴ ἀπορραγῇ*: τὴν ἀρχήν is the adverbial idiom “at all, in the first place”, not “the beginning”. The verb is “be broken or torn off”, stronger than the “cut” words above. Other reading: so as not to be torn away at all
- *τὴν τοῦ μέρους τάξιν*: τάξις is a post or rank in a formation: “the station of the part”. Other reading: its post as a part

</details>

### 8.35

Just as the nature of rational beings [has given] each of the rational beings its other powers […], so we have received this one too from it. For in the way that that nature turns round everything that stands in its way and goes against it, gives it a place in what is fated, and makes it a part of itself, so too the rational animal can make every obstacle into material for itself and use it for whatever its impulse was set on.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὥσπερ τὰς ἄλλας δυνάμεις ἑκάστῳ τῶν λογικῶν σχεδὸν ὅσον ἡ τῶν λογικῶν φύσις*: The Greek is damaged here: the clause has no verb. “Has given” is supplied, in square brackets, on the strength of “we have received … from it” in the second half. From memory, unchecked: editors treat the sentence as corrupt or as having lost some words. Other reading: Just as each of the rational beings has had nearly all its other powers from the nature of rational beings, so we have received this one too from it
- *σχεδὸν ὅσον*: These two words, literally “almost as much as”, do not join to anything in the sentence as it stands. They are left untranslated, and their place is marked by the bracketed dots. Other reading: its other powers, almost as many as the nature of rational beings itself has
- *ταύτην*: “This one” points forward to the power described in the next sentence. Other reading: so we have received the following power too from it
- *ἐκείνη*: On the Greek as given, “that nature” is the nature of rational beings named in the first sentence. But what is said of it, that it gives every obstacle a place in what is fated and makes it a part of itself, is what Marcus says elsewhere of the nature of the whole. From memory, unchecked: editors have proposed “of the whole” in place of the second “of rational beings”. Other reading: For in the way that the nature of the whole turns round everything that stands in its way
- *ἐπιπεριτρέπει*: A compound of the verb “turns round” used in 5.20, and the same English is kept. Other reading: turns to its own purpose
- *κατατάσσει εἰς τὴν εἱμαρμένην*: Literally “posts it into the fated”, into the order of what is destined. Other reading: fits it into destiny
- *οἷον ἂν καὶ ὥρμησεν*: The verb is the one behind “impulse”. Literally “towards whatever sort of thing it had set out”. Other reading: for whatever purpose it had set out on

</details>

### 8.36

Do not let the impression of your whole life confound you. Do not take in, in one sweep of thought, what hardships and how many are likely to have come on you. Instead, at each of the things present, ask yourself: “What is there in this task that is unbearable and not to be endured?” For you will be ashamed to admit it. Then remind yourself that it is neither the future nor the past that weighs on you, but always the present; and this shrinks if you mark it off by itself alone and convict your mind if it cannot hold out against this, stripped bare.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἡ τοῦ ὅλου βίου φαντασία*: “The impression of the whole life”: the picture of one’s life taken all at once. “Your” is supplied. Other reading: the picture of your life as a whole
- *συγχείτω*: Literally “pour together”: to throw into confusion. Other reading: Do not let it overwhelm you
- *συμπερινόει*: A compound: to go round a number of things together in thought, to take them in at once. Other reading: do not think over all together
- *ἐπιγεγενῆσθαι*: The form is a perfect infinitive, “to have come on (you)”, where the sense may seem to want a future, “are likely to come”. The English translates the perfect as it stands: the picture of a whole life includes what is past, and the chapter goes on to name the past beside the future. From memory, unchecked: editors have proposed the future here. Other reading: what hardships and how many are likely to come on you
- *τοῦ ἔργου*: “The task” or “the business in hand”; it can also be loosely “the matter”. Other reading: What is there in this that is unbearable
- *αἰσχυνθήσῃ γὰρ ὁμολογῆσαι*: The Greek does not say what would be admitted: either what the unbearable thing is, or that there is one. Other reading: For you will be ashamed to confess what it is
- *κατασμικρύνεται*: “Is made small”, passive. The English has “shrinks”. Other reading: and this is cut down to size
- *ἀπελέγχῃς τὴν διάνοιαν*: ἀπελέγχω is to refute or convict by cross-examination. διάνοια here is the faculty, “mind”. Other reading: and put your mind to shame
- *ψιλὸν*: “Bare, stripped”: the present on its own, without the past and future added. It is a different word from “alone” (μόνον) just before. Other reading: against this alone

</details>

### 8.37

Surely Pantheia or Pergamus is not sitting by Verus’s coffin now? Or Chabrias or Diotimus by Hadrian’s? Ridiculous. And if they were sitting there, would the dead be aware of it? And if they were aware, would they be pleased? And if they were pleased, would these who sit by them be immortal? Was it not so fated for these too, first to become old women and old men, and then to die? So what were those others going to do afterwards, once these had died? All this is a rank smell and gore in a bag.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μήτι*: A question word that expects the answer no. “Surely … not” carries that. Other reading: Is Pantheia or Pergamus sitting by Verus’s coffin now?
- *σορῷ*: A vessel for the remains of the dead: a coffin or an urn for ashes. The word does not decide between them, and it names the vessel, not the building that holds it. Other reading: by the urn of Verus
- *Πάνθεια ἢ Πέργαμος*: People of the household of Verus, as Chabrias and Diotimus were of Hadrian’s. Pantheia is recalled as the mistress of Lucius Verus (from memory, unchecked).
- *ἔμελλον αἰσθάνεσθαι*: The verb has no stated subject. The sense requires the dead men, since “these” two questions later marks the sitters off from them. “The dead” is supplied in the English. Other reading: would they have noticed?
- *ἡσθήσεσθαι*: “To be pleased”. It chimes in sound with the verb for “be aware” just before, a play English cannot keep. Other reading: would it give them pleasure?
- *οὗτοι*: “These”, the ones sitting by the coffin, against “those” (ἐκεῖνοι), the dead, two sentences on. The Greek has only the two pronouns. “Who sit by them” and later “others” are added to keep the two groups apart. Other reading: would the mourners be immortal?
- *γράσος πᾶν τοῦτο καὶ λύθρος ἐν θυλάκῳ*: γράσος is the rank smell of a goat or of sweat, λύθρος is blood mixed with dirt, θύλακος is a sack. “All this” is not defined: the body, or the whole business. Other reading: The whole thing is stench and filthy blood in a sack.

</details>

### 8.38

If you can look keenly, look, judging, he says, with the wisest.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *φησί*: “He says” marks a quotation, and the speaker is not named. The Greek does not show how much of the line is quoted, so the English uses no quotation marks. Other reading: “If you can look keenly, look and judge,” it says, “with the wisest.”
- *σοφωτάτοις*: A plural form, “wisest”, with no noun, and the Greek as given does not construe securely: it could be “together with the wisest men” or “by the wisest standards”.
