The English keeps the form and leaves it as open as the Greek. From memory, unchecked: editors have changed it to an adverb, “most wisely”. Other reading: judging most wisely
- *βλέπε κρίνων*: Literally “look, judging”: the looking is to be done with judgment. It could also be heard as “see to it that you judge”. Other reading: see that you judge
- *ὀξὺ βλέπειν, βλέπε*: One verb comes twice, so the English has “look” both times. The first phrase is the usual one for being sharp-sighted. Other reading: If you can see sharply, see

</details>

### 8.39

In the make-up of the rational animal I see no virtue that rises up against justice, but I do see one that rises up against pleasure: self-control.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κατεξαναστατικὴν*: A rare adjective from the verb “to rise up against” used in 5.15, and the same English is kept. The second clause does not repeat it; it is supplied there. Other reading: I see no virtue opposed to justice, but opposed to pleasure I see self-control
- *τὴν ἐγκράτειαν*: Literally “having power over oneself”. Other reading: self-mastery

</details>

### 8.40

If you take away your judgment about what seems to distress you, you yourself stand in the safest place. “Who is ‘yourself’?” Reason. “But I am not reason.” Granted. Then let reason, for its part, not be the one to distress itself, and if anything else of yours is in a bad way, let that form its own judgment about itself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὑπόληψιν*: The glossary word “judgment”. The verb at the end of the passage (ὑπολαβέτω) is the same word, so “form its own judgment” is used there to let the link be seen. Other reading: your opinion, your assumption
- *τοῦ λυπεῖν σε δοκοῦντος*: The form can be neuter, the thing that seems to distress you, or masculine, the person who seems to. The English takes it as the thing, which is the wider reading. Other reading: your judgment about the person who seems to distress you
- *λυπεῖν*: The verb covers bodily pain, grief and annoyance. “Distress” can be said of both body and mind, and it is kept for the second occurrence (λυπείτω). Other reading: what seems to be hurting you … let reason not be the one to hurt itself
- *ἐν τῷ ἀσφαλεστάτῳ ἕστηκας*: The verb is a perfect with present sense, “you stand”, and it is kept as a present, not made a future. The superlative can mean “the safest place” or simply “complete safety”. Other reading: you yourself stand in complete safety
- *τίς αὐτός;*: The dashes of the edition mark changes of speaker in a short exchange. The objector’s two lines are put in quotation marks and the answers are left without. The question picks up the emphatic “you yourself” (αὐτὸς) of the first sentence. Other reading: “Who is this ‘self’?”
- *οὐκ εἰμὶ λόγος*: Said flatly, with no qualification. The objector probably means “not reason only”, but the Greek has no “only” and none is added. Other reading: “But I am not just reason.”
- *ὁ μὲν λόγος αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν μὴ λυπείτω*: The Greek doubles the pronoun, “itself … itself”, to say that the distress would be reason’s own doing; “not be the one to” carries that. “For its part” gives the contrast with “anything else” in the next clause. Other reading: let reason at least not distress itself
- *εἰ δέ τι ἄλλο σοι κακῶς ἔχει, ὑπολαβέτω αὐτὸ περὶ αὑτοῦ*: αὐτὸ is taken as the subject, “let it, itself, judge”. It can also be the object, “let it suppose that about itself”. The “anything else of yours” is not named; the body is the likely candidate. Other reading: and if anything else of yours is in a bad way, let it suppose so about itself

</details>

### 8.41a

A hindrance to sensation is a bad thing for an animal nature. A hindrance to impulse is likewise a bad thing for an animal nature. And there is something else that likewise hinders, and is a bad thing for, the way a plant is made. In the same way, then, a hindrance to mind is a bad thing for a nature that has mind. Now carry all of this over to yourself. Does pain, does pleasure touch you? That is for sensation to see to. Did something come to stand in the way of your impulse? If your impulse was without reservation, then it is already a bad thing for you as a rational being. But if you accept the common lot, you have not yet been harmed or hindered. What is the mind’s own, however, no one else is in the habit of hindering: for neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant, nor slander, nor anything whatever touches it,

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ζωτικῆς φύσεως*: “A nature that has life”, here animal life, the level that has sensation and impulse. The genitive is “an evil of” such a nature; the English has “a bad thing for”. Other reading: an evil of the living nature
- *τῆς φυτικῆς κατασκευῆς*: “The plant constitution”; “the way a plant is made” matches the rendering of κατασκευή in 10.33 and 7.53. Other reading: the constitution of plants
- *νοερᾶς φύσεως*: The glossary gives “of mind” for νοερός. “A nature that has mind” keeps “mind” so that the link with “a hindrance to mind” can be heard. Other reading: a thinking nature
- *ὄψεται ἡ αἴσθησις*: Literally “sensation will see”: the idiom for “that is its affair”, as in 5.25. Other reading: let sensation look to it
- *ἔνστημα*: Something that “stands in the way”: the noun of the verb so rendered in 8.47 and 10.33. Other reading: Did an obstacle meet your impulse?
- *ἀνυπεξαιρέτως*: A Stoic term: without the “reservation” (ὑπεξαίρεσις), the unspoken clause “if nothing prevents” with which a wise person frames every impulse. Other reading: If you set out unconditionally
- *ὡς λογικοῦ*: “As of a rational one”: a bad thing for you in so far as you are rational. “Being” is supplied. The word for “already” before it answers “not yet” in the next clause. Other reading: an evil of you as rational
- *εἰ δὲ τὸ κοινὸν λαμβάνεις*: Literally “but if you take the common”. What “the common” is is not clear: the lot common to all, the general rule that impulses meet obstacles, or the usual reservation. The English takes the first. Other reading: but if you take the usual reservation for granted
- *οὐδεὶς ἄλλος εἴωθεν ἐμποδίζειν*: Literally “no one else is accustomed to hinder”. The Greek does not say else than whom; the sense is no one but the mind itself, or but you. Other reading: no one other than the mind itself ever hinders
- *σίδηρος*: “Iron”: the sword or the knife. Other reading: nor steel
- *οὐχ ὁτιοῦν ἅπτεται,*: The passage ends here with a comma, part-way through the chapter and the sentence. The comma is kept and nothing is supplied. Other reading: nor anything at all touches it.

</details>

### 8.41b

once it has become a “rounded sphere, in stillness”.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὅταν γένηται*: This is a subordinate clause only, and the English begins in lower case to show it. Its main clause stands in the part of 8.41 that is not given, which says that nothing at all touches the mind; “it” is the mind. ὅταν with the aorist subjunctive is “once” or “whenever”. Other reading: whenever it becomes
- *σφαῖρος κυκλοτερὴς μονίῃ*: A quotation of verse, from memory, unchecked, a line of Empedocles that goes on with a word meaning “rejoicing”, which governs the dative μονίῃ. Marcus stops before that word, so the dative is left hanging. The English gives it as “in stillness” and adds nothing from the rest of the line. Other reading: a “rounded sphere”, in stillness (with the dative outside the quotation); or, with the rest of the line supplied, “a rounded sphere rejoicing in its stillness”
- *μονίῃ*: A rare poetic noun that can be derived from μένω, “stay”, giving “rest, stillness, steadfastness”, or from μόνος, “alone”, giving “solitude”. The English takes the first. From memory, unchecked, scholars are divided on which the poet meant. Other reading: in solitude
- *κυκλοτερὴς μονίῃ*: From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts are said to end here with μένει, “it stays”, which gives the clause a verb of its own, and μονίῃ is an editor’s restoration from the same verse quoted at greater length in 12.3. The English follows the text as given. Other reading: once it has become a rounded sphere, it stays so
- *σφαῖρος*: A masculine form of the usual feminine σφαῖρα, “ball, sphere”, the poet’s name for his perfectly round whole. Marcus applies it to the mind as an image, so the English has no capital. κυκλοτερής, “rounded, circular”, repeats the idea of roundness, and both words are kept. Other reading: a well-rounded Sphere; or: a round ball

</details>

### 8.42–43

I do not deserve to cause myself distress, for I have never yet willingly distressed anyone else.

One thing gladdens one person, another another. What gladdens me is if I have my ruling part sound: not turning away from any human being or from any of the things that happen to human beings, but looking at everything with kindly eyes, accepting it, and using each thing according to its worth.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οὐκ εἰμὶ ἄξιος*: Literally “not worthy”: the speaker has not earned it. Other reading: It is not right that I should distress myself
- *ἑκὼν*: “Willingly, on purpose.” Other reading: I have never intentionally distressed another
- *ἐὰν ὑγιὲς ἔχω τὸ ἡγεμονικόν*: A conditional clause, and the “if” is kept. ὑγιές is “healthy, sound”. Other reading: but me, to keep my ruling part healthy
- *ἀποστρεφόμενον*: The participles that follow (turning away, looking, accepting, using) all describe the ruling part, not the speaker. Other reading: a ruling part that does not turn away
- *εὐμενέσιν ὀφθαλμοῖς*: “With well-meaning eyes”; the same word as “in a kindly spirit” in 8.47. Other reading: with friendly eyes
- *χρώμενον ἑκάστῳ κατ’ ἀξίαν*: “Using each according to worth”: ἑκάστῳ can be each thing or each person, and the worth is the worth of that thing or person. Other reading: and dealing with each as it deserves

</details>

### 8.44

Look: make a gift of this present time to yourself. People who chase fame after death instead do not take into account that those people will be others of the same kind as these whom they find hard to bear; and those people too are mortal. And what is it to you at all, if those people echo with sounds of such a kind, or hold a judgment of such a kind about you?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τοῦτον ἰδοὺ τὸν χρόνον σεαυτῷ χάρισαι*: The Greek has only “this time”: the time that is here now, set against the time of later fame. “Present” is added so that the words are not heard as “on this occasion”. The verb is to give freely, as a favour or present. Other reading: Look: grant this time to yourself.
- *ὑστεροφημίαν*: A compound, literally “after-fame”: what is said of a person later. “After death” is the sense but “death” is not in the word. Other reading: what will be said of them afterwards
- *μᾶλλον*: “Rather”: they chase later fame in preference to the present time just mentioned. The English reads “instead”. Other reading: People who prefer to chase fame after death
- *ἄλλοι τοιοῦτοι μέλλουσιν ἐκεῖνοι εἶναι, οἷοί εἰσιν οὗτοι οὓς βαροῦνται*: The Greek has only “those” and “these”: “those” are the people among whom the later fame would live, “these” the people of the present. “Those people” is kept for the one Greek word all three times. The last verb is literally to be weighed down by someone. Other reading: that those will be others such as these who weigh on them
- *φωναῖς τοιαύταις ἀπηχῶσιν*: The verb means to sound back, echo or ring out; the noun covers voices, sounds and words. The phrase makes their talk about you into mere noise. Other reading: if those people ring out with voices of such a kind
- *ὑπόληψιν τοιαύτην*: The word “such”, here and with “sounds”, can point back to “of the same kind” above, the sounds and the judgment that people of that kind produce. It can also be indefinite, “this or that”. “Of such a kind” leaves both possible. Other reading: if those people echo with this or that sound, or hold this or that judgment about you
- *ὑπόληψιν*: The Stoic word for a judgment or opinion taken up about something; “judgment” follows the glossary. Other reading: an opinion of such a kind about you

</details>

### 8.45a

Pick me up and throw me wherever you want. For there too I will have the divinity within me gracious, that is, content if the state it is in and the way it acts follow from its own make-up.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἆρόν με καὶ βάλε*: The Greek does not say who is addressed (fortune, a god, anyone at all). “You” is left unexplained. Other reading: Lift me up and cast me
- *τὸν ἐμὸν δαίμονα*: δαίμων is the divine being that each person has within, which Marcus elsewhere treats as one’s own mind and reason. The Greek has only the possessive, “the daimon that is mine”. The English reads “the divinity within me” because “spirit” with a possessive would be heard today as a mood. Other reading: the daimon that is mine; the guardian spirit that is mine
- *ἵλεων*: ἵλεως is the word for a god who is favourable, and of a person it means kindly or cheerful. The English reads “gracious”, the word used of a god. Marcus glosses it himself in the next words. Other reading: well disposed; cheerful; serene
- *ἀρκούμενον, εἰ*: The clause with εἰ can state what the divinity is content with (content if it is and acts so), or a condition on the whole promise (it will be gracious, provided it is and acts so). The English takes the first and so leaves out the comma that the edition has before εἰ. Other reading: that is, content, provided that the state it is in and the way it acts follow from its own make-up
- *ἔχοι*: ἔχοι is read as intransitive, “is in a certain state”, sharing the phrase κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς with ἐνεργοίη. “The state it is in” and “the way it acts” stand for the two Greek verbs. ἔχοι could also be taken as “holds” with an object left unsaid. Other reading: if it holds its ground and acts
- *κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ*: Literally “according to what comes next in order after its own make-up”, that is, what follows from the way it is made. κατασκευή is the make or build of a thing. Other reading: in keeping with its own constitution

</details>

### 8.45b

Is this worth it, that because of it my soul should be in a bad way and be worse than itself: brought low, craving, shrinking in, taking fright? And what will you find that is worth that?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἆρα τοῦτο ἄξιον*: The passage is the second part of a chapter. “This” points back to something not given here, and it is not supplied. Other reading: Is this thing worth such a price
- *χείρων ἑαυτῆς*: Literally “worse than itself”, that is, worse than it is in its right state. The literal phrase is kept. Other reading: fall below itself
- *ὀρεγομένη*: Literally “stretching out” after something, the ordinary verb for desiring. In this list of bad states it is given as “craving”; the literal sense may be meant as a pair with the next word. Other reading: reaching out
- *συνδυομένη*: A rare word: literally “sinking in together”, taken as shrinking into itself. The reading is thought to be doubted, and a word meaning “bound, fettered” to have been proposed (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: fettered
- *πτυρομένη*: Used of a horse that shies: startled, scared. Other reading: panicking
- *καὶ τί εὑρήσεις τούτου ἄξιον*: The person changes from the first person to “you will find”, and the change is kept. τούτου, “worth this”, means worth such a cost to the soul; “that” keeps it apart from the first “this”. Other reading: And what will you find that is worth this?

</details>

### 8.46–47

Nothing can happen to any human being that is not a human occurrence, nor to an ox that is not of the ox kind, nor to a vine that is not of the vine kind, nor to a stone that is not proper to a stone. So if what happens to each is what is both usual and natural, why would you resent it? For the common nature was bringing you nothing that could not be borne.

If you are distressed because of something outside you, it is not that thing that troubles you but your own verdict about it, and to wipe that out at once is in your power. But if what distresses you is something in your own disposition, who prevents you from putting your principle right? In the same way, if you are distressed because you are not doing some particular thing that seems sound to you, why not do it rather than be distressed? “But something stronger stands in the way.” Then do not be distressed, for the cause of its not being done does not lie with you. “But life is not worth living if this is not done.” Then leave life in a kindly spirit, just as the one who is doing it dies too, and at the same time gracious towards the things that stand in the way.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀνθρωπικὸν σύμπτωμα*: σύμπτωμα is a chance event, often a mishap. “Occurrence” keeps it neutral and keeps it apart from the verb “happen” (συμβαίνειν) beside it. Other reading: a mishap of the human kind
- *οὐ γὰρ ἀφόρητόν σοι ἔφερεν*: The Greek plays on one root: the common nature “brought” (ἔφερεν) nothing that cannot be “borne” (ἀφόρητον). “Bringing” and “borne” are set close together, which is as near as English comes. The verb is imperfect, kept as “was bringing”; it can also be heard as “was never going to bring”. Other reading: For what the common nature brought you was not something unbearable.
- *ἡ κοινὴ φύσις*: The nature common to all things, that is, the nature of the whole. “The common nature” is kept because the same phrase in 5.25 is set against the speaker’s own nature. Other reading: the nature that all things share
- *δυσχεραίνοις*: The verb ranges from “be annoyed” to “find hard to bear”. “Resent” is used here and for the same verb in 10.3 and 7.64. Other reading: why would you be annoyed?
- *κρῖμα*: κρῖμα is the finding one arrives at. The glossary keeps “judgment” for ὑπόληψις, so “verdict” stands for κρῖμα and κρίσις throughout this section. Other reading: your own judgment about it
- *ἤδη*: ἤδη can go with “wipe out” (“at once”) or with “is in your power” (“here and now, as things stand”). The English takes the first. Other reading: and wiping that out is, here and now, in your power
- *τὸ δόγμα*: δόγμα is “principle” throughout this translation; here it is the belief a person holds, the thing in their own disposition that distresses them. “Your” renders the Greek article. Other reading: who prevents you from putting your belief right?
- *ἐνεργεῖς*: The argument runs on one verb in four forms (ἐνεργεῖς, ἐνεργεῖσθαι, ἐνεργουμένου, ὁ ἐνεργῶν). “Do” and “be done” are kept for all of them. Elsewhere in this section the noun ἐνέργεια is “activity”. Other reading: you are not carrying out some particular activity
- *ᾗ καὶ ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἀποθνῄσκει*: ᾗ is “in the way that” or “just as”. ὁ ἐνεργῶν has no object: the English takes it as the person who does manage to do the thing, who also dies; it could be simply “the one who is active”. Other reading: in the same way as the active person dies too
- *τοῖς ἐνισταμένοις*: The form can be neuter (“the things that stand in the way”) or masculine (“the people who stand in the way”). The neuter is taken because the objection above speaks of “something stronger”. Other reading: gracious towards those who stand in your way

</details>

### 8.48

Remember that the ruling part becomes unconquerable when, gathered into itself, it is content with itself, not doing anything it does not want to do, even if it takes its stand without reason. What, then, when it judges about something with reason as well, and after looking all round it? This is why the mind free of passions is a citadel, for a human being has nothing better fortified to flee to, where they would from then on be beyond capture. So whoever has not seen this is ignorant, and whoever has seen it and does not flee to it is unfortunate.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *εἰς ἑαυτὸ συστραφὲν*: The participle is of something twisted or rolled together, as troops close up or an animal coils. The English reads “gathered into itself”. Other reading: when it has turned in on itself
- *κἂν ἀλόγως παρατάξηται*: παρατάσσομαι is to draw up in line of battle, which goes with “unconquerable”. The sense is that it cannot be forced even when its resistance is mere stubbornness; “takes its stand” keeps something of the battle line. Other reading: even if it draws up its line without reason
- *καὶ μετὰ λόγου καὶ περιεσκεμμένως*: The first καί can be “also”, answering “without reason” just before, or the first half of “both … and”. The English takes it as “as well”, which marks the step from the weaker case to the stronger. Other reading: when it judges about something both with reason and after looking all round it
- *περιεσκεμμένως*: Literally “having looked round”: with circumspection. Other reading: with reason and deliberately
- *διάνοια*: The glossary gives “thought” and allows “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here the faculty is meant, and νοῦς does not occur in the passage. Other reading: thought that is free of passions is a citadel
- *παθῶν*: πάθη in the Stoic sense: the disturbing emotions such as fear, craving, grief. Other reading: free of emotions
- *ὀχυρώτερον*: ὀχυρός is said of a place that is fortified and hard to take, so the word carries on the citadel. The Greek has the adjective alone, with no noun for “stronghold”. Other reading: a human being has nothing stronger
- *ἐφ’ ὃ καταφυγὼν ἀνάλωτος λοιπὸν ἂν εἴη*: Literally “to which having fled for refuge he would thereafter be not to be taken”. The fleeing and the safety are split between two clauses, and “they” stands for the unmarked “human being”. Other reading: nothing better fortified in which to take refuge and be impregnable from then on
- *ἀτυχής*: Literally “without good fortune”. It may be said with some edge, of one who has the refuge and does not use it. Other reading: is wretched

</details>

### 8.49

Say nothing more to yourself than what the impressions that lead the way report. It has been reported that so-and-so is speaking ill of you. That has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported. I see that the child is sick. I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see. So always stay like this with the first impressions and say nothing further yourself from within, and nothing happens to you. Or rather, do say something further, as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *αἱ προηγούμεναι φαντασίαι*: The participle means “going before, leading the way”. It is most likely meant of time, the impressions that arrive first, which the later phrase “the first impressions” (τῶν πρώτων φαντασιῶν) supports; “lead the way” keeps it a different word from “first”, as it is in the Greek. It can also mean “leading, principal”. Other reading: than what the principal impressions report
- *ἀναγγέλλουσιν*: The image is of a messenger bringing news. The same verb returns three times (ἤγγελται) and “report” is kept for all of them. Other reading: than what the impressions that lead the way announce
- *ὁ δεῖνά*: The Greek word for an unnamed person, “so-and-so”. Other reading: a certain person
- *τὸ παιδίον*: “The child”, a small child. The article may stand for “my”, which would make the example his own; the English leaves it as the Greek has it. “The child” is repeated in the next sentence, where the Greek leaves the subject unspoken. Other reading: I see that my child is sick.
- *μηδὲν αὐτὸς ἔνδοθεν ἐπίλεγε*: The verb is “say in addition”, to add a comment to what was reported. It is built on the “say” of the first sentence (λέγε) and returns in the last, so “say … further” is used both times. Other reading: and add nothing yourself from within
- *οὐδέν σοι γίνεται*: A present, “nothing happens to you”, kept as a present. It could be heard as “nothing is the matter with you”. Other reading: and nothing comes of it for you
- *μᾶλλον δὲ ἐπίλεγε*: The Greek has only “or rather, say further”. “Something” is supplied, and what is to be said is not spelled out. Other reading: Or rather, do add a comment
- *ὡς γνωρίζων ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ συμβαινόντων*: The participle is “recognising, being acquainted with”, a little more than knowing: he is to speak as someone to whom each thing that happens is familiar. κόσμῳ is the glossary’s “universe”; “the world” would also fit. Other reading: as one who knows each thing that comes about in the world

</details>

### 8.50

A bitter cucumber? Leave it. Brambles in the path? Turn aside. That is enough. Do not go on to say, “And why did these things come to be in the universe at all?” Because you will be laughed at by a person who studies nature, just as you would be laughed at by a carpenter and a shoemaker if you blamed them because you see, in the workshop, shavings and trimmings from the things being made. And yet they, at least, have somewhere to throw these, whereas the nature of the whole has nothing outside it. But the wonderful thing about this craft is that nature, having drawn a boundary around itself, changes into itself everything inside that seems to be decaying and growing old and to be useless, and that it makes other, fresh things again out of these very things, so that it neither needs substance from outside nor has any further need of a place to throw out what is too rotten. So its own space is enough for it, and its own material, and its own craft.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἄφες*: “Let go of it, leave it”: a physical instruction, like “turn aside” in the next line. It can mean dropping the cucumber, throwing it away or simply leaving it alone. Other reading: Throw it away.
- *ἀρκεῖ, μὴ προσεπείπῃς*: ἀρκεῖ (“it is enough”) returns at the end as ἀρκεῖται (“is content with, finds enough in”), so “enough” is used in both places. The verb after it is “say in addition”. Other reading: That will do; do not add,
- *ἀνθρώπου φυσιολόγου*: A φυσιολόγος is one who gives an account of nature, a natural philosopher. The English reads “a person who studies nature” to stay plain. Other reading: by a natural philosopher
- *καταγινώσκων*: “Condemning, finding fault”. The Greek gives no object; the English supplies “them”, the craftsmen, though it could be the workshop or the craft that is blamed. Other reading: if you found fault because you see
- *ξέσματα καὶ περιτμήματα*: The first word is what is scraped or planed off, the carpenter’s waste; the second is what is cut away round the edge, the shoemaker’s. Other reading: scrapings and offcuts
- *ἔξω οὐδὲν ἔχει*: Either “has nothing outside itself”, there being nothing beyond it, or “has no outside place” to throw things. The two come to much the same; the English leans to the first. Other reading: has no outside at all
- *περιορίσασα ἑαυτὴν*: Literally “having marked a boundary round itself”, that is, having confined itself to itself. “Nature” and “craft” are both feminine in Greek, so the form alone does not say which does this; the run of the sentence and the last line, where nature is content with its own craft, show that nature is meant, and the English names it. Other reading: having limited itself to itself
- *οὐσίας*: οὐσία here is the stuff things are made of. The English reads “substance” to keep it apart from ὕλῃ (“material”) in the last sentence, though the two seem to mean the same thing here. Other reading: needs no matter from outside
- *τὰ σαπρότερα*: A comparative: “the more rotten things”, or “the things that are too far gone”. The English takes the second. Other reading: the more rotten parts

</details>

### 8.51a

Not to be slovenly in actions, not to make a muddle in dealings with people, not to wander in impressions, not to shrink together or leap out in the soul at all, not to be without leisure in life.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐπισύρειν*: The whole passage is a string of infinitives used as instructions, with no “you”; it is kept impersonal. This verb is literally to drag or trail, and so to do a thing in a careless, trailing way. Other reading: Not to drag in actions
- *ἐν ταῖς ὁμιλίαις φύρειν*: φύρω is to mix up or knead together, and so to confuse. ὁμιλίαι can be conversations or dealings with people generally; the English takes the wider sense, which includes talk. Other reading: not to be confused in conversation
- *ἀλᾶσθαι*: To wander or rove. The Greek says “in impressions” (φαντασίαι), not “in thoughts”. Other reading: not to stray among impressions
- *καθάπαξ*: “Once for all”, and with a negative “not at all”. It is taken with both verbs that follow. Other reading: nor, in a word, to shrink together or leap out in the soul
- *συνέλκεσθαι ἢ ἐκθόρνυσθαι*: Literally “to be drawn together or to leap out”: the soul contracting (as in grief or fear) and bursting out (as in elation or anger). Both are kept as bodily images. Other reading: to be cast down or carried away
- *ἀσχολεῖσθαι*: ἀσχολία is the lack of leisure, being taken up with business. Other reading: not to be all business in life

</details>

### 8.51b

They kill, they cut up like meat, they hound with curses. What, then, is that to the mind staying clean, sane, self-controlled, just? It is as if someone stood beside a clear, sweet spring and insulted it, yet it does not stop welling up with water fit to drink; even if they throw in mud, even if dung, it will very quickly scatter these and wash them out, and will in no way be stained. How, then, will you have an ever-flowing spring and not a well? If you guard yourself at every hour so as to be free, and with that to act kindly, simply and modestly.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Κτείνουσι, κρεανομοῦσι, κατάραις ἐλαύνουσι*: Three verbs with no subject and no object: “they” are unnamed, and the Greek does not say whom they kill. Nothing is added. Other reading: They kill you, cut you to pieces, drive you out with curses.
- *κρεανομοῦσι*: Literally “they divide up as meat”, the word for portioning a carcass. The meat is kept. Other reading: they butcher
- *τί οὖν ταῦτα πρὸς τὸ*: Literally “what, then, are these things towards the mind’s remaining”: what bearing do they have on it. Other reading: How does that stop the mind from staying
- *διάνοιαν*: “Mind” rather than the glossary’s “thought”, because the faculty is meant and νοῦς does not occur here. Other reading: to your thought staying clean
- *φρενήρη, σώφρονα*: φρενήρης is “sound in mind”; σώφρων is the virtue of self-control or moderation. Other reading: sound, temperate
- *οἷον εἴ τις*: The comparison has no main clause of its own (“as if someone …”), and the construction then passes to plain statements about the spring. “It is” is supplied. Other reading: As if someone standing by a clear, sweet spring were to abuse it
- *βλασφημοίη αὐτήν*: βλασφημέω is abuse in words. “Insulted” makes that plain and keeps it apart from the “curses” of the first sentence, which are another Greek word. Other reading: and cursed it
- *βαφήσεται*: Literally “will be dyed”: take the colour of what is thrown in. Other reading: will in no way be dyed
- *φρέαρ*: A dug well or cistern of standing water, as against a spring that flows of itself. Other reading: and not a cistern
- *ἂν φυλάσσῃς σεαυτὸν πάσης ὥρας εἰς ἐλευθερίαν*: As given: “if you guard yourself at every hour for freedom”, the εἰς being the end you are guarded for; the English reads “so as to be free”. From memory, unchecked: the verb has been doubted and another verb (“grow”) proposed. Other reading: If at every hour you grow into freedom
- *μετὰ τοῦ εὐμενῶς καὶ ἁπλῶς καὶ αἰδημόνως*: Literally “together with the kindly and simply and modestly”, three adverbs under one article, with no verb. “To act” is supplied to carry them, and “with that” gives “together with”: the three go along with the freedom. Other reading: for freedom, together with kindness, simplicity and modesty

</details>

### 8.52–53

Whoever does not know what the universe is does not know where they are. Whoever does not know what it is by nature for does not know who they are, nor what the universe is. And whoever is missing any one of these could not even say what they themselves are by nature for. What, then, does a person seem to you to be who runs from the praise of those who clap, or chases it, people who know neither where they are nor who they are?

Do you want to be praised by a person who curses themselves three times an hour? Do you want to please a person who is not pleased with themselves? Is a person pleased with themselves who regrets nearly everything they do?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὅ τι ἐστὶ κόσμος*: The noun has no article here or below: “what a universe is”. The word also means order. The English keeps the glossary’s “the universe”. Other reading: what a universe is
- *ὁ δὲ μὴ εἰδὼς πρὸς ὅ τι πέφυκεν*: The subject of the last verb is not stated. It can be the universe just named or the person. The English takes the universe, because the next sentence adds an emphatic “they themselves” to the same verb, which reads as a contrast with a different subject here. Other reading: Whoever does not know what they are by nature for
- *πέφυκεν*: Literally “has grown” or “is by nature”, with a preposition of aim: what a thing’s nature fits it for. No maker is named. Other reading: what it has come to be for
- *ἕν τι τούτων ἀπολιπὼν*: The participle can mean having left out, or falling short in. “These” are the points of knowledge just listed. Other reading: whoever has left out any one of these
- *εἴποι*: An optative with no particle, where “could say” would normally have one. The English reads it as “could say”. Other reading: may they not even say what they themselves are by nature for
- *ὁ τὸν τῶν κροτούντων ἔπαινον φεύγων ἢ διώκων*: Literally “the one fleeing or pursuing the praise of the clappers”. The verb for clapping is used of applause and of any rattling noise. Running from praise is odd beside chasing it, but that is what the Greek as given says; from memory, unchecked: the words have been suspected, with blame as the thing fled. Other reading: who runs from the blame of those who clap, or chases their praise
- *τρὶς τῆς ὥρας*: Literally “three times in the hour”. The noun can also mean a season or a moment. Other reading: three times every hour
- *ἀρέσκειν θέλεις ἀνθρώπῳ ὃς οὐκ ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ; ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ*: One verb, “please”, three times: please a person who does not please themselves. English “please oneself” means to do as one likes, so the English reads “is pleased with themselves” and keeps the root. Other reading: Do you want to please a person who does not satisfy themselves?
- *μετανοῶν*: To change one’s mind afterwards, to regret. Other reading: who repents of nearly everything they do

</details>

### 8.54

No longer only to breathe together with the surrounding air, but from now on also to think together with the mind that surrounds all things. For the power of mind is poured out everywhere and has spread all through, for the one able to draw it in, no less than the power of air for the one able to breathe it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μηκέτι μόνον συμπνεῖν*: The Greek uses bare infinitives as a rule set down for himself, with no “you”. The infinitive is kept and not turned into a command. Other reading: Do not any longer only breathe together
- *συμπνεῖν*: Literally “breathe with”; in ordinary Greek the word also means “be in accord with”, which prepares the second half. Other reading: to be of one breath with
- *συμφρονεῖν*: Built to match “breathe with”: “think with”. Its usual sense is “be of one mind with, agree with”; “think together with” keeps the pairing. Other reading: to be of one mind with
- *τῷ περιέχοντι πάντα νοερῷ*: Literally “the thing of mind that surrounds all things”. περιέχω is “surround” and also “contain, hold”; “surround” is kept to match the air. “Mind” is used for νοερόν here and “power of mind” for the adjective in the next sentence. Other reading: the intelligence that contains all things
- *διαπεφοίτηκε*: “Has gone through and through”: pervaded. The one “everywhere” in the Greek serves both verbs. Other reading: has passed through all things
- *τῷ σπάσαι δυναμένῳ*: σπάω is “draw, pull in”, as one draws breath or a drink. The dative is “for” the one who can. Other reading: for anyone able to take it in
- *ἡ ἀερώδης*: “The airy (power)”: the word “power” is carried over from the first half. Other reading: than the air is

</details>

### 8.55–56

Wickedness in general does no harm to the universe, and wickedness in the particular case does no harm to the other person. It is harmful only to the one who has also been given the power to be rid of it, as soon as they wish to.

To my faculty of choice, my neighbour’s faculty of choice is just as much a matter of indifference as their bit of breath and their bit of flesh. For however true it is that we have come to be for one another’s sake, still each of our ruling parts has its own authority. For otherwise my neighbour’s wickedness would be an evil for me, which god decided against, so that my being unfortunate should not depend on someone else.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Γενικῶς*: The adverb means “as a kind” or “taken generally” and is set against κατὰ μέρος, “in the particular case”. The English takes the first as wickedness taken all together and the second as one person’s particular wickedness. Other reading: Generically, wickedness does no harm to the universe
- *τὸν ἕτερον*: Literally “the other one” of a pair: the person on the receiving end of a particular piece of wickedness. The English keeps it as “the other person”. Other reading: does no harm to anyone else
- *ᾧ ἐπιτέτραπται καὶ ἀπηλλάχθαι αὐτῆς*: The verb is “it has been entrusted” or “it has been permitted”, for which the English has the slightly fuller “has been given the power”. καὶ is “also”: the one person wickedness harms is the same person who can also be free of it. The perfect infinitive suggests being rid of it once and for all. Other reading: to whom it has also been left to be quit of it
- *Τῷ ἐμῷ προαιρετικῷ*: τὸ προαιρετικόν is the part of a person that chooses, a term at home in Epictetus (from memory, unchecked). The glossary has no entry; “faculty of choice” is used for both occurrences. Other reading: To my will
- *ἐπίσης ἀδιάφορόν ἐστιν*: ἀδιάφορον is the Stoic technical term for what is neither good nor bad. The English reads “a matter of indifference”, which keeps the term without suggesting that the neighbour’s faculty of choice does not care. ἐπίσης with the following ὡς καὶ gives “just as much … as”. Other reading: is equally a thing neither good nor bad for it
- *τὸ πνευμάτιον αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ σαρκίδιον*: Both nouns are belittling diminutives of “breath” and “flesh”, kept with “bit of”. The Greek pronoun is masculine singular for the neighbour; the English has “their”. Other reading: his poor breath and his poor flesh
- *τὴν ἰδίαν κυρίαν ἔχει*: κυρίαν here is a noun, “authority” or “mastery”. The subject is plural (“our ruling parts”) with “each” and a singular verb, rendered “has its own authority”. Other reading: each is its own master
- *ἐπεί τοι ἔμελλεν ἡ τοῦ πλησίον κακία ἐμοῦ κακὸν εἶναι*: ἐπεί τοι is “since otherwise”, and the past tense ἔμελλεν says what would have followed if each ruling part did not have its own authority. κακία (“wickedness”) and κακόν (“an evil”) share one root, an echo the English does not carry because “wickedness” is kept for κακία throughout. ἐμοῦ is literally “of mine”; “for me” takes it as an evil that falls on the speaker, as the closing words suggest. Other reading: For otherwise my neighbour’s badness would be something bad of mine
- *ὅπερ οὐκ ἔδοξε τῷ θεῷ*: Literally “which did not seem good to the god”, the ordinary Greek phrase for a decision. The English reads “which god decided against”, since the purpose clause that follows suits a decision that it should not be so. “god” is lower case, as the glossary asks, although the Greek has the article. Other reading: which was not what god decided
- *τὸ ἐμὲ ἀτυχεῖν*: Literally “my being unlucky”; the verb ranges from “to meet misfortune” to “to fail” or “to be unhappy”. The English keeps “being unfortunate”. ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ is “in another’s power”, rendered “depend on someone else”. Other reading: so that my unhappiness should not be in another’s power

</details>

### 8.57

The sun seems to be poured down, and indeed it is poured in every direction, yet it is not poured out. For this pouring is an extension; its beams, at any rate, are called aktines (“rays”) from ekteinesthai (“to be extended”). You could see what a ray is if you watched the sun’s light coming through something narrow into a shaded room. For it extends in a straight line and leans, so to speak, against whatever solid thing it meets that shuts off the air beyond; there it stands, and it does not slip down or fall. So the pouring and spreading of thought should be like that: in no way a pouring out, but an extension. It should not lean on the obstacles it meets with force or like a torrent, nor fall down, but stand and light up whatever receives it. For whatever does not give the beam passage will deprive itself of the beam.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὁ ἥλιος κατακεχύσθαι δοκεῖ*: 'The sun' stands for its light. The verb form can be passive ('be poured down') or reflexive ('pour itself down'), and δοκεῖ can be 'seems' or 'is thought'. Other reading: The sun is thought to pour itself down
- *οὐ μὴν ἐκκέχυται*: 'Poured out' in the sense of spilled away and used up. I kept the same verb 'pour' so the three forms (down, everywhere, out) stay visible. Other reading: yet it does not run out
- *ἡ γὰρ χύσις αὕτη τάσις ἐστίν*: τάσις is stretching, extension or tension, a term of Stoic physics. “Extension” is used because the next clause derives “ray” from the verb “to be extended”. Other reading: For this pouring is a stretching
- *ἀκτῖνες γοῦν αἱ αὐγαὶ αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐκτείνεσθαι λέγονται*: Marcus derives the word for rays (aktines) from the verb “to be extended” (ekteinesthai) because they sound alike. The Greek words are given in Latin letters so the claim still makes sense in English.
- *ἐσκιασμένον οἶκον*: Literally a “shaded” house or room. Other reading: a darkened house
- *ὥσπερ διερείδεται*: The verb means to lean on or brace oneself against something; ὥσπερ (“so to speak”) marks it as a figure. The text of this word has been doubted, and another reading gives “is divided”; that doubt was not checked against a critical edition’s notes. Other reading: and presses, so to speak, against
- *διεῖργον τὸν ἐπέκεινα ἀέρα*: The participle goes with the solid thing: it bars the way to the air on the far side. It could also be taken as the solid thing marking off the air beyond. Other reading: that separates off the air beyond
- *ἐνταῦθα δὲ ἔστη καὶ οὐ κατώλισθεν οὐδὲ ἔπεσε*: The Greek verbs are past tense, either a general truth or the moment of watching. I used the English present. Other reading: there it has stopped, and it did not slip down or fall
- *τῆς διανοίας*: The word covers thought, thinking and the mind. Other reading: of the mind
- *μὴ βίαιον μηδὲ ῥαγδαίαν τὴν ἐπέρεισιν ποιεῖσθαι*: The noun for leaning picks up the verb used of the sunbeam; the second adjective is the one used of a driving storm. No subject is stated: it may be thought or a general “one”. Other reading: one should not make the contact forced or violent
- *αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑαυτὸ στερήσει τῆς αὐγῆς τὸ μὴ παραπέμπον αὐτήν*: The last verb means to escort, convey or let pass. The sense is open: the thing that does not let the beam through, or the thing that does not take it in, as against “whatever receives it” just before. Other reading: For whatever does not take the beam in will deprive itself of it
- *τὴν χύσιν καὶ διάχυσιν*: Both nouns, and the “pouring out” after them, are built on one root. English cannot keep that without strain. Other reading: the pouring and wide pouring

</details>

### 8.58

Whoever fears death fears either the absence of sensation or sensation of another kind. But if you no longer have sensation, you will have no sensation of anything bad either; and if you acquire a rather different kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of living thing, and you will not stop living.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀναισθησίαν φοβεῖται ἢ αἴσθησιν ἑτεροίαν*: αἴσθησις is “sensation, perception, feeling”. “Sensation” is kept for every form, including the verb αἰσθήσῃ (“you will have no sensation of”), so that the argument can be followed. Other reading: fears either not feeling or feeling in a different way
- *εἴτε οὐκέτι αἴσθησιν*: The clause as given has no verb: the accusative needs “you have”, understood from κτήσῃ in the next clause (from memory, unchecked, editors supply a verb here). The Greek also moves here from “whoever” to “you”, which is kept. Other reading: if it is sensation no longer
- *ἀλλοιοτέραν αἴσθησιν κτήσῃ, ἀλλοῖον ζῷον ἔσῃ*: ἀλλοιοτέραν is a comparative, “rather different” or “more different”. ζῷον (“living thing”, also “animal”) is echoed by ζῆν (“living”), and the echo is kept. Other reading: if you get an altered sensation, you will be an altered creature

</details>

### 8.59

Human beings have come into being for one another’s sake. So either teach them or bear with them.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *γεγόνασιν ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν*: The same thought and nearly the same wording as in 11.18, and it is rendered the same way. Other reading: People exist for the sake of one another
- *ἢ δίδασκε οὖν ἢ φέρε*: The two commands have no object in the Greek; the English adds “them” and “with them”. φέρω is to carry, to endure. Other reading: So either teach or endure

</details>

### 8.60

An arrow travels in one way, the mind in another. Yet the mind, both when it is being cautious and when it turns about in considering something, travels straight none the less, and toward what is set before it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἄλλως βέλος, ἄλλως νοῦς φέρεται*: βέλος is any missile, an arrow or a javelin. φέρεται, “is carried, travels”, is the same verb in both sentences, and “travels” is kept for it. Other reading: A missile is carried one way, the mind another.
- *εὐλαβῆται*: To be cautious, to take care; εὐλάβεια is the Stoic word for reasonable caution. Other reading: when it is on its guard
- *περὶ τὴν σκέψιν στρέφηται*: Literally “turns about around the inquiry”. The turning is set against the straight line that follows, so “turns” is kept. Other reading: when it is occupied with an inquiry
- *οὐδὲν ἧττον*: “No less”: either “none the less” (in spite of the caution and the turning) or “no less than the arrow”. The English takes the first. Other reading: travels straight no less than the arrow does
- *ἐπὶ τὸ προκείμενον*: What lies before it: its target, or the matter in hand. Other reading: to its mark

</details>

### 8.61

To enter into each person’s ruling part, and also to allow every other person to enter into one’s own ruling part.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Εἰσιέναι*: An infinitive used as a note of what is to be done, with no person. The reflexive later is third person, so the English stays impersonal with “one’s own”. Other reading: Enter into each person’s ruling part, and let every other person enter into yours
- *παρέχειν*: To offer or to allow: either holding oneself open or simply not preventing. Other reading: to offer every other person entry
- *ἑκάστου*: “Of each”, with no noun: each person one deals with. Other reading: of everyone

</details>

## Book 9

### 9.1

Whoever does injustice is impious. For since the nature of the whole has made rational animals for the sake of one another, to help one another as each deserves and in no way to harm one another, whoever goes against its will is clearly impious towards the eldest of the gods. And whoever says what is false is also impious, towards the same goddess. For the nature of the whole is the nature of the things that are, and the things that are stand in close kinship to all that is the case. Further, this nature is also named Truth, and it is the first cause of all things that are true. So whoever says what is false willingly is impious in so far as they do injustice by deceiving; and whoever does so unwillingly, in so far as they are out of tune with the nature of the whole, and in so far as they are disorderly, fighting against the nature of the universe. For whoever is carried by their own doing towards what is opposite to the things that are true is fighting; for they had received starting points from nature beforehand, and by neglecting them they are now unable to tell false things from true. And again, whoever pursues pleasures as goods and runs from pains as evils is impious. For such a person must often find fault with the common nature, as allotting something to the worthless and the worthy against what they deserve, because often the worthless live among pleasures and get the things that produce them, while the worthy fall into pain and the things that produce it. Further, whoever fears pains will at some time also fear something that is going to be in the universe, and that is already impious. And whoever pursues pleasures will not hold back from doing injustice, and that is plainly impious. Now towards the things to which the common nature is equally disposed (for it would not make both if it were not equally disposed to both), those who want to follow nature, being of one mind with it, must also be equally disposed. So whoever is not, for their own part, equally disposed towards pain and pleasure, or death and life, or good repute and ill repute, which the nature of the whole uses equally, is clearly impious. When I say that the common nature uses these equally, I mean that they happen equally, in sequence, to the things that come to be and the things that come after them, by a certain original impulse of providence, by which from a certain origin it set its impulse towards this ordering of the universe, having conceived certain principles of the things that were to be and marked off powers to generate such existences, changes and successions.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὁ ἀδικῶν ἀσεβεῖ*: The first verb is “to do wrong”, from the root of “justice”; the second is “to fail in reverence towards the gods”. “Does injustice” and “is impious” are kept throughout so the chain of the argument shows. Other reading: The wrongdoer sins against the gods
- *ὠφελεῖν μὲν ἄλληλα κατ’ ἀξίαν*: Literally “according to worth”. The opposite phrase, “against worth”, comes later in the passage, and the two are rendered to match. Other reading: to benefit one another according to worth
- *εἰς τὴν πρεσβυτάτην τῶν θεῶν*: “Eldest” also means most to be honoured. The word for nature is feminine in Greek, which is why the next sentence calls her a goddess. Other reading: towards the most venerable of the gods
- *ὁ ψευδόμενος*: The verb covers both lying and saying what is false without meaning to. Since Marcus goes on to an unwilling case, “says what is false” is used. Other reading: And the liar is also impious
- *τὰ δέ γε ὄντα πρὸς τὰ ὑπάρχοντα πάντα οἰκείως ἔχει*: An obscure sentence. The second participle can mean “the things that exist”, which is hard to tell apart from “the things that are”, or “the things that are the case”, a sense the Stoics use of what is truly so. The second is taken, because the sentence is given as the ground for calling false speech impious; the point of the kinship is not stated. Other reading: and the things that are stand in close kinship to all the things that exist
- *ἀκοσμεῖ μαχόμενος τῇ τοῦ κόσμου φύσει*: A play on words: the verb “is disorderly” is built on the word kosmos, which means both “order” and “the universe”. English cannot keep the play without adding a word. The verb before it, “out of tune”, is a musical word for disagreeing. Other reading: in so far as they break order, fighting against the nature of the world-order
- *φερόμενος παρ’ ἑαυτόν*: The last two words can mean “through himself, by his own fault” or “contrary to himself”. The first is taken, which the next clause about neglect supports. Other reading: whoever is carried, against themselves, towards what is opposite to the things that are true
- *ἀφορμὰς*: Literally “starting points”, also “means, resources”: what nature gives one to begin from. Other reading: for they had received the means from nature beforehand
- *τοὺς δὲ πόνους*: The word covers pain and toil. Set against pleasure here, it is “pain”, as in 6.33. Other reading: and runs from hardships as evils
- *τοῖς φαύλοις καὶ τοῖς σπουδαίοις*: The Stoic pair for people of no worth and people of real worth. They are not the words used for bad and good things elsewhere in the passage, so “the worthless” and “the worthy” keep the two pairs apart. Other reading: to the bad and the good
- *ἐπίσης ἔχει*: Literally “holds itself equally”. The adverb “equally” comes seven times in the passage and carries the argument, so one word is kept for it. Other reading: the things towards which the common nature is indifferent
- *ἀντὶ τοῦ συμβαίνειν ἐπίσης κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τοῖς γινομένοις καὶ ἐπιγινομένοις*: Literally “I say X in place of Y”, that is, “by X I mean Y”. The datives may be things or people: those that come to be and those that follow them. Other reading: I mean that they befall equally, one after another, those who are born and those who are born after them
- *ὁρμῇ τινι ἀρχαίᾳ τῆς προνοίας*: The adjective means “ancient” and “belonging to the beginning”, and the noun “beginning” follows in the next clause; “original” and “origin” show that pair, as “impulse” twice shows the noun and its verb. The subject of the verb is not stated: providence or the common nature. Other reading: by a certain ancient impulse of providence, by which from some beginning it set out towards this ordering
- *ἐπὶ τήνδε τὴν διακόσμησιν*: The noun is one word, “the setting in order”, built on kosmos. “Of the universe” spells out what the word contains. Other reading: towards this present arrangement of things
- *συλλαβοῦσά τινας λόγους τῶν ἐσομένων*: The participle means “having gathered together” and also “having conceived” as a womb does; with “powers to generate” following, “conceived” is taken. The noun is elsewhere “reason”; in the plural here it is the Stoic term for the rational principles, like seeds, from which things unfold, so “principles” is used. Other reading: having gathered together certain reasons for the things that were to be
- *δυνάμεις γονίμους ἀφορίσασα ὑποστάσεών τε καὶ μεταβολῶν καὶ διαδοχῶν τοιούτων*: Literally “having marked off fertile powers of such comings-to-exist, changes and successions”. The first genitive can mean things that exist or their coming into existence. Other reading: and set apart fertile powers of such substances, changes and successions

</details>

### 9.2

It would have been the mark of a finer man to go from among people without having tasted lying, or any pretence or luxury or vanity. But at any rate to breathe one’s last having at least grown sick of these things is the next best course. Or have you chosen to stay sitting beside vice, and does not even experience yet persuade you to flee from the plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague, far more so than any such unhealthy mixture and change of this air that is poured around. For the latter is a plague of living creatures, in so far as they are living creatures; the former is a plague of human beings, in so far as they are human beings.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Χαριεστέρου μὲν ἦν ἀνδρός*: The past tense without ἄν says what would have been right but did not happen. χαριέστερος is “more graceful, more accomplished”, here “finer”. ἀνδρός is the word for a man, so “man” is kept. Other reading: It was the part of a more accomplished man
- *πάσης ὑποκρίσεως καὶ τρυφῆς καὶ τύφου*: πάσης (“all”) agrees with ὑποκρίσεως and may run on to the nouns after it. “Any” stands for it because of the negative, and is placed so that its reach is as open in the English as in the Greek. τῦφος is literally smoke and is used of puffed-up self-importance, here “vanity”. Other reading: or pretence of any kind, or luxury, or conceit
- *κορεσθέντα γε τούτων ἀποπνεῦσαι*: κορεσθέντα is “sated, glutted”: having had so much of these things as to be sick of them, which “grown sick of” says without suggesting that they were enjoyed. ἀποπνεῦσαι is “to breathe out”, that is, to die. The Greek is impersonal here, so “one’s”. Other reading: to breathe one’s last at least sated with them
- *δεύτερος πλοῦς*: A proverb, literally “second sailing”: the next best way when the best is closed. From memory, unchecked, it was explained as taking to the oars when the wind fails. “Course” gives the sense and keeps a trace of the sailing. Other reading: the second sailing
- *προσκαθῆσθαι τῇ κακίᾳ*: The verb is “to sit beside, to stay settled by”, and is also used of an army sitting before a town. κακία is “vice” or “badness”. Other reading: to settle down with badness
- *πεῖρα πείθει*: The two words chime in the Greek (peira peithei). The English does not reproduce the sound. Other reading: trial persuades
- *διαφθορὰ διανοίας*: The glossary gives “thought” for διάνοια and “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty that is ruined, so “mind”. Other reading: the ruin of thought
- *ἡ τοῦ περικεχυμένου τούτου πνεύματος τοιάδε τις δυσκρασία καὶ τροπή*: πνεῦμα is “breath” or “air”, and the Greek says “poured around” without saying around whom. δυσκρασία is a bad mixture, the medical word for an unhealthy state, here of the air; τροπή is a turn or change. From memory, unchecked, there was a real epidemic in Marcus’s reign. Other reading: some such distemper and alteration of this surrounding breath
- *αὕτη μὲν γὰρ ζῴων λοιμός*: αὕτη points to the nearer thing, the plague of the air, and ἐκείνη to the farther, the corruption of the mind. “The latter” and “the former” keep the pointing without adding words. Other reading: For the plague of the air is a plague of animals as animals; the plague of the mind is a plague of human beings as human beings

</details>

### 9.3

Do not despise death, but be well pleased with it, since this too is one of the things nature wills. For as it is with being young and growing old, with growing and reaching one’s prime, with getting teeth and a beard and grey hair, with begetting and carrying a child and giving birth, and with all the other natural activities that the seasons of life bring, so it is with being dissolved. This, then, is what fits a human being who has reasoned it out: not to be offhand toward death, nor violent, nor disdainful, but to wait for it as one of the natural activities; and, as you now wait for the time when the unborn child will come out of your wife’s womb, in the same way to await the hour in which your little soul will drop out of this husk. But if you also want a layman’s rule that touches the heart, what will most put you at ease about death is to stop and look at the things you are about to leave, and [at what kind of] characters [your soul] will no longer be mixed up with. For there must be no taking offence at them at all; rather one must even care for them and bear with them gently, yet remember that the release will not be from people who hold the same principles as you. For this alone, if anything at all, would pull one back and hold one in life: if one were allowed to live together with those who have made the same principles their own. But as it is you see how much weariness there is in the discord of living together, so that one says: “Come sooner, death, in case I too should perhaps forget myself.”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μὴ καταφρόνει θανάτου*: καταφρονεῖν runs from “despise” to “think little of, make light of”. In 12.34 the same attitude is spoken of with approval, so “despise” is used in both places and the tension is left visible. Other reading: Do not make light of death
- *κατὰ ἄνθρωπόν ἐστι λελογισμένον*: λελογισμένον can agree with ἄνθρωπον (“a human being who has reasoned”) or be neuter with τοῦτο (“this is a thing reasoned out”). The English takes it with the human being; “it” is added. Other reading: This, then, is the considered course that fits a human being
- *μὴ ὁλοσχερῶς μηδὲ ὠστικῶς μηδὲ ὑπερηφάνως*: Three adverbs with a range. ὁλοσχερῶς is “in the gross, summarily”, so carelessly; ὠστικῶς is “in a pushing way”, which could mean pushing toward death or shoving it away, and “violent” leaves that open; ὑπερηφάνως is “haughtily”. Other reading: not carelessly, nor impatiently, nor arrogantly
- *πότε ἔμβρυον ἐκ τῆς γαστρὸς τῆς γυναικός σου ἐξέλθῃ*: γυνή is “woman” or “wife”; with σου the English reads “your wife”. The words “as you now wait” read like a real circumstance of the writer, but they could be a general illustration. Other reading: when the child will come out of your woman’s belly
- *τοῦ ἐλύτρου τούτου*: ἔλυτρον is any case or covering (a pod, a shell, a sheath). After the comparison with birth it may suggest the membrane round an unborn child; the English reads “husk”. ψυχάριον just before is a diminutive, kept as “little soul”. Other reading: out of this sheath
- *ἰδιωτικὸν παράπηγμα ἁψικάρδιον*: παράπηγμα is literally a peg-board calendar or table, and so a rule to steer by. ἰδιωτικόν is “of the layman”, that is, not a philosopher’s argument. ἁψικάρδιον is “that takes hold of the heart”. Other reading: an unphilosophical maxim that grips the heart
- *ἡ ἐπίστασις ἡ ἐπὶ τὰ ὑποκείμενα*: ἐπίστασις is a stopping to attend. τὰ ὑποκείμενα is “the things lying before you”, the objects or circumstances of your life; whether this covers only things or people as well is open, and the English keeps it general. Other reading: close attention to the objects before you
- *ἠθῶν οὐκέτι ἔσται ἡ*: The Greek as given does not construe: the edition marks a gap after ἡ where a feminine noun is missing, and there is no relative word before ἠθῶν. The words in square brackets are supplied; from memory, unchecked, editors read a relative (“what kind of”) here and supply “soul”. ἐμπεφυρμένη is “kneaded in with” and can imply being soiled. Other reading: and with characters the … will no longer be mixed up
- *ἀλλὰ καὶ κήδεσθαι καὶ πρᾴως φέρειν*: καί before κήδεσθαι is read as “even”. It can also be the first half of “both … and” with the καί that follows. δεῖ (“must”) governs the whole sentence. Other reading: but both care for them and bear with them gently
- *εἴπερ ἄρα*: A hedge: “if anything at all (would)”. The two verbs that follow have no object in the Greek; the impersonal “one” is supplied. Other reading: For this alone, if indeed anything, could have drawn you back and kept you in life
- *ἐν τῇ διαφωνίᾳ τῆς συμβιώσεως*: διαφωνία is literally being out of tune, discord. It answers ὁμοδογματούντων, people whose principles sound together with yours, so the musical word is kept. συμβίωσις is “living together”, echoing συζῆν in the sentence before. Other reading: in the disagreement of those you live with
- *μή που καὶ αὐτὸς ἐπιλάθωμαι ἐμαυτοῦ*: To forget oneself here is to lose hold of what one is and of one’s principles. καὶ αὐτός (“too”) implies that the others have already done so, and που adds “perhaps”. Other reading: before I too lose sight of what I am

</details>

### 9.4–5

Whoever does wrong does wrong at their own cost. Whoever acts unjustly does injustice to themselves, making themselves bad.

Often the one who does not do something acts unjustly, not only the one who does something.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἑαυτῷ ἁμαρτάνει*: The dative can mean “for themselves, to their own cost” or “against themselves”. The English takes the first, the more natural force of a bare dative, which also keeps this clause apart from the next, where the Greek has the accusative and the person is the one wronged. Other reading: Whoever does wrong does wrong against themselves
- *ὁ ἀδικῶν ἑαυτὸν ἀδικεῖ*: A different verb from the first clause: ἁμαρτάνω is “do wrong, go wrong”, ἀδικέω is “act unjustly, do injustice to”. The two are kept apart in English, here and in chapter 5. Other reading: Whoever wrongs another wrongs themselves
- *ἑαυτὸν, ἑαυτὸν κακὸν ποιῶν*: The Greek as given has ἑαυτὸν twice with a comma between. The first has a grave accent directly before the comma, where this copy otherwise has an acute before a stop, so it is read as an accidental doubling and translated once. From memory, unchecked: editions print the word once here, and some read a verb “makes bad” instead of “making bad”. Other reading: does injustice to themselves, themselves, by making themselves bad
- *ὁ μὴ ποιῶν τι*: τι can be “something” (a particular thing left undone) or, after the negative, “anything”. The parallel with ὁ ποιῶν τι, “the one who does something”, decides for “something”. Other reading: the one who does nothing

</details>

### 9.6

It is enough that the present judgment should have a firm grasp of what is there, that the present action should be social, and that the present disposition should be well pleased with everything that happens from the external cause.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἀρκεῖ*: The Greek has no “that” or “if”: three nouns, each with an adjective as predicate, are the subject of “is enough”. “That … should” is used so as neither to assert that the three are already so nor to add a bare “if”. Other reading: It is enough if the present judgment has a firm grasp of what is there, the present action is social, and the present disposition is well pleased
- *ἡ παροῦσα*: Said three times: the one that is here now. “The present” is kept each time, and “your”, which the Greek does not have, is not added. Other reading: your judgment at this moment
- *καταληπτικὴ*: A Stoic term, from the word for a grasp: said of an impression or judgment that takes hold of the thing as it really is, and so is sure. “Firm” gives the sureness, and “of what is there” is added to complete the English. Other reading: a present judgment that is certain; a present judgment that grasps its object
- *κοινωνικὴ*: κοινωνικός is “social” throughout this translation: directed to the community of human beings, done for the common good. It does not mean sociable. Other reading: the present action be for the common good
- *εὐαρεστικὴ πρὸς*: An adjective for a settled readiness to be pleased with something. The English must choose how warm it is, and reads “well pleased with”. Other reading: content with; ready to accept
- *τῆς ἐκτὸς αἰτίας*: Singular with the article: the one cause that lies outside, as against what one causes oneself. It is kept singular, and “you” is not added. Other reading: from external causes; from a cause outside you

</details>

### 9.7

To wipe out an impression. To stop an impulse. To quench desire. To keep the ruling part in one’s own power.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐξαλεῖψαι φαντασίαν*: The four phrases are infinitives used as instructions, with no “you”; they are kept impersonal. The Greek nouns have no article; English needs one for “impression” and “impulse”, and can do without for “desire”. Other reading: Wipe out the impression.
- *σβέσαι ὄρεξιν*: The verb is to put out a fire. ὄρεξις is desire, the reaching for a thing. Other reading: To extinguish appetite.
- *ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ ἔχειν τὸ ἡγεμονικόν*: The reflexive can point to the unnamed person (“in one’s own power”) or to the ruling part (“in its own power”). It is taken of the person, the one who is to do the keeping, which is the regular use of the word. Other reading: To keep the ruling part in its own power.

</details>

### 9.8–9

One soul has been divided among the animals without reason, and one soul that has mind has been portioned out among the rational ones, just as there is one earth for all earthy things, and we see by one light and breathe one air, all of us that have sight and a soul.

All things that share in something common hurry toward what is of their own kind. Everything earthy tends toward earth. Everything wet flows together. What is airy does the same, so that it takes things to hold them apart, and force. Fire is carried upward because of the elemental fire, yet it is so ready to be kindled together with every fire here that even everything material that is a little drier is easy to kindle, because less of what hinders kindling is mixed into it. So too, then, everything that shares in a common nature of mind hurries toward its kin in the same way, or even more. For the better it is compared with the rest, the readier it is to mix with what is its own and to be poured together with it. At any rate, right from the start, among the animals without reason there were found swarms and herds and the rearing of nestlings and what one might call loves; for here there were already souls, and the thing that draws together was found growing stronger in what is better, of a kind that did not exist in plants, or in stones or timber. Among the rational animals there were states and friendships and households and gatherings, and in wars treaties and truces. Among those better still, even out of things that stand apart there came to be, in a way, a union, such as there is among the stars. In this way the climb toward the better was able to produce a shared feeling even in things that stand apart. See, then, what is happening now. For only the beings that have mind have now forgotten their hurrying toward one another and their leaning together, and only here is the flowing together not to be seen. And yet, though they run away, they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same; for nature prevails. You will see what I mean if you watch closely. At any rate, one would sooner find something earthy touching nothing earthy than a human being split off from a human being.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *μία νοερὰ ψυχὴ μεμέρισται*: νοερός is “of mind, able to think”. “Mind” is kept as the one word for it through the passage (“one soul that has mind”, “a common nature of mind”, “the beings that have mind”) so the chain can be followed. The verb differs from “divided” in the first clause and has a different English verb. Other reading: one thinking soul has been shared out
- *ὅσα ὁρατικὰ καὶ ἔμψυχα*: A neuter plural (“whatever things can see and have soul in them”) attached to verbs in “we”. ἔμψυχα is literally “ensouled”, in ordinary Greek simply “alive”; “soul” is kept because the sentence is about soul. Other reading: all of us creatures that can see and are alive
- *πρὸς τὸ ὁμογενὲς σπεύδει*: σπεύδω is “hurry, press eagerly toward”, and also “strive”. “Hurry” is used for the verb both times and “hurrying” for the noun σπουδή near the end, since the argument turns on the repetition. Other reading: strive toward what is of their own kind
- *ῥέπει*: The word for a scale pan going down: to incline, to tend. “Tends” is used so that “leaning” can be kept for a different word near the end. Other reading: Everything earthy sinks toward earth
- *ὥστε χρῄζειν τῶν διειργόντων καὶ βίας*: The Greek has no subject: “so that there is need of things that keep apart, and of force”. The clause may cover the wet as well as the airy. Other reading: so that barriers and force are needed
- *διὰ τὸ στοιχειῶδες πῦρ*: Literally “because of the elemental fire”. It is taken as the pure fire of the upper region, toward which fire down here rises; the words could also name the fiery element within the flame itself. Other reading: because of the element of fire in it
- *συνεξάπτεσθαι*: Three words in this sentence are made from one verb for setting alight. “Kindle” is used for all three. Other reading: to catch light together
- *πᾶν τὸ ὑλικὸν*: ὑλικός is “material, made of matter”, but ὕλη is also the ordinary word for wood and fuel, and that sense is close to the surface here. “Even” is taken with the whole phrase: not only fire itself but anything material. Other reading: even all fuel that is a little drier
- *ὅσῳ γάρ ἐστι κρεῖττον παρὰ τὰ ἄλλα*: κρείττων is “better”, also “stronger” or “superior”. The word returns four times as the rungs of a ladder; “better” is kept each time and not “higher”, since the Greek has no image of height until the “climb” later on. Other reading: For the higher it stands above the rest
- *εὐθὺς γοῦν*: εὐθύς is “straight away” and can mark the first moment in time or the first case in a list; the past tenses that follow tell the ladder of beings as if it were a history. “Right from the start” leaves both senses possible. γοῦν, “at any rate”, brings in the evidence, as it does again in the last sentence. Other reading: To begin with, at any rate,
- *ἐκ διεστηκότων*: A school term: wholes made of members that stand physically apart, as opposed to one continuous body. The same word comes back as διεστῶσιν in the next sentence; “things that stand apart” is used for both. Other reading: even out of separated things
- *τρόπον τινὰ*: “In a way” stands between “things that stand apart” and “union” and could soften either. It is taken with the union. Other reading: even out of things that in a way stand apart there came to be a union
- *συμπάθειαν*: A Stoic term for parts of the universe being affected together, as if by one feeling. The English word “sympathy” now means pity, so the English reads “a shared feeling”. Other reading: sympathy
- *τὸ σύρρουν ὧδε μόνον οὐ βλέπεται*: μόνον is taken with ὧδε: “here alone it is not seen”. μόνον οὐ can also be an idiom for “all but”, but “is all but seen” gives no sense here. “The flowing together” repeats the word used of water above. Other reading: and in this one case the running together is not seen
- *φεύγοντες περικαταλαμβάνονται*: The participle turns masculine: the neuter “beings that have mind” have become people. The verb is one word, “overtake and surround”; the English needs two. Other reading: though they flee, they are caught all the same

</details>

### 9.10

A human being bears fruit, and so does god, and so does the universe; each bears it in its own seasons. But if usage has made the phrase well worn, in its strict sense, for the vine and things like it, that makes no difference. And reason has fruit, both shared and its own, and from it come other things of much the same kind as reason itself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *καὶ θεὸς*: No article: “god” or “a god”. The English reads “god” with a small letter and no article. Other reading: and so does a god
- *ἡ συνήθεια κυρίως τέτριφεν*: The verb is the one for rubbing a thing smooth by use, and of words it means making them well worn, current. The Greek gives it no object; the English supplies “the phrase”, that is, “bear fruit”. κυρίως is taken as “in the proper, strict sense”; it can also mean “chiefly”. Other reading: But if usage has chiefly worn the phrase in on the vine and things like it
- *οὐδὲν τοῦτο*: Literally “this is nothing”. Other reading: that is nothing
- *ὁ λόγος δὲ*: λόγος is “reason” but also “speech, word, account”. The English takes “reason”, as the thing that bears fruit in a human being; the sentence may also glance at “speech” after the remark on usage. Other reading: And speech has fruit
- *καὶ κοινὸν καὶ ἴδιον καρπὸν*: “Fruit both common and private”: fruit shared with everyone and fruit that belongs to reason itself. The Greek does not say more. Other reading: fruit both for all in common and for itself
- *τοιαῦθ’ ἕτερα, ὁποῖόν τι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ λόγος*: “Other things of some such kind as reason itself is”: what reason produces is like reason, as fruit is like the plant. The small word τι loosens the likeness a little, which “much the same” gives. Other reading: and what grows from it is more of the same sort of thing as reason itself

</details>

### 9.11

If you can, teach them otherwise; and if not, remember that kindness has been given to you for this. The gods too are kind to such people, and toward some things they even work with them, toward health, toward wealth, toward reputation: so good are they. You may be so too; or tell me, who is stopping you?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *μεταδίδασκε*: The Greek has no object; the English adds “them”. The verb is to teach someone into a different view, as in 9.42. Other reading: If you can, show the better way
- *τοῖς τοιούτοις*: “Such people” are not named: those who go wrong and cannot be taught. Other reading: to people of that kind
- *οὕτως εἰσὶ χρηστοί*: χρηστός is good in the sense of kind and helpful. Since “kind” is used for εὐμενής, the English reads “good”. Other reading: so generous are they
- *ἔξεστι δὲ καὶ σοί*: Literally “it is open to you also”. The Greek does not say to do what; it is taken as to be kind as the gods are. Other reading: It is in your power too

</details>

### 9.12

Toil, not as someone miserable, and not as someone who wants to be pitied or admired, but want one thing only: to move and to hold back as civic reason thinks right.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πόνει*: The verb means to labour and also to bear hardship or pain. “Toil” is used because it carries both the work and its hardness. Other reading: Bear your hardship
- *ὡς ἄθλιος*: “As a miserable person”: someone suffering under the labour, to be pitied. The word comes from the word for a struggle or contest, which may be felt after “toil”. Other reading: not like someone wretched
- *κινεῖσθαι καὶ ἴσχεσθαι*: Both forms can be middle (“to move and to check oneself”) or passive (“to be set moving and to be held back”). The English takes the middle: what is wanted is the person’s own moving and stopping, with reason setting the measure. Other reading: to be set in motion and to be held in check
- *ὁ πολιτικὸς λόγος*: Literally “the political reason”: reason as it belongs to a πόλις, a community of fellow citizens. “Civic” keeps the adjective wide. The Greek does not say which city, and the Stoics also call the universe a city. Other reading: as the reason of a citizen (or: the reason of the community) thinks right
- *ἀξιοῖ*: The verb is “thinks fit”, “claims as right”, “demands”. The English takes the milder “thinks right”. Other reading: requires

</details>

### 9.13

Today I got out of all that hemmed me in, or rather I threw out all that hemmed me in; for it was not outside but inside, in my judgments.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *περιστάσεως*: Literally “what stands around”: one’s circumstances, and especially hard ones, a crisis. The picture matters, since he goes on to say it was not “outside” at all, so the English reads “all that hemmed me in”, where “me” is supplied. The Greek repeats the noun and the English repeats the phrase. Other reading: Today I got out of every difficulty, or rather I threw every difficulty out
- *ἐξῆλθον*: This verb and ἐξέβαλον both begin with ἐξ-, “out”: “went out of” against “threw out”. The pair is kept with “got out of” and “threw out”. Other reading: Today I escaped all that hemmed me in, or rather I cast it out
- *ἔξω γὰρ οὐκ ἦν*: No subject is expressed; “it” is supplied, meaning all that hemmed him in. Other reading: for they were not outside
- *ἐν ταῖς ὑπολήψεσιν*: The Greek has only the article, “in the judgments”; the English reads “my”, as English does where Greek leaves the owner to be understood. Other reading: but within, in the judgments

</details>

### 9.14

All these things are familiar in experience, lasting a day in time, and filthy in their matter. Everything now is as it was in the time of those we have buried.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>
