- *Πάντα ταῦτα*: The chapter does not say what “all these things” are. The English leaves it as open as the Greek. Other reading: All of this
- *συνήθη μὲν τῇ πείρᾳ*: Literally “customary by experience”: things known from having been met again and again. The dative could also be heard as “to experience”, that is, to the person who has had it. Other reading: well known by experience
- *ἐφήμερα*: Literally “lasting a day”. The English keeps the image of the single day, although “in time” follows it. Other reading: short-lived in time
- *ῥυπαρὰ δὲ τῇ ὕλῃ*: The adjective means dirty or grimy, and by extension mean or sordid. The physical sense is kept because the dative names the material the things are made of. Other reading: sordid in their material
- *ἐκείνων οὓς κατεθάψαμεν*: The preposition before this phrase can mean “in the time of” or “in the case of”. The English takes it as time. The verb is a plain past, which English gives as a perfect. Other reading: Everything now is just as it was with those we buried.

</details>

### 9.15

Things stand outside the doors, themselves by themselves, knowing nothing about themselves and pronouncing nothing. What, then, pronounces on them? The ruling part.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὰ πράγματα*: πράγματα are things, affairs, the objects and events one has to deal with. Other reading: Outward things
- *ἔξω θυρῶν ἕστηκεν*: The image is of things standing outside the doors; the Greek does not say whose doors. The phrase that follows is literally “themselves upon themselves”, that is, on their own. Other reading: stand outside our doors, on their own
- *μηδὲν μήτε εἰδότα περὶ αὑτῶν*: αὑτῶν with the rough breathing is reflexive, “about themselves”, and belongs to both participles, though the English states it once. The question that follows has the plain αὐτῶν, “about them”. Other reading: having no knowledge of themselves and making no declaration about themselves
- *ἀποφαινόμενα*: ἀποφαίνεσθαι is to declare, to give a verdict. The same verb comes back in the question, so “pronounce” is used both times. Other reading: nor making any statement

</details>

### 9.16

The bad and the good of the rational and civic animal lie not in what it undergoes but in what it does, just as its virtue and its vice lie not in what it undergoes but in what it does.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πείσει*: The noun means being acted on, set against the noun for acting, which is “activity” in 5.20 and 8.7. The Greek has two abstract nouns; the English turns them into clauses. Other reading: not in passive experience but in activity
- *πολιτικοῦ*: “Belonging to a city, fitted for life as a citizen”; “civic”, as in 7.72. Other reading: the rational and political animal
- *κακὸν καὶ ἀγαθόν*: Neuter adjectives used as nouns: what is bad for it and what is good for it. The Greek has no verb; “lie” is supplied. Other reading: The evil and the good of the rational and civic animal

</details>

### 9.17

For a stone that has been thrown upward, it is nothing bad to be carried down, and nothing good to be carried up.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ κατενεχθῆναι*: The two infinitives are passive forms of one verb (φέρω, “carry”) with opposite prefixes, down and up. The passive is also the ordinary Greek for a thing moving down or up, with no carrier in view. “Be carried” is kept for both so that the pairing shows and the stone, which was thrown, stays passive in both directions. Other reading: to come down … to go up; or: to fall … to rise
- *οὐδὲν κακὸν*: Literally “nothing bad”, with “nor good” following and no second “nothing”; “nothing” is repeated in the second half for the English. κακόν and ἀγαθόν are the ordinary words for bad and good, and can also be heard as nouns, “an evil” and “a good”. Other reading: it is no evil to be carried down, nor a good to be carried up
- *Τῷ ἀναρριφέντι λίθῳ*: A dative of the one concerned, with the article used generically, and a participle of completed action: the stone has already been thrown when its coming down is judged. The English reads “a stone” and “upward”, since “thrown up” has another sense in English. Other reading: For the stone that has been thrown up
- *τὸ ἀνενεχθῆναι*: The Greek names the coming down first and the going up second, though the stone goes up first; the Greek order is kept. The aorist infinitive marks the event, not a past time, so the English does not read “to have been carried up”. Other reading: nor good to have been carried up

</details>

### 9.18

Pass inside, right inside, into their ruling parts, and you will see what judges you are afraid of, and what sort of judges they are of themselves as well.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἔσω ἔσω*: “Inside” is written twice. The English takes the doubling as emphasis; it could also be a copying slip for a single word. Other reading: Pass inside
- *τίνας κριτὰς φοβῇ*: “What judges”, with the sense of what kind. The verb is present: you fear them now. Other reading: what kind of judges you fear
- *οἵους καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν ὄντας κριτάς*: Literally “being what sort of judges about themselves too”. The pronoun as printed is reflexive. The small word given as “as well” can also be “even”. Other reading: and what poor judges they are even of themselves

</details>

### 9.19

All things are in change. You yourself too are in continual alteration and, in a certain respect, in perishing, and so is the whole universe.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κατά τι φθορᾷ*: κατά τι limits the claim: “in some respect” or “in part”. The English takes “in a certain respect”, since elsewhere in the notebook perishing is treated as a kind of alteration (10.7). φθορά is the noun of “perish” in the neighbouring passages, so “perishing” is kept. Other reading: and in part in decay
- *ἐν διηνεκεῖ ἀλλοιώσει*: ἀλλοίωσις is “becoming other”, alteration; “alteration” is kept for it and “change” for μεταβολή across the section. Other reading: in unbroken transformation

</details>

### 9.20

Another person’s wrongdoing must be left there.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐκεῖ*: Literally “there”: in the place where it arose, that is, with the person who did it. The English keeps “there”, the same word as in 9.38 (“the evil is there”), so that the two sayings answer each other. Other reading: Another person’s wrongdoing must be left where it is.
- *ἁμάρτημα*: The word covers anything from a mistake to a moral fault. The English keeps “wrongdoing”, as for the same family of words in the neighbouring passages. Other reading: Another person’s error
- *δεῖ καταλιπεῖν*: Impersonal: “it is necessary to leave”. The English uses a passive (“must be left”) so as not to supply “you”. Other reading: one must leave it there

</details>

### 9.21

The ending of an activity, the stopping and, as it were, the death of an impulse, of a judgment: nothing bad. Now pass on to the ages of life: childhood, for example, adolescence, youth, old age. For every change of these too is a death. Surely that is nothing terrible? Now pass on to your life under your grandfather, then your life under your mother, then your life under your father; and as you find many other things perishing and changing and ending, ask yourself: “Surely that is nothing terrible?” In the same way, then, neither is the ending and stopping and change of your whole life.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὁρμῆς, ὑπολήψεως παῦλα καὶ οἷον θάνατος*: How the genitives divide is open. The English follows the word order, in which each noun comes after its genitives: “ending” with the activity, “stopping and, as it were, death” with impulse and judgment. All three genitives could instead be the subject and “a stopping and a kind of death” the predicate. Other reading: The ending of an activity, of an impulse, of a judgment is a stopping and, as it were, a death
- *τὴν τοῦ μειρακίου, τὴν νεότητα*: Literally “the age of the lad” (the teens) and “youth” (young adulthood). English has no fixed pair for these; the English reads “adolescence, youth”. Other reading: boyhood, young manhood
- *μήτι δεινόν*: A question that expects the answer no, which “surely” gives. “That is” is added in English. Other reading: Is that anything terrible?
- *τὸν ὑπὸ τῷ πάππῳ, εἶτα τὸν ὑπὸ τῇ μητρί, εἶτα τὸν ὑπὸ τῷ πατρί*: The Greek has only articles; “your” is supplied each time. These are stages of Marcus’s own upbringing; the “father” is probably his adoptive father Antoninus (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: the life under the grandfather, then the one under the mother, then the one under the father
- *διαφθορὰς καὶ μεταβολὰς καὶ ἀπολήξεις*: Three plural nouns, turned into “things perishing and changing and ending” because the first has no natural English plural. “Changing” and “ending” still echo “change” and “ending” elsewhere in the passage. Other reading: many other destructions and changes and endings
- *οὐδὲ ἡ τοῦ ὅλου σου βίου λῆξις καὶ παῦλα καὶ μεταβολή*: There is no predicate: “terrible” is understood from the questions before, and the English is left as short as the Greek. λῆξις is from the same root as ἀπόληξις above, so both are “ending”. Other reading: So then neither is the close, the pause and the change of your whole life anything terrible.

</details>

### 9.22

Run to your own ruling part, and to that of the whole, and to this person’s. To your own, so that you make it a just mind. To that of the whole, so that you remember along with it what you are a part of. To this person’s, so that you take note whether there is ignorance there or intent, and at the same time reckon that it is akin.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἡγεμονικὸν*: The Stoic term for the governing part of the soul, here “the ruling part” as in the glossary. The whole is said to have one as well. Other reading: your own governing mind
- *καὶ τὸ τούτου*: Literally “and that of this one”. The Greek does not say who: presumably the person in front of you, the one whose act is in question. The form could be masculine or neuter; the English reads “this person’s”. Other reading: and to that of this man
- *νοῦν δικαικὸν*: The adjective (δικαϊκός, given here without its diaeresis) is a rare one meaning “just” or “concerned with justice”. From memory, unchecked, some editors have doubted the word. It is translated as it stands. Other reading: so that you make it a mind set on justice
- *συμμνημονεύσῃς*: The prefix adds “together with” or “at the same time” to “remember”. The English gives it as “along with it”; the “it” is supplied, and the Greek does not state what the remembering goes together with. Other reading: so that you also remember what you are a part of
- *τίνος μέρος εἶ*: τίνος can be “of what” or “of whom”. The English takes “what”, the whole just named. Other reading: whose part you are
- *πότερον ἄγνοια ἢ γνώμη*: There is no verb and no subject: “whether ignorance or γνώμη”. γνώμη ranges over judgment, purpose and knowledge, and the two words echo each other in sound. The English takes the contrast as between acting in ignorance and acting on a considered purpose, and supplies “there is” and “there”. Other reading: whether it is ignorance or judgment (or: or knowledge)
- *ὅτι συγγενές*: Literally “that it is akin”, neuter, so it is the other person’s ruling part that is akin. The Greek does not say to what: to your own, to that of the whole, or to both. Other reading: and at the same time reckon that it is akin to yours

</details>

### 9.23

Just as you yourself help to complete a civic whole, so too let every action of yours help to complete a civic life. So any action of yours that does not refer, whether directly or at a distance, to the social goal tears your life apart and does not let it be one, and it is seditious, like the person in a citizen body who, for their own part, stands apart from such harmony.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πολιτικοῦ συστήματος*: πολιτικός is “of citizens, of the city”; “civic” is used for both occurrences. σύστημα is an organised whole made of members, a different word from the one given as “the whole” elsewhere (τὸ ὅλον). Other reading: a civic system
- *συμπληρωτικὸς*: An adjective: “such as to fill up together”, said of a member without which the whole is not complete. “Help to complete” gives the “together” of the Greek prefix; the Greek has no noun such as “part” here. Other reading: you yourself go to make up a civic whole
- *ζωῆς πολιτικῆς*: Two words for life in this passage: ζωή here (being alive, life as lived) and βίος in the next sentence (a life as a course or career). English has one word for both. Other reading: a life lived as a citizen
- *τὴν ἀναφοράν*: “Reference”, a carrying-back of the act to what it is for. Other reading: that is not directed
- *εἴτε προσεχῶς εἴτε πόρρωθεν*: Literally “whether next in line or from afar”: directly or through other steps. Other reading: whether closely or from far off
- *ἐπὶ τὸ κοινωνικὸν τέλος*: κοινωνικός, “social”, is the adjective of κοινωνία, community. τέλος is “end” in the sense of what a thing is for; “goal” avoids the other sense of “end”. Other reading: to the end that is community
- *διασπᾷ τὸν βίον*: The Greek has “the life” with no possessive. “Your” is supplied because the action is yours; it could be read more generally. Other reading: tears life apart
- *στασιώδης*: The adjective of στάσις, faction or civil strife inside a city: “of the nature of civil strife”. Other reading: and it is a kind of civil strife
- *ἐν δήμῳ*: δῆμος is the people as a political body; it can also mean the popular assembly or a democracy. Other reading: in a popular assembly
- *μέρος διιστάμενος*: “Their own part” is taken as adverbial (“as far as they are concerned”) and the verb as “stands apart”. It could also be taken as “withdrawing their own share (or party)”. The verb is the one used elsewhere for things that “stand apart”. Other reading: who pulls their own party away from such harmony
- *συμφωνίας*: Literally “sounding together”, a musical word also used for agreement. Other reading: agreement

</details>

### 9.24

Children’s tantrums and toys, and “little breaths carrying corpses”, so that the scene of the Calling Up of the Dead strikes home more vividly.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Παιδίων ὀργαὶ καὶ παίγνια*: There is no verb, and the Greek does not say what is being called this. The first noun is fits of anger. The second is first of all playthings, and can also be games or play; the English takes the objects. Other reading: Children’s fits of anger and children’s games
- *πνευμάτια νεκροὺς βαστάζοντα*: The edition marks this as a quotation. It seems to echo a saying of Epictetus that Marcus cites at 4.41, “you are a little soul carrying a corpse”, here in the plural and with “little breath” for the soul (from memory, unchecked). “Little breaths” matches 9.36. Other reading: “little souls carrying dead bodies”
- *ἐναργέστερον προσπεσεῖν*: A result clause with an infinitive: “so as to strike more vividly”. The Greek does not say whom it strikes, and “strikes home” lets the English name no one either. Other reading: so that it comes home to you more clearly
- *τὸ τῆς Νεκυίας*: Literally “the (matter) of the Nekyia”; “the scene” fills in the bare article. Nekyia, a calling up of the dead, is the traditional title of book 11 of the Odyssey, where Odysseus meets the shades. The English translates the title and does not add Homer, since other works bore the name (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: so that what is in the Nekyia strikes home more vividly

</details>

### 9.25

Go to the quality of the cause; mark the cause off from the material and look at it. Then also set the limit of the time: the longest that this thing, with its own particular quality, can by nature last.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ποιότητα τοῦ αἰτίου*: The first word is “quality”, literally “what-sort-ness”. The second is “the causal”, the active element in a thing, set against “the material” in the next phrase. The English is “the cause”. Other reading: Go to what sort of thing the causal element is
- *αὐτὸ περιγράψας*: The verb means to draw a line around a thing, and so to mark it off. The pronoun is neuter and so points to the cause, not to the quality, and the English names it. It could also be the thing under examination as a whole. Other reading: isolate the thing itself from the material and study it
- *ὑλικοῦ*: The adjective from the word for timber or stuff: “the material”. Stoic analysis divides each thing into its material and its cause. Other reading: from the matter
- *περιόρισον*: A different verb from the earlier one, but again one of drawing a boundary: to fix the limits of something. The English is “set the limit”. Other reading: Then determine the time as well
- *ὅσον πλεῖστον ὑφίστασθαι πέφυκε*: Literally “how much at the most it is by nature such as to subsist”. The English is “the longest that this thing can by nature last”. Other reading: the utmost length of time it is of a nature to exist
- *τὸ ἰδίως ποιόν*: Literally “the thing qualified in a way of its own”. It seems to be the Stoic technical term for an individual as marked by its own particular quality (from memory, unchecked). The word repeats the root of “quality” in the first sentence, and the English repeats “quality”. Other reading: this individually qualified thing

</details>

### 9.26

You have endured countless things because you were not content with your ruling part doing the kind of things it is made to do. But enough.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἀνέτλης*: A verb from epic and tragic poetry, rare in prose, so the opening has a raised, almost quoted sound that plain English cannot easily keep; whether it echoes a particular line of verse is not established here (from memory, unchecked). The tense is a simple past, which can be “you endured” or “you have endured”. Other reading: You bore
- *μύρια*: Literally “ten thousand things”, the usual Greek for a number past counting. The Greek does not name what was endured; troubles are understood. Other reading: ten thousand troubles
- *διὰ τὸ μὴ ἀρκεῖσθαι τῷ σῷ ἡγεμονικῷ ποιοῦντι*: Literally “through not being content with your ruling part doing”. The discontent is with the ruling part’s simply doing its own work, as if that were not enough. Other reading: because it was not enough for you that your ruling part should do
- *οἷα κατεσκεύασται*: Literally “such as it has been constructed”: the kind of things that fit the way the ruling part is made, with “to do” supplied. The Greek tense describes a present state, so the English reads “is made”. The verb could instead have “the things” as its subject. Other reading: doing those things, such as have been made ready for it
- *ἀλλὰ ἅλις*: Two words that break off: “but enough”. The Greek does not say enough of what, the enduring or the talk about it, and the English leaves it as bare. Other reading: But that is enough of that.

</details>

### 9.27

When someone else blames you or hates you, or people voice things of that kind, go to their little souls, pass inside and see what sort of people they are. You will see that you need not be torn apart so that these people may think this or that of you. You must wish them well, however; for by nature they are friends, and the gods too help them in every kind of way, through dreams, through oracles, yet toward the things those people care about.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐκφωνῶσιν*: The Greek moves from the singular “another” to a plural verb, and stays in the plural. The shift is marked with “people”. Other reading: or utters things of that kind
- *τὰ ψυχάρια αὐτῶν*: A diminutive of ψυχή (soul), said with pity or contempt. Other reading: their poor souls
- *σπᾶσθαι*: To be pulled, wrenched or convulsed: the torment of anxiety over their opinion. The words οὐ δεῖ before it are taken as “need not”, following “you will see”; they can also mean “must not”. Other reading: that you must not be racked
- *τί ποτε περὶ σοῦ δοκῇ*: Literally “that some particular thing may seem to them about you”: that they should hold one opinion of you or another. Other reading: so that these people may have any opinion of you whatever
- *φύσει γὰρ φίλοι*: No verb and no “your”: by nature they are friends, which is taken as friends to you. φίλοι can also mean “dear”. Other reading: for by nature they are dear to you
- *πρὸς ἃ ἐκεῖνοι διαφέρονται*: διαφέρομαι usually means to differ or quarrel. The English takes a sense found in later Greek, to be concerned about something, to set store by it (from memory, unchecked). The point is that the gods help them even toward things that are not truly good. Other reading: yet toward the things those people quarrel over

</details>

### 9.28a

The cycles of the universe are the same, up and down, from age to age. And either the mind of the whole has an impulse towards each thing, and if that is so, accept what its impulse is towards; or it had an impulse once, and the rest follows as a consequence, and why do you strain? For in a way: atoms, or things without parts. In sum: if it is god, all is well; if it is randomness, do not act at random yourself as well.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ταὐτά*: The breathing mark makes this a contraction of τὰ αὐτά, “the same things”. Without it the word would be ταῦτα, “these things”. The English follows the mark. Other reading: These are the cycles of the universe
- *ἐγκύκλια*: Literally “things that go in a circle”. The word can also mean what is ordinary and recurring. “Cycles” keeps the image of going round. Other reading: the ordinary run of the universe
- *ἡ τοῦ ὅλου διάνοια*: διάνοια is “thought” elsewhere in this translation. Here it is the faculty that has impulses, so the English reads “mind”. Other reading: the thought of the whole
- *ὁρμᾷ*: The verb and its relatives (ὁρμητόν, ὥρμησε) come three times and carry the argument, so “impulse” is used for all three. The Stoic term is ὁρμή; the verb more literally means “sets itself moving towards”. Other reading: either the mind of the whole sets itself moving towards each thing
- *καὶ τί ἐντείνῃ*: Literally “and why do you stretch yourself tight?”. The join with what goes before is abrupt, and the text here may have been doubted (from memory, unchecked). The words are translated as they stand. Other reading: and what are you straining at?
- *τρόπον γάρ τινα ἄτομοι ἢ ἀμερῆ*: The sentence has no verb and no stated subject, and how it follows from the question before it is not clear; the text may be damaged (from memory, unchecked). The English gives the words as they stand and supplies nothing. ἀμερῆ means things that have no parts and so cannot be divided. Other reading: for in a way it is atoms, or indivisible things
- *τὸ δ’ ὅλον*: This can be the set phrase “on the whole, in sum” or the noun “the whole”, which is named two sentences earlier. The English takes it as the set phrase. Other reading: As for the whole: if it is god, all is well
- *εἴτε θεός*: The Greek is only “if god”, matched by “if the random”. It can mean “if what runs things is god” or “if there is a god”. The English keeps the two halves parallel. Other reading: if there is a god, all is well
- *μὴ καὶ σὺ εἰκῇ*: There is no verb: literally “not you too at random”. “Act” is supplied. εἰκῇ, “at random, without plan or purpose”, is the same word used just before of what runs things, where the English reads “randomness”. Other reading: do not be random yourself as well

</details>

### 9.28b–29a

Any moment now earth will cover us all. Then earth itself will change, and those things too will change without end, and those again without end. For a person who reflects on wave after wave of changes and alterations, and on their speed, will look down on everything mortal.

The substance of the whole is a torrent: it carries everything along.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἤδη*: “Already”, with a future verb: at any moment, very soon. Other reading: Soon
- *κἀκεῖνα εἰς ἄπειρον μεταβαλεῖ*: “Those things” has no stated referent in the Greek; it must mean what the earth changes into. The English leaves it as bare as the Greek. εἰς ἄπειρον is “to infinity”. Other reading: and what it changes into will change without end, and that in turn without end
- *ἐπικυματώσεις*: A rare word: waves coming on top of waves. The image is kept. Other reading: the surging waves of changes and alterations
- *καὶ τὸ τάχος*: “The speed” is taken as a second object of “reflects on”, the speed of the changes. The following genitive παντὸς θνητοῦ then goes with “will look down on”. Other reading: who reflects on the waves of change and on the speed of everything mortal will feel contempt
- *καταφρονήσει*: “Will think down on”: hold as of little account. It need not carry scorn. Other reading: will think little of everything mortal
- *Χειμάρρους*: A winter torrent, a stream swollen by storm that sweeps things away. Other reading: a river in flood
- *ἡ τῶν ὅλων οὐσία*: “The substance of the whole”, on the pattern of the glossary’s “the nature of the whole”. Some editors are believed to read αἰτία, “cause”, here in place of οὐσία (from memory, unchecked); the English translates the text as given. Other reading: The cause of the whole is a torrent
- *πάντα φέρει*: φέρει is “carries”, of a current bearing things away. The same verb can mean “brings”. Other reading: it sweeps all things away

</details>

### 9.29b

And how cheap, too, are these little people who are busy with public affairs and, as they suppose, practical in a philosophic way: full of snot. Man, what then? Do what nature now demands. Set out, if it is given to you, and do not look around to see whether anyone will know. Do not hope for Plato’s republic, but be content if the smallest thing goes forward, and think of the outcome of even this as a small thing. For who will change a principle of theirs? And without a change of principles, what is there but the slavery of people who groan and pretend to be persuaded? Go on now and tell me of Alexander and Philip and Demetrius of Phalerum. It is for them to see whether they saw what the common nature wanted and schooled themselves; but if they played the tragic hero, no one has condemned me to imitate them. The work of philosophy is simple and modest: do not lead me off into solemn conceit.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὡς εὐτελῆ δὲ καὶ*: The passage begins in the middle of chapter 9.29, so “and … too” looks back to something outside it. Other reading: And how cheap as well
- *ὡς οἴεται*: The verb is singular. With the neuter plural subject it can mean “as they think”; it could also be “as he thinks” or “as people think”. Other reading: as one supposes
- *φιλοσόφως πρακτικὰ ἀνθρώπια*: ἀνθρώπια is a belittling diminutive, “little people”. Literally “these little people of public affairs and, as they think, practical in a philosophic way”. Other reading: these little men of politics who think they are putting philosophy into practice
- *μυξῶν μεστά*: “Full of mucus”: snotty-nosed, like small children. Other reading: drivelling
- *ἄνθρωπε, τί ποτε*: A bare “man, what ever?” with the verb left out. The edition marks a break before it with a dash; the English begins a new sentence instead. Other reading: Man, what are you to do?
- *ὅρμησον, ἐὰν διδῶται*: The verb of ὁρμή, “impulse”: start, set yourself moving. “If it is given” has no stated giver; “to you” is supplied. Other reading: act on the impulse, if you are allowed
- *τὴν Πλάτωνος πολιτείαν*: πολιτεία is “constitution, state” and also the title of Plato’s book describing a perfect city. The English reads “Plato’s republic”, the state itself, which is what one could hope for. Other reading: Plato’s Republic, the book
- *εἰ τὸ βραχύτατον πρόεισι*: The words can be the subject, “the smallest thing”, or a measure of how far things go forward. The English takes the first, since “this very thing” in the next clause picks it up. Other reading: if things go forward by the smallest step
- *ὡς μικρόν τί ἐστι διανοοῦ*: As the Greek stands: “think of the outcome of this very thing as something small”. Some editors may read the opposite, “as no small thing” (from memory, unchecked). The English translates what is given. Other reading: and count even that result as no small thing
- *δόγμα γὰρ αὐτῶν τίς μεταβαλεῖ*: “Theirs” has no stated reference inside this passage: the people one would be trying to reform. The noun is singular and has no article. Other reading: For who can change what people believe?
- *πείθεσθαι προσποιουμένων*: πείθεσθαι is both “to be persuaded” and “to obey”. Other reading: who pretend to obey
- *Ἀλέξανδρον καὶ Φίλιππον καὶ Δημήτριον τὸν Φαληρέα*: Alexander the Great, his father Philip of Macedon, and Demetrius of Phalerum, a philosopher and statesman who governed Athens in the late fourth century BC (the last detail from memory, unchecked). Other reading: Alexander, Philip and Demetrius the Phalerean
- *ὄψονται*: An idiom: “they will see to it”, that is, it is their own business. Literally “they will see whether they saw”. Other reading: They will see whether they saw what the common nature wanted
- *ἡ κοινὴ φύσις*: “The common nature”: nature as shared by all things, the same as the nature of the whole. Other reading: universal nature
- *ἐτραγῴδησαν*: “Played tragedy”: acted a grand part, struck heroic poses. Other reading: if they merely put on a tragic show
- *σεμνοτυφίαν*: A compound of “solemn” and τῦφος, the “conceit” of 6.13: pompous self-importance. Other reading: pomposity

</details>

### 9.30–31

To look down from above on countless herds and countless rites, on every kind of voyage in storms and in calms, and on the differences among those coming to be, coming together, and passing away. Think too of the life lived long ago by others, the life that will be lived after you, and the life being lived now among the barbarian peoples; and how many do not even know your name, how many will very quickly forget it, how many who perhaps praise you now will very quickly blame you; and that neither being remembered is of any account, nor reputation, nor anything else at all.

Freedom from disturbance about the things that happen from the cause outside; justice in the things done through the cause that comes from you. That is, impulse and action ending in just this, acting socially, as being what is according to nature for you.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐπιθεωρεῖν*: An infinitive used as an instruction, with no person. It is kept as “To look”; the next sentence turns to a direct command, “Think”. Other reading: Look down from above on
- *ἀγέλας μυρίας*: ἀγέλη is a herd of animals, and also any crowd or band of people. “Herds” is kept. Other reading: countless crowds
- *τελετὰς μυρίας*: τελετή is a religious rite, especially a rite of initiation. Other reading: countless ceremonies of initiation
- *διαφορὰς γινομένων, συγγινομένων, ἀπογινομένων*: One verb with three prefixes: coming to be, being or coming together, being away. The forms can be people or things, and the middle word can mean keeping company (also of sexual union) or combining. The English takes all three of people, since the herds, rites and voyages before them are human scenes. Other reading: the variety of what comes to be, comes together and passes away
- *ἐπαινοῦντες ἴσως νῦν σε τάχιστα ψέξουσι*: “Perhaps” stands inside the phrase about praise, between “praising” and “now”, and the English takes it there. It could be taken with the verb that follows. Other reading: how many who praise you now will perhaps very quickly blame you
- *ἀξιόλογόν γε*: Literally “worth speaking of”, with a small word of emphasis. “Of any account” carries both. Other reading: is worth mentioning
- *τὸ σύμπαν*: Used as an adverb, “altogether”, “at all”. Other reading: nor, in short, anything else
- *Ἀταραξία μὲν*: The sentence has no verb: two nouns set down like headings. ἀταραξία is the state of not being disturbed. Other reading: Calm about the things that happen
- *παρὰ τὴν ἐκ σοῦ αἰτίαν*: παρά with this case here means “owing to”. The pair is the cause outside you and the cause that is you. Other reading: in the things whose cause lies in you
- *κοινωνικῶς πρᾶξαι*: “Socially” follows this translation’s fixed word for κοινωνικός. It does not mean being sociable: it means acting as a member of the human community, for the common good. Other reading: ending in just this, acting for the common good
- *ὡς τοῦτό σοι κατὰ φύσιν ὄν*: The Greek gives this as the ground on which the person acts, “as being”, and not as the writer’s own statement of a cause. Other reading: because this is according to nature for you

</details>

### 9.32a

You can strip away many needless things among those that trouble you, things that rest wholly on your judgment, and you will at once make plenty of open room for yourself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πολλὰ περισσὰ περιελεῖν*: περισσὰ is “more than is needed”. Three words in the sentence begin with περι- (περισσὰ, περιελεῖν, περιποιήσεις), a sound play English cannot keep. Other reading: Many of the things that trouble you are superfluous and you can remove them
- *ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα*: Literally “lying wholly upon your judgment”, with the preposition that gives “up to you” elsewhere in the section. The participle may give the reason; it is left as a plain description, since the Greek has no “since”. ὅλα is taken as “wholly”, not “all of them”. Other reading: since all of them lie in your own judgment
- *εὐρυχωρίαν*: Literally “wide space”, room to move. The image of space is kept. Other reading: a great deal of freedom
- *ἤδη*: “Already” or “at once”: the room comes with the stripping away, not later. Other reading: and you will already have made plenty of room for yourself
- *περιποιήσεις ἤδη σεαυτῷ*: The Greek as given stops here without a full stop: the sentence runs on in the rest of the chapter, which says by what means the room is made. Only what is given is translated, and the full stop that closes it is an addition. Other reading: and you will at once make plenty of open room for yourself, …

</details>

### 9.32b–33

By having encompassed the whole universe in thought, and by surveying everlasting eternity, and by thinking of the swift change of each particular thing: how short is the stretch from coming to be to dissolution, and how gaping the time before the coming to be, just as the time after the dissolution is likewise boundless.

Everything you see will very quickly perish, and those who have looked on as it perished will very quickly perish themselves, and whoever dies in extreme old age will be brought level with the one who died before their time.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τῷ τὸν ὅλον κόσμον περιειληφέναι*: The passage begins in mid-sentence with a dative infinitive, “by having encompassed”, which depends on a main clause that is not given. It is left as a fragment and nothing is supplied; only the capital letter is added. No “you” is expressed in the fragment. Other reading: by having embraced the whole universe
- *τῇ γνώμῃ*: γνώμη is the mind as it judges and forms a view. The glossary keeps “thought” for διάνοια and “mind” for νοῦς, neither of which occurs here; “thought” is used as the plainest fit. Other reading: in your mind
- *περινοεῖν*: Literally “to think around”, with the same prefix as περιειληφέναι, “to have encompassed”. “Surveying” gives the looking all round in ordinary English, at the cost of the word “think”. Other reading: and by thinking round everlasting eternity
- *ἀχανὲς*: “Yawning, gaping”: a gulf with no visible far side. The image is kept, as with the same word in 12.32. Other reading: how vast the time before the coming to be
- *ὡς καὶ τὸ μετὰ τὴν διάλυσιν ὁμοίως ἄπειρον*: The second ὡς may be a comparative “just as” or another “how”. With καὶ and ὁμοίως (“likewise”) beside it, the English takes it as “just as”. Other reading: and how the time after the dissolution is likewise boundless
- *ἐπιδόντες*: The verb can mean simply to look on, or to live to see something. The English takes the plainer sense. Other reading: and those who have lived to see it perish
- *τῷ προώρῳ*: “The untimely one”, the one who dies before the due season. Greek uses the masculine as the general form; the English has “whoever” and “their”. Other reading: will be made equal to the one who died young

</details>

### 9.34

What the ruling parts of these people are, what sort of things they are in earnest about, and for what sort of things they love and honour. Think of yourself as looking at their little souls naked. When they suppose that they do harm by blaming or do good by singing praises, how much conceit.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τίνα τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ τούτων*: There is no verb. It can be a direct question or the heading of something to consider; the English keeps it as a thing to consider, running on into the two clauses that follow. τὸ ἡγεμονικόν is the Stoic term for the part of the soul that directs the rest, “the ruling part”. Other reading: What are the ruling parts of these people?
- *ἐσπουδάκασι*: A perfect with present force: what they are busy about and take seriously now. English has to choose between effort and seriousness. Other reading: what sort of things they have put their effort into
- *δι’ οἷα φιλοῦσι καὶ τιμῶσι*: The two verbs have no object in the Greek and the English gives them none. The sense is the kind of reasons for which these people give their love and honour. Other reading: and what sort of things make them love and honour a person
- *γυμνὰ νόμιζε βλέπειν*: The imperative can mean “consider that you see” or “make it your practice to see”. The English takes the first. Other reading: Make it your habit to look at their little souls naked.
- *ψυχάρια*: A diminutive of the word for soul, belittling in tone. Other reading: their souls
- *δοκοῦσι*: The verb can mean “they think” or “they seem”. The English takes it as what they themselves think, which fits the word for conceit that follows. Other reading: When they seem to do harm by blaming or good by singing praises
- *ὅση οἴησις*: Literally “how great the conceit”, with a word of measure. The noun covers self-importance and also mere supposing, so it answers the verb “suppose” just before. Other reading: how great the delusion

</details>

### 9.35

Loss is nothing other than change. And in this the nature of the whole delights, the nature in accordance with which all things come about well, and from eternity have come about in the same kind of way, and without end there will be others like them. Why then do you say that all things have come about badly and all things will always go badly, and that among so many gods no power, it seems, has ever been found to set these things right, but the universe has been condemned to be held fast in bad things without a break?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἡ ἀποβολὴ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ μεταβολή*: A play on two words from the same verb: ἀποβολή, a throwing away or loss, and μεταβολή, a throwing over or change. The English words do not echo each other. Other reading: A casting off is nothing but a casting over into something else
- *τούτῳ δὲ χαίρει*: τούτῳ is neuter, “this”, and so points to the fact or process of change in general, not to the feminine noun μεταβολή. Other reading: And change is what the nature of the whole delights in
- *ὁμοειδῶς*: “In the same form”: the adverb of ὁμοειδής, rendered “of the same kind” in 7.49 and 6.37. Other reading: and from eternity came about in just the same way
- *τί οὖν λέγεις ὅτι*: Either “why then do you say that” or “what then are you saying: that”. The English takes the first. Other reading: What then are you saying? That all things have come about badly
- *ἐν τοσούτοις θεοῖς*: “Among so many gods”; ἄρα in the same clause marks the inference as one the speaker would be forced to, given as “it seems”. Other reading: and so, with all those gods, no power was ever found
- *ἐν ἀδιαλείπτοις κακοῖς συνέχεσθαι*: κακοῖς is the plural noun that goes with the adverb κακῶς, “badly”, just before, and both answer καλῶς, “well”. “Bad things” keeps the family together. συνέχεσθαι is to be held fast or gripped. Other reading: to be gripped by unceasing evils

</details>

### 9.36

The rottenness of the matter that underlies each thing: water, dust, little bones, a goatish reek. Or again: marble is calluses of the earth, gold and silver are sediment, clothing is little hairs, and purple dye is blood, and all the rest is of this kind. And the little breath too is another thing of this kind, changing out of these things and into these.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὸ σαπρὸν*: A neuter adjective used as a noun, “the rotten (side)”, with no verb: a heading followed by a list. The English keeps it verbless. Other reading: How rotten is the matter that underlies each thing
- *τῆς ἑκάστῳ ὑποκειμένης ὕλης*: The dative “each” can be neuter (each thing) or masculine (each person). The English reads “each thing”, because the list goes on to marble, gold and clothing. Other reading: of the matter that underlies each person
- *γράσος*: The word names the smell of a goat and is used of the rank smell of the unwashed body. The English keeps the goat. Other reading: the rank smell of sweat
- *ἢ πάλιν*: As punctuated, “or again” closes the first list and opens a second. It could also be run on into the next clause. Other reading: or, to take it another way,
- *πῶροι γῆς*: The noun means a porous stone (tufa) and also a callus or hard lump formed in the body. The English takes the bodily sense, which keeps the image in one word. Other reading: marble is hardened lumps of earth
- *ὑποστάθμαι*: What settles at the bottom of a liquid: sediment, dregs. The plural is kept as a mass noun in English. Other reading: gold and silver are dregs
- *αἷμα ἡ πορφύρα*: The noun is the purple dye, or cloth dyed with it, and not the colour, so the English says “purple dye”. The blood is that of the shellfish the dye came from, which the Greek does not mention and the English does not add. Other reading: the purple robe is blood
- *τὸ πνευμάτιον*: The diminutive of pneuma, the breath that for the Stoics is the stuff of life and soul. The English keeps the diminutive and the image of breath, as in 9.24 of this section. Other reading: the little soul; the bit of breath that is our life
- *ἐκ τούτων εἰς ταῦτα μεταβάλλον*: Literally “changing out of these into these”, the same pronoun twice. It may mean out of such things and into such things again, or from some of these materials into others. The English repeats “these” as the Greek does and leaves both open. Other reading: changing from one of these things into another

</details>

### 9.37a

Enough of the wretched life, the grumbling, the aping. Why are you troubled? What in this is new? What puts you beside yourself? The cause? Look at it. Or the material? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing. But toward the gods too, now at last, become simpler and better.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἅλις τοῦ ἀθλίου βίου καὶ γογγυσμοῦ καὶ πιθηκισμοῦ*: Three nouns joined by “and”; “wretched” stands only with “life” but may colour all three. πιθηκισμός is playing the ape: mimicry, putting on an act. The dash that follows in the Greek is replaced with a new sentence. Other reading: Enough of this wretched life of grumbling and monkey tricks.
- *τί σε ἐξίστησι*: The verb is to put someone out of their place, and so out of their wits. “Beside yourself” is the English idiom with the same picture. Other reading: What is upsetting you?
- *τὸ αἴτιον*: “The cause” and “the material” (ἡ ὕλη) are the usual two-part analysis of any thing in this book: the active principle that makes it what it is, and the stuff it is made of. The questions ask which of the two is the trouble. Other reading: Is it the form of the thing?
- *ἀλλ’ ἡ ὕλη*: ἀλλά here brings in the second of two alternatives, so the English says “or”. ὕλη is the stuff a thing is made of, often rendered “matter”; “material” avoids the other sense of “the matter”. Other reading: But the matter?
- *ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς θεοὺς ἤδη ποτὲ*: “But also toward the gods”: the turn is abrupt in the Greek, and no link is added. ἤδη ποτέ is “now at last”, with a note of impatience. Other reading: And in your dealings with the gods as well, it is high time
- *ἁπλούστερος καὶ χρηστότερος*: ἁπλοῦς is single, without doubleness: simple, straightforward. χρηστός is good in the sense of decent, honest, kind; “better” matches “very good” for the same word at 12.5. Other reading: more straightforward and kinder

</details>

### 9.37b

To have observed these things for a hundred years or for three comes to the same.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἴσον*: “Equal”, with no verb: the hundred years and the three are declared equal. It stands at the end of the English sentence as “comes to the same”, and the Greek “and” between the two spans becomes “or”. Other reading: It is equal, to have observed these things for a hundred years and for three.
- *ἑκατὸν ἔτεσι*: A dative of time, which in Greek of this period can express duration. The English takes it as “for a hundred years”. It could be pressed as “in” or “over” a hundred years. Other reading: over a hundred years or over three
- *ταῦτα*: “These things” points back to the earlier part of the chapter, which is not in this passage and which speaks of looking at the cause and the matter of things. Nothing is supplied. Other reading: all this
- *ἱστορῆσαι*: The verb is to inquire into, and also to observe, to come to know by seeing. The English takes it as observing, since the earlier part of the chapter twice says “look at it”. The aorist views the looking as a whole, hence “to have observed”. Other reading: To look into these things; to have been a witness of these things

</details>

### 9.38

If the person did wrong, the evil is there. But perhaps they did not do wrong.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἥμαρτεν*: The verb has no expressed subject: “he, she or someone did wrong”. The English supplies “the person” and then “they”, since the Greek does not single out a man. Other reading: If he did wrong
- *ἐκεῖ τὸ κακόν*: Literally “there the bad”: the bad thing lies there, with the one who did it, and not with you. No verb is expressed, and “is” is supplied. τὸ κακόν could be “the harm” as well as “the evil”; ἐκεῖ is “there”, as in 9.20. Other reading: the harm is theirs

</details>

### 9.39a

Either everything happens, one thing upon another, as to one body, from one source that has mind, and the part must not find fault with what comes about for the sake of the whole; or there are atoms, and nothing else but a stirred brew and a scattering. Why, then, are you troubled?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πηγῆς νοερᾶς*: Literally “a spring that has mind”. The image is of water from one source. νοερός is “having mind”, from νοῦς, “mind”. Other reading: from one intelligent spring
- *ὡς ἑνὶ σώματι ἐπισυμβαίνει*: The verb is “happens” with two prefixes, “upon” and “together”. The English gives the first as “one thing upon another”; it could also mean simply “happens to”. “As to one body” can mean that things happen to the universe as to a single body, or that they happen as things do within a single body. Other reading: all things befall it as they befall a single body
- *ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὅλου*: “On behalf of the whole”, which can be “for its good” or “in its interest”. Other reading: what is done in the interest of the whole
- *κυκεὼν*: A drink made by stirring barley meal and other things into liquid; it separates unless kept stirred. It is used as an image of a mere mixture, and the English keeps it as a brew. Other reading: nothing but a hotchpotch and a dispersal
- *ταράσσῃ*: “Troubled”, literally “stirred up”, which may answer the image of the stirred drink. Other reading: why then are you in turmoil?

</details>

### 9.39b

Do you say to the ruling part: “You are dead, you are ruined, you have turned into a wild beast, you are playing a part, you are running with the herd, you are grazing”?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τῷ ἡγεμονικῷ λέγεις*: This is the end of a chapter and its construction is open. With the question mark at the end, the whole is taken as one question, with the six verbs as statements made to the ruling part. They can also be read as questions put to the ruling part, and some editors are thought to change λέγεις to an imperative (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: You say to your ruling part: “Are you dead? Are you ruined? Have you turned into a wild beast? Are you playing a part, running with the herd, grazing?”
- *ἔφθαρσαι*: Perfect passive of φθείρω: destroyed, spoilt, or morally corrupted. “Ruined” is used because it can be heard in each of these ways, as the Greek can. Other reading: you are corrupted
- *τεθηρίωσαι*: Literally “you have been made a wild beast” (θηρίον). Other reading: you have been brutalised
- *ὑποκρίνῃ*: The actor’s verb: you play a part, you pretend. Same rendering as in 2.16. Other reading: you are pretending
- *συναγελάζῃ, βόσκῃ*: Both are words used of animals: to gather in a herd (ἀγέλη) and to feed at pasture. Other reading: you herd together, you feed

</details>

### 9.40

Either the gods can do nothing or they can. Now if they cannot, why do you pray? But if they can, why do you not rather pray that they grant you not to fear any of these things, not to desire any of them, not to be pained at any of them, rather than that any of them be absent or be present? For certainly, if they can work with people, they can work with them toward these things too. But perhaps you will say: “The gods have left these things up to me.” Then is it not better to use what is up to you in freedom than to let what is not up to you make a difference to you, in slavery and degradation? And who told you that the gods do not also lend a hand with the things that are up to us? Begin, at any rate, to pray about these, and you will see. This man prays: “How may I sleep with that woman?” You: “How may I not desire to sleep with that woman?” Another: “How may I be rid of that one?” You: “How may I not want to be rid of that one?” Another: “How may I not lose my little child?” You: “How may I not be afraid of losing it?” In short, turn your prayers round like this and watch what happens.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *οὐδὲν δύνανται*: The verb is “can”, “have power”. The argument repeats it six times, so the English keeps “can” throughout. Other reading: Either the gods have no power or they have power.
- *εὔχῃ. διδόναι αὐτοὺς*: The full stop after εὔχῃ in the text as given breaks one sentence in two, a slip of the digitised copy; the English reads a single question ending at the question mark after παρεῖναι. “You” after “grant” is added: the Greek says only “that they give the not fearing”. Other reading: why not rather pray for them to give freedom from fear of any of these things
- *τι τούτων*: “These things” has nothing before it to point to. It means the things people pray to get or to be spared, as the examples at the end show. Other reading: any of the things in question
- *ἐπ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτὰ οἱ θεοὶ ἐποίησαν*: Literally “the gods made them upon me”, that is, placed them in the speaker’s power: the objection is that there is then no need to pray for them. The English says “left” for “made” so that “up to” can stand as in the rest of the passage. The quotation marks are added. Other reading: The gods have put these things in my own power.
- *ἣ διαφέρεσθαι πρὸς τὰ μὴ ἐπὶ σοὶ*: ἣ is a slip for ἢ, “than”. The verb διαφέρεσθαι πρός can mean to treat a thing as making a difference, to be concerned about it, or to be at odds with it. The English takes the first, as for the noun of the same idiom at 6.41. Other reading: than to be at odds with what is not up to you
- *μετὰ δουλείας καὶ ταπεινότητος*: Literally “with slavery and lowness”, set against “with freedom”. ταπεινότης is the state of one brought low, abject. Other reading: like a slave and a beggar
- *συλλαμβάνουσιν*: The verb is to take hold together with someone, to help with a task. It is a different word from “work with” (συνεργεῖν) above, so the English gives it a different phrase. Other reading: that the gods do not help us even with the things that are up to us
- *πῶς κοιμηθῶ μετ’ ἐκείνης*: Each prayer is put as a question beginning “how”, which is a request, not a real question. The quotation marks are added. The verb is literally “to go to bed”. Other reading: Let me sleep with that woman.
- *πῶς στερηθῶ ἐκείνου*: The verb is literally “be deprived of”. ἐκείνου can be a man or a thing, and “that one” leaves it open. In the answer the Greek has no object, and “of that one” is repeated to complete the English. Other reading: How may I be rid of that man?
- *πῶς μὴ χρῄζω τοῦ στερηθῆναι*: χρῄζω is to need and also to want, to crave. “Want” is taken because the answer runs parallel to “not desire” in the answer before. Other reading: How may I not need to be rid of that one?
- *τὸ τεκνίον*: A diminutive of “child”, tender in tone. The Greek word is neuter, which is why the English has “it”. Other reading: my little one

</details>

### 9.41a

Epicurus says: “In my illness my conversations were not about the sufferings of the little body, nor,” he says, “did I talk about such things to those who came in. Instead I went on inquiring into the leading questions of nature, and stayed on this very point: how the mind, though it has its share in such motions in the bit of flesh, stays untroubled, keeping its own good. Nor did I give the doctors the chance,” he says, “to put on airs as though they were doing something. Rather, life went on well and nobly.” So do the same as he did, in illness, if you are ill, and in any other circumstance. For not to stand away from philosophy in anything whatever that befalls, and not to chatter along with someone who is a layman and has not studied nature,

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *αἱ ὁμιλίαι*: ὁμιλίαι are one’s dealings and talk with others; it can also mean a teacher’s lectures. Other reading: my lectures
- *φησίν*: “He says” is put in twice inside the quotation, as Greek does; both are kept. Other reading: he goes on
- *σωματίου*: Diminutive of “body”, “little body” throughout the section. σαρκιδίῳ below is the same kind of diminutive of “flesh”. Other reading: of my poor body
- *ἐλάλουν*: λαλεῖν is plain “talk”. “Chatter” is kept for συμφλυαρεῖν at the end of the passage, which is “talk nonsense along with”. Other reading: did I chatter
- *τὰ προηγούμενα φυσιολογῶν*: φυσιολογέω is to give an account of nature, the Epicurean name for natural philosophy. τὰ προηγούμενα is most likely “the leading, principal matters”; it can also mean “what went before”, that is, the subjects he had been on already. Other reading: I went on with my earlier inquiries into nature
- *πρὸς αὐτῷ τούτῳ ὤν*: “Being at this very thing”: occupied with this one point. Other reading: and was intent on just this
- *συμμεταλαμβάνουσα*: “Taking a share along with”: the mind does share in what the flesh undergoes. The participle could be “though it shares” or simply “while it shares”. Other reading: while it shares in
- *ἀταρακτεῖ*: The verb of ἀταραξία, the Epicurean word for freedom from disturbance. Other reading: stays calm
- *καταφρυάττεσθαι*: From a verb for a horse snorting and prancing: to give oneself airs over someone. The Greek does not say over whom. Other reading: to swagger over me
- *ὥς τι ποιοῦσιν*: “As though doing something”, that is, something that mattered. Other reading: as if they were achieving something important
- *ὁ βίος ἤγετο εὖ καὶ καλῶς*: Literally “life was led well and finely”. The Greek does not say whose life. καλῶς is “finely, nobly”, a word of worth and not of happiness. Other reading: my life went on well and happily
- *ταὐτὰ οὖν ἐκείνῳ*: The Greek has no verb: “the same things, then, as he”. “Do” is supplied. Other reading: The same, then, as he did
- *ἰδιώτῃ καὶ ἀφυσιολόγῳ*: ἰδιώτης is a layman, one with no training in philosophy; the second word is “without knowledge of the study of nature”. The English keeps the “and” and takes the two as describing one person; they could be two. Other reading: with the layman and with the one ignorant of nature
- *συμφλυαρεῖν,*: The passage ends here with a comma, part-way through the sentence: the infinitives “not to stand away … not to chatter” are left without their verb. The comma is kept and nothing is supplied. Other reading: nor to join in the nonsense of the layman … (is …)

</details>

### 9.41b

… is common to every school. To be occupied only with what is being done now, and with the instrument through which you act.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πάσης αἱρέσεως κοινόν.*: The passage begins in the middle of a sentence. These words are its predicate, “common to every school”, and the subject stands before the cut: not leaving philosophy whatever happens, and not joining in the chatter of the untrained. The English adds “is” and a mark of omission, so that the words are not read as a heading for the sentence that follows. Other reading: Common to every school.
- *αἱρέσεως*: αἵρεσις is literally a “choice”, and then a school of philosophy that one chooses to follow. The English takes it in that second sense. Other reading: common to every sect; common to every choice of a way of life
- *πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ νῦν πρασσομένῳ εἶναι*: The verb is an infinitive with no finite verb, and the English keeps it so. It can be read as an instruction, as the infinitive often is in this notebook, or as one more thing that every school holds. πρὸς with the dative and εἶναι means to be at something, busy with it. Other reading: Be intent only on what is being done now
- *τῷ ὀργάνῳ*: ὄργανον is a tool, an instrument, or an organ of the body. The Greek does not say which instrument is meant: it could be the body, the mind, or whatever means the action uses. The English keeps the open word. Other reading: and with the tool through which you act
- *δι’ οὗ πράσσεις*: The verb has no object: “through which you act”, not “with which you do it”. It is the only second person in the passage. Other reading: the instrument you are doing it with

</details>

### 9.42

Whenever you take offence at someone’s shamelessness, ask yourself at once: “Is it possible, then, for there to be no shameless people in the universe?” It is not possible. Then do not demand the impossible. For this person too is one of those shameless people who must exist in the universe. Have the same thought ready to hand for the scoundrel, and for the faithless person, and for everyone who does wrong in any way whatever. For as soon as you are reminded that it is impossible for this kind of people not to exist, you will be kinder toward each one of them. It is useful too to think at once of this: what virtue nature has given to a human being to meet this wrong. For it has given, as an antidote, gentleness against the unfeeling person, and against another some other power. And in general you are free to teach the one who has gone astray to think otherwise; for everyone who does wrong misses what they were aiming at and has gone astray. And what harm have you in fact suffered? For you will find that none of those you are provoked at has done anything of a kind that was going to make your mind worse; and it is there that what is bad for you, and what harms you, has its whole existence. And what new or strange thing has happened, if the untaught person does what an untaught person does? See whether you ought not rather to blame yourself, because you did not expect that this person would do this wrong. For you did have from reason the means to reflect that this person was likely to do this wrong, and yet you forgot it and are surprised that they have done wrong. Above all, whenever you blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For plainly the wrong is yours, whether you trusted that a person with such a disposition would keep faith, or whether, in doing a favour, you did not do it as something finished in itself, nor so as to have received the whole fruit at once from the act itself. For what more do you want when you have done good to a person? Is it not enough that you have done something in accord with your own nature, but you look for a wage for it? As if the eye demanded a return because it sees, or the feet because they walk. For just as these have come into being for one particular thing, and in doing it according to their own build they receive in full what is their own, so too a human being, who is by nature a doer of good, whenever they do some good, or in some other way work together toward things of the middle kind, has done what they were built for, and has what is their own.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *προσκόπτῃς*: Literally to strike or stumble against something. The English takes the settled figurative sense, “take offence”, and keeps it for this verb in 10.30 and 6.20. Other reading: Whenever you stumble against someone’s shamelessness
- *ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἀναίσχυντοι μὴ εἶναι*: “The universe” is the settled rendering of ὁ κόσμος and is kept here because the argument is about what the order of things must contain. “In the world” would be the more natural English. Other reading: for there to be no shameless people in the world
- *τὸν ἀγνώμονα*: ἀγνώμων has a wide range: without consideration, unfeeling, unfair, senseless, also ungrateful. The English reads “unfeeling”, the sense that gentleness best answers, and keeps “ungrateful” for ἀχάριστος later in the passage. Other reading: against the inconsiderate person (or: the ungrateful person)
- *μεταδιδάσκειν*: The verb means to teach someone so that they change their view. It is rendered “teach … to think otherwise” here and “teach otherwise” where it recurs in this section. Other reading: you are free to re-educate the one who has gone astray
- *πᾶς γὰρ ὁ ἁμαρτάνων ἀφαμαρτάνει τοῦ προκειμένου*: A play on words: ἁμαρτάνω (to do wrong) originally means to miss a mark, and ἀφαμαρτάνω is to miss it altogether. τὸ προκείμενον is what is set in front of a person, their target. The English cannot repeat the one root. Other reading: for everyone who errs errs from the mark set before them
- *ἡ διάνοιά σου*: The settled rendering of διάνοια is “thought”, with “mind” where the faculty is meant. Here it is the faculty that could be made worse, so “mind”. Other reading: that was going to make your thought worse
- *ἐνταῦθα πᾶσαν τὴν ὑπόστασιν ἔχει*: “There” points back to the mind: what is bad and harmful for you exists only in it. The Greek says only “there”; the English adds no noun but puts “it is there that” first, so that the word is heard to point back to the mind. Other reading: has its whole existence here, in the mind
- *ἀφορμὰς ἐκ τοῦ λόγου*: ἀφορμαί are starting points or resources. λόγος is taken as the faculty of reason, as in the settled list; it could also be “the argument”, meaning the reasoning just given. Other reading: you did have starting points from the argument
- *ἐπίστευσας ὅτι τὴν πίστιν φυλάξει*: The Greek repeats one root three times: ἄπιστος (faithless), ἐπίστευσας (you trusted), πίστιν (faith, trust). English needs “trusted” for the verb, so the chain is only partly visible. Other reading: you had faith that such a person would keep faith
- *τὴν χάριν διδοὺς μὴ καταληκτικῶς ἔδωκας*: χάρις (a favour) is the root of ἀχάριστος (ungrateful: one who returns no favour). καταληκτικῶς is a rare adverb, from the verb “to come to an end”; it is taken as giving in a way that ends with the giving and looks for nothing further. Other reading: in bestowing the kindness you did not bestow it once and for all
- *ἀπέχει τὸ ἴδιον*: ἀπέχω is the word used on receipts: to have received payment in full. It answers the “wage” and “return” just before, so the English reads “receive in full what is their own”. Other reading: they have their own payment in full
- *εὐεργετικὸς πεφυκώς*: εὐεργετικός, apt to do good to others, comes twice in the sentence. The English has “a doer of good” and “do some good”, so that the one word is heard both times. Other reading: who is by nature beneficent, whenever they do something beneficent
- *εἰς τὰ μέσα συνεργητικὸν*: τὰ μέσα, “the middle things”, is taken as the Stoic name for things that are neither good nor bad in themselves, such as health and wealth, toward which people can work together. It could instead mean what lies in the middle between people, the common interest. Other reading: or in some other way contribute to the common good
- *κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν κατασκευὴν*: κατασκευή (how a thing is constructed) and κατεσκεύασται at the end are the same word; the English has “build” and “built”. The usual philosophical English is “constitution”. Other reading: acting according to their own constitution … what they were constituted for

</details>

## Book 10

### 10.1

Will you ever, soul, be good and simple and one and bare, plainer to see than the body wrapped round you? Will you ever taste the loving and affectionate disposition? Will you ever be full and in need of nothing, longing for nothing and desiring nothing, whether living or lifeless, for the enjoyment of pleasures? Nor time in which to enjoy them longer? Nor a place or a country or a mild climate? Nor people who suit you well? But will you be content with your present state and take pleasure in all that is present, and persuade yourself that all things are present to you, from the gods, that all things are well with you and will be well, all that pleases them and all that they are going to give for the preservation of the perfect living being, the good and just and beautiful one, which begets all things and holds them together and surrounds them and takes them into itself as they are dissolved for the birth of others like them? Will you ever be such as to live as a fellow citizen with gods and human beings in such a way that you neither find any fault with them nor are condemned by them?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὦ ψυχή*: Marcus addresses his soul directly, and every “you” in the passage is the soul (the Greek forms are feminine). The Greek has no “my”. Other reading: Will you ever, my soul, be good
- *φανερωτέρα*: “More visible”, “more manifest” than the body around it: the soul is to show more plainly than its covering. Other reading: more in the open than the body that surrounds you
- *τῆς φιλητικῆς καὶ στερκτικῆς διαθέσεως*: Two near synonyms for a state inclined to love: φιλέω is the general word, στέργω the affection of family. The English has “loving and affectionate”. Other reading: the state of one who loves and cherishes
- *ἐν ᾧ ἐπὶ μακρότερον ἀπολαύσεις*: ἀπολαύσεις here can be the verb “you will enjoy” or again the noun “enjoyments” of the line before. It is taken as the verb. Other reading: Nor time for longer enjoyments?
- *ἀέρων εὐκρασίας*: Literally “a good blending of airs”, the Greek way of saying a temperate climate. Other reading: or a good mixture of airs
- *ἀνθρώπων εὐαρμοστίας*: Literally “a good fitting together of people”. It can be people who fit well with you, or harmony among people. The same root is “well fitted” in 6.16. Other reading: Nor harmony among the people around you?
- *ἀλλὰ ἀρκεσθήσῃ*: The Greek punctuation carries the question through to the end of this long sentence, so “but will you be content …?” is still asked, not asserted. Other reading: but you will be content with your present state
- *πάντα σοι παρὰ τῶν θεῶν πάρεστι*: Literally “all things are present to you from the gods”. The main verb is “are present”, repeating the word used twice just before, so the English says that the soul has everything, and has it from the gods. The words can also be heard as a statement only about where its present things come from. Other reading: that all you have comes from the gods
- *ὅσα φίλον αὐτοῖς*: φίλον with the dative is the idiom “it pleases them”; the adjective is singular beside the plural “all that”. A verb such as “to give” can be supplied from the next clause. Other reading: all that is dear to them
- *ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ*: σωτηρία is keeping a thing safe and whole. “Preservation” is used because “safety” suggests rescue from a danger. Other reading: for the safety of the perfect living being
- *τοῦ τελείου ζῴου*: “The perfect living being” is the universe, thought of as one living thing. ζῷον is the ordinary word for an animal; here “living being” reads better. Other reading: the perfect animal
- *συμπολιτεύεσθαι*: “To live as a fellow citizen with”: the universe as a city shared by gods and people. Other reading: to share one community with gods and human beings

</details>

### 10.2

Watch what your nature asks for, taking yourself as something governed by nature only. Then do it and accept it, unless your nature as an animal is going to be put in a worse state. Next you must watch what your nature as an animal asks for, and all of this is to be taken up, unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state. And what is rational is by that very fact also civic. Using these rules, then, do not busy yourself with anything further.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὡς ὑπὸ φύσεως μόνον διοικουμένου*: φύσις here has its narrow Stoic sense: the power of growth and nourishment that governs plants, below the soul that governs animals. So the first step is what you need simply as a growing body. ὡς with the participle means “regarded as”, not a statement that this is all you are. Other reading: as one governed only by the nature of a growing thing
- *ποίει αὐτὸ καὶ προσίεσο*: προσίεσο is “let it come to you, admit it”. Other reading: do it and allow it
- *ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις*: ζῷον is a being with soul and sensation, one step above a thing that only grows. The English reads “animal” here so that the three steps stay apart: a growing thing, an animal, a rational animal. In other passages of this section, where no such ladder is in play, the word is “living being”. Other reading: your nature as a living being
- *χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαί*: Literally “is going to be disposed worse”. Other reading: is going to be the worse for it
- *ἔστι δὲ τὸ λογικὸν εὐθὺς καὶ πολιτικόν*: εὐθύς is “straight away, immediately”: being rational brings being civic with it at once. πολιτικός is “civic” as in 3.6. Other reading: and the rational is at once also made for a city
- *μηδὲν περιεργάζου*: περιεργάζομαι is to do more than is needed, to fuss, or to meddle in what is not one’s business. The English takes the prefix as “beyond what these rules ask”. Other reading: do not fuss over anything

</details>

### 10.3

Everything that happens either happens in such a way that you are fitted by nature to bear it, or in such a way that you are not fitted by nature to bear it. So if it happens to you in a way you are fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it, but bear it as you are fitted by nature to do. And if in a way you are not fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it: for it will perish once it has used you up. Remember, though, that you are fitted by nature to bear everything that it rests with your own judgment to make bearable and endurable, through the impression that it is good for you, or is your duty, to do so.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πέφυκας*: “You are so made by nature.” The word comes six times and one phrase is kept for it each time. Other reading: you are naturally able to bear it
- *φέρειν. μὴ δυσχέραινε*: The text given has a full stop after φέρειν where the sense needs a comma; the English reads one sentence. Other reading: bear, do not be annoyed
- *φθαρήσεται γάρ σε ἀπαναλῶσαν*: Literally “for it will be destroyed, having used you up”: what cannot be borne ends with the one it destroys. Other reading: for it will come to an end when it has consumed you
- *ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει ἐστὶ τῇ σῇ*: “It is up to your judgment”: the same construction as “in your power” (ἐπὶ σοί) elsewhere. Other reading: which it is in the power of your judgment to make bearable
- *φορητὸν καὶ ἀνεκτὸν*: Two near-synonyms. The first is from the same root as “bear” (φέρειν). Other reading: bearable and tolerable
- *κατὰ φαντασίαν τοῦ συμφέρειν ἢ καθήκειν*: συμφέρειν (“to be good for”) echoes φέρειν (“to bear”), a play English cannot keep. καθήκειν is the Stoic word for what it is appropriate or due for one to do; the English has “is your duty”. Other reading: by picturing it as to your advantage, or as fitting for you
- *τοῦτο ποιεῖν*: “To do this” most naturally means to make the thing bearable, that is, to bear it. Other reading: to act so

</details>

### 10.4

If someone is mistaken, teach them kindly and show them what they are failing to see. But if you cannot, blame yourself, or not even yourself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *σφάλλεται*: Literally “is tripped up”, so “is mistaken”. The Greek names no subject; the English supplies “someone”. Other reading: If someone trips
- *διδάσκειν εὐμενῶς*: The commands are infinitives with no person; “you cannot” in the next sentence shows who is addressed, so the English uses imperatives. Other reading: the thing is to teach kindly
- *τὸ παρορώμενον*: “What is being overlooked”: what the person is failing to see, as in 11.13. Other reading: point out what has been overlooked

</details>

### 10.5

Whatever happens to you was being made ready for you beforehand, from all time, and the interweaving of causes was spinning together, from eternity, both your existence and the happening of this.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐξ αἰῶνος*: Two different expressions are used: this one, “from the age”, and ἐξ ἀιδίου, “from the everlasting”. They are given as “from all time” and “from eternity”. Other reading: from the beginning of time ... from everlasting
- *προκατεσκευάζετο*: A past tense of continuing action, with a prefix meaning “beforehand”: “was being prepared in advance”. The verb is the ordinary one for building or fitting something out. The same tense is used for “was spinning”. Other reading: was prepared for you in advance
- *ὑπόστασιν*: Literally “what stands under”: a thing’s real existence, its coming to be something. Other reading: your very being / your substance
- *τὴν τούτου σύμβασιν*: The noun is from the same verb as “happens” at the start. “Of this” is the particular thing that happens to you. Other reading: and this event’s falling to you

</details>

### 10.6

Whether it is atoms or nature, let this first be laid down: that I am a part of the whole, which is governed by nature. Next, that I stand in a kind of kinship to the parts that are of the same kind as I am. For if I remember these things, then insofar as I am a part, I will not be displeased with anything that is allotted from the whole. For nothing that is good for the whole is harmful to the part. For the whole has nothing that is not good for itself. All natures have this in common, but the nature of the universe has this in addition, that it is not even forced by any cause from outside to produce anything harmful to itself. So by remembering that I am a part of a whole of this kind, I will be well pleased with everything that comes about. And insofar as I stand in a kind of kinship to the parts of the same kind, I will do nothing unsocial. Rather I will make those of my own kind my aim, and I will lead my every impulse toward what is good for all in common and lead it away from the opposite. When these things are carried through in this way, life must flow well, just as you would think that a citizen’s life flows well when that citizen goes forward through actions that profit the citizens, and welcomes whatever the city allots.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Εἴτε ἄτομοι εἴτε φύσις*: The Epicurean account (atoms moving at random) against the Stoic one (an ordering nature). The Greek has no verb. The next clause already says the whole is “governed by nature”, which sits oddly with leaving the question open; it is translated as it stands. Other reading: Whether there are atoms or a nature
- *ἔχω πως οἰκείως*: οἰκείως ἔχειν is to be related to something as to what belongs to one’s own household. πως, “in some way”, softens it. Other reading: to be in some way closely bound to
- *τὰ ὁμογενῆ μέρη*: “The parts of the same kind”, or of the same birth. The words “as I am” are supplied. Other reading: the kindred parts
- *οὐδενὶ δυσαρεστήσω*: δυσαρεστεῖν and εὐαρεστεῖν later in the passage are a matched pair; the English reads “displeased” and “well pleased”. Other reading: to resent nothing
- *οὐδὲν γὰρ βλαβερὸν τῷ μέρει ὃ τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρει*: Word order in the Greek: “for nothing is harmful to the part which is good for the whole”. The English turns it round so the relative clause is not misread as describing the part. συμφέρει is “is good for” by the glossary; in τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον below, “what is good for all in common”, the words “for all” are supplied. Other reading: for nothing harms the part that benefits the whole
- *ἀκοινώνητον*: The negative of κοινωνικός, “social”: an act that takes no share in the common life. The Greek answers it at once with κοινῇ, “in common”, an echo the English does not keep. Other reading: nothing that breaks the common bond
- *στοχάσομαι τῶν ὁμογενῶν*: στοχάζομαι is to aim at a target, and so to have something in view; the English keeps the picture of aiming without the sound of an attack. The genitive may be masculine (those of the same kind) or neuter (the parts of the same kind), and the possessive is supplied. Other reading: to have regard for the parts of the same kind
- *τούτων δὲ οὕτως περαινομένων*: Glossary rendering, “carried through”. Other reading: When this is accomplished in this way
- *εὐροεῖν*: “To flow well”. From memory, unchecked: “a good flow of life” is an early Stoic description of happiness. The image is kept. Other reading: life must go smoothly
- *ἐπινοήσειας*: The passage is in the first person, but this verb is second person, “you would think”, and is kept so. The citizen is masculine in the Greek but stands for any citizen, so the English avoids “he”. Other reading: just as one would think

</details>

### 10.7

The parts of the whole, all that are by nature contained by the universe, must perish; but let “perish” be said in the sense of “be altered”. Now if this is by nature both bad and necessary for them, the whole would not be well managed, with its parts going into alteration and built in various ways for perishing. For did nature itself set out to treat its own parts badly, and to make them both liable to fall into what is bad and bound by necessity to fall into what is bad, or did such things come about without nature noticing? For both are unbelievable. And if someone were to leave nature out of it and explain these things by the way they naturally are, even so it would be ridiculous to say that the parts of the whole are naturally such as to change, and at the same time to be surprised or annoyed as though at something happening against nature, especially when the dissolution is into the things out of which each is put together. For it is either a scattering of the elements out of which it was compounded, or a turning of the solid into the earthy and of the breath-like into the airy, so that these too are taken back up into the reason of the whole, whether the whole is burned up in fire at each cycle or renewed by everlasting exchanges.
