And do not picture the solid and the breath-like as the ones that date from the first birth. For all of this took its inflow yesterday and the day before, from food and from the air drawn in. So what changes is this that it took in, not what your mother bore. But suppose that this binds you very closely to that individually qualified thing, which, I think, has no bearing on what is being said now.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *λεγέσθω δὲ τοῦτο σημαντικῶς τοῦ ἀλλοιοῦσθαι*: Literally “let this be said as signifying being altered”. The sentence fixes the sense of φθείρεσθαι for the rest of the chapter; the English repeats “perish” in quotation marks so that the reader sees which word is being defined. Other reading: but let this be said in a way that signifies being altered
- *διαφόρως*: The adverb can mean “in different ways” or “to an outstanding degree”. The English takes the first: the parts are built for perishing in their several ways, which the chapter goes on to list (scattering, turning into earth, turning into air). Other reading: and built above all for perishing
- *κακοῦν*: The verb is formed from κακόν, “bad”, which stands beside it twice in the same sentence and once in the sentence before. “Bad” and “badly” are kept throughout so that the repetition is heard; “harm” would be more natural English for the verb. Other reading: set out to harm its own parts
- *ἀφέμενος τῆς φύσεως κατὰ τὸ πεφυκέναι*: A play on φύσις (nature as the power that orders things) and πεφυκέναι (to be so by nature). The person imagined drops nature as an agent and says only that things are naturally like this. “Naturally” is used for πεφυκέναι both times it comes, because the argument ends by setting it against παρὰ φύσιν, “against nature”. Other reading: dropping the term “nature” and explaining these things by the way they are constituted
- *θαυμάζειν ἣ δυσχεραίνειν*: ἣ is read as ἢ, “or” (a slip of the digitised text). θαυμάζειν covers both “be surprised” and “wonder at”; the context of complaint points to surprise. Other reading: to wonder or to be displeased
- *τοῦ δὲ πνευματικοῦ εἰς τὸ ἀερῶδες*: τὸ πνευματικόν is what in a living thing is of the nature of πνεῦμα, breath, the Stoic vital breath. “The breath-like” pairs with “the solid”. Other reading: and of the part that is spirit into the airy
- *εἰς τὸν τοῦ ὅλου λόγον*: λόγος here is the reason that governs the whole and from which things are generated, into which the elements are taken back; it is not “the reason for” the whole. The glossary’s “reason” is kept. Other reading: into the generative principle of the whole
- *εἴτε κατὰ περίοδον ἐκπυρουμένου εἴτε ἀιδίοις ἀμοιβαῖς ἀνανεουμένου*: The two genitive participles agree with τοῦ ὅλου, so “the whole” is supplied as their subject. The first alludes to the Stoic teaching that the universe is consumed by fire at the end of each cycle; the second is the alternative of a universe that lasts for ever by exchange. Other reading: whether it is periodically turned to fire or renewed by everlasting exchanges
- *ἐχθὲς καὶ τρίτην ἡμέραν*: Literally “yesterday and the third day”, an idiom for “very recently”. The literal shape is kept. Other reading: only the other day
- *ἐκείνῳ σε λίαν προσπλέκει τῷ ἰδίως ποιῷ*: The verb “binds” has no subject expressed in the Greek, and the text of the sentence is thought doubtful (from memory, unchecked). The English supplies “this”, the matter recently taken in, from the sentence before; the subject could also be what the mother bore. τὸ ἰδίως ποιόν is the Stoic term for the individual as marked by a quality peculiar to it, which persists while its matter changes. Other reading: But suppose that what your mother bore ties you too closely to the individually qualified thing, which has no bearing on the present argument

</details>

### 10.8

Having given yourself these names: good, modest, truthful, clear-minded, like-minded, high-minded, take care that you never come to bear other names; and if you do lose these names, go back to them quickly. Remember that “clear-minded” was to mean for you a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded; “like-minded”, the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns; and “high-minded”, the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind. So if you keep yourself in these names, without craving to have others call you by them, you will be a different person and will enter a different life. For to go on being such as you have been up to now, and to be torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life, someone like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites. So put yourself aboard these few names, and if you can stay on them, stay, like someone who has moved to some Islands of the Blessed. But if you sense that you are falling away and are not prevailing, go away with a good heart to some corner where you will prevail, or even leave life altogether, not in anger, but simply, freely and modestly, having at least done this one thing, and only this, in your life: to leave it in this way. Toward remembering the names, though, it will help you greatly to remember the gods, and that what they want is not to be flattered, but for all rational beings to become like them, and for the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἔμφρων, σύμφρων, ὑπέρφρων*: Three words built on one root (phron, “mind, thinking”): emphron, “in one’s mind, sensible”; symphron, “of one mind with”; hyperphron, “with mind above”, usually a word of blame (“haughty”) that is here turned to a good sense. Three words ending in “minded” are used so that the play shows; the definitions that follow carry the meaning, and “high-minded” is not meant in its ordinary English sense. Other reading: sensible, in agreement, above it all
- *αἰδήμων*: The word covers a sense of shame, self-respect and respect for others. The English reads “modest”, and “modestly” for the adverb near the end. Other reading: self-respecting
- *μετονομάζῃ*: The form can be passive (“are renamed”) or middle (“rename yourself”). “Come to bear other names” leaves open who does the renaming, as the Greek does. Other reading: take care that you never change your names
- *κἂν ἀπολλύῃς ταῦτα τὰ ὀνόματα, καὶ ταχέως ἐπάνιθι*: The second “and” in the Greek sits awkwardly before “go back quickly”. It is read as marking the main clause (“then too”) and left untranslated; it may be a fault in the text. Other reading: and if you lose these names, then also go back to them quickly
- *διαληπτικὴν ἐπίστασιν καὶ τὸ ἀπαρενθύμητον*: The first phrase is “attention that distinguishes”, stopping over each thing and telling it apart. The last word is rare: the state of not letting something slip past unconsidered. Other reading: an attention that takes each thing apart, and freedom from carelessness
- *τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως*: Literally “the common nature”, the nature shared by all things, which is the nature of the whole. The literal phrase is kept. Other reading: what the nature of the whole assigns
- *τὴν ὑπέρτασιν τοῦ φρονοῦντος μορίου ὑπὲρ*: The Greek explains the name by its own parts: “high-minded” is the stretching high (hyper) of the part that has mind (phron) above (hyper again) the things listed. “Lifting high”, “has mind” and “above” are chosen so that the explanation can be heard in English. “Above” is repeated where the Greek has it once. Other reading: the raising of the part that thinks above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh
- *λείαν ἣ τραχεῖαν κίνησιν τῆς σαρκὸς*: “Smooth or rough movement of the flesh” is a way of saying pleasure and pain. The image is kept. The second word as given is a slip for “or”. Other reading: above pleasure or pain in the flesh
- *ἀναισθήτου*: The word is “without perception”: dull, not noticing what is happening to oneself. “Senseless” is used, and “sense” for the verb of the same root further on (“if you sense that you are falling away”). Other reading: someone thoroughly dull
- *φιλοψύχου*: Literally “life-loving”, always said with blame: holding on to life at any price. Other reading: cowardly
- *θηριομάχοις*: Men who fight wild animals in the arena. The English reads “beast-fighters”. Other reading: men who fight wild beasts in the arena
- *παραβληθησόμενοι τοιοῦτοι*: A future participle: “going to be thrown, such as they are”. It may state simply what awaits them or, more bitterly, what they are being kept for; “to be thrown” leaves both open. Other reading: though they will be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites
- *ἐμβίβασον*: The verb is the regular word for putting someone on board a ship. With the islands that follow, the picture of a boat is kept. Other reading: so set yourself upon these few names
- *μακάρων τινὰς νήσους*: The Islands of the Blessed: in Greek story, the far-off islands where favoured heroes live on after death without toil. Other reading: to certain islands of the blessed
- *ἐκπίπτεις καὶ οὐ περικρατεῖς*: The first verb is “fall out, fall away”; it is also the usual word for being driven into exile or cast ashore, which fits the picture of a settler. The second verb and the later “you will prevail” share a root, so “prevail” is used for both. Other reading: that you are being cast out and are not keeping the mastery
- *ἕν γε τοῦτο μόνον πράξας*: Literally “having done this one thing only, at least”. The Greek says both “at least” and “only”, and both are kept. Other reading: having done this one thing at any rate in your life
- *καὶ εἶναι τὴν μὲν συκῆν τὰ συκῆς ποιοῦσαν*: This is read as still depending on “they want”: the gods want the fig tree to be doing a fig tree’s work, and so on. It can also be read as depending on “remember”, a statement of what makes each thing what it is. Other reading: and that it is doing the work of a fig tree that makes a fig tree, of a dog a dog, of a bee a bee, of a human being a human being

</details>

### 10.9

Farce, war, panic, numbness, slavery: day by day those sacred principles of yours will be wiped out, all those that you picture without study of nature and let go by. But everything must be looked at and done in such a way that at one and the same time the practical side is carried out and the contemplative side is at work, and that the self-assurance which comes from knowledge of each thing is kept, unnoticed but not hidden. For when will you enjoy simplicity? When dignity? When the recognition, in each case, of what the thing is in its substance, what place it has in the universe, how long it is in its nature to last, what it is put together from, who can have it, and who can give it and take it away?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μῖμος, πόλεμος, πτοία, νάρκα, δουλεία*: Five bare nouns with no verb. μῖμος is the mime, a low stage farce; πτοία is fright or flutter; νάρκα is numbness. How the list connects with what follows is left to the reader, as in the Greek. Other reading: A stage farce, a war, a fright, a stupor, a slavery
- *ἀπαλείψεταί*: Future middle, read here as passive, “will be wiped out”, with the principles as subject. Other reading: day by day it will wipe out those sacred principles of yours
- *ὁπόσα ἀφυσιολογήτως φαντάζῃ καὶ παραπέμπεις*: The text here is doubted, and ἀφυσιολογήτως may be an editor’s correction (from memory, unchecked). As given: “all those you picture without study of nature and send on their way”, with the relative attached to “principles”. It can also be taken loosely, of everything pictured in that way, and παραπέμπεις can mean let pass, dismiss or neglect. Other reading: wiped out, whenever you form impressions without study of nature and let them pass
- *τὸ πρακτικὸν ἅμα συντελεῖσθαι καὶ ἅμα τὸ θεωρητικὸν ἐνεργεῖσθαι*: Literally “the practical” and “the contemplative”: either the two sides of a task or the two powers of the person. The English reads “side”. The Greek says “at once” twice, which “at one and the same time” carries. Other reading: that the power to act is brought to completion and the power to contemplate is exercised at the same time
- *αὔθαδες*: Usually a bad word, “self-willed, stubborn”. Here it is good: the self-assurance that knowledge gives. Other reading: the confidence
- *λανθάνον, οὐχὶ κρυπτόμενον*: “Escaping notice, not being hidden”: not put on show, but not concealed either. Other reading: unobtrusive, yet not concealed
- *γνωρίσεως*: γνώρισις is getting to know a thing, recognising it in the single case. It is a different word from ἐπιστήμη, “knowledge”, just above. Other reading: the knowledge of each thing
- *κατ’ οὐσίαν*: οὐσία is both “being, essence” and the Stoic “substance”, the stuff of things. The English reads “in its substance”, as in 3.11. Other reading: in its essence
- *τίσι δύναται ὑπάρχειν*: The dative can be “to whom it can belong” or “to what things it can belong”. It is taken of persons, because “who can give it” comes next. Other reading: what it can belong to

</details>

### 10.10

A little spider thinks a great deal of itself for having hunted down a fly; someone else for a little hare, another for a sprat in a hand net, another for little boars, another for bears, another for Sarmatians. For are these not robbers, if you examine their principles?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἀράχνιον*: A diminutive of the word for spider; the same form can also mean a spider’s web. Other reading: A spider
- *μέγα φρονεῖ*: Literally “thinks big”: is proud. Other reading: is proud
- *ἄλλος δὲ λαγίδιον*: “Another” is masculine, so a person and not another spider, which is why the English reads “someone else” the first time. The participle “having hunted” is carried over from the first clause. The hare is a diminutive. Other reading: another man when he has caught a leveret
- *ὑποχῇ ἀφύην*: The first word is a kind of fishing net held under the catch; the second is small fry, a named tiny fish such as a sprat or an anchovy. Other reading: an anchovy in a scoop net
- *συίδια*: A diminutive of the word for pig or boar. Among things hunted it is presumably wild boar. Other reading: piglets
- *Σαρμάτας*: A people beyond the Danube against whom Marcus himself fought as emperor, so the last hunter is himself.
- *οὗτοι γὰρ οὐ λῃσταί*: There is no verb, and the particle “for” opens the question. The noun covers robbers, bandits and pirates. Other reading: Why, are these not bandits
- *τὰ δόγματα*: “The principles”, the Stoic word for the settled beliefs a person acts on. The Greek has “the”; the English reads “their”. Other reading: if you examine the beliefs behind it

</details>

### 10.11a

How all things change into one another: get yourself a method for contemplating it, attend to it constantly, and train yourself in this field. For nothing so produces greatness of mind.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *θεωρητικὴν μέθοδον*: “A method of contemplation”; the “how” clause that opens the sentence is its object. θεωρητικός is the word rendered “contemplative” in 10.9. Other reading: Acquire a systematic way of observing how all things change into one another
- *περὶ τοῦτο τὸ μέρος*: Literally “about this part”: this department of philosophy or of study. The English reads “field”. Other reading: in this part
- *οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως μεγαλοφροσύνης ποιητικόν*: The same words as in 3.11. The section cut falls here; the chapter goes on in the Greek. Other reading: for nothing is so apt to make a mind great

</details>

### 10.11b

Such a person has stripped off the body and, having taken in that very soon they will have to leave all these things behind as they go from among people, has given their whole self over: to justice in what they do themselves, and to the nature of the whole in the other things, those that happen. What anyone will say or think about them, or do against them, they do not even let into their mind, being content with these two things: if they themselves act justly in what is being done now, and if they love what is being allotted to them now. They have let go of all busyness and all eager pursuits, and want nothing else than to keep a straight course right through, by way of the law, and to follow god, who keeps a straight course right through.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐξεδύσατο τὸ σῶμα*: The passage starts in mid-chapter and the verb has no stated subject. “Such a person” is supplied: it points back to the chapter’s first sentence, not in this passage, which is about training in the study of how all things change into one another. “They” is used because the Greek names no one and its masculine forms are the general ones; the image is of taking off a garment. Other reading: He has stripped off the body
- *ὅσον οὐδέπω*: An idiom, literally “all but now”: very soon, at any moment. Other reading: any moment now
- *ἀνῆκεν ὅλον ἑαυτὸν*: ἀνίημι is “let go, hand over, dedicate”, and ὅλον ἑαυτόν is “the whole of himself”, here “their whole self”. The past forms here and below (ἐξεδύσατο, ἀφῆκε) are put as English perfects, because the present verbs beside them describe the resulting state. Other reading: gave himself up wholly
- *ὑπολήψεται*: The verb belonging to ὑπόληψις, for which the glossary gives “judgment”. Here it is another person’s opinion of the one described, and “judge about” is not natural English, so “think”. περὶ αὐτοῦ (“about them”) goes with both “say” and “think”. Other reading: or what judgment anyone will form of them
- *οὐδ’ εἰς νοῦν βάλλεται*: Literally “does not even cast it into the mind”. “Mind” is kept for νοῦς. Other reading: does not even give it a thought
- *εἰ αὐτὸς δικαιοπραγεῖ τὸ νῦν πρασσόμενον*: After “content with these two things” the Greek has “if”, not “that”, and the English keeps it. The second “if” repeats the one εἰ, which governs both verbs. Other reading: that they themselves act justly in what is being done now
- *ἀσχολίας δὲ πάσας καὶ σπουδὰς*: ἀσχολία is being occupied, having no leisure; σπουδή is eager effort or a thing pursued in earnest. πάσας (“all”) stands once in the Greek and is taken with both nouns. Other reading: all occupations and strivings
- *εὐθεῖαν περαίνειν διὰ τοῦ νόμου*: εὐθεῖαν is “a straight [road]”, with the noun left out, and περαίνειν is to carry a thing through to its finish. The glossary’s “carried through” does not sit with “course” in English, so “keep … right through” stands for it, in the same words both times. διὰ τοῦ νόμου could be “through” or “by means of” the law. Other reading: to travel a straight road to its finish through the law
- *εὐθεῖαν περαίνοντι ἕπεσθαι τῷ θεῷ*: περαίνοντι is dative and agrees with τῷ θεῷ, so it is god who keeps the straight course and the person who follows. From memory, unchecked, this echoes Plato’s Laws, book 4, where god goes straight to his goal and justice follows. Other reading: to follow god as he travels a straight road to its finish

</details>

### 10.12a

What need is there of guessing, when you are free to look at what has to be done, and, if you see it clearly, to go that way with good will and without turning back; and if you do not see it clearly, to hold off and use the best advisers; and if some other things stand in the way of this, to go forward as present means allow, in a considered way, holding to what appears just? For to reach this is best, since failure, at any rate, is falling away from this.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὑπονοίας*: ὑπόνοια is a surmise, a suspicion, a guess at what lies under the surface. It could be suspicion of other people or anxious conjecture about how things will turn out. The English has “guessing”, since the word is set against looking at what has to be done. Other reading: What need is there of suspicion
- *συνορᾷς*: “See it all together”, take it in at a glance. The English has “see it clearly”. Other reading: if you can see the whole of it
- *ἐπέχειν*: To hold back, to suspend action or judgment. Other reading: to suspend judgment
- *κατὰ τὰς παρούσας ἀφορμὰς*: ἀφορμή is a starting point, and so the means or opening one has to act from. The English has “as present means allow”. Other reading: to go forward from the openings that are there
- *λελογισμένως*: An adverb from the verb “to reckon, to reason”: in a reasoned or considered way. It describes how one goes forward. Other reading: with reasoning
- *ἥ γε ἀπόπτωσις ἀπὸ τούτου ἐστίν*: Literally “since the falling away, at least, is from this”, which is obscure as given. It is taken to mean that the only failure there is, is failing to hit what is just. From memory, unchecked: editors have doubted the verb and some read a command. Other reading: since if you are to fail, let it be in aiming at this

</details>

### 10.12b

Someone who follows reason in everything is something at once unhurried and quick to move, at once cheerful and composed.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *σχολαῖόν τι*: Neuter predicates with a masculine subject: such a person is “something” unhurried, and so on. σχολαῖος is leisurely, unhurried, sometimes slow. Other reading: something leisurely
- *εὐκίνητόν*: Easily moved: quick to act, nimble. It is set in deliberate contrast with “unhurried”. Other reading: ready to move
- *φαιδρὸν*: Bright, beaming, cheerful. “Cheerful” is used because “bright”, said of a person, would be heard as “clever”. Other reading: radiant
- *συνεστηκὸς*: Literally “standing together”: firm, compact, collected. Other reading: steady
- *ὁ τῷ λόγῳ κατὰ πᾶν ἑπόμενος*: The passage is the close of a chapter. The masculine article is generic, so the English has “someone who”. Other reading: the man who follows reason in everything

</details>

### 10.13

Ask yourself as soon as you come out of sleep: will it make any difference to you if what is just and right is blamed by someone else? It will not. Have you forgotten that these people who snort and prance in their praise and blame of others are like this in bed and like this at table, and what things they do, what they run from, what they chase, what they steal, what they seize, not with hands and feet but with the most precious part of themselves, the part that becomes, when it wants to, good faith, a sense of shame, truth, law, a good spirit?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πυνθάνεσθαι ἑαυτοῦ*: The Greek is an infinitive used as an instruction (“to ask oneself”), but the question that follows is in the second person (σοι). The English is in the second person throughout. Other reading: One should ask oneself, as soon as one comes out of sleep
- *ψέγηται*: The English translates the verb as given, “is blamed”. From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts have γένηται (“is done”) here and ψέγηται is an editor’s correction; with γένηται the question is whether it matters who does the right thing. Other reading: if what is just and right is done by someone else
- *φρυαττόμενοι*: The verb is used of a spirited horse snorting and prancing, and then of people giving themselves airs. “Snort and prance” keeps the animal image; the one Greek verb covers both movements. Other reading: who give themselves airs
- *τοιοῦτοι μὲν*: Literally “are such in bed, such at table”: the word points at what the reader already knows about them without saying it. The English points in the same way with “like this”. Other reading: are what they are in bed and what they are at table
- *ἐπὶ τῆς κλίνης*: The word means a bed and also the couch on which one reclined to eat. Paired with “table” it could be either; the English takes it as the bed. Other reading: on the dining couch
- *ὃ γίνεται ὅταν θέλῃ*: As given, the relative is the subject: the most precious part itself becomes good faith, shame and the rest “when it wants”. The subject of “wants” could also be the person. From memory, unchecked: some editors print a dative here, giving “by which there come to be”. Other reading: the part by which, when a person wants, there come to be good faith, a sense of shame, truth, law, a good spirit
- *πίστις*: The word covers both trusting and being worthy of trust. In a list of good qualities it is the keeping of faith, so the English reads “good faith”. Other reading: trust
- *ἀγαθὸς δαίμων*: A daimon is the divine spirit that attends a person; to have a good one is the root sense of the Greek word for happiness (eudaimonia). The English reads “a good spirit” and adds nothing to say what kind of spirit. Other reading: a good guardian spirit; or: happiness

</details>

### 10.14

To nature, which gives everything and takes everything back, the person who is educated and modest says: “Give what you want. Take back what you want.” And that person says this not in bold defiance, but only in obedience to it and good will toward it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *πεπαιδευμένος καὶ αἰδήμων*: One article, so one person with both qualities. πεπαιδευμένος is the ordinary word for “educated”, and also “trained”. αἰδήμων is having a sense of shame and respect; “modest” is taken because the next sentence sets this person against over-boldness. Other reading: the person who has been trained and is respectful
- *ἀπολαμβανούσῃ*: ἀπολαμβάνω is to take back or receive back what one is owed, as a lender does. The same verb returns in ἀπόλαβε, so “take back” is used both times. Other reading: which gives all things and receives them again
- *δὸς ὃ θέλεις*: θέλεις is “want”, “wish” or “will”. “Want” is kept, as for ὅπου θέλεις in 8.45a in this section. Other reading: Give what you will; take back what you will
- *καταθρασυνόμενος*: A rare verb built on the word for over-boldness, with a prefix that means “against”: making oneself bold against someone. It can be resistance or mere show. The English reads “bold defiance”, which the sentence sets against obeying; no object is expressed. Other reading: not out of bravado; not as a show of boldness
- *πειθαρχῶν μόνον*: μόνον stands after “obeying” and can limit that word alone or both participles, or mean “simply”. The English keeps “only” and puts it before both. Other reading: but simply obeying it, and with good will toward it
- *εὐνοῶν αὐτῇ*: εὐνοέω is to be well disposed or loyal to someone. αὐτῇ is nature, a feminine noun in Greek, and goes with both participles. “It” is written because “her” would add a personification the grammar alone does not require, though nature is here spoken to as “you”. Other reading: obeying her and loyal to her

</details>

### 10.15

What is left now is little. Live as on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether there or here, if a person, wherever they are, lives in the universe as in a city. Let human beings see, let them study, a true human being living according to nature. If they do not bear it, let them kill that person. For that is better than to live that way.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ ὑπολειπόμενον τοῦτο*: Literally “this that is left”: of life, which the Greek does not say. “Now” stands for “this”. Other reading: The time you have left is short
- *ὡς ἐν ὄρει*: Translated as it stands. The Greek does not say whether the mountain stands for living apart or for living in full view; the next sentences fit the second, “there or here” fits the first. Other reading: as if you were away in the hills
- *ἐάν τις πανταχοῦ ὡς ἐν πόλει τῷ κόσμῳ*: The clause has no verb in the Greek as given. “Lives” is supplied from “live” just before; whether a word has dropped out or the verb is simply understood cannot be told from this text. πανταχοῦ (“everywhere”) is taken apart, as “wherever they are”, and τῷ κόσμῳ shares the “in” of “in a city”: the universe treated as one’s city. Other reading: if a person lives everywhere in the universe as in a city
- *ἱστορησάτωσαν*: “Inquire into, examine, get to know by looking.” Other reading: let them look closely at
- *οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἄνθρωπον ἀληθινὸν*: The same word stands twice side by side, so “human beings” and “human being”. ἀληθινός is “true, real, genuine”. Other reading: let people see a real person
- *εἰ μὴ φέρουσιν, ἀποκτεινάτωσαν*: Neither verb has an object in the Greek. “It” and “that person” are supplied; “him” is avoided, since ἄνθρωπον does not single out a man. Other reading: If they do not bear him, let them kill him
- *κρεῖττον γὰρ ἢ οὕτως ζῆν*: “Better than to live so.” “So” is open: living as those people live, or living on in the way they would allow. “That way” keeps it open while pointing away from the life according to nature just described. Other reading: for that is better than living as they do

</details>

### 10.16

No longer to discuss at all what kind of man the good man is, but to be such a man.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *διαλέγεσθαι*: To converse, discuss or argue a question, the word for philosophical talk. It is an infinitive used as a note of what is to be done, with no person, and the English keeps it so. Other reading: Stop arguing altogether about what the good man is like, and be one
- *τὸν ἀγαθὸν ἄνδρα*: The Greek has the word for a man, not the general word for a person, so the English keeps “man”. Other reading: the good person
- *Μηκέθ’ ὅλως*: “No longer” and “at all” together: the discussing is to stop entirely. Other reading: Not any more, in any way

</details>

### 10.17–18

An impression, constantly, of the whole of eternity and the whole of substance, and that all particular things are, set against substance, a fig seed, and set against time, a turn of a drill.

Fixing attention on each object, think of it as already dissolving and in change, and as it were in the course of rotting or scattering, or in whatever way it is the nature of each thing, so to speak, to die.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *συνεχῶς φαντασία*: The sentence has no verb: it is a note to self, “[have] constantly an impression of”. The English leaves it verbless. φαντασία is the Stoic term, “impression”. Other reading: Keep constantly before you the picture of the whole of eternity
- *τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας*: οὐσία is the stuff of which everything is made, “substance” or “being” or “matter”. “Substance” is used throughout this section. Other reading: and the whole of matter
- *κεγχραμίς*: The tiny seed inside a fig. The image is of something almost too small to see. Other reading: a grain
- *τρυπάνου περιστροφή*: A twist of a borer or drill: an instant of motion. Other reading: the twist of a gimlet
- *τῶν ὑποκειμένων*: Literally “the things that lie under”: either the things presented to one, the things at hand, or more generally existing things. “Object” is meant to cover both. Other reading: each of the things in front of you
- *ἐφιστάντα ἐπινοεῖν*: An infinitive used as an instruction, with an accusative participle and no person expressed (“for one who attends to each thing, to think”). The English uses an imperative. ἐφιστάναι is to bring the attention to rest on something. Other reading: One should stop at each thing and think of it
- *ὥσπερ θνῄσκειν*: ὥσπερ softens “to die”, since it is said of things as well as living beings: “to die, as it were”. Earlier οἷον does the same for the rotting and scattering. Other reading: or as each thing is by nature made to die, as it were

</details>

### 10.19

What they are like when eating, sleeping, mating, emptying their bowels, and the rest. Then what they are like when lording it and giving themselves airs, or getting angry and scolding from a position of superiority. Yet a little while ago they were slaves, to how many, and for what sort of things. And in a little while they will be in the same sort of case.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὀχεύοντες*: A word used of male animals covering females. Applied to people it is blunt. Other reading: coupling
- *ἀποπατοῦντες*: Literally “stepping aside”, the ordinary word for relieving the bowels. Other reading: relieving themselves
- *ἀνδρονομούμενοι*: A very rare word of uncertain sense, built from “man” and a root for managing or ruling, and middle or passive in form. “Lording it” is a guess from its parts and from the context of pride, and should not be read as certain. From memory, unchecked: editors doubt the word and have proposed others. Other reading: when playing the man
- *γαυρούμενοι*: To prance or plume oneself, used of a proud horse. Other reading: and strutting
- *ἐξ ὑπεροχῆς ἐπιπλήττοντες*: Literally “rebuking from superiority”: from a higher position. Other reading: and scolding from above
- *ἐδούλευον πόσοις καὶ δι’ οἷα*: The verb is to be a slave. It is probably meant of serving and courting others, not of legal slavery, but the image is kept. “To how many, and for what” is an exclamation inside the sentence. Other reading: they were dancing attendance on how many, and for what ends
- *ἐν τοιούτοις ἔσονται*: Literally “they will be in such things”. The English takes it as pointing back to the slavery just mentioned; it can also point to the bodily state of the opening, or forward to death. Other reading: they will be in such a state

</details>

### 10.20

What the nature of the whole brings to each is good for each, and it is good at the time when nature brings it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Συμφέρει ἑκάστῳ ὃ φέρει ἑκάστῳ*: A play on words: “brings” (φέρει) and “is good for”, literally “brings together” (συμφέρει), which means to benefit or be to the advantage of. English cannot keep the echo, so the sense is kept. Other reading: What the nature of the whole brings to each benefits each
- *ἑκάστῳ*: The form can be masculine or neuter: each person or each thing. “Each” leaves it open. Other reading: to each thing
- *ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις*: Literally “the nature of the wholes”, a set phrase for the nature of the universe taken as a whole. Other reading: the nature of all things
- *καὶ τότε συμφέρει ὅτε ἐκείνη φέρει*: 'Then ... when': the benefit is tied to the moment of the bringing. The Greek does not add 'only' or 'exactly'; a stronger wording would be an interpretation. Other reading: and it is good for them exactly when nature brings it

</details>

### 10.21

“The earth loves the rain, and the holy sky loves,” and the universe loves to bring about whatever is to come. So I say to the universe: “I love along with you.” And is that, too, perhaps said in this sense: “this loves to happen”?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐρᾷ δὲ ὁ σεμνὸς αἰθήρ*: The quoted line of verse stops here without saying what the sky loves. The English leaves it just as bare. Other reading: and the holy sky loves it too
- *σεμνὸς αἰθήρ*: αἰθήρ is the bright upper air or heaven; σεμνός is “revered”, “holy”, “majestic”. Other reading: the majestic heaven
- *ἐρᾷ δὲ ὁ κόσμος ποιῆσαι*: The poet’s words end before this; from here Marcus speaks, reusing the poet’s verb. It is the verb of being in love and of strong desire. “Loves” is used for it throughout so that the last sentence can be heard. Other reading: and the universe longs to bring about
- *κόσμος*: The word means both the universe and its order. 'Universe' is used here and in 4.23. Other reading: the world
- *ὃ ἂν μέλλῃ γίνεσθαι*: The verb can mean simply “is about to” or “is destined to”. The plain future sense is translated. Other reading: whatever is destined to happen
- *σοὶ συνερῶ*: One compound verb, “I love together with you”; no object is given, so what is loved is left to the context. Other reading: I long along with you
- *μήτι δὲ οὕτω κἀκεῖνο λέγεται*: The particle μήτι usually opens a question expecting “no” (as in 6.43), but it can also float a tentative suggestion. It is taken as a suggestion here, since the sentence completes the thought. Other reading: Surely that, too, is not said in this sense: “this loves to happen”?
- *φιλεῖ τοῦτο γίνεσθαι*: An everyday Greek idiom: “loves to happen” means “tends to happen, usually happens”. The literal “loves” is kept because Marcus’s point depends on hearing the love in it. It is a different Greek verb from the “loves” of the lines above. Other reading: This tends to happen

</details>

### 10.22

Either you live here, and by now you are used to it; or you are going out from here, and that is what you wanted; or you are dying, and you have completed your service. Besides these there is nothing. So be of good heart.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἤδη εἴθικας*: The form is the active perfect of ἐθίζω, which usually means “you have accustomed [someone]”. With no object given it is taken as “you have got used to it”. Other reading: and by now you have made it your habit
- *ἔξω ὑπάγεις*: Literally “you are going off outside”: ἔξω answers “here”, and “from here” is added to bring that out. The Greek does not say where “here” or “outside” is. It is not death, which is the third case. Other reading: you are withdrawing elsewhere
- *τοῦτο ἤθελες*: An imperfect: “this is what you were wanting”. Other reading: and that was your own wish
- *ἀπελειτούργησας*: From λειτουργία, a public service a citizen carried out for his city. The verb is “to finish one’s service, to be discharged”. Other reading: your duty is done
- *εὐθύμει*: “Be in good spirits, be cheerful.” Other reading: be cheerful

</details>

### 10.23–24

Let it always be clear that the country place over there is just like this, and how everything here is the same as on the top of the mountain or on the seashore or wherever you like. For you will find exactly what Plato says: “putting a sheepfold round himself on a mountain,” he says, “and milking the bleaters.”

What is my ruling part to me, and what kind of thing am I making it now, and what am I using it for now? Can it be empty of mind? Can it be cut loose and torn away from community? Can it be melted into the bit of flesh and blended with it, so that it turns as the flesh turns?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τοιοῦτο ἐκεῖνο ὁ ἀγρός ἐστι*: The wording does not construe cleanly: literally “that, the country place, is such”, with a neuter “that” beside the masculine noun and no “this” expressed. The English takes ἐκεῖνο as pointing to the country place one longs for (“over there”) and supplies “this” for the place where one is; ἀγρός is “country place” to match 4.3. From memory, unchecked: editors doubt the text. Other reading: that this place is just what that country retreat is
- *ἄντικρυς*: “Outright”, “exactly”. The Greek says only “you will find outright the words of Plato”, that is, find them borne out. Other reading: For you will find Plato’s saying plainly true
- *σηκὸν ἐν ὄρει*: A σηκός is a pen or fold for animals; the English has “sheepfold” so that “pen” is not misread. From memory, unchecked: the words come from the Theaetetus of Plato, where a ruler shut inside his city wall is compared to a herdsman in a mountain fold; Marcus quotes loosely. Other reading: “putting a pen round himself in the hills”
- *βδάλλων βληχήματα*: Literally “milking bleatings”, the sound standing for the animals that make it. The English has “the bleaters” so that it can be read; the text here has also been doubted (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: “and milking bleatings”
- *μήτι κενὸν νοῦ ἐστι*: μήτι opens a question asked with misgiving: “can it be that …?”, “it is not …, is it?”. The English has “Can it be” for all three questions. Other reading: It is not empty of mind, is it?
- *κοινωνίας*: κοινωνία is sharing, fellowship, the common life of rational beings; the adjective is “social” in the glossary. The English has “community”. Other reading: cut loose and torn away from society
- *συντρέπεσθαι*: “To turn together with it”: to be swayed whichever way the flesh is swayed. From memory, unchecked: another reading gives a verb meaning “to be nourished with it”. Other reading: so that it is moved by every movement of the flesh

</details>

### 10.25

Whoever flees from their master is a runaway slave. And the law is master, so whoever breaks the law is a runaway slave too. But whoever is distressed or angry or afraid, too, does not want one of the things appointed by the one who governs all things to have happened, or to be happening, or to be going to happen; and the one who governs all things is law, as the one who deals out all that falls to each. So whoever is afraid or distressed or angry is a runaway slave.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *δραπέτης*: The word means specifically a slave who has run away from a master, not any fugitive. “Runaway slave” is written each time so that the conclusion of the argument uses the same words as its first step. Other reading: a runaway
- *κύριος δὲ ὁ νόμος*: κύριος is the master of a slave, and more widely one who has authority, a lord. “The law” has the article and is the subject; “master” has none, and the English reads “is master”. The small word δέ adds the second step of the argument, so it is “and”, not “but”. Other reading: and our master is the law
- *καὶ ὁ παρανομῶν οὖν δραπέτης*: καί can be “also” (the lawbreaker too is a runaway) or a plain “and” joining the two clauses. “Too” is read: the closing step of the argument has its “so” without καί, and the next sentence goes on with “but” and another “too”. Other reading: and so whoever breaks the law is a runaway slave
- *ὁ λυπούμενος*: λύπη covers pain, grief and distress; in Stoic lists it is the name for one of the main passions. “Distressed” is the widest plain word. Other reading: whoever grieves, or: whoever is in pain
- *οὐ βούλεταί τι γεγονέναι ἢ γίνεσθαι ἢ γενήσεσθαι*: Literally “does not want something to have happened or to be happening or to be going to happen”: one “not” governs the three tenses, which answer distress (past), anger (present) and fear (future) only loosely. Greek “does not want” regularly means “wants it not to be so”. In the Greek “of the things appointed” comes after the three tenses; the English brings it forward as “one of the things appointed”. Other reading: wishes that one of the things appointed had not happened, or were not happening, or would not happen
- *τεταγμένων*: The verb is to set in order, to station, to assign. “Appointed” keeps the sense of things set in their place by an authority. Other reading: the things arranged, or ordered
- *τοῦ τὰ πάντα διοικοῦντος*: The form could be masculine (“the one who governs”) or neuter (“that which governs”). The masculine ὅς that follows suggests a person, though it could also take its gender from νόμος (“law”). διοικεῖν is to manage a household or a city. Other reading: that which administers everything
- *ὅς ἐστι νόμος, νέμων ὅσα ἑκάστῳ ἐπιβάλλει*: A play on words that carries the argument: νόμος (“law”) is explained from νέμων (“dealing out, allotting”), as if law were by its name the one who allots. English cannot show it; “as the one who deals out” lets the explanation be heard without a “because” that the Greek does not have. The Greek relative clause (“who is law”) is made a clause of its own, with “the one who governs all things” repeated; ἑκάστῳ can be each person or each thing, and ἐπιβάλλει is “falls to one’s share”. Other reading: who is law, because he allots to each whatever is each one’s portion

</details>

### 10.26

A man lets seed go into a womb and goes away, and from then on another cause takes it over, works on it and brings a baby to completion. From what a thing, what a thing! Again: he lets food go down through the throat, and from then on another cause takes it over and makes perception and impulse and, in sum, life and strength and other things (how many, and what things!). So: to look at these things that come about under such a veil, and to see the power just as we see the power that presses downward and the power that rises upward, not with the eyes, but no less clearly.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀφεὶς ἀπεχώρησε*: The Greek names no subject. The participle is masculine and the act is a man’s, and the tense is a past used for what generally happens. The English is “A man” and the present tense. Other reading: He let seed go into a womb and went away
- *ἄλλη αἰτία παραλαβοῦσα*: Literally “another cause, having received it”, as one takes over a thing handed on. The same phrase is repeated word for word in the second half, and the English repeats too. Other reading: a different cause takes charge of it
- *ἐξ οἵου οἷον*: Three words: “out of what sort of thing, what sort of thing”. The edition prints a question mark, but the words read as an exclamation of wonder and are punctuated so. The same word of wonder returns in the bracket below, “what things!”. Other reading: From what kind of beginning, what kind of result?
- *ἀφῆκε*: The same verb as for the seed, “let go, released”, and “lets … go” is kept so the parallel shows. The subject is again unstated: “he” carries on from “a man”, since the Greek names no new subject, though anyone who eats is meant. Other reading: a person lets food go down through the throat
- *τὸ ὅλον*: Used as an adverb: “on the whole, in general”, summing up the list. The English is “in sum”. Other reading: and, altogether, life and strength
- *ἐγκαλύψει*: A noun meaning a veiling or wrapping up. It is kept as an image: a veil under which the work goes on unseen. Other reading: that come about in such concealment
- *θεωρεῖν*: This and the next verb are infinitives with no person, the form of a note to oneself. They are kept impersonal as “to look” and “to see”. Other reading: So look at these things, and see the power
- *τὴν βρίθουσαν καὶ τὴν ἀνωφερῆ*: Two adjectives with “power” understood, each describing the power itself: the one that presses down with weight and the one that tends upward. Heavy things are seen to fall and light things to rise, but the power is not seen by the eyes. Other reading: the force that makes things heavy and the force that makes them rise

</details>

### 10.27

Think continually how all things of the kind that happen now happened before as well, and think of them as going to happen. And set before your eyes whole plays and scenes of the same kind, all that you have come to know from your own experience or from older history: for example the whole court of Hadrian, and the whole court of Antoninus, and the whole court of Philip, of Alexander, of Croesus. For all of those were of this kind, only with other people.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Συνεχῶς ἐπινοεῖν*: An infinitive used as an instruction, with no person, though “your own experience” and “you have come to know” follow in the second person. The English uses the bare command. Other reading: To think continually
- *πάντα τοιαῦτα, ὁποῖα νῦν γίνεται*: τοιαῦτα, “of such a kind”, opens the chapter and returns in its last clause. The English reads “of the kind” and “of this kind” so that the echo can be heard. “Of the same kind” in between stands for a different Greek word (ὁμοειδεῖς, “alike in form”) that carries the same thought. Other reading: all things such as happen now … all of those were just the same
- *καὶ ἐπινοεῖν γενησόμενα*: Literally “and to think [them] going to happen”: things of the same kind will happen again. Other reading: and think that they will happen
- *δράματα καὶ σκηνὰς ὁμοειδεῖς*: σκηνή is the stage, and so a scene or stage setting. “Of the same kind” may go with the scenes only or with both nouns. Other reading: whole dramas and their stages, all alike
- *Ἀντωνίνου*: Presumably the emperor Antoninus Pius, the writer’s predecessor. Philip and Alexander are the kings of Macedon, Croesus the king of Lydia. Other reading: the whole court of Antoninus Pius
- *μόνον δι’ ἑτέρων*: Literally “only through others”: carried out by other people. After “plays and scenes” this can be heard as a change of cast, but the Greek has no word for actors and the English adds none. Other reading: only with other actors

</details>

### 10.28

Picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on their little bed, alone, in silence. Picture also how we are bound, and that to the rational living creature alone it has been given to follow willingly what happens, while simply to follow is a necessity for all.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Φαντάζου*: The verb of φαντασία, “impression”: “form the impression of, picture to yourself”. Other reading: Form an impression of
- *λυπούμενον ἢ δυσαρεστοῦντα*: λυπούμενον is “pained, grieved”; δυσαρεστοῦντα is “displeased, discontented”. Other reading: grieved or discontented
- *ὁ οἰμώζων ἐπὶ τοῦ κλινιδίου μόνος σιωπῇ*: οἰμώζω is to cry out in grief, to lament, yet σιωπῇ is “in silence”: a lament kept inside, set beside the squealing of the piglet. “Laments” lets both words stand. κλινίδιον is a small bed or couch, a diminutive like χοιρίδιον, “piglet”. Other reading: the one who wails on a couch, alone and without a sound
- *τὴν ἔνδεσιν ἡμῶν*: An accusative with no verb in the Greek as given, so the sentence does not construe as it stands. “Picture also” is supplied, carried over from the opening, and “how we are bound” stands for the noun ἔνδεσις, a binding or fastening-in: being tied to what happens. If the full stop before these words were taken away, they could be the object of “laments”. Other reading: Like it too is the one who, on a little bed, alone, in silence, laments our binding
- *μόνῳ τῷ λογικῷ ζῴῳ δέδοται τὸ ἑκουσίως ἕπεσθαι τοῖς γινομένοις*: ἕπεσθαι is “to follow”, the same word as “to follow god” in 10.11, and ἑκουσίως (“willingly”) goes with it. τοῖς γινομένοις is “the things that come about”. Other reading: only the rational animal has been granted to go along with events of its own will
- *τὸ δὲ ἕπεσθαι ψιλὸν*: ψιλόν is “bare”: following by itself, without the willingness. Other reading: but bare following

</details>

### 10.29

At each of the things you do, one by one, stop and ask yourself whether death is something terrible because of being deprived of this.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Κατὰ μέρος*: “Part by part”: taking the things you do singly, not in the mass. The English reads “one by one”. Other reading: In detail, at each thing you do
- *ἐφιστάνων*: The participle can mean “halting” or “fixing your attention”. The English reads “stop”. Other reading: fix your attention and ask yourself
- *διὰ τὸ τούτου στέρεσθαι*: Literally “because of being deprived of this”, and the English keeps that. The Greek does not say who is deprived. The question plainly expects the answer no, but the Greek only asks. Other reading: whether death is to be feared because it takes this away from you

</details>

### 10.30

Whenever you take offence at someone’s wrongdoing, turn at once to yourself and reckon up what wrong of a similar kind you do: for example, judging money to be a good, or pleasure, or a scrap of reputation, and so on, kind by kind. For when you put your mind to this you will quickly forget your anger, as it strikes you at the same time that they are being forced: for what are they to do? Or, if you can, take away from them what is forcing them.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *μεταβὰς*: “Having crossed over”: shifting from the other person to yourself. The Greek does not say where to; “to yourself” is supplied from the sense. Other reading: pass over at once and reckon up
- *τὸ δοξάριον*: A diminutive of δόξα (reputation), said with contempt. Other reading: petty fame
- *εἶδος*: The phrase is literally “and by kind”: a short way of saying “and so on through each sort of case”. Other reading: and the like, class by class
- *τούτῳ γὰρ ἐπιβάλλων*: ἐπιβάλλω with a dative is to apply oneself, or one’s mind, to something. Other reading: for if you fix on this
- *βιάζεται*: The form can be passive (“is forced”) or middle (“uses force”). It is taken as passive, with “what are they to do?” following: the person is forced by their own false judgment. Other reading: that they are acting with violence
- *τὸ βιαζόμενον*: Read as middle, “that which forces”. It could be passive, “the part of them that is forced”. Other reading: take away from them the compulsion they are under

</details>

### 10.31a

When you see Satyrion, picture Socraticus or Eutyches or Hymen; and when you see Euphrates, picture Eutychion or Silvanus; and with Alciphron picture Tropaeophorus; and when you see Severus, picture Crito or Xenophon; and when you look at yourself, picture one of the Caesars; and with each person the one who corresponds. Then let this come to you along with it: where, then, are those people? Nowhere, or wherever it may be. For in this way you will continually look on human things as smoke and nothing, especially if you remember along with it that what has once changed will not exist any more in boundless time. Why then do you strain? Why is it not enough for you to get across this short stretch in good order?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Σωκρατικὸν φαντάζου ἢ Εὐτύχην ἢ Ὑμένα*: Σωκρατικὸν can be a man’s name, Socraticus, or “a Socratic” (a follower of Socrates). The English takes it as a name and the two “or” as a list of three, like the pairs of plain names that follow. The words can also be read as a Socratic who is then named as one of two men. Other reading: picture a Socratic, either Eutyches or Hymen
- *φαντάζου*: The verb belongs with φαντασία, “impression”: form the impression of, call up the image of. “Picture” is used throughout. Other reading: call up the impression of
- *Ἀλκίφρονα Τροπαιοφόρον*: Here the Greek leaves out “when you see”; the English marks that with the shorter “with”. Most of the people named in this passage cannot be identified here; Crito and Xenophon were followers of Socrates. Other reading: and Alciphron, picture Tropaeophorus
- *οὐδαμοῦ ἢ ὁπουδή*: The second word is “wherever, no matter where”: either nowhere, or somewhere that does not matter. Other reading: Nowhere, or who knows where.
- *οὐκέτι ἔσται ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ χρόνῳ*: οὐκέτι is “no longer”. The boundless time is the endless time still to come. Other reading: will never be again in all the endless time
- *τί οὖν ἐντείνῃ*: As given, “why do you strain yourself?”. Other editions are recalled as printing a different text at this point (from memory, unchecked); the English follows what stands here. Other reading: Why then are you so tense?
- *κοσμίως διαπερᾶσαι*: The verb is “to cross over, to get to the other side”, so the short thing is a stretch to be crossed; “stretch” is supplied. κοσμίως is “in good order, decently, with composure”. Other reading: to pass through this short time decently

</details>

### 10.31b

What material, what a subject, you are running away from! For what are all these things but exercises for a reason that has looked exactly, and as a student of nature, at the things in life? Stay, then, until you have made these things too your own, as a strong stomach makes everything its own, as a bright fire makes flame and light out of whatever you throw into it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οἵαν ὕλην καὶ ὑπόθεσιν φεύγεις*: Can be an exclamation or a question. The passage begins mid-chapter, so “all these things” points to what came before it. ὑπόθεσις here is the subject set before one to work on; in 8.1 and 11.7, where it is the footing of a life, the English has “situation”. Other reading: What kind of material and what subject are you running away from?
- *γυμνάσματα λόγου*: The genitive can be “exercises for reason” or “exercises of reason”. Other reading: the exercises of a reason that has seen
- *φυσιολόγως*: “In the manner of one who studies nature”; the same root as ἀφυσιολογήτως in 10.9. Other reading: scientifically
- *ἐξοικειώσῃς σεαυτῷ*: To make a thing οἰκεῖον, one’s own, at home with oneself; of the stomach, to assimilate. “Make your own” and “makes its own” are kept for both. Other reading: until you have assimilated these things too
- *φλόγα ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐγὴν ποιεῖ*: αὐγή is brightness, the light a fire gives. Other reading: makes flame and a blaze out of it

</details>

### 10.32–33

Let it not be possible for anyone to say truthfully of you that you are not straightforward or that you are not good, but let anyone who is going to judge any of these things about you be mistaken. All of this is in your power: for who prevents you from being good and straightforward? You have only to decide not to go on living unless you are going to be such a person, for reason does not require you to live either, if you are not such.

With this material, what is it that can be done or said in the soundest way? For whatever it is, it is possible to do it or say it, and do not make the excuse that you are being prevented. You will not stop groaning until this has come over you: that what luxury is to those who live for pleasure, that is what it is for you to do, with the material that is supplied and comes to hand, the things that belong to the way a human being is made. For one must judge everything that it is possible to do in accordance with one’s own nature to be an enjoyment. And it is possible everywhere. Now a cylinder is not granted everywhere to be carried along in its own motion, nor is water, nor fire, nor the other things that are governed by nature or by a soul without reason: for the things that bar them and stand in their way are many. But mind and reason can make their way through everything that falls against them, in the way their nature is and in the way they wish. Set this ease before your eyes, the ease with which reason will be carried through all things as fire is carried up, as a stone down, as a cylinder down a slope, and look for nothing more. For the remaining obstacles either belong to the little body, the dead thing, or, without a judgment and the giving in of reason itself, they break no one and do nothing bad at all. Otherwise the one affected would themselves at once become bad. At any rate with all other made things, whatever bad thing happens to any of them, the thing affected itself becomes worse because of it. But here, if it must be said, the human being becomes both better and more praiseworthy by using rightly the things that befall them. In general, remember that nothing harms one who is by nature a citizen that does not harm the city, and nothing harms the city that does not harm the law. And of these so-called strokes of bad luck not one harms the law. So what does not harm the law harms neither city nor citizen.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἁπλοῦς*: ἁπλοῦς is literally “single, simple”: a person with no folds or double dealing. “Straightforward” is used. Other reading: that you are not simple
- *ψευδέσθω*: The verb covers both saying what is false and being mistaken. Since the person is said to “judge”, not to speak, the English has “be mistaken”; set against “say truthfully” it could also be “be saying what is false”. Other reading: but let anyone who is going to judge any of these things about you be saying what is false
- *οὐδὲ γὰρ αἱρεῖ λόγος μὴ τοιοῦτον ὄντα*: αἱρεῖ λόγος is a fixed phrase for what reason dictates or what the argument proves; literally reason “takes” or “chooses”. The clause is elliptical: “you to live” is supplied from the clause before. Other reading: for reason does not choose life either for one who is not such
- *ἡδυπαθοῦσιν ἡ τρυφή;*: The text as given puts a question mark here, which would make the first clause a question. That breaks the pair οἷον … τοιοῦτο (“what … that”), so the English sets the mark aside and reads one statement running on. The capital on Οὐ is the edition’s paragraph inside chapter 33, not a new chapter. Other reading: Will you not stop groaning before you have come to feel what luxury is to those who live for pleasure? That is what it is for you to do …
- *τοῦτο πάθῃς*: Literally “until you undergo this”: the point is to come to feel it, not merely to think it. Other reading: until you experience this
- *κατασκευῇ*: κατασκευή is how a thing is built or constituted. “The way a human being is made” lets the link to κατασκευασμάτων further on (“made things”) be heard. Other reading: what belongs to the human constitution
- *ἀπόλαυσιν γὰρ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν*: The Greek is impersonal (“one must”), so “one” is kept. ὑπολαμβάνειν is the verb of ὑπόληψις (“judgment”), so “judge” is kept, though “count as” is the more natural English. Other reading: For you should count as enjoyment everything …
- *κυλίνδρῳ*: A cylinder or roller, the stock Stoic example of a thing that moves by its own shape once pushed. The Greek word is the name of the solid, so “cylinder” is kept. Other reading: a roller
- *ὑπὸ φύσεως ἢ ψυχῆς ἀλόγου*: “Without reason” can go with “soul” alone or with both nouns. The English takes it with “soul” alone: in Stoic terms plants are governed by “nature” and animals by a soul that lacks reason. Other reading: by a nature or a soul that is without reason
- *τοῦ σωματίου ἐστὶ τοῦ νεκροῦ*: σωμάτιον is a diminutive of “body”, used slightingly; “little body” is written wherever it occurs. τοῦ νεκροῦ calls the body “the corpse” or “the dead thing”. Other reading: belong to this poor body, the corpse
- *ἐνδόσεως*: ἔνδοσις is a slackening or giving way, here of reason itself. “Giving in” is used. Other reading: and the surrender of reason itself
- *οὐ θραύει*: The verb has no object in the Greek. “No one” is supplied, because the same verb is used of the person (“broken”) in 4.49b. Other reading: they do not crush
- *κακὸς ἂν εὐθὺς ἐγίνετο*: The argument runs on κακόν, κακός, χεῖρον. “Bad”, “bad”, “worse” are kept so that the chain shows, and “harm” is kept for βλάπτει at the end of the chapter. Other reading: would at once become evil himself
- *εἰ δεῖ εἰπεῖν, καὶ κρείττων*: Literally “if one must say it”. The first καί is taken with the second as “both … and”; it can also be “even” or “actually”, in contrast with “becomes worse” just before. Other reading: But here, if one may say so, the human being actually becomes better and more praiseworthy
- *τὸν φύσει πολίτην*: Literally “the by-nature citizen”: the human being as a citizen, by nature, of the city that is the universe. φύσει could also be taken loosely as “the true citizen”. Other reading: the true citizen
- *ἀκληρημάτων*: ἀκλήρημα is a piece of bad luck, literally a bad lot drawn. It is a different word from ἀτύχημα (“misfortune”) used in 4.49. Other reading: these so-called misfortunes

</details>

### 10.34

For someone who has been steeped in the true principles, even the shortest saying, one that lies open to everybody, is enough as a reminder of freedom from grief and fear. For example: “Leaves, some the wind pours to the ground: so the generation of men.” Your little children are little leaves too; little leaves too are these that shout convincingly and applaud, or on the contrary curse, or quietly find fault and mock; and little leaves in the same way are those who will receive in succession the fame that comes after death. For all these “come on in the season of spring”. Then the wind has thrown them down; then the forest grows others in their place. Shortness of life is common to all, but you run from all things and chase all things as if they were going to last for ever. A little while and you will close your eyes, and already someone else will be mourning the one who carried you out.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *δεδευμένῳ*: As given, the perfect participle of “to wet, to soak”, so “steeped”. Other editions are recalled as printing a word meaning “bitten” here (from memory, unchecked); the English follows what stands. Other reading: For someone who has been bitten by the true principles
- *ἐν μέσῳ κείμενον*: Literally “lying in the middle”, an idiom for what is common property, within everyone’s reach. “Saying” is supplied: the Greek has only “the shortest thing”. Other reading: the most ordinary saying
- *φύλλα τὰ μέν τ’ ἄνεμος χαμάδις χέει· ὣς ἀνδρῶν γενεή*: Homer, from the leaves speech in the Iliad (book 6, from memory, unchecked), with the lines between left out. The two phrases quoted further on are from the same lines. The English keeps the broken grammar of the abridged quotation. Other reading: “The wind scatters some leaves on the ground: such is the race of men.”
- *φυλλάρια*: A diminutive of “leaves”, set beside the diminutive for “children”. “Little” is kept each time it recurs. Other reading: mere leaves
- *ἀξιοπίστως*: “In a way that wins belief”. It may be meant straight (they sound sincere) or with an edge (they only sound it). Other reading: with every appearance of sincerity
- *τὰ διαδεξόμενα τὴν ὑστεροφημίαν*: Literally “those who will receive in succession the after-fame”: the later people who will each in turn hold what is said of a person once dead. The Greek does not say whose fame; in context it is the fame of the one addressed. Other reading: those who will take over your fame after you
- *ἔαρος ἐπιγίγνεται ὥρῃ*: In Homer the season is the subject (“the season of spring comes on”). As given here it is dative, “in the season of spring”, with “all these” as subject. Other reading: “the season of spring comes on”
- *φεύγεις καὶ διώκεις*: The standard pair for avoiding and pursuing. The English keeps the literal running and chasing, and repeats “all things” for both verbs where the Greek has it once. Other reading: you avoid and pursue everything
- *ἤδη*: “Already, presently”: the mourner’s own turn follows at once. “Carried you out” is the regular Greek expression for carrying a body out to burial. Other reading: and the one who carried you out to burial will soon be mourned by someone else

</details>

### 10.35

The healthy eye must see everything that can be seen, and not say, “I want the green things”; for that belongs to someone whose eyes are diseased. And healthy hearing and healthy smell must be ready for everything that can be heard and smelled, and the healthy stomach must be the same toward all foods, as a mill is toward everything it was built to grind. So too the healthy mind must be ready for everything that happens. But the mind that says, “Let the little ones be kept safe,” and “Let everyone praise whatever I do,” is an eye that looks for the green things, or teeth that look for the soft things.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὰ χλωρὰ*: The color word runs from pale green to yellowish; here it is green as the color that is easy on sore eyes. Other reading: pale things
- *ὀφθαλμιῶντός*: A participle: “of one who is suffering from ophthalmia”, a soreness of the eyes. The English gives it plainly. Other reading: that is what a person with sore eyes does
- *στόμαχον*: The word can mean the gullet or the stomach. With food and a mill, “stomach”. Other reading: gullet
- *ὁμοίως ἔχειν ὡς μύλην*: “To be disposed alike” toward all foods, as a mill or millstone is. “Alike” can go with “all foods” (the same toward each) or with the comparison (in the same way as a mill); the English is worded so that both are heard. Other reading: must take all foods just as a millstone takes all that it was made to grind
- *διάνοιαν*: The faculty, set beside eye, hearing and stomach, so “mind” and not the glossary’s first choice “thought”. Other reading: thought
- *τὰ τεκνία σῳζέσθω*: A diminutive, “little children”, and a verb that is both “be kept safe” and “survive”. The Greek has “the”, not a possessive, and the English follows it. Other reading: “Let my little ones live”
- *ἡ δὲ λέγουσα*: Literally “but the one that says”, feminine, picking up “mind”. The English repeats the noun. Other reading: But the one that says

</details>

### 10.36

No one is so fortunate that, as they die, there will not be some people standing by who welcome the bad thing that is happening. Say the person was good and wise: may there not, at the very last, be someone who says to themselves: “Shall we at last get a breathing space from this minder? He was not hard on any of us, but I could feel that he was quietly condemning us.” That, then, in the case of the good person. But in our case how many other things there are on account of which many a person is longing to be rid of us! So you will think of this as you die, and you will go out more easily, reasoning: “I am leaving a life of this kind, in which my very partners, for whom I struggled so much, prayed, took thought, those very people want me to go, hoping perhaps to get some other relief out of it. Why, then, would anyone hold on to a longer stay here?” Still, do not for that reason go away less kindly toward them, but keeping to your own habit: friendly, well-disposed and gracious. And, on the other hand, not as one being torn away; rather, just as in a person who dies an easy death the little soul slips easily out of the body, such too must the withdrawal from these people be. For nature tied you to these people too and put you together with them, but now it unties. I am being untied, as from my own people, it is true, yet not pulled back but without force; for this too is one of the things that accord with nature.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀσπαζόμενοι τὸ συμβαῖνον κακόν*: ἀσπάζεσθαι is “to greet gladly, to welcome”. κακόν, “bad thing”, is said from the ordinary point of view, not as Marcus’s own verdict on death. Other reading: who are glad of the misfortune that is befalling him
- *μὴ τὸ πανύστατον ἔσται τις*: The Greek before this is a bare statement (“was good and wise”) used as a supposition; “Say the person” is added. A question with μή is hesitant and often expects the answer no, but the argument needs such a person to exist, so it is read as a tentative “may there not be”. σπουδαῖος is the Stoic word for the good, serious person. Other reading: The person was earnest and wise. Surely at the very end there will not be someone who says to themselves …?
- *ἀναπνεύσομέν ποτε ἀπὸ τούτου τοῦ παιδαγωγοῦ*: The edition punctuates this as a question; it could be an exclamation. A παιδαγωγός was the slave who escorted, supervised and corrected a boy, not a teacher, and “minder” gives that status. The verb is literally “breathe again from”. Other reading: At last there will be room to breathe, away from this tutor!
- *πολὺς ὁ ἀπαλλακτιῶν ἡμῶν*: ἀπαλλακτιάω is “to long to be rid of”. ἡμῶν is a first-person plural: Marcus means himself and people like him as against the truly good person, and the plural is kept. Other reading: many a one wants to be rid of me
- *αὐτοὶ οἱ κοινωνοί*: κοινωνοί are sharers or partners, from the same root as κοινωνικός (“social” in this project). The possessive is supplied. Other reading: the very companions
- *ἄλλην τινὰ τυχὸν ἐκ τούτου ῥᾳστώνην ἐλπίζοντες*: ἄλλην τινά is “some other” relief, perhaps “some further”. ἐκ τούτου is “from this”, that is, from the departure, or possibly “after this”. Other reading: hoping perhaps for some further relief after this
- *τί ἂν οὖν τις ἀντέχοιτο τῆς ἐνταῦθα μακροτέρας διατριβῆς*: It is open whether this question still belongs to the dying person’s reasoning or is Marcus’s own comment. It is kept inside the quotation, because it draws the conclusion of that reasoning and the next sentence turns back to “you”. Other reading: (outside the quotation) Why, then, would anyone cling to a longer stay here?
- *καὶ μὴ πάλιν ὡς ἀποσπώμενος*: πάλιν here is “on the other hand, conversely”: not unkindly, but not clinging either. It could also be heard as “again”. Other reading: And, again, not as one being torn away
- *ἐξειλεῖται*: Literally “is unrolled, unwound out of”. The English reads “slips out”; the image is of something coming free without a tug. Other reading: is unwound from the body
- *τούτοις ἡ φύσις συνῆψε καὶ συνέκρινεν, ἀλλὰ νῦν διαλύει*: The verbs have no object; “you” is supplied, though the next word is first person and the object may be the speaker. καί before τούτοις is “too”, looking back to the soul and the body. διαλύειν is also the usual word for the dissolving of a person at death (as in 9.3 and 12.36), so “untie” loses a second sense, while “put together” matches 12.36. Other reading: For nature bound me to these people too and combined me with them, but now she dissolves the bond. I am being dissolved
- *οὐ μὴν ἀνθελκόμενος*: The form is passive (“pulled back”) or middle (“pulling back, resisting”). The passive is taken, parallel to “torn away” above and to “pull one back” for the same verb in 9.3. Other reading: yet not pulling back

</details>

### 10.37

Train yourself, as far as you can, with everything that anyone does, to ask in your own mind: “To what end is this person doing this?” But begin with yourself, and examine yourself first.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἔθισον*: The verb “accustom” stands without an object. The English supplies “yourself”. Other reading: Make it a habit
- *ὡς οἷόν τε*: “As far as possible” sits between “every” and “thing done”, so it may limit the habit or the “every”. The English leaves it loose, as the Greek does. Other reading: with as nearly everything as possible that anyone does
- *ἐπὶ τί ἀναφέρει*: Literally “to what does this person refer this?”, the regular Stoic expression for what an action is referred to, which can be an aim or a standard. The English puts it as a plain question about the end. Other reading: What is this person referring this to?
- *κατὰ σαυτόν*: Literally “by yourself”: privately, inwardly. The English reads “in your own mind”. Other reading: to ask yourself privately

</details>

### 10.38

Remember that what pulls the strings is that thing hidden inside. That is oratory, that is life, that, if one must say it, is the human being. Never picture along with it the vessel-like thing that surrounds it and these little tools moulded around it. For they are like a carpenter’s axe, differing only in being grown on. For without the cause that moves them and holds them in check these parts are in fact of no more use than the weaver’s shuttle, the writer’s pen and the charioteer’s little whip.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ νευροσπαστοῦν*: “What pulls the strings”, as of a puppet worked by cords. Other reading: the puppet-master
- *ἐκεῖνο ῥητορεία*: ῥητορεία is oratory, public speaking. It sits oddly beside “life” and “the human being”, and the word may have been doubted (from memory, unchecked). It is translated as it stands. Other reading: that is the power of speech
- *εἰ δεῖ εἰπεῖν*: “If one must say it”: an apology for the bold wording. Other reading: if the word may be allowed
- *συμπεριφαντάζου*: A compound of the verb of “impression”: do not take in, in the same picture, what lies around it. Other reading: never include in your thought of it
- *τὸ περικείμενον ἀγγειῶδες*: “The vessel-like thing lying round it”: the body as a container. Other reading: the vessel that encloses it
- *τὰ ὀργάνια ταῦτα τὰ περιπεπλασμένα*: ὀργάνια is a diminutive of ὄργανον, which is both “tool” and bodily “organ”. The comparison with the carpenter’s axe turns on the first sense, so the English reads “little tools”. Other reading: these organs moulded round it
- *σκεπάρνῳ*: A carpenter’s axe or adze, a tool for shaping wood. Other reading: an adze
- *καθότι προσφυῆ ἐστιν*: “In that they are grown on”: attached by growth. Other reading: in that they are part of the body’s growth
- *ἰσχούσης*: ἴσχω is to hold, hold back or check: the cause that sets the parts moving and stops them. Other reading: the cause that moves and sustains them
- *ἢ τῆς κερκίδος τῇ ὑφαντρίᾳ*: Literally “than [there is use] of the shuttle to the weaver, of the pen to the writer, of the little whip to the charioteer”. The comparison is compressed: “without the cause that moves them” has to be carried over to the three tools, and the English puts those words first so that they are heard over both halves. ὑφαντρίᾳ is a woman weaver. Other reading: than the shuttle is without the weaver, the pen without the writer, or the whip without the charioteer

</details>

## Book 11

### 11.1

What is the rational soul’s own: it sees itself, it analyses itself, it makes itself whatever it wishes, it gathers for itself the fruit it bears (for the fruits of plants, and what corresponds to them in animals, are gathered by others), and it reaches its own end wherever the limit of life comes upon it. It is not as with dancing and acting and things of that kind, where the whole action falls short of its end if something cuts in, but at every part, and wherever it is overtaken, it makes what was set before it full and in need of nothing more, for itself, so that it can say: “I have what is mine in full.” Further, it goes round the whole universe and the void around it and its shape, and it stretches out into the boundlessness of time, and it takes in the periodic rebirth of the whole and considers it from every side, and it observes that those after us will see nothing newer and that those before us saw nothing more remarkable, but that in a way a person of forty, if they have any mind at all, has seen all that has been and all that will be, in that it is all of one kind. Also the rational soul’s own are love of those near it, and truthfulness, and a sense of shame, and valuing nothing above itself, which is law’s own too. In this way, then, right reason and the reason of justice turn out not to differ at all.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὰ ἴδια τῆς λογικῆς ψυχῆς*: ἴδιος runs through the passage (τὰ ἴδια, τοῦ ἰδίου τέλους, ἴδιον twice), and the last step, that what is the soul’s own is also law’s own, depends on it. The English keeps “own” in all four places. Other reading: The properties of the rational soul
- *ἑαυτὴν διαρθροῖ*: διαρθρόω is literally to give something its joints, and so either to set out distinctly, to analyse, or to shape in detail. The English takes the first, since making itself what it wishes follows as a separate item. Other reading: it gives itself its articulate shape
- *ἀτελὴς γίνεται ἡ ὅλη πρᾶξις*: ἀτελής (incomplete) answers τέλους (end) just before: the soul reaches its end wherever it stops, while a dance cut short is left without one. “End” is kept in both places to show the link. Other reading: the whole action becomes incomplete
- *ἀπροσδεὲς ἑαυτῇ τὸ προτεθὲν*: The dative ἑαυτῇ, “for itself”, is taken with the main statement: the soul makes its task full for itself. It could also go with the participle, giving “what it set before itself”. The participle is passive: what was set before it, what was proposed. Other reading: it makes what it set before itself full and in need of nothing more
- *ἀπέχω*: ἀπέχω is the word for acknowledging payment in full, as on a receipt. The English adds “in full” to carry that sense. Other reading: have received
- *τὴν περιοδικὴν παλιγγενεσίαν τῶν ὅλων*: This is the Stoic teaching that the universe is destroyed and born again in cycles. τῶν ὅλων is plural, “of all things together”; the English follows the glossary’s “the whole”. Other reading: the cyclical regeneration of all things
- *περινοεῖ καὶ θεωρεῖ ὅτι*: περινοεῖ is taken with the rebirth, as a second verb beside “takes in”: both are compounds of περί, like “goes round” before them. Only θεωρεῖ is taken with the clause that follows. Both verbs can instead govern that clause. Other reading: and it takes in the periodic rebirth of the whole, and it grasps and observes that
- *οὐδὲ περιττότερον εἶδον*: περιττός is what goes beyond the ordinary: either “more remarkable” or simply “more”. The English takes the first. Other reading: saw nothing more
- *κατὰ τὸ ὁμοειδές*: Literally “in accordance with the sameness of kind”. It may give the ground (everything is of one kind) or limit the claim (has seen it all, as far as its kind goes). “In that” leans to the first.
