Other reading: has seen, as far as their kind goes, all that has been and all that will be
- *αἰδὼς*: αἰδώς covers shame, modesty and respect for others. The English has “a sense of shame”. Other reading: modesty
- *τὸ μηδὲν ἑαυτῆς προτιμᾶν*: ἑαυτῆς is taken as a genitive of comparison with προτιμᾶν: to rank nothing above itself. Other reading: to prefer nothing to itself
- *λόγος ὀρθὸς καὶ λόγος δικαιοσύνης*: λόγος is “reason” in both phrases, as in the glossary; the second could also be “the principle of justice”. The verb διήνεγκε is an aorist, taken as stating a result (“turn out not to differ”), not a past event. Other reading: In this way, then, right reason did not differ at all from the principle of justice.

</details>

### 11.2

You will look down on delightful singing, on dancing and on the pankration, if you divide the tuneful voice into each of its notes and ask yourself at each one whether this gets the better of you, for you will be ashamed; and with dancing, if you do the corresponding thing at each movement or pose; and the same with the pankration too. In general, then, except for virtue and what comes from virtue, remember to run to the parts, and by dividing them to come to look down on them; and carry the same thing over to the whole of life as well.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὠιδῆς ἐπιτερποῦς*: ᾠδή is a song or singing; it has no article, and the English takes the activity, “singing”, beside “dancing”. “Delightful” can by its form go with the singing alone or with the singing and the dancing; the English leaves it with the singing. Other reading: delightful singing and dancing (or: a delightful song)
- *παγκρατίου*: The pankration was an athletic contest, all-in fighting that joined boxing and wrestling. The English keeps the name, which English also uses for the contest. Other reading: all-in fighting
- *καταφρονήσεις*: To think little of, to despise. The noun from the same verb (καταφρόνησιν) closes the argument, so “look down on” is used in both places. Other reading: You will despise
- *τὴν μὲν ἐμμελῆ φωνὴν*: φωνή is voice or sound, and ἐμμελής is “in tune”, “melodious”. The English takes the singing voice. Other reading: the melodious sound
- *εἰ τούτου ἥττων εἶ*: Literally “whether you are less than this”, the regular idiom for being overcome by something, giving in to it. “This” is the single note. Other reading: whether you are too weak to resist this one
- *διατραπήσῃ γάρ*: The verb means to be turned aside, and so to be put out of countenance or ashamed. The English takes “ashamed”; what you will be ashamed of (saying yes) is left unsaid, as in the Greek. It could also mean that you will be put off the thing itself. Other reading: for you will be put off it (or: for you will shrink from saying so)
- *τὸ ἀνάλογον ποιήσας*: A participle (“having done the corresponding thing”) with no finite verb of its own; it hangs loosely on “you will look down on”. The English gives it as “if you do”, parallel to the first “if” clause. Other reading: and in the case of dancing, having done the like
- *σχέσιν*: A held position, as against a movement: a pose or attitude of the body. Other reading: at each movement or posture
- *ἐπὶ τὰ κατὰ μέρος τρέχειν*: Literally “to run to the things part by part”, the particulars as against the whole. The English keeps “run” (the verb of 9.22) and “parts”, so that “the whole of life” at the end answers it. Other reading: to go straight to the details
- *τῇ διαιρέσει αὐτῶν*: Literally “by the division of them”. “Them” may be the things divided or the parts; the English “them” is open in the same way. The noun is not from the verb used above for dividing the voice (καταμερίσῃς), though the English has “divide” for both. Other reading: by analysing them
- *ἐπὶ τὸν βίον ὅλον μετάφερε*: “Carry it over to the whole life”: either life as a whole or the whole of one’s life. The English takes the first, as the counterpart of “the parts”. Other reading: apply the same to your whole life as well

</details>

### 11.3

What a soul it is that is ready, if it must this moment be released from the body, and either be extinguished or be scattered or hold together. But this readiness should come from a judgment of one’s own, not by way of bare opposition, as with the Christians, but in a reasoned and dignified way, and in a way that could convince someone else too, without theatrics.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οἵα ἐστὶν ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ ἕτοιμος*: οἵα can be an exclamation (“what a soul!”) or a description (“of what kind is the soul”). The English takes it as an exclamation of admiration. Other reading: Of what kind is the soul that is ready
- *σβεσθῆναι ἢ σκεδασθῆναι ἢ συμμεῖναι*: Three possible fates of the soul at death: to go out like a flame, to be dispersed, or to stay in one piece. The images are kept; συμμεῖναι is “hold together” here and in 4.21. Other reading: to be snuffed out, to be dispersed, or to survive
- *ἵνα ἀπὸ ἰδικῆς κρίσεως ἔρχηται*: The ἵνα clause has no governing verb: literally “that this readiness may come”. It is read as an instruction and “should” is supplied. ἰδικός is “one’s own” or “particular, specific”; κρίσις is a judgment or decision, a different word from the glossary’s ὑπόληψις. Other reading: see that this readiness comes from a judgment made on the particular case
- *κατὰ ψιλὴν παράταξιν*: παράταξις is a drawing up in line of battle, and so opposition or defiance; ψιλή is “bare, mere”. The English takes it as mere opposition, but it could mean a readiness that comes from mere drill, like troops standing where they have been ranked. Other reading: not by mere drill
- *ὡς οἱ Χριστιανοί*: This is thought to be the only mention of Christians in the book, and some editors suspect that the words are a reader’s comment that entered the text; they sit loosely in the sentence (from memory, unchecked). They are translated as they stand. Other reading: not by way of bare opposition, but in a reasoned and dignified way (with the three words left out)
- *ὥστε καὶ ἄλλον πεῖσαι*: A result clause: in such a way as to convince another person too. It can go with what precedes or with ἀτραγῴδως, which follows; the English attaches it to the manner as a whole. Other reading: and, if it is to convince anyone else, without theatrics
- *ἀτραγῴδως*: Literally “untragically”: without the gestures of the tragic stage. Other reading: without tragic show

</details>

### 11.4–5

I have done something as a social being: then I have been benefited. See that this always comes to hand, and never stop.

What is your craft? To be good. And how does that come about well, except from points of theory, some about the nature of the whole, others about the make-up proper to the human being?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κοινωνικῶς*: The adverb of κοινωνικός, “social”: as a member of the community, for the common good. The glossary word is kept, in the phrase “as a social being”. Other reading: I have done something for the common good
- *οὐκοῦν ὠφέλημαι*: Perfect: “I have been benefited”, the benefit being in the act itself. Other reading: then I have my reward
- *τοῦτο ἵνα ἀεὶ πρόχειρον ἀπαντᾷ*: ἵνα with the subjunctive standing alone as a command: “see that this always meets you ready to hand”. The English joins the verb and the adjective in “comes to hand”. Other reading: Let this thought always be ready when you need it
- *μηδαμοῦ παύου*: Literally “stop nowhere”. What is not to stop is not said: the doing of such acts, or the keeping of the thought at hand. Other reading: and do not leave off at any point
- *τέχνη*: A craft, skill or profession. Other reading: What is your profession?
- *ὴ ἐκ θεωρημάτων*: ὴ is a slip in the copy for ἢ, “than”: “how … other than from”, though the Greek has no “other” for it to lean on. θεωρήματα are the propositions a science or craft rests on, literally “things contemplated”; the English reads “points of theory”. The Greek ends with a full stop; the English has a question mark. Other reading: except from theorems
- *τῆς ἰδίας τοῦ ἀνθρώπου κατασκευῆς*: κατασκευή is how a thing is built, its constitution. Other reading: the particular constitution of man

</details>

### 11.6

First, tragedies were brought on as reminders of the things that happen, and that it is in the nature of these things to happen this way, and that what charms you on the stage should not weigh on you on the larger stage. For you see that these things have to be carried through this way, and that even those who cry out “O Cithaeron!” bear them. And some things are said usefully by those who write the plays. This above all, for example: “But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.” And again: “For one should not be angry with events.” And: “To reap life like a fruitful ear of grain.” And everything of that kind. After tragedy, the Old Comedy was brought on. It had a tutor’s frankness and, by its very plainness of speech, reminded people, not uselessly, of freedom from conceit. It was for some such purpose that Diogenes too took these things up. As for the Middle Comedy after it, and lastly the New, which little by little slipped down into cleverness at imitation, consider just what it has been taken up for. For it is not unknown that some useful things are said by these writers too; but the whole undertaking of this kind of poetry and play-making, just what aim did it look to?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *παρήχθησαν*: “Were brought forward, introduced”; the verb is also the ordinary one for bringing something on stage. “Brought on” is used here and for the Old Comedy, where the verb is repeated. “First” could also be read as “at first, originally”. Other reading: Tragedies were first introduced as reminders
- *τούτοις μὴ ἄχθεσθε*: The Greek slips into a direct command to an audience in the plural: “do not be weighed down by these things”. The English turns it into “should not weigh on you” so that the sentence runs on. ψυχαγωγεῖσθε before it is literally “you have your souls led”, said of being entertained. Other reading: and that: “what entertains you on the stage, do not be vexed by on the larger stage”
- *ὁρᾶτε γὰρ*: The form can be “you see” or the command “see”. With “for” it is taken as a statement. Other reading: For see that these things have to be carried through this way
- *περαίνεσθαι*: “To be carried through, completed”; the word suits both a plot and events in life. “To their end” is not added, since in English it would be heard as dying. Other reading: that this is how these things must be accomplished
- *ʽἰὼ Κιθαιρών.ʼ*: The cry of Oedipus in Sophocles’ Oedipus the King, addressed to Mount Cithaeron, where he was left to die as a baby (from memory, unchecked). ἰώ is a cry of grief. Other reading: “Alas, Cithaeron!”
- *ἔχει λόγον καὶ τοῦτο*: “This too has a reason”, or “this too makes sense”. The line and the two that follow are verse quotations, all three thought to be from lost plays of Euripides (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: this too is reasonable
- *καὶ παῖδ’ ἐμώ*: A dual: “my two children”. The form does not say whether they are sons. Other reading: I and my two sons
- *τοῖς πράγμασιν γὰρ οὐχὶ θυμοῦσθαι*: As quoted, the line is a bare infinitive, “for not to be angry with things”, and stops before the word that governs it. The full verse is thought to end with a word for “one must” (from memory, unchecked), so “one should” in the English is supplied. πράγματα is “things, affairs, circumstances”. Other reading: “For to be angry with things is not ...”
- *βίον θερίζειν ὥστε κάρπιμον στάχυν*: Again an infinitive cut loose from its sentence; in the original it probably said that life must be reaped. ὥστε is the poetic “like”. κάρπιμον is “bearing fruit”. Other reading: “that life is harvested like a ripe ear of grain”
- *παιδαγωγικὴν παρρησίαν*: παρρησία is saying everything openly: frankness, outspokenness. The adjective is from παιδαγωγός, the attendant who minded a boy and corrected his behaviour, so the sense is frankness that disciplines and teaches. Other reading: an educating outspokenness
- *τῆς ἀτυφίας*: “Absence of τῦφος”, the smoke of vanity and self-importance: so modesty, freedom from conceit. The comedy is said to remind people of this quality. Other reading: reminding people of modesty
- *πρὸς οἷόν τι καὶ Διογένης ταυτὶ παρελάμβανε*: Diogenes is the Cynic philosopher, known for blunt speech. “These things” is vague: probably this manner of plain speaking, possibly actual lines or devices of comedy. The verb is the same one used just after of comedy being “taken up”, so “took up” is used for both. Other reading: With some such end in view Diogenes too adopted this sort of thing
- *μετὰ ταύτην ἡ μέση κωμῳδία καὶ λοιπὸν ἡ νέα πρὸς τί ποτε παρείληπται*: “After it” belongs to the Middle Comedy, which came after the Old, as “after tragedy” does above. The verb is singular and treats the Middle and the New as one thing. ποτε sharpens the question, here and in the last sentence; “just what” gives it in both places. Other reading: After this, consider whatever the Middle Comedy, and lastly the New, has been taken up for
- *ἣ κατ’ ὀλίγον ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκ μιμήσεως φιλοτεχνίαν ὑπερρύη*: The verb is “slid, sank gradually”. φιλοτεχνία is love of craft, and so ingenuity or clever workmanship; “from imitation” says that the cleverness lies in lifelike representation. “Which” most naturally refers to the New Comedy, the nearest noun, but can be read of this later comedy as a whole. Other reading: comedy which by degrees sank into a love of craft in mimicry
- *ἡ ὅλη ἐπιβολὴ*: ἐπιβολή is a setting oneself to something: design, attempt, undertaking. σκοπός at the end is a mark aimed at; the English reads “aim”. Other reading: the whole design of this kind of poetry and play-making

</details>

### 11.7

How plainly it comes home that there is no other situation in life so suited to philosophy as this one in which you now happen to be.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πῶς ἐναργὲς προσπίπτει*: An exclamation. προσπίπτει, “strikes, falls upon”, is the word used of impressions; it has no object, so the English reads “comes home”. Other reading: How clearly it strikes you
- *βίου ὑπόθεσιν*: ὑπόθεσις as in 8.1: the footing or position of a life. The English reads “situation in life”. Other reading: no other calling in life
- *εἰς τὸ φιλοσοφεῖν*: “For philosophising”: the practice, not the subject. Other reading: for the practice of philosophy

</details>

### 11.8a

A branch cut off from the branch next to it cannot help being cut off from the whole plant as well. So too a human being split off from one human being has fallen away from the whole community. Now a branch is cut off by someone else; but it is the human being who separates themselves from their neighbour, by coming to hate and turning away, and they do not know that they have at the same time cut themselves away from the whole civic body as well. Yet there is this gift from Zeus, who put the community together: we are allowed to grow together again with the one next to us and again to help to complete the whole. But when this kind of division happens many times, it makes what withdraws hard to unite and hard to restore. And in general, the branch that sprouted together from the beginning and has stayed together, sharing one breath, is not like the one grafted in again after being cut off, whatever it is that the gardeners say.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τοῦ προσεχοῦς κλάδου*: προσεχής is “adjoining, next in line”. The same word is used later of the person “next to us”, and “next to” is kept for both. Other reading: from the neighbouring branch
- *φυτοῦ*: The general word for anything planted; a tree is meant, but the Greek says “plant”. Other reading: the whole tree
- *ἀποσχισθεὶς*: A different verb from the “cut off” used of the branch: “split, torn off”. A third verb, “cut away”, comes later; the three are kept apart. Other reading: severed from one human being
- *μισήσας καὶ ἀποστραφείς*: Two past participles, “having come to hate and having turned away”; they give the acts by which the separation is made. The Greek names no object for the hatred. Other reading: when they hate their neighbour and turn their back
- *πολιτεύματος*: πολίτευμα: a state, a constitution, or the body of citizens. “Civic body” is used, as in 4.4. Other reading: the whole commonwealth
- *τοῦ συστησαμένου τὴν κοινωνίαν Διός*: Zeus is the chief god of the Greeks, for the Stoics a name for the reason that governs the universe. The verb is “set up, put together”, from which the word for a whole made of members (σύστημα) comes. Other reading: of Zeus, who founded the community
- *συμπληρωτικοῖς*: An adjective: “such as to fill up the whole together”. “Help to complete” is used as in 9.23; the Greek has no noun such as “parts”. Other reading: and once more to go to make up the whole
- *τὸ κατὰ τὴν τοιαύτην διαίρεσιν*: A roundabout phrase, “the matter of such a division”, given simply as “this kind of division”. Other reading: what happens in such a separation
- *συμβλαστήσας*: Three words in a row begin with the prefix “together”: sprouted together, breathing together, stayed together. The Greek does not say with what; the rest of the plant is understood. Other reading: the branch that sprouted with the plant from the beginning and has stayed with it
- *σύμπνους*: “Breathing together”, of one breath. The verb of the same make is given as “breathe together with” in 8.54. Other reading: and has stayed of one breath
- *ὅ τι ποτὲ λέγουσιν οἱ φυτουργοί*: Open: literally “whatever it is that the plant-workers say”, which can be a concession (“whatever the gardeners may say”), a shrug at their trade word for grafting, or a pointer to a saying of theirs. The English keeps the literal wording so that all three stay possible. The chapter’s closing sentence, which belongs to the next passage, follows at once and runs roughly: to grow on the same stock, but not to hold the same principles. Other reading: or whatever the gardeners call it

</details>

### 11.8b–9

To grow on the same stem, but not to hold the same principles.

Just as those who stand in your way as you go forward in accord with right reason will not be able to turn you aside from sound action, so let them not knock you out of your kindness toward them either; but keep watch over yourself on both counts alike: not only in steady judgment and action, but also in gentleness toward those who try to hinder you or are otherwise annoyed. For this too is weakness, to be harsh with them, just as it is to abandon the action and give in from fright. For both are equally deserters from their post: the one who has flinched, and the one who has become estranged from a person who is by nature kin and friend.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὁμοθαμνεῖν*: A rare verb from θάμνος (a bush or shrub): to belong to the same plant. This is the closing maxim of a chapter about a branch cut from its tree and grafted back; the earlier part is not given here, so who is to do this is not said, and only the words that stand are translated. Other reading: To share one trunk
- *ὁμοδογματεῖν*: To hold the same δόγματα, “principles” in the settled list. The two verbs are built alike in Greek (same bush, same principles); English cannot match the pair in one word each. Other reading: but not to share one mind
- *προιόντι σοι κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον*: ὀρθὸς λόγος, “right reason”, is a fixed Stoic phrase. “In accord with right reason” is taken with “go forward”. Other reading: those who, in accord with right reason, cannot turn you as you advance
- *ἐκκρουέτωσαν*: To knock out or drive off, as from a position. The image is kept. Other reading: let them not shake you out of
- *τῆς εὐσταθοῦς κρίσεως*: κρίσις is the act of judging. The settled list keeps “judgment” for ὑπόληψις, which does not occur in this passage, so “judgment” is used here. Other reading: steady decision
- *δυσχεραίνοντας*: To be annoyed, or to make difficulties. “Annoyed” is kept, as for the same verb in 11.18. Other reading: or are otherwise troublesome
- *λειποτάκται*: A military word: those who leave their place in the line. Other reading: deserters from the ranks

</details>

### 11.10

“No nature is inferior to art”; for the arts imitate the natures. If that is so, the nature that is the most complete of all natures and embraces the most would not fall short of the ingenuity of art. Now all the arts make the inferior things for the sake of the superior; so the common nature does too. And it is from this that justice is born, and from justice that the rest of the virtues have their existence; for what is just will not be kept if we either care about the things in between, or are easily deceived, hasty and changeable.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οὐκ ἔστι χείρων οὐδεμία φύσις τέχνης*: The edition prints this as a quotation and names no source. “Art” is any craft or skill, not fine art only. Other reading: No nature is worse than a craft
- *ἡ πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων τελεωτάτη καὶ περιληπτικωτάτη φύσις*: Greek says “the most complete of all the others”, an idiom for “of them all”. The second adjective means “most containing”: the nature that takes in all the rest. Other reading: the nature that is the most perfect and the most comprehensive of all
- *τῆς τεχνικῆς εὐμηχανίας*: Literally “the craftsmanly skill at contriving”. Other reading: the resourcefulness of the crafts
- *ἔνθεν μὲν γένεσις δικαιοσύνης*: “From here” points back to what has just been said, most naturally the making of the inferior for the sake of the superior. The Greek does not spell it out. Other reading: And from there justice has its origin
- *ὑφίστανται*: The verb means “come to stand, have their basis”. Other reading: the other virtues are founded on it
- *διαφερώμεθα πρὸς τὰ μέσα*: Literally “the middle things”: the things between good and bad, called “indifferent things” in 5.20. The verb can mean “care about, treat as making a difference” or “quarrel over”; the first is taken. Other reading: if we quarrel over the middle things
- *προπτωτικοὶ καὶ μεταπτωτικοὶ*: A pair on one root: literally “apt to fall forward” (assenting too soon) and “apt to fall over to another side” (changing one’s judgment). Other reading: rash and unstable

</details>

### 11.11

The things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you, but in a way you yourself go to them. At least let your judgment about them be quiet, and they will stay unmoving, and you will be seen neither pursuing nor avoiding.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Εἰ μὲν Οὐκ ἔρχεται*: As given, the passage opens with Εἰ μὲν (“If, on the one hand”) and then a word with a capital letter, as though the sentence began there; nothing answers “on the one hand”, and the negative is the one used in statements. The English begins at the capital and leaves the first two words untranslated. Probably the edition bracketed them and the brackets were lost in copying (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: If the things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you, but in a way you yourself go to them, then at least let your judgment about them be quiet
- *αἱ διώξεις καὶ φυγαὶ*: Literally “pursuits and flights”: chasing some things and running from others. The same pair returns as verbs at the end, so “pursue” and “avoid” are kept in both places. Other reading: the things you are thrown into turmoil chasing and running from
- *θορυβοῦσί σε*: The verb is from θόρυβος, the noise of a crowd, and is also used of one person being disturbed or confused. “Let your judgment be quiet” answers it. Other reading: raise a clamour in you
- *τὸ γοῦν κρῖμα*: κρῖμα is a ruling or decision, a different word from ὑπόληψις, which is “judgment” in the glossary. “Judgment” is used here as the plainer word, and nothing in the passage depends on the difference. Other reading: at least let your verdict on them keep still
- *ἀτρεμοῦντα*: “Not trembling”, at rest. Other reading: and they will stay quite still

</details>

### 11.12

The sphere of the soul is true to its own form when it neither stretches out toward anything nor runs together inward, neither coils up nor sinks in on itself, but shines with a light by which it sees the truth, the truth of all things and the truth within itself.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Σφαῖρα ψυχῆς αὐτοειδής*: A sentence without a verb. αὐτοειδής is a very rare word, apparently “having its own form”; it is taken as the predicate and “is true to” is supplied. The text here is thought to have been doubted and emended (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: The soul is a sphere of its own form when
- *ἐκτείνηται ἐπί τι*: The verbs describe ways the sphere loses its shape; the first pair is outward and inward. ἐπί τι is “toward something”, which may suggest reaching after an object of desire. Other reading: reaches out after anything
- *σπειρᾶται*: As printed this is from σπειράομαι, “to be coiled” (σπεῖρα, a coil). Another reading, σπείρηται, “is scattered”, would make an opposite to the next verb (from memory, unchecked). The English translates the text as given. Other reading: nor is scattered
- *συνιζάνῃ*: To settle together, to collapse on itself; the prefix means “together”. Other reading: nor collapses
- *φωτὶ λάμπηται*: The verb is middle: the sphere shines with a light. A passive sense, “is lit by a light”, would make the light come from outside. Other reading: is lit by a light
- *τὴν πάντων καὶ τὴν ἐν αὑτῇ*: αὑτῇ with the rough breathing is reflexive, “in itself”, that is, in the soul. “The truth” is repeated so that the two articles are clear in English. Other reading: the truth of all things and the one in it

</details>

### 11.13

Will someone despise me? That is for them to see to. But I will see to it that I am not found doing or saying anything that deserves to be despised. Will they hate me? That is for them to see to. But I am kind and well-disposed to everyone, and ready to show this very person what they are failing to see, not with reproach, nor as if making a show of putting up with them, but genuinely and good-heartedly, like the famous Phocion, if indeed he was not pretending. For what is within must be like this, and a human being must be seen by the gods to be one who is not disposed to be indignant at anything and makes a grievance of nothing. For what is bad for you, if you yourself are now doing what is proper to your nature, and are accepting what is now in season for the nature of the whole, a human being straining toward this: that what is good for all in common should come about, by whatever means?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὄψεται*: Literally “that person will see”, an idiom for “that is their affair”. Marcus then uses the same verb of himself, ὄψομαι. “See to” is kept in both. Other reading: That is their concern.
- *ἐγὼ εὐμενὴς καὶ εὔνους παντὶ καὶ τούτῳ αὐτῷ ἕτοιμος*: There is no verb; the English supplies a present, and after the two futures a future is as possible. “This very person” can go with what follows (ready to show them) or with what precedes (well-disposed to everyone, and to them). Other reading: will be kind and well-disposed to everyone and to this very person, ready to show
- *χρηστῶς*: χρηστός is good in the sense of decent, kind and useful. Since “kind” is used for εὐμενής, the English reads “good-heartedly”. Other reading: sincerely and decently
- *οἷος ὁ Φωκίων ἐκεῖνος*: Phocion was an Athenian general and statesman of the fourth century BC, remembered for bearing no grudge against the city that condemned him (from memory, unchecked). ἐκεῖνος marks him as well known. Other reading: as Phocion did in the well-known story
- *ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν βλέπεσθαι ἄνθρωπον*: The “must” of the sentence governs both halves: what is within must be like this, and a human being must be seen by the gods to be of this kind. The obligation lies on the person. Other reading: and the gods must see a human being who is not disposed to be indignant at anything
- *δεινοπαθοῦντα*: To complain loudly of what one suffers, to treat it as an outrage. “At nothing” earlier in the clause is taken with this word too. Other reading: and does not cry out at hard treatment
- *τί γάρ σοι κακόν*: The passage begins in the first person and here turns to the second; the change is kept. κακόν is “bad”, as elsewhere in this section. Other reading: For what harm is there to you
- *τεταμένος*: “Stretched”, that is, pulled taut toward something; “straining” keeps the image. Some editors are believed to print a word meaning “stationed” here instead (from memory, unchecked); the text as given is translated. Other reading: a human being posted to see that the common good is brought about
- *ὅτου δὴ τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον*: The phrase is “through whatever”, and the form can also mean “through whomever”. συμφέρον is rendered “what is good for” as settled. Other reading: that the common benefit should come about through whoever it may be

</details>

### 11.14

Despising one another, they fawn on one another; and wanting to be above one another, they take the lower place beneath one another.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀρεσκεύονται*: From the word for an over-eager pleaser: to play up to someone, to fawn. It has the same root as “please” in 6.59 and 8.53 but is a harsher verb. Other reading: they try to please one another
- *ὑπερέχειν*: Literally “to hold oneself over”, to be superior. The spatial sense is kept because the next verb answers it with “under”. Other reading: wanting to outdo one another
- *ὑποκατακλίνονται*: Literally “to lie down beneath”, used of taking the lower place on a dining couch and so of giving way to someone. Other reading: they give way to one another

</details>

### 11.15

How rotten and counterfeit is the person who says: “I have chosen to be straightforward with you.” What are you doing, man? This is not a thing to announce beforehand. It will show of itself. It ought to be written on the forehead. At once the voice has that ring, at once it stands out in the eyes, just as the one who is loved at once knows everything in the look of the lovers. In short, the straightforward and good person must be like someone who stinks like a goat, so that whoever stands near notices as soon as they come up, whether they want to or not. But a studied straightforwardness is a dagger. Nothing is more shameful than a wolf’s friendship: shun this above all things. The good and straightforward and kind person has these things in the eyes, and it does not escape notice.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κίβδηλος*: The word for base or adulterated coin. The image is kept as “counterfeit”. Other reading: How rotten and false
- *ἁπλῶς σοι προσφέρεσθαι*: ἁπλῶς, “simply, without folds”, belongs with ἁπλοῦν and ἁπλότητος below. “Straightforward” is used for all of them. Other reading: to deal with you in simplicity
- *τοῦτο οὐ δεῖ προλέγειν*: οὐ δεῖ can mean “one should not” or “there is no need”. The English wording leaves room for both: after “rotten and counterfeit” the first fits, and “it will show of itself” supports the second. Other reading: There is no need to announce this beforehand
- *εὐθὺς ἡ φωνὴ τοιοῦτον ἠχεῖ*: Literally “at once the voice sounds such a thing”: the voice itself carries the character, with no need to announce it. Other reading: the voice at once sounds of it
- *ὡς τῶν ἐραστῶν ἐν τῷ βλέμματι πάντα εὐθὺς γνωρίζει ὁ ἐρώμενος*: ἐραστής and ἐρώμενος are the lover and the one loved in a Greek love affair; the lovers are plural and the beloved singular. Both numbers are kept. Other reading: as the beloved reads everything at once in a lover’s glance
- *οἶον γράσωνα*: The copy has οἶον, a slip for οἷον (“like”). γράσων is the goat-smelling person of 5.28: goodness should be as impossible to miss as a strong smell. Other reading: like someone with rank armpits
- *ἐπιτήδευσις δὲ ἁπλότητος σκάλμη ἐστίν*: ἐπιτήδευσις is the deliberate practice or cultivation of something, here a straightforwardness that is put on. σκάλμη is a rare word for a knife or short sword; its meaning is given from memory, unchecked. Other reading: A put-on simplicity is a concealed knife
- *λυκοφιλίας*: “Wolf-friendship”: the friendship of wolves, which is a pretence and ends in an attack. The image is kept. Other reading: than false friendship
- *ἔχουσι ταῦτα καὶ οὐ λανθάνει*: The subject has one article for three adjectives, the first verb is plural and the second singular. The plural is probably a slip in the text, unless three persons are meant; the English has one person and a singular throughout. Other reading: The good, the straightforward and the kind have these things in their eyes, and they do not go unnoticed

</details>

### 11.16

To live life through in the finest way: this power is in the soul, if a person is indifferent toward the things that are indifferent. And a person will be indifferent if they look at each of these things taken apart and as a whole, and remember that none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one somehow escapes notice, to wipe it out at once; and remember that this kind of attention will be for a short time, and after that life will be over. But what is hard in it, if these things are otherwise? For if they are according to nature, rejoice in them and let them be easy for you. And if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry toward that, even if it brings no reputation. For there is pardon for everyone who looks for their own good.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Κάλλιστα διαζῆν, δύναμις αὕτη ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ*: The opening is loose: an infinitive phrase, then “this power [is] in the soul”. The English keeps the looseness with a colon. κάλλιστα is “most finely, most nobly”. Other reading: The power to live life through in the noblest way is in the soul
- *πρὸς τὰ ἀδιάφορά τις ἀδιαφορῇ*: A play on one word. τὰ ἀδιάφορα is the Stoic term for things neither good nor bad in themselves, such as health, wealth, reputation and death; the verb says to be toward them as they are. Other reading: if one makes no difference of the things that make no difference
- *διῃρημένως καὶ ὁλικῶς*: Two adverbs: “dividedly and wholly”, that is, looking at the thing split into its parts and also as one whole. Other reading: by analysis and as a whole
- *ὑπόληψιν περὶ αὐτοῦ ἡμῖν ἐμποιεῖ*: ὑπόληψις is “judgment” by the glossary; κρίσεις in the next clause is “verdicts” to keep the two words apart, though Marcus seems to mean much the same by both. Other reading: none of them produces in us an opinion about itself
- *κἄν που λάθῃ*: No subject is given: “even if perhaps it escapes notice”. The English takes the subject to be a verdict that got written without being noticed. που is “somehow, perhaps” and need not mean a place. Other reading: and, even if one has been written unawares
- *ὅτι ὀλίγου χρόνου ἔσται ἡ τοιαύτη προσοχὴ*: A bare “that” in the Greek, with no “and remember”; the English supplies the two words, taking the clause as a second thing to remember. The same Greek word can mean “because”, giving a reason for what goes before. Other reading: because this kind of attention will be for a short time
- *τί μέντοι δύσκολον ἄλλως ἔχειν ταῦτα;*: Word for word: “What, however, [is] hard [in] these things being otherwise?” The English keeps “hard”, which “easy” in the next sentence answers, and leaves “otherwise” as bare as the Greek, where the likeliest sense is “other than you would wish”. From memory, unchecked: some editors change ἄλλως to καλῶς, giving “what is hard about getting these things right?” Other reading: Yet what is so hard to bear if these things are other than you would wish?
- *κἂν ἄδοξον ᾖ*: ἄδοξον is “without reputation”: either bringing no fame or held in low regard. Other reading: even if it is looked down on
- *παντὶ γὰρ συγγνώμη*: συγγνώμη is pardon or allowance that is available, not a forgiveness already given. The Greek has no verb: “for to everyone [there is] pardon who seeks their own good”. Other reading: for anyone may be excused for seeking their own good

</details>

### 11.17–18

Where each thing has come from, and what underlying materials each is made of, and what it is changing into, and what it will be like when it has changed, and that it will suffer nothing bad.

And first: what my relation to them is, and that we have come into being for one another’s sake; and that, on another account, I have come into being to stand at their head, as a ram stands at the head of a flock or a bull of a herd. But go back further and start from this: if not atoms, then nature is what governs the whole; if that is so, the worse things are for the sake of the better, and the better for the sake of one another. Second: what sort of people they are at table, in bed, and so on; and above all, what compulsions their principles have laid on them; and these very things, with what conceit they do them. Third: that if they do these things rightly, one should not be annoyed; and if not rightly, then plainly they do them against their will and in ignorance. For every soul is deprived against its will, as of the truth, so too of dealing with each person as they deserve. At any rate they are aggrieved to hear themselves called unjust and unfeeling and greedy and, in a word, prone to do wrong to their neighbours. Fourth: that you yourself also do many wrongs and are another of the same kind; and if you do hold back from certain wrongs, you still have the disposition that brings them on, even if it is through cowardice or hunger for reputation or some such bad thing that you hold back from wrongs like theirs. Fifth: that you have not even grasped for certain whether they are doing wrong; for many things are done with some further purpose in view, and in general one must first learn many things in order to pronounce on another’s action with a sure grasp. Sixth: that, whenever you are extremely indignant or even take it hard, human life is a moment long, and in a little while we are all laid out. Seventh: that it is not their actions that trouble us, for those are in their ruling parts, but our own judgments. At any rate, take away the verdict that this is something terrible, and be willing to let it go, and the anger is gone. How, then, will you take it away? By reasoning that it is not shameful. For if what is shameful is not the only bad thing, you too must do many wrongs and become a robber and anything at all. Eighth: how much harder are the things that our fits of anger and distress over such things bring on than the things themselves are at which we are angry and distressed. Ninth: that kindness is unbeatable, if it is genuine and not a grin or play-acting. For what will the most insolent person do to you, if you go on being kind to them and, if the chance comes, gently advise them and teach them otherwise, at your ease, at the very moment when they are trying to do you harm: “No, child. We are made by nature for something else. I shall certainly not be harmed; it is you who are being harmed, child.” And show, with a light touch and in general terms, that this is so: that not even bees do it, nor any of the creatures that are by nature herd animals. And it must be done neither with irony nor with reproach, but with affection and with no bite in your soul; and not as in a lecture room, nor so that someone else standing by may admire, but to that person alone, even if some others are standing around. Remember these nine headings as gifts you have received from the Muses, and begin at last to be a human being, while you live. One must guard against flattering them just as much as against being angry with them, for both are unsocial and lead to harm. And in your fits of anger have this ready to hand: that it is not flying into a rage that is manly, but that what is gentle and mild, as it is more human, is also more masculine; and that it is this that has a share of strength and sinew and manly courage, not the one who is indignant and discontented. For the closer this is to freedom from passion, the closer it is to power. And just as distress belongs to a weak person, so does anger; for both have been wounded and have given in. And if you like, take a tenth gift too, from the Leader of the Muses: that to require bad people not to do wrong is madness, for it aims at the impossible. And to allow them to be such to others, but to require that they not do wrong to you, is unfeeling and tyrannical.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἐκ τίνων ἕκαστον ὑποκειμένων*: The chapter is a list of headings with no main verb. Here the Greek has only “and out of what underlying things each”; the English supplies “is made of”. ὑποκείμενα are the underlying materials a thing consists of. Other reading: and out of what underlying things each has come
- *τίς ἡ πρὸς αὐτούς μοι σχέσις*: The chapter opens with “And”, as if continuing, and “them” is never explained: it is the people who offend, as the rest shows. Both are left as they stand. The first heading speaks in the first person; from the fourth the Greek turns to the second. Other reading: First, how one stands in relation to other people
- *προστησόμενος αὐτῶν*: A future participle of purpose: to stand in front of them, which covers both leading and protecting. The word λόγος just before it is here an account or way of reckoning, not reason. Other reading: and, from another point of view, born to protect them
- *ἄνωθεν δὲ ἔπιθι*: ἄνωθεν is “from above”, here from higher up in the argument, from an earlier starting point. It can also mean “over again”. Other reading: But go over it again from the beginning
- *εἰ μὴ ἄτομοι, φύσις ἡ τὰ ὅλα διοικοῦσα*: A compressed either-or with no verbs: if things are not atoms (the Epicurean view), then they are governed by nature. The English supplies “then” and “is what”. τὰ ὅλα is rendered “the whole” as settled. Other reading: if there are not just atoms, there is a nature governing all things
- *ὲν τῷ κλιναρίῳ*: κλινάριον is a small bed or couch. After “at table” it is taken as the bed; it could be the dining couch. The grave accent on ὲν is a slip in the copy for ἐν. Other reading: on the couch
- *οἵας ἀνάγκας δογμάτων κειμένας ἔχουσι*: Literally “what necessities of principles they have lying on them”. The word “laid” belongs to the compulsions, and the principles are taken as their source: what these people hold forces them to act as they do. Other reading: what fixed constraints of belief they are subject to
- *οἵου τύφου ποιοῦσιν*: “These very things” may be what their principles compel or their conduct at table and in bed; the Greek does not say. τῦφος is literally smoke: conceit, a puffed-up delusion. Other reading: and how puffed up they are in doing just what they do
- *ἄχθονται γοῦν ἀκούοντες ἄδικοι καὶ ἀγνώμονες*: ἀκούω with a nominative is the idiom “to be called”. ἀγνώμων is rendered “unfeeling”, as at the end of the passage and in 9.42; it also means inconsiderate, unfair or senseless. Other reading: they are pained when they hear the words unjust, inconsiderate
- *τήν γε ἕξιν ἐποιστικὴν ἔχεις*: ἕξις is a settled state of character, here “disposition”. ἐποιστικός is a rare word, “apt to bring on”: the state from which such wrongs come. Other reading: you still have the habit that tends that way
- *κατείληφας*: The Stoic term for a secure grasp of something as true (κατάληψις); καταληπτικῶς at the end of the sentence is the same word, so the English has “grasp” for both. Other reading: you are not even sure whether they are doing wrong
- *οἰκονομίαν*: Literally “by management”: done as part of some arrangement, for a purpose beyond the act itself that the onlooker does not know. The English has to spell this out a little. Other reading: many things are done for reasons of policy
- *ἐξετάθημεν*: A past tense, “were stretched out”, the word for laying out a corpse. The past treats the near future as already done; the English uses a present. Other reading: in a little while all have been laid out
- *τὴν ὡς περὶ δεινοῦ κρίσιν*: κρίσις is the act of judging. Since “judgments” has just been used for ὑπολήψεις, the English has “verdict” here to keep the two Greek words apart. “And be willing to let it go” is moved after the object. Other reading: take away, and be willing to let go, the judgment that it is something terrible
- *λογισάμενος ὅτι οὐκ αἰσχρόν*: The Greek does not say what is “not shameful”: it is taken to be what has been done to you, which brings no shame on you. The next sentence rests on the Stoic rule that only the shameful is bad. Other reading: By reflecting that being wronged is no disgrace to you
- *λῃστὴν καὶ παντοῖον γενέσθαι*: παντοῖον is “of every kind”: a person who will turn into anything, do anything. Other reading: become a robber and whatever else you please
- *σεσηρὸς*: A participle of the verb for drawing back the lips and showing the teeth: a fixed or mocking grin. The image is kept as “a grin”. Other reading: not a smirk
- *εἰ οὕτως ἔτυχε*: Literally “if it so happened”: if the occasion arises. Other reading: if it should so happen
- *εὐσχολῶν*: “Being at leisure”: unhurried, with time to spare for the other person, at the very moment of being attacked. Other reading: taking your time
- *πρὸς ἄλλο πεφύκαμεν*: The verb is the one used two lines later of creatures that “are by nature” herd animals. The English has “made by nature” and “are by nature” so that the two are heard together. Other reading: born for something else
- *εὐαφῶς καὶ ὁλικῶς*: εὐαφῶς is “with a good touch”, tactfully. ὁλικῶς is “in a general way”, taken as speaking of the general rule and not of this person’s fault. Other reading: tactfully and as a universal truth
- *ἤτοι πρὸς μόνον καὶ ἐὰν ἄλλοι τινὲς περιεστήκωσι*: The Greek as given does not fully construe: ἤτοι, “either”, has no “or” to answer it, and some words seem to have dropped out. The English leaves “either” untranslated and supplies “that person”; nothing is added to fill the gap. Other reading: but either to that person alone, even if some others are standing around
- *παρὰ τῶν Μουσῶν*: The Muses are nine, like the nine headings. The Leader of the Muses below (Μουσηγέτης) is a title of Apollo. Other reading: as gifts from the nine Muses
- *οὐχὶ τὸ θυμοῦσθαι ἀνδρικόν*: The sentence plays on four words: ἀνδρικόν (manly), ἀνθρωπικώτερον (more human), ἀρρενικώτερον (more male) and ἀνδρεία (courage, literally manliness). The English has “manly”, “human”, “masculine” and “manly courage”, the last so that the end of the sentence answers its beginning. Other reading: what is gentle and mild is more human and so more of a man’s part, and manliness belongs to it
- *ἥμερον*: ἥμερος is the word for tamed animals and cultivated plants; of a person it means mild, civilised, and is praise. “Mild” is used because “tame” belittles a person in English. Other reading: what is gentle and tame
- *τούτῳ μέτεστιν*: “This” points back to what is gentle and mild, and the same pronoun returns in the next clause. The form could also be masculine, the person who has that quality, set against “the one who is indignant”. Other reading: strength and sinew and manly courage belong to the gentle person
- *ἀπαθείᾳ*: ἀπάθεια is the Stoic term for being free of the passions, not for dullness or indifference. Other reading: the nearer this is to being unmoved
- *τὸ μὴ ἀξιοῦν ἁμαρτάνειν τοὺς φαύλους*: ἀξιόω is to think something right and so to claim or require it of others; the English has “require” both times it occurs. The negative goes with the infinitive in sense. Other reading: to expect bad people not to do wrong
- *ἄλλοις μὲν εἶναι τοιούτους*: The dative “to others” is taken with “be such”: to accept that they behave like this toward other people. Other reading: to grant others that such people exist
- *ἄγνωμον καὶ τυραννικόν*: The same word as ἀγνώμονες earlier in the passage, so “unfeeling” is kept: it is unfeeling to accept that others are wronged and claim exemption only for yourself. Beside “madness” in the sentence before it could also mean senseless. Other reading: is unreasonable and tyrannical

</details>

### 11.19

Four turns that the ruling part takes must above all be guarded against without a break and, whenever you catch them, wiped away, saying over each one as follows: “This imagining is not necessary.” “This one dissolves community.” “This that you are about to say is not from yourself.” For count it among the most absurd things not to speak from yourself. The fourth is the one for which you will reproach yourself: that this is the mark of the more divine part in you being beaten and lying down under the less worthy and mortal portion, that of the body, and under its rough or smooth movements.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τροπὰς*: Literally “turnings”: turns the ruling part (τὸ ἡγεμονικόν) takes away from its course. The English keeps “turns” and adds no “aside”, which the Greek leaves unsaid. Other reading: four lapses of the ruling part
- *ἀπαλειπτέον*: “Must be wiped off”, the same image of wiping a writing surface clean as ἐξαλείφω elsewhere. The form does not say by whom; the “you” comes only from the verb before it. Other reading: must be rubbed out
- *φάντασμα*: Not φαντασία (“impression”) but φάντασμα, which in Stoic usage is a picture in the mind with nothing real behind it. “Imagining” keeps the two apart. Other reading: This impression is not necessary.
- *λυτικὸν κοινωνίας*: Literally “apt to loosen fellowship”. κοινωνία is the noun behind κοινωνικός (“social”); the English reads “community”. Other reading: This one loosens the bond between people.
- *τοῦτο οὐκ ἀπὸ σαυτοῦ μέλλεις λέγειν*: Literally “this you are about to say not from yourself”. “Not from yourself” is taken as the point of the sentence, as the clause that follows shows: the words are not your own real thought. Other reading: You are not going to say this from yourself.
- *ἐν τοῖς ἀτοπωτάτοις*: ἄτοπος is literally “out of place”, and so strange or absurd. The English gives the sense, since nothing in the sentence turns on the literal one. Other reading: among the most out-of-place things
- *καθὸ σεαυτῷ ὀνειδιεῖς, ὅτι*: The first three turns are each met by a sentence to say; the fourth is put differently, as the ground of a reproach you will make to yourself, and its content follows with ὅτι. The change of construction is kept. Other reading: The fourth is when you will reproach yourself that this is a case of
- *τοῦτο ἡττωμένου ἐστὶ*: Literally “this is of the more divine part being beaten”: the Greek genitive says whose sign or whose doing a thing is. The English reads “is the mark of”. Other reading: that this is the more divine part in you being beaten
- *ὑποκατακλινομένου*: The verb is to lie down in the lower place, as on a dinner couch, and so to give way to someone. The image is kept as “lying down under”. Other reading: giving way to
- *ἀτιμοτέρᾳ*: Literally “of less honour” or “of less value”, a comparative answering “more divine”. Other reading: the less honourable and mortal portion
- *τραχείαις ἢ λείαις κινήσεσιν*: “Rough or smooth movements” is school language for pain and pleasure felt in the body; both this and “the portion of the body” are taken to depend on “lying down under”, so “under” is repeated. From memory, unchecked: the wording at this point has been doubted and some editions print something else (“gross pleasures”). Other reading: and its pains or pleasures

</details>

### 11.20

Your bit of breath and all the fiery part that is mixed into you, though by nature they tend upwards, all the same obey the ordering of the whole and are held here in the compound. And all the earthy part in you, and the wet, though they tend downwards, have all the same been raised up and stand in a position that is not naturally theirs. So even the elements heed the whole: once they have been posted somewhere by force, they stay until, from there in turn, the signal for dissolution is given. Is it not terrible, then, that only the part of you that is of mind is disobedient and resents its own post? And yet nothing forced is ordered of it, only the things that are in accordance with its nature. Still it does not bear them, but is carried the opposite way. For the movement towards acts of injustice and acts of self-indulgence, towards angers and griefs and fears, is nothing other than the movement of one who is deserting nature. And whenever the ruling part is discontented with any of the things that happen, then too it leaves its own post. For it has been made for holiness and reverence for the gods no less than for justice. For these too come under good fellowship, or rather they come before acts of justice.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὸ μὲν πνευμάτιόν σου*: A diminutive of the word for breath or air, one of the four elements in the body here. The diminutive is slightly belittling. Other reading: Your little portion of air
- *τῇ τῶν ὅλων διατάξει*: The Greek has a plural, “the wholes”, Marcus’s usual phrase for the universe, rendered “the whole” throughout. The noun means an arrangement and is used of troops drawn up; “ordering” is meant to carry both arranging and commanding, since “posted” and “ordered” further on are from the same root. Other reading: the arrangement of the universe
- *ἐπὶ τοῦ συγκρίματος*: “The compound” is the body seen as a mixture of the elements. Other reading: here in the mixture that is you
- *ὑπακούει*: A different verb from “obey” in the first sentence: literally “listen to”, “answer a call”. “Heed” keeps it apart from “obey” and “disobedient”, the pair the argument runs on. Other reading: So even the elements obey the whole
- *ἐπειδάν που καταταχθῇ σὺν βίᾳ*: The verb is a military one, “to be posted”. “By force” can go with being posted, as the edition punctuates, or with staying. Other reading: once they have been posted somewhere, they stay there under force until
- *ἐκεῖθεν πάλιν τὸ ἐνδόσιμον τῆς διαλύσεως σημήνῃ*: The noun is the note given to start a song or a movement, a cue. “From there” is from the whole that posted them, and the adverb is taken as “in turn” (the order that posted them is answered by one that breaks them up), not as “a second time”. The verb has no stated subject. Other reading: until from there the cue is given for them to be dissolved back again
- *τὸ νοερόν σου μέρος*: The adjective is built on the Greek noun for mind. “Of mind” is the wording kept for it throughout the translation. Other reading: only the intelligent part of you
- *τῇ ἑαυτοῦ χώρᾳ*: The word means “place”, and also a soldier’s station. “Post” is taken because of the military verbs around it, and kept for the second occurrence. Other reading: resents its own place
- *ἀφισταμένου τῆς φύσεως*: Literally “of one standing away from nature”. The verb is used of rebels and deserters, and that sense is taken. Other reading: of one who is withdrawing from nature
- *θεοσέβειαν*: A compound, “god-reverence”, that does not say whether one god or many is meant. The plural is taken, as in “the eldest of the gods” in 9.1. Other reading: reverence for god
- *ἐν εἴδει ἐστὶ τῆς εὐκοινωνησίας*: Literally “are in the form of good fellowship”, that is, are a kind of it. The noun is very rare; it is built on the root of the word rendered “social” elsewhere. Other reading: For these too are a kind of good fellowship
- *πρεσβύτερα τῶν δικαιοπραγημάτων*: Literally “older than”, which in Greek also means higher in rank or more to be honoured. “Come before” is meant to allow both. Other reading: or rather they are older than acts of justice

</details>

### 11.21

“A person who does not always have one and the same aim in life cannot be one and the same through the whole of life.” The saying is not enough unless you also add what kind of aim this must be. For just as judgment is not alike about all the things that in one way or another seem good to the majority, but is alike about those of a certain kind, that is, the common goods, so too the aim to be set up must be the social and civic one. For whoever directs all their private impulses toward this aim will make all their actions alike, and in this way will always be the same.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *εἷς καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς δι*: The edition marks the first sentence as a quotation; the source is not named. The Greek has simply “he for whom” and “this one”, and “a person” is supplied. “One and the same” is said first of the aim and then of the person, and the same English is kept for both. Other reading: that man cannot be one and the same through his whole life
- *τοῦ βίου σκοπός*: σκοπός is the mark an archer aims at. “Aim” is used for it throughout. Other reading: target in life
- *τὸ εἰρημένον*: Literally “what has been said”. Other reading: What has been said is not enough
- *τῶν ὁπωσοῦν τοῖς πλείοσι δοκούντων ἀγαθῶν*: ὁπωσοῦν (“in whatever way”) is taken with “seem good”. οἱ πλείονες is “the majority, most people”. Other reading: all the things most people somehow or other think good
- *ὑπόληψις ὁμοία ἐστίν*: ὑπόληψις is a judgment taken up about something. “Alike” is understood as the same from one person to the next, and is kept for the same adjective in the last sentence. The Greek does not repeat “is alike” after “but”; it is repeated for clarity. Other reading: people do not judge alike about all the things
- *τουτέστι τῶν κοινῶν*: “The common ones”: goods that are shared, or that concern everyone; the Greek does not say which more exactly. “Goods” is supplied from the clause before, so that “common” is not heard as “ordinary”. Other reading: that is, the shared ones
- *τὸν κοινωνικὸν καὶ πολιτικὸν*: Two adjectives, “social” and “of citizens (of the city)”. In Greek the first is made from the word “common” just used, a link that “social” does not show; “social” is kept because it is the word for κοινωνικός throughout this translation. Other reading: the communal and civic one
- *ὑποστήσασθαι*: “To set under oneself”: to lay down as a basis. Other reading: must be laid down as one’s foundation
- *πάσας τὰς ἰδίας ὁρμὰς*: ἴδιος is “one’s own”, and also “private” as against “common” above; “private” is used so that the contrast can be heard. ὁρμή is the Stoic “impulse”, the movement toward an action. Other reading: all their own impulses
- *κατὰ τοῦτο*: “In accordance with this”: either “in this way, by this means” or “in this respect”. The first is taken, as the result of aiming everything at one mark. Other reading: and in this respect will always be the same

</details>

### 11.22

The mountain mouse and the house mouse, and this one’s fright and its being scared away.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τὸν μῦν τὸν ὀρεινὸν καὶ τὸν κατοικίδιον*: The Greek as given does not construe on its own: everything is in the accusative with no verb, as if after an unspoken “think of” or “remember”. The English leaves a bare phrase and supplies no verb. The reference is taken to be the fable of the country mouse and the town mouse. Other reading: Think of the mountain mouse and the house mouse
- *ὀρεινὸν*: Literally “of the mountains” or hill country, the mouse that lives in the wild. English tradition says “country mouse”. The English keeps the Greek’s word. Other reading: the country mouse
- *τούτου*: “Of this one”, pointing to the nearer of the two, the house mouse. The English keeps “this one” and does not name it. Other reading: the fright of the house mouse
- *πτοίαν*: A fluttering fear, a state of alarm or agitation. Other reading: this one’s panic
- *διασόβησιν*: A rare noun from a verb meaning to scare off or throw into confusion. It may be the mouse’s being scared away, or its own agitated running about. The English takes the first, which is what the verb says. Other reading: and its scurrying in alarm

</details>

### 11.23

Socrates used to call the principles of the many, too, “Lamias”, things to frighten children.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *καὶ*: “Too” or “even”: it may add this saying to others, or mean that he gave the name even to what most people hold. Other reading: Socrates used to call even the principles of the many “Lamias”
- *τὰ τῶν πολλῶν δόγματα*: δόγμα is “principle” throughout this translation, the word Marcus uses for what a person holds and lives by; here it is what most people hold. “Principles” is kept so that the word can be recognised from passage to passage. Other reading: the beliefs of most people
- *Λαμίας*: Lamia was a child-eating monster of Greek nursery tales, used to scare children into behaving. The name and the plural are kept. Other reading: bogeys
- *παιδίων δείματα*: Literally “terrors of little children”: things children are frightened of. Other reading: the terrors of small children

</details>

### 11.24

At their public shows the Spartans used to set the benches for foreign visitors in the shade, while they themselves sat wherever they happened to.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Λακεδαιμόνιοι*: “Lacedaemonians”, the formal name of the Spartans. The English uses the name a reader of today knows. Other reading: The Lacedaemonians
- *τοῖς μὲν ξένοις*: ξένος is both “foreigner” and “guest”: visitors from other cities. μέν and δέ set them against the Spartans themselves, which the English gives with “while”. Other reading: for their guests
- *ἐν ταῖς θεωρίαις*: “At the viewings”: public spectacles or festivals where people sat to watch. Other reading: at their festivals
- *οὗ ἔτυχεν*: Literally “where it chanced”: anywhere, with no care for comfort. Other reading: and sat themselves anywhere

</details>

### 11.25

Socrates to Perdiccas, on not going to him: “So that I may not die the worst of deaths,” he said, that is, so that I may not, after receiving a kindness, be unable to do one in return.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τῷ Περδίκκᾳ ὁ Σωκράτης*: There is no verb: “Socrates to Perdiccas”, as a heading for the saying. Perdiccas was a king of Macedon. From memory, unchecked: other ancient writers tell this of his son Archelaus. Other reading: Socrates said to Perdiccas
- *περὶ τοῦ μὴ ἔρχεσθαι παρ’ αὐτόν*: Literally “about the not coming to him”: his reason for refusing the king’s invitation. Other reading: on why he would not come to his court
- *τῷ κακίστῳ ὀλέθρῳ ἀπόλωμαι*: Literally “perish by the worst destruction”; noun and verb are close in sense, which “die the worst of deaths” keeps. Other reading: So that I may not come to the worst of ends
- *τουτέστι*: “That is”: the explanation that follows keeps the speaker’s own voice, so it may be Socrates’ own words or Marcus’s gloss put in Socrates’ mouth. The Greek as given closes the quotation before it, and the English does the same. Other reading: “So that I may not die the worst of deaths, that is, receive a kindness and be unable to return it.”
- *μὴ εὖ παθῶν οὐ δυνηθῶ ἀντευποιῆσαι*: παθῶν is a slip in the copy for παθών. The Greek pairs “being done good” with “doing good in return”, kept as “receiving a kindness” and “do one in return”. The first is a participle, so what is feared is being unable to repay. Other reading: so that I may not be well treated and be unable to treat him well in return

</details>

### 11.26

In the writings of the Epicureans a rule was laid down: to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐπικουρείων*: The English follows the text as given. From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts read “of the Ephesians” here and “Epicureans” is an editor’s correction, made because Seneca reports a similar precept from Epicurus. Other reading: In the writings of the Ephesians
- *γράμμασι*: The word covers anything written: writings, books, or letters. Other reading: In the letters of the Epicureans
- *παράγγελμα ἔκειτο*: Literally “an instruction lay”, that is, stood written or was laid down as a rule. The tense is past and continuing. Other reading: there stood a precept
- *συνεχῶς ὑπομιμνῄσκεσθαι*: The verb is the same as “are reminded” in 11.27; here the form can be “to remind oneself” or “to be reminded”. “Constantly” is the same word as in 5.27. Other reading: to be continually reminded of
- *τῶν παλαιῶν τινος τῶν ἀρετῇ χρησαμένων*: Literally “some one of the ancients, of those who made use of virtue”. The Greek has the singular: one such person, not the ancients in general. Other reading: some one of the ancients who lived by virtue

</details>

### 11.27

The Pythagoreans: to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn, so that we are reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way, and of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι·*: A nominative with no verb, like a heading, followed by an infinitive that gives their instruction. The English keeps it as a jotting and does not supply “say” or “tell us”. Other reading: The Pythagoreans tell us to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn
- *ἕωθεν*: Literally “from dawn”. It is used both for “at dawn” and more loosely for “early in the morning”. Other reading: early in the morning
- *ἀφορᾶν*: The verb is to look away from other things and fix the eyes on one; the Greek names no direction. “Our” is supplied from the “we” of the next verb. Other reading: to look up at the sky
- *τῶν ἀεὶ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως τὸ ἑαυτῶν ἔργον διανυόντων*: The participle can be masculine (“those who”) or neuter (“the things that”); the last clause shows the stars are meant, so the English reads “those that”. Other reading: the beings who for ever complete their own task
- *κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως*: A set pair for what never varies (a phrase of Plato’s, from memory, unchecked). The first half is literally “according to the same things”; “along the same lines” is the English for it. Other reading: in the same respects and in like manner
- *διανυόντων*: The verb is to bring to completion, and is also used of finishing a journey, which suits the stars’ courses. The English reads “complete”. Other reading: carry out; accomplish
- *καὶ τῆς τάξεως καὶ τῆς καθαρότητος καὶ τῆς γυμνότητος*: Three more things to be reminded of. The Greek has only the article, “the order, the purity, the nakedness”; “their” is supplied, since the last clause gives a star as the reason. The three can also be read as things named in themselves. Other reading: and of order, purity and nakedness
- *οὐδὲν γὰρ προκάλυμμα ἄστρου*: Literally “for there is no covering of a star”, with no verb. The noun is anything hung in front to hide: a curtain, a veil. Other reading: for nothing covers a star

</details>

### 11.28

What Socrates was like with the sheepskin tied round his waist, when Xanthippe had taken his cloak and gone out; and what Socrates said to his companions, who were embarrassed and drew back when they saw him dressed like that.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Οἷος ὁ Σωκράτης*: No main verb: a note to himself, “what kind of man Socrates was”, pointing at a story Marcus knew. From memory, unchecked: the story does not survive elsewhere, so what Socrates said is not known. Other reading: Think what Socrates was like
- *τὸ κῴδιον ὑπεζωσμένος*: “Having girded on the fleece underneath”: wearing a sheepskin tied round the middle in place of clothes. Other reading: wearing only the sheepskin as an undergarment
- *ἡ Ξανθίππη*: Xanthippe was Socrates’ wife. The cloak she took was his outer garment, perhaps the only one. Other reading: when Xanthippe took the cloak and went out
- *αἰδεσθεῖσι καὶ ἀναχωρήσασιν*: “Having felt shame and having withdrawn”: they were ashamed, for him or at seeing him so, and stepped back or went away. Other reading: who were ashamed and went away

</details>

### 11.29–30

In writing and reading you will not rule before you have been ruled. This is much more so in life.

You are by nature a slave; you have no share in reason.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἄρξεις πρὶν ἀρχθῇς*: The verb means to rule or command, and also to begin; here it is active and then passive of the same verb. In the setting of writing and reading the sense is the master and the pupil: no one gives the rules before having been given them. “Rule … been ruled” keeps the one verb and its sense of command. Other reading: you will not lead before you have been led (in sense: you will not teach before you have been taught)
- *τοῦτο πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν τῷ βίῳ*: The Greek has no verb: “this, much more, in life”. “Is so” is supplied. Other reading: This holds much more in life.
- *Δοῦλος πέφυκας, οὐ μέτεστί σοι λόγου*: The words scan as a line of spoken verse (an iambic trimeter) and read like a quotation from a play; from memory, unchecked, the line is counted as a fragment of an unknown dramatist. The Greek as given has no quotation marks and none are added. The two halves stand side by side with only a comma; the English uses a semicolon and adds no “because”. Other reading: “You are a born slave, you have no say.”
- *οὐ μέτεστί σοι λόγου*: The last word is open. In a stage line spoken to a slave it would mean speech: “you have no right to speak”. In this notebook the word is nearly always “reason”, and with “by nature” that sense gives a connected thought, so the English reads “reason”, the settled rendering. Other reading: you have no say
- *πέφυκας*: The perfect can mean “you are by nature” or “you were born”. The English reads “by nature”, the sense that goes with “reason” in the second half; “you were born” goes with “you have no say”. Other reading: You were born a slave

</details>

### 11.31–32

And my own heart laughed.

And they will find fault with virtue, speaking harsh words.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἐμὸν*: The possessive belongs to the speaker of the verse and not necessarily to Marcus. The chapter is a bare line of poetry with no comment. The particle after it can be “and” or “but”. Other reading: But my heart laughed.
- *ἐγέλασσε φίλον κῆρ*: A line-end from Homer, probably Odyssey 9.413, Odysseus after tricking the Cyclops (from memory, unchecked). The epic adjective, literally “dear”, usually means little more than “one’s own”, and is taken so. Other reading: and my dear heart laughed
- *Μέμψονται*: A future with no stated subject, hence “they”. The verb is to blame or find fault with. Other reading: They will blame virtue
- *ἀρετὴν*: The line appears to be Hesiod, Works and Days 186, where the transmitted text has two small words at this point (“then” and “them”) and no mention of virtue (from memory, unchecked). The wording here may be Marcus’s own adaptation or a copying change. The English translates the line as it stands here. Other reading: And they will find fault with them, speaking harsh words.
- *χαλεποῖς βάζοντες ἔπεσσιν*: Literally “speaking with harsh words”. The line does not say whether the words are aimed at virtue or are simply the way these people talk. Other reading: railing at it in harsh words

</details>

### 11.33

To ask for a fig in winter is the act of someone mad. Such is the person who asks for their child when it is no longer given.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Σῦκον χειμῶνος*: The saying appears to come from Epictetus, Discourses 3.24, as do the neighbouring chapters of book 11 (from memory, unchecked). Only what stands here is translated. Other reading: A fig in wintertime
- *μαινομένου*: A genitive with no verb: “(it is the part) of one who is mad”. The participle is masculine but general, so the English says “someone”. Other reading: is a madman’s act
- *ζητεῖν*: The verb is to seek or look for, and also to ask for or want. It is used of the fig and of the child, so one English verb serves both. “Ask for” is used because “look for a child” would be heard as searching for one who is lost. Other reading: To look for a fig in winter; the person who looks for their child
- *τὸ παιδίον*: Literally “the little child”. The article can stand for a possessive, and the English takes it so. Other reading: the one who asks for the child
- *ὅτε οὐκέτι δίδοται*: A present passive: “when it is no longer given” or “granted”. The Greek does not say by whom, and the English keeps the passive. Other reading: when it is no longer granted to them

</details>

### 11.34–35

A person kissing their small child, Epictetus used to say, should add inwardly: “Tomorrow, perhaps, you will die.” “Those are words of ill omen.” “Nothing is of ill omen,” he said, “that points to some work of nature. Otherwise the ears of grain being reaped is of ill omen too.”

Unripe grape, ripe grape, raisin: all changes, not into what is not, but into what is not now.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Καταφιλοῦντα τὸ παιδίον*: Impersonal: “[one] kissing the child”, with a diminutive for “child”. The English uses “a person … their”. The saying is from the Discourses of Epictetus (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: When you kiss your little child
- *ἔνδον ἐπιφθέγγεσθαι*: The verb is “to utter over or in addition”, as one adds a word over an act. ἔνδον is “within”, that is, not aloud. Other reading: should whisper within
- *ἀποθανῇ*: As accented, second person future, “you will die”, spoken to the child. With the accent moved it would be a third person subjunctive, which does not construe here. Other reading: “Tomorrow, perhaps, it will die.”
- *δύσφημα ταῦτα*: The edition marks the objection off with dashes, and the English uses quotation marks for the change of speaker. δύσφημος is “of ill omen”, said of words one should not utter for fear of bringing the thing on. Other reading: “That is unlucky talk.”
- *σημαντικόν*: “That signifies, that is a sign of.” The sentence is “nothing [is] ill-omened [that is] significant of some natural work”. Other reading: that names some process of nature
- *ἢ καὶ τὸ τοὺς στάχυας θερισθῆναι δύσφημον*: Literally “or else the ears of grain being reaped [is] ill-omened too”. It can be read as a statement that follows from the objection, as here, or as a question. Other reading: Or is it also ill-omened for the ears of grain to be reaped?
- *Ὄμφαξ, σταφυλή, σταφίς*: Three single nouns: the unripe grape, the ripe bunch, the dried grape. English has no three matching single words. Other reading: Green grape, cluster, raisin

</details>

### 11.36–38

“There is no robber of the power to choose.” That is the saying of Epictetus.

“One must find an art,” he said, “for giving assent, and in the field of the impulses keep up attention, so that they are with a reservation, so that they are social, so that they are according to worth; and keep away from desire altogether, and use aversion towards none of the things that are not up to us.”

“So the contest,” he said, “is not about just anything, but about being mad or not.”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Λῃστὴς προαιρέσεως οὐ γίνεται*: Literally “a robber of choice does not come to be”: no one can rob a person of their choice. From memory, unchecked: the words are in the Discourses of Epictetus, the Stoic teacher (about AD 50 to 135). Other reading: No one can rob you of your choice.
- *προαιρέσεως*: προαίρεσις is the word Epictetus uses for the faculty of choosing, the one thing that is fully one’s own. The English reads “the power to choose”, because “a robber of choice” would be heard today as “a favourite robber”. Other reading: a robber of the will
- *Τέχνην*: τέχνη is an art or skill with rules. The sentence depends on δεῖ, “it is necessary”, with no person named; the English reads “one must” and lets the one phrase carry all four verbs, as the Greek does. Other reading: We must find a method for assenting
- *ἐν τῷ περὶ τὰς ὁρμὰς τόπῳ*: τόπος (“place”) is the term Epictetus uses for one of the fields of training: assent, impulse, and desire and aversion. The English reads “field”. Other reading: in the topic concerning the impulses
- *τὸ προσεκτικὸν φυλάσσειν*: Literally “to guard the attentive [power]”: to keep attention awake. Other reading: to keep watch over the power of attention
- *ἵνα μεθ’ ὑπεξαιρέσεως, ἵνα κοινωνικαί, ἵνα κατ’ ἀξίαν*: The three clauses have no verb; “they are” is supplied, the impulses being the subject. ὑπεξαίρεσις is the “reservation” (“if nothing prevents”); κατ’ ἀξίαν is “according to the worth” of the thing aimed at. Other reading: so that they are conditional, for the common good, and in proportion to worth
- *ὀρέξεως μὲν παντάπασιν ἀπέχεσθαι, ἐκκλίσει δὲ*: ὄρεξις (“desire”, reaching for a thing) and ἔκκλισις (“aversion”, turning from a thing) are a fixed pair. “Altogether” is kept as the Greek has it. Other reading: to abstain entirely from desire, and to turn away from nothing that is not up to us
- *περὶ τοῦ τυχόντος*: Literally “about what happens along”: any ordinary matter. “Not about just anything” gives the idiom in the English that matches it. Other reading: is not about some trivial thing
- *ἀγών*: A contest, as in the games or in court, and so a struggle. Other reading: So the struggle

</details>

### 11.39

Socrates used to say: “What do you want? To have the souls of rational beings or of irrational ones?” “Of rational beings.” “Of which rational beings? Sound ones or bad ones?” “Sound ones.” “Then why do you not look for them?” “Because we have them.” “Then why do you fight and fall out?”

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὁ Σωκράτης ἔλεγε*: The tense is “used to say” or “was saying”. The exchange is not known from Plato or Xenophon (from memory, unchecked). The Greek as given marks each change of speaker with a dash; the English uses quotation marks. Other reading: Socrates said
- *λογικῶν ψυχὰς ἔχειν ἢ ἀλόγων*: Literally “to have souls of rational ones or of irrational ones”. λογικός is “rational” throughout this translation; “beings” is added. Other reading: To have rational souls or irrational ones?
- *ὑγιῶν ἢ φαύλων*: ὑγιής is “healthy”, “sound”; φαῦλος is “bad”, “worthless”. The pair is not an exact opposite in Greek either. Other reading: Healthy ones or worthless ones?
- *τί οὖν οὐ ζητεῖτε*: The verb has no object: “why do you not seek?” “Them” is supplied, the souls just named. Other reading: Then why do you not go looking?
- *μάχεσθε καὶ διαφέρεσθε*: “Fight and differ”: the second verb is to be at odds, to quarrel. Other reading: Then why do you fight and disagree?

</details>

## Book 12

### 12.1

All those things you pray to reach by a roundabout road you can have already, if you do not begrudge yourself. That is: if you leave all the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present toward piety and justice. Piety, so that you love what is allotted, for nature brought it to you and you to it. Justice, so that, freely and without winding about, you speak the truth and do what accords with law and with what each deserves. And do not be hindered by another person’s badness, or judgment, or voice, or even by the sensation of the bit of flesh that has grown up around you, for the part that suffers will see to that. So if, whenever it is that you come close to your exit, you leave everything else behind and honor only your ruling part and what is divine in you, and if what you fear is not that you will some day stop living but rather never beginning to live according to nature, then you will be a human being worthy of the universe that gave you birth.
