You will stop being a stranger in your own country, stop wondering at what happens every day as if it were unexpected, and stop hanging on this and that.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *διὰ περιόδου*: Literally “by way of a circuit”. The English takes it of a roundabout route; it can also be taken of time, a cycle or period that has to pass first. Other reading: that you pray to reach in the course of time
- *ὁσιότητα καὶ δικαιοσύνην*: ὁσιότης is right dealing toward the divine, as justice is toward people. “Piety” is the nearest plain word; the next sentence defines it as loving what is allotted. Other reading: holiness and justice
- *χωρὶς περιπλοκῆς*: Literally “without entwining”: without twisting or winding, said of speech that goes round about and of dealings that are not straight. “Without winding about” keeps the image and covers both the speaking and the doing. Other reading: without evasion
- *κατ’ ἀξίαν*: “According to worth”: in proportion to what is deserved. The Greek does not say whose worth, a person’s or a thing’s, and “each” leaves that open. Other reading: and do what accords with law and with the worth of each thing
- *μὴ ἐμποδίζῃ δέ σε*: A subjunctive as given. The English reads it as standing on its own, as a command; it may still depend on the “so that” before it. The Greek is active, “let neither … hinder you”; the English is passive to carry the list. Other reading: and so that nothing may hinder you, neither …
- *μήτε κακία ἀλλοτρία μήτε ὑπόληψις μήτε φωνὴ*: “Another person’s” stands with “badness” and can carry over to the two nouns after it, so that these are what others think and say; or the judgment may be one’s own. The English is built so that the words can carry over in the same way. “Judgment” is this translation’s word for ὑπόληψις. Other reading: by another person’s badness, or by your own judgment, or by anything said
- *ὄψεται γὰρ τὸ πάσχον*: An idiom: “it will see”, meaning “that is its own business”. The part that suffers is the flesh, as against the ruling part. Other reading: for that is the business of the part that is affected
- *ὅτε δήποτε πρὸς ἐξόδῳ γένῃ*: “At whatever time you come to be near the exit.” It may be general (whenever that turns out to be) or pointed (now that you are at last near it). The English keeps it general. Other reading: now that you are at last close to your exit
- *ἀλλὰ τό γε μηδέποτε ἄρξασθαι κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν*: The Greek verb form here carries no time: “never beginning” covers both never having begun so far and never coming to begin. The fear of stopping, by contrast, is put in the future. Other reading: but that you never began to live according to nature
- *κρεμάμενος ἐκ τοῦδε καὶ τοῦδε*: Literally “hanging from this and this”. The image is of depending on one thing after another, or one person after another: the Greek form can be either, and “this and that” leaves it open. Other reading: depending on this person and that

</details>

### 12.2–3

God sees all ruling parts bare of their material vessels and husks and refuse. For with only the part of himself that is of mind he touches only what has flowed out of himself into these and been channelled off. If you too make a habit of doing this, you will strip away most of your distraction. For someone who does not look at the surrounding scraps of flesh is hardly likely to busy themselves with gazing at clothing and a house and reputation and that kind of wrapping and stage scenery.

There are three things of which you are made up: a little body, a little breath, mind. Of these the other two are yours so far as you must take care of them, but only the third is properly yours. So if you separate from yourself, that is, from your thought, all that others do or say, or all that you yourself have done or said, and all that troubles you as something to come, and all that belongs to you, without your choosing it, from the little body that surrounds you or the little breath born with you, and all that the whirl streaming round outside sets spinning, so that the power of mind, lifted clear of what is bound up with it by fate, and clean, lives set loose by itself, doing what is just and willing what happens and saying what is true; if, I say, you separate from this ruling part the things fastened onto it by attachment, and what of time lies ahead or has gone by, and make yourself like the sphere of Empedocles, “rounded, rejoicing in its encircling solitude”, and practise living only what you are living, that is, the present: then what is left until you die, at least, you will be able to live through untroubled, kindly, and gracious toward your own guardian spirit.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *φλοιῶν καὶ καθαρμάτων*: φλοιός is bark, husk or rind, any outer covering; κάθαρμα is what is thrown away in cleaning, refuse. The three nouns (vessels, husks, refuse) are all images for the body and its coverings. Other reading: bare of their material vessels and bark and impurities
- *εἰς ταῦτα*: “Into these” can point to the vessels and husks, into which the ruling parts have flowed from god, or to the ruling parts themselves. The English leaves it as “these”. Other reading: what has flowed out of himself into these ruling parts
- *τὸν πολὺν περισπασμὸν σεαυτοῦ περιαιρήσεις*: τὸν πολὺν with a noun is “the greater part of” or “all this great”; the English has “most of”. σεαυτοῦ can go with the verb (“strip from yourself”) or with the noun (“your distraction”). The Greek also plays on the prefix περι- (“around”) here and in the next sentence: distraction, stripping away, surrounding flesh, wrapping. Other reading: you will strip away from yourself that great distraction
- *ἦ πού γε*: After a negative this idiom means “much less”: one who does not look at the flesh will, still less, spend time gazing at clothes. The Greek has no “not” here and puts it as a half question; the English has “is hardly likely to”. Other reading: will someone who does not look at the surrounding scraps of flesh busy themselves, do you suppose, with gazing at clothing and a house and reputation?
- *σκηνὴν*: σκηνή is a tent or hut and also the stage building and its scenery. With θεώμενος, the verb for watching a show, the English takes the theatre sense. Other reading: that kind of wrapping and tent
- *σωμάτιον, πνευμάτιον*: Both are diminutives, with a belittling tone. πνευμάτιον is the breath that keeps the body alive, not “spirit” in the modern sense, so the English has “a little breath”. Other reading: a poor body, a puff of breath
- *ὃ ἐὰν χωρίσῃς*: As given, the relative ὃ (“which”) has no construction with what follows, since the object of “separate” is the string of “all that” clauses. The English treats it as a loose connective, “So”; from memory, unchecked, some editors print διό (“therefore”). The long “if” clause is taken up again further down. Other reading: Which third part, if you separate from yourself
- *τῆς σῆς διανοίας*: The passage has both νοῦς and διάνοια. The English keeps “mind” for νοῦς and νοερός and “thought” for διάνοια, as the glossary prefers, though διάνοια here is the faculty. Other reading: that is, from your understanding
- *τοῦ συμφύτου πνευματίου*: σύμφυτος is inborn, grown together with something. The English takes it with “you”, carried over from the body “that surrounds you”; it can also mean grown together with the body. Other reading: the little breath that has grown with it
- *τῶν συνειμαρμένων*: A rare word built on εἱμαρμένη, fate: the things fated together with it, bound up with it by fate. The English spells the sense out. Other reading: lifted clear of the things that share its fate
- *προσπαθείας*: προσπάθεια is passionate attachment to something, a clinging. The English has “attachment”. Other reading: the things that hang on it through its passions
- *κυκλοτερὴς μονίῃ περιηγέι γαίων*: The epic forms show these words are a line of verse quoted from Empedocles, so they are set in quotation marks, which the Greek as given does not have; the line may begin at σφαῖρος. μονίη can be “solitude” (from μόνος) or “rest”, “staying still” (from μένω), and περιηγής is “circular” or “encircling”. The English has “its encircling solitude”. Other reading: rounded, rejoicing in its circular stillness
- *ἵλεως τῷ σαυτοῦ δαίμονι*: ἵλεως is “gracious”, the word for a god who is well disposed; here it is you who are so toward your δαίμων, the divine being assigned to each person, which Marcus identifies with the mind. “Guardian” is supplied in the English so that “spirit” is not heard as your own soul or mood. The dative may go with all three words or only with the last. Other reading: untroubled, and kindly and gracious toward the god within you

</details>

### 12.4

I have often wondered how it is that each person loves themselves more than everyone else, yet sets less value on their own judgment about themselves than on that of others. At any rate, if a god appears beside someone, or a sensible teacher, and tells them to turn over nothing in their mind and think nothing to themselves that they will not at the same moment bring out, crying it aloud, they will not put up with this for even one day. So it is that we feel more shame before those near us, at what they will think of us, than before ourselves.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *μᾶλλον πάντων*: Literally “more than all”, which can be all people or all things. The English takes people, since the sentence goes on to set each person against “the others”. Other reading: more than everything
- *ὑπόληψιν*: The judgment or opinion one holds; “judgment” follows the glossary. Other reading: their own opinion of themselves
- *ἐν ἐλάττονι λόγῳ τίθεται*: An idiom: to put in a lesser account. λόγος here is “account” or “reckoning”, not reason. Other reading: holds in less account
- *θεὸς ἐπιστὰς*: The participle is used of a god or a dream figure appearing and standing by a person. Other reading: if a god stood over someone
- *καθ’ ἑαυτὸν ἐνθυμεῖσθαι καὶ διανοεῖσθαι*: Two verbs for inward thinking, the second from the word the glossary gives as “thought”. “By oneself” means privately, inside. Other reading: to have no idea and no thought in private
- *γεγωνίσκων ἐξοίσει*: Literally “will bring out, shouting it”: the verb is to cry out so as to be heard. Other reading: that they will not at once shout out loud
- *αἰδούμεθα*: To feel shame before someone, to stand in awe of them or respect them. Other reading: So much more do we respect our neighbours
- *τοὺς πέλας*: Literally “those nearby”, the usual phrase for other people. Other reading: our neighbours

</details>

### 12.5

How can it be that the gods, who arranged all things well and with love for humankind, overlooked this one thing only: that some people, and very good ones, who had made a great many contracts, so to speak, with the divine, and who through holy deeds and sacred rites had come to be on the closest terms with the divine, once they have died, do not come to be again any more, but are completely extinguished? But if this really is so, be sure that if it ought to have been otherwise, they would have made it otherwise. For if it were just, it would also be possible, and if it were in accord with nature, nature would have brought it about. So from its not being so, if indeed it is not so, be assured that it ought not to have come about so. For you see for yourself that in prying into this you are arguing a case of justice with god. And we would not be reasoning with the gods like this unless they are best and most just. And if that is so, they would not have let anything in the order of things be neglected unjustly and against reason.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ὥσπερ συμβόλαια θεμένους*: συμβόλαια are contracts or business dealings between parties; “so to speak” (ὥσπερ) marks it as a figure. The English keeps the commercial image. Other reading: who had had, as it were, the most dealings with the divine
- *μηκέτι αὖθις γίνεσθαι*: Literally “no longer come to be again”. The verb is the general one for coming into being, so it does not decide between being born again and existing again in some other way. Other reading: are never born again
- *ἀπεσβηκέναι*: The verb is used of a flame or lamp that has gone out. “Extinguished” keeps the image. Other reading: have gone out completely
- *ἐκ δὴ τοῦ μὴ οὕτως ἔχειν, εἴπερ οὐχ οὕτως ἔχει*: The same word “so” (οὕτως) changes what it points to: earlier, “if this really is so” meant that the good are completely extinguished, and here “its not being so” means its not being the other way, that they come to be again. The English keeps “so” each time, as the Greek does. Other reading: So from the fact that it is not that other way, if indeed it is not
- *πιστούσθω σοι τὸ μὴ δεῆσαι οὕτως γίνεσθαι*: A third-person command: “let it be made sure for you”. The infinitive δεῆσαι is a past form and answers “ought” (ἔδει) above, so the English says “ought not to have”. The sense is that the other arrangement was not called for; the word can also mean bare need. Other reading: let it be your assurance that there was no need for it to come about so
- *παραζητῶν*: A rare compound of “to seek”. The prefix marks the search as beside the point or as going beyond what is proper; “prying” takes the second. Other reading: in raising this needless question
- *δικαιολογῇ πρὸς τὸν θεόν*: The verb is to plead one’s case, to argue what is just, as before a court. The Greek has the singular with the article here, between plurals before and after: god in general, not one god already named. Other reading: you are pleading your rights against the god
- *διελεγόμεθα*: The verb is to talk a thing through with someone, to reason it out. “Reasoning” is used so that it is not confused with “arguing a case of justice” (δικαιολογῇ) just before. Other reading: we would not be talking with the gods like this
- *εἰ μὴ ἄριστοι καὶ δικαιότατοί εἰσιν*: The Greek has a plain present, “if they are not”, where an unreal condition would lead one to expect “if they were not”. The English keeps the present, which states their goodness as a fact. Other reading: if they were not best and most just
- *περιεῖδον*: This answers “overlooked” (παρεῖδον) in the first sentence with a near twin: there the verb is to look past, here to look on and let happen. English cannot keep the echo. Other reading: they would not have overlooked anything
- *τῶν ἐν τῇ διακοσμήσει*: Literally “of the things in the setting-in-order”, a noun from the same root as κόσμος and the regular Stoic word for the ordering of the universe. The English uses the common phrase “the order of things”. Other reading: anything in the ordering of the universe

</details>

### 12.6

Practise even the things you have given up on. For in fact the left hand, though for lack of practice it is no good at anything else, holds the bridle more firmly than the right, because this is what it has had practice in.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἔθιζε*: An active imperative, “accustom”, with no “yourself” expressed; the things given up on are its object. The same root returns in ἀνέθιστον and εἴθισται, so one English word, “practise” (“practice”), is kept for all three. Other reading: Accustom yourself even to the things you have given up on.
- *ἀπογινώσκεις*: The verb is to give something up as hopeless. It does not say whether these are tasks thought to be beyond one’s power or anything written off, and “have given up on” leaves that as open as the Greek. Other reading: the things you despair of
- *καὶ γὰρ*: The two particles together can be “for in fact”, or the first can be “even” (or “too”) and go with the left hand. The English reads “for in fact”; the “though” that follows already carries the surprise. Other reading: For even the left hand
- *ἀργὸς οὖσα*: Literally “being not working”: the adjective covers idle, slow and of no use, and the participle is read as a concession, “though”. “No good at” is used so that the hand is not heard as lazy. Other reading: which is idle (or: slow) at everything else
- *πρὸς τὰ ἄλλα*: With its article the phrase means “the rest”, all the other things, so the English reads “anything else”. Other reading: at other things
- *τοῦ χαλινοῦ*: The word is the bridle or the bit; what the hand actually holds is the reins. The literal “bridle” is kept. Other reading: holds the reins
- *κρατεῖ*: With the genitive the verb means to have hold of, or to have mastery over. The English takes the physical grip. Other reading: masters the bridle more strongly than the right
- *τοῦτο γὰρ εἴθισται*: The form can be read with “this” as subject (“this has become habitual”) or with the hand as subject (“it has been accustomed to this”). The English takes the hand as subject and writes “has had practice in”, which keeps the word “practice” and the passive sense of the Greek perfect. Other reading: for this has become its habit

</details>

### 12.7–9

What a person ought to be like, in body and in soul, when death catches them. The shortness of life. The gaping expanse of time behind and ahead. The weakness of all matter.

To look at what is causal, bare of its husks. The aims of actions. What pain is. What pleasure is. What death is. What reputation is. Who is the cause of a person’s own busyness. How no one is hindered by another. That everything is judgment.

And in the use of principles one must be like the all-in fighter, not the gladiator. For the gladiator puts down the sword he uses and picks it up; but the other always has his hand, and needs only to clench it.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὁποῖον δεῖ καταληφθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ θανάτου*: The chapter is a list of headings with no main verb; the accusatives that follow depend on an unstated “think of”, and they are left as bare headings. Ὁποῖον is masculine, “what kind of man”, with no man singled out, so the English has “a person” and “them”. Other reading: In what state of body and soul death ought to find one
- *τὴν ἀχάνειαν*: A yawning gulf, an immensity. αἰών, which follows, is unbounded time. Other reading: the abyss of eternity behind and before
- *Γυμνὰ τῶν φλοιῶν*: φλοιός is bark, rind or husk. Other reading: stripped of their bark
- *τὰ αἰτιώδη*: “The causal things”: the cause or active principle in each thing, as against its matter, which closes the paragraph before. The infinitive θεάσασθαι has no verb governing it. Other reading: the causes of things, seen bare of their coverings
- *τὰς ἀναφορὰς τῶν πράξεων*: ἀναφορά is the “carrying back” of an act to its end: what the act is done with reference to. The English reads “aims”. The same root is in 3.13 (συναναφορᾶς), where it is “referring”. Other reading: what actions are referred to
- *τί πόνος*: πόνος is toil, hardship or pain; set beside pleasure, it is taken as pain. Other reading: what toil is
- *τίς ὁ ἑαυτῷ ἀσχολίας αἴτιος*: Literally “who [is] the one who is to himself the cause of want of leisure”. ἀσχολία is busyness, being taken up with things, and so trouble. The implied answer is each person themselves. Other reading: who it is that makes trouble for himself
- *παγκρατιαστῇ, οὐχὶ μονομάχῳ*: The pankration (“all powers”) was a Greek contest of boxing and wrestling combined, fought with bare hands; the English reads “all-in fighter”. μονομάχος is a gladiator. Other reading: like a pancratiast, not a gladiator
- *ἀποτίθεται καὶ ἀναιρεῖται*: ἀναιρεῖται can be middle, “takes up”, or passive, “is killed”. It is taken as middle, with the sword as object of both verbs: he has his weapon only when he picks it up. Other reading: the one lays aside the sword he uses, and is killed
- *συστρέψαι*: To twist together: here, to ball the hand into a fist. Other reading: has only to close it

</details>

### 12.10

See things as being of this kind, dividing them into matter, cause, purpose.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Τοιαῦτα*: Literally “such”, “of this kind”, said of the things. Nothing in the sentence answers “such”: it may point back to the chapter before, which is not part of this passage, or forward to the division that follows, and the English leaves it as open as the Greek. Some editions may print a fuller text in which words meaning “as they are” answer “such” (from memory, unchecked). Other reading: See things in this way, dividing them into matter, cause, purpose.
- *ὁρᾶν*: An infinitive used as an instruction to oneself, written as a command. Other reading: To see things as being of this kind
- *ὕλην, αἴτιον, ἀναφοράν*: Three bare nouns with no “and”. “Matter” is the noun; the related adjective in 12.17b and 8.11 is given as “material”. “Cause” is the Stoic active element that shapes the matter, not an earlier event, and the third word is literally “reference”, what the thing is referred to, narrowed to “purpose” as in 12.17b. Other reading: into matter, cause, reference

</details>

### 12.11a

How great a power a human being has: to do nothing other than what god is going to praise, and to accept everything god assigns to them, whatever it is.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ἡλίκην ἐξουσίαν*: An exclamation. ἐξουσία is the power to do a thing in the sense that it lies with one to do it, and ranges over freedom to act and authority. The English reads “power”, as in “it is in a person’s power”. Other reading: What freedom a human being has
- *ἄνθρωπος*: No article: any human being. The English reads “a human being” and “them” so as not to single out a man. Other reading: a man … to him
- *μέλλει ὁ θεὸς ἐπαινεῖν*: μέλλει with the infinitive is “is going to” or “is sure to”, and ἐπαινεῖν is “praise” and also “approve”. The English keeps the plainer future and “praise”. Other reading: what god will approve
- *δέχεσθαι*: The verb is “receive” or “accept”, and can be as warm as “welcome”. The English reads “accept”, as for δέχομαι in 8.23 in this section. Other reading: to welcome
- *ὃν νέμῃ*: As given, ὃν (“whom”) does not construe with the neuter πᾶν or with the subjunctive. It is read as a slip of the digitised copy for ὃ ἂν νέμῃ, “whatever he assigns” (from memory, unchecked, that the edition prints ὃ ἂν). “Whatever it is” gives the indefinite force of that reading. Other reading: everything that god assigns to them

</details>

### 12.11b–12

What follows in order on nature.

The gods are not to be blamed, for they go wrong in nothing, willingly or unwillingly. Nor are people, for they go wrong in nothing except unwillingly. So no one is to be blamed.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ φύσει*: A phrase without a verb, cut from its sentence: “the next-in-order to nature”, what comes in sequence with nature. It does not construe alone and is left a fragment, in a paragraph of its own because the passage gives it as the end of chapter 11. It can also be taken with the sentence that follows; from memory, unchecked, editors differ on whether these words end chapter 11 or begin chapter 12. Other reading: As to what comes next in the order of nature: the gods are not to be blamed
- *οὐδὲν γὰρ ἑκόντες ἢ ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνουσι*: The verb is to miss the mark, to go wrong; it covers error as well as wrongdoing. “Willingly or unwillingly” denies both ways of going wrong. Other reading: for they do no wrong, either on purpose or against their will
- *οὐδὲν γὰρ οὐχὶ ἄκοντες*: The verb is carried over from the clause before, and the English repeats it. Literally “for nothing not unwillingly”: whatever they go wrong in, they do against their will, the Socratic teaching that no one goes wrong willingly. Other reading: for they do no wrong that is not against their will

</details>

### 12.13

How ridiculous, and what a stranger, is the person who is surprised at anything at all that happens in life.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πῶς γελοῖος*: An exclamatory “how”, covering both adjectives. The edition ends the sentence with a full stop and the English does the same. Other reading: How ridiculous and how much a stranger
- *ξένος*: A foreigner or stranger, as in 4.29, where the one who does not know what happens is a stranger to the universe. The word can also mean “strange”, but the link with 4.29 favours “stranger”. Other reading: How ridiculous and strange is the person
- *θαυμάζων*: The verb covers being surprised, wondering and marvelling. “Surprised” is used, since the point is being caught unprepared. Other reading: who wonders at; who is astonished at
- *ὁτιοῦν*: “Anything whatever”. The English keeps the full force with “anything at all”. Other reading: at any one of the things that happen in life

</details>

### 12.14–15

Either a necessity of fate and an order that cannot be overstepped, or a providence that can be appeased, or a jumble of randomness with no one in charge. If, then, it is a necessity that cannot be overstepped, why do you strain against it? If it is a providence that allows itself to be appeased, make yourself worthy of the help that comes from the divine. And if it is a jumble with nothing ruling it, be glad that in such a rough sea you yourself have in yourself a mind that rules. And if the sea carries you away, let it carry away the poor flesh, the bit of breath, the rest; for the mind it will not carry away.

Or does the light of a lamp shine until it goes out, and not lose its brightness, while the truth and justice and self-control in you will go out first?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀπαράβατος*: Literally “not to be stepped past”. It can mean that no one can break it, or that it does not itself step aside. Other reading: an order that never deviates
- *ἱλάσιμος*: A rare word from the verb for making a god well-disposed by prayer or offering, which comes again two sentences later. “Appeased” is used for both. Other reading: a providence that can be won over
- *φυρμὸς εἰκαιότητος ἀπροστάτητος*: Literally “a mixing-up of randomness without anyone standing over it”. εἰκαιότης is from the adverb for “at random, without purpose”. Other reading: a purposeless confusion with no one presiding
- *ἀντιτείνεις*: Literally “stretch against”, the image of pulling the other way. Other reading: why do you resist?
- *ἀνηγεμόνευτος*: “Without a ruler”. It is set against νοῦν ἡγεμονικόν, “a ruling mind”, in the same sentence, the word Marcus uses for the ruling part of the soul. “Rule” is used for both. Other reading: a leaderless jumble ... a mind to lead you
- *κλύδωνι*: Rough water, the swell and wash of waves. The word comes twice; the English reads “rough sea” and then “the sea”. Other reading: in such a surge
- *τὸ σαρκίδιον, τὸ πνευμάτιον*: Both are diminutives, “little flesh” and “little breath”, and they belittle. English has no single form for this, so “poor” and “bit of” are used. Other reading: the scrap of flesh, the puff of breath
- *ἢ τὸ μὲν τοῦ λύχνου φῶς*: The second chapter is taken to begin here, where the subject changes. The digitised text marks no break at this point; editions are believed to divide here (from memory, unchecked).
- *σωφροσύνη*: Soundness of mind shown as moderation and self-command. Other reading: moderation
- *προαποσβήσεται*: Literally “will go out beforehand”. Before what is not said: the sense is before you yourself do, as the lamp’s light lasts until the lamp goes out. The verb is the lamp’s verb with two prefixes, so “go out” is used for both. Other reading: will be put out before you are

</details>

### 12.16

In the case of someone who has given the impression of having done wrong: “But how do I know whether this is a wrong?” And if they did do wrong, that they have condemned themselves, and so this is like tearing one’s own face. That whoever does not want the bad person to do wrong is like someone who does not want the fig tree to bear sap in its figs, or babies to cry, or the horse to neigh, or any of the other things that have to be. For what are they to do, having a disposition like that? So if you are vigorous, cure that disposition.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *φαντασίαν παρασχόντος*: φαντασία is “impression” as settled: the person has produced the impression that they did wrong. Other reading: someone who appears to have done wrong
- *τί δαὶ οἶδα*: δαί is a colloquial particle that sharpens a question. It is rendered with “But”. Other reading: And how
- *ὅτι κατέκρινεν αὐτὸς ἑαυτόν*: The Greek has only “that …”, a thought to be held ready, with no verb of saying; so too the next sentence. The bare “that” is kept in both places. Other reading: then tell yourself that they have condemned themselves
- *τῷ καταδρύπτειν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ὄψιν*: καταδρύπτω is to tear with the nails, as mourners did. ὄψις is the face, or possibly the eyes. The Greek does not say what “this” is; it is taken to be the wrongdoing. Other reading: like tearing at one’s own eyes
- *ὀπὸν*: ὀπός is the sharp milky juice of the fig tree. English has no single plain word; the English reads “sap”. Other reading: to have acrid juice in its figs
- *τί γὰρ πάθῃ*: An idiom, literally “what is the person to undergo?”, used for “what else can they do?”. It is taken of the bad person, who cannot help it with such a disposition. ἕξις is rendered “disposition”, as in 11.18. Other reading: For what is to become of a person in such a condition?
- *γοργὸς*: γοργός is fierce, vigorous, quick to act. The English gives the plain sense and adds no mockery; the Greek may be straight praise or a slight taunt. Other reading: So if you are fierce
- *ταύτην θεράπευσον*: “That” is feminine in the Greek and points to the disposition just named. It is most naturally the other person’s; it could be read as a turn back to your own. Other reading: treat this condition of yours

</details>

### 12.17a

If it is not fitting, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it. For let your impulse be …

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *καθήκει*: The verb behind the Stoic term for a fitting act, often given as “duty”. The English keeps the plain “fitting”. Other reading: If it is not your duty
- *ἡ γὰρ ὁρμή σου ἔστω*: The Greek as given stops here in mid-sentence, with no word to say what the impulse is to be; the English adds nothing and marks the break with three dots. In the edition the chapter goes on with words that the section division leaves to the next passage, and whether they complete this sentence is not clear. Taking the words as complete, with “yours” as the thing said of the impulse, is possible but strained. Other reading: For let the impulse be yours

</details>

### 12.17b

Always see in full what that thing itself is which produces the impression in you, and open it out, dividing it into the cause, into the material, into the purpose, into the time within which it will have to be over.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *εἰς τὸ πᾶν*: The words can be an adverb with “see” (“altogether, in full”, or “in every case”), or what is looked at, “look to the whole”, meaning the whole of the thing or the universe. The English takes “in full” because the question “what that thing is” follows at once as what is to be seen. The passage starts in mid-chapter, and the sentence before it, not translated here, breaks off at “for let your impulse be”, so these words may once have belonged to that sentence. Other reading: Always look to the whole: what that thing itself is which produces the impression in you
- *ὁρᾶν*: The verbs here (“see”, “open out”) are infinitives, the notebook form for an instruction to oneself, and are written as commands. “See” is kept for this verb here and in 12.10; “look” is left for the different verb of 6.3. Other reading: Always to look in full at what that thing itself is … and to open it out
- *τὸ τὴν φαντασίαν σοι ποιοῦν*: Literally “the thing making the impression for you”; the dative “for you” can also be heard as “on you”. “Impression” is the Stoic term φαντασία: how a thing presents itself to the mind. Other reading: the thing that makes the impression on you
- *ἀναπτύσσειν*: An image: to unfold or unroll something folded up, as one opens a scroll or a folded cloth. It is kept as “open it out”. Other reading: and unfold it
- *τὸ αἴτιον*: “The cause” here is the Stoic term for the active element that shapes a thing and makes it what it is, set against its material. It is not an earlier event that brought the thing about. Other reading: the causal element, the shaping principle
- *εἰς τὸ αἴτιον, εἰς τὸ ὑλικόν, εἰς τὴν ἀναφοράν, εἰς τὸν χρόνον*: The Greek says “into” four times and has no “and”: four separate heads, counted off one by one. The English keeps all four. Other reading: into the cause, the material, the purpose and the time
- *τὴν ἀναφοράν*: Literally “the reference”, “the carrying back”: what the thing is referred to. The word has a range (relation, reference, the end something is directed to), and the English narrows it to “purpose”, as also in 12.10. The sister passage 8.11 asks at this point in the same list “What does it do in the universe?”, which supports the narrower sense. Other reading: into the reference, what it relates to
- *πεπαῦσθαι αὐτὸ δεήσει*: The infinitive is a perfect: not “will have to stop” but “will have to have stopped”, to be over and done, which the English gives as “will have to be over”. “It” is neuter and so is the thing, not the impression (which is feminine in Greek). Other reading: the time within which it will have to have ceased

</details>

### 12.19–21

Notice at last that you have in yourself something stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions and that, in a word, pull you about on strings. What is my thought at this moment? Can it be fear? Suspicion? Desire? Anything else of that kind?

First, not at random and not without a point of reference. Second, to take as the point of reference nothing other than the social end.

That before long you will be no one and nowhere, nor will any of the things you now see be, nor any of the people now living. For it is the nature of all things to change, to turn and to perish, so that other things may come to be after them.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Αἴσθου ποτὲ*: ποτέ with a command is “at some point”, with a note of impatience: “at last”, “for once”. Other reading: Notice, some time,
- *κρεῖττόν τι καὶ δαιμονιώτερον*: κρεῖττον is both “stronger” and “better”. The second word is formed from δαίμων, the divine being within a person, so “more divine”. Other reading: something better and more godlike
- *νευροσπαστούντων*: The verb for working a puppet by its strings. The Greek word carries the image by itself; “on strings” is the English for it here, as in 2.2 and 7.3. Other reading: the things that pull your strings
- *ἡ διάνοια*: “Thought” is this translation’s word for διάνοια: here the thinking part as a whole and the state it is in at this moment, not one thought. The Greek changes here from the second person to the first. Other reading: What is my mind at this moment?
- *μὴ φόβος*: A question with μή: it expects or hopes for the answer no, or asks with some unease. “Can it be” stands for the first and the rest are left bare. Other reading: It is not fear, is it?
- *ἄνευ ἀναφορᾶς*: Literally “without a reference”: without something the action is referred back to. The next sentence uses a near twin, “to make the referring”. “Point of reference” stands for both. Neither sentence has a main verb. Other reading: First, not at random and not without an aim. Second, to aim at nothing other than the social end.
- *τὸ κοινωνικὸν τέλος*: “Social” is this translation’s word for κοινωνικός: the end that concerns the community, the common good. Other reading: the good of the community as its end
- *Ὅτι μετ’ οὐ πολὺ*: The chapter opens with a bare “That”, as a thought to keep in mind. It is kept. Other reading: Remember that before long

</details>

### 12.22

That all things are judgment, and this judgment is up to you. So take the judgment away when you wish, and, just as for someone who has rounded the headland, there is calm: all things steady, and a bay without a wave.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Ὅτι πάντα ὑπόληψις*: The sentence opens with a bare “That”, with no verb of saying or remembering; it reads as a heading for something to keep in mind. It is kept bare, here and in 2.15, and no “remember” is added. πάντα is plural, “all things”, and returns in “all things steady”. Other reading: Remember that everything is what you judge it to be
- *καὶ αὕτη ἐπὶ σοί*: “And this is up to you”: the pronoun is feminine and points to the judgment, so the English reads “this judgment” to keep it from being heard as “this fact”. Other reading: and it is in your power
- *ἆρον*: The verb is to lift, and so to lift away, remove. The form is a single act, “take it away”. Other reading: So remove the judgment when you choose
- *ὥσπερ κάμψαντι τὴν ἄκραν*: A sailing image: literally “just as to one who has bent round the cape”. The Greek has no “you” and no verb here; it may be felt as “for you, as for a sailor who …”. Other reading: and, like someone who has doubled the cape, you find calm
- *γαλήνη, σταθερὰ πάντα καὶ κόλπος ἀκύμων*: Three items with no verb; “there is” and a colon are supplied. γαλήνη is the calm of the sea; σταθερὰ is steady, standing firm; ἀκύμων is literally “waveless”. Other reading: calm, everything still, and a waveless gulf

</details>

### 12.23

Any single activity, whichever it is, that stops at the right time suffers nothing bad in that it has stopped; nor has the one who did this action suffered anything bad just in this respect, that it has stopped. In the same way, then, the sum made up of all the actions, which is a life, if it stops at the right time, suffers nothing bad just in this respect, that it has stopped; nor has the one who brought this chain to a stop at the right time been put in a bad state. The right time and the limit are given by nature: sometimes by one’s own nature too, when the stopping comes in old age, but in every case by the nature of the whole, with the changing of whose parts the entire universe stays always young and in its prime. And everything that benefits the whole is always fine and in season. So for each person the stopping of life is not a bad thing, since it is not a shameful thing either, if indeed it is both outside one’s choice and not unsocial; and it is a good thing, if indeed it comes at the right time for the whole, benefits the whole and is carried along with the whole. For in this way a person is also carried by god: the one who is carried in the same way as god and is carried, in their purpose, toward the same things.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Μία καὶ ἡτισοῦν ἐνέργεια κατὰ καιρὸν παυσαμένη*: Marcus says ἐνέργεια (“activity”) and then πρᾶξις (“action”) for the same thing; two English words are kept. καιρός is the right moment, “the right time” throughout, including for καίριον near the end. The whole chain on παύομαι is kept as “stop”. Other reading: Any one activity whatever, ceasing in due season
- *τὸ ἐκ πασῶν τῶν πράξεων σύστημα*: σύστημα is a composite whole. “Sum” keeps “the whole” free for τὸ ὅλον later in the passage. Other reading: the system composed of all one’s actions
- *ὁ καταπαύσας ἐν καιρῷ τὸν εἱρμὸν τοῦτον κακῶς διετέθη*: The one who “brought the chain to a stop” is, by the parallel with “the one who did this action”, the person whose life it is, though it could be heard as whoever ends it. κακῶς διετέθη is a past passive, literally “was put into a bad condition”. Other reading: nor has the one who ended this series at the right time been badly dealt with
- *ὅταν ἐν γήρᾳ*: There is no verb and no subject. The English supplies “the stopping comes”. Other reading: when one is old
- *ἧς τῶν μερῶν μεταβαλλόντων*: A genitive absolute inside a relative clause, which can give the means (“through the changing of whose parts”) or only the accompanying circumstance. “With” leaves both open. Other reading: through the changing of whose parts
- *καλὸν δὲ ἀεὶ πᾶν καὶ ὡραῖον*: καλόν is “fine, beautiful, noble”. ὡραῖον is “in season, in bloom”, which picks up both the theme of timing and “young and in its prime” just before. Other reading: always beautiful and in bloom
- *εἴπερ καὶ ἀπροαίρετον καὶ οὐκ ἀκοινώνητον*: ἀπροαίρετον is “not within one’s choice” (προαίρεσις). οὐκ ἀκοινώνητον is “not unsocial”, that is, not against the common interest. The step “not bad, since not shameful” rests on the Stoic view that only the shameful is bad. Other reading: since it is not chosen and does not go against the community
- *συμφέρον καὶ συμφερόμενον*: A play on φέρω, “carry”: συμφέρον (literally “bearing together”), συμφερόμενον (“carried along with”), θεοφόρητος (“god-carried”, normally “inspired”) and φερόμενος twice; “carried” is kept for all but the first. συμφέρον is “benefits” here, not the glossary’s “is good for”, so that it is not confused with ἀγαθόν (“a good thing”) in the same sentence. “The whole” is repeated three times where the Greek has it once. Other reading: is good for it and in step with it. For in this way a person is inspired by god
- *τῇ γνώμῃ φερόμενος*: γνώμη is “judgment, mind, intention”. The English reads “purpose”, which fits being carried toward something and keeps “judgment” for ὑπόληψις and “mind” for νοῦς in this project. κατὰ ταὐτά just before is “in the same way” or “along the same lines”. Other reading: carried in judgment toward the same things

</details>

### 12.24

These three things must be kept ready to hand. About what you do: whether it is neither at random nor otherwise than Justice herself would have acted. About what happens from outside: that it comes either by chance or by providence, and that one must neither blame chance nor bring a charge against providence. Second: what each thing is like from seed to the receiving of a soul, and from the receiving of a soul to the giving back of the soul; and out of what kind of things it is put together and into what kind of things it is dissolved. Third: that if you were suddenly lifted high into the air and looked down on human affairs and their many turns, you will despise them, seeing at the same time how much there is that dwells all around, in the air and in the ether; and that however often you are lifted up, you will see the same things: how alike in kind, how short-lived. And over these things, the puffed-up pride.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *εἰ μήτε εἰκῇ*: The clause has no verb. εἰ is taken as “whether”, a question to put to oneself about each action. It could be “if”, with the thought left hanging. Other reading: About what you do: that it be neither at random nor otherwise than
- *κατ’ ἐπιτυχίαν*: ἐπιτυχία is how things happen to fall out. The pair is chance against providence. Other reading: either by accident or by providence
- *δεύτερον τό*: The Greek says “second” here although no “first” was named: the first of the three is the double point about what you do and what happens from outside. Other reading: The second is this:
- *ψυχώσεως*: The moment a living thing gets its soul, set against the later moment of “giving back the soul”, that is, dying. Other reading: from seed to quickening, and from quickening to the giving up of life
- *τὴν πολυτροπίαν*: Literally “many-turning-ness”: the variety of human affairs, or their shiftiness. “Many turns” keeps the image and both senses. Other reading: human affairs and their variety
- *ὅτι καταφρονήσεις*: The grammar is loose: “if you were to look” (a supposed case) is followed by “that you will despise” (a plain future). The mismatch is kept. Other reading: that you would despise them
- *ὅσον τὸ περιοικοῦν ἐναερίων καὶ ἐναιθερίων*: Literally “how great is what dwells around, of those in the air and those in the ether”. The ether is the bright upper air above the air that is breathed. It can be the number of those living there or the extent of the region so lived in, and whether these are living beings or simply everything up there is not said; the word “dwells” points to beings. Other reading: how great is the company that dwells all around, of beings in the air and in the ether
- *τὸ ὁμοειδές, τὸ ὀλιγοχρόνιον*: Two adjectives used as nouns, said of the things seen: that they are of one kind and that they last a short time. Other reading: the sameness, the shortness of their time
- *ἐπὶ τούτοις ὁ τῦφος*: No verb: “over these, the τῦφος”. The word is literally smoke (so translated in 2.17), and so empty pride or delusion. Here it is taken as people’s pride in such things, and “puffed-up” keeps something of the smoke. Other reading: And these are what people are puffed up about.

</details>

### 12.25–26

Throw out the judgment: you are saved. Who then is stopping you from throwing it out?

Whenever you take something hard, you have forgotten that all things come about according to the nature of the whole; and that the wrong done is another’s; and, on top of these, that everything that comes about has always come about in this way, and will come about, and is coming about now everywhere; and how great is the kinship of a human being with the whole human race, for it is a sharing not of a little blood or a little seed but of mind. And you have forgotten too that each person’s mind is a god and has flowed from there; that nothing is anyone’s own, but even one’s little child and little body and the little soul itself have come from there; that everything is judgment; that each person lives only the present, and this is what they lose.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *σέσωσαι*: A perfect: the saving is already done the moment the judgment is thrown out. Other reading: and you are safe
- *ἐπελάθου τοῦ*: A simple past, “you forgot”. English needs “you have forgotten”. The list that follows hangs on this verb, repeated once. Other reading: you forgot this: that
- *τὸ ἁμαρτανόμενον ἀλλότριον*: ἀλλότριον is “belonging to another”, and so also “not your concern”. The English keeps the first, the literal sense, as in 12.1. Other reading: that the wrong done is not your affair
- *αἱματίου ἢ σπερματίου*: Both words are belittling diminutives, like the child, body and soul further on. Each is kept as “little”. Other reading: not of a drop of blood or a bit of seed
- *νοῦ κοινωνία*: κοινωνία is having something in common, a partnership. It is the noun behind this translation’s “social”. Other reading: a community of mind
- *θεὸς καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἐρρύηκεν*: θεός has no article, so “a god” or “god”. “From there” is left as vague as the Greek: from the divine source. Other reading: each person’s mind is god and has flowed from that source
- *πάνθ’ ὑπόληψις*: “Everything is judgment”: everything is as you judge it to be. The same word as in the first line of the passage. Other reading: that all is as you take it
- *καὶ τοῦτο ἀποβάλλει*: “And loses this.” “Only” stands with “lives” in the Greek and is not repeated with “loses”. Other reading: and it is only this that they lose

</details>

### 12.27

Go back continually over those who were exceedingly indignant at something, those who were at their height in the greatest fame or disasters or enmities or fortunes of whatever kind. Then stop and consider: where is all that now? Smoke and ash and a tale, or not even a tale. And let everything of this kind come to you along with it, for example: Fabius Catullinus in the country, and Lusius Lupus in the gardens, and Stertinius at Baiae, and Tiberius on Capri, and Velius Rufus, and in general the setting store by anything whatever, together with self-importance; and how cheap everything is that people strain after, and how much more philosophical it is, in the material one has been given, to show oneself just, self-controlled, following the gods, without affectation. For the vanity that smoulders under a cover of having none is the most troublesome of all.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *ἀναπολεῖν*: An infinitive used as an instruction, with no person; so are the verbs that follow. The English uses the bare command. Other reading: To go back continually over
- *ἀκμάσαντας*: “Who were at their height, who flourished”, used here of misfortunes and enmities as well as of fame. Other reading: those who stood at the peak of the greatest fame or disasters
- *ἐφιστάνειν*: “To halt and fix the attention.” The question follows without a verb of asking. Other reading: then put the question:
- *Λούσιος Δοῦπος*: As given, the second name is “Dupus”, which is taken to be a slip of the copy for Λοῦπος, Lupus, and is corrected in the English. Apart from Tiberius, the emperor who withdrew to Capri, these men cannot be identified here. Other reading: Lusius Dupus
- *Φάβιος Κατουλλῖνος ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ*: The list has no verb: a name and a place each time, and for Velius Rufus a name only. The English leaves it so. “In the country” can also be “on his estate”. Other reading: Fabius Catullinus on his country estate
- *ἡ πρὸς ὁτιοῦν μετ’ οἰήσεως διαφορά*: διαφορά ranges over difference, distinction and disagreement. With πρός, “towards”, the English reads it as the opposite of indifference, treating a thing as making a difference, which suits the men just named at their country places. οἴησις is a high opinion of oneself. Other reading: and in general distinction in anything whatever, or a quarrel over anything whatever, joined with conceit
- *τὸ κατεντεινόμενον*: A neuter participle, “what is strained after” or “the straining”. “People” is added in the English. Other reading: how cheap all straining is
- *ἐπὶ τῆς δοθείσης ὕλης*: ὕλη is “material, stuff to work on”: the circumstances handed to a person, as timber is handed to a carpenter. Other reading: on the material that has been given
- *ἀφελῶς*: “Simply, plainly, without affectation”. It stands just before the verb and may go with the whole of “show oneself just, self-controlled, following the gods”, or only with the last item. Other reading: following the gods simply
- *ὁ γὰρ ὑπὸ ἀτυφίᾳ τῦφος τυφόμενος*: A play on one root three times: τῦφος is smoke, and so vanity; ἀτυφία is being without it; τυφόμενος is “smouldering”. The Greek says only “under freedom from vanity”, and “a cover of” is added to make the image plain. χαλεπώτατος is “hardest”, to bear or to deal with. Other reading: For the pride that prides itself on having no pride is the most insufferable of all.

</details>

### 12.28

To those who ask: “Well, where have you seen the gods, or from what have you grasped that they exist, that you revere them as you do?” First, they are visible even to the eye. Second, though, I have not seen my own soul either, and yet I honour it. So with the gods too: from what I experience of their power on every occasion, from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πρὸς τοὺς ἐπιζητοῦντας*: A heading with no verb. The prefix of the verb can mean asking further or asking insistently, or it may add nothing; the English reads the plain “ask”, since no earlier question stands in the passage for “further” to follow. Other reading: To those who go on to ask; To those who press the question
- *ποῦ γὰρ ἰδὼν*: The particle γὰρ in a question marks it as a challenge and is not “for” here; “Well,” stands for it. The question is the questioners’ own words, so it is set in quotation marks, which the Greek does not have. Other reading: Why, where have you seen
- *κατειληφὼς*: The Stoic school’s word for a sure grasp of a fact (katalepsis). The same verb comes back at the end (καταλαμβάνω), so the English reads “grasp” both times. Other reading: from what have you made sure that they exist
- *οὕτως σέβεις*: Literally “you revere in this way”, with “them” supplied; “so” can point to the manner or to the degree, and “as you do” keeps both. The verb also covers acts of worship. “Revere” is used so that the noun of the same root in 4.16 (σεβασμὸν) can be “reverence”. Other reading: that you worship them so devoutly
- *καὶ ὄψει ὁρατοί εἰσιν*: Literally “they are visible even to sight”. The small word καὶ can be “even” or “also” (visible to sight as well as known in other ways); the English reads “even”. The Greek does not say which gods: the sun, moon and stars, which were counted as gods, are probably meant, but nothing is added. Other reading: they are visible to the eye as well
- *ἐξ ὧν τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶν ἑκάστοτε πειρῶμαι*: The verb means to make trial of or to have experience of something. The adverb ἑκάστοτε is “each time” or “on every occasion”, and so can also be “constantly”. Other reading: from the proofs of their power that are met with again and again
- *αἰδοῦμαι*: A third verb, after “revere” (σέβεις) and “honour” (τιμῶ): it means respect mixed with shame or awe before someone. Three English verbs are kept for the three Greek ones. Other reading: and respect them

</details>

### 12.29

What keeps a life safe: to see each thing through and through, what it is in itself, what in it is the material and what the cause; with the whole soul to do what is just and to say what is true. What is left but to enjoy living, joining one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap?

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Σωτηρία βίου*: Two words with no verb: “safety of life” or “the saving of a life”. The English turns them into a clause. Other reading: The salvation of life is this
- *ὅλου αὐτὸ τί ἐστιν ὁρᾶν*: With the preposition before it the phrase is “through the whole”: either seeing the whole of each thing or seeing it thoroughly. αὐτὸ τί ἐστιν is “what it is itself”. Other reading: to see what each thing is in itself, as a whole
- *τί μὲν αὐτοῦ τὸ ὑλικόν, τί δὲ τὸ αἰτιῶδες*: The two Stoic principles: the matter a thing is made of and the cause that shapes and moves it. Marcus uses the pair often. Other reading: what its matter is and what its causal part
- *ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς*: The same words as in 3.6, where the English has “with your whole soul” because a command is addressed to “you”. Here the Greek is impersonal throughout and the article is kept. Other reading: with your whole soul
- *συνάπτοντα ἄλλο*: “Fastening one good onto another”, like links in a chain. ἀγαθόν is neuter, “a good thing”; in context it is probably a good act. Other reading: linking one good deed to the next
- *διάστημα*: An interval, here of time left empty between one good and the next. Other reading: the briefest interval

</details>

### 12.30

One light of the sun, even if it is divided by walls, by mountains, by countless other things. One common substance, even if it is divided by countless bodies, each with its own quality. One soul, even if it is divided by countless natures and individual outlines. One soul that has mind, even if it seems to be separated. Now the other parts of the things just named, such as breaths and the matter that underlies things, are without sensation and have no attachment to one another; and yet even those are held together by what makes them one and by the weight that bears toward the same place. But thought, in a way of its own, stretches toward what is of the same kind and joins with it, and the social feeling is not divided.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *κἂν διείργηται τοίχοις*: The first four sentences have no verb “is”, and are left so. The verb διείργω (“keep apart, bar off”) comes four times in the passage; “divided” is used every time, including the last sentence, where the repetition makes the point. Other reading: There is one light of the sun, even if it is shut off by walls
- *ἰδίως ποιοῖς σώμασι μυρίοις*: ἰδίως ποιόν is a Stoic term for an individual thing marked off by a quality that is its own. The dative is read as in the first sentence, “by”: the one thing is divided by the many. It could also be heard as “among”. Other reading: even if it is shared out among countless individually qualified bodies
- *ἰδίαις περιγραφαῖς*: περιγραφή is a line drawn around something: an outline or limit. ἰδίαις is “own, individual”; “countless” may cover the outlines as well as the natures. Other reading: by countless natures and their own boundaries
- *μία νοερὰ ψυχή*: νοερά is “of mind, able to think”; “that has mind” keeps “mind” for this word, as in the other passages. διάνοια in the last sentence is a different word and is given as “thought”. Other reading: One thinking soul
- *διακεκρίσθαι*: A different verb from “divided”: “to be separated out, distinguished”. The change is marked with “separated”. Other reading: even if it seems to have been split up
- *τὰ μὲν οὖν ἄλλα μέρη τῶν εἰρημένων*: “The other parts of the things said” is loose in the Greek too. It is taken as the portions of the things just listed other than the soul that has mind. It could also mean the remaining constituents of the bodies and natures just mentioned. Other reading: the remaining parts of the wholes just mentioned
- *πνεύματα καὶ ὑποκείμενα*: πνεῦμα is breath or wind, and in Stoic physics the breath that holds a body together; ὑποκείμενα are “things that underlie”, the material a thing is made of. Both are kept literal, and the plural “breaths” is kept because separate portions are meant. Other reading: such as currents of air and material things
- *ἀναίσθητα*: “Without perception or feeling.” “Sensation” is used so that “feeling” can be kept for a different word in the last sentence. Other reading: without feeling
- *ἀνοικείωτα*: A negative made from the Stoic word for treating something as one’s own (οἰκείωσις): “not made one another’s own, with no sense of belonging to one another”. Other reading: and have no kinship with one another
- *τὸ ἑνοῦν*: “That which makes one”, from the word “one” that opens each of the first four sentences. This is a correction, and the manuscripts have τὸ νοοῦν, “that which thinks” (from memory, unchecked). The English translates the text given. Other reading: by what thinks
- *τὸ ἐπὶ τὰ αὐτὰ βρῖθον*: Literally “that which weighs down toward the same things”: a pull like weight toward a common point. Other reading: and by what presses toward the same things
- *διάνοια δὲ ἰδίως*: διάνοια is “thought, understanding, mind”. ἰδίως, “in a way peculiar to itself”, picks up the words given above as “its own quality” and “individual outlines”, used there of what divides. Other reading: But mind, in a special way,
- *συνίσταται*: “Combines, joins, holds together” with its own kind; the parts of the word are “stand” and “together”. Other reading: and stands together with it
- *οὐ διείργεται τὸ κοινωνικὸν πάθος*: “The social feeling” is taken as the subject. It could instead be an accusative of respect, with thought still the subject. πάθος is something undergone, a feeling; κοινωνικόν, “social”, is the adjective of the word for community. Other reading: and is not divided in its social feeling

</details>

### 12.31

What are you looking for? To breathe? Or to have sensation? To have impulse? To grow? And then to stop? To use your voice? To think? Which of these seems to you worth longing for? But if each of them is easy to despise, go on to the last thing, following reason and god. But to value these things, to be vexed that by being dead a person will be deprived of them, conflicts with that.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *τὸ διαπνεῖσθαι*: Literally “to be blown through”: breathing, or the passing of air through a body, the lowest function of life. From memory, unchecked, Marcus uses the word elsewhere of plants, and some editions print a different verb here, “to go on living”. Other reading: To go on breathing?
- *ἀλλὰ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι*: “But” in a string of questions: “or, if not that, then”. Other reading: Well then, to have sensation?
- *τὸ λήγειν αὖθις*: “To cease in turn”, set against “to grow”: to stop growing, or to decline. The Greek does not say what stops. Other reading: And then to stop growing?
- *ἐπὶ τελευταῖον*: “To the last”: the one thing left when the others have been set aside. Other reading: go on to what remains at the end
- *ἀλλὰ μάχεται τὸ τιμᾶν ταῦτα, τὸ ἄχθεσθαι*: “But it fights”: the Greek does not say with what, and “with that”, meaning following reason and god, is supplied. “These things” are taken as the functions listed, and being vexed as what valuing them comes to. The words can also be read as two things set against each other, with “these” as reason and god, though for that the Greek would regularly put “being vexed” in another case. Other reading: But honoring these conflicts with being vexed that by being dead a person will be deprived of the others
- *διὰ τοῦ τεθνηκέναι*: “Through having died”, the state of being dead and not the act of dying. Other reading: to be vexed that death will take them from one

</details>

### 12.32

How small a part of boundless, gaping eternity has been portioned out to each one: for it vanishes very quickly into the everlasting. And how small a part of the whole of substance, and how small a part of the whole of soul. And on how small a clod of the whole earth you crawl. Reflecting on all this, picture nothing as great except this: to act as your own nature leads, and to undergo things as the common nature brings them.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πόστον μέρος*: πόστος asks “which in a series”, so “what fraction”. The force is “how tiny a fraction”. “How small a part” is used each of the four times the word comes. Other reading: What fraction of boundless, gaping eternity
- *ἀχανοῦς*: “Yawning, gaping”: a gulf with no visible far side. The image is kept, as with the same word in 9.32. Other reading: of boundless and vast eternity
- *ἑκάστῳ*: “To each”, with nothing added in the Greek; the second person comes only with “you crawl”. Other reading: to each person
- *τῆς ὅλης ψυχῆς*: “The whole soul”: the soul of the universe, of which each soul is a part, as each body is a part of the whole substance. Other reading: of the universal soul
- *βωλαρίῳ*: A diminutive: a little clod or lump of earth. Literally “on what fraction of a clod of the whole earth”. Other reading: on how tiny a lump of the whole earth you creep
- *μηδὲν μέγα φαντάζου*: The verb is from the root of φαντασία, “impression”: do not form the impression that anything is great. “Picture” is used, as elsewhere in this section. Other reading: imagine nothing to be great
- *ὡς μὲν ἡ σὴ φύσις ἄγει ποιεῖν, πάσχειν δὲ ὡς ἡ κοινὴ φύσις φέρει*: ποιεῖν and πάσχειν are the standing pair “to do” and “to have done to one”; πάσχειν need not mean suffering. ἄγει (“leads”) and φέρει (“brings, carries”) are also a pair, kept as “leads” and “brings”. Both halves have ὡς, “as”; “things” and “them” are added because English “undergo” and “brings” need an object. Other reading: to do as your own nature leads, and to bear what the common nature brings

</details>

### 12.33

How is the ruling part using itself? For everything lies in that. As for the rest, it is either within choice or outside it: dead things and smoke.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πῶς ἑαυτῷ χρῆται τὸ ἡγεμονικόν*: A question to keep asking, with no verb of asking expressed. The present can be “how does it use” or “how is it using”. Other reading: How does the ruling part use itself?
- *ἐν γὰρ τούτῳ τὸ πᾶν ἐστι*: Literally “for in this is the all”, an idiom for “everything depends on this”. τούτῳ may be the ruling part or the way it uses itself. Other reading: for everything depends on this
- *ἢ προαιρετικά ἐστιν ἢ ἀπροαίρετα*: προαίρεσις is choice, the Stoic term for moral purpose. The Greek states flatly that the rest is either a thing of choice or not, and then, with no connecting word, “dead things and smoke”; the English keeps that shape, with a colon. It is striking that even what falls within choice seems to be dismissed with the rest, and this is not softened. Other reading: As for the rest, whether it falls within choice or outside it, it is dead things and smoke.
- *νεκρὰ καὶ καπνός*: νεκρά is neuter plural: “dead things” or “corpses”. Other reading: corpses and smoke

</details>

### 12.34–36

What most rouses one to despise death is that even those who judge pleasure good and pain bad have despised it all the same.

A person for whom only what comes at the right time is good, for whom performing more actions in line with right reason is equal to performing fewer, and to whom it makes no difference whether they look on the universe for a longer or a shorter time: to that person not even death is a thing to fear.

Man, you have been a citizen in this great city. What difference does it make to you whether for five years or for three? For what accords with the laws is equal for each. So what is terrible if you are sent away from the city not by a tyrant, nor by an unjust judge, but by nature, which brought you in, just as if the magistrate who engaged a comic actor were to dismiss him from the stage? “But I have spoken not the five acts but the three.” Well said; in life, however, the three are the whole play. For what is complete is fixed by the one who was responsible then for the putting together and is responsible now for the dissolving; you are responsible for neither. So go away graciously, for the one who dismisses you is gracious too.

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- *Πρὸς θανάτου καταφρόνησιν ἐγερτικώτατον*: ἐγερτικώτατον is “most rousing, most awakening”. καταφρόνησις is the noun of the verb in 9.3, where Marcus tells himself not to despise death; “despise” is kept in both places so that the tension can be seen. Other reading: The strongest incentive to think little of death
- *οἱ τὴν ἡδονὴν ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸν πόνον κακὸν κρίνοντες*: The Epicureans are meant, though not named. πόνος is “pain” or “toil”; against pleasure the English reads “pain”. Other reading: those who judge pleasure a good and toil an evil
- *τὸ εὔκαιρον μόνον ἀγαθὸν*: εὔκαιρον is “well-timed, in season”. “What comes at the right time” matches καιρός in 12.23. μόνον could also be heard as “simply”. Other reading: for whom the good is simply what is in season
- *τούτῳ οὐδὲ ὁ θάνατος φοβερόν*: οὐδέ can be “not even” or “not … either”. φοβερόν is neuter, “a fearful thing”. Other reading: to that person death is not a fearful thing either
- *Ἄνθρωπε*: The address is “human being”, not specifically a male, and it is blunt. “Man” is used as the nearest natural English form of address. Other reading: Human being,
- *εἰ πέντε ἔτεσιν ἢ τρισί*: Translated as given. From memory, unchecked: the words “or for three” are not secure in the transmission, and other editors print a different number (“or a hundred”). “Three” here prepares the three acts below. Other reading: whether for five years or for a hundred
- *τὸ γὰρ κατὰ τοὺς νόμους ἴσον ἑκάστῳ*: ἴσον is “equal” or “fair”. “Equal” is kept because the previous chapter uses ἐν ἴσῳ (“is equal to”). Other reading: For what follows the laws is fair to everyone.
- *ὁ παραλαβὼν στρατηγός*: στρατηγός is literally “general” and is also the standard Greek for the Roman praetor, the magistrate who put on public shows; the English says “magistrate”. παραλαβών is “who took him on”. Other reading: the general who took him on
- *οὐκ εἶπον τὰ πέντε μέρη*: μέρη is “parts”, here the acts of a play. εἶπον is the verb “say, speak”, and the answer καλῶς εἶπας (“you have said well”, that is, “you are right”) picks it up; the English has “spoken” and “Well said”. Other reading: But I have not played the five parts, but the three.
- *ὁ τότε μὲν τῆς συγκρίσεως. νῦν δὲ τῆς διαλύσεως αἴτιος*: The full stop after συγκρίσεως in the text as given breaks one phrase and is read as a comma. ἐκεῖνος is masculine, so it is not grammatically “nature” (feminine): it is god, or the magistrate of the image. αἴτιος and ἀναίτιος are both rendered with “responsible”; the Greek does not say whose putting together is meant, and the English leaves it unsaid too. Other reading: the one who was then the cause of your being combined and is now the cause of your being dissolved; you are the cause of neither
- *ἄπιθι οὖν ἵλεως*: ἵλεως is used of gods (“propitious”) and of people (“cheerful, kindly”). The same word is used of the one leaving and of the one dismissing, so one English word is kept, “gracious”, as also in 10.36. Other reading: So go in good cheer, for the one who releases you is kindly too.

</details>
